## Questions

### Why did falling interest rates encourage deferred maintenance?

When values rise from falling yields, spending capital that reduces near-term income looks unattractive and the asset can be sold before deferred work becomes urgent. The incentive was to defer, and many ageing buildings carry the result.

### Does the end of cheap money make buildings worse investments?

Not necessarily. It makes them different investments. Return depends more on income and physical performance, which rewards owners who understand their buildings and plan capital deliberately.

papers.title: The Building That Has to Earn Its Hedge
papers.question: Is commercial property really an inflation hedge once capital expenditure is taken into account?
papers.answer: A building hedges inflation only if its income can rise with prices and its capital needs do not inflate faster than that income. Because construction and building-services costs can rise faster than general inflation, deferred works become more expensive each year, and a building with a heavy capital programme can lose much of its hedge.
papers.summary: Property is sold as an inflation hedge. Whether a building actually behaves like one depends on its leases and on how fast its own capital needs inflate.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: The hedge is a claim, not a property
Capex is a short position on construction costs
Testing the hedge on one building
Lease structure decides who holds the risk

papers.contentMarkdown:
Real assets are meant to protect capital when money loses value. Land is finite, replacement cost rises with prices, rents follow. If the macro view in [The Movement to Real](/insights/the-movement-to-real) is right and inflation runs warmer than central bank targets for a long time, that protection matters more than it has for a generation.

But a building is not land. It is a machine sitting on land, and machines wear out on a schedule that inflation does not care about. Whether a particular building hedges inflation is a question about that building, not about property as a class.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. In Australia, construction cost indices ran well ahead of the Consumer Price Index from 2021: the Cordell Construction Cost Index, a private index, recorded 11.9 per cent growth in residential construction costs over 2022, its largest annual rise on record outside the introduction of the GST, before slowing to 2.6 per cent in the year to June 2024 with costs still around 30 per cent above pre-pandemic levels. Construction costs outpacing consumer prices is episodic rather than a constant. Producer price indexes in Britain and the United States showed similar pressure in the same period. Lease indexation practice varies by market and lease. Deepened 4 November 2026 with construction and consumer price series from the BLS (via AGC), the ABS and BCIS.

## The hedge is a claim, not a property

The case for property as an inflation hedge rests on income. If rents rise with prices, the real value of the income holds. That depends on the lease. Fixed annual reviews below inflation, long terms without market reviews and incentives that eat into effective rent can all leave income trailing prices for years.

Even where the lease works, income is only half the picture. The other half is what the building will ask of its owner over the same period, and that half is rarely modelled with the same care.

## Capex is a short position on construction costs

Every planned replacement in a building is, in effect, a commitment to buy construction at some future price. Roofing, lifts, chillers, switchboards, fire systems: all of these are priced in the construction and services markets, and those markets have their own inflation. In the years after 2020, building costs in Australia, Britain and the United States rose faster than consumer prices, driven by materials, labour shortages and long equipment lead times. The pressure eased from 2024, but the episode showed how quickly the gap can open, and the energy-price shock of 2026 has brought input costs back into view.

An owner with a large deferred programme is therefore short construction inflation. Each year of deferral is a year in which the eventual cost can rise faster than the income meant to pay for it. The hedge leaks through the plant room.

A building with a light capital programme and well-indexed leases is a strong hedge. A building with a heavy programme and soft leases can be a weak one, whatever the asset class says.

## What the numbers show

The gap between construction prices and general inflation is no longer a theoretical risk. It has been measured in all three markets, and in the United States it is large. Construction prices against consumer pricesMeasureConstruction pricesConsumer pricesGapUnited States, Feb 2020 to Dec 2025+42.5% (new nonresidential building, BLS PPI)+25.7% (CPI-U)16.8 pointsUnited States, new office only+50.3%+25.7%24.6 pointsUnited States, peak year (2022)+19.9%+8.0%11.9 points in one yearAustralia, Sep 2021 to Sep 2026About +35% (ABS building construction output index)Not compared over the same periodAnnual non-residential building inflation 4.8% to September 2026United Kingdom, forecast to Q3 2031+14.1% (BCIS all-in tender price index)Not forecast hereTender prices +3.2% in the year to Q3 2026

US: BLS producer price indexes as tabulated by the Associated General Contractors of America. Australia: ABS producer price indexes. UK: BCIS five-year forecast.

Put simply: works priced at $1 million in February 2020 would have cost about $1.43 million by the end of 2025, while rent indexed to consumer prices rose about 26 per cent. A building whose income tracked inflation and whose capital plan tracked construction lost about a sixth of its real capacity to fund its own renewal in under six years.

The gap did not open evenly. Most of it arrived between 2021 and 2023, when US construction prices rose 5.2, 19.9 and 7.9 per cent in successive years. In 2024 and 2025 they rose only 0.1 and 1.6 per cent. The lesson is not that construction inflation always runs hot. It is that it moves in surges that income rarely matches, and a capital plan that assumes general inflation will be caught out by the next surge.

## Testing the hedge on one building

A practical test needs three inputs. First, the income path: how the leases index, when they review to market and when they expire. Second, the capital path: the register’s ten-year programme, by horizon. Third, an assumption about construction cost escalation relative to general inflation, which can be varied. With those, an owner can see whether net income after capital holds its real value under a warmer inflation regime, or leaks.

Two buildings with identical leases can give opposite answers. One has a light programme spread across the decade and keeps most of its hedge. The other has a heavy mid-decade programme in roofing, plant and facade, priced in a construction market that has run ahead of CPI, and gives a large part of its hedge back. The difference is invisible in a valuation and obvious in a register.

## Lease structure decides who holds the risk

Who actually bears that capital inflation depends on the lease. Under fully net structures common in the United States, many outgoings and some capital items pass to tenants, though structural and major replacement items often stay with the owner. In Australian and British leases, the line between recoverable outgoings, tenant repair obligations and landlord capital varies widely by lease and by asset. We explore the mechanics in [Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases); the point here is that the same building can be a good hedge for one owner and a poor one for another, depending on what the leases say.

## Earning the hedge

Earning the hedge is mostly a matter of knowing the capital position early. If the major replacements over the next decade are visible, with a sensible range and timing for each, an owner can decide which to bring forward before costs rise, which to defer with confidence, and which to stage. That is a different posture from discovering the chiller is failing in a hot summer and buying a replacement at whatever price the market sets that month.

It also changes how an acquisition should be read. A building bought as an inflation hedge should be tested against its own capital programme, priced in the same inflationary world the hedge is meant to protect against. If the programme is heavy and early, part of the hedge has already been spent.  In the register

Inflation exposure sits in the timing columns: large items in the 2–5 yr horizon are the ones most sensitive to construction cost movements before they are bought.   Key signal

An owner with a heavy deferred capital programme is effectively short construction inflation, which can erode the inflation protection the asset is meant to provide.

## Questions

### Why can construction costs rise faster than general inflation?

Construction and building-services prices respond to materials, specialist labour supply and equipment lead times, which can move independently of consumer prices. When those markets are tight, the cost of planned building works can rise faster than rents.

### Does bringing capital works forward always beat inflation?

No. Replacing a system early gives up remaining service life and ties up capital. The useful question is item by item: what the remaining life is, what failure would cost, and how sensitive the price is to waiting.

papers.title: Industrial Policy Comes Home
papers.question: What does the return of industrial policy mean for industrial and logistics buildings?
papers.answer: As governments in Australia, Britain and the United States steer capital toward domestic manufacturing, energy and defence supply chains, demand grows for buildings that can host production rather than storage. Production asks for power, floor capacity, services, compliance and resilience that many existing sheds were never built to provide, so the gap between specification and requirement becomes a capital question.
papers.summary: Governments in all three of our markets are directing capital back toward domestic production. Production asks more of a building than storage ever did.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: The money is real, and it moves
What production asks of a building

papers.contentMarkdown:
For thirty years the rich world exported its production and imported finished goods. The buildings followed. Factories closed or became warehouses, and the industrial real estate that boomed was the distribution box: big, simple, low in services, built to hold goods rather than make them.

That arrangement is being reversed by policy. The details differ and will keep changing, but the direction is shared. Australia, Britain and the United States now all speak openly about industrial strategy, supply-chain security and domestic capability in energy, defence, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing. Capital is being steered toward making things at home.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Australia’s Future Made in Australia Act 2024 received royal assent on 10 December 2024, establishing a National Interest Framework for public investment; the UK published its Modern Industrial Strategy on 23 June 2025; the United States enacted the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of July 2025 then curtailed US clean-energy incentives: wind and solar projects lose the main credits unless construction began by 4 July 2026 or they are in service by the end of 2027, and the commercial building energy-efficiency deduction ends for construction beginning after 30 June 2026. Individual programmes change with governments; the direction of policy, toward domestic capability in energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing and defence, is shared. Deepened 4 November 2026 with US Census manufacturing construction spending, 2022 to August 2026.

## Policy with a postcode

Industrial policy has a physical address. A subsidy for battery assembly, a defence contract, a critical-minerals processing plant: each of these lands in a building somewhere, usually in an existing industrial precinct because that is where zoning, labour and transport already are. The demand shows up first as enquiries for sites and existing sheds, long before any new plant is built.

This is the practical expression of the macro argument in [The Movement to Real](/insights/the-movement-to-real). Capital cycles reward the sectors that went unfunded for years. Domestic production capacity is one of them, and it needs buildings.

## The money is real, and it moves

Industrial policy is visible in concrete. In the United States, construction spending on manufacturing facilities rose from about $125 billion in 2022 to about $236 billion in 2024, as the CHIPS and Science Act and clean-energy incentives drew in semiconductor, battery and solar plants. It then eased: $220 billion in 2025, and an annual rate of about $171 billion by August 2026, as some projects completed and some incentives were cut back. Policy instruments and the evidence of buildingMarketInstrumentBuilding signalUnited StatesCHIPS and Science Act (2022); clean-energy manufacturing credits, narrowed in 2025Manufacturing construction $125bn (2022), $202bn (2023), $236bn (2024), $220bn (2025); about $171bn annual rate (August 2026)AustraliaFuture Made in Australia Act 2024 (assent 10 December 2024)A national interest framework for public investment in strategic industriesUnited KingdomModern Industrial Strategy (23 June 2025)Eight priority sectors, with an emphasis on energy costs and grid connection for industry

US Census Bureau construction spending (TLMFGCONS, via FRED). Australian and UK instruments as enacted or published; their effect on construction is not yet separately measured.

The American series carries a warning as well as a signal. Policy can move capital quickly, and it can move it back. An owner positioning industrial stock for production should underwrite the physical capability, which lasts, rather than a particular incentive, which may not.

## What production asks of a building

A warehouse needs a dry roof, a flat slab, clear height, docks and enough power for lighting, racking and a few chargers. A production building asks much more. Electrical capacity sized for process equipment. Floor slabs that can take point loads and vibration. Compressed air, process water, extraction and drainage. Fire and hazardous-materials compliance for what is stored and made. Often round-the-clock operation, which changes how plant and envelope wear.

Each of those requirements is a line in a capital programme. Each can also be a reason a building cannot be used at all without major works.

The difference between a storage shed and a production building is mostly invisible from the street. It sits in the switchboard, the slab and the services.

## A production readiness reading

A production readiness reading asks six questions of each building in an industrial portfolio. What is the incoming electrical supply, and what would increasing it involve? What is the slab designed for, and what condition is it in? Can the roof structure take extraction plant, solar or both? What does the fire strategy permit in terms of process, storage and hazardous materials? Are there process services, compressed air, water, drainage, gas, to build on? And what does the site allow for vehicles, hardstand and expansion?

The answers sort a portfolio into three groups: buildings that can host production with modest works, buildings that can with significant works, and buildings that are distribution boxes and will stay that way. Each group has a different capital strategy and a different place in the market that industrial policy is creating.

## The specification gap

Much of the existing industrial stock in all three markets was built for distribution or light industry. Some of it can adapt. Some cannot without works that approach the cost of building new. The gap between what a shed was designed for and what a production occupier now needs is where value is being made and lost.

Power is usually the binding constraint. Increasing a site’s electrical supply can involve network studies, new substations and long lead times on transformers and switchgear, as we discuss in [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function). Floor capacity is the next: a slab designed for racking loads may not take heavy machinery without strengthening. Roof structures may not take the extraction plant or solar arrays that come with the new use.

## Reading the shed for production

The question for an owner of industrial stock is which of these buildings could host the occupiers that policy is creating, what it would take, and in what order. That is a building question before it is a leasing one: supply capacity, slab, structure, services, fire strategy, hazardous materials.

Portfolios of sheds are worth reading in two layers, the familiar income and location layer and a physical-capacity layer that asks what each building can become. The second layer is where the next decade of value is likely to be decided. Industrial policy is political and reversible, so this view will be revised with the programmes that drive it.  In the register

Production readiness surfaces in a register through electrical supply, slab and structure, fire services and roof structure items, frequently carrying wide ranges until supply capacity and loads are confirmed.   Key signal

Industrial policy creates demand for buildings that can host production, and the binding constraints are usually power supply, floor capacity and services rather than location.

## Questions

### Can an existing warehouse be converted to manufacturing use?

Sometimes. It depends on electrical supply, floor slab capacity, roof and structural capacity, services and fire compliance for the intended process. Each needs checking against the specific occupier’s requirements before value is assumed.

### Why is electrical supply often the main constraint?

Increasing a site’s supply can require network approvals, new substations and equipment with long lead times. Unlike most building works, it is partly outside the owner’s control.

papers.title: Energy Becomes a Building Function
papers.question: Why is a building’s electrical capacity becoming a key factor in commercial property value?
papers.answer: As heating, transport and equipment electrify while grids struggle to add connections, the electrical capacity a building already holds becomes scarce and valuable. Switchboards, substations, supply agreements and gas services move from background utilities into core capital lines that shape what a building can be used for and what it will cost to keep competitive.
papers.summary: Electrification and grid constraint are turning a building’s energy capacity into one of its most valuable and least understood attributes.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: The switchboard as a capital line
Why the supply is hard to add
What this asks of the register

papers.contentMarkdown:
For most of the last century, energy was something a building consumed. It arrived through a gas main and an electrical supply sized when the building was designed, and nobody thought about either until a bill or a fault forced them to. Energy was an operating cost, not a building attribute.

That is changing quickly. Heating is moving from gas to electric heat pumps. Vehicles are moving from fuel to charging. Occupiers are adding equipment that draws more power. Rooftops are generating. And in all three of our markets, electricity networks are struggling to connect new demand as fast as it arrives.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. A 2024 National Renewable Energy Laboratory report found distribution transformer lead times of up to two years, roughly four times pre-2022 norms. Since then the picture has split: distribution transformers have eased to around 30 weeks, while large power transformers average more than two years and generator step-up units passed 160 weeks in early 2026, according to Wood Mackenzie data cited by the Congressional Research Service. In Britain, connections reform cut the queue for new generation and storage from over 700 gigawatts to 283 in December 2025, with revised offers issued through 2026. In Victoria, new homes and most new commercial buildings must be all-electric from 1 January 2027; elsewhere gas restrictions vary and some have been reversed. Deepened 4 November 2026 with electrical plant lead times (Wood Mackenzie data, secondary reporting) and the December 2025 results of Britain’s connections reform.

## Capacity is the new location

Grid connection has become one of the slowest parts of any project. Network operators in Australia, Britain and the United States have all faced long queues for new connections and upgrades, and the equipment that sits between the grid and a building, transformers and high-voltage switchgear, has had long lead times. A building that already holds a generous supply has something a newer competitor may wait years for.

This is why we think of electrical capacity the way the market has always thought of location. It is partly fixed, hard to add, and it determines what a site can be used for. The argument runs through [When the Shed Becomes a Power Station](/insights/when-the-shed-becomes-a-power-station) for industrial stock, but it applies to offices, retail and mixed-use buildings too.

## The switchboard as a capital line

Inside the building, the main switchboard is where this becomes physical. An older board may be at the end of its life, short of spare capacity, or built to standards that make modification difficult. Replacing it can mean a shutdown, temporary supply and coordination with the network. It is rarely a large line in isolation, but it often gates everything else: electrified heating, chargers, solar and batteries all need somewhere to connect.

In many ageing buildings the switchboard is the quiet bottleneck. Nothing on the electrification wish-list can happen until it does.

## Why the supply is hard to add

Increasing a building’s electrical supply is rarely a matter of asking. It usually involves an application to the network operator, a study of local network capacity, and sometimes a new or upgraded substation, either on site or in the street. The equipment involved, transformers and high-voltage switchgear, has had long lead times since 2022. In the United States, federal laboratory research documented waits of up to two years for distribution transformers at the 2024 peak; those have since eased, but large power transformers still commonly take more than two years. Australian and British owners report similar delays for substation equipment and network works.

The consequence is that supply capacity behaves like a scarce asset. An owner who already holds it can offer electrified heating, fleet charging or process loads quickly. One who does not may wait years, at a cost that is partly outside their control. That asymmetry is now showing in leasing conversations for industrial and logistics space, and it is starting to appear in office and mixed-use buildings planning to electrify.

## The equipment queue

The difficulty of adding supply is not only the network’s capacity. It is the equipment needed to connect to it. Lead times for electrical plant lengthened sharply from 2021 and have only partly eased. Wood Mackenzie data as reported by POWER magazine and other trade sources; secondary reporting. Australian and UK lead times follow the same global supply chain but are not separately published.

Prices moved with the queues: power transformer prices were reported to have risen about 77 per cent since 2019. For a building, the practical point is that a supply upgrade needing a new transformer is a multi-year programme item, and it should enter the capital plan years before the load it serves.

## Britain reorders the queue

Britain’s transmission connection queue had grown beyond 700 gigawatts, far more than the system could ever connect. Reform approved by Ofgem in 2025 reordered it around readiness and strategic need. The results published in December 2025 left 283 gigawatts of generation and storage and 99 gigawatts of demand in the new pipeline. Only about 13 gigawatts of new transmission demand can connect before 2030, with a further 86 gigawatts from 2030 to 2035.

At distribution level, UK Power Networks reported that 59 per cent of its customers secured a place in the reformed queue and that the queue more than halved. Reform reallocates capacity rather than creating it. For a building or a site that needs a larger connection, the queue position is now a property attribute in its own right.

## Reading the energy chain

In a register, the energy chain reads in order: incoming supply and its agreement; main switchboard, age, capacity and spare ways; sub-mains and distribution; heating and hot water plant and its fuel; roof capacity for generation; space and fire strategy for storage; and metering and controls. Each link has its own condition and timing. The useful judgement is about the weakest link, because that is the one that sets the pace for the rest.

## Gas: from utility to liability

The other side of the shift is gas. Gas boilers and gas services were once the cheap, reliable default. In many jurisdictions they now face carbon limits, disclosure, rising network charges and, for new buildings, outright restriction. A building that relies on gas for heating has a conversion in its future even if the date is uncertain.

That conversion is not a like-for-like swap. Heat pumps run at lower temperatures, may need different distribution, take roof or plant space and add electrical load. The [After Rent](/insights/after-rent) paper makes the case that electrification is ultimately about control, not compliance. Whatever the motive, the capital consequence is the same: gas-dependent plant has a shortened useful life in the minds of tenants, lenders and buyers, whatever its physical condition.

## What this asks of the register

In a Capital Strategy, energy capacity should be read as a system rather than a set of separate items. The supply, the main board, distribution, heating plant, roof capacity for generation and the space for storage or charging belong to one story. Reading them together tells an owner what the building can become and in what order the works need to happen.

It also changes how to read timing. A switchboard with five years of physical life may still need to move earlier if it blocks a heating conversion that a tenant or a regulation requires. That is a decision, not a condition rating, and it belongs in the conversation with the owner. If connection queues clear and equipment lead times normalise, capacity becomes easier to add and this argument loses some of its force; we will say so when it does.  In the register

Energy capacity appears across several rows: supply and main switchboard, distribution, heating plant, roof structure and generation, each with its own timing but one shared dependency.   Key signal

Electrical capacity is becoming as decisive for commercial property as location, and the switchboard often gates every other electrification decision.

## Questions

### Why does gas heating shorten a plant’s useful life?

Carbon limits, disclosure, network charges and occupier expectations can make gas-dependent plant obsolete before it is physically worn out. The physical condition may be fine while the economic life is shrinking.

### What should an owner check first about a building’s energy capacity?

The size and age of the incoming supply and main switchboard, the spare capacity available, and whether a supply increase would need network works. Those answers frame every later electrification decision.

papers.title: What AI Takes Out of the Building
papers.question: How will artificial intelligence change the physical requirements of commercial buildings?
papers.answer: AI subtracts routine desk work from offices and routine control from building operations, while adding demand for power, connectivity and monitoring. The result is buildings that hold fewer people doing more consequential work, run by software that exposes the age of their controls, and draw more on electrical and digital infrastructure.
papers.summary: AI removes routine work from offices and routine decisions from building operations. Both subtractions change what a building needs to be.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: The building learns to run itself
What the market shows so far

papers.contentMarkdown:
The common story about AI and property is short: AI makes office workers more productive, firms need fewer of them, offices empty out. In [The 10% Office](/insights/the-10-office) we argued that this misses what is actually happening inside firms. The work that remains is the work that needs people together.

This paper takes the next step. AI is a subtraction, but it subtracts in two places at once: from the work done in buildings and from the work of running them. Both have physical consequences.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. The International Energy Agency reported in April 2026 that data centre electricity use grew 17 per cent in 2025 to about 485 terawatt-hours and projects around 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, about 3 per cent of global electricity demand. The description of building management system obsolescence reflects common practice experience; controller support and integration capability should be confirmed with the system vendor for any particular building. Deepened 4 November 2026 with early market evidence on AI and office demand.

## Subtraction first

The first subtraction is desk volume. Drafting, formatting, reconciling and first-pass analysis are moving to software. The floor space that housed that work, rows of workstations and the storage and back-office functions around them, has less reason to exist.

What remains is denser in meaning but not necessarily in people. Rooms for decisions, client work, teaching and the conversations where trust is built. These ask for different things from a building: better acoustic separation, flexible meeting space, good air and light, reliable connectivity, and services that cope with uneven occupancy, empty on Friday and full on Tuesday.

For the base building, uneven occupancy is a services problem. Plant sized for steady full occupancy runs inefficiently at partial load. Older systems without good zoning heat and cool whole floors for a handful of people.

## The building learns to run itself

The second subtraction is in operations. Building management has been largely a matter of schedules, set points and someone responding to complaints. Analytics and AI-driven controls can now predict loads, detect faults and tune plant continuously. That only works if the building can be read and controlled: sensors, metering, networked controllers and plant that responds to commands.

Software-defined operation exposes the age of the controls. A building with a closed, obsolete management system cannot benefit, however good the software above it.

Many buildings from the 1990s and 2000s carry management systems whose controllers are no longer supported, built on proprietary protocols that are hard to integrate. Their replacement used to be discretionary. It is becoming the condition of participating in how buildings will be run.

## A controls reading

Reading a building’s readiness for software-defined operation comes down to a few questions. What is the building management system, which version, and is it supported? Are the controllers on an open protocol, such as BACnet, or a closed proprietary one? How much of the plant is metered and sub-metered, and how much reports its state? Do the major items, chillers, boilers or heat pumps, air-handling units, accept commands at variable output, or only on and off? And is there a secure network path from the building’s systems to the software that would analyse them, separated from tenants and the internet in the way current cyber guidance expects?

Many buildings of the 1990s and 2000s answer poorly on most of these. That is not a crisis. It is a capital line, and it is often one of the cheapest ways to improve both performance and energy ratings in an older building.

## What arrives

AI also adds. It adds compute, which needs power and cooling, whether in a data hall or a server room on a floor. It adds connectivity requirements, from fibre into the building to coverage across it. It adds monitoring, which turns parts of the building into data sources. The building-as-host argument in [The Building as Host to Machines](/insights/the-building-as-host-to-machines) develops this further.

## What the market shows so far

If AI were simply emptying offices, the evidence would show it in vacancy. What it shows instead is concentration, and in places AI is adding demand rather than removing it. AI and office demand: early evidenceSignalReadingSourceAI-related firms’ share of London office take-up, Q1 202611%ColliersMidtown Manhattan prime office vacancy, Q3 20261.9%CBREUS national office vacancy, Q3 202618.2%, with ten straight quarters of positive net absorptionCBRE

Early and partial evidence. AI’s effect on headcount is a slower variable than leasing cycles.

The subtraction this paper describes is real at the level of tasks and desks. At the level of buildings, the first effect has been to sharpen the divide between space that people want to be in and space they do not. The capital question is the one this paper ends on: whether the base building’s services and controls can support fewer, more purposeful occupants.

## Capital follows the subtraction

The capital consequence is a shift in where money goes: less into floor-plate fit-out at scale, more into the base-building systems that make a smaller, better-used building work. Zoned and responsive mechanical plant, modern controls, electrical capacity, connectivity, and the quality of the shared spaces that bring people in.

The dividing line in office stock may not run between prime and secondary at all. It may run between buildings whose services and controls can adapt to fewer, more purposeful occupants, and buildings that cannot without a deep refurbishment. Much of this depends on how far and how fast firms actually change the way they work, and occupancy evidence over the next few years will test it.  In the register

These shifts appear as building management system, controls, metering and mechanical zoning items, often rated for functional rather than physical obsolescence.   Key signal

AI subtracts desk work and routine operations at the same time, moving capital toward base-building controls, responsive plant and connectivity rather than floor-plate fit-out.

## Sources

## Questions

### Does AI mean office buildings need less capital spending?

It changes where capital goes more than how much. Fit-out at scale may shrink, while controls, responsive mechanical plant, electrical capacity and shared spaces become more important.

### Why are older building management systems a problem?

Many use unsupported controllers and closed protocols that cannot integrate with modern analytics. Without replacement, the building cannot benefit from data-driven operation.

papers.title: Climate as Physical Risk
papers.question: How does physical climate risk affect the capital planning of commercial buildings?
papers.answer: Heat, flood, storm and fire act on specific building elements: roof drainage, plant location, cooling capacity, envelope and site levels. Insurers are already pricing these exposures, so physical climate risk becomes a capital question about which elements need to change, and when, rather than a disclosure exercise.
papers.summary: Climate risk has mostly been treated as a reporting exercise. For buildings it is a physical one, and insurers are pricing it before most owners do.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: Where the risk reaches the asset

papers.contentMarkdown:
Most of the attention on climate in commercial property has gone to transition risk: emissions targets, disclosure rules, energy ratings. Australia’s mandatory climate reporting began phasing in from 2025, Britain finalised its own sustainability reporting standards in 2026, and in the United States federal rules have stalled while California presses ahead. Portfolio reports have grown thick with scenarios.

Physical risk is different. It does not live in a report. It lives in the box gutter that overflows in a cloudburst, the switchroom in the basement, the chiller that cannot keep up on the fourth day of a heatwave.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Flood Re supports flood cover for eligible households in the UK and does not extend to commercial property. Australian mandatory climate-related financial reporting under AASB S2 began for the largest entities from financial years starting 1 January 2025, with further groups from July 2026 and July 2027. Britain published final UK Sustainability Reporting Standards on 25 February 2026. In the United States, the SEC proposed rescinding its climate disclosure rule on 29 May 2026, California’s climate-risk reporting law has been enjoined since November 2025, and its emissions reporting law is proceeding. The IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report describes increasing frequency and intensity of heat extremes and heavy rainfall across many regions. Insurance market conditions vary by location and change over time. Deepened 4 November 2026 with Marsh rate data for Q3 2026, APRA’s premium series and ACCC findings.

## From disclosure to drainage

Disclosure asks an owner to describe exposure. Buildings ask an owner to deal with it. The two meet only when the reported risk is translated into elements, actions and timing. A flood exposure becomes a question about where the main switchboard, lift motors and pumps sit relative to likely water levels. A heat exposure becomes a question about cooling capacity, plant ratings and envelope performance. A storm exposure becomes a question about roof fixings, gutters, downpipes and facade anchors.

Many existing buildings were designed for a climate envelope that is shifting. Drainage sized for historic rainfall intensities, plant selected for historic peak temperatures, roofs fixed for historic wind loads. None of that makes a building unsafe by default. It does mean the margins are thinner than they were.

## Insurance prices the building

Insurers have been pricing physical risk ahead of most owners, though not in a straight line. Headline commercial property rates have been falling since 2024 as reinsurance capacity returned: Marsh reported global property rates down 10 per cent in the third quarter of 2026. That is the insurance cycle, not the hazard. Exposure still reaches a building through deductibles, sub-limits, exclusions and rebuild-cost inflation, and in the most exposed locations through cover that is hard to place at all. Australian home premiums rose an average of 7.2 per cent a year between 2010 and 2025, against 3.1 per cent wage growth, according to APRA. In Britain, the Flood Re scheme supports household flood cover but does not extend to commercial property, which is priced on its own exposure.

When insurance becomes the first place a physical risk is priced, the building’s condition and configuration start to show up in its operating cost, its financeability and its sale.

An owner who can show what has been done, flood barriers, raised plant, upgraded drainage, can argue for better terms. One who cannot is priced on the assumption that nothing has.

## Where the risk reaches the asset

Because headline commercial rates are falling, it is tempting to read physical risk as easing. The signals in the market say otherwise, once they are separated. Insurance signals at reviewSignalReadingSourceGlobal commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 10%, after falls of 12% and 9% in the two previous quartersMarsh Global Insurance Market IndexUS commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 10%MarshPacific (Australia and New Zealand) commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 14%MarshAustralian home premiums, 2010 to 2025Up 7.2% a year on average, against 3.1% wage growthAPRADriver of Australian premiumsBuilding cost inflation identified as a key factorACCC insurance monitoring

Commercial rates reflect the reinsurance cycle as well as hazard; household premiums in exposed regions have continued to rise.

Physical risk reaches a commercial building through more than the premium. Deductibles and sub-limits for flood, storm and hail determine how much of a loss the owner carries. Rebuild-cost inflation raises the sum insured, and with it the premium, even where the rate falls. Lenders increasingly ask for evidence of resilience before they will finance an exposed asset. And in the most exposed locations, the question is not price but whether cover can be placed at all.

For the register, this means the resilience items in this paper, plant location, drainage capacity, roof drainage and cooling margins, are not only about avoiding damage. They are about keeping the building insurable on terms that a buyer and a lender will accept.

## The elements climate reads first

Physical climate risk concentrates in a familiar set of elements. Roof drainage and box gutters. Basements, ground-floor plant and electrical rooms. Cooling plant and its capacity margin. Facade sealants, fixings and glazing. External ground levels and site stormwater. Bushfire-exposed vents, gutters and combustible elements on urban fringes.

These are ordinary register items. What changes is how they are read. A gutter at mid-life might be a 6–10 year item on condition alone, and a 2–5 year item once its capacity against current rainfall intensity is considered. That is the kind of judgement we discuss in [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): risk changes the case for acting, while timing still follows the evidence.

## A resilience reading

A resilience reading starts with exposure and ends with elements. Exposure comes from hazard mapping and history: flood levels, overland flow paths, bushfire overlays, wind regions, heat. Elements come from the building: where the main switchboard, lift motors, pumps and generators sit relative to plausible water levels; how roof drainage, box gutters and overflows are sized against current rainfall intensities; how much margin cooling plant has on hot days; how facades and roof fixings are designed for wind; what vents, gutters and combustible elements face fire.

Joining the two produces a short list of targeted works: raising or protecting critical plant, adding overflow capacity, upgrading fixings, ember-proofing vents, adding cooling margin. Most are modest. Their value lies as much in what they show an insurer or lender as in what they prevent.

## Holding the line

The step itself is modest. Identify the elements that carry the building’s climate exposure, check them against current conditions rather than design-era assumptions, and decide which deserve earlier attention. Most will be targeted works rather than wholesale change.

Portfolio heat maps hide this. Two buildings on the same flood map can carry very different exposure depending on where their plant sits and what has already been done, which is a reason to look below the map at the building. Insurance markets move, and the pressure on particular elements will follow claims evidence rather than this paper.  In the register

Physical climate exposure appears through roof drainage, basement and ground-level plant, cooling capacity, facade and site stormwater items, with impact ratings that reflect consequence rather than condition alone.   Key signal

Physical climate risk acts on specific elements, and insurers are pricing it now, which makes plant location, drainage and cooling margins capital questions rather than disclosure items.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.

- [AR6 Synthesis Report](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/), Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [UK government finalises sustainability reporting standards](https://www.iasplus.com/en/news/2026/02/uk-issb), IAS Plus, Deloitte, February 2026. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Rescinded, required, pending: mapping US climate disclosure rules in 2026](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2026/09/rescinded-required-pending-mapping-us-climate-disclosure-rules-in-2026), Jones Day, September 2026. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Global commercial insurance rates fall 5% in Q3 2026](https://www.marsh.com/en/corp/about/news/global-commercial-insurance-falls-5-percent-q3-2026.html), Marsh. Accessed 3 November 2026.

- [Pacific insurance rates](https://www.marsh.com/en/services/international-placement-services/insights/pacific-insurance-rates.html), Marsh Global Insurance Market Index. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Insurance monitoring report, July 2025](https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/accc-insurance-monitoring-report-july-2025.pdf), Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What building elements are most exposed to physical climate risk?

Typically roof drainage and gutters, basement and ground-floor electrical and mechanical plant, cooling capacity, facade sealants and fixings, and site stormwater, plus bushfire-exposed elements in fringe locations.

### Is climate disclosure the same as climate resilience?

No. Disclosure describes exposure. Resilience comes from physical changes to specific elements, which need to be identified, prioritised and timed in a capital plan.

papers.title: The Building as Host to Machines
papers.question: What do automation, batteries and on-site computing ask of a commercial building?
papers.answer: Machines need power, cooling, floor capacity, connectivity and fire protection in quantities that people never did. As occupiers add compute, automated handling, batteries and charging, the building’s electrical, structural, mechanical and fire systems become the limit on what it can host.
papers.summary: Occupiers increasingly bring machines rather than people: compute, robots, batteries and chargers. Machines are demanding tenants, and they ask the building for things it may not have.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: How dense the machines have become
Machines want the floor to behave
What hosting asks of the owner

papers.contentMarkdown:
Buildings were designed around people. Floor loads assumed desks and filing. Ventilation assumed breathing. Power assumed lights and a computer per person. Fire strategies assumed paper, furniture and fit-out.

A growing share of what occupiers bring through the door is not people. It is servers and network equipment, robotic picking systems, battery storage, charging banks for vehicles and forklifts, sensors and the infrastructure that connects them. Machines are a new kind of tenant, and they are demanding ones.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. NFPA 855 sets requirements for the installation of stationary energy storage systems in the United States and is widely referenced elsewhere; fire services in Australia and Britain, including the London Fire Brigade, have issued guidance on lithium-ion battery risks from e-bikes, scooters and storage. The IEA projects data centre electricity demand of around 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, roughly double 2025. Specific requirements depend on the jurisdiction, the system and the insurer. Deepened 4 November 2026 with Uptime Institute rack density data and a summary of battery installation standards in each market.

## Machines want power and cooling

Machines convert electricity into work and heat. A rack of modern computing equipment can draw as much power as a whole floor of office workers once did, and all of it ends up as heat that must be removed. An automated warehouse runs conveyors, shuttles and chargers continuously. A fleet depot may need more power at night than the building uses all day.

The building’s supply, switchboards, distribution and cooling plant were sized for a different load profile. Adding machines often means adding capacity, and as [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) sets out, capacity is now one of the hardest things to add.

## How dense the machines have become

The pace of change is easiest to see in computing racks, the clearest case of a machine asking more of a building than people ever did. Rack power density: typical against AIMeasureReadingSourceAverage rack density, excluding purpose-built high-density sitesAbout 7.5 kW (2025)Uptime Institute Global Data Center SurveyMost common rack densityAbout 11 kW (2026), up from 9 kWUptime Institute, 2026 surveyOperators whose densest rack is below 30 kW82% (2025)Uptime InstituteOperators with a rack of 50 kW or more9% (2025)Uptime InstitutePoint at which liquid cooling is typically usedAbove about 50 kW per rackUptime InstituteLeading AI racks100 kW and more, with designs moving towards several hundredUptime Institute

Uptime Institute survey data as reported by Data Center Knowledge and others.

For a building that was never designed as a data hall, the lesson is that a single AI rack can draw what an entire floor of offices once did, and reject the same heat into one small room. Hosting that is a question of supply capacity, cooling plant, structure and, increasingly, water for liquid cooling, not of floor area.

## Battery rules by market

The fire question has its own standards, and they differ. In the United States, NFPA 855 governs the installation of stationary energy storage systems. In Australia, AS/NZS 5139 covers battery systems connected through inverters, mainly at smaller scale, with larger installations relying on fire engineering and insurer requirements. In Britain, PAS 63100 sets out fire protection for domestic battery storage, and commercial installations rely on fire engineering and insurer guidance. For an owner, the consistent points are separation, ventilation, detection and access for firefighters, and an insurer who has been told before the system is installed, not after.

## Machines want the floor to behave

Automated handling systems ask for slab flatness and load capacity that older industrial floors may not meet. Very narrow aisle and high-bay racking concentrates loads at the feet of tall structures. Robots tolerate far less unevenness than forklifts and people. Heavy batteries and equipment cabinets put point loads on suspended floors in offices and mixed-use buildings.

A slab that has served for twenty years can become the reason a building cannot host the next occupier. Floor capacity is rarely on a marketing sheet, and it is expensive to change.

## Machines change the fire question

Lithium-ion batteries are the clearest example. Battery storage, e-bike and scooter charging, forklift fleets and vehicle chargers bring a fire hazard that behaves differently from the fires most building fire strategies were designed around. Fire authorities and insurers in all three of our markets have been issuing guidance and tightening expectations on where batteries sit, how they are separated and how fires would be fought.

For an existing building, this can mean new compartmentation, detection, suppression, ventilation or simply a different location for the equipment. It can also mean that an insurer prices the building differently once the machines arrive.

## A hosting capacity statement

Owners who expect machine-heavy occupiers benefit from preparing a short hosting capacity statement for each building, drawn from the register. Spare electrical capacity at the main switchboard and the supply, and what increasing it would involve. Cooling headroom in the base-building plant and space for supplementary cooling. Floor loading and, for industrial space, slab flatness and joint condition. Riser and cable path capacity. And the fire strategy’s position on batteries, charging and high-value equipment.

A statement like this answers a prospective occupier’s first questions quickly and honestly. It also tells the owner which buildings to market to which kind of occupier, and which upgrades would widen the field.

## What hosting asks of the owner

An owner does not control what occupiers bring, but does control what the base building can support. The useful work is to know the limits before the enquiry arrives: spare electrical capacity, cooling headroom, slab capacity and flatness where relevant, riser space for cabling, and what the fire strategy would need to accept batteries or charging.

Those limits belong in the Capital Strategy as facts and as decisions. Some buildings will host machines easily. Some can with targeted works. Some cannot, and knowing that early is as valuable as knowing the opposite. How much of this reaches ordinary commercial stock, rather than purpose-built facilities, is the open question we are watching.  In the register

Hosting capacity shows up across supply and switchboard, mechanical cooling, slab and structure, risers and fire services rows, often as conditional allowances tied to a specific future use.   Key signal

As occupiers bring machines rather than people, electrical capacity, cooling headroom, floor performance and battery fire strategy decide what a building can host.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.

- [Lithium-ion batteries](https://www.london-fire.gov.uk/safety/lithium-batteries/), London Fire Brigade. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Energy and AI](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai), International Energy Agency, 2025. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [National Construction Code](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/), Australian Building Codes Board. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Key Questions on Energy and AI: executive summary](https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai/executive-summary), International Energy Agency, April 2026. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [For high-density AI, available data center space may not be usable (Uptime Institute survey data)](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/cooling/for-high-density-ai-available-data-center-space-may-not-be-usable), Data Center Knowledge. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [AI rack density’s real limits: power, cooling, failure risk (Uptime Institute 2026 survey)](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/ai-data-centers/ai-rack-density-s-real-limits-power-cooling-failure-risk), Data Center Knowledge. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Why do lithium-ion batteries change a building’s fire strategy?

Battery fires can develop and spread differently from ordinary fit-out fires and can be hard to extinguish. Where batteries are stored or charged, separation, detection, ventilation and suppression may need to change, and insurers may reassess the risk.

### Can any warehouse floor take automated handling equipment?

Not necessarily. Automated systems can require tighter floor flatness and higher load capacity than older slabs provide. The slab should be checked against the specific system before committing.

papers.title: Retail as Service Infrastructure
papers.question: How is the role of retail buildings changing, and what does that mean for their capital needs?
papers.answer: Retail space is shifting from places that display goods to places that deliver services: health and medical uses, food, fitness, collection and returns, and local fulfilment. These uses ask more of loading, services, hydraulics, power, accessibility and opening hours, so the capital needs of retail buildings move from shopfront refresh toward services and infrastructure.
papers.summary: The shop is becoming a service point: collection, returns, health, food and local logistics. The building has to work harder and longer than the one it replaced.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: Services ask more of the building
A flexibility reading for a retail asset
Reading retail for its next use

papers.contentMarkdown:
For decades a shop was a room for showing goods. Its building needed a good frontage, a dry roof, lighting, some air conditioning and a back door for deliveries. Online shopping took a large part of the selling away, and the predicted outcome was empty strips and dead malls.

Some of that happened. But in many places something else filled the space: services that cannot be delivered through a screen. Medical and allied health, childcare, gyms, food and hospitality, personal services, and the collection, returns and local fulfilment that online retail itself depends on.  Research note

This paper is a thesis about the changing use of retail buildings drawn from market observation in Australia, Britain and the United States. Building requirements for medical, food, fitness and fulfilment uses vary by jurisdiction, classification and tenancy; the building surveyor or code official for the property determines what a change of use triggers. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a practice table of what service uses ask of a retail tenancy.

## The shop as a node

The common thread is that the retail building becomes a node in a service network rather than an end point. A pharmacy fulfils online orders. A supermarket runs a dark-store operation behind its shopfront. A former department store hosts a clinic, a gym and a fulfilment floor. A neighbourhood strip becomes the place where people collect, return, eat and see a physiotherapist.

This is consistent with the wider argument of this publication. Value moves toward what a building can do. For retail, what it can do is increasingly a matter of services, access and hours rather than footfall alone.

## Services ask more of the building

Each of these uses asks for something the original shop did not. Medical and allied health tenancies need hydraulics, accessible amenities, ventilation and sometimes specialist electrical and waste arrangements. Food uses need grease management, exhaust, fire separation and more power. Gyms bring floor loading, acoustic and ventilation demands. Fulfilment needs loading, cold-chain power and vehicle access at hours the original design never anticipated.

The retail building of the next decade is open longer, works harder and carries more services per square metre than the one it replaces.

## What each service use asks

The demands differ by use, and the differences decide which tenancies can take which occupiers without major works. What service uses ask of a retail tenancyUseHydraulics and drainageMechanical and exhaustStructure and acousticsOtherMedical and allied healthBasins in rooms, accessible amenitiesHigher ventilation rates, sometimes negative pressureAcoustic privacy between roomsAccessibility, extended hoursFood and beverageGrease arrestor, floor wastes, water supplyKitchen exhaust to roof, make-up airFloor finishes and loads for equipmentFire separation, waste storageFitnessShowers and change roomsHigh fresh-air and cooling loadsImpact and vibration isolation, floor loadsLong hoursClick-and-collect and fulfilmentMinimalMinimalFloor loads for storage, dock or loading accessVehicle access and parkingChildcareChild-scale amenities, food preparationVentilation and heating to standardOutdoor play spaceLicensing requirements set the building standard

Moyne Ross practice, generalised. Requirements vary by jurisdiction and operator.

A tenancy with drainage capacity at its boundary, a riser to the roof and a structural slab can host most of this list. A tenancy without them can host the last row and little else. That is the flexibility reading in practical form.

## A flexibility reading for a retail asset

For each tenancy and for the base building, a flexibility reading asks: what drainage and water capacity is available at the tenancy boundary, and where could a grease arrestor go? What exhaust paths exist to the roof? What electrical capacity is spare at the tenancy and at the main board? What separation exists between tenancies, and what would a change of use require? Where can deliveries happen, and at what hours? Are accessible amenities and paths of travel already compliant?

Centres and strips that score well can re-let to service uses quickly as fashion and homewares tenants leave. Those that score poorly face either a capital programme to catch up or a narrower tenant market. Both outcomes are better known in advance.

## The big box problem

Large single-occupier boxes, department stores and big-format retail present the hardest case. Deep floor plates, few windows, central escalators and services designed for one tenant do not divide easily. Subdividing for several uses can trigger fire, accessibility and services upgrades across the whole building. The question is often similar to the one in [Conversion Is an Engineering Question First](/insights/conversion-is-an-engineering-question): whether the existing structure and services can carry the new pattern of use at a sensible cost.

## Reading retail for its next use

This changes where capital should go. Shopfront and finishes refreshes matter less than the infrastructure that lets a space accept a range of service tenants: capacity in hydraulics and drainage, electrical supply, mechanical exhaust paths, loading and access, and fire separation between tenancies.

A centre whose base building can host medical, food and fulfilment uses has more paths forward than one whose services were sized for fashion and homewares, and that flexibility is a better guide to its future than its current tenancy mix. Whether service uses prove durable or a temporary filler is still being decided on the ground, and this reading will follow the evidence.  In the register

Service-led retail shows up as hydraulics and drainage, exhaust and ventilation, electrical supply, fire separation and accessibility items, frequently tied to tenancy changes rather than age alone.   Key signal

Retail buildings are becoming service infrastructure, which moves capital needs from frontages and finishes toward hydraulics, power, exhaust, access and fire separation.

## Sources

## Questions

### What does converting a shop to a medical tenancy usually require?

Commonly additional hydraulics and accessible amenities, ventilation changes, electrical work and compliance upgrades. The extent depends on the use and on what the local building rules trigger.

### Why are department stores hard to repurpose?

Deep floor plates, limited daylight and services designed for one occupier make subdivision difficult, and splitting the building can trigger fire, access and services upgrades across the whole asset.

papers.title: Conversion Is an Engineering Question First
papers.question: What makes an office building suitable or unsuitable for conversion to residential use?
papers.answer: Conversion feasibility is decided mainly by engineering: floor-plate depth and daylight, floor-to-floor height, structure, the ability to run plumbing and ventilation to many units, fire separation and the facade’s thermal and acoustic performance. Many offices fail one or more of these tests, which is why only a fraction of vacant office stock is genuinely convertible.
papers.summary: Office-to-residential conversion is pitched as a policy and planning story. Whether a building can actually be converted is decided by its depth, structure, services and envelope.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.
papers.contentMarkdown:
With office vacancy high in many cities and housing short almost everywhere, converting offices into homes has become one of the most discussed ideas in real estate. Governments in all three of our markets have encouraged it. Britain extended permitted development rights to allow many commercial buildings to become housing without a full planning application, and widened them again in 2024 by removing the floor-space cap and vacancy test. American cities have offered incentives and zoning changes. Australian cities have explored the same path.

Planning permission, though, is rarely what stops a conversion. The building does.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. In England, Class MA permitted development rights, introduced from 1 August 2021, allow buildings in Commercial, Business and Service use to change to residential subject to prior approval. From 5 March 2024 the 1,500 square metre cap and the three-month vacancy requirement were removed; the building must still have been in that use for two years. New York adopted a dedicated conversion tax incentive in 2024 and citywide zoning reform in December 2024. Australian cities have explored similar measures. Engineering feasibility applies regardless of the planning route. Deepened 4 November 2026 with US pipeline and English completion data and practitioner figures for conversion constraints (REBusinessOnline, citing Ware Malcomb).

## Depth and light

Homes need daylight and natural ventilation in places offices do not. A deep office floor plate, common in buildings from the 1970s onward, can leave a large central core of space too far from a window to be a habitable room. Designers can carve light wells or use the centre for storage and services, but each response costs area and money.

This single factor rules out a large share of office stock before anything else is considered.

## Plumbing is the hidden cost

An office has a few wet areas stacked around the core. An apartment building has a kitchen and a bathroom in every unit. Running new soil, waste and water services to dozens of units means new risers, penetrations through slabs, falls for drainage and often raised floors to carry pipework, which eats into floor-to-floor height.

Most conversions are a plumbing project with a building attached. That is where the cost, the risk and the delay concentrate.

Ventilation follows the same pattern. Each unit needs extraction and fresh air, and the central systems that served open office floors are rarely suited to many small separate dwellings.

## How much conversion is happening

Conversion is growing, but from a small base, and pipeline is not delivery. Office and commercial conversion activityMarketMeasureFigureUnited StatesOffice-to-apartment pipeline, start of 202690,300 units, up 28% in a year and about four times the 2022 levelNew York CityUnits in the conversion pipeline16,358Washington DCUnits in the conversion pipeline8,479ChicagoUnits in the conversion pipeline4,360EnglandOffice-to-residential completions under permitted development6,695 (2023-24), falling to 5,154 (2024-25)EnglandClass MA (commercial to residential) completions454, 803 and 1,048 (2022-23 to 2024-25, latest provisional)

RentCafe data via NAIOP; MHCLG housing supply statistics. US figures are pipeline, not completions.

England is the instructive case. Class MA, the permitted development right for converting commercial premises to homes, was relaxed on 5 March 2024 to remove the 1,500 m² floorspace cap and the vacancy test. Completions under it are rising, but total office-to-residential output under permitted development has fallen. Removing planning friction did not remove the engineering.

## The physical tests, in numbers

Practitioners put figures on the constraints this paper describes. Residential conversion typically needs one to three feet of additional floor-to-floor allowance for the services, plumbing and sprinklers that homes require. Floor plates deeper than roughly 80 to 120 feet from core to facade struggle to give every room daylight. Where cities have used subsidy to close the gap, the sums are large: Chicago has committed more than $315 million of tax increment finance to six projects totalling 1,765 homes.

None of these is a rule. They are the screens a feasibility study runs first, and they explain why the conversion candidates that work tend to be older, narrower buildings with generous floor heights, rather than the deep-plan offices with the highest vacancy.

## Fire, sound and the facade

Residential use changes the fire strategy. Each unit becomes its own compartment, escape routes change, and sprinkler and detection requirements may increase. Acoustic separation between units, which offices never needed, must be built in. And the facade, often designed for an office that was cooled more than heated and occupied by day, may need upgrading for thermal comfort, condensation control and openable windows.

In older buildings these works sit alongside the issues described in [What Age Conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals): hazardous materials in the way of new penetrations, concrete condition, and facade materials that may not meet current expectations.

## A conversion screen

A first engineering screen for conversion can be run on most office buildings before any design work. Floor-plate depth from window to core, against the depth at which habitable rooms can still get daylight. Floor-to-floor height, against the space needed for new services and acceptable ceiling heights. Structural grid and floor capacity. Number and location of risers, and where new wet stacks could run. Facade type, openability and condition. Fire stair and lift provision against residential needs. Hazardous materials likely to be disturbed.

Buildings that pass most of these screens are worth designing. Those that fail two or more are usually better candidates for refurbishment in their existing use or for the redevelopment question discussed in [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset).

## Feasibility before enthusiasm

None of this means conversion is a bad idea. Narrow plates, generous floor-to-floor heights, good structural grids and facades with openable or replaceable glazing can convert well. Many older, smaller office buildings fit that description better than the large post-war towers.

The point is order. Conversion should start with an engineering reading of the building, which then informs the planning and financial case, rather than the other way round. The analysis in [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) shows the other side of the same decision: sometimes the honest answer is that the land, not the building, carries the value. New retrofit methods could loosen the screen described here; it is a current reading of what is practical, not a permanent one.  In the register

Conversion feasibility is read across structure, floor-to-floor, hydraulics and risers, mechanical ventilation, fire services and facade rows, usually as scenario allowances rather than base-case capital.   Key signal

Office-to-residential conversion succeeds or fails on depth, plumbing, ventilation, fire separation and facade performance long before planning rules are tested.

## Sources
