- [Work item WK92482: standard guide for facility condition assessments](https://astm.org/workitem-wk92482), ASTM International. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How is a capital reading different from a building condition report?

A condition report describes the state of elements and defects. A capital reading adds what should be done, how the cost is built, when it falls, how much it matters and how confident the evidence is, producing a decision-ready capital view.

### What are the three layers Moyne Ross uses to read a building?

Structure, services and space: the elements that hold up and enclose the building, the systems that make it work, and the internal environment and amenities that make it usable.

papers.title: Documented, Observed, Inferred
papers.question: How should evidence about a building’s condition be graded in a capital assessment?
papers.answer: Evidence should be graded by its source: documented evidence comes from records or supplied material, observed evidence from what is visible in available evidence, and inferred evidence from reasoning about era, type and context. Keeping these grades separate on every line prevents a reasonable inference from being treated as a confirmed fact and makes the confidence of each figure clear.
papers.summary: Every claim about a building comes from somewhere: a record, something seen, or reasoning from context. Keeping those three apart is how a capital view stays honest.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: A public example of inference hardening

papers.contentMarkdown:
An assessment of a building is a collection of claims. The roof is metal deck. The chillers were replaced around 2008. The facade panels are precast concrete. The building was completed in the mid-1970s. Some of those claims come from a document. Some come from what can be seen. Some are reasoned from context.

All three kinds are legitimate. The problem arises when they are mixed up, and an inference starts to behave like a fact.  Research note

The three evidence grades are published in the Moyne Ross Capital Register and llms.txt descriptions. The safeguard that a planning application or permit date alone does not establish a construction year is a Moyne Ross method rule. Deepened 4 November 2026 with examples of each evidence grade and the RAAC lifespan claim as a public example of inference hardening.

## Three grades

Documented evidence is supported by a record or supplied material: a drawing, a maintenance log, a compliance certificate, a survey, a permit with a clear scope, an owner’s confirmation. Observed evidence is visible in what is available to the assessment: a photograph, aerial or street imagery, a site inspection, a listing image. Inferred evidence is reasoned from era, type and contextual signals: a building of this age and type in this location probably has this kind of plant or these materials.

Each grade has a place. Inference is often the only evidence available for concealed elements, and it can be very good inference. It is still inference.

The danger is not inference. It is inference that has forgotten it is one.

## What each grade looks like

The grades are easiest to apply when each comes with examples of its evidence and of what would move it up. Evidence grades in practiceGradeTypical evidenceExampleWhat would upgrade itDocumentedDrawings, invoices, maintenance logs, compliance certificates, test resultsChillers replaced in 2015, per invoice and commissioning reportAlready the strongest grade; it can still be out of dateObservedInspection, photographs, imagery, nameplates seen in listing materialPonding visible on the roof in imagery from two separate yearsA document confirming the cause, or a closer inspectionInferredThe building’s era, type, location and comparable buildingsAsbestos-containing materials likely in a 1972 officeObservation, then a survey or test result

Moyne Ross practice.

## A public example of inference hardening

The clearest recent example of an inference hardening into fact is the 30-year lifespan widely attributed to reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete during the 2023 school closures in England. The figure was repeated across news reports, professional commentary and guidance. The Institution of Structural Engineers has since said the claim is misleading, traced to a 1995 exchange of correspondence, with no specific data behind it.

Every mechanism this paper describes is visible in that case: a figure repeated without its source, summarised without its caveats, and finally treated as an engineering fact. A register that grades evidence would have carried it as inferred and unsupported, and priced the investigation rather than the date. [What Age Conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals) sets out the case in full.

## How inference hardens

Inference hardens into assumed fact in predictable ways. It is repeated across documents without its source. It is summarised into a headline. It fills a field that has no way of saying how it was derived. An inferred construction year appears in a report, is copied into the next one, and becomes the building’s age.

Dates are a common example. A planning application or permit tells you that work was proposed or approved at a certain time. It does not, on its own, establish when a building was completed. A capital view that treats the permit date as the construction date may misjudge the age of every system in the building.

## Grades and confidence

Evidence grade feeds directly into confidence. A line whose condition and cost basis rest on documented evidence can carry high confidence. One resting on inference should carry lower confidence and, where the stakes justify it, an action to confirm. This is what lets an owner see where the capital position is firm and where it is soft.

It also shapes how uncertainty is priced, which is the subject of [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know).

## Three statements about one roof

Documented: “The roof was re-sheeted in 2014; invoice and scope supplied by the owner.” Observed: “Aerial imagery from 2015 onward shows a uniform new profile across the western bays.” Inferred: “Buildings of this type and era in this location typically had asbestos cement roofing originally; the eastern bays may retain it.” Each statement is useful. Each supports a different level of confidence. And each tells the reader what would strengthen it: the inferred statement points directly to a hazardous materials survey.

Keeping the grade visible stops the inferred statement from being read as the documented one six months later in someone else’s report.

## Why it matters more now

Assessments increasingly draw on public data, imagery and AI-assisted reading of documents. These tools are powerful at producing plausible statements. Plausibility is not evidence. A disciplined method has to keep asking of every claim: where did this come from? [What Public Evidence Can Tell You](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) discusses the limits of desktop reading, and the Moyne Ross [approach to AI](/ai) sets out how models are kept inside this discipline.  In the register

Each row’s condition text states its evidential basis, and confidence reflects whether the line rests on documented, observed or inferred evidence.   Key signal

Keeping documented, observed and inferred evidence separate on every line prevents plausible inference from hardening into assumed fact.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [IStructE statement and FAQs: reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC)](https://www.istructe.org/resources/news/istructe-statement-reinforced-autoclaved-aerated-c/), Institution of Structural Engineers. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is inferred evidence unreliable?

Not necessarily. Inference from era, type and context can be well founded and is often the only evidence for concealed elements. It should simply be labelled as inference and carry appropriate confidence.

### Does a planning permit date show when a building was built?

Not on its own. A permit or application shows when work was proposed or approved. Completion needs a source that actually fixes or bounds the construction date.

papers.title: Pricing What You Don’t Know
papers.question: How should uncertainty be priced in a building capital plan?
papers.answer: Uncertainty should be made visible rather than hidden. A capital plan can carry an investigation allowance for the work needed to find out, a range for the possible outcome, a conditional allowance for works that depend on the investigation, and a confidence rating, so that the owner sees both the likely position and the size of what is unknown.
papers.summary: Every building assessment meets things it cannot see. The honest response is neither silence nor a confident guess, but a visible allowance, a range and the action that would resolve it.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: How wide a range should be

papers.contentMarkdown:
No assessment sees everything. Foundations are buried. Structural timbers sit behind ceilings. Concrete hides its reinforcement. Cladding hides its fixings. Records go missing. In a desktop read, most of the building is unseen.

There are two common bad responses. One is silence: leave out what cannot be confirmed, and present a tidy number that understates the risk. The other is false precision: give the unknown a single confident figure as if it were known. Both mislead.  Research note

This paper describes the Moyne Ross approach to uncertainty: investigation allowances, ranges, conditional allowances kept distinct from anticipated expenditure, and confidence ratings. The heritage example draws on the published CMP 003 asset study. Deepened 4 November 2026 with AACE International’s estimate classification as a reference for how range width should track evidence.

## Four tools

A capital plan has four tools for carrying uncertainty honestly. An investigation allowance pays for finding out: a roof survey, a structural assessment, a hazardous materials survey. A range shows the spread of plausible outcomes rather than a single point. A conditional allowance carries works that will only be needed if the investigation finds a problem, kept distinct from anticipated expenditure. And a confidence rating tells the reader how firm each line is.

Used together, they let an owner see the likely capital position and, separately, the size of what is not yet known.

## How wide a range should be

Cost engineers have a long-standing way of saying how wide an estimate’s range should be: tie it to how much is known. AACE International’s cost estimate classification sets out the expected accuracy of an estimate by the maturity of the information behind it. Expected accuracy by estimate classClassInformation availableTypical low rangeTypical high rangeClass 5Concept only, very little definition−20% to −50%+30% to +100%Class 4Feasibility; limited definition−15% to −30%+20% to +50%Class 3Budget authorisation; meaningful definition−10% to −20%+10% to +30%Class 2Control estimate; substantial definition−5% to −15%+5% to +20%Class 1Bid or tender check; full definition−3% to −10%+3% to +15%

AACE International Recommended Practice 18R-97, cost estimate classification. Ranges are typical, not limits.

Two lessons carry straight into a capital plan. A range that is too narrow for the evidence is not more accurate, only more confident. And the ranges are asymmetric: when less is known, the upside risk is larger than the downside. That is why a register built from early evidence carries wide, upward-skewed ranges on the lines that matter, and why investigation is often the cheapest way to narrow them.

## The heritage example

The fire station in [The Economics of Heritage](/insights/the-economics-of-heritage) shows the pattern clearly. A significant share of near-term spend was investigation rather than remediation: foundations, roof structure, fire compliance. Beside it sat explicit worst-case ranges for the risks those investigations would resolve. The building was not presented as cheaper or more expensive than it was. It was presented as partly unknown, with a plan to find out.

The cost of an investigation is usually small beside the cost of being wrong. Pricing it explicitly is how a plan earns trust.

## Keeping the base honest

Conditional allowances need care. If every possible problem is added to the base programme, the plan becomes a worst case and loses credibility. If none is shown, the plan becomes a best case. The register keeps them separate: anticipated works in the base, conditional works beside it, each with its trigger. This is the same discipline as [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): checks can sit in the near term while the works they may lead to sit later.

## A worked uncertainty

A 1960s office has precast facade panels whose fixings cannot be seen. The register carries three lines. An investigation item in the first year: inspection of a sample of fixings from access equipment, with a modest cost. A base-programme item in years two to five: cleaning, sealant renewal and minor concrete repair, priced with a range. And a conditional allowance beside the programme, not inside it: remedial fixing works if the inspection finds corrosion, priced as a wide range with its trigger stated.

The owner sees the likely programme, the size of the unknown and the small cost of resolving it. After the inspection, the conditional line either disappears or moves into the base with a narrower range. Either way, the plan stays honest.

## Uncertainty in the rating

Uncertainty also belongs in the building’s overall position. In the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index), an element that needs a check, or a hazard suspected but not yet seen, is carried as an open question until it is resolved. A building with many open questions reads differently from one whose questions have been answered, and resolving them moves the band in whichever direction the evidence points.

What an owner gets from this is a clear list of what to investigate first. Resolving the largest uncertainties early usually narrows the range of the whole programme and makes every later decision easier.  In the register

Uncertainty appears as investigation items, ranges in the cost basis, conditional allowances kept distinct from anticipated works, and a confidence rating on every line.   Key signal

Honest capital plans show both the likely position and the size of the unknown, using investigation allowances, ranges, conditional allowances and confidence.

## Questions

### What is the difference between a provisional sum and a contingency?

Terms vary by market, but generally a provisional or conditional allowance is tied to a specific identified uncertainty, while a contingency is a general margin across a project. A capital plan is clearer when specific uncertainties are named.

### Why not include every possible defect in the capital plan?

Adding every possible problem to the base turns the plan into a worst case and undermines its credibility. Keeping conditional works separate, with their triggers, shows the likely position and the risk around it.

papers.title: What Public Evidence Can Tell You
papers.question: How much can be learned about a commercial building from public evidence without an inspection?
papers.answer: Public evidence such as aerial and street imagery, planning and permit records, heritage registers, energy rating databases, sales material and published documents can establish a building’s form, materials, major plant, some history and many visible conditions. It cannot confirm concealed elements, internal condition or operating performance, so a desktop read is a strong first view that needs evidence-led refinement.
papers.summary: A surprising amount about a building is on the public record: its form, its roof, its permits, its energy rating, its planning history. Reading it well is a first read, not a final one.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.
papers.contentMarkdown:
Not long ago, understanding a building meant visiting it, requesting documents and waiting. Much of that is still necessary for a final view. But a great deal can now be learned before anyone sets foot on site, from evidence that is publicly available.

This paper describes what that evidence can establish, what it cannot, and how Moyne Ross uses it as a first read.  Research note

Public evidence sources named here are general categories. Energy disclosure regimes cited, NABERS and the Commercial Building Disclosure programme in Australia, EPCs in Britain and city benchmarking in the United States, are covered in Part VI with their sources. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of public evidence sources by market.

## What the record shows

Aerial imagery shows roof form, materials, plant locations, solar, ponding, patch repairs and changes over time when historic imagery is available. Street-level imagery shows facades, windows, entrances, signs of movement or staining, and how a building has changed. Planning and permit records show what works were proposed or approved and when. Heritage registers show protections. Energy and emissions disclosure regimes, such as NABERS in Australia, EPCs in Britain and city benchmarking in the United States, show recorded performance for many buildings.

Sales and leasing material, annual reports, tenant announcements and published documents often add specifications, floor areas, plant details and recent works.

## Where the public record lives

The sources differ by market, but the categories are the same. The table names the main public sources a first read draws on and what each tends to say about capital. Public evidence by marketEvidenceAustraliaUnited KingdomUnited StatesWhat it says about capitalEnergy performanceNABERS ratings; Commercial Building Disclosure for offices of 1,000 m² and overEnergy Performance Certificates; Display Energy Certificates for public buildingsLocal benchmarking data, such as New York’s annual disclosuresPlant efficiency, controls, and exposure to performance rulesPlanning and permitsState planning portals and council registersLocal planning portalsLocal permit recordsWhat has been renewed, altered or approved, and whenHeritage and controlsState heritage registers and planning overlaysThe National Heritage List for England and equivalentsLocal landmark designationsWhat can be changed, and at what premiumHazard mappingState and council flood studiesEnvironment Agency flood mapsFEMA flood mapsExposure of plant, basements and drainageImagery and listingsAerial and street imagery; sale and leasing materialThe sameThe sameRoof condition, plant, alterations and their dates

Moyne Ross practice. Coverage and access vary by state, council and county.

None of these sources is complete on its own, and several date quickly. Their value comes from being read together, with each finding graded as documented, observed or inferred and dated to its source.

## What it cannot show

Public evidence cannot show what is behind finishes or below ground. It rarely shows internal plant condition, maintenance history, compliance certification or how systems actually perform. It can be out of date. Listings are written to sell. Permits may never have been acted on.

A desktop read sees a great deal of the outside of a building and very little of its inside. Its job is to frame the right questions, not to answer all of them.

This is why [evidence grading](/insights/documented-observed-inferred) matters so much in desktop work. Much of what a desktop read concludes about concealed elements is inference, and it should be labelled so.

## Evidence that ages

Public evidence has dates, and they matter. Aerial imagery may be months or years old. Street views can predate a refurbishment. A listing describes the building as the seller wished to present it on a particular day. An energy rating has a validity period and may predate plant changes. A permit records a proposal, not necessarily what was built.

A careful desktop read records the date of each piece of evidence it relies on and treats newer, more specific evidence as stronger. Where evidence conflicts, it says so rather than choosing silently.

## A first read, then sharper

Moyne Ross uses public evidence to produce a first read of a building’s capital position: a ten-year view built from what can be established, with its uncertainties visible. That first read is not the final word. As the owner’s records, surveys and knowledge are brought in, lines firm up, ranges narrow and some conclusions change.

The [Melbourne office](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) and [Preston fire station](/insights/the-economics-of-heritage) studies were both desktop assessments using public evidence. Both reached useful conclusions, and both were explicit about what would need confirming.

## Why the first read matters

A good first read changes what happens next. It tells an owner where the capital is likely to sit, which uncertainties matter most and what to investigate first. It focuses the expensive parts of due diligence, site inspections, specialist surveys, intrusive investigation, on the questions that will move the answer.

It also tends to change the brief. An owner who sees the first read often asks different questions than they would have asked beforehand, which is the argument of [Hearing the Building as It Is](/insights/hearing-the-building-as-it-is).  In the register

Desktop-derived rows state their evidential source in the condition text, and lines that rest on public evidence alone carry confidence to match.   Key signal

Public evidence can establish much of a building’s form, history and visible condition, making a desktop read a strong first view that frames the questions further evidence must answer.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Commercial Building Disclosure program](https://www.cbd.gov.au/), Australian Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Energy Performance Certificates](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/energy-performance-certificates), UK Government collection. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [ENERGY STAR for buildings](https://www.energystar.gov/buildings), US Environmental Protection Agency. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Commercial Building Disclosure: is your building disclosure affected?](https://www.cbd.gov.au/node/27), Australian Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Find an energy certificate](https://find-energy-certificate.service.gov.uk/), UK Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [The National Heritage List for England](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/), Historic England. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [FEMA Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home), Federal Emergency Management Agency. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Can a desktop assessment replace a physical inspection?

No. It can provide a strong first view and focus later work, but concealed elements, internal plant condition and compliance status generally need inspection, records or specialist investigation to confirm.

### What public records are most useful for understanding a commercial building?

Aerial and street imagery, planning and permit histories, heritage registers, energy rating and benchmarking databases, and published sales or leasing material are typically the most informative.

papers.title: Why Cost Is the Wrong Rating
papers.question: Why shouldn’t a building’s condition rating be based on the total cost of its capital works?
papers.answer: Total cost scales with building size, location and market prices, so a cost-based rating says more about scale than about the building’s position, and it inherits all the uncertainty in the estimates. A better rating reads the judgement in the register instead: for each element, whether it needs attention, how serious it is and how soon. The MR Index works this way, and no costs take part in its band.
papers.summary: Rating a building by the size of its capital bill is easy and misleading. Big buildings look bad, small ones look good, and the judgement that matters disappears into a number.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: The index most public owners use
How the MR Index reads it

papers.contentMarkdown:
The quickest way to rate a building’s capital position is to add up its capital bill and compare it with something: floor area, value, a benchmark. More cost, worse building. It is simple, it looks objective, and it is the way many systems have done it.

We think it is the wrong way, and the reasons say something about what a rating is for.  Research note

The MR Index method and its five bands are published in the Moyne Ross methodology reference. Since October 2026 the band has been read from the register’s judgements, element by element, rather than its costs; the cost-weighted measures used before then are still calculated for reference. The MR Index is calculated by the platform, not by the AI model. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the Facility Condition Index, its published bands and its limitations.

## Cost measures size first

A large building has larger capital needs than a small one in almost every case. A building in an expensive market has higher costs than one elsewhere. Dividing by floor area or value helps, but only partly, because costs do not scale neatly with either. A rating built on cost ends up describing scale and market as much as the building.

Cost also carries every uncertainty in the estimates beneath it. Planning allowances are ranges. Prices move. A rating built on a total inherits all of that noise.

## The index most public owners use

The most widely used condition rating among public and institutional owners is a cost ratio. The Facility Condition Index, published by the US National Association of College and University Business Officers in 1991, divides the cost of deferred maintenance and renewal by the building’s current replacement value. It is simple, comparable across a portfolio and easy to explain to a finance committee. Facility Condition Index bands, as commonly publishedSourceGoodFairPoorCriticalClassic scheme used by many institutions (APPA)Under 5%5% to 10%Over 10%International Facility Management Association scale0 to 5%5% to 10%10% to 30%Over 30%Some current software defaultsUnder 10%10% to 30%30% to 60%Over 60%

Designing Buildings; published institutional assessments. The variation in bands is itself part of the problem.

The FCI has real strengths, and its weaknesses are the ones this paper describes. It depends entirely on the replacement value in the denominator, which drifts if it is not re-indexed and differs with method. It weighs a deferred handrail and a deferred fire panel by their cost, not their consequence. And the bands are not agreed: the same building can be good on one published scale and fair on another. A rating built on judgement rather than cost avoids all three.

## The judgement is the signal

What actually distinguishes one building’s capital position from another is the judgement in its register. How much of the programme is work the building cannot defer? How firm is the evidence? Is there a single finding, a structural question, a facade issue, that could reshape everything? How much falls in the near term for good reason? How much is driven by compliance obligations? Is the burden spread or concentrated in one system?

A rating should tell you what kind of decade a building faces. The size of the bill is one input. The shape of the judgement is the answer.

## How the MR Index reads it

The [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) is built on three of those questions, asked of every element in the completed register: does it need attention, how serious is it, and how soon. Read across the whole building, the answers place it on a band from MR 1, minimal requirements, to MR 5, major intervention. No costs, floor areas or rates take part, so the rating does not drift as prices move and can be recalculated from any stored register. The score is calculated by code, not guessed, and it describes condition, not the building’s quality or attractiveness.

A prime building in a strong location can score MR 4 and still be an excellent acquisition. A modest building can score MR 2 and still be a poor one. The rating is a decision aid, not a verdict.

## Two buildings, one total

Two buildings each carry a ten-year capital requirement of three million dollars. In the first, the requirement is spread across roof, plant, lifts and finishes, mostly in years six to ten, supported by records and with few unknowns. In the second, half of it sits in a single facade question that cannot be resolved without investigation, most of it falls in the first five years, and a material share is driven by compliance.

A cost-based rating scores them the same. The MR Index separates them because it never looks at the totals. In the first building, most elements needing attention are planned renewals late in the decade. In the second, an essential facade element needs a check now and important elements need works within five years. Consequence and timing put the second building in a heavier band, and resolving the facade question will move it. That is the information an owner or buyer needs, and it comes from the register’s judgement rather than its total.

## Costs still matter

None of this means costs are unimportant. They remain in the register, line by line, with their basis visible, because owners need to plan and fund the work. They are there to plan and fund the work, not to grade the building. Moyne Ross does not publish cost tables, which go stale, and a capital plan is not a reinstatement valuation or a quantity surveyor’s estimate.

the overall rating should rest on judgement about what the building needs, how serious it is and how soon, rather than on the dollar total.  In the register

The MR Index reads each element’s attention, impact and timing from the register; the cost basis stays on every line for planning and plays no part in the band.   Key signal

A cost-based rating mostly measures size and inherits estimate noise, while a judgement-based rating describes the kind of decade a building faces.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Facility condition index (FCI)](https://designingbuildings.co.uk/wiki/Facility_condition_index_FCI), Designing Buildings. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How does the MR Index rate a building without using costs?

For each element it reads whether attention is needed, how serious it is and how soon. Read across the whole building, those judgements set the band from MR 1 to MR 5; the size of the bill plays no part.

### Does a high MR Index score mean a building is a bad investment?

No. It describes condition, not asset quality or attractiveness. A building that needs a lot of attention can be well worth taking on if that is understood and priced.

papers.title: The Register, Not the Report
papers.question: Why is a line-by-line capital register more useful than a traditional building report?
papers.answer: A traditional report presents conclusions at a point in time and ages quickly, while a register holds each element as a structured line with its evidence, reasoning and timing that can be challenged, filtered, updated and recombined. Reports are best treated as views produced from the register rather than the record itself.
papers.summary: A report freezes a building at a date. A register can keep up with it. The difference decides whether building advice is a document or a working tool.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: What changes when a line changes

papers.contentMarkdown:
For most of the history of building consultancy, the product has been a report. Bound, then PDF. An executive summary, sections on each building element, photographs, a cost table at the back. Careful work, often excellent, and frozen on the day it was issued.

Buildings do not freeze. Tenants change, systems age, surveys resolve questions, regulations move. Within a year or two, much of a report describes a building that no longer quite exists.  Research note

This paper describes the Moyne Ross approach in which issued reports are drawn from the register and what is shown together must agree. It is a method statement, not a criticism of report-based practice, which remains appropriate for many purposes. Deepened 4 November 2026 with regulatory and standards moves toward structured building records.

## What a report does well

Reports are good at telling a story. They can explain context, weigh considerations, give a professional opinion and present it in a form a board or lender can read. Those strengths matter, and a good narrative remains an important way to communicate about a building.

Their weakness is structural. The conclusions sit in prose and tables that are hard to update, hard to compare across buildings and hard to challenge line by line. The reasoning behind a figure is often in the author’s head or a working file, not in the document.

## What a register does differently

A register holds each element as a structured line: condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence. Each line can be read alone, challenged alone and updated alone. The reasoning behind each number travels with it. Lines can be filtered by system, horizon, confidence or impact, summed into a position and compared across a portfolio.

A report is a view of the building on one day. A register is the building’s capital record, from which any number of views can be drawn.

When new evidence arrives, the affected lines change and everything that depends on them, totals, horizons, the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index), updates with them. Nothing has to be rewritten from scratch.

## Registers are becoming the expectation

The shift from documents to structured records is not only a Moyne Ross preference. Regulators and standards bodies are moving the same way. Structured building records in regulation and standardsWhereWhatStatus at reviewEnglandThe golden thread of information for higher-risk buildings under the Building Safety Act 2022Required: digital, kept up to date, available to those who need itEuropean UnionRenovation passports and digital building logbooks in the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (2024)Being transposed by member statesUnited StatesASTM work item for a facility condition assessment standard aimed at capital planningOpened 2024, alongside the transactional E2018 guideInternationalISO 19650 information management for buildingsWidely used for new construction; less so for existing stock

UK Building Safety Act 2022; Directive (EU) 2024/1275; ASTM International; ISO.

The common thread is that a building’s information should outlive the document it was first written in, and be kept current by whoever changes the building. That is the register’s premise.

## Reports as views

This does not make reports obsolete. It changes their role. A technical due diligence report, a capital strategy report for a board, a short brief for a lender: each can be produced from the register, written for its reader, and consistent with every other view because they share one source. When the register changes, the next report reflects it.

Moyne Ross works this way. The register is the record. Reports are written from it, and what is shown together must agree.

## What changes when a line changes

Suppose a roof survey narrows a facade allowance from a wide range to a tight one and moves its timing from years two to five into years six to ten. In a report-based world, someone must rewrite the relevant section, the cost table, the summary, the horizon split and any rating, and hope they all agree. In a register-based world, the line changes; the totals, horizons, MR Index and any report drawn afterwards follow automatically, and the previous version is kept for the record.

Over a decade of ownership, the difference is the difference between advice that stays current and advice that is current once.

## Why it matters to owners

Capital advice kept this way stays current and stays challengeable. A question about a particular line can be answered by reading the line. A change of plan can be tested against the register rather than commissioning a new report. Over years, the register becomes the building’s memory, which is the argument of [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record).

For portfolios, structured registers make comparison possible. Forty buildings described in forty reports are forty stories. Forty registers are a dataset.  In the register

The register itself is the record: every report, summary and rating is drawn from its rows, so a change to one line flows through to every view.   Key signal

A register keeps a building’s capital record current and challengeable line by line, with reports produced as consistent views of it rather than standalone documents.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Work item WK92482: standard guide for facility condition assessments](https://astm.org/workitem-wk92482), ASTM International. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Does a capital register replace a written report?

Not entirely. Narrative reports remain useful for boards, lenders and transactions. The difference is that they are produced from the register, so they stay consistent and can be refreshed when the register changes.

### Why does structured capital data matter for portfolios?

Structured registers can be filtered, summed and compared across buildings, which makes portfolio-level capital planning and benchmarking possible in a way that separate reports do not.

papers.title: Australia: Supply Constraint and the Staircase Code
papers.question: What regulatory and market conditions shape capital planning for commercial buildings in Australia?
papers.answer: Australian commercial property combines constrained, costly new supply with a National Construction Code adopted at different times by each state, mandatory energy disclosure for larger offices through NABERS, state-based fire safety maintenance regimes, combustible cladding programmes and phased mandatory climate reporting. Together these make existing buildings more valuable and their capital planning more consequential.
papers.summary: Australian commercial property sits between slow, expensive new supply and a building code that changes state by state. Both make the existing building more valuable and its capital plan more consequential.
papers.limitations: A building-and-capital reading of one or more national regimes, current at the review date. Rules change and vary by state, city and lease; it is not legal advice and the governing instrument and qualified advisers should be consulted.
papers.contentMarkdown:
Australia is the home market of Moyne Ross, and its commercial property has a particular character. New supply is slow and expensive. Regulation is national in name and state-based in practice. Energy performance has been disclosed for larger offices for more than a decade. And much of the stock is younger than in Britain, but ageing fast.

This note reads the Australian setting for its capital consequences. It is not legal advice, and rules differ between states and change over time.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. NCC 2025 was published by the Australian Building Codes Board with adoption available from 1 May 2026. Victoria adopted from that date; the ACT and Western Australia commenced then with transitions to 2027; New South Wales, Queensland and South Australia’s building provisions are deferred to 1 May 2027; Tasmania reverted to NCC 2022 from 5 June 2026 until May 2027; the Northern Territory remains on NCC 2022. The state positions were confirmed from secondary summaries and should be read against each regulator’s current notice. The Commercial Building Disclosure programme requires a Building Energy Efficiency Certificate for most office space of 1,000 square metres or more offered for sale or lease. Mandatory climate-related reporting under the Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards began for the largest entities from financial years starting 1 January 2025, with further groups from 1 July 2026 and 1 July 2027. Victoria requires new homes and most new commercial buildings to be all-electric from 1 January 2027. Deepened 4 November 2026 with an adoption table by jurisdiction.

## Slow, costly new supply

Construction costs in Australia rose sharply in the years after 2020, with labour shortages, materials prices and builder insolvencies all contributing. Planning and approvals add time. The result is that replacing an existing building, or adding new stock, is slow and dear. That strengthens the position of existing buildings in well-located precincts, and raises the stakes of keeping them competitive.

It also explains a pattern seen in [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset): in tightly held locations, the land and the consent can be worth more than the building on them.

## The staircase code

The [National Construction Code](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/) sets technical requirements for new building work, but each state and territory decides when to adopt each edition. NCC 2025 illustrates the result. Its energy provisions include mandatory on-site solar for new commercial buildings, and adoption has become a staircase. Victoria adopted from 1 May 2026. Western Australia and the ACT began on 1 May 2026 with transitions that allow NCC 2022 until 2027. New South Wales, Queensland and South Australia’s building provisions are deferred to 1 May 2027. Tasmania applied the new edition for a few days in June 2026 and then returned to NCC 2022 until May 2027. The Northern Territory remains on NCC 2022 with no adoption date. Two codes will run side by side until at least 2027. [When the Shed Becomes a Power Station](/insights/when-the-shed-becomes-a-power-station) sets out what this means for industrial stock.

For existing buildings, the code matters mostly when major work is done. Significant alterations can bring parts of a building toward current requirements, and the extent depends on the state, the work and the building surveyor’s assessment.

In Australia the code is national, the timing is local, and the trigger for existing buildings is usually the next major project.

## Where each state stands

The staircase is easiest to see laid out. The position below is as published at review; states continue to adjust their adoption, so the governing instrument should be checked for any particular project. NCC 2025 adoption by jurisdictionJurisdictionBuilding Code (Volume One)NoteVictoriaFrom 1 May 2026First moverWestern AustraliaFrom 1 May 2026Transition allows NCC 2022 until 1 May 2027ACTFrom 1 May 2026Transition allows NCC 2022 until 1 May 2027New South WalesFrom 1 May 2027DeferredQueenslandFrom 1 May 2027Deferred, with variations flaggedSouth AustraliaFrom 1 May 2027Plumbing provisions from 1 May 2026TasmaniaReverted to NCC 2022 from 5 June 2026Briefly adopted, then withdrawnNorthern TerritoryNot adoptedRemains on NCC 2022

Australian Building Codes Board; state adoption notices as summarised by Cyberate. Check the current state instrument before relying on a date.

For an owner the consequence is that the same building type, built in the same year, can be governed by different editions on either side of a state border. A national portfolio cannot assume one standard for new work, and a register that records the edition a building was approved under is more useful than one that records only its age.

## What the 2025 edition actually changes

For commercial classes, NCC 2025 concentrates on four areas: mandatory on-site solar photovoltaics for new Class 3 and Class 5 to 9 buildings, tighter commercial energy efficiency across Section J, strengthened water management provisions to reduce water ingress in commercial and apartment buildings, and revised car park fire safety provisions. Residential energy provisions were largely held at NCC 2022 levels, with building ministers signalling a pause on further residential changes toward the end of the decade.

The adoption picture is uneven and still settling. Victoria moved first. The ACT and Western Australia began on the same date with transitions. New South Wales, Queensland and South Australia deferred to May 2027, with Queensland flagging variations. Tasmania applied the edition for a few days in June 2026 and then returned to NCC 2022. The Northern Territory has not adopted it. Two codes will run side by side until at least 2027, and in the Territory for longer. For an owner of an existing building, the practical consequence is that the standard a major alteration will be assessed against depends on the state and the date, and a building surveyor’s advice is needed early.

## Disclosure and safety regimes

Under the [Commercial Building Disclosure](https://www.cbd.gov.au/) programme, most office spaces of 1,000 square metres or more must disclose an energy efficiency certificate, including a NABERS Energy rating, when offered for sale or lease. NABERS ratings have become a market signal for offices well beyond the legal requirement.

Fire safety maintenance is state-based. Victoria requires owners to maintain essential safety measures and produce annual reports. New South Wales requires annual fire safety statements. Other states have equivalent regimes. These records are among the first things a buyer’s adviser will ask for.

Combustible cladding remains a live issue, with state programmes and building audits following the cladding fires of the last decade, and with implications for insurance and finance as well as safety.

## Reporting, strata and leases

Mandatory climate-related financial reporting under the Australian sustainability reporting standards began for the largest entities from financial years starting 1 January 2025, with a second group from 1 July 2026 and a third from 1 July 2027. For property owners, this brings physical climate risk and transition plans into formal disclosure, as discussed in [Climate as Physical Risk](/insights/climate-as-physical-risk).

Strata ownership is common in Australian commercial property, especially small offices, medical suites and industrial units, with state rules on maintenance planning and funds; [Why Shared Buildings Defer](/insights/why-shared-buildings-defer) covers the dynamics. And make-good obligations at lease end are a standard feature of Australian leases, explored in [Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases). Adoption and variations are still settling, and this note is reviewed every six months.  In the register

Australian registers commonly carry essential safety measures and fire services, cladding identification, NABERS-relevant mechanical and controls items, and code-triggered upgrades as conditional allowances tied to major works.   Key signal

In Australia, slow and costly new supply raises the value of existing buildings while state-by-state code adoption, disclosure and fire safety regimes shape when their capital falls due.

## Questions

### Which Australian offices must disclose a NABERS Energy rating?

Under the Commercial Building Disclosure programme, most office spaces of 1,000 square metres or more must disclose a Building Energy Efficiency Certificate, including a NABERS Energy rating, when offered for sale or lease. Exemptions and details should be checked with the programme.

### Do existing Australian buildings have to comply with the latest NCC?

Generally not simply because a new edition is adopted. Requirements usually apply to new building work, and significant alterations can trigger upgrades to parts of an existing building depending on the state and the work.

papers.title: Britain: When the Energy Rating Becomes a Letting Rule
papers.question: How do minimum energy efficiency standards affect commercial property in England and Wales?
papers.answer: Under the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards, privately rented non-domestic property in England and Wales generally needs an EPC rating of at least E to be let unless an exemption applies. In June 2026 the government confirmed its intention that, from 2031, privately rented non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres should reach EPC B where cost-effective, subject to secondary legislation, which makes energy upgrades a central capital question for larger buildings.
papers.summary: In England and Wales, a building’s energy certificate decides whether it can lawfully be let. The bar for larger commercial buildings is set to rise sharply, and that turns an energy rating into a capital plan.
papers.limitations: A building-and-capital reading of one or more national regimes, current at the review date. Rules change and vary by state, city and lease; it is not legal advice and the governing instrument and qualified advisers should be consulted.

sections.heading: Why it is a capital plan

papers.contentMarkdown:
Britain has the oldest building stock of our three markets and some of the most direct links between a building’s technical performance and its ability to earn income. The clearest example is the energy rating. In England and Wales, a commercial building’s Energy Performance Certificate is not just a label. Below a threshold, it decides whether the building can lawfully be let.

This note reads the British setting for its capital consequences, focusing on England and Wales; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regimes. It is not legal advice.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026 against the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero interim response of 18 June 2026 and subsequent professional commentary. The EPC B expectation from 2031 for privately rented non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres, where cost-effective, depends on secondary legislation and a fuller government response still to come; penalties, exemptions, shell-and-core treatment and compliance windows remain open questions. Scotland and Northern Ireland operate separate regimes; in Scotland, non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres that are sold or let need an energy Action Plan under 2016 regulations. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a comparison of the regime before and after the June 2026 interim response, and CBRE’s August 2025 estimate of stock below EPC B.

## MEES today and in 2031

The Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards currently prevent landlords letting privately rented non-domestic property with an EPC rating below E, unless a valid exemption is registered. For years the market expected the bar to rise to B by 2030 for all commercial lettings, possibly with an interim step to C.

On 18 June 2026 the government published an [interim response](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/non-domestic-private-rented-sector-minimum-energy-efficiency-standards-epc-b-implementation/outcome/minimum-energy-efficiency-standards-mees-in-the-non-domestic-private-rented-sector-interim-response) setting a more targeted course. From 2031, privately rented non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres are expected to need EPC B where cost-effective. Smaller buildings stay at the E minimum for now. The interim C milestone was dropped. Secondary legislation and a fuller response are still to come, so the detail may change. In Scotland, MEES does not apply; instead, non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres that are sold or let need an Action Plan setting out energy and emissions improvements.

For larger British commercial buildings, the energy upgrade is no longer a sustainability option. It is the condition of continuing to let.

## The rule then and now

The June 2026 interim response changed the shape of the regime, not just its dates. The comparison below is the planning position at review; secondary legislation is still needed to bring the 2031 standard into force. Non-domestic MEES in England and WalesBefore June 2026After the June 2026 interim responseCurrent minimumEPC E for new and existing lettingsEPC E, unchangedInterim milestoneEPC C proposed for 2027DroppedLong-term standardEPC B by 2030 proposed for all lettingsEPC B from 2031 for buildings over 1,000 m², where cost-effectiveBuildings under 1,000 m²Covered by the proposed trajectoryRemain at EPC ECost-effectiveness testSeven-year paybackSeven-year payback retainedPenaltiesUp to £150,000 per breachUp to £150,000 per breach

RICS and Jones Day summaries of the UK Government’s interim response, 18 June 2026. Scotland operates a separate regime.

The scale of exposure is large. CBRE estimated in August 2025 that 60 per cent of UK city-centre office stock by floor area had an EPC below B. Not all of it will be caught, because buildings under 1,000 m² and works that fail the payback test fall outside, but the larger, better-located buildings most likely to be institutionally owned are exactly the ones the 2031 standard targets.

## Why it is a capital plan

Moving a building from D or C to B is rarely one project. It typically involves some combination of heating and cooling plant replacement, often electrification; controls and metering; lighting; fabric improvements to roofs, walls and glazing; and sometimes on-site generation. These works interact, and their order matters. A building whose gas boilers have ten years of physical life may need them replaced well before then to meet the standard.

This is [economic obsolescence](/insights/three-kinds-of-obsolescence) in its clearest form. Plant that works perfectly can become the reason a building cannot be let. Many investors had already adopted B as an informal target for major refurbishments while waiting for the rules, and the 2026 response makes that approach more concrete for larger assets.

## A worked pathway

Consider a 1990s multi-let office of 4,000 square metres with gas boilers, electric chillers, a proprietary building management system and a rated EPC of D. A credible pathway to B typically runs in this order. First, controls and metering, so the building can be operated and measured properly; this is cheap and often improves the rating on its own. Second, lighting, where any remaining fluorescent or early LED can be replaced with controlled LED. Third, heating plant: boilers replaced with heat pumps at the end of their life or earlier, with the switchboard and supply checked for the added load. Fourth, fabric: roof insulation, glazing and air-tightness, usually the most expensive and most disruptive step, sometimes avoidable if the first three deliver the rating.

The 2031 date makes the order matter. Plant that falls due in 2028 should be replaced with the standard in view, not like for like. A refurbishment planned for 2029 should carry the rating as an objective. Lease events, breaks and renewals set when access and recovery are possible. The register, read against the leases, shows where the pathway fits.

## What stays uncertain

Three things could change the pathway. The final legislation may set compliance windows and milestones that differ from the interim response. The 1,000 square metre threshold may move or be measured in ways that catch or release particular buildings. And the reform of EPC methodology itself, with new-style certificates and the non-domestic carbon metric retained, could shift ratings without any change to the building. Owners planning now should design for B as a working target and keep the register flexible on timing.

## Safety, materials and heritage

The [Building Safety Act 2022](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-building-safety-act) created a stricter regime for higher-risk residential buildings, generally those at least 18 metres or seven storeys with two or more residential units. Mixed-use buildings with residential above commercial can fall within it, which matters for owners of town-centre and conversion assets.

Britain also has era-specific materials issues, including reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete in some roofs and floors from the 1950s to the 1990s, discussed in [What Age Conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals). And a large share of older commercial stock is listed or in conservation areas, where listed building consent shapes what can be done to meet energy and safety expectations.

## Leases and lease end

British commercial leases often place repairing obligations on tenants, through full repairing and insuring leases for single-let buildings and service charges in multi-let ones. At lease end, dilapidations claims address the building’s condition against the lease. These structures change who carries which capital lines and when, as [Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases) sets out, and they can interact awkwardly with energy upgrades that benefit the landlord’s ability to re-let. Threshold, date, exemptions and the EPC methodology itself could all still move; this note is reviewed every six months and revised when the rules settle.  In the register

British registers for larger let buildings increasingly carry an EPC pathway as a sequence of mechanical, controls, lighting and fabric rows, with timing set by the letting standard as well as physical condition.   Key signal

For larger commercial buildings in England and Wales, the expected EPC B standard from 2031 turns energy performance into a sequenced capital plan that can override physical condition.

## Questions

### What EPC rating is needed to let commercial property in England and Wales?

Currently at least E, unless a valid exemption is registered. The government has said it intends to require EPC B from 2031 for privately rented non-domestic buildings over 1,000 square metres where cost-effective, subject to secondary legislation.

### Does the 2031 EPC B target apply to small commercial units?

According to the June 2026 interim response, privately rented non-domestic buildings below 1,000 square metres are expected to remain subject to the existing E minimum for now, with no set deadline for a higher standard.

papers.title: United States: City Performance Standards and the Reserve Study
papers.question: How do building performance standards and local rules affect commercial building capital planning in the United States?
papers.answer: The United States has no single national building regime; codes, energy benchmarking and building performance standards are adopted locally. Cities such as New York, through Local Law 97, now set emissions limits for large existing buildings that tighten over time, while lender-driven property condition assessments, net leases and post-Surfside reserve and inspection rules in some states shape when and by whom capital is spent.
papers.summary: In the United States, building rules are made city by city and state by state. A growing number of cities now cap what existing buildings may emit, and that turns plant replacement into compliance.
papers.limitations: A building-and-capital reading of one or more national regimes, current at the review date. Rules change and vary by state, city and lease; it is not legal advice and the governing instrument and qualified advisers should be consulted.

sections.heading: Reading a building against a performance standard

papers.contentMarkdown:
In Australia and Britain, the building rules that matter most are set nationally or by large states. In the United States they are set by thousands of jurisdictions. Model codes are adopted and amended locally. Energy policy for existing buildings is driven largely by cities and a handful of states. The result is a patchwork, and capital planning has to start with the address.

This note reads the American setting for its capital consequences. It is not legal advice.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Local Law 97 applies to most New York City buildings over 25,000 square feet, with emissions limits from 2024 and materially stricter limits from 2030; Urban Green Council’s analysis of 2024 benchmarking data found that 43 per cent of covered buildings already meet the 2030 limits; the penalty is 268 dollars per tonne above the limit. Washington DC’s mayor proposed pausing that city’s standard in 2025. Florida’s milestone inspection and structural integrity reserve study requirements apply to condominium and cooperative buildings of three or more habitable storeys. Other city and state standards cited are current as understood at the review date and vary in metric and timetable. Deepened 4 November 2026 with Local Law 97 first-year compliance data and a summary of other performance standards.

## Cities cap existing buildings

Building performance standards limit the energy use or emissions of existing buildings, not just new ones. New York City’s [Local Law 97](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll97-greenhouse-gas-emissions-reductions.page) is the best known. It applies to most buildings over 25,000 square feet, set its first limits from 2024 and tightens them significantly from 2030, with a penalty of 268 dollars per tonne of emissions above the limit. Urban Green Council’s analysis of 2024 benchmarking data found that only 43 per cent of covered buildings already meet the 2030 limits.

Other cities and several states have adopted their own standards, including Boston, Washington DC, Denver, Colorado, Maryland and Washington State, each with its own metrics and timetables. Several have faced delays, and in 2025 Washington DC’s mayor proposed pausing implementation there. Many more cities require annual energy benchmarking and publish the results.

Where a performance standard applies, the replacement of a gas boiler is no longer just a maintenance decision. It is a compliance strategy with a penalty attached to getting it wrong.

## What the first year showed

New York’s Local Law 97 reached its first compliance deadline in 2025, and the results are the first real evidence of how owners respond to a performance standard with penalties attached. Of 29,031 buildings required to report, about 7 per cent did not file. Of those that did, about 95 per cent met their emissions limits. Penalties collected so far are modest, around $270,000 from roughly fifteen buildings, against a statutory rate of $268 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent over the limit.

The first period was always going to be the easy one; the limits tighten sharply from 2030. What the first year shows is that most owners can meet a lenient limit with operational changes and modest works, and that the capital question arrives at the second step, when plant replacement and electrification become hard to avoid. Selected building performance standards in force or adoptedJurisdictionCoversKey point at reviewNew York City (LL97)Buildings over 25,000 sq ftFirst period 2024 to 2029; tighter limits from 2030; $268 per tCO2e over the limitWashington State (CBPS)Tier 1 commercial over 220,000 sq ftFirst compliance deadline 1 June 2026Evanston and West HollywoodLocal building stockAdopted standards in 2025Benchmarking onlyMore than 35 jurisdictionsAnnual energy reporting; no performance cap

NYC Department of Buildings via Facilities Dive; Institute for Market Transformation. About fifteen state and local governments had adopted performance standards by 2025.

## Reading a building against a performance standard

A performance standard converts a building’s energy use into an emissions figure using factors for electricity, gas and steam, and compares it with a limit set by occupancy type and floor area. The reading an owner needs is therefore in four steps. Benchmark the current position from the energy data most cities already require. Model the limits for each compliance period against that position. Identify which measures close the gap, in order of cost and disruption: controls and operations, lighting, heating plant and electrification, envelope. And time those measures against plant life and lease events so that compliance is achieved by replacement at the right moment rather than by premature spend or penalty.

In the register, the same works appear as ordinary plant, controls and fabric rows. What changes is their timing field, which is set by the compliance period as well as by condition, and their cost basis, which records the penalty exposure that makes the timing matter.

## The condition assessment culture

American commercial real estate has a well-established due diligence product in the property condition assessment, commonly performed to the ASTM E2018 standard and often required by lenders. It typically identifies immediate costs and projects replacement reserves over a term, frequently around ten to twelve years, alongside a separate Phase I environmental site assessment. [Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) compares it with Australian and British practice.

Lender-driven assessments are efficient and consistent, but they are often designed around a loan rather than an owner’s strategy. A capital plan built for decisions asks different questions of the same building.

## Net leases and reserves

Net leases are common, especially triple-net structures in single-tenant retail, industrial and some office assets, where tenants carry taxes, insurance and many operating costs. Even so, structural and major replacement items often remain with owners, and the line between repair and capital varies by lease.

In shared residential and mixed-use buildings, reserve studies estimate future capital needs. After the 2021 collapse at Surfside, Florida introduced mandatory milestone structural inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominium buildings of three or more habitable storeys, a reminder that underfunded shared buildings can become a safety issue, as discussed in [Why Shared Buildings Defer](/insights/why-shared-buildings-defer).

## Insurance and physical risk

The United States is where insurance retreat from physical risk is most visible, with insurers withdrawing from or repricing exposed regions. For owners, building-level resilience, plant location, roof systems, flood protection, increasingly shows up in insurance terms. [Climate as Physical Risk](/insights/climate-as-physical-risk) develops this. Local standards change with local politics and litigation, and this note is reviewed every six months.  In the register

American registers in performance-standard cities carry plant and controls rows timed against compliance periods, with penalty exposure recorded in the cost basis rather than merged into the works cost.   Key signal

In US cities with building performance standards, emissions limits that tighten over time turn plant replacement and controls upgrades into compliance timing decisions.

## Questions

### Which buildings does New York City’s Local Law 97 cover?

Most buildings over 25,000 square feet, with emissions limits that began in 2024 and become significantly stricter from 2030. Exemptions and alternative pathways apply to some building types.

### What is a property condition assessment?

A due diligence report on a commercial property’s physical condition, commonly prepared to the ASTM E2018 standard, typically identifying immediate repair costs and projecting replacement reserves over a term, often for a lender.

papers.title: Same Thing, Different Name
papers.question: What are the equivalent terms for building due diligence, lease obligations and capital funds in Australia, Britain and the United States?
papers.answer: The same concepts carry different names across the three markets: technical due diligence, building survey and property condition assessment; make good, dilapidations and restoration obligations; outgoings, service charges and common area maintenance; sinking funds, reserve funds and reserve studies; NABERS, EPCs and ENERGY STAR. Knowing the equivalents avoids comparing different things as if they were the same.
papers.summary: Australia, Britain and the United States describe building capital with different words for the same ideas. A short field guide for owners and investors working across all three.

sections.heading: Areas, costs and the standards behind them

papers.contentMarkdown:
Building physics is universal. A roof leaks in Melbourne, Manchester and Minneapolis for the same reasons. The language around it is not. Owners and investors who work across Australia, Britain and the United States often find that the same idea has three names, and that similar names can mean slightly different things.

This field guide sets out the equivalents that matter most for building capital. They are close equivalents, not identical: scope and legal effect differ.  Research note

Terms are given as commonly used in professional practice in each market at the review date. Legal definitions, measurement standards and professional titles vary within countries as well as between them; where a term has legal effect, the governing instrument and local advice decide. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of measurement and cost terms across the three markets.

## Due diligence and surveys
- Technical due diligence (Australia, also used in Britain) · building survey or building condition survey (Britain) · property condition assessment, often to ASTM E2018 (United States). Each assesses physical condition and likely capital needs before a transaction.
- Building consultant or building surveyor in the consultancy sense (Australia) · chartered building surveyor (Britain) · property condition assessor or consultant (United States). In Australia, a registered building surveyor is also the statutory role that issues building permits, which is a different job.
- Environmental site assessment, contamination report (Australia) · environmental report (Britain) · Phase I environmental site assessment, often to ASTM E1527 (United States).

[Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) compares how these are scoped.

## Leases and recoveries
- Make good (Australia) · dilapidations, reinstatement and yielding up (Britain) · surrender condition or restoration obligations (United States). What a tenant must do to the premises at lease end.
- Outgoings (Australia) · service charge (Britain, multi-let) · common area maintenance, operating expenses and pass-throughs (United States).
- Gross and net leases (Australia) · full repairing and insuring lease (Britain) · gross, modified gross and triple-net leases (United States).

[Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases) reads what these structures mean for capital.

## Areas, costs and the standards behind them

Some of the most expensive mistranslations are about area and cost, because a figure can be correct and still not mean what the reader assumes. Measurement and cost terms across the three marketsConceptAustraliaUnited KingdomUnited StatesLettable office areaNet lettable area (PCA method of measurement)Net internal area, or IPMS under RICS standardsRentable area under BOMA standardsRecoverable running costsOutgoingsService chargeOperating expenses, common area maintenanceRestoring premises at lease endMake goodDilapidations, reinstatement, yielding upRestoration, surrender conditionShared-building reserveSinking fund or capital works fundReserve or sinking fund (often voluntary)Reserve fund, set by a reserve studyPre-purchase building reportTechnical due diligenceBuilding survey or technical due diligenceProperty condition assessment

Moyne Ross summary. Standards change; confirm which edition a figure was measured or prepared under.

The habit that prevents most errors is the first one this paper names: ask what the number includes, and under which standard it was produced.

## Shared buildings and funds
- Strata title, owners corporation or body corporate (Australia) · leasehold flats with a freeholder or residents’ management company, or commonhold (Britain) · condominium and homeowners association (United States).
- Sinking fund, capital works fund or maintenance fund (Australia) · reserve or sinking fund within the service charge (Britain) · reserve fund, with a reserve study to set it (United States).

## Three habits that prevent mistranslation

First, ask what the number includes. A capital figure may or may not include design fees, contingency, preliminaries, tax and access costs, and the conventions differ by market. Second, ask what the area is. Net lettable area, net internal area and rentable square feet are measured differently and can differ by ten per cent or more for the same floor. Third, ask what the horizon is. A ten-year forecast, a twelve-year reserve table and a schedule of immediate works are not the same instrument, and only one of them is comparable with another building’s ten-year forecast.

Moyne Ross keeps these on the cost basis of every line: currency, measurement basis, inclusions and exclusions, base date. It is unglamorous, and it is what makes cross-border comparison honest.

## Performance and measurement
- NABERS ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure (Australia) · Energy Performance Certificates and Display Energy Certificates (Britain) · ENERGY STAR scores and city benchmarking (United States).
- Net lettable area (Australia) · net internal area (Britain) · rentable and usable square feet, often to BOMA standards (United States). Floor area definitions differ, so capital per square metre or square foot is only comparable once the basis is aligned.
- Essential safety measures and annual fire safety statements (Australian states) · fire risk assessment under fire safety legislation (Britain) · fire inspections and code compliance under local adoption of model codes (United States).   In the register

Moyne Ross registers use one structure across markets, structure, services and space with the same six fields, while the cost basis records currency, measurement basis and local terminology so lines are not blended across jurisdictions.   Key signal

Equivalent terms across Australia, Britain and the United States are close but not identical, so capital figures should only be compared once scope, measurement and currency are aligned.

- [E2018 revision](https://newsroom.astm.org/e2018-revision), ASTM International. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is make good the same as dilapidations?

They address the same idea, a tenant’s obligations about the premises’ condition at lease end, but the legal framework, process and typical outcomes differ between Australia and Britain. Lease terms and local advice govern the detail.

### Can capital costs per square metre be compared across countries?

Only with care. Floor area definitions, currency, tax treatment and what is included in each cost can all differ, so the basis needs aligning before comparison.

papers.title: Due Diligence Across Three Markets
papers.question: How does technical due diligence on commercial buildings differ between Australia, Britain and the United States?
papers.answer: All three markets assess physical condition and likely capital needs before a transaction, but practice differs: Australian technical due diligence typically covers condition, statutory compliance and a capital forecast; British building surveys and technical due diligence add a strong focus on lease obligations, deleterious materials and statutory matters; and US property condition assessments, often lender-led and prepared to ASTM E2018, emphasise immediate costs and replacement reserves over a set term.
papers.summary: Technical due diligence, the building survey and the property condition assessment answer similar questions in different ways. Knowing the differences helps investors read what each actually tells them.
