- [The MR Index: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/mr-index), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How is a Capital Strategy different from a building condition report?

A condition report describes the state of the building. A Capital Strategy turns that and other evidence into a ten-year view of actions, costs, timing, impact and confidence, with an overall position and decisions for the owner.

### What horizons does a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy use?

Within one year, years two to five, and years six to ten, across a ten-year view.

papers.title: Hearing the Building as It Is
papers.question: Why should an initial building assessment be made before considering the owner’s plans?
papers.answer: An initial read made on the building’s current, business-as-usual terms captures what the evidence says before intentions shape it. Owner plans, tenant expectations and transaction goals can bias which issues are noticed and how they are weighed, and the first read often changes what the brief should be. Intentions are then overlaid in a second stage.
papers.summary: The first read of a building should listen to the building, not to the plans for it. Briefing too much too early bends the evidence toward the answer someone already wants.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: What the first read holds back

papers.contentMarkdown:
Most building advice begins with a brief. The owner explains the plan: a refurbishment, a sale, a new tenant, a five-year hold. The adviser then reads the building in light of it.

That sounds efficient, and for some questions it is. But for the first read of a building’s capital position, we think it is the wrong order.  Research note

This paper states a Moyne Ross method principle: the first read is made on the building’s current, business-as-usual terms, and the owner’s intentions are applied afterwards. The observations about attention and briefing are general and drawn from practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of what the first read records and what it holds back.

## Briefs bend evidence

A brief tells the reader what matters before the reader has looked. An owner planning a sale may unconsciously steer attention away from issues a buyer will find. An owner planning a refurbishment may lead the adviser to discount systems the refurbishment would replace, even if the refurbishment never happens. A tenant’s fit-out plan may focus attention on one floor while the roof above it is the real story.

None of this requires bad faith. It is how attention works. Knowing the answer someone wants changes which questions get asked.

The first read should be the building speaking for itself. Everything else can be layered on once that voice has been heard.

## Business as usual

The Moyne Ross first read assumes the building continues in its current use, on its current terms. What is its condition? What will it need over ten years if nothing about its use changes? What is uncertain? This business-as-usual baseline is the reference against which every later plan can be measured.

It is built from the address and the evidence available, often [public evidence](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) at first, read with the discipline described in [Documented, Observed, Inferred](/insights/documented-observed-inferred). Its uncertainties are visible, and its conclusions are a starting point rather than a verdict.

## What the first read contains

A first read sets out the building’s profile as established from evidence: use, age and how it was dated, construction, size and the main systems. It sets out a ten-year register on business-as-usual terms, with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence on every line. It carries an overall capital position and MR Index band. And it states plainly what is uncertain and what would resolve it.

It does not assume a refurbishment, a sale or a new tenant. Those come next, and they are easier to reason about because the baseline is already there.

## What the first read holds back

The discipline of the first read is as much about what it leaves out as what it contains. The first read and what follows itThe first read recordsHeld back until the owner is heardThe building’s profile, dated from evidenceThe owner’s plans for use, tenancy and timingEvery element, graded documented, observed or inferredBudgets and preferred spending patternsA business-as-usual register: what the building needs in its current useOptions for refurbishment, repositioning or saleThe uncertainties and what would resolve themWhich uncertainties the owner wants resolved first

Moyne Ross practice.

Holding the second column back is not indifference to the owner. It is what makes the first column trustworthy: a baseline written before anyone said what they hoped it would show.

## The read changes the brief

One of the most useful things a first read does is change the questions. An owner who expected to discuss tenancy refresh learns that the facade and fire services are the dominant issue. An owner planning to sell learns that a cheap investigation now could remove the largest uncertainty a buyer would price. An owner thinking about electrification learns that the switchboard gates everything.

If the brief had come first, those findings might have been framed as peripheral. Coming first, the read sets the agenda for the conversation.

## Then the owner

Hearing the building as it is does not mean ignoring the owner. It means sequencing. Once the baseline exists, the owner’s plans, records, knowledge and constraints are brought to bear, line by line, on the decisions it contains. That second movement is described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).

The baseline stays on the record. It is what lets an owner see exactly what their plans change, and what they do not.  In the register

The first read produces a business-as-usual register: condition, action, timing and confidence on the building’s current terms, which later strategies are measured against.   Key signal

A first read made on the building’s own terms, before the owner’s plans are applied, avoids bending evidence and often changes what the brief should be.

## Questions

### Does a first read ignore what the owner knows?

No. It sets a baseline from the evidence before plans are applied. The owner’s records and knowledge can still improve that evidence, and their intentions are applied in the next stage.

### Why is a business-as-usual baseline useful?

It shows what the building needs if its use does not change, so the effect of any plan, refurbishment, sale or new tenant, can be measured against it clearly.

papers.title: Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear
papers.question: How do an owner’s plans change a building’s capital strategy?
papers.answer: Once a baseline capital view exists, the owner’s intentions, such as hold period, refurbishment plans, tenant arrangements, sale timing and appetite for risk, change the right action and timing on many lines without changing the building’s condition. Applying them line by line, with the owner’s records and knowledge, turns a capital view into a strategy the owner can act on.
papers.summary: The building does not change when its owner’s plans do. The strategy does. Bringing intentions to the register is where a capital view becomes a direction to act on.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: The same building under three intentions

papers.contentMarkdown:
A first read tells an owner what the building will ask of them on its current terms. It does not tell them what to do. That depends on what they want from the building, and two owners of the same building can rightly reach very different answers.

This is the second movement of a Capital Strategy: bringing the owner’s intentions, records and knowledge to bear on the decisions the first read raises.  Research note

This paper describes the second movement of a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy. How intentions are applied in any engagement depends on the owner, the building and the agreed scope. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a grid of one register read under three intentions.

## Intentions change actions, not condition

An owner planning a deep refurbishment in three years should not replace a lobby finish now. An owner selling next year may resolve a large uncertainty before marketing. An owner holding for twenty years may bring a roof forward to install solar. A tenant committing to a long lease may change which systems matter and who pays for them. In each case the building’s condition is unchanged. The right action and timing are not.

This is why the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) reference says the same score can lead to different decisions. The capital position is a fact about the building. The strategy is a fact about the building and its owner together.

## Records sharpen the read

Owners also bring evidence. Maintenance logs, compliance records, drawings, recent works, warranties, surveys and tenant information can confirm, narrow or overturn lines from the first read. An inferred plant age becomes documented. A wide range for a facade becomes a narrow one after an inspection report is supplied. A suspected issue is closed.

The first read listens to the building. The second listens to the owner. A good strategy needs both voices, in that order.

## Three intentions, one building

Take a 1990s office with a mid-decade chiller replacement, a lobby in need of refresh and an energy rating below where the market is heading. An owner selling in eighteen months resolves the largest uncertainty, documents the plant, and leaves the replacement to the buyer with clear information. An owner holding for ten years replaces the chiller with electrified plant at the right moment, sequences the switchboard first and times the lobby with a lease event. An owner repositioning for a different tenant market brings plant, lobby and energy works together into one refurbishment.

The building is identical in all three. The register lines are the same. The actions and timing differ, and each strategy can be read against the same baseline.

## The same building under three intentions

The worked example in this paper is clearest as a grid: the same register lines, read under three different plans. One 1990s office, three intentionsRegister lineHold for ten yearsRefurbish in three yearsSell within eighteen monthsChiller replacement, mid-decadePlan and fund on its own clockFold into the refurbishment scopeDisclose with its evidence; consider early works only if they protect the priceLobby refreshDo it when the leasing case supports itDefer: the refurbishment replaces itA modest refresh may help presentationEnergy rating below the marketImprove controls and plant over the holdDesign the refurbishment to the target ratingExplain the pathway and its cost to buyersLow-confidence facade allowanceInvestigate early and refineInvestigate as part of designInvestigate before marketing so the buyer does not

Moyne Ross illustration. The condition of each line is the same in every column; only the action and timing change.

## Working through the decisions

Bringing intentions to bear means working through the register with the owner: which lines matter most to their plans, which decisions are urgent, which can wait, which depend on each other, and which need investigation before anyone can decide. [A Building Is Forty Decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) describes the shape of that work.

The outcome is a direction the owner can act on, with the reasoning visible: what will be done, when, why, and what remains open.

## Keeping the baseline

The baseline from the first read stays on the record beside the tailored strategy. That matters for two reasons. It shows the owner exactly what their plans change. And if the plans change, as they often do, the strategy can be re-tailored from the same baseline rather than rebuilt.

It also guards against a subtle risk: that a strategy shaped around an intention drops issues the intention made inconvenient. With the baseline visible, nothing disappears without a reason.  In the register

Tailoring changes the action and timing fields on affected rows and records the owner’s reason in the cost basis, while the business-as-usual baseline remains available for comparison.   Key signal

Owner intentions change the right action and timing on many lines without changing the building, so a strategy applies them to a stable baseline rather than replacing it.

## Questions

### Can two owners of the same building have different capital strategies?

Yes. Hold period, refurbishment plans, tenancy, sale timing and risk appetite all change the best action and timing for many items, even though the building’s condition is the same.

### What owner records improve a capital strategy most?

Maintenance and works history, compliance records, drawings, recent surveys, warranties and lease and tenant information typically narrow uncertainty and confirm or correct the first read.

papers.title: The Living Record
papers.question: Why should a building’s capital strategy be maintained as a living record?
papers.answer: A capital strategy kept current, with each line updated as evidence arrives, works are done and plans change, becomes the building’s memory. It preserves knowledge across managers and owners, keeps decisions grounded in current evidence, supports sale and finance, and avoids the cost of rediscovering the building every few years.
papers.summary: A building outlives its reports, its managers and often its owners. A capital record that is kept current becomes the building’s memory, and memory is worth money.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.
papers.contentMarkdown:
Ask most owners for the history of their building and they will produce a folder, or several. Reports from different years, by different advisers, in different formats. Invoices for works. Certificates. Some drawings. A great deal of knowledge sits in the heads of a facility manager or a former owner, and leaves with them.

Buildings forget. Every few years someone has to rediscover them.  Research note

This paper describes how Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy as a versioned register in a private, invitation-only place for the owner. Retention and access arrangements are set out in the Moyne Ross terms and privacy policy. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of recurring regulatory evidence that refreshes a building record.

## Memory as an asset

A living record is a capital register that is kept current. When a survey arrives, the affected lines change. When works are done, they are recorded and the next cycle is set. When a plan changes, the strategy is re-tailored and the reason noted. Each version is kept, so the record shows how understanding of the building developed over time.

A building with a living record carries its knowledge with it. A building without one loses most of what anyone learned about it at every handover.

## Why it is worth keeping

The benefits compound. Decisions are made on current evidence rather than old reports. Uncertainty narrows over time instead of being re-estimated from scratch. Managers and advisers can change without the building losing its history. Lenders and insurers can be shown a credible picture. And at sale, as [What the Next Buyer Will Read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read) argues, the buyer verifies rather than discovers.

There is also a simpler benefit. Rediscovering a building every few years is expensive and slow. Updating a record is not.

## What keeps a record current

A record stays alive because the building keeps producing evidence. Much of it arrives on a regulatory calendar. Recurring evidence that refreshes a building’s recordEvidenceWhereHow oftenAnnual fire safety statementNew South WalesEvery yearEssential safety measures reportVictoriaEvery yearBuilding Energy Efficiency Certificate for offices of 1,000 m² and overAustraliaValid for up to 12 months, needed when space is sold or leasedFire risk assessmentEngland and WalesKept under regular review, and after significant changeEnergy benchmarking disclosureNew York City and other US jurisdictionsEvery yearFacade inspection for buildings over six storeysNew York CityEvery five years

State and city regulations as summarised at review; obligations depend on building type and size.

Each of these is a small update to the register if the record is kept, and a box of paper if it is not. The difference compounds: after a few cycles, a kept record knows the building better than any single report could.

## What a good record holds

A living record holds the current register with its reasoning; every previous version with what changed and why; completed works with their scope, date and evidence; investigations and their results; the decisions agreed with the owner; and the documents that support them, drawings, certificates, warranties, surveys. It is organised so that any line can be traced from today’s figure back to the evidence that produced it.

Kept this way, the record is useful to everyone who will ever have to make a decision about the building, which over its life is a long list.

## Versions and agreement

A living record needs discipline. Versions should be clear: what was known at each point and what changed. Anything shown together, a strategy, a report, a summary, should agree, which is why reports are best drawn from the register as views rather than written separately, as [The Register, Not the Report](/insights/the-register-not-the-report) explains. And updates should follow evidence, not convenience.

Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy in a private place for the owner, by invitation, where the current version, its history, the notes and what has been agreed sit together.

## Beyond the single owner

Over a long enough period, a building’s living record matters more than any single owner’s tenure. It is the baton described in [Patient Capital and the Long Building](/insights/patient-capital-and-the-long-building): the most useful thing one owner can pass to the next. It is also, in aggregate, how a practice learns. Every record that improves over time teaches something about how buildings of that kind actually behave.  In the register

A living register keeps every version, records completed works and resolved uncertainties on their rows, and carries the reasons for each change.   Key signal

A capital record kept current becomes the building’s memory, preserving knowledge across managers and owners and turning sale and finance into verification rather than discovery.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Commercial Building Disclosure: is your building disclosure affected?](https://www.cbd.gov.au/node/27), Australian Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How often should a building capital plan be updated?

Whenever material evidence arrives, works are completed or plans change, with a periodic review even when nothing obvious has changed. The aim is that the record always reflects current knowledge.

### What should a living building record contain?

The current capital register with its reasoning, a version history, completed works, resolved and open uncertainties, supporting documents and the decisions agreed with the owner.

papers.title: A Register Read End to End
papers.question: How should an owner or investor read a building capital register?
papers.answer: Start with the capital position and its split across one year, two to five years and six to ten years, then the MR Index band, then where the capital concentrates by system. Next look for gating items and low-confidence lines, then read the near-term rows and their reasons, and finally the cost basis on the largest lines. That order moves from the shape of the decade to the evidence behind it.
papers.summary: A Capital Register can hold forty or more lines. Read in the right order, it tells a clear story in minutes. A practical guide for owners and investors.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: Find the concentration and the gates
One row, read field by field
Read confidence and the near term
Five questions to ask any register

papers.contentMarkdown:
A full Capital Register is dense. Every element of structure, services and space, each with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence. Read top to bottom, it can feel like an inventory. Read in the right order, it tells a story quickly.

This guide sets out the order we recommend. The [Capital Register reference](/methodology/capital-register) shows a real row from a 1970s distribution warehouse, which is a useful companion.  Research note

The worked row referred to is published in full on the Moyne Ross Capital Register methodology reference. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a field-by-field reading of the register row in the methodology reference.

## Start with the shape

Begin with the capital position: the ten-year total and its split across the first year, years two to five and years six to ten. The split says more than the total. A front-loaded programme means decisions now. A mid-decade bulge means planning time. A back-loaded programme means a building in a quiet phase that will not stay quiet.

Then read the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) band. It summarises how much of the building needs attention, how serious and how soon, in one position from MR 1 to MR 5. It is not a verdict on the building. It tells you what kind of decade to expect.

## Find the concentration and the gates

Next, see where the capital concentrates. Is it spread across many systems, or dominated by one, a roof, a facade, central plant? Concentration tells you where attention and investigation will pay off most.

Then look for gating items: single findings that could reshape the programme if confirmed. A structural question, a concealed facade issue, a hazardous material in the way of planned works. These usually sit as investigation items with conditional allowances, as described in [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know).

Read the shape before the rows. Most of what matters is visible in the split, the band, the concentration and the gates.

## One row, read field by field

The methodology reference shows a single row from an issued strategy: metal deck roofing across the older bays of a 1970s distribution warehouse. Reading it field by field shows what each part is for. Reading a register rowFieldWhat the row saysThe question it answersConditionSevere oxidation and coating breakdown across the older bays; water ingress risk to stock belowWhat state is it in, and what is the consequence if nothing is done?ActionStaged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, with a roofing consultant’s inspection firstWhat should be done, and in what order?Cost basisPlanning range $1.8 million to $3.4 million for 20,000 to 25,000 m², excluding GST, Q3 2026; purlins excludedHow was the figure built, and what does it leave out?Impact4, EssentialHow much does this matter to the building?ConfidenceMediumHow firm is the evidence?Timing$35,000 in year one; $2.6 million in years two to five; nothing in years six to tenWhen does the money fall?Item total$2.64 millionWhat does it add to the decade?

Moyne Ross Capital Register methodology reference.

Read together, the fields say something no single one does. The roof matters a great deal, but the money is not urgent: the first year buys an inspection, and the works follow once their scope is known. The exclusion of purlins is the line a buyer’s adviser would circle first.

## Read confidence and the near term

Filter for low-confidence lines. They show where the evidence is thin and where the capital position could move. Then read every first-year line and ask the question from [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): why must this happen within twelve months? A good register answers it on each row.

On the warehouse example in the reference, the roof row shows the pattern clearly: strong evidence from aerial imagery, a large exposure, a modest first-year amount for a roofing consultant’s inspection, and the main re-sheeting in years two to five.

## Five questions to ask any register
- Why must each first-year item happen within twelve months?
- Which single findings could reshape the programme, and what would it cost to resolve them?
- Where does the capital concentrate, and is that concentration supported by strong evidence?
- Which lines rest on inference, and does their confidence say so?
- Which lines depend on each other, and is the sequence right?

A register that answers these well is one an owner can act on. One that cannot is one to question.

## Finish with the cost basis

Finally, read the cost basis on the largest lines. How was each figure built? What scope, quantity and assumptions does it rest on? What is included and excluded? How firm is it? This is where you can challenge a number intelligently, and where an owner’s own knowledge, a recent quote, a known constraint, can sharpen it.

Read this way, a register of forty lines becomes a short list of questions worth asking. That list is usually the start of the conversation described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).  In the register

The reading order follows the register’s own structure: capital position by horizon, MR Index band, concentration by system, gating and low-confidence rows, first-year rows, then the cost basis on the largest lines.   Key signal

Reading a register from its shape to its evidence, split, band, concentration, gates, confidence, near term, cost basis, turns a dense schedule into a short list of decisions.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [The Capital Register: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/capital-register), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What is the most important number in a capital register?

Usually not the total, but how it splits across the near term, middle years and later years, together with where it concentrates. Those show what kind of decisions the building will demand and when.

### How can an owner challenge a figure in a capital register?

By reading its cost basis: the scope, quantity, assumptions, inclusions, exclusions and confidence behind it, and testing them against the owner’s own knowledge, quotes or records.

papers.title: Hold, Improve, Reposition or Exit
papers.question: How does a building’s capital strategy inform whether to hold, improve, reposition or sell it?
papers.answer: The four basic paths for a building, holding it largely as is, improving it within its current use, repositioning it for a different market or use, or exiting, each imply a different capital programme and risk. A Capital Strategy makes each option legible by showing what the building needs regardless, what each path adds or avoids, and what remains uncertain, so the owner can compare them on evidence.
papers.summary: Every capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. The register does not make the choice. It makes each option legible.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: When the building is not the answer
A public test of refurbish against rebuild

papers.contentMarkdown:
However detailed the analysis, a capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. Broadly there are four paths. Hold it largely as it is and maintain it well. Improve it within its current use. Reposition it, for a different tenant market or a different use. Or exit.

The register does not choose between them. What it can do is make each option legible, so the choice rests on evidence rather than instinct.  Research note

The four-path framing is a general asset strategy convention. The redevelopment example draws on the published CMP 007 asset study. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the Marks & Spencer Marble Arch case as a public test of refurbishment against redevelopment.

## What the building needs regardless

Every option starts from the same base: what the building needs whatever path is chosen. Safety, current compliance obligations, items failing or causing damage. These are the floor. Even an owner who intends to sell must usually deal with some of them, or price them into the sale.

Above the floor, the paths diverge.

## Four paths, four programmes

Holding as is means following the business-as-usual register: renew systems as they come due, defer consciously where sensible, keep the building competitive within its current market. Improving means adding works that raise performance within the current use: better controls, an energy upgrade, a lobby, end-of-trip facilities. Repositioning means accepting a larger programme to reach a different market or use, a deeper refurbishment, a conversion, a change of tenant type. Exiting means deciding what to do before sale, which uncertainties to resolve and which works to leave to the buyer.

The same register supports all four paths. What changes is which lines are taken up, when, and what is added.

Each path also carries different risk. Holding exposes the owner to obsolescence. Improving exposes them to whether the market rewards the improvement. Repositioning exposes them to construction, approvals and leasing risk. Exiting exposes them to what [the next buyer will read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read).

## A simple comparison table

For each path, set out four figures from the register: the base programme every path must fund; the additional works the path implies; the conditional allowances still open; and the timing against leases. Add a short note on the main risk each path carries. On one page, an owner can see the capital implication of each option on the same evidence, which is usually enough to narrow the choice to one or two before any detailed feasibility work begins.

## When the building is not the answer

Sometimes the evidence points beyond all four. When the capital needed to keep a building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the land supports something else, redevelopment becomes the rational path, as [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) describes. A good capital strategy says so plainly when it is true.

## A public test of refurbish against rebuild

The most visible recent test of this decision is Marks & Spencer’s store at Marble Arch on London’s Oxford Street. The retailer applied in 2021 to demolish the 1930s building and replace it with a new nine-storey building of shops and offices, arguing that the existing store could not be adapted. Westminster approved the scheme, but the government called it in, and in July 2023 the then Secretary of State refused it, citing among other things whether refurbishment had been properly explored and the embodied carbon of demolition.

In March 2024 the High Court quashed that refusal, finding that national planning policy had been misapplied. In December 2024 the decision was remade and permission granted. The case did not settle the general question of retrofit against rebuild, but it made one thing plain: the case for redevelopment now has to be argued from evidence about the existing building, including what refurbishment could achieve and at what carbon and capital cost. The Marble Arch timelineDateEvent2021Application to demolish and rebuild; approved by Westminster City CouncilJune 2022Called in by the Secretary of StateJuly 2023Permission refused1 March 2024High Court quashes the refusal5 December 2024Permission granted on redetermination

Mishcon de Reya; Dezeen; CIBSE Journal.

For an owner weighing the four paths, the lesson is that exit by redevelopment is no longer a quiet choice in many cities. The register that shows what the existing building needs, and what it could become, is the evidence such a decision will be asked for.

## Choosing on evidence

Owners compare paths through the register: the base they must fund anyway, the additional programme each path implies, the uncertainty that remains, and the timing against leases and plans. The comparison does not need to be elaborate to be useful. What matters is that each option is costed and timed on the same evidence.

This is also where the ideas in Capital Made Physical become practical. Whether a building should be held, improved, repositioned or sold depends in part on the forces in [Part I](/insights/the-movement-to-real) and the futures in Part II. The register brings those general arguments down to one building’s options.  In the register

Options are compared on one register: the base rows every path must fund, the additional rows each path adds, and the conditional allowances that remain open under each.   Key signal

Hold, improve, reposition and exit each imply a different capital programme and risk, and a register makes them comparable on the same evidence.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [RICS Valuation, Global Standards (Red Book)](https://www.rics.org/profession-standards/rics-standards-and-guidance/sector-standards/valuation-standards/red-book), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Government grants planning permission for the redevelopment of Marks & Spencer’s flagship store on Oxford Street](https://www.mishcon.com/news/government-grants-planning-permission-for-the-redevelopment-of-marks-and-spencers-flagship-store-on-oxford-street?publication=7403), Mishcon de Reya. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Marks & Spencer gets go-ahead for Oxford Street flagship store demolition](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/12/05/marks-spencer-approval-flagship-store-demolition/), Dezeen. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [High Court overturns Gove’s M&S decision](https://www.cibsejournal.com/news/high-court-overturns-goves-ms-decision/), CIBSE Journal. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What capital works must be done even if a building is being sold?

Typically safety issues, current compliance obligations and failing elements causing damage, or else they are priced into the sale. Discretionary improvements can usually be left to the buyer.

### When does redevelopment make more sense than refurbishment?

Often when the capital needed to keep the existing building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the site supports a more valuable use or form. The decision depends on the building, the land and approvals.

papers.title: Physical Assets Under Management
papers.question: What would continuous, ongoing management of a building’s capital position look like?
papers.answer: Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced.
papers.summary: The investment world manages financial assets continuously. Buildings are mostly advised on in episodes. The argument of this publication ends with the case for treating physical assets the way capital treats money.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: An established discipline, applied to buildings

papers.contentMarkdown:
A financial portfolio is never left alone for five years. It is monitored, rebalanced and reported on continuously. Decisions are made as information arrives. The manager is judged by outcomes over time.

Buildings, which are often a large part of those same portfolios, are usually treated differently. Advice arrives in episodes: a due diligence report at purchase, a condition survey at refinancing, a vendor report at sale. Between episodes, the building’s capital position drifts, and nobody is watching it as a whole.  Research note

This closing thesis describes a direction for building advice rather than a service offering. The comparison with continuing service arrangements for lifts and major plant refers to common industry practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the ISO 55000 asset management series and a comparison of episodic and continuous advice.

## Episodes and drift

Episodic advice made sense when assessing a building was slow and expensive, and when reports were the only practical output. Each engagement started from scratch, produced a document and ended. The knowledge it created aged on a shelf.

The cost of that model is drift. Systems age past their planned replacement. Uncertainties remain unresolved. Regulations change. Plans change. By the next episode, much of the previous advice is out of date and the building has to be rediscovered, which is the problem [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record) addresses.

## A different shape of advice

The tools now exist to change that shape. A building can be read quickly from evidence, held as a structured register, and kept current as things change. The expensive part of the old model, rediscovering the building, shrinks. What remains, and grows in importance, is judgement: deciding which of the building’s [forty decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) to make now, which to defer, which to reopen.

When reading a building becomes fast, the value moves to staying with it.

Other industries already work this way with physical equipment. Lifts, escalators and major plant are commonly maintained under continuing service arrangements by people who know the installed base intimately. The idea here is similar, applied to a building’s whole capital position rather than to one system.

## What would make it work

Continuous advice on a building’s capital position needs three things. A structured, versioned register that can be updated cheaply as evidence arrives. A method that keeps judgement visible and challengeable, so that changes are explained rather than asserted. And people who know the building well enough to notice what matters and to talk to its owner about it. The first two are now practical. The third is the part that cannot be automated, and the part owners value most.

## An established discipline, applied to buildings

Continuous management of physical assets is not new. Infrastructure owners, utilities and public estates have run it for decades, and it has an international standard: the ISO 55000 series on asset management, first published in 2014 and revised in 2024. Its premise is the one this paper argues for buildings: decisions about physical assets should be made over their whole life, from current evidence, and recorded so they can be reviewed. Episodic advice and continuous managementEpisodicContinuousTriggerA transaction, a lease event or a failureA calendar, and any new evidenceOutputA report at a dateA register kept current, with its historyUncertaintyFixed at the date of the reportNarrowed as evidence arrivesAcross a portfolioReports in different formats and datesComparable registers on one basisWho carries the knowledgeWhoever read the last reportThe record itself

Moyne Ross summary; asset management principles follow the ISO 55000 series.

Commercial property has been slow to adopt this way of working because its assets change hands and its advice is bought transaction by transaction. That is exactly why the record matters: it is the part of the discipline that survives a change of owner.

## Physical assets under management

Seen at portfolio scale, a set of live registers begins to look like assets under management: physical rather than financial, but held, monitored and decided on continuously. Each register improves as evidence accumulates. Across many buildings, patterns emerge about how real systems age, what works cost and which decisions paid off. That is the argument of [It’s Not About Owning Data](/insights/its-not-about-owning-data) carried to its conclusion: the advantage lies in turning evidence into decisions, repeatedly.

## Where the thesis ends

Capital Made Physical began with a claim that capital is turning back toward the physical, that buildings are becoming operating infrastructure rather than financial wrappers. If that is right, buildings deserve the continuous attention that capital gives to everything else it cares about.

That is the world this publication describes and the one Moyne Ross is built for: buildings read as capital, held as living records, and decided on with care over time, by people who know them. This is the most speculative paper in Capital Made Physical. Within a few years the evidence will show whether owners want continuous attention to their buildings and whether it can be delivered economically, and the paper will be rewritten either way.  In the register

In this model the register never closes: every row is a standing decision, revisited as evidence, markets and the owner’s plans change.   Key signal

As reading a building becomes fast, the value of building advice moves from producing documents to staying with the building and its decisions over time.

## Questions

### How is continuous building advice different from periodic condition surveys?

Periodic surveys produce a snapshot that ages until the next one. Continuous advice keeps a living register current and works through decisions as evidence and plans change, so knowledge accumulates instead of being rediscovered.

### Why compare buildings with financial assets under management?

Both are significant capital that changes value with time and circumstances. Financial assets are managed continuously; the argument is that physical assets increasingly warrant similar ongoing attention to their capital position.

methods.title: The Capital Register
methods.summary: The line-by-line capital document behind every Capital Strategy: condition, action, timing, cost, impact and confidence on every row, with the cost basis behind every figure.
methods.text:
Methodology / The Capital Register

# The Capital Register

Every element of the building, costed across the decade, with the evidence for every cost carried on its own row.

It sits at the centre of every Moyne Ross Capital Strategy. This page shows what you receive, how to read it, and why each number can be challenged.

What you receive

One row, from a real strategy 1970s distribution warehouse · Q3 2026

Roof · Item 4.1 **Metal deck roofing across the distribution warehouse**

1. **01 · Condition** Severe oxidation and coating breakdown across the older bays; water ingress risk to stock below.
2. **02 · Action** Staged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, with a roofing consultant’s inspection first.
3. **03 · Cost basis** Planning range $1.8M–$3.4M for 20,000–25,000 m², ex GST, Q3 2026. Purlins excluded.
4. **04 · Impact** 4 · Essential
5. **05 · Confidence** Medium
6. **06 · Timing** 1 yr *$35K* 2–5 yr *$2.6M* 6–10 yr *None*

Item total **$2.64M**

     01

## What you receive

A Capital Strategy is a reviewed, ten-year view of what your building will ask of your capital, why, and how sure we are. It comes in six connected parts. The register is the engine room; this is what sits around it.

Illustrative excerpt with sample figures, in the layout of an issued strategy.

1. **The story** An executive summary in plain words: where the building stands, what matters most, and what is still uncertain.
2. **The capital position** The ten-year total, and how it falls across the next year, years two to five, and years six to ten.
3. **The MR Index** One score for the decade ahead, from MR 1 to MR 5, calculated from the register. [How to read it](https://moyneross.com/methodology/mr-index).
4. **The register** Every element of structure, services and space, row by row: condition, action, cost, timing, impact and confidence.
5. **The cost basis** Behind every priced line, how the number was built, what it includes and excludes, and how firm it is.
6. **A living record** Your building’s private place in the portal, by invitation, with report and spreadsheet exports, updated as evidence and plans change.

Then, with you: the questions worth investigating, the options the building could support, and the next sensible step.

      02

## One method, different answers

The method is the same on every row. What changes is what the evidence supports. The roof above is a large, well-evidenced exposure. The five rows below each reach a different kind of answer, reproduced from issued strategies and anonymised.

      01

### Urgency, earned

Most of a decade's capital never belongs in the first year. This row does: the failure is active, and water is reaching an occupied room below.

Early learning centre, regional Victoria · built 2018 · Q3 2026

External Elements · Item 6.6 **Landscaping & Play Areas: Upper Play Deck Waterproofing & Drainage Outlet Failure (Timber-Framed Structure)**

1. **Impact** 4 · Essential
2. **Confidence** Medium
3. **Timing** 1 yr *$152.5K* 2–5 yr *None* 6–10 yr *None*

Condition, action and cost basis

1. **Condition** The upper play deck's turf-over-membrane system is failing as one continuous sequence. Inadequate membrane falls and outlet restrictions cause persistent water ponding and biological growth. Saturation is tracking through the plywood substrate into the children's room below and bleeding down the rear elevation, presenting an imminent risk of premature fungal decay and structural loss across concealed joists, blocking, and LVL framing if unaddressed.
2. **Action** Allow for full turf strip-out and bituminous membrane removal across the confirmed multi-bay extent, reinstated with a flanged clamping-ring outlet, tapered firring to falls, reworked upstand flashing, a sub-turf drainage layer, structural timber framing repair from localized joist/blocking replacement through to full LVL deck relay, and render/soffit make-good, a range of $95,000–$195,000. A specialist waterproofing and structural engineering inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included.
3. **Includes** Turf strip-out and disposal, full bituminous membrane removal and replacement with a flanged clamping-ring outlet termination, tapered firring to falls, continuous upstand flashing reworked at the parapet and post-penetration cluster, a drainage layer beneath reinstated turf, spot render and soffit make-good at the confirmed staining path, and structural timber repair ranging from multi-bay joist/blocking replacement to full LVL deck relay.
4. **Excludes** Remediation beyond the deck footprint and its confirmed drainage path, structural upgrades beyond like-for-like member replacement, internal reinstatement to the room below (costed separately at 5.3).

Item total **$152.5K**

     02

### Where the evidence stops

Impact 4, and no works figure. Nothing yet supports one, so the register prices the inspection and stops there.

 1912 heritage building, inner-north Melbourne · Q4 2026

Substructure · Item 1.1 **Foundations: Original masonry footings beneath the original building**

1. **Impact** 4 · Essential
2. **Confidence** Low
3. **Timing** 1 yr *$4.5K* 2–5 yr *None* 6–10 yr *None*

Condition, action and cost basis

1. **Condition** Original early-twentieth-century foundations are likely shallow masonry footings beneath the two-storey brick shell. No major façade displacement is apparent across the visible street elevations, but concealed footing geometry and movement history remain unknown across the full approximately 564 m² building. Differential movement could crack heritage masonry and disrupt later structural alterations.
2. **Action** Commission a structural engineer to inspect accessible lower-level fabric, review visible cracking and assess footing performance before major fit-out, rooftop works or façade intervention. The objective is to confirm structural capacity and movement risk at the original-building and later-alteration interfaces.
3. **Includes** Site inspection, visible crack review, accessible lower-level observations and concise structural advice.
4. **Excludes** Trial pits, geotechnical testing, monitoring, design documentation and remedial works.

Item total **$4.5K**

     03

### Heritage fabric

Conservation repair rather than replacement: compatible materials, protection of original fabric, and exclusions that keep the range honest.

 1912 heritage building, inner-north Melbourne · Q4 2026

Façades · Item 3.1 **Masonry/Brickwork: Principal heritage street elevations**

1. **Impact** 3 · Important
2. **Confidence** Medium
3. **Timing** 1 yr *$8.5K* 2–5 yr *$137.5K* 6–10 yr *None*

Condition, action and cost basis

1. **Condition** The principal elevations retain extensive red face brickwork, projecting pilasters and decorative white masonry dressings. Local staining, aged pointing and weathered decorative interfaces are visible, particularly around parapet-level details. The façade is a prominent heritage asset; moisture entry through open joints or failed flashings could accelerate brick and internal-finish damage.
2. **Action** Allow for conservation cleaning, mortar renewal, local brick and dressings repair, and parapet weathering works to the heritage elevations, a range of $85,000–$190,000. A heritage façade specialist inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included.
3. **Includes** Access, cleaning, local repointing, brick replacement, decorative repair and minor flashings.
4. **Excludes** Full façade reconstruction, structural rebuilds, hidden lintel replacement and permit fees.

Item total **$146K**

     04

### An inference, labelled as one

No fault is reported, and the row says so. It names the statutory regime that sets the inspection, and keeps the age-based reasoning visible as reasoning.

 1990s broadcasting and office tower, Japan · Q4 2026

Fire Services · Item 9.1 **Fire Detection & Alarm Systems**

1. **Impact** 4 · Essential
2. **Confidence** Medium
3. **Timing** 1 yr *¥4M* 2–5 yr *¥122.5M* 6–10 yr *None*

Condition, action and cost basis

1. **Condition** Fire detection and alarm infrastructure across a 21-storey occupied tower is a life-safety system subject to mandatory periodic inspection under Japan's Fire Service Act. At 30+ years, original-era detection panels and field devices are a plausible candidate for parts obsolescence even absent any reported fault.
2. **Action** Allow for fire alarm control panel and detector network replacement across all floors, a range of ¥85,000,000–¥160,000,000. A fire engineer inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included.
3. **Includes** Fire alarm control panel replacement, detector network renewal, integration with smoke management.
4. **Excludes** Sprinkler system works (priced separately), structural fire separation works.

Item total **¥126.5M**

     05

### Sound work, left alone

Coatings refreshed in 2023 are not pulled forward. The recoat sits in years seven to nine, with a review before it.

 1990 office building, inner south-east Melbourne · Q3 2026

Façades · Item 3.6 **External Coating Systems: Architectural Masonry Paint & Render**

1. **Impact** 2 · Planned
2. **Confidence** Low
3. **Timing** 1 yr *None* 2–5 yr *None* 6–10 yr *$60K*

Condition, action and cost basis

1. **Condition** External acrylic elastomeric paint system applied to concrete spandrels, parapets, and side/rear masonry boundary walls. Facade coatings were selectively refreshed during the late 2023 works, presenting uniform adhesion and colour retention with minor road grime accumulation on upper returns.
2. **Action** Allow for commercial pressure washing, localized crack priming, and dual-coat elastomeric repainting of all external concrete and masonry surfaces, a range of $35,000–$78,000. A painting specialist inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included.
3. **Includes** Access plant, surface prep, crack patching, two-coat exterior paint.
4. **Excludes** Structural render replacement.

Item total **$60K**

       03

## Every number can be challenged

Each finding is graded by where it comes from. **Documented** findings rest on records or supplied material, **observed** findings on what the evidence shows, and **inferred** findings on the building’s era, type and context. The grade travels with the finding, so an assumption never quietly becomes a fact.

The cost basis is the audit trail, and it shows how each number was built. Every priced line carries one: what kind of figure it is, the quantity it was applied to, what it includes and excludes, and its date. A planning allowance is presented as a planning allowance, not as a market price, so a quotation or a new survey can be tested against it line by line.

The register puts a price on uncertainty instead of hiding it. Where the evidence stops short, the register says so. Partial evidence gets a range and the assumptions that could move it. Where investigation is the right next step, it is priced as its own line rather than hidden behind “to be confirmed”. Inspection tightens the ranges; the discipline is the same either way.

That makes the register a shared reference as the plan develops. A quote, a survey or a change of direction can be brought in, and the position updated within the agreed engagement.

    04

## What the register is not

The register isn’t a condition report, a maintenance schedule or a compliance checklist. Those answer technical questions: what the building is, what to do about it routinely, what regulators need to see. The Capital Register is a capital document. It tells the owner what the building will ask of their capital over the next ten years, how sure we are, and when.

See the method in use in [When the Building is Not the Asset](https://moyneross.com/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) and [The Economics of Heritage](https://moyneross.com/insights/the-economics-of-heritage). The thinking behind it is set out in [Timing Is Not Risk](https://moyneross.com/insights/timing-is-not-risk), [Documented, Observed, Inferred](https://moyneross.com/insights/documented-observed-inferred), [Pricing What You Don’t Know](https://moyneross.com/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know) and [The Register, Not the Report](https://moyneross.com/insights/the-register-not-the-report); [A Register Read End to End](https://moyneross.com/insights/a-register-read-end-to-end) shows how to read one.

Moyne Ross / Capital Register

## Every building is a capital story. See yours.

Send us an address. Your building’s first read arrives as a register like the one above, before anything is agreed.

[How the engine works →](https://moyneross.com/ai#engine)

methods.title: The MR Index
methods.summary: The decision layer: how much attention a building needs and how soon, read element by element and placed on a band from MR 1 to MR 5. No costs take part; it is calculated from the register, not guessed by a model.
methods.text:
Methodology / The MR Index

# The MR Index

How much of the building needs attention, how serious it is and how soon. One reading, on a scale from MR 1 to MR 5.

Every Capital Strategy carries one. This page explains what the Index is reading, how a building ends up on a band, and what the band is telling you.

How it is read

One reading, five bands Illustrative building · forty elements

Element by element **Each square is one element of the building**

- Needs nothing
- Needs a check
- Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon

Reads as **MR 3 · Mid-cycle refresh**

     01

## Why a single score

A Capital Register runs to forty lines or more. The first question anyone asks of it is simpler than that: how bad is it?

The MR Index answers that first. It gives back one position for the decade ahead, so an owner, a board or a buyer sees the shape of what is coming at a glance, then turns to the register for the why.

- **Condition, not cost**: A large building is not marked down for being large, and an expensive repair counts for no more than a cheap one of the same seriousness. The costs stay in the register, for planning.
- **The same way, every time**: The band is worked out from the register itself, line by line. Nobody decides it, and it does not drift as prices move.

It tells you where the building stands. What to do about it is the conversation that follows.

**1** Minimal **2** Routine **3** Mid-cycle **4** Elevated **5** Major

    02

## Three questions, every element

By the time the register is complete, every element of the building, from the footings to the fire panel, has been looked at and judged. The Index asks the same three things of each one.

1. **Does it need attention?** Over the next ten years, will this element need work, need someone to look before anyone can say, or need nothing at all?
  - Works
  - A check
  - Nothing
2. **How serious?** If it were left, what would it cost the building: its safety, its function, its value?
  - Essential
  - Important
  - Planned
  - Routine
3. **How soon?** Is this a matter for the coming year, the middle of the decade, or later?
  - Within a year
  - Years two to five
  - Years six to ten

    03

## The band reads the whole building

Picture the building as a field of squares, one for each element. Light up the ones that need attention, more strongly the more serious and the sooner. The band is a reading of that whole picture.

A building with a few faint squares late in the decade reads lightly. A building where most of the field is lit, much of it strongly, reads heavily. Three examples, drawn to the same scale:

**MR 1** Minimal requirements

**MR 3** Mid-cycle refresh

**MR 5** Major intervention

- Needs nothing
- Needs a check
- Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon

Illustrative buildings of forty elements. A real register commonly reads between thirty and fifty.

    04

## The five bands

The reading lands on one of five bands. Each describes a kind of decade, not a verdict on the building. Where the lines between them fall is set against buildings Moyne Ross has assessed, and reviewed as that library grows.

1. **MR 1** **Minimal requirements** Little needs attention, and nothing serious any time soon.
2. **MR 2** **Routine profile** What is needed is routine or already planned, and spread across the decade.
3. **MR 3** **Mid-cycle refresh** A clear set of elements needs attention, some of them important. This decade needs a plan.
4. **MR 4** **Elevated programme** Serious elements need attention, often within a few years, or too many questions are still open.
5. **MR 5** **Major intervention** So much of the building needs serious, early attention that the decision itself changes.

    05

## What the Index is, and is not

The Index says what condition a building is in. It is not a verdict on whether the building is good, beautiful or worth buying.

- **Not a valuation**: A prime building in a tightly held precinct can read MR 5 and still be the right acquisition. A heritage building often reads heavily simply because so much of it deserves care. Nor is the Index a cost estimate; the register carries the costs.
- **Same band, different decisions**: Someone holding for ten years reads an MR 4 one way; someone weighing a refurbishment or a change of use reads it another. The Index is the shared starting point. The plan comes from your objectives.
- **Since October 2026**: The Index has read condition rather than cost since October 2026. Earlier strategies were banded from cost-weighted measures, still kept for reference, and any of them can be read again under the current method.

Sample / Capital Strategy

# A sample Capital Strategy Industrial warehouse and office, outer-eastern Melbourne

This is a real Moyne Ross Capital Strategy, version 2, issued on 6 November 2026, with the address and other identifying details changed. It shows what a client receives: a ten-year view of what the building is likely to need, when, and at what cost, line by line in a Capital Register, with the MR Index.

Costs are planning allowances in Australian dollars at Q4 2026, not quotes. The assessment is desktop-based: public records, imagery and listing material, reviewed by Moyne Ross before release.

[Open the interactive strategy →](https://moyneross.com/samples/strategy)

- **Ten years**: $331,225planning allowances, Q4 2026
- **Next year**: $12,5003.8% of the ten years
- **Years 2–5**: $217,22565.6% of the ten years
- **Years 6–10**: $101,50030.6% of the ten years
- **MR Index**: MR 2Routine profile
- **Building**: 599 m²15 costed lines in 13 sections

## Executive summary

A two-storey precast tilt-panel warehouse on a steel portal frame, with a glazed office frontage and steel mezzanine, most likely built between 2010 and 2012. The slab, portal frame and precast panels appear sound, with no visible cracking or corrosion, and the offices and roller shutter present well. Most of the capital falls in the 2–5 YR window, with a smaller share later and little in the first year beyond inspections.

The roof is the largest single matter. The low-pitch metal deck shows weathering and lap staining, and no anchors or fall protection are apparent beside the translucent sheets. The roof is common property, so the cost reaches the owner through owners corporation levies, and rooftop solar is best planned once the restoration is done. The unit is vacant, which suits access works before a tenant is in place. A roofing contractor inspection in 1 YR should come first, as it settles the scope of the restoration.

### Key considerations

- **Roofs & Rainwater Goods** No anchors, static line or edge protection are apparent on a roof that carries translucent sheets, which presents a fall-through hazard. Have a roof-safety specialist inspect in 1 YR, so that anchor and sheet protection can be installed in 2–5 YR before any roof access is needed.
- **Roofs & Rainwater Goods** The low-pitch metal deck shows weathering, discoloured lap lines and staining, and the extent of fastener and sheet failure is not established. A roofing contractor inspection in 1 YR decides the scope of the 2–5 YR restoration, which in turn sets the timing of any solar installation.
- **Building Code Compliance** The first-floor offices are reached by an internal stair only, and no lift is visible. Engage an access consultant in 1 YR to establish whether performance solutions or ground-floor service delivery will suffice, or whether a platform lift is needed in 2–5 YR.
- **Superstructure** The steel mezzanine and its guarding appear in order, but the design documents and load rating are not established. A structural engineer's review in 1 YR confirms the safe working load before the unit is leased or sold.
- **Substructure** The title dates the shell to 2010–2012, but a conflicting third-party record gives 2003. A building inspector should confirm the date from approval records and review the mezzanine, fire and electrical certificates in one visit in 1 YR, which fixes the lifecycle basis for the services.

## How to read this register

### How To Read The Register

- **One row, one element**: Each row is an element of the building: its condition, the action it needs, when that falls, what it is expected to cost, how much it matters and how firm the evidence is.
- **Cost basis**: Every priced row carries the reasoning behind its number: the scope assumed, the quantities, what is included and excluded, the cost date and how firm the footing is. A planning allowance is presented as a planning allowance, not as a market price.
- **Timing**: Every allowance carries an intervention window in years. The next-year column is reserved for work whose whole window sits inside the next twelve months. Any other window is shown, as a single placement, in the horizon that holds its midpoint; the window itself is stated in the cost basis.

### Evidence

- **Desktop or inspection**: Unless this strategy records a site inspection, the assessment is desktop-based: public records, imagery and material supplied by the client. A desktop assessment cannot establish concealed conditions or replace an inspection where one is needed.
- **Documented, observed, inferred**: Documented findings are supported by records or supplied material. Observed findings are visible in the evidence available. Inferred findings are reasoned from the building’s era, type and context, and are labelled as such.
- **Where the evidence stops**: Where nothing yet supports a works figure, the register prices the investigation that would, and stops there. Where an inspection is included, its fee is a separate line added to the works midpoint rather than absorbed into the range.

### Impact

- **Essential**: Critical to operation, life safety or compliance. Failure would risk shutdown, a safety incident or regulatory action.
- **Important**: Significant effect on operation or commercial value. Failure would cause material disruption.
- **Planned**: Standard lifecycle work within expected replacement cycles.
- **Routine**: Minor work that can be deferred without material consequence.

### Confidence

- **High**: Strong, asset-specific evidence for the scope. Any benchmark, quote or tender relied on is identified at item level.
- **Medium**: Building-specific evidence combined with standard assumptions for buildings of this type and scale.
- **Low**: Limited evidence, concealed elements or atypical systems. The range is wider, and the investigation that would narrow it is included.

### Work Codes

- **CAP**: Capital expenditure: lifecycle replacement, restoration or end-of-life renewal.
- **R&M**: Repair and maintenance beyond routine thresholds.
- **BCC**: Building code compliance: statutory, certification or code-upgrade work.
- **ENV**: Environmental: efficiency, carbon and environmental compliance.

### Costs

- **Planning allowances**: Costs are planning allowances in the strategy currency at Q4 2026. Each row states its own inclusions, exclusions and treatment of preliminaries and tax; these are not assumed to be uniform across the register.
- **Separate interventions**: Works are planned as discrete interventions unless a row says otherwise. Coordinated procurement may reduce duplicated access and preliminaries; no saving is assumed without project-specific evidence.
- **Before commitment**: This Capital Strategy is a planning tool based on the evidence available at the time. It identifies likely capital needs, priorities and areas of uncertainty, but does not replace site inspection, detailed investigation, design, certification or specialist advice. Significant works and expenditure should be verified before commitment.

engagement.text:
## Working with Moyne Ross

Moyne Ross works with owners, investors, asset managers and their advisers across commercial and multi-unit property (office, industrial, retail, mixed use and multi-unit residential) in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Portfolios are scoped individually.

To begin, use Start your strategy (https://moyneross.com/contact): send the building's address and anything worth knowing. An address is enough. Assistants can open the form already filled in; see https://moyneross.com/assistants.

The relationship has three stages. Each is available on its own; none has to be taken.

- [Your strategy](https://moyneross.com/#how-we-work): Moyne Ross prepares a ten-year Capital Strategy for the building and looks it over before it reaches the client. It arrives by email, ready to open, and stands on its own.
- [Working it through](https://moyneross.com/#how-we-work): where the client wants to go further, the questions the strategy raises are worked through together, bringing in their plans and records, until the direction is settled.
- [Ongoing](https://moyneross.com/#how-we-work): for those who hold the building, the strategy stays live. As quotes arrive and plans change it keeps up: a record of the building that stays true.

The Capital Strategy is released once the client agrees the Moyne Ross terms and pays a fixed fee of 950 in local currency: AUD in Australia, GBP in the United Kingdom, USD in the United States. Anything beyond that is agreed with the client for the building, before it begins.

A sample Capital Strategy, for an industrial warehouse and office, with identifying details changed: https://moyneross.com/samples/capital-strategy (the full register as a readable page; the interactive version is at https://moyneross.com/samples/strategy).

Portal access is by personal invitation. Each building has a private place for its strategy, our notes and what has been agreed. A plain-English summary of how Moyne Ross works sits at the top of the Terms (https://moyneross.com/terms#in-brief).

## Frequently asked

### What is a Capital Strategy?

A structured ten-year view of a commercial building: what each part of it is likely to need, when, and what it is likely to cost. It is set out line by line in a Capital Register, with an MR Index that reads how much attention the building needs and how soon.

### What does it cost?

The Capital Strategy is a fixed fee of 950 in local currency (AUD, GBP or USD). It is released once the client agrees the terms and pays. Working it through, and ongoing support, are scoped and priced for each building and agreed before they begin.

### What do I need to provide?

The building's address. Reports, plans, photographs or other records help and are taken into account if supplied, but are not required.

### Is it a building inspection?

No. It is a planning tool built from the evidence available: the address, public records, imagery and any documents supplied, read by the Moyne Ross platform and reviewed by the practice before release. Where the evidence is thin it says so, and names the inspection or specialist check worth commissioning. It does not replace site inspection, detailed investigation, design, certification or specialist advice.

### Which countries and buildings?

Commercial and multi-unit property in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. For homes, see Homechecker (https://homechecker.com.au).

### How is AI used?

AI helps read documents, research the building and draft structured assessment material. It does not make the final capital calculation, calculate the MR Index, publish a strategy or replace professional judgement. Every strategy is reviewed before release. More: https://moyneross.com/ai

Every completed strategy adds structured building observations to the private Moyne Ross intelligence library. The public research archive contains only material Moyne Ross has chosen to publish.

pages.title: Accessibility Lifts
pages.question: How do platform lifts and stair lifts fail, and when does a failure make a building inaccessible?
pages.answer: Accessibility lifts are often the least reliable equipment in a building and the only step-free route between levels. They fail at drives, batteries and safety edges; units from small makers become unrepairable; external units corrode. The safety failures are bypassed interlocks and safety edges, no way to call for help or lower a stranded user, and inclined units obstructing escape stairs. A unit out of service means the building is not accessible.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about accessibility lifts; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Platform lifts, stair lifts

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Accessibility lifts provide step-free access where a full passenger lift is impractical: vertical platform lifts over short rises, inclined platform lifts that travel along a stair, stair lifts with seats, low-rise passenger lifts, and home lifts in houses and small apartment buildings. They are the only accessible route between levels in many existing buildings, so when one fails, people who use wheelchairs or cannot manage stairs are excluded from part of the building.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical platform lift (open or enclosed) | Entrances, mezzanines, stages, heritage buildings | Short rises; screw, chain or hydraulic drive; slow; hold-to-run controls |
| Inclined platform lift | Existing stairs in schools, churches, offices | Runs on the stair; folds away; restricts the stair |
| Stair lift with seat | Houses, small residential buildings | For people who can transfer to a seat |
| Low-rise passenger lift | Small apartment buildings, offices | Between a platform lift and a full lift |
| Home lift | Houses and townhouses | Domestic duty; often battery or screw driven |

Many units were installed to meet access requirements during refurbishments and then left without proper maintenance. Several are supplied by small manufacturers whose parts and support disappear. Battery-backed units depend on batteries that fail quietly.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform lift drive (screw, chain or hydraulic) | 15 to 25 years | Use; lubrication; exposure |
| Controls and safety circuits | 10 to 15 years | Manufacturer support; exposure |
| Batteries | 3 to 5 years | Charging; temperature |
| Safety edges and sensors | 5 to 10 years | Damage; exposure |
| Gates and doors | 10 to 20 years | Abuse; interlocks |
| Stair lift rails and carriages | 10 to 15 years | Use |

What shortens life:

- External exposure: units at entrances get wet, corrode and suffer electrical faults.
- Lack of use: seldom-used units seize and their batteries die.
- Misuse and vandalism: gates forced, controls damaged.
- Unsupported manufacturers, which leave units unrepairable.

Units used daily by the same person, such as in a house, wear differently from units used occasionally by many visitors in a public building; the second group often fails from neglect rather than wear.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Drive and battery failures

Screw and nut drives wear, chains stretch, hydraulic systems leak, and batteries that provide travel or emergency lowering fail. A unit that stops part way leaves the user stranded.

### Safety edge and interlock failures

Platforms have safety edges and pans under them that stop travel if they touch an obstruction, and gates and doors with interlocks so they cannot open mid-travel. Damaged edges and bypassed interlocks expose users and bystanders to crushing and falls.

### Entrapment without communication

Users stranded on a stopped platform, often alone and with limited mobility, need a way to call for help and a means of emergency lowering. Many units have neither, or have a phone on a retired line.

### Unreliability

Accessibility lifts are often the least reliable equipment in a building. Repeated breakdowns, long waits for parts and units left out of service mean the building is not accessible, which is a discrimination risk for owners and occupiers.

### Control and usability problems

Hold-to-run controls that are hard to operate, keys that staff cannot find, and call points out of reach make units unusable even when they work.

### Stair obstruction

Inclined platform lifts and stair lifts reduce stair width; when left unfolded or broken down they can obstruct an escape stair.

### Electrical and control faults

Control boards, limit switches and wiring in compact units are exposed to damp and dust; intermittent faults that clear when reset are common and usually precede a failure that leaves the unit out of service.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Unit working on test, with smooth travel and levelling at both landings.
- Safety edges and pans intact; gates and doors interlocked.
- Emergency lowering and call device present and working.
- "Out of order" signs; keys and call buttons accessible to users.
- Corrosion and water at external units.
- Stair width with inclined units folded and unfolded.

### In the records

- Maintenance and breakdown history.
- Manufacturer and parts support.
- Inspection or examination certificates.
- Complaints from users about access.

- A call button or intercom at each landing that a wheelchair user can reach, and signage explaining how to get help to operate the unit.
- Folded inclined platforms that block part of a stair even when not in use.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit stops part way or will not start | Battery, drive or safety circuit fault | Battery test; fault codes |
| Frequent breakdowns and long waits for parts | Unsupported manufacturer or end of life | Parts support status |
| Unit works only with staff help | Key or call arrangements, not the lift | Observation |
| Corrosion and electrical faults at an entrance unit | Weather exposure | Inspection |
| Platform continues when the edge is pressed | Safety edge fault | Test |

> An accessibility lift out of service means part of the building is not accessible. Treat repeated or prolonged outages as an accessibility failure, not just a maintenance issue.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety edges or interlocks failed; no emergency call or lowering; unit obstructing an escape stair | safety | Take out of service and fix now |
| Unit out of service, leaving no accessible route | failure | Restore now or provide an alternative |
| Thorough examination or inspection due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Repeated breakdowns; worn drives; failing batteries | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Unit unsupported or at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No maintenance contract; usability not checked | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |
