sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A lift consultant or accessibility lift specialist, ideally with an access consultant for usability.

- Function test over full travel with a typical load, including emergency lowering.
- Safety tests: safety edges, pans, gate and door interlocks, overspeed and slack chain protection.
- Battery and drive inspection.
- Communication test: emergency call device and its line.
- Usability review: controls, reach, keys, signage and how users summon help.
- Records review: breakdowns, downtime, parts support.
- Stair review for inclined units on escape stairs.

The report should state safety, reliability, usability and remaining life, and whether a different solution (a low-rise lift or ramp) would serve better.

- Alternatives review: whether a ramp, a different route, or a low-rise passenger lift would provide more reliable access than repairing or replacing the existing unit.
- Escape review with the fire strategy, so a person using the lift can also leave the building in an emergency.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Maintenance contract with planned visits and agreed response times, since many units have none.
- Battery replacement on a cycle.
- Safety device repair and interlock replacement.
- Emergency communication with a working line and battery backup.
- Weather protection for external units: canopies, enclosures, drainage.
- Replacement with a supported product, or with a low-rise passenger lift or ramp where space allows.
- Usability fixes: accessible controls, signage, call points, and procedures so users are not left waiting for staff.

- Spare parts strategy: hold critical spares on site for units whose parts have long lead times.
- Remote monitoring so faults are reported to the maintenance contractor without waiting for a user complaint.
- Evacuation planning for people who rely on the lift, recorded in personal emergency evacuation plans where used.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Batteries are replaced on a cycle. Repairs are itemised. Replacement is a lump sum per unit, with builders' work; replacing a platform lift with a low-rise lift or ramp is a larger project that may be justified by reliability. Downtime has an indirect cost in access complaints and legal risk.

Safety and accessibility rectification are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance and batteries are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010 and the National Construction Code set access requirements, with low-rise platforms and lifts covered by parts of the AS 1735 series; the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 applies where access is not provided; lifts are plant under work health and safety laws.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 81-41 covers vertical lifting platforms and BS EN 81-40 stair lifts and inclined platforms; Approved Document M sets access requirements; the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments; LOLER requires thorough examination of lifting platforms.
- United States. ASME A18.1 covers platform lifts and stairway chairlifts; the 2010 ADA Standards set where and how they may be used; state elevator authorities inspect them.

Discrimination complaints in all three countries commonly arise from broken accessibility lifts.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Maintenance contract and breakdown history.
- Inspection or thorough examination certificates.
- Manufacturer and parts support details.
- Emergency call device line and test records.
- Access complaints or discrimination claims.
- Access audit for the building.

- Downtime records showing how long the unit has been out of service.
- Personal emergency evacuation plans for regular users.
- Records of any alternative access offered during outages.

pages.title: Air Handling Units (AHUs)
pages.question: How do air handling units fail, what does each failure look like, and when do they affect health rather than just comfort?
pages.answer: Air handling units fail first at their wet parts: drain pans that do not drain, wet internal insulation and fouled coils grow microbes and cause the musty smell people notice when air conditioning starts. Seized outside air dampers starve buildings of fresh air and raise carbon dioxide. Fans wear at bearings and belts; old belt-driven fans waste energy. Rooftop casings corrode. Hygiene and outside air are health issues, not just comfort issues.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about air handling units (ahus); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fans, coils, filters, casings

sources.title: Standard 180: Standard Practice for Inspection and Maintenance of Commercial HVAC Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
An air handling unit conditions and moves air for a zone, a floor or a whole building. Inside its casing are fans, filters, heating and cooling coils, often heat recovery, sometimes humidification, dampers for outside, return and exhaust air, sound attenuators and a drain pan under the cooling coil. Units sit in plant rooms, on roofs or in ceiling voids, and serve the ductwork and terminal units downstream.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Casing and panels | Contain air; insulate; keep out water on rooftop units | Corrosion; air leakage; wet or shedding internal insulation |
| Fans and motors | Move air | Bearing wear; belt wear; imbalance; motor failure; old forward-curved fans inefficient |
| Filters | Remove particles | Bypass around frames; overloaded filters; wrong grade |
| Cooling coils | Cool and dehumidify | Fouled fins; corrosion; leaks; freeze damage |
| Heating coils | Heat | Fouling; leaks; freeze damage |
| Drain pans | Collect condensate from cooling coils | Corrosion; standing water; microbial growth; overflow |
| Heat recovery (wheels, plates, run-around coils) | Recover energy from exhaust air | Seals; cross-leakage; fouling; drive failure |
| Humidifiers | Add moisture | Scale; water quality; microbial risk with adiabatic types |
| Dampers and actuators | Control outside air and economy cycle | Seized dampers; failed actuators; stuck positions |
| Attenuators | Reduce noise | Fibrous media degrading or wet |

Units vary from large site-built units in office plant rooms serving several floors, through packaged rooftop units on retail and industrial buildings (often with gas heating or direct expansion cooling built in), to dedicated outdoor air units supplying ventilation to fan coils or chilled beams. Hospitals, laboratories and cleanrooms have units built to stricter hygiene and filtration standards.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AHU casing (indoor) | 25 to 30 years | Condensation; drain pan leaks |
| AHU casing (rooftop) | 15 to 25 years | Weather; coastal exposure; panel seals |
| Fans | 20 to 25 years | Maintenance; balance |
| Fan motors (including EC motors) | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; heat |
| Belts | 2 to 4 years | Tension; alignment |
| Cooling and heating coils | 15 to 25 years | Cleaning; water treatment; coastal air |
| Heat recovery wheels | 15 to 20 years | Seals; drives |
| Humidifiers | 10 to 15 years | Water quality |
| Damper actuators | 10 to 15 years | Use; controls |
| Filters | Months to a year | Dust load; grade |

What shortens life:

- Neglected filters, which let dust foul coils and fans and raise fan energy.
- Blocked drains and standing condensate, which corrode drain pans and casings and grow microbes.
- Coastal and industrial air on rooftop casings and coils.
- Freezing in cold climates where frost protection fails.
- Poor access inside units, so parts are never cleaned or inspected.
- Running 24 hours when schedules have been lost or overridden.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Hygiene failures

Cooling coils produce condensate. If the drain pan does not drain because it is flat, corroded, or the trap is dry or the wrong depth for the fan pressure, water stands in the pan and grows bacteria and fungi. Wet fibrous insulation inside casings and attenuators does the same. Air carries spores and odours downstream. This is the commonest cause of musty smells from air conditioning and a recognised indoor air quality hazard.

### Coil fouling and failure

Dust bypassing filters coats coil fins and cuts heat transfer; the coil then cannot cool or dehumidify fully and the chilled water system sees less temperature difference (low delta T). Coils corrode at fins and tube joints, and chilled water coils leak; heating and cooling coils burst when frozen.

### Fan and drive wear

Bearings wear and run hot; belts slip and shed; pulleys wear; fans lose balance and vibrate. Older forward-curved and belt-driven fans use far more energy than modern direct-drive plug fans with electronically commutated motors.

### Damper and outside air faults

Outside air dampers seized shut starve the building of fresh air, raising carbon dioxide and complaints; seized open, they waste energy and can freeze coils. Economy cycle failures lose free cooling. Minimum outside air settings drift as controls change.

### Casing corrosion and leakage

Panels corrode from condensation and drain pan leaks; seals harden; rooftop units let in rain. Leakage into a unit from the plant room or out of the unit wastes energy and bypasses filters.

### Heat recovery faults

Wheels lose seals and leak exhaust air into supply; drives fail and wheels stop; plate heat exchangers foul. Recovery efficiency falls without obvious signs.

### Humidifier risks

Steam humidifiers scale; adiabatic (spray or pad) humidifiers can grow Legionella and other bacteria if water quality and maintenance lapse.

### Contaminated intakes

Outside air intakes near cooling towers, car park exhausts, kitchen exhausts, loading docks or flues draw contaminants into the building.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### At the unit

- Nameplate data: manufacturer, year, airflow, fan type.
- Water on the plant room floor; corrosion at the base of casings; rust stains below rooftop units.
- Drain pan condition: standing water, slime, rust; trap present and full.
- Filters overloaded, missing, or bypassed around frames.
- Coil fins dirty, flattened or corroded.
- Noise and vibration; belt dust; hot bearings.
- Dampers and actuators: position against what the controls show.
- Internal insulation wet, shedding or mouldy.

### In the building

- Musty smells when air conditioning starts.
- Stuffiness, high carbon dioxide and complaints in meetings rooms.
- Dust deposits around supply grilles.
- Temperature and humidity complaints.

### In the records

- Maintenance logs: filter changes, belt changes, coil cleaning.
- Hygiene inspection reports.
- Indoor air quality monitoring.
- BMS trends: fan status, damper position, supply temperature.
- Energy consumption.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Musty smell at start-up | Microbial growth in drain pans, coils or wet insulation | Standing water and slime in the pan; wet insulation; swab results |
| High carbon dioxide in occupied spaces | Outside air damper closed or minimum set too low | Damper position; outside air flow measured |
| Cannot reach supply temperature; low chilled water delta T | Fouled cooling coil or failed valve | Coil pressure drop; air and water temperatures across the coil |
| Water on the floor or ceiling below | Blocked drain or dry trap | Drain flow; trap depth against fan pressure |
| Vibration and noise | Bearing wear, belt problems or imbalance | Vibration analysis |
| Rising fan energy | Overloaded filters or fouled coils | Filter pressure drop |
| Water carried into ductwork | Coil face velocity too high or eliminators missing | Airflow measurement |

> Musty smells from air conditioning are not cosmetic. They are a sign of microbial growth in the unit, and a hygiene inspection should follow.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella risk from an adiabatic humidifier; heavy microbial growth in a unit serving a healthcare or occupied space; contaminated intake near a cooling tower or exhaust | safety | Isolate or clean now; hygiene and engineer review |
| Unit failed serving an occupied or critical space; major leaks | failure | Repair now |
| Outside air below code minimum; failed dampers; corroded drain pans; fouled coils | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Units at the end of their life; inefficient fans | lifecycle | Plan replacement or refurbishment |
| No hygiene inspection; outside air not measured | check | Inspect and measure |
| Normal wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a hygiene specialist where microbial issues are suspected.

- Unit inspection with panels open: casing, fans, motors, belts, filters, coils, drain pans and traps, humidifiers, heat recovery, dampers and actuators, attenuators.
- Airflow measurement: supply, return and outside air, against design and code minimums.
- Coil performance: air and water temperatures and flows; pressure drop.
- Fan performance: airflow, pressure, power, vibration.
- Hygiene inspection: visual, swabs and dust samples to AS/NZS 3666.2, BESA TR/19 or ASHRAE 180 practice.
- Indoor air quality: carbon dioxide, particulates, temperature and humidity in served spaces.
- Intake review: distance to towers, exhausts, flues and docks.
- Controls review: schedules, setpoints, economy cycle, outside air control.

The report should give the condition of each unit, airflow and outside air against requirements, hygiene status, and whether to repair, refurbish in place, or replace.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Hygiene remediation: clean coils, drain pans and casings; replace wet insulation with closed-cell or faced material; fix drain falls and traps.
- Filter upgrade: better grades and sealed frames to stop bypass.
- Fan upgrade: replace belt-driven fans with direct-drive plug fans and electronically commutated motors, often a large energy saving.
- Coil replacement where corroded or leaking; coatings for coastal sites.
- Damper and actuator replacement and outside air control with carbon dioxide sensors.
- Heat recovery repair or addition.
- Refurbishment in place: new internals within the existing casing, where the casing is sound and access is difficult.
- Replacement of the whole unit, sized to current loads and ventilation needs.
- Intake relocation where contamination is the problem.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection, airflow measurement and hygiene testing are lump sums. Component replacements (fans, motors, coils, dampers, humidifiers) are itemised per unit. Refurbishment in place is a lump sum per unit and avoids the cost of getting a new unit into a plant room. Replacement is a lump sum per unit including access (cranes for rooftop units, partial dismantling or wall openings for plant rooms), electrical and controls integration, and commissioning. Hygiene cleaning and filter changes recur.

Replacement and refurbishment are lifecycle; outside air and hygiene rectification can be code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Fan upgrades to direct-drive EC fans often pay back through energy savings and can sit in an energy line.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 1668.2 for ventilation; AS/NZS 3666.1 and 3666.2 set design, installation and maintenance of air-handling systems for microbial control, and in several states maintenance of air-handling systems is an essential safety measure. NABERS Indoor Environment rates indoor air quality.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document F sets ventilation; BS EN 16798-3 covers non-residential ventilation performance; BESA TR/19 sets ventilation hygiene; air-conditioning systems over 12 kW need energy inspection at least every five years; healthcare follows HTM 03-01.
- United States. ASHRAE 62.1 sets ventilation rates, ASHRAE 180 inspection and maintenance practice, ASHRAE 241 control of infectious aerosols, and ASHRAE 170 healthcare ventilation; the International Mechanical Code applies.

Healthcare, laboratory and cleanroom units follow additional standards for filtration and hygiene in all three countries.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Maintenance logs: filter, belt and coil cleaning records.
- Hygiene inspection reports and any microbial sampling.
- Airflow and outside air test and balance reports.
- Indoor air quality monitoring (CO₂, particulates).
- Installation dates and nameplate data for each unit.
- BMS trends for fans, dampers and supply temperatures.
- Energy consumption data.
- Drawings showing intake locations relative to exhausts and towers.

pages.title: Ancillary Structures
pages.question: How do sheds, carports, shade structures and other minor structures fail, and which findings are hazards?
pages.answer: Minor structures fail at their bases and in wind. Timber posts rot at ground level and pergolas and carports lean; shade sails overload masts and fixings in storms when left up; flagpoles and signs crack by fatigue at their bases; car park canopy posts are struck by vehicles. Older sheds often hold weathered asbestos cement. Many were added without approval or engineering. Leaning or wind-damaged structures over people are falling hazards.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ancillary structures; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Sheds, gazebos, monuments, water features

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Ancillary structures are the minor buildings and structures on a site that are not part of the main building: sheds, garages and carports, bin and bike enclosures, pergolas and gazebos, shade sails and canopies over car parks and play areas, flagpoles, signage structures, monuments and memorials, and decorative water features. Individually small, they are numerous, often built without the scrutiny given to the main building, frequently altered or added informally, and sometimes contain the oldest and most hazardous materials on a site.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sheds, garages and outbuildings | Houses, schools, depots, older commercial sites | Asbestos cement sheeting; decayed timber; unapproved construction |
| Carports and car park shade structures | Apartments, retail, offices | Fixings and posts corroding; vehicle impact; wind |
| Shade sails | Play areas, schools, car parks, courtyards | Mast and fixing failure in wind; fabric degradation |
| Pergolas and gazebos | Residential and hospitality courtyards | Timber decay at post bases; connections |
| Bin and bike enclosures | Apartments and commercial sites | Damage; fire risk; vermin |
| Flagpoles and signage structures | Commercial and public sites | Fatigue cracking at the base; corrosion; wind |
| Monuments, memorials and sculptures | Public and institutional sites | Stability; heritage; materials |
| Water features | Lobbies, plazas, gardens | Leaks; Legionella; slips; electrical safety |

Because many of these were added after the main building, they may lack approval, engineering or proper foundations. They are usually exposed to weather on all sides, and their structural margins in wind are often smaller than the main building's.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Structure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel sheds and carports | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; coastal exposure; impact |
| Timber pergolas and structures | 15 to 30 years | Decay at post bases; treatment; maintenance |
| Shade sail fabric | 8 to 12 years | UV; tension; wind |
| Shade sail masts and fixings | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; footing design |
| Flagpoles | 20 to 30 years | Fatigue; corrosion at the base |
| Asbestos cement sheds | Past life wherever weathered | Weathering; damage |
| Water feature equipment | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; pumps |

What shortens life:

- Wind: shade sails, signs and flagpoles carry high wind loads relative to their size, and cyclic loading fatigues them.
- Ground contact: timber posts set in soil or concrete rot at the base.
- Vehicle impact on carport and canopy posts.
- Coastal and industrial exposure.
- Informal alterations: added roofs, enclosures and loads.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Wind failure

Shade sails act like sails: they load masts and fixings heavily in storms, and many are designed to be taken down before severe winds but are left up. Masts bend, footings pull out, and fixings to buildings tear out. Freestanding signs and flagpoles fail by fatigue cracking at welds and base plates after years of wind cycling, often without visible warning.

### Post base decay

Timber posts embedded in soil or concrete stay wet at the base and rot from inside; the structure then leans or collapses, sometimes onto people. Steel posts corrode at ground level where water and debris collect.

### Vehicle impact

Carport and canopy posts in car parks are struck by vehicles; bent or cracked posts and loosened base plates weaken the whole structure.

### Asbestos and hazardous materials

Older sheds, garages and outbuildings are often clad or roofed in asbestos cement sheeting, which weathers, cracks and breaks. Damage and removal must be managed under asbestos rules.

### Unapproved or unengineered structures

Structures added informally may lack footings, engineering, fire separation from the main building or boundary setbacks. Their condition is often unknown and their compliance doubtful.

### Fire risk

Bin enclosures, storage sheds and combustible structures close to buildings are fire sources; bin fires against walls and under eaves spread into buildings.

### Water feature hazards

Fountains and ponds leak, grow algae and Legionella, create slip hazards, and combine water with electrical equipment.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Leaning structures; posts loose, cracked or rotted at ground level.
- Shade sails sagging, torn or with distorted masts; fixings pulling from walls.
- Rust at flagpole and sign bases; cracking at welds and base plates.
- Impact damage on carport and canopy posts.
- Grey corrugated or flat cement sheeting on sheds and garages of the right era.
- Bin enclosures built against walls and under eaves.
- Water features with green water, slime, leaks or exposed electrics.

### In the records

- Approvals and engineering for each structure.
- Shade sail installation certificates and wind instructions.
- Asbestos register entries for outbuildings.
- Inspection records for signs and flagpoles.
- Water feature maintenance records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pergola or carport leaning | Post base decay or impact damage | Probe or inspect at ground level |
| Shade sail masts bent after a storm | Wind overload; sail not removed | Inspection; design wind rating |
| Rust bleeding from a flagpole or sign base | Corrosion at the base and possible fatigue | Inspection; non-destructive testing of welds |
| Cracked cement sheeting on an old shed | Weathered asbestos cement | Sampling |
| Structure with no record of approval | Informal addition | Council or authority records |
| Algae and slime in a water feature | Inadequate treatment | Water testing |

> Leaning structures, damaged shade sail masts and corroded sign or flagpole bases over areas people use are falling hazards. Exclude people until an engineer has assessed them.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaning or damaged structures over occupied areas; damaged asbestos cement; water features with exposed electrics; bin stores against walls with fire risk | safety | Exclude, make safe or remove now |
| Structure collapsed or unusable | failure | Remove or rebuild |
| Approval or compliance required by an authority | deadline | By the required date |
| Decay or corrosion starting; worn shade fabric | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Structures and fabrics at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Unapproved structures; no engineering | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects; a structural engineer assesses structures that are leaning, damaged or carry significant wind loads; a licensed asbestos assessor samples suspect materials.

- Inventory of every ancillary structure on the site, with type, age, material, location and use.
- Condition inspection of posts, footings, connections, roofs and cladding, with probing of timber at ground level.
- Wind-loaded structures: shade sails, signs and flagpoles checked for masts, welds, base plates and fixings, with non-destructive testing of welds on tall poles and signs.
- Approvals check against council or authority records.
- Hazardous materials: asbestos sampling of cement sheeting and other suspect materials in older structures.
- Fire separation: distance of bin stores, sheds and combustible structures from the main building.
- Water features: leaks, electrical safety, water treatment and Legionella risk.

The report should list each structure with its condition, safety status, approval status and recommended action, including whether it should be kept, repaired, replaced or removed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Post base repairs: replace decayed timber posts with posts on stirrups or galvanised bases above ground, or replace with steel.
- Impact protection: bollards and post guards for carport and canopy posts in car parks.
- Shade sail works: replace fabric on cycle, upgrade masts and footings to engineered designs, and set procedures for taking sails down before severe winds.
- Sign and flagpole works: repair or replace corroded bases, and replace poles with fatigue cracking.
- Asbestos removal of weathered sheds and outbuildings by licensed contractors, or encapsulation where sound and undisturbed.
- Removal of redundant or unsafe structures.
- Approvals: obtain retrospective approval or remove non-compliant structures.
- Bin store relocation or fire-rated enclosures away from the building.
- Water feature treatment or decommissioning.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and engineering are lump sums. Repairs are itemised per structure or per post. Shade sail fabric is replaced on a cycle and is best carried as a recurring line; masts and footings are lump sums. Sign and flagpole replacement is per item. Asbestos removal is a lump sum per structure including licensed removal and clearance. Demolition of redundant structures is a lump sum.

Safety items are immediate; asbestos and approval issues are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Minor structures may be exempt development under state planning rules if they meet size and setback limits, otherwise they need approval; AS/NZS 1170.2 sets wind actions and shade structures in cyclonic regions need particular care; asbestos in outbuildings is managed under work health and safety and state asbestos rules.
- United Kingdom. Outbuildings may fall under permitted development or need planning permission and building regulations approval depending on size, use and location; the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 govern asbestos in non-domestic premises; signs may need advertisement consent.
- United States. Accessory structures follow local zoning and building codes, with permits above set sizes; ASCE 7 sets wind loads, and signs and flagpoles in high-wind areas need engineered foundations; asbestos is regulated by the EPA and states for renovation and demolition.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Approvals, permits and engineering for each ancillary structure.
- Shade sail installation certificates, design wind ratings and take-down procedures.
- Asbestos register entries for outbuildings.
- Inspection records for signs, flagpoles and shade structures.
- Water feature maintenance and water treatment records.
- Records of structures added after the main building was completed.
- Incident records involving these structures.

pages.title: Architectural & Decorative Features
pages.question: How do cornices, stone, terracotta and render ornament fail, how do you tell the causes apart, and when is it a public danger?
pages.answer: Ornament fails at the hidden metal that holds it on. Iron cramps and steel anchors rust, expand and split the stone or terracotta along their line, releasing the piece they were holding. Unprotected cornice tops feed water straight to those fixings. Crazed terracotta glaze lets water into hollow units. Cracks along a straight line with rust at the end, missing pieces and netting at street level mean the façade needs a close-up hammer survey now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about architectural & decorative features; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cornices, corbels, string courses, parapets, mouldings

sources.title: Preservation Brief 7: The Preservation of Historic Glazed Architectural Terra-Cotta

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Architectural and decorative features are the projecting and ornamental parts of a façade: cornices, string courses, parapet balustrades, pediments, window surrounds, columns and pilasters, finials, brackets and sculpture, in natural stone, terracotta and faience, cast stone, render on armatures, pressed metal and, more recently, glass-reinforced concrete and fibreglass. They are concentrated on buildings from the mid nineteenth century to about 1940, and on later buildings in the classical or art deco manner.

Two facts decide how they fail. First, most ornament is held in place by hidden metal: iron or steel cramps, dowels and armatures, or anchors tying hollow terracotta units back to a steel frame. Second, projections shed water poorly unless their top surfaces were protected, typically with lead, copper or a weathered top, so water sits exactly where the hidden metal is.

| Material | Typical period | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandstone and limestone with iron cramps and dowels | Nineteenth and early twentieth century | Cramp corrosion cracking and displacing stone; contour scaling and delamination of sandstone |
| Glazed architectural terracotta and faience | About 1880 to 1940, especially offices, banks, theatres and department stores | Hollow units on steel anchors; glaze crazing lets water in; anchor corrosion; frost spalling |
| Cast stone | 1900s to 1950s | Reinforcement close to the surface; cracking along bars |
| Render mouldings on armatures or brick cores | Victorian and Edwardian stock, interwar | Delamination from the backing; hidden armature corrosion |
| Pressed metal | Late nineteenth and early twentieth century | Corrosion from behind; fixing failure |
| GRC and fibreglass replacements | From the 1980s | Fixing condition; UV and coating wear |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural stone | 100 to 300 years | Stone type and bedding; pollution; salts; water on top surfaces |
| Terracotta and faience | 80 to 120 years and more | Glaze integrity; anchor condition; joint maintenance |
| Iron cramps and anchors | 50 to 100 years before they jack the stone | Water at the fixing |
| Render ornament | 40 to 80 years | Bond; armature corrosion; water from above |
| Lead and copper weatherings | 50 to 100 years | Fixing and detailing; theft in some areas |
| Lime mortar joints in ornament | 30 to 60 years | Exposure; top surfaces |

What shortens life:

- Missing weatherings on cornices and string courses, so water sits on the top surface and runs into joints.
- Cement repairs and cement pointing, which trap moisture and force decay into the stone or terracotta beside them.
- Impermeable coatings painted over stone and render.
- Abrasive or acid cleaning, which removes the protective surface of stone and the glaze of terracotta.
- Vegetation and birds: roots in joints, guano holding moisture.
- Pollution, which forms sulfate crusts on limestone and marble.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Corrosion jacking of hidden metal

Iron cramps and dowels set in stone, and steel anchors holding terracotta, rust when water reaches them. The rust expands and splits the unit along the line of the fixing, often shearing off a corner or the front of a moulding. The fixing that was holding the piece in place is now what releases it. Cracks that follow the line of a hidden cramp, often with rust staining, are the signature.

### Terracotta failure

Terracotta units are hollow, fired clay with a glaze or slip on the face. Crazed or cracked glaze lets water into the body; the water freezes or carries salts, and the glaze and face spall off. Water inside the unit reaches the steel anchors and, often, the steel frame behind. Units were frequently filled with brick or mortar, which holds water.

### Stone decay

Sandstone scales in sheets parallel to the surface (contour scaling) from salt crystallisation, and stone laid with its bedding planes parallel to the face (face-bedded) delaminates. Limestone and marble form black gypsum crusts in polluted air that blister and fall away taking the surface with them. Soft stone erodes, losing the detail of mouldings.

### Render ornament delamination

Render mouldings run on site or cast over brick cores and metal armatures lose their bond to the backing as water gets behind them. They sound hollow, crack around their perimeter, and can fall as a large piece.

### Cornice and projection failure

A cornice is a cantilever of stone or terracotta held in place by its own back weight and by cramps, sometimes by the parapet above. Water on the unprotected top surface penetrates the joints, corrodes the cramps and decays the backing. Removing or lowering a parapet above, often done in past alterations, reduces the weight holding the cornice in.

### Failed previous repairs

Cement patches and plastic repairs debond and fall; steel pins used in earlier repairs corrode in turn; resin repairs discolour.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Missing pieces of moulding; fresh breaks lighter in colour than the weathered surface.
- Cracks along the line of mouldings and at the ends of units; rust staining from joints and cracks.
- Crazed, spalled or missing glaze on terracotta; replaced units in a different colour.
- Vegetation growing from cornices and parapets; birds nesting in projections.
- Netting over ornament, scaffolding sheds or hoardings at street level.
- Aerial imagery of the top surfaces of cornices and parapets: weatherings missing, vegetation, ponding.

### Close up on site

- Hollow sound when tapped; movement of units under hand pressure.
- Sheet-like scaling and blistering of stone surfaces; black crusts.
- Open joints on top surfaces; failed or missing lead and copper.
- Previous cement patches debonding; corroded pins exposed.

### In the records

- Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings with unsafe findings, and make-safe records.
- Records of fragments falling, and insurance or council correspondence about them.
- Conservation management plans and heritage consents for previous repairs.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crack following a straight line through a stone unit, rust stain at its end, corner displaced | Cramp or dowel corrosion | Metal detector locates the cramp on the crack line; opening up shows rust |
| Sheets of stone lifting parallel to the face | Contour scaling from salts, or face-bedded stone | Salts in the debris; bedding planes visible parallel to the face |
| Glaze crazed and spalled across terracotta units | Water in the body of the unit; frost or salt | Moisture in the unit; spalls concentrated on exposed and top surfaces |
| Terracotta units cracking along joints with rust staining | Anchor corrosion behind the units | Opening shows corroded anchors or frame |
| Black crust blistering on limestone or marble | Gypsum crust from pollution | Sheltered areas worst; surface loss when crust falls |
| Hollow render moulding cracked around its edges | Delamination from the backing | Tapping; probing behind |
| Cornice top with vegetation and open joints, staining below | Missing weathering; water at the cramps | Aerial imagery; joints open on top |

> Ornament falls in pieces, and a small piece from a high cornice is lethal. Any ornament above a footpath, entrance or courtyard that has not been hammer-tapped close up should be treated as unknown, not sound.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, cracked or displaced ornament over a public or occupied area; recent fragments fallen | safety | Remove loose material and protect below immediately (netting, sidewalk shed, exclusion) |
| Ordinance finding of unsafe condition | deadline | Timing set by the ordinance; protection immediately |
| Active cramp or anchor corrosion cracking units, without displacement; widespread terracotta spalling | condition | Programme re-anchoring and repair in the near term |
| Weatherings and joints at age; surface erosion without loss of detail | lifecycle | Renewal on cycle with access for other façade work |
| Heritage façade over a footpath with no close-up survey on record | check | Close-up hammer survey before sizing works |
| Surface soiling, minor erosion | nil | Cleaning by appropriate method when warranted |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer or building surveyor with conservation experience leads, with a conservator or stonemason. Where the building is listed or heritage-registered, a conservation architect advises on method and consents.

- Close-up hammer survey of every unit over public areas and a sample elsewhere, removing anything loose at the time and recording it unit by unit on elevation drawings.
- Metal detection and ground-penetrating radar to locate cramps, dowels and anchors; borescope through joints.
- Opening up at representative locations to see anchor condition and the frame behind terracotta.
- Material analysis: stone identification, petrographic examination, mortar analysis, salt analysis.
- Infrared thermography to locate delamination in terracotta and render.
- Review of past repairs and their materials.

The report should map defects unit by unit, distinguish make-safe items from repairs, and specify methods and materials appropriate to the fabric.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Make safe: remove loose pieces and store them for reinstatement; netting or sidewalk sheds until repaired.
- Re-anchoring: remove corroded cramps and replace with stainless steel; drilled stainless pins set in resin or grout through units into sound backing.
- Weatherings: lead or copper flashings over cornices and string courses; repointing of top joints with lime mortar.
- Stone repair: indents (new stone pieced in), lime mortar repairs for small losses, replacement units cut to profile.
- Terracotta repair: crack repair and glaze consolidation for minor damage; replacement units from a specialist manufacturer, or GRC or cast stone substitutes where approved.
- Removal of harmful earlier repairs: cement patches, impermeable coatings, corroded steel pins.
- Cleaning by low-pressure water, poultices or other methods suited to the material, not abrasive blasting.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Survey is a lump sum plus access. Repairs are priced per unit, per anchor, per linear metre of cornice or string course, or by area for repointing and cleaning. Access, often by scaffold over a footpath, dominates. Protective netting and sidewalk sheds are recurring costs until the work is done. Replacement terracotta has long lead times.

Two-part lines are normal. Make-safe and ordinance repairs are code compliance or repairs and maintenance; re-anchoring and weatherings are lifecycle; conservation repairs follow the heritage approval process.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. State heritage legislation (for example the Heritage Act 2017 in Victoria and the Heritage Act 1977 in New South Wales) and local planning heritage overlays control works to listed fabric; the Burra Charter of Australia ICOMOS sets conservation practice. There is no periodic façade inspection regime; the owner's duty to the public is general.
- United Kingdom. Works to listed buildings need listed building consent under the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990; BS 7913 guides the conservation of historic buildings and BS 8221-1 and BS 8221-2 cover cleaning and repair; Historic England publishes technical guidance on stone, terracotta and lime.
- United States. The Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties and the National Park Service Preservation Briefs (Brief 7 covers glazed architectural terra-cotta) set practice; local landmarks commissions control listed buildings. New York's FISP examines ornament on buildings over six storeys every five years, and its parapet rule requires annual observation of street-facing parapets; Chicago, Boston and San Francisco have similar regimes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Façade inspection reports, ordinance filings and make-safe records.
- Records of falling fragments and any incident reports.
- Heritage listing, conservation management plan and consents for past works.
- Specifications and records of previous repairs, with materials used.
- Netting, shed or hoarding records and their duration.

- Records of cleaning methods used on the façade.

pages.title: Automatic Sprinkler Systems
pages.question: How do sprinkler systems fail, when is a system no longer adequate for a building, and which findings leave a building unprotected?
pages.answer: Sprinkler systems fail more often from what changes around them than from wear. Warehouses store more, higher or different goods than the design allows; fit-outs add rooms without heads and block spray patterns; valves closed for works stay closed. Internally, dry systems corrode where water is trapped, wet systems suffer microbial corrosion and pinhole leaks, and town main pressures fall. A perfect system can be inadequate for its current use.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about automatic sprinkler systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Sprinkler heads, valve sets, pipework

sources.title: NFPA 25 Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
An automatic sprinkler system discharges water onto a fire from heat-activated heads above it, controlling or extinguishing the fire before it spreads. It comprises a water supply (town main, storage tanks, fire pumps), control valves and alarm valve sets, pipework (risers, mains, branch lines), sprinkler heads, flow and tamper switches connected to the fire alarm, and a fire brigade booster or inlet. Each head opens independently when its glass bulb or fusible link reaches its rated temperature; only heads near the fire operate.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet pipe | Most heated buildings | Pipes full of water; simplest and most reliable |
| Dry pipe | Unheated spaces at risk of freezing: car parks in cold climates, loading docks, cold stores | Pipes full of air; water enters when a head opens; corrosion where water remains |
| Pre-action and deluge | Data rooms, heritage, special hazards | Covered on the specialist suppression page |
| Residential and domestic | Apartments, aged care, houses | Fast-response heads designed for life safety in dwellings |
| Storage protection (ESFR, in-rack) | Warehouses and logistics | Designed for a specific storage height, arrangement and commodity |

A sprinkler system is designed for a hazard: the building's use, ceiling heights, and in warehouses the commodity, packaging, storage height and racking. When the use changes, the system may no longer be adequate even though nothing in it has deteriorated. This is the most important and most overlooked sprinkler finding in industrial and retail buildings.

Codes have extended sprinkler requirements over time: new residential buildings over 11 metres in England since 2020, new apartment buildings of four storeys and more in Australia from the 2019 code amendments, and most new multi-family buildings in the United States. Older buildings of the same type are often unsprinklered, which is a fire safety strategy matter rather than a defect.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black steel wet pipework | 50 years and more | Water chemistry; microbiologically influenced corrosion |
| Galvanised dry pipework | 20 to 40 years | Water left in pipes; condensation |
| CPVC pipework | 30 to 50 years | Chemical incompatibility |
| Standard sprinkler heads | 50 years, then sample testing | Environment; corrosion; loading |
| Fast-response heads | 20 years, then sample testing | Environment |
| Alarm and dry pipe valves | 25 to 40 years with internal inspection | Water quality; maintenance |
| Control valves | 30 years and more | Exercising |
| Flow and tamper switches | 15 to 25 years | Electrical components |

What shortens life:

- Water left in dry pipe systems after trip tests, which corrodes pipe from the inside.
- Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) in wet systems, producing pinhole leaks.
- Oxygen introduced by frequent draining and refilling.
- Corrosive atmospheres: car parks, swimming pools, cold stores, industrial processes.
- CPVC contact with incompatible products: some cable sheaths, sealants, spray foam and oils.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Change of hazard

A warehouse designed for low storage of ordinary goods that now holds high-piled plastics, or racking taller than the design height, overwhelms the system: too few heads open, too little water, and the fire outruns it. Retail and industrial tenancies change commodity and layout far more often than sprinkler systems are redesigned.

### Obstruction and shielding

Storage stacked too close to heads, new ductwork, cable trays, lights and partitions below or beside heads, and ceilings lowered in fit-outs block the spray pattern or create unsprinklered areas. Heads painted, taped, bagged during works or loaded with dust and grease respond late or not at all.

### Internal corrosion and leaks

Dry pipe systems corrode where trapped water sits at low points; wet systems suffer MIC, which produces tubercles and pinhole leaks and can block small pipes. Corrosion products can block heads. Leaks in occupied buildings cause damage and lead to systems being shut down.

### Impairments

Control valves closed for works and not reopened leave parts of a building unprotected. Supervised valves report closure to the fire panel; unsupervised valves do not.

### Water supply decline

Town main pressures fall as networks change; tanks lose capacity to sediment and corrosion; pumps deteriorate. A system that met its design at commissioning may not now, and only a flow test shows it.

### Head defects and recalls

Certain sprinkler heads have been subject to recalls; corroded heads and those in hot or corrosive areas can fail to open; heads replaced with the wrong temperature rating, response type or coverage break the design.

### CPVC cracking

CPVC sprinkler pipe used in residential and light hazard buildings cracks when exposed to incompatible chemicals, sometimes years after installation.

### Freezing

Wet pipes in unheated spaces freeze and burst; dry systems with poor drainage freeze at low points.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the building

- Storage within the clearance zone below heads; racking taller than the design; changed commodities.
- Heads painted, taped, bagged, loaded with dust, or corroded.
- New partitions, ceilings, ductwork and lights below or around heads; rooms without heads.
- Signs of leaks and corrosion on pipework; drips and staining below.
- Spare head cabinet: stocked with heads matching those installed.
- Valve room: control valves open and secured; gauges reading; signage.
- Booster or brigade inlet accessible and in good order.

### In the records

- Design certificate and hydraulic calculations, with the hazard classification and storage design.
- Routine service records: weekly or monthly valve checks, alarm tests, flow tests.
- Long-interval inspections: internal pipe inspections and head sampling.
- Impairment log.
- Leak history.
- Changes of use or tenancy since design.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warehouse storing more, higher or different goods than designed | Hazard change beyond design | Design certificate against current storage |
| Pinhole leaks in wet pipework | Microbiologically influenced corrosion | Pipe section examination; water testing |
| Leaks at low points of a dry system | Trapped water corrosion | Drain and inspect low points |
| Flow test below the design point | Water supply decline or obstruction | Flow test against design curve |
| Fire panel shows valve closed | Impairment not cleared | Valve inspection |
| Rooms without heads after fit-out | Coverage gap | Survey against layout |
| Cracked CPVC fittings | Chemical incompatibility | Products in contact |

> A sprinkler system can be in perfect condition and still be inadequate for what the building now stores. In warehouses and retail, the design basis against current use is the first thing to check.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control valves closed; storage hazard beyond design; heads covered or obstructed over large areas; water supply below design | safety | Restore protection or reduce the hazard now; fire watch until done |
| Leaks causing damage; system out of service | failure | Repair now with impairment management |
| Routine and long-interval inspections due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Corrosion, MIC, head defects, coverage gaps after fit-outs | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Pipework or heads at end of life; sample testing due | lifecycle | Plan replacement |
| No design certificate; use changed; no recent flow test | check | Design review and testing |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer leads, with the sprinkler maintenance contractor; for storage buildings, the review is against the storage design standards.

- Design review: design certificate, hazard classification, hydraulic calculations, storage design basis, against the building's current use, layout and storage.
- Coverage and obstruction survey of all areas, including new rooms, ceilings and storage.
- Head survey: type, temperature, response, condition, recalls, painting and loading; sample removal and laboratory testing at the age the standard sets.
- Internal pipe inspection: flushing, opening at representative points, internal camera inspection, and pipe sampling for MIC where leaks occur.
- Water supply flow test at the design point.
- Valve inspection: control valves open and supervised; alarm and dry pipe valves internally inspected.
- Records review: service history, impairments, leaks.

The report should state whether the system matches the current hazard, coverage and obstruction issues, water supply adequacy, internal condition, and works needed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restore protection: open and supervise valves; remove covers; clear storage from below heads; manage impairments with permits and fire watches.
- Match storage to the system: reduce storage height or change commodities, or redesign the system (more water, larger heads, in-rack sprinklers).
- Coverage additions after fit-outs.
- Head replacement: recalled, painted, corroded or aged heads.
- Corrosion treatment: replace corroded sections; nitrogen inerting of dry and pre-action systems; MIC treatment and replacement of affected pipe.
- Water supply improvement: pumps, tanks, larger connections.
- Dry system drainage and auxiliary drains at low points.
- CPVC protection: identify and isolate incompatible products; replace cracked sections.

- Spare heads: restock the spare head cabinet with heads matching each type installed, with the correct wrench.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine and long-interval inspections are recurring contracts, with lump sums for internal pipe inspections, head sampling and flow tests. Head replacement is per head. Coverage additions per head with design. Redesign for storage is a lump-sum project, possibly with pumps and tanks. Pipework replacement is by length, with access and ceiling works dominating in occupied buildings.

Inspections and safety rectification are code compliance; pipework and heads at end of life are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance. A change of use that requires redesign is usually borne by the project that changes the use.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets where sprinklers are required, including newer requirements for apartment buildings; AS 2118.1 governs design and installation; AS 1851 sets routine service, including weekly or monthly checks, annual flow tests, and long-interval inspections and testing; sprinklers are essential safety measures with annual certification.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B sets where sprinklers are required, including new residential buildings over 11 metres; BS EN 12845 with the LPC Rules covers commercial systems and BS 9251 residential systems, with weekly tests, quarterly to annual inspections and long-interval inspections; insurers often set additional requirements.
- United States. NFPA 13, 13R and 13D govern design; NFPA 25 sets inspection, testing and maintenance, including weekly to annual checks, five-yearly internal pipe assessments, and testing of sample heads at 50 years (20 for fast-response) and periodically thereafter; the International Building and Fire Codes set where sprinklers are required.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Design certificate, hazard classification and hydraulic calculations.
- Routine service records and annual certification.
- Flow test results against the design curve.
- Internal pipe inspection and head sampling reports.
- Impairment log.
- Leak and repair history.
- Storage arrangement and commodity description for warehouses.
- Insurer surveys and recommendations.

- Records of recalled heads identified and replaced.
- Fit-out records showing sprinkler alterations and who certified them.

pages.title: Basement, Cellars & Retaining Walls
pages.question: How do basements and retaining walls fail, and when is a leaning wall dangerous?
pages.answer: Basements leak at cracks, joints and penetrations; whether leaks follow rain or run all year separates surface water from groundwater. Retaining walls fail when drainage behind them blocks and water pressure builds: they rotate, bulge and crack, often after heavy rain. Timber sleeper walls rot at the posts below ground. Loads added behind walls overload them. A wall leaning or moving next to people, buildings or boundaries is a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about basement, cellars & retaining walls; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Perimeter walls, structural integrity, damp-proofing, tanking

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Basements and cellars are rooms below ground, enclosed by walls that hold back soil and often groundwater. Retaining walls hold back soil at changes in level on a site: driveways, embankments, terraces, and the edges of basement excavations. Both resist earth pressure, and both must manage water, because water behind a wall both adds pressure and finds its way through.

| Form | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry cellar walls | Older houses and terraces | Damp and salts; no waterproofing; bowing under earth pressure |
| Reinforced concrete basement walls | Modern buildings and car parks | Leaks at cracks, joints and penetrations |
| Diaphragm, secant and contiguous pile walls | Deep basements in cities | Leaks between piles; joint seals |
| Cantilever concrete or blockwork retaining walls | Sites, driveways, landscaping | Rotation; cracking; blocked drainage |
| Timber sleeper walls | Australian residential sites | Decay of sleepers and posts; overturning |
| Crib, gabion and gravity walls | Embankments and landscaping | Movement; corrosion of gabion wire |
| Anchored and soil-nailed walls | Deep cuts and constrained sites | Anchor corrosion; monitoring |

Basement waterproofing follows three broad approaches, set out in Britain as Types A, B and C: a barrier applied to the structure (tanking), a structurally integral watertight concrete, and a drained cavity that accepts some water and pumps it away. Many buildings combine them. Which approach the building has decides how leaks are fixed.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete walls | Life of the building | Cracking; reinforcement corrosion |
| Applied tanking membranes | 20 to 40 years | Movement; installation quality |
| Drained cavity membranes and pumps | Membranes 30 years and more; pumps 10 to 15 | Pump maintenance |
| Timber sleeper retaining walls | 10 to 25 years | Treatment; drainage; soil contact |
| Blockwork and concrete retaining walls | 50 years and more | Drainage; reinforcement |
| Ground anchors | 25 to 50 years | Corrosion protection |
| Agricultural drains behind walls | 15 to 30 years | Silting; roots |

What shortens life:

- Blocked drainage behind retaining walls and basement walls, which raises water pressure.
- Surcharge loads: new structures, vehicles, fill and pools placed behind walls that were not designed for them.
- Tree roots pushing on and through walls.
- Rising groundwater and changed drainage on and around the site.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Water ingress

Water enters basements through cracks, construction joints, tie holes, service penetrations and the junction between walls and floors. Leaks that run in wet weather point to surface water; leaks that run all year point to groundwater. Efflorescence, tide marks and mould follow, and stored goods and services are damaged.

### Hydrostatic and earth pressure

A wall designed for drained soil fails when its drainage blocks: water pressure adds to earth pressure and the wall rotates, bulges or cracks. Many retaining wall failures follow heavy rain on walls with blocked weep holes or failed drains.

### Rotation and bowing

Cantilever retaining walls rotate forward at the top; masonry cellar walls bow inward under earth pressure where floors do not restrain them. Movement that continues leads to collapse.

### Timber sleeper decay

Timber sleepers and posts rot where they are in contact with wet soil, and walls lean and collapse, often after a decade or two. Posts rot below ground first, so a wall can look sound until it fails.

### Surcharge

Driveways, car parking, new buildings, pools and fill placed close behind a wall add load it was never designed for.

### Anchor and reinforcement corrosion

Ground anchors and soil nails lose capacity as their steel corrodes; reinforcement in walls corrodes where water penetrates cracks.

### Radon and ground gases

Basements in radon-affected areas and on contaminated land collect radon or other ground gases through cracks and joints. Radon is a recognised cause of lung cancer; testing is advised in affected areas in Britain and the United States.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Retaining walls leaning forward, bulging or cracked; fence and handrail lines out of true.
- Weep holes blocked or dry after rain; water seeping through the wall face.
- Timber sleepers soft at the base; posts loose.
- Ground cracking or slumping behind walls; loads placed close behind them.
- Basement walls with damp patches, efflorescence, tide marks and mould.
- Water entering at joints and penetrations; sump pumps running constantly.

### In the records

- Waterproofing specification and warranty.
- Retaining wall design and approvals.
- Leak and flood history.
- Monitoring of wall movement.
- Radon test results in affected areas.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basement leaks only in wet weather | Surface water reaching the wall | Correlation with rainfall; surface drainage |
| Basement leaks all year | Groundwater | Groundwater levels |
| Retaining wall leaning more after heavy rain | Blocked drainage and water pressure | Weep holes and drains inspected |
| Timber wall leaning with soft posts | Decay below ground | Probe posts |
| Wall cracked behind a new driveway or structure | Surcharge | Loads against design |
| Inward bowing of cellar walls | Lack of restraint and earth pressure | Survey; restraint details |

> A retaining wall that is leaning, bulging or moving next to a footpath, driveway, building or boundary is a safety finding. Keep people and loads away and get an engineer's assessment.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retaining wall leaning or moving beside a public area, building or boundary; radon above action levels | safety | Exclude people and loads, prop or remediate now |
| Basement flooding; wall collapse | failure | Repair now |
| Seepage, efflorescence, blocked drainage, early rotation | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Sleeper walls and pumps at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Walls without design approval; radon untested in affected areas | check | Assess |
| Minor damp | nil | Monitor |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural or geotechnical engineer leads; a waterproofing specialist joins for basements.

- Wall survey: verticality, bulging and cracking, with fixed survey points for monitoring over time.
- Drainage inspection: weep holes, drains behind walls by CCTV, outlets and surface drainage.
- Leak tracing: mapping wet areas, monitoring in wet and dry periods, and testing at joints and penetrations.
- Timber probing of sleepers and posts at and below ground.
- Load review: what sits behind the wall against its design.
- Design and approval check for retaining walls above the height that needs approval.
- Radon testing in affected areas.

The report should state structural stability, the waterproofing approach and its failures, drainage condition, and remedies.

For basements, testing in both a dry and a prolonged wet period is often needed before the source of water can be confirmed and the right waterproofing repair chosen.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restore drainage: clear or replace drains behind walls, open weep holes, fix surface drainage.
- Crack and joint injection with polyurethane or epoxy resins.
- Drained cavity systems on the inside of basements with sumps and pumps where external access is impossible.
- External tanking where walls can be excavated.
- Retaining wall strengthening: buttresses, anchors or soil nails, or rebuilding.
- Sleeper wall replacement with concrete or masonry systems.
- Remove surcharge loads or redesign the wall for them.
- Radon mitigation: sealing and sub-floor depressurisation.

- Joint and penetration seals: hydrophilic strips, injection hoses and puddle flanges at service penetrations, which are the commonest leak points.
- Surface water management: regrading, drainage channels and downpipe connections so rainwater is carried away from basement and retaining walls.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation and monitoring are lump sums. Injection is priced by length of crack or joint; drained cavity systems by area with pumps; external tanking by area with excavation; retaining wall rebuilding by length and height. Drainage repairs by length. Pumps recur on cycle.

Rebuilding and new waterproofing are lifecycle; drainage and injection are repairs and maintenance; unsafe walls are immediate.

Basement leak repairs in occupied car parks and plant rooms often need out-of-hours access and protection of services, which can exceed the cost of the injection itself.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4678 governs earth-retaining structures; the National Construction Code covers damp and weatherproofing; councils require approval for retaining walls above set heights, often around a metre, and walls near boundaries can involve neighbours.
- United Kingdom. BS 8102 sets the protection of below-ground structures against water, with grades of environment and Types A, B and C; BS EN 1997 covers geotechnical design; the UK Health Security Agency maps radon-affected areas.
- United States. The International Building Code covers damp-proofing and waterproofing (Section 1805) and retaining walls (Section 1807); the EPA recommends radon testing and mitigation above its action level.

In all three jurisdictions, a retaining wall on or near a boundary can affect a neighbour's land, and responsibility depends on who built it and whose land it supports; failures often lead to disputes, so ownership and approvals should be established early. Strata and condominium buildings usually treat basement structure and waterproofing as common property.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Waterproofing specification, type and warranty.
- Retaining wall designs and approvals.
- Leak, flood and pump records.
- Movement monitoring data.
- Drainage drawings.
- Radon test results in affected areas.

- Survey plans showing walls in relation to boundaries.
- Geotechnical reports for the site.
- Records of loads or structures added behind walls.
- Correspondence with neighbours about shared walls.

pages.title: Bathrooms & Wet Areas
pages.question: How do bathrooms and wet areas leak, how do you find the source, and when does resealing stop being enough?
pages.answer: Wet areas fail at the membrane nobody sees: gaps at wall-floor junctions, around the waste, at the threshold and at tap penetrations let every shower soak the substrate, and in apartments water appears in the ceiling below. Leaks that follow showering point to the membrane, screen or floor; constant leaks point to pipes. Regrouting stops water briefly but does not repair a failed membrane: strip and re-waterproof. Fans venting into the roof grow mould.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about bathrooms & wet areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Bathrooms, ensuites, powder rooms, WCs, laundry wet areas \u2014 waterproofing, tiling, fixtures, fittings

sources.title: TCNA Handbook for Ceramic, Glass, and Stone Tile Installation

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Bathrooms and wet areas are the bathrooms, ensuites, showers, toilets and laundries in homes and apartments. Functionally they must contain water, remove moisture, deliver safe hot water, drain properly and stay hygienic. Their most important component is one nobody sees: the waterproofing membrane under the tiles and behind the shower walls. Wet area leaks are among the most common and costly defects in residential buildings, especially apartments, where a failed shower floods the unit below and damages structure for years before it shows.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waterproofing membrane | Liquid or sheet membrane under tiles, turned up walls, over hobs and at door thresholds | Continuity at junctions, penetrations and wastes |
| Floor falls and wastes | Screed falling to floor wastes with puddle flanges | Water draining to the waste, not ponding or escaping |
| Tiles, grout and sealant | Ceramic or stone tiles with grout; flexible sealant at junctions | Not waterproof on their own; movement joints |
| Shower enclosure | Screen, hob or hobless step-down, waterstop at the entry | Containing spray and water flow |
| Fixtures and plumbing | WC, basin, bath, taps, mixers, wastes | Leaks at seals, connections and penetrations |
| Exhaust ventilation | Fan ducted to outside | Removing moisture, preventing mould |
| Substrate | Concrete slab, fibre cement or timber floor; wall sheets | Movement; rot if wet |

Era is a strong guide. Many bathrooms built before the 1980s have no membrane at all and rely on tiles and grout; later bathrooms have membranes of varying quality; current standards demand membranes with continuous upturns, flashing at thresholds, and floors falling to the waste. Timber-framed floors move and crack tiles and membranes more than concrete.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waterproofing membrane | 15 to 25 years if well installed; can fail within months if not | Installation quality; substrate movement |
| Grout | 5 to 15 years before cracking and staining | Cleaning; movement |
| Silicone sealant at junctions | 3 to 10 years | Mould; movement; cleaning |
| Tapware and mixers | 10 to 20 years | Water quality |
| Shower screens and seals | 10 to 20 years; seals 3 to 7 | Use; hardware |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Run hours; dust |
| Bathroom refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years | Leaks; wear; style |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Poor membrane installation: thin coats, unreinforced junctions, membranes stopped short at walls and doors, and wastes without puddle flanges.
- Substrate movement in timber floors and lightweight walls cracking tiles and membranes.
- Hobless showers without adequate falls and waterstops, letting water flow across the floor.
- Neglected sealant at junctions and around screens.
- Weak or unused exhaust leaving moisture in the room.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Membrane failure

Water reaches the substrate through gaps in the membrane at wall-floor junctions, around the floor waste, at the shower entry and threshold, and where taps, mixers and pipes penetrate the wall. Grout and tiles are not waterproof; once the membrane fails, every shower soaks the substrate. In apartments water travels along the slab and appears in the ceiling below or in adjoining rooms, sometimes metres away.

### Threshold and waterstop failure

At bathroom doors and shower entries, water flows along the floor or wicks under the tiles beyond the wet area. Missing or poorly sealed waterstop angles let water reach skirtings, carpets and timber floors outside the bathroom, which swell and rot.

### Inadequate falls

Floors that do not fall to the waste, or fall the wrong way, leave water ponding against walls and doorways and push it toward weak points in the membrane.

### Plumbing leaks

Leaking mixer bodies and connections inside walls, toilet pan seals, cistern connections, bath wastes and pipe joints leak constantly, unlike membrane leaks that follow showering.

### Substrate damage

Water in timber floors and framing causes rot and termite attack; in fibre cement and plasterboard, swelling and mould; in concrete slabs, corrosion of reinforcement over time.

### Mould and condensation

Bathrooms without effective exhaust, or with fans discharging into the roof space, stay humid after showers; mould grows on ceilings, grout and sealant. Fans venting into roof spaces cause condensation and mould there too.

### Slips and scalding

Smooth wet tiles cause falls, especially for older people. Hot water without tempering to safe temperatures scalds children and the elderly.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the bathroom

- Cracked, loose or drummy (hollow-sounding) tiles, especially near the shower and waste.
- Discoloured, missing or cracked grout; mouldy or split silicone at junctions.
- Water ponding on the floor after a shower; water crossing the threshold.
- Exhaust fan weak, noisy or discharging into the ceiling space.
- Mould on ceilings and around the shower.
- Moisture meter readings elevated at the base of walls and around the shower.

### Around and below

- Swollen skirtings, door frames and vanity bases near the bathroom door.
- Stained, bubbling or mouldy ceilings in the room or unit below.
- Damp carpet or lifting floor coverings outside the bathroom.
- Rot and termite damage in timber floors below, seen from the sub-floor.

### In the records

- Waterproofing certificates and installer details.
- Leak complaints from neighbours below.
- Previous repairs and resealing.
- Building defect claims.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling stain below appears after showers and dries between | Membrane, screen or shower floor failure | Flood test of the shower floor; spray test of the screen |
| Stain below that is wet all the time | Pressurised pipe or fitting leak | Pressure test; water meter with outlets closed |
| Swollen skirting or door frame outside the bathroom | Water escaping at the threshold or waterstop | Moisture readings; flood test |
| Drummy tiles around the waste | Water under tiles from membrane or waste flange failure | Lift a tile; inspect the flange |
| Stain below the WC | Pan seal or cistern connection leak | Dye test in the cistern and pan |
| Mould on the ceiling | Inadequate exhaust or fan not ducted outside | Fan airflow; duct route |

> Leaks that follow showering point to the membrane, screen or floor; leaks that are constant point to pipes. Regrouting and resealing can stop water at the surface for a while, but they do not repair a failed membrane.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water damaging structure, electrical fittings or another dwelling; hot water above safe temperatures for vulnerable occupants | safety | Stop use of the shower or fix now |
| Active leak to the unit below; rotted floor | failure | Repair now |
| Defect warranty or tribunal deadlines | deadline | Act within the period |
| Cracked grout, failed sealant, weak exhaust, mould | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Bathroom at end of refurbishment cycle, or no membrane in an older bathroom | lifecycle | Plan a full strip and re-waterproof |
| Moisture readings elevated with no visible damage | check | Investigate further |
| Normal | nil | Routine resealing |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or wet area specialist leads; a plumber joins for pressure testing; in apartments, access to the unit below is essential.

- Moisture mapping with a meter around the shower, at wall bases, at the threshold and outside the door, and on the ceiling below.
- Thermal imaging to trace wet areas in walls and ceilings.
- Flood test: plug the waste and flood the floor or shower base for a set period, then check below and around for water.
- Spray and use tests of screens and fixtures.
- Dye tests of WC pans and cisterns.
- Pressure test of hot and cold pipework, or a meter test with all outlets closed.
