- Invasive inspection: lift a tile at the waste or threshold, or open the ceiling below, to see the membrane and substrate.
- Exhaust check: airflow and where the duct discharges.
- Sub-floor inspection below timber-floored bathrooms for rot and termites.

The report should identify the source of each leak with evidence, the extent of substrate damage, whether the membrane can be repaired or must be replaced, and in strata buildings whether the cause is common property or within the lot.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Regrout and reseal as maintenance or a short-term measure where the membrane is sound; it does not fix membrane failure.
- Penetrating sealers and surface coatings applied over tiles as temporary measures, with the understanding that they rarely last.
- Strip and re-waterproof: remove tiles and screed, repair the substrate, install a compliant membrane with reinforced junctions, upturns, waste flanges and threshold waterstops, re-screed to falls and retile. This is the only lasting fix for a failed membrane.
- Plumbing repairs of mixers, connections, pan seals and wastes.
- Shower screen repair: new seals, adjustment or replacement.
- Exhaust: replace weak fans with ducted fans discharging outside, with run-on timers or humidity control.
- Substrate repair: replace rotted timber and swollen sheets; treat termite damage.
- Safety: slip-resistant floor tiles and tempering valves on hot water.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Regrouting and resealing are small items but recur. Strip and re-waterproof is priced per bathroom and is a significant project, with temporary loss of the bathroom and making good of adjoining finishes and the ceiling below. Plumbing repairs are itemised. Exhaust upgrades are per fan with ducting. In apartments, consequential damage below often costs as much as the bathroom itself.

Full re-waterproofing is lifecycle or a defect repair; leaks are failures; resealing is repairs and maintenance; in new buildings, claims may fall under statutory warranties.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 3740 sets waterproofing of domestic wet areas, with a revised edition in 2021 tightening falls, upturns and threshold details; the National Construction Code requires exhaust from bathrooms and laundries to discharge to the outside in newer homes; state home building laws provide statutory warranties against defects (for example in New South Wales), and strata law decides whether the membrane is common property or part of the lot, which varies by plan.
- United Kingdom. BS 5385 covers wall and floor tiling, including wet areas; Approved Document F sets extract ventilation rates; NHBC Standards set warranty requirements for new homes; leasehold terms decide responsibility in flats.
- United States. The International Residential and Plumbing Codes set shower pan and wet area requirements, with membranes commonly to ANSI A118.10 and practice to the TCNA Handbook; exhaust fans must discharge outdoors; condominium declarations set responsibility.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Waterproofing certificates and installer details.
- Leak complaints from the unit below or neighbours.
- Records of previous repairs, regrouting and resealing.
- Building defect claims and warranty details for newer buildings.
- Strata plan and by-laws defining membrane ownership.
- Plumbing compliance certificates for renovations.

- Moisture or thermal imaging reports from earlier investigations.

pages.title: Building Maintenance Units (BMU)
pages.question: How do building maintenance units and façade access systems fail, how is their position established, and when are they unusable?
pages.answer: Façade access equipment carries people at height, so its position is set by certification as much as wear. An overdue inspection, missing logbook or uncertified anchors means it cannot be used and façade maintenance stops. The physical failures are fatigue cracks at welds and the slewing ring, worn brakes, degraded ropes, water in sockets and track fixings, and obsolete controls that keep a unit out of service for months. Units over ten years old need a major inspection.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about building maintenance units (bmu); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cradles, gantries, track/guide systems

sources.title: 29 CFR 1910.27 Scaffolds and rope descent systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Building maintenance units and façade access equipment are the permanent systems used to reach the outside of a building for cleaning, inspection and repair. They are lifting equipment that carries people at height, so their condition is set by statutory inspection and certification as much as by wear, and a failed or uncertified system stops façade maintenance altogether.

| Form | Where it is found | Key components |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof-mounted BMU (track or rail mounted) | Towers and large offices | Carriage on rails or a track, slewing ring, jib or luffing arm, hoists, wire ropes, cradle, controls, counterweight |
| Monorail with trolley and cradle | Mid-rise offices, atria, curved façades | Monorail track fixed to the structure or parapet, trolley, hoist, cradle |
| Davit system | Mid-rise buildings | Fixed or portable davit arms in sockets along the roof edge; cradle or rope access from them |
| Parapet clamps and outriggers | Older and lower buildings | Temporary suspension points clamped to parapets |
| Rope access anchors | Most buildings over a few storeys | Permanent anchors for rope descent systems and abseil work |
| Atrium and internal gantries | Retail centres, atria, institutional buildings | Gantries or travelling platforms on rails |
| Façade restraint system | Tall buildings with cradles | Restraint rails, buttons or sockets on the façade that tie the cradle to the building in wind |

The system must reach every part of the façade that needs maintenance. A building's façade access strategy sets which equipment serves which elevation. Façade changes over time, such as new canopies, louvres, signs or balconies, can leave elevations that the equipment can no longer reach.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMU structure, carriage and track | 25 to 40 years | Coastal exposure; maintenance; fatigue at highly stressed welds |
| Slewing ring bearing | 20 to 30 years | Lubrication; use |
| Controls and electrical systems | 15 to 25 years | Obsolescence of parts; water ingress |
| Hoists and brakes | 15 to 25 years | Use; maintenance |
| Wire ropes | Replaced on condition, typically 5 to 10 years | Use, corrosion, damage; discard criteria |
| Cradle | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; impact damage |
| Davit arms and sockets | 25 to 40 years | Water in sockets; coating |
| Rope access anchors | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; roof works disturbing fixings; recertification |

What shortens life:

- Infrequent use: equipment used once or twice a year seizes, corrodes and is neglected between uses.
- Coastal and rooftop exposure: salt, UV and water on equipment stored uncovered on the roof.
- Water in davit sockets and track fixings, which corrodes the base and leaks through the roof membrane.
- Lapsed maintenance contracts and lapsed certification.
- Obsolete controls, which turn a minor fault into a long outage.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Structural fatigue and corrosion

The jib, carriage and slewing assembly carry cyclic loads at high stress points. Fatigue cracks start at welds and section changes; corrosion reduces section at connections and fixings. Track and rail fixings corrode where water collects, and where they penetrate the roof, they leak.

### Stability

Roof-mounted units rely on counterweight and rail clamps to stay on the roof under load and wind. Altered counterweights, worn clamps or modified units have led to instability incidents; regulators in Australia have issued safety alerts on BMU stability.

### Wire rope deterioration

Ropes lose strength through broken wires, corrosion, abrasion and kinking. They are discarded against defined criteria; a rope that is not inspected to those criteria can fail.

### Hoist, brake and drive wear

Hoist brakes, gearboxes and drives wear with use and seize without it. Brake failure on a hoist carrying people is the critical mechanical failure.

### Control obsolescence and water

Controls, limit switches and safety devices age, take in water and become unsupported. Parts become unavailable and the unit stays out of service while controls are re-engineered.

### Anchor and socket corrosion

Davit sockets fill with water and corrode from the inside. Rope access anchors corrode at their base, and roof works that disturb the membrane around them can compromise their fixing. Anchors that are not inspected and recertified on schedule cannot be relied on.

### Loss of coverage

Façade alterations and new rooftop plant can block reach or travel, leaving elevations that can only be reached by hired equipment.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From aerial imagery and the roof

- Equipment present: track, carriage, monorail, davits, anchors; covered or uncovered.
- Corrosion on the unit, track and fixings; ponding around track fixings and sockets.
- Rooftop plant or structures in the travel path of the unit.

### On site

- Inspection tags and the logbook: current, overdue or missing.
- Rust at welds, connections and the slewing ring; oil leaks from hoists and gearboxes.
- Wire ropes with broken wires, corrosion or kinks.
- Controls cabinet condition, water ingress, labels and warning signs.
- Davit sockets full of water or debris; anchors loose or corroded.
- Façade restraint points present and usable.

### In the records

- Periodic and major inspection reports, with outstanding defects.
- Plant registration, design registration and load test records.
- Maintenance contract and service reports; unit out of service for extended periods.
- Façade access strategy and whether it still covers every elevation.
- Anchor certification with dates; rescue plans.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
BMU problems are diagnosed more from records than from sight. The question is less "what is wrong" than "can this equipment be used, and for how long".

| What you find | What it means | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspection overdue or logbook missing | Equipment cannot lawfully be used | Last inspection date against the required interval |
| Major inspection never done on a unit more than ten years old | Hidden structural condition unknown | Records; Australian guidance calls for a major inspection at that age |
| Unit out of service for months, waiting on parts | Control obsolescence | Manufacturer support status; service reports |
| Corrosion at track fixings and leaks below them | Water at roof penetrations | Membrane condition at the fixings; leak log |
| Hired equipment used for some elevations | Coverage gap | Façade access strategy against the current façade |
| Anchors without certification records | Anchors cannot be relied on | Certification records and intervals |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structural crack, brake fault, failed safety device, or failed inspection item on equipment carrying people | safety | Tag out of service immediately; repair before any use |
| Equipment out of service with façade maintenance stopped; anchors uncertified | failure | Restore now or arrange alternative access; façade inspections and cleaning depend on it |
| Periodic inspection or certification due | deadline | Timing set by the regulation or standard |
| Corrosion, wear and leaks at fixings without a failed item | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Controls approaching obsolescence; unit approaching end of structural life | lifecycle | Plan modernisation or replacement |
| Unit more than ten years old with no major inspection; coverage of the current façade unknown | check | Major inspection and coverage study |
| Minor wear in a maintained, certified system | nil | Routine servicing |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A competent person, usually the maintenance contractor or an independent lifting equipment inspector, carries out periodic and major inspections. A façade access consultant assesses coverage and strategy.

- Records review: logbook, inspection reports, registrations, load tests, maintenance reports.
- Periodic inspection of the structure, mechanisms, ropes, brakes, controls and safety devices at the statutory interval.
- Major inspection: strip-down and non-destructive testing of welds, slewing ring and highly stressed components, with load testing, at the interval set by the standard or the inspector.
- Wire rope examination against discard criteria.
- Anchor and davit socket inspection and proof load testing where required.
- Coverage study: mapping the reach of the equipment against the current façade, including additions since installation.

The report should state whether the equipment is fit for use, defects by priority, the date of the next periodic and major inspection, remaining service life, and any elevations not covered.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Repair of defects found at inspection; rope replacement; brake and hoist overhaul.
- Control modernisation: replacement of controls and electrical systems on a sound structure, often the main mid-life investment.
- Track and fixing refurbishment with renewal of the roof membrane at penetrations.
- Replacement of the unit at end of structural life, with crane lift, roof works and recommissioning.
- Strategy change: replacing a BMU with davits or rope access anchors where the façade allows, or adding a monorail or davits to cover a gap.
- Façade restraint installation where the cradle has none.
- Anchor replacement and recertification.

- Records: restore the logbook and keep it with the equipment.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Periodic inspection and servicing are a recurring contract per unit. Major inspections and control modernisation are lump sums. Replacement is a lump sum including crane hire, roof works and commissioning. Where equipment is out of service, hired access (swing stages, rope access or mobile platforms) is a recurring cost for each cleaning and inspection cycle.

Inspection and certification are code compliance; servicing is repairs and maintenance; modernisation and replacement are lifecycle. A major inspection is often the check line that sizes a replacement envelope.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. BMUs are designed to AS 1418.13 and used, inspected and maintained to AS 2550.13, which sets the logbook and certificate formats; their designs are registrable plant under the work health and safety regulations. Regulators have issued safety alerts on BMU stability and on major inspections for units more than ten years old.
- United Kingdom. Equipment lifting people needs a thorough examination at least every six months under the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998, alongside PUWER 1998 and the Work at Height Regulations 2005. BS 6037-1 covers permanently installed suspended access equipment and BS EN 1808 the safety requirements for suspended access equipment.
- United States. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.66 governs powered platforms for building maintenance; 29 CFR 1910.27 requires rope descent anchorages to be inspected annually and certified at least every ten years. ANSI/IWCA I-14.1 and ASME A120.1 set further requirements for window cleaning and building maintenance platforms.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Logbook, current periodic inspection certificate and the last major inspection report.
- Plant and design registration and load test records.
- Maintenance contract and service reports for the last two years.
- Façade access strategy and any coverage study.
- Anchor certification records and the rigging plan.
- Manufacturer support status for the controls.
- Rescue plan for work at height on the façade.

pages.title: Building Management & Control System (BMCS)
pages.question: How do building management systems fail, how do you assess one, and when does obsolescence or cyber exposure force replacement?
pages.answer: A BMS fails quietly. Controllers and software lose vendor support; sensors drift; operators put points in manual and they stay there, so plant runs nights and weekends; sequences no longer fit the building; alarms are suppressed. Proprietary systems lock owners to one contractor. Internet-exposed systems with default passwords are a security risk. Assess a BMS by its trend data and overrides, not its hardware.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about building management & control system (bmcs); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Central server, software, field controllers, sensors

sources.title: DA28 Building Management and Control Systems
CIBSE Guide H: Building control systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A building management system (BMS, also called a building automation system) monitors and controls the building's mechanical plant and often lighting, metering, hydraulics and interfaces to fire, lifts and security. It is layered: a head end (server, software and operator workstations, now often cloud-hosted), a network, field controllers (direct digital controllers) in plant rooms and on floors, and sensors and actuators at the equipment. Its value lies in the control sequences it runs, the data it holds, and the people who can use it.

| Layer | What it includes | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head end | Server, software, graphics, alarms, trend logging | Unsupported operating systems and software; lost licences; single-vendor lock-in |
| Network | IP backbone, field buses (BACnet, Modbus, LonWorks, proprietary) | Old field buses; insecure connections to the internet |
| Field controllers | Plant controllers, unitary controllers on terminal units | Obsolescence; parts unavailable; proprietary programming |
| Sensors | Temperature, humidity, CO₂, pressure, flow, energy meters | Drift; failure; poor location |
| Actuators and outputs | Valve and damper actuators, drives, relays | Failure; overridden; disconnected |
| Integrations | Fire, lifts, lighting, metering, security, tenant systems | Undocumented; broken after changes |

Open protocols (BACnet in particular) allow equipment from different manufacturers to work together and allow more than one contractor to service the system. Many older systems are proprietary, so only one contractor can maintain or extend them, and that contractor sets the price of every change.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head end software | 5 to 10 years before major upgrade | Operating system and vendor support |
| Head end hardware | 5 to 8 years | IT refresh |
| Plant controllers | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support; parts |
| Unitary controllers | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Sensors | 10 to 15 years with calibration | Drift; type |
| Actuators | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Network infrastructure | 10 to 15 years | Protocol support |

What shortens life:

- Vendor end of support for controllers and software.
- Proprietary lock-in, which raises the cost of every repair and extension.
- Lost documentation: points lists, control narratives, network diagrams.
- No calibration of sensors.
- Cyber exposure that forces urgent replacement.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Obsolescence

Controllers and software become unsupported: no spare parts, no security patches, no engineers who know the programming. Head ends running on unsupported operating systems are common. A single controller failure can then take plant out of automatic control for weeks.

### Sensor drift and failure

Temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and pressure sensors drift over years; a supply air sensor reading two degrees low makes the chiller work harder all year. Failed sensors default to values that hide the problem.

### Overrides and manual operation

Operators put points in manual to deal with complaints or faults, and they stay there. Plants run 24 hours because schedules were overridden; valves are held open; alarms are suppressed. Over time the building runs on overrides rather than sequences.

### Poor or lost control sequences

Sequences written for the original design no longer fit after fit-outs and plant changes; they were often never fully commissioned. Heating and cooling fight; outside air is wrong; chillers and boilers stage poorly.

### Missing or poor data

Trend logging is not set up, history is lost, meters are not connected. Without data, faults cannot be diagnosed and energy cannot be managed.

### Cyber security exposure

BMS connected to the internet for remote access, with default passwords and unpatched software, can be found and controlled by attackers. Building systems have been used as entry points into corporate networks. National cyber security agencies publish guidance on securing building control systems.

### Integration failures

Interfaces to fire systems (for smoke mode and plant shutdown), lifts and metering are undocumented and break when either side changes. The first sign may be a failed fire test.

### Hardware failures

Controller power supplies and batteries fail, losing programs or clocks; network switches and gateways fail; head end servers fail without backups. Without current backups of controller programs, recovery means reprogramming from scratch.

### Ownership of software and passwords

Programming tools, software licences, controller programs and administrator passwords are often held by the installing contractor rather than the owner. Changing contractor then means paying for access to the owner's own system, or replacing it.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### At the head end

- Software and operating system versions.
- Alarm list: number of active and suppressed alarms.
- Points in manual override.
- Trend data availability.
- Graphics matching the plant.
- Remote access arrangements and passwords.

### In the field

- Controller models and ages; labels.
- Sensors damaged, missing or in poor locations.
- Actuators disconnected or held by cable ties.

### In the building

- Plant running at night and weekends.
- Comfort complaints.
- Energy use higher than benchmarks.

### In the records

- Points list, control narratives, network diagrams, as-built drawings.
- Maintenance contract and contractor.
- Software licences.
- Calibration records.
- Penetration tests or security assessments.

- No current backup of controller programs or the head end.
- Licences and passwords held only by the contractor.
- Several separate BMS in one building from different eras or tenants.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant running at night | Schedules overridden or lost | Schedule review; trends |
| Many points in manual | Workarounds for faults | Point list |
| Hundreds of suppressed alarms | Alarm fatigue | Alarm list |
| Only one contractor can work on it | Proprietary system | Protocol and licensing |
| BMS reachable from the internet | Insecure remote access | Security assessment |
| Energy high despite modern plant | Poor sequences or drifted sensors | Trends; calibration |

> A BMS is assessed by what it does, not what it is. Trend data over a few weeks usually reveals more than an inspection of the hardware.

Sensors that read the same value for weeks are usually failed rather than steady.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMS exposed to the internet with default credentials; fire interface failing | safety | Isolate and secure now; test fire interfaces |
| Head end or controllers failed, plant uncontrolled | failure | Restore now |
| Unsupported controllers and software; drifted sensors; overrides | condition | Upgrade and recommission in the near term |
| System at end of support | lifecycle | Plan replacement, preferably open protocol |
| No documentation or security assessment | check | Audit |
| Normal maintenance | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A controls engineer leads, independent of the incumbent contractor where possible, with a cyber security specialist for any system with remote access.

- Inventory of the head end, network devices, controllers, sensors and actuators, with manufacturer, model, firmware and software versions, and vendor support status.
- Trend analysis over at least several weeks: plant start and stop times against occupancy, setpoints, simultaneous heating and cooling, outside air, chilled and hot water temperatures, chiller and boiler staging.
- Override and alarm review: points in manual, suppressed and standing alarms, and why.
- Sensor calibration of key points (supply air, chilled water, outside air temperature and humidity, CO₂, static pressure, flow) against reference instruments.
- Functional testing: command actuators and confirm response at the equipment.
- Documentation review: points list, control narratives, network diagrams, as-built drawings, backups.
- Ownership review: who holds licences, programming tools, source programs and passwords.
- Cyber security assessment: remote access paths, internet exposure, credentials, patch levels, segmentation from corporate networks.
- Integration testing with fire (smoke mode, plant shutdown), lifts, metering and lighting.

The report should give the support status of each layer, the operating faults found in the trends, the security position, the integration status, and a migration plan: recommission, upgrade in stages, or replace.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Recommissioning: release overrides, restore schedules, calibrate sensors, retune and rewrite sequences to current loads, rationalise alarms. Often the best value of any building services work.
- Head end upgrade to supported software and hardware, with proper backups.
- Staged migration: replace controllers plant by plant with open-protocol controllers, using gateways to keep old and new working together during the transition, rather than a single change-over.
- Specification of the new system around open protocols, owner ownership of licences, programs and passwords, documentation deliverables and training, so that any competent contractor can service it.
- Cyber security hardening: remove direct internet exposure, use secure remote access, change default credentials, patch, segment the building network from corporate IT, log access.
- Analytics: fault detection and diagnostics that read BMS data and flag faults automatically.
- Integration repair and testing with fire and other systems, documented.
- Documentation: points lists, narratives and network diagrams brought up to date.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and trend analysis are lump sums. Recommissioning is priced per system or per plant item. Controller replacement is priced per controller or per point, with field wiring, sensors, actuators and programming. A head end upgrade is a lump sum. Analytics is a recurring subscription. Cyber hardening is a lump sum with recurring monitoring.

Replacement and staged migration are lifecycle; recommissioning and calibration are repairs and maintenance; cyber hardening and fire interface rectification are risk or code compliance driven. The usual shape is two-part: an audit first, then a migration envelope sized from it.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AIRAH DA28 is the industry guide to building management and control systems; NABERS Energy ratings depend heavily on control performance; the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre publishes guidance on operational technology security that applies to building systems; fire interfaces are tested as part of essential safety measures.
- United Kingdom. CIBSE Guide H covers building control systems; BS EN ISO 16484 covers building automation and control; the National Cyber Security Centre publishes operational technology guidance; BSRIA publishes BMS specification and commissioning guidance.
- United States. ASHRAE 135 defines BACnet, ASHRAE Guideline 13 guides specifying building automation systems, and Guideline 36 sets high-performance sequences; CISA publishes guidance on securing building and industrial control systems; building performance standards make control performance a compliance matter.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Points list, control narratives and network diagrams.
- Head end, controller and firmware versions, with vendor support status.
- Backups of controller programs and the head end.
- Who holds licences, programming tools and passwords.
- Maintenance contract and scope.
- Several weeks of trend data for key plant.
- Any cyber security assessment or penetration test.
- Fire and lift interface test records.

pages.title: Canopies & Awnings
pages.question: How do awnings and canopies fail, what are the warning signs, and when is an awning over a footpath unsafe?
pages.answer: Tied street awnings fail at the anchorages where their rods enter the masonry: corrosion inside the wall, cracked soft brick around the plate, then pull-out that can cascade along the frontage. A sagging fascia, one slack rod among taut ones, or rust bleeding where a rod enters the wall means closing the footpath. Blocked box gutters cause ponding collapse. Visual soundness of the frame does not clear the hidden anchorages.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about canopies & awnings; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Structural and finishing elements

sources.title: Planning Circular BS 13-001 Safety of awnings over public lands

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Canopies and awnings are roofed projections from a façade that shelter entrances, footpaths, shopfronts and loading docks. Many project over public land, which makes their failures public safety failures, and the classic Australian street awning has a failure mode that is entirely hidden inside the wall.

| Form | Where it is found | How it is held up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tied street awning | Retail strips and main streets, late nineteenth century to about the 1960s, Australia especially | Steel frame cantilevered from the façade, hung from tie rods angled up to anchorages in the wall above |
| Cantilevered awning | Retail and mixed use from the mid twentieth century | Steel or concrete beams fixed back into the structure with no ties; relies on the back-span and connection |
| Post-supported verandah awning | Heritage shopping streets | Posts at the kerb carrying a beam; posts in the footpath |
| Entrance canopy | Offices, apartments, institutions | Steel, concrete or glass, cantilevered or suspended on rods or cables |
| Glass canopy | Entrances from the 1990s | Laminated glass on point fixings or brackets, often with suspension rods |
| Loading dock canopy | Industrial and logistics | Steel portal extension or cantilever with sheet roof |
| Fabric and retractable awnings | Retail and hospitality | Frame and fabric; mechanical arms |

A tied awning carries its load through the tie rods into anchorages built into the masonry above: a plate, a bolt through the wall, or a hook built into a pier. The anchorage is inside the wall or behind internal finishes, it is often corroded, and the masonry around it is often old lime-mortared brick. The awning roof hides box gutters that, when blocked, add a large water load.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel awning frame | 40 to 70 years | Paint cycle; water at connections |
| Tie rods, turnbuckles and clevises | 30 to 60 years | Corrosion at threads and where rods enter the wall |
| Anchorages in masonry | 30 to 60 years | Water reaching the anchorage; masonry condition |
| Roof sheeting and box gutters | 20 to 40 years | Maintenance of gutters; coastal exposure |
| Soffit linings (pressed metal, fibre cement, timber) | 20 to 50 years | Water from above; hazardous materials in older linings |
| Glass canopy fittings | 25 to 40 years | Stainless grade; sealant at fittings |
| Fabric | 8 to 15 years | UV; wind damage |

What shortens life:

- Blocked gutters on the awning roof, which add a water load the frame was never designed for and keep connections wet.
- Added loads: illuminated signs, air conditioning units, people walking on the roof to reach signage or windows.
- Water at the wall line through failed flashings, running down to the anchorages.
- Vehicle impact on posts and low fascias.
- Façade alterations that cut into the masonry around anchorages, or new shopfronts that remove the pier an anchorage sits in.
- Coastal exposure and road salt in colder climates.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Anchorage failure

The tie rod passes through or into the wall to a plate or hook. Water running down the façade reaches the point where the rod enters the wall and corrodes the rod and anchorage inside the masonry, out of sight. The masonry around the anchorage, often soft brick in lime mortar, cracks and loosens. When an anchorage pulls out or a rod snaps, the load transfers to neighbouring rods; if they are in similar condition, the failure progresses along the awning. The fatal Bathurst collapse in 1998 and later collapses in New South Wales followed this pattern.

### Tie rod and fitting corrosion

Rods corrode at threads, turnbuckles and clevis pins, where section is thinnest and water sits. A rod that has lost tension because its anchorage has moved, or that has been adjusted to take up sag, signals a problem elsewhere.

### Ponding and overload

A blocked box gutter turns the awning roof into a tank. The water load deflects the frame, deflection holds more water, and the awning can collapse in a single storm. Signs, plant and people on the roof add load the original design did not allow for.

### Cantilever connection failure

Cantilevered awnings depend on the connection to the structure: bolts into a slab edge or beams built into the wall with a back-span inside. Corrosion of bolts, spalling of the slab edge, or decay of the back-span lets the awning rotate.

### Glass canopy failure

Point fittings and suspension rods corrode or loosen; glass breaks from impact, thermal stress or nickel sulphide inclusions where toughened glass is used without lamination.

### Post failure

Posts at the kerb on post-supported awnings are struck by vehicles and corrode at the footpath line, where water and salt collect.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Fascia line sagging, out of level or stepped along the frontage.
- Tie rods slack, bent, missing or at different angles; turnbuckles visibly adjusted on some rods and not others.
- Rust staining and cracking in the masonry where rods enter the wall.
- Signs, plant or lighting on or under the awning; evidence of people walking on the roof.
- Vegetation, debris or ponding visible on the awning roof in aerial imagery; staining from overflowing gutters.
- Damaged or leaning posts; soffit linings stained, sagging or missing.

### Close up on site

- Rod condition at threads and fittings; section loss.
- Masonry around anchorages: cracked, loose, previously repaired.
- Anchorage plates inside the building where accessible, behind linings or in ceiling spaces.
- Frame connections and fascia corrosion; gutter condition and outlet size.
- Glass canopy fittings: corrosion, missing caps, glass type markings.

### In the records

- Council awning inspection notices and engineer's certificates, with dates.
- Previous structural repairs, rod replacements or propping.
- Gutter cleaning records.
- Approvals for signage on the awning.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One slack rod among taut ones | Anchorage moved or rod failed | Masonry cracked at that anchorage; rod pulls out or turns freely |
| Uniform sag along the fascia | Connection rotation at the wall or general overload | All rods equally stretched; cracking along the wall line; added signage or water load |
| Local dip at one bay | Failed rod, anchorage or frame connection at that bay | Inspection of that bay's rod and fixings |
| Rust bleeding from the wall at rod entry points | Anchorage corrosion inside the wall | Opening up exposes the plate or hook |
| Staining from the gutter line, deflection worst after rain | Blocked box gutter and ponding | Gutter full of debris; outlets undersized or blocked |
| Glass canopy panel cracked with no impact | Thermal stress or nickel sulphide inclusion | Glass type; fracture origin |

> A tied awning over a footpath with any visible sag, slack rod or cracking at an anchorage is a public safety matter. The anchorages that decide its strength are hidden, and visual soundness of the frame does not clear them.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sag, slack or failed rod, cracked anchorage, damaged post, or glass breakage over a footpath or entrance | safety | Close the footpath below or prop immediately; engineer within days |
| Ponding on the roof with deflection | failure | Clear and relieve the load now; engineer to assess |
| Rod and frame corrosion without movement; cracked masonry around anchorages without displacement | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Roof sheeting, gutters and linings at age | lifecycle | Renewal on cycle |
| Council notice requiring certification | deadline | Timing set by the council |
| Tied awning more than ten years old with no engineer's certificate on record | check | Structural inspection with opening up of anchorages |
| Fabric wear, minor coating wear | nil | Routine care |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer inspects every awning. For tied awnings, the method set out in Practice Note 18 of the Association of Consulting Structural Engineers of New South Wales, attached to NSW Planning Circular BS 13-001, is the benchmark: staged inspection, opening up, assessment, rectification and certification.

- Visual inspection of the whole frame, every rod and fitting, the roof and gutters, and the soffit.
- Opening up of every anchorage, or a representative sample where the same detail repeats, to expose the plate, bolt or hook inside the wall.
- Masonry assessment around anchorages: mortar strength, cracking, the pier's capacity.
- Measurement of fascia level and rod tension, recorded for comparison.
- Load capacity check including signage, plant and any public access onto the roof.
- Glass canopies: fitting inspection, glass identification, and assessment of post-breakage behaviour.

The report should certify the awning as structurally adequate, or list the rectification needed and any propping or closure until it is done.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Anchorage replacement: new through-bolted plates or chemical anchors into sound masonry, or a new anchorage in the floor structure where the masonry is poor.
- Rod replacement with new rods and fittings, galvanised or stainless.
- Conversion to cantilever: new beams fixed back into the floor structure so the awning no longer depends on ties.
- Frame repair: treat corrosion, replace sections, repaint.
- Roof and gutter renewal with larger outlets and overflows; remove debris and added loads.
- Replacement of the whole awning where the frame and anchorages are both at end of life.
- Glass canopies: replace monolithic toughened glass with laminated glass; renew fittings.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is priced per awning, with opening up and making good as rates. Works are priced per awning bay or per linear metre of frontage, with anchorage replacement per anchorage. Footpath closure permits, traffic control, out-of-hours work and propping add materially. Certification recurs where a council regime applies.

Two-part lines are normal: inspection with opening up, then conditional rectification. Certification is code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle; propping and closure are immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. NSW Planning Circular BS 13-001 records repeated awning collapses in New South Wales since 1998, advises that awnings over ten years old warrant inspection, and notes that councils may require engineer certification; several councils, including Wagga Wagga, run awning policies with periodic certification. Awnings over public land usually need council approval under local government legislation. Design follows AS/NZS 1170 for actions, AS 4100 for steel and AS 1288 for glass.
- United Kingdom. Structures over the highway need consent under the Highways Act 1980; the owner's duty of care to the public falls under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957. Design follows Approved Document A and the Eurocodes.
- United States. International Building Code Section 3105 governs awnings and canopies, with loads to ASCE 7. Façade ordinances in New York, Chicago and other cities include canopies, marquees and appurtenances in the periodic examination.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Engineer's certificates for the awning, current and previous.
- Council notices, approvals and correspondence.
- Drawings of the awning and its anchorages.
- Repair, rod replacement and propping records.
- Gutter cleaning records.
- Approvals for signs and plant on the awning.

- Records of people accessing the awning roof.
- Insurance notes on the awning.

pages.title: Central Cooling Plant
pages.question: How do chillers and central cooling plant fail, how do you read their operating data, and when does refrigerant rather than wear end their life?
pages.answer: Chillers often reach the end of their economic life on refrigerant before wear: R22 and R123 are almost gone, and HFCs are being phased down. Mechanically, condenser tubes foul without good water treatment, evaporator tubes rupture if flow fails, hermetic motors burn out and contaminate the circuit, and drives and controls lose parts support early. Rising approach temperatures, refrigerant top-ups and high purge run time are the early signs. Low delta T looks like a chiller problem but starts in the building.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about central cooling plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Chillers, compressors, associated primary pumps

sources.title: Ozone protection and synthetic greenhouse gas management
sources.publisher: Australian Government Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water

sources.title: Fluorinated gases (F gas): guidance for users, producers and traders

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Central cooling plant produces chilled water for a whole building or campus: one or more chillers, their primary pumps, the chilled water pipework in the plant room, and the controls that sequence them. It works with the heat rejection plant (cooling towers, dry coolers or air-cooled condensers, which have their own page) and the air handling and terminal units that deliver the cooling to spaces.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-cooled centrifugal | Large offices, hospitals, campuses; 1960s onward | Most efficient at full load; surge at low load on older fixed-speed machines; longest life |
| Oil-free magnetic-bearing centrifugal | Retrofits and new plant from the 2000s | Excellent part-load efficiency; electronics-dependent; fewer mechanical wear parts |
| Water-cooled screw | Mid-size commercial and industrial | Robust; good part-load with variable speed; oil management matters |
| Air-cooled screw or scroll | Smaller offices, retail, apartments, where towers are unwanted | No cooling tower; condenser coils outdoors set the life |
| Absorption (lithium bromide) | Sites with waste heat or cheap gas; hospitals, tri-generation | Crystallisation and corrosion risks; vacuum must be maintained |
| Heat pump and heat recovery chillers | Electrification projects from the 2010s | Produce heating and cooling; replace boilers as well as chillers |
| Reciprocating | Older plant, 1970s to 1990s | Mostly replaced; spares scarce |

Distribution arrangements matter as much as the machines. Constant primary systems run fixed flow through each chiller. Primary-secondary systems decouple chiller flow from building flow through a bypass. Variable primary systems vary flow through the chillers themselves. Each has its own way of going wrong, and most chilled water problems that look like chiller problems start in the distribution system or at the coils.

Plant capacity is sized for a design load that may no longer exist. Tenancy changes, more efficient lighting, higher occupant densities, data rooms and longer hours all move the load, so a plant can be both old and wrongly sized.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-cooled centrifugal chiller | 20 to 30 years | Water treatment; overhaul history; refrigerant |
| Water-cooled screw chiller | 20 to 25 years | Oil management; run hours |
| Air-cooled chiller | 15 to 20 years | Condenser coil corrosion, especially near the coast |
| Absorption chiller | 20 to 25 years | Vacuum integrity; corrosion inhibitor |
| Primary pumps | 15 to 25 years; seals and bearings 5 to 10 | Run hours; alignment; water quality |
| Starters and variable speed drives | 10 to 20 years | Heat and dust in the plant room; harmonics |
| Plant controls and chiller panels | 10 to 15 years before parts support ends | Manufacturer support |
| Chilled water pipework (steel) | 40 to 60 years | Water treatment; external condensation and insulation |

Industry service-life tables (ASHRAE's service life database and CIBSE Guide M) give median lives in this range; the spread between a well-run and a neglected plant is wider than the spread between machine types.

What shortens life:

- Poor water treatment on the condenser water side, which fouls and corrodes tube bundles.
- Low flow and low temperature conditions that freeze and rupture evaporator tubes.
- Oversizing after load reductions, which makes chillers cycle on and off at low load.
- Refrigerant leaks that are topped up rather than repaired, bringing in moisture and air.
- Deferred overhauls past the manufacturer's run-hour intervals.
- Hot, dusty plant rooms that age drives and starters.
- Coastal air on air-cooled condensers.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Refrigerant obsolescence

A chiller's economic life is often set by its refrigerant before its mechanical life. CFCs (R11, R12) went out of production in developed countries in 1996. HCFCs (R22, R123) are in the last stage of phase-out: R22 production and import ended in the United States in 2020 and servicing with it has been banned in Britain since 2015. HFCs (R134a, R410A, R407C) are being phased down under the Kigali Amendment, with Australia and the United States both stepping down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036 and new high-GWP refrigerants restricted in new chillers. As a refrigerant becomes scarce, a leak or a compressor failure becomes a replacement decision.

### Tube bundle fouling, corrosion and rupture

Condenser tubes carry tower water and foul with scale, biofilm and silt when water treatment lapses; fouling raises condensing pressure, power draw and wear. Corrosion and erosion thin the tubes, especially at the inlet ends. Evaporator tubes can freeze and rupture if water flow drops while the chiller is running, or during low-temperature operation; a rupture floods the refrigerant circuit with water and usually ends the machine.

### Compressor and motor failure

Bearings wear, oil degrades and loses its lubricating properties, and oil migration leaves compressors running dry. In hermetic machines, where the refrigerant cools the motor, a winding failure burns the insulation and contaminates the whole refrigerant circuit with acid. Centrifugal compressors surge at low load: flow reverses briefly, with a characteristic noise, and repeated surge damages bearings and impellers.

### Air and moisture in low-pressure machines

Low-pressure centrifugal chillers (R11, R123) run below atmospheric pressure on the evaporator side, so leaks draw air and moisture in rather than letting refrigerant out. A purge unit removes them; high purge run time means a leak, and moisture forms acids that attack the motor and bearings.

### Low delta T

When chilled water returns from the building only a few degrees warmer than it left, chillers cannot load fully, so more chillers and pumps run to meet the same load. The cause is usually in the building: fouled or bypassing coils, failed control valves, three-way valves left from earlier systems, or bypasses open. The symptom appears at the plant and is often misread as a capacity shortfall.

### Pump failure

Mechanical seals leak, bearings wear, couplings misalign, impellers erode and motors fail. Pumps running against throttled valves or at the wrong point on their curve wear faster. A pump failure without standby takes a chiller out of service.

### Starters, drives and controls

Starters, variable speed drives and chiller control panels fail with heat and age, and their parts stop being made long before the chiller is worn out. A ten-year-old drive or a twenty-year-old control panel can strand a sound machine.

### Air-cooled condenser coil corrosion

Aluminium fins on copper tubes corrode quickly in salt air, separating from the tubes and losing heat transfer; capacity falls on the hottest days, when it is most needed.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the plant room

- Nameplates: manufacturer, model, serial, year and refrigerant. Year and refrigerant together fix most of the position.
- Oil stains under compressors and at fittings; refrigerant leak detector alarms; the smell of oil.
- Corrosion and condensation on chilled water pipework; damaged insulation.
- Pump seals weeping; noisy bearings; vibration on base frames.
- Number of chillers and pumps running against the load at the time.
- Plant room heat, ventilation, housekeeping, and refrigerant detection and alarm equipment.

### In operating data

- Condenser approach (refrigerant condensing temperature minus leaving condenser water temperature) rising over time.
- Evaporator approach rising.
- Chilled water supply temperature drifting up on hot afternoons.
- Low chilled water delta T across the building.
- High purge run time on low-pressure machines.
- Energy per unit of cooling rising.

### In the building

- Comfort complaints concentrated on hot afternoons.
- More chillers running than the load warrants.
- Temporary chillers hired in summer.

### In the records

- Service reports with recurring faults and deferred recommendations.
- Refrigerant log: additions and leak tests.
- Oil analysis, vibration analysis and eddy current tube test results.
- Overhaul history against run hours.
- Energy ratings and consumption trends.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condenser approach rising over months | Fouled or scaled condenser tubes | Tube inspection; water treatment records; approach falls after cleaning |
| Evaporator approach rising | Low refrigerant charge or fouled evaporator | Refrigerant log; leak test; evaporator inspection |
| Refrigerant added at each service | Leak | Refrigerant log; leak test locates it |
| High purge run time on an R123 or R11 machine | Air leak on the low-pressure side | Purge records; leak test under pressure |
| Chillers cannot load; more chillers and pumps running than the load needs | Low delta T in the building | Supply and return temperatures; coil and valve condition |
| Surging noise at light load | Oversized centrifugal at low load | Load profile; surge events in logs |
| Acidic oil or refrigerant | Moisture or motor winding failure | Oil and refrigerant analysis |
| Capacity loss on hot days on an air-cooled unit | Condenser coil corrosion or fouling, or hot air recirculating | Coil condition; plant screen or wall blocking airflow |

> Treat a chiller problem as a system problem until proven otherwise. Low delta T, failed valves and fouled coils produce the same symptoms at the plant as a failing chiller, and replacing the chiller will not fix them.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ammonia or large refrigerant leak; plant room without required refrigerant detection or ventilation; pressure relief discharging into the room | safety | Isolate and ventilate now; plant room safety measures before restart |
| Chiller failed with no standby capacity in a building that needs cooling (hospital, data, summer occupancy) | failure | Restore or hire temporary plant now |
| Refrigerant service restrictions in force for the refrigerant used | deadline | Plan replacement or conversion before the next major leak or repair |
| Rising approaches, recurring leaks, worn pumps, unsupported drives or controls | condition | Repair, retube or upgrade in the near term |
| Chiller approaching end of life on run hours and age with no current faults | lifecycle | Plan replacement, sized to current load |
| No tube testing, oil analysis or load study on record; capacity questioned after tenancy changes | check | Plant condition and load assessment before sizing works |
| Normal wear in a maintained plant | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with the chiller service contractor present. On large plant the investigation is planned around the cooling season so that machines can be opened.

- Records review: service reports, refrigerant log, oil and vibration analysis, energy data, overhaul history.
- Plant inspection of chillers, pumps, starters, drives, pipework and plant room safety equipment.
- Eddy current testing of condenser and evaporator tubes to measure wall loss and find defects.
- Oil and refrigerant analysis for acids, moisture, metals and contaminants.
- Vibration analysis of compressors and pumps.
- Performance testing: measured cooling output against power input across load.
- Load assessment: trended building load against installed capacity, to size any replacement correctly.
- Refrigerant position: current and forthcoming restrictions for the refrigerant in use.
- Distribution check: delta T, valves, bypasses and coil condition before blaming the chiller.

The report should give remaining life for each machine and pump, the refrigerant position, whether to overhaul, retrofit or replace, and the correct size and configuration for any replacement.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Water treatment and tube cleaning to restore condenser performance.
- Leak repair rather than topping up.
- Overhaul: compressor rebuild, bearing and seal replacement, motor rewind, at run-hour intervals.
- Retubing of bundles with significant wall loss.
- Variable speed drive retrofit on centrifugal and screw machines for part-load efficiency.
- Controls upgrade to supported chiller panels and plant sequencing.
- Refrigerant conversion to a lower-GWP alternative where the manufacturer supports it for that machine.
- Fix the distribution: replace failed valves, remove three-way valves and bypasses, clean coils, to cure low delta T.
- Replacement sized to the current load: often fewer or smaller machines, with variable speed, in a configuration that allows staged replacement; heat recovery or heat pump chillers where the building is electrifying.

Interactions: chiller replacement involves rigging and access (often through roofs, façades or by crane), electrical supply works, temporary cooling, controls integration and sometimes heat rejection and pump replacement at the same time.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment and testing are lump sums. Overhauls, retubing, drive retrofits and controls upgrades are lump sums per machine. Replacement is a lump-sum project including the machines, rigging and crane hire, pipework and electrical connection, controls integration, commissioning, and temporary cooling for the change-over, which can be a large share on occupied buildings.

Replacement and major overhaul are lifecycle; repairs and leak repair are repairs and maintenance; refrigerant-driven replacement and plant room safety measures carry code compliance elements. The usual shape where condition or load is uncertain is two-part: assessment first, then replacement or retrofit sized from it.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Refrigerants are controlled under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989, with HCFC imports reduced to a small servicing allowance that ends by 2030, HFC imports phased down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036, and refrigerant handling licensed through the ARC scheme. Refrigerating system safety follows AS/NZS 5149, and pressure equipment in-service inspection AS/NZS 3788. Offices of 1,000 m² and more need a current energy certificate under the Commercial Building Disclosure programme when sold or leased, and NABERS ratings drive lettability.
- United Kingdom. The GB fluorinated gas regulations restrict refrigerants by global warming potential and require leak checks at intervals set by the CO₂-equivalent charge; R22 servicing has been banned since 2015. Refrigerating system safety follows BS EN 378; pressure systems need a written scheme of examination under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000. Air-conditioning systems over 12 kW need an energy inspection at least every five years, and let commercial buildings need an EPC of at least E under the minimum energy efficiency standards.
- United States. Refrigerant management follows Clean Air Act Section 608; the AIM Act phases HFCs down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036, and EPA rules limit the global warming potential of refrigerants in new chillers from 2025. ASHRAE 15 governs refrigerating system safety and ASHRAE 90.1 efficiency. Building performance standards, such as New York City's Local Law 97, set emissions limits that drive plant replacement on a legislated timetable.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Mechanical maintenance contract and two years of service reports with recommendations.
- Refrigerant log, leak test records and refrigerant type for each machine.
- Installation and overhaul dates; run hours.
- Eddy current, oil and vibration test results.
- Water treatment reports for the condenser water system.
- Energy consumption data and energy ratings.
- Comfort complaint log and records of temporary chiller hire.
- Plant room refrigerant detection and alarm records.

pages.title: Central Heating Plant
pages.question: How do boilers and heating systems fail, how do you read the signs, and when does fuel policy change the replacement decision?
pages.answer: Heating plant fails mostly through its water. Leaks topped up with fresh water bring in oxygen and minerals, corroding steel and iron, building magnetite sludge and blocking condensing boiler heat exchangers. Cast iron sections crack from thermal shock; non-condensing boilers corrode when run too cool. Combustion faults risk carbon monoxide. Gas restrictions and electrification policy now shape replacement: a like-for-like gas boiler may be stranded before it wears out.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about central heating plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Boilers (condensing/non-condensing), hydronic radiators, primary pumps

sources.title: National Board Inspection Code
sources.publisher: National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Central heating plant produces heat for space heating and often for domestic hot water: boilers or heat pumps, their burners and gas trains, primary pumps, pressurisation and expansion equipment, water treatment, calorifiers and plate heat exchangers, and the hydronic distribution to radiators, convectors, coils and underfloor circuits. The flues that serve boilers have their own page.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron sectional boiler | Older offices, schools, apartment blocks | Long-lived; sections crack from thermal shock; low efficiency |
| Steel shell (fire-tube) boiler | Larger commercial and institutional plant | Robust; tube and furnace corrosion; pressure vessel |
| Condensing boiler (often modular or cascade) | Most plant installed since the 2000s | High efficiency if return water is cool; heat exchangers sensitive to water quality |
| Steam boiler | Hospitals, laundries, older US buildings, industrial | High-risk pressure plant; traps and condensate return corrode |
| Air-to-water heat pump | Electrification projects; new buildings | Lower flow temperatures; needs electrical capacity; refrigerant rules apply |
| District heat connection | Some campuses and city centres | Heat exchanger and metering only on site |
| Hydronic distribution | All wet systems | Pipework, valves, radiators, underfloor circuits; water quality decides life |

Fuel policy now shapes heating plant as much as condition. Victoria has barred gas connections to new homes needing a planning permit since 2024 and the ACT has barred new gas network connections since late 2023; Britain's policy is moving buildings off fossil-fuel heating; New York City's Local Law 154 requires all-electric new buildings. A gas boiler replaced like for like today may be a stranded asset before it wears out.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron sectional boiler | 25 to 35 years | Thermal shock; water quality |
| Steel shell boiler | 25 to 30 years | Water treatment; firing cycles |
| Condensing boiler | 15 to 20 years | Water quality; heat exchanger material |
| Burners and gas trains | 15 to 20 years | Maintenance; combustion tuning |
| Air-to-water heat pump | 15 to 20 years | Coastal exposure; cycling; refrigerant |
| Primary pumps | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; water quality |
| Pressurisation units and expansion vessels | 10 to 20 years | Diaphragm life; pressure setting |
| Calorifiers | 20 to 25 years | Water quality; temperature regime |
| Steel distribution pipework | 40 to 60 years | Oxygen ingress; water treatment |
| Radiators | 40 years and more | Internal corrosion from oxygenated water |

What shortens life:

- Oxygen in the water, from leaks topped up with fresh water, from open vents, or from older plastic pipe without an oxygen barrier, which corrodes steel and iron and forms magnetite sludge.
- Hard make-up water that scales heat exchangers.
- Lapsed water treatment in closed systems.
- Thermal shock from cold return water into hot cast iron boilers.
- Non-condensing boilers running too cool, so flue gases condense and corrode them.
- Short cycling of oversized boilers.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Water-side corrosion and sludge

A closed heating system should hold the same water for years. When it leaks and is topped up, each fill brings fresh oxygen and minerals: steel and cast iron corrode, magnetite sludge accumulates in boilers, radiators and valves, and heat exchangers scale. Condensing boilers with narrow aluminium or stainless passages are particularly sensitive; blocked or corroded heat exchangers are the commonest reason they are replaced early.

### Thermal shock and cracking

Cast iron sections crack when cold water reaches a hot boiler, for example when a pump starts after a period off. A cracked section leaks into the combustion chamber.

### Fire-side corrosion

Non-condensing boilers are designed to keep flue gases above their dew point. Run with low return temperatures, they condense acidic water inside, corroding tubes and furnaces. Steam boilers corrode at tubes and in the condensate return.

### Combustion faults

Burners drift out of adjustment, nozzles and heat exchangers soot up, and combustion becomes incomplete. The result is lower efficiency and, at worst, carbon monoxide production. Flame safeguards and gas valves age and must be tested.

### Pressurisation and expansion faults

Expansion vessel diaphragms fail and lose their gas charge; system pressure swings, relief valves discharge, and air is drawn in at high points. A relief valve that discharges regularly is a symptom, not a fault in itself.

### Distribution faults

Radiators pinhole from internal corrosion; valves seize; thermostatic radiator valves fail; pipes leak at joints in walls and ceilings; underfloor circuits lose flow from sludge. Older systems that were drained and refilled often are worst affected.

### Steam system faults

Steam traps fail open, wasting steam, or closed, flooding equipment; condensate pipework corrodes from carbonic acid; water hammer damages fittings. Steam boilers are high-hazard pressure equipment with inspection obligations.

### Heat pump specific faults

Air-to-water heat pumps lose capacity in cold weather and defrost frequently; outdoor coils corrode near the coast; compressors fail from short cycling when the system volume is too small. They need lower flow temperatures than boilers, so radiators and coils sized for boilers may not heat the building.

### Hot water storage and Legionella

Where the heating plant also heats domestic hot water through calorifiers or plate heat exchangers, the stored water must stay hot enough to control Legionella: stored at 60 °C or more and distributed hot enough that it does not fall into the growth range at outlets. Calorifiers that run cool to save energy, have cold stratified water at the base, or feed long dead legs carry a public health risk. Plate heat exchangers foul with scale on the hard-water side and lose output.

### Controls and oversizing

Boiler plant is commonly much larger than the load it serves, because of conservative original design, later fabric improvements and changes of use. Oversized boilers fire and stop repeatedly (short cycling), which wastes fuel and wears burners and ignition systems. Lost weather compensation, failed optimum start and poor boiler sequencing waste energy and mask the real load.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the plant room

- Nameplates: type, year, output, fuel; pressure vessel registration plates and tags.
- Water on the floor; staining at boiler sections; weeping valves and pump seals.
- Make-up water meter readings rising; pressurisation unit running often.
- Relief valve discharge pipes with scale or water marks.
- Soot at burner and flue connections; smell of combustion products.
- Corroded pipework, damaged insulation, missing labels.

### In the building

- Cold radiators or radiators cold at the bottom (sludge) or top (air).
- Uneven heating; long warm-up times.
- Leaks at radiators and in ceilings.
- Hot water temperature complaints.

### In the records

- Service and combustion test reports.
- Water treatment analysis: pH, inhibitor level, iron, conductivity.
- Make-up water volumes.
- Pressure vessel inspection reports.
- Gas safety records and burner certification.
- Energy consumption and gas bills.

- Flue gas temperatures well above design: fouled heat exchangers.
- Return water temperature too high for condensing boilers to condense, which wastes their efficiency.
- Calorifier temperatures below 60 °C; cold water at the base of stores.
- Boilers firing and stopping every few minutes in mild weather.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High make-up water use; system pressure falling | Leaks | Make-up meter; inspection of pipework, radiators and boiler |
| Black water when radiators are bled; cold bottoms on radiators | Magnetite sludge from oxygen ingress | Water analysis shows high iron; filter catch |
| Condensing boiler locking out, low flow faults | Blocked heat exchanger | Pressure drop across the boiler; water quality |
| Relief valve discharging, pressure swinging | Failed expansion vessel | Vessel charge pressure; diaphragm |
| Water in the combustion chamber of a cast iron boiler | Cracked section | Leak visible from inside; history of cold starts |
| Corrosion inside a non-condensing boiler | Running too cool | Return temperature records |
| Building cannot reach temperature after a heat pump retrofit | Emitters sized for higher flow temperatures | Heat loss vs emitter output at heat pump flow temperature |

| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boilers cycling every few minutes | Oversizing or poor controls | Load profile from gas data; burner run hours vs starts |
| Condensing boilers achieving non-condensing efficiency | High return temperatures from the building | Return temperature; bypasses; three-port valves |
| Calorifier stored below 60 °C | Setpoint lowered or plant undersized for hot water | Temperature records; Legionella sampling |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leak, carbon monoxide or spillage, failed flame safeguard or safety valve, inadequate plant room ventilation | safety | Isolate now; gas fitter and engineer before restart |
| No heating in winter in residential, healthcare or education buildings; major leaks | failure | Restore now or provide temporary heat |
| Pressure vessel inspection or gas safety check due | deadline | Timing set by the regulation |
| Sludge, corrosion, failed expansion vessel, poor combustion | condition | Repair and treat in the near term |
| Boilers at the end of their life; fuel policy affecting replacement choice | lifecycle | Plan replacement, including the electrification option |
| No water treatment records; no assessment of heat pump readiness | check | Assess before replacing |
| Normal wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a licensed gas fitter, the maintenance contractor and a water treatment specialist. The investigation is best done at the start of the heating season, when faults show and plant can still be taken offline.

- Records review: service and combustion reports, water treatment logs, make-up water volumes, pressure vessel inspections, gas safety records, energy data.
- Plant inspection of boilers, burners and gas trains, pumps, pressurisation units, expansion vessels, calorifiers, heat exchangers and pipework, with pressure vessel registration plates checked.
- Combustion analysis of each burner at high and low fire: oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, flue temperature, efficiency.
- System water analysis to BSRIA BG 50 practice: pH, inhibitor concentration, total and dissolved iron, copper, conductivity, bacteria; a filter or strainer inspection to see what the water carries.
- Make-up water metering over several weeks to quantify leaks.
- Internal inspection of boilers and pressure vessels at the statutory interval, with ultrasonic thickness testing of shells and tubes where corrosion is suspected.
- Pipework survey: ultrasonic thickness readings on suspect runs; thermography of radiators and distribution.
- Load assessment: heating load derived from gas consumption against heating degree days, to size replacement plant to the real load rather than the nameplate.
- Hot water review: calorifier temperatures, dead legs, Legionella risk assessment.
- Electrification readiness: building heat loss, emitter output at heat pump flow temperatures, electrical supply capacity, outdoor space, structural capacity for plant, noise constraints.

The report should give remaining life for each boiler and major component, water quality and its consequences, the safety position, the real heating load, and a replacement strategy that compares like-for-like gas, hybrid and full electric options against the building's fuel and emissions obligations.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Water treatment programme: find and fix leaks first, then clean and flush (chemically where sludge is heavy), dose with inhibitor, fit magnetic and side-stream filtration, add deaeration where air is a problem, and monitor quarterly. Water treatment is the cheapest life extension available for every component in the system.
- Component repairs: expansion vessel and pressurisation unit replacement, pump replacement with variable speed, valve replacement, burner overhaul or replacement, heat exchanger cleaning.
- Controls: weather compensation, optimum start and stop, boiler sequencing, and return temperature control so condensing boilers condense.
- Boiler replacement: modular condensing boilers sized to the measured load, after the system has been cleaned so that new heat exchangers are not fouled by old sludge, with new flue, gas train and controls.
- Hybrid systems: heat pumps carrying the base load with boilers for peaks and backup, which lowers emissions without a full emitter upgrade.
- Full electrification: heat pumps at flow temperatures typically in the 45 to 55 °C range, with emitter upgrades (larger radiators, fan convectors), buffer vessels, fabric improvements to reduce the load, electrical supply upgrade, and space for outdoor units with noise control.
- Hot water: restore storage temperatures, remove dead legs, or move to point-of-use or heat pump hot water.
- Distribution: replace corroded pipework sections and pinholed radiators; replace non-barrier plastic pipe that admits oxygen.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment, combustion testing and water analysis are lump sums. Water treatment is a recurring contract, with a one-off clean and flush. Component repairs are itemised. Boiler replacement is a lump-sum project including boilers, flue system, gas train and supply, pumps, controls, commissioning and temporary heating where the building is occupied in winter.

Electrification adds lines that can exceed the plant cost: heat pumps and outdoor plant platforms, emitter upgrades through the building, electrical supply upgrade with the network operator, structural works for plant, and fabric improvements. Running cost and emissions comparisons belong in the strategy rather than in the register line.

Replacement is lifecycle; pressure vessel and gas safety obligations are code compliance; water treatment and repairs are repairs and maintenance; electrification driven by a building performance standard carries a deadline.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Gas installations follow AS/NZS 5601.1 and commercial gas appliances AS 3814; boilers and pressure vessels are classified by hazard level under AS 4343, built to AS/NZS 1200, registered under the work health and safety regulations and inspected in service to AS/NZS 3788. Victoria and the ACT restrict new gas connections.
- United Kingdom. The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 apply, with IGEM standards for non-domestic installations; pressure systems need a written scheme of examination under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000; BSRIA BG 50 and BS 7593 guide water treatment; Approved Document L governs efficiency.
- United States. Boilers are built to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code with controls to ASME CSD-1, and inspected by jurisdictional boiler inspectors under the National Board Inspection Code; NFPA 54 covers gas and NFPA 85 larger boiler combustion systems. Local Law 97 and Local Law 154 in New York drive electrification.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Service and combustion test reports for the last two years.
- Water treatment reports and make-up water records.
- Pressure vessel registration, written scheme of examination and inspection reports.
- Gas safety records and burner certification.
- Gas and electricity consumption data for at least two heating seasons.
