- Legionella risk assessment and hot water temperature logs.
- Installation dates for boilers, burners, pumps and calorifiers.
- Any electrification, decarbonisation or heat pump feasibility study.
- Obligations under any building performance standard that applies.

pages.title: Chimney Stacks & Flues
pages.question: How do chimney stacks and flues fail, how do you read a leaning or stained chimney, and when is it dangerous?
pages.answer: Chimneys fail from exposure on all faces and from what goes up them. Stacks lean away from the weather as sulfates from flue gases swell the mortar on the wetter side; a large lean with open joints is a falling hazard. Brown stains on a breast mean tar or acid condensate through an unsuitable flue. Cracked liners leak carbon monoxide. Disused stacks still need capping, ventilation and support, and a breast removed below without support leaves the stack hanging.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about chimney stacks & flues; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Masonry condition, pointing, flashings, flue liners

sources.title: NFPA 211 Chimneys, Fireplaces, Vents and Solid Fuel-Burning Appliances

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Chimney stacks and flues carry combustion gases from appliances out of the building. The element covers masonry stacks with their pots, cappings, flaunching and flashings; flue liners (clay, concrete, pumice, stainless steel); prefabricated metal flues; boiler and generator flues on commercial buildings; kitchen exhaust ducts; and industrial stacks. It includes decommissioned stacks, which still stand above the roof and still need to be stable and weathertight.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry stack with unlined or parged flue | Houses and terraces before about 1950 | Gas leakage through the masonry; sulfate attack and lean |
| Masonry stack with clay or concrete liners | Houses from the mid twentieth century | Cracked liners; open joints |
| Stainless flexible or rigid liner in an old flue | Relined chimneys | Liner life; incorrect for the appliance |
| Twin-wall metal flue | Wood heaters, boilers, generators | Joints; support; clearances to combustibles |
| Commercial kitchen exhaust duct | Restaurants, institutions | Grease build-up and duct fires |
| Tall masonry or steel stack | Industrial and institutional | Banding and lightning protection; structural condition |
| Decommissioned stack | All older buildings | Damp from open pots; lean; removed breasts below |

Commercial and institutional buildings carry flues of their own: boiler flues rising through risers, generator exhausts, kitchen exhaust ducts, laboratory fume exhausts and, on older industrial and hospital sites, tall free-standing stacks. These follow appliance and fire codes as much as building codes, and their failures show up as fire, fume and condensation problems as well as fabric problems.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry stack | 80 to 120 years | Exposure on all faces; flue gases; frost |
| Flaunching and pointing | 20 to 40 years | Exposure |
| Lead flashings | 50 to 80 years | Fixing in chases |
| Clay liners | 50 to 80 years | Chimney fires; thermal shock |
| Stainless liners | 15 to 30 years | Fuel type; condensate; grade |
| Twin-wall flues | 20 to 30 years | Fuel; installation |

What shortens life:

- Exposure on all faces: stacks get wetter than walls and dry less.
- Flue gases: sulfates from coal and oil, acid condensate from modern efficient appliances, tar from smouldering wood.
- Cement repairs on lime-built stacks.
- Missing damp-proof trays where the stack passes through the roof.
- Wrong liner for the fuel.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Lean from sulfate attack

Sulfates from flue gases condense in the flue lining and mortar, more on the wetter side of the stack. Mortar expands on that side, and the stack bends away from the prevailing weather. A leaning stack can be stable for decades, but a large lean, cracked joints and loose upper courses mean it may fall in a storm.

### Weathering

Frost and salts spall bricks; pointing erodes; flaunching around the pots cracks and lets water into the flue; pots loosen.

### Flashing failure

Apron, step and back gutter flashings lift and pull from their chases; back gutters fill with debris. Water runs down inside the stack and into the building, often appearing on chimney breasts below.

### Liner failure and gas leakage

Cracked or open-jointed liners, and unlined flues with decayed parging, let gases and smoke into rooms, roof spaces and adjoining dwellings. Carbon monoxide leakage is the life-safety failure.

### Tar and condensate staining

Wet tar from wood, and acid condensate from efficient gas boilers in unlined flues, soak through to the inside and stain chimney breasts brown; the staining is a sign of an unsuitable flue.

### Removed chimney breasts

Chimney breasts removed from lower floors without supporting what remains above leave the stack and upper breasts hanging on the masonry. Gallows brackets or steel beams are needed; without them the stack can drop.

### Kitchen exhaust fires

Grease builds up in commercial kitchen exhaust ducts and ignites; ducts without access for cleaning are the problem.

### Tall stacks

Tall masonry stacks are held by steel bands that corrode and loosen; their tops weather fastest; lightning protection conductors corrode and detach. Steel stacks corrode internally from acid condensate. These are structural items needing periodic engineering inspection.

### Chimney fires

Creosote and soot build up in wood and coal flues and ignite. A chimney fire cracks liners and masonry and can spread to timbers built into or against the stack.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Lean visible by sighting against vertical lines; cracks in stack joints.
- Spalled bricks, eroded pointing, cracked flaunching, missing or loose pots.
- Lifted flashings; vegetation on stacks.
- Pots open on decommissioned stacks; cowls or caps present.

### In the roof space

- Damp, efflorescence and staining on the stack where it passes through.
- Mortar fallen from joints; holes in the masonry.
- Chimney breast removed below with no support.

### Inside the building

- Brown staining and damp on chimney breasts; smoke smell; soot.
- Carbon monoxide alarm activations.
- Missing breasts on lower floors.

### In the records

- Chimney sweep and CCTV inspection records.
- Gas safety certificates; appliance register.
- Liner installation certificates.
- Decommissioning records.
- Building approvals for breast removal.

- Timbers in the roof space built into or touching the stack, which are a fire risk in working flues.
- Scorching or cracking on breasts after a chimney fire.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack bending away from the prevailing weather | Sulfate attack on mortar | Joints open on the weather side; mortar white and soft |
| Brown staining on the chimney breast | Tar or acid condensate through an unsuitable flue | Appliance type; flue unlined |
| Damp on breasts after rain, dry otherwise | Water entry at the top or flashings | Flaunching, cap or flashing defects |
| Damp on breasts of a disused flue in all weather | Open pot and no ventilation | Pot open; fireplace sealed |
| Smoke or fumes in other rooms or adjoining dwellings | Liner failure | Smoke test; CCTV |

> Any flue serving a working appliance that shows signs of leakage, or where carbon monoxide alarms have activated, must be taken out of use until tested.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack leaning with open joints or loose upper courses; loose pots; breast removed without support; flue gas leakage | safety | Make safe now; appliance out of use |
| Water entering the building through the stack | failure | Repair now |
| Cracked flaunching; eroded pointing; lifted flashings without leaks | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Liners and flashings at age | lifecycle | Renew on cycle |
| Gas safety check due under landlord rules | deadline | Annual |
| Working flue with no inspection record; appliance changed | check | Inspect and test before use |
| Minor weathering | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects the stack; a structural engineer assesses lean; a licensed gas fitter, chimney sweep or flue specialist inspects the flue.

- External inspection from the roof or a platform.
- Plumb measurement of the stack.
- CCTV inspection of the flue.
- Smoke test for leakage.
- Appliance and flue compatibility check against the appliance's requirements.

The report should state stack plumb and condition, flashing condition, flue lining condition from CCTV, whether each flue suits the appliance connected to it, and the status of disused flues.

- Moisture and salts survey of chimney breasts, to separate rain entering at the top, condensate from appliances, and hygroscopic salts left by years of coal and wood burning, which draw moisture from the air and keep plaster damp after the source has stopped.
- Support check wherever breasts have been removed: look in the roof space and the floor below for gallows brackets, steel beams or corbelling carrying the remaining masonry, and for approvals.
- Carbon monoxide testing in rooms served and in adjoining dwellings with appliances running, since leaking flues often affect neighbours first.
- Kitchen exhaust inspection of the duct from hood to discharge through access panels, measuring grease deposits against the cleaning standard.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Repoint and reflaunch in lime-based mortar for lime-built stacks.
- Rebuild the upper courses or the stack from the roof line.
- Renew flashings with a damp-proof tray.
- Reline with a liner suited to the appliance.
- Cap and ventilate decommissioned flues.
- Remove redundant stacks above the roof with approvals.
- Support stacks over removed breasts with gallows brackets or steel beams.

- Liners matched to the fuel: suitable stainless grades for wood and oil, condensate-resistant liners for condensing gas appliances, and cast-in-place pumice or ceramic liners where an old stack needs structural support as well.
- Cowls and bird guards on working flues; capping with ventilation on disused flues, and a vent at the base of disused breasts so the flue can dry.
- Damp-proof trays built in where stacks are rebuilt at roof level.
- Bands, ladders and lightning protection repaired on tall industrial stacks.
- Grease duct programme: access panels at changes of direction and a cleaning frequency set by the cooking volume.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Repairs are lump sums per stack; rebuilds by height; relining per flue. Scaffold dominates on roofs. Flue inspections and sweeping recur.

Rebuild is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; flue compliance is code compliance.

Where a stack is redundant, removal above the roof can be cheaper than repair over the long term, subject to heritage and planning controls.

A stack rebuild carries scaffold, demolition to below the defect, rebuild, new pots and flaunching, flashings and tray, and often relining in the same visit. Capping a disused flue is a small item per flue but needs the same access. Support for stacks over removed breasts is a structural lump sum and a safety item. Kitchen exhaust cleaning recurs at the frequency the standard sets for the cooking type.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Solid fuel appliances follow AS/NZS 2918 and gas appliances and flues AS/NZS 5601.1; commercial kitchen exhaust follows AS 1668.1.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document J covers combustion appliances and fuel storage; the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require annual landlord gas safety checks; BS 5440 covers gas flues.
- United States. NFPA 211 governs chimneys and venting systems, with levels of inspection; NFPA 54 covers gas, NFPA 96 commercial kitchen exhaust; International Building Code Chapter 21 covers masonry chimneys.

Removing a chimney breast or stack is structural work needing building approval in all three jurisdictions. In Britain, work to a stack shared with a neighbour usually needs a party wall notice under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996. Heritage controls in Australia, Britain and the United States frequently protect chimneys as part of a building's character, which can rule out removal and set the materials for repair.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Sweep and CCTV inspection records.
- Gas safety certificates and the appliance register.
- Liner installation certificates.
- Decommissioning records.
- Approvals and engineering for chimney breast removal.

- Approvals and engineering for any breast or stack removal.
- Carbon monoxide alarm records and any incidents.
- Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates.
- Heritage listing where chimneys are protected.

pages.title: Cladding & Wall Systems
pages.question: How do cladding systems fail, what does each failure look like, and which findings are urgent?
pages.answer: Cladding fails in two ways. Most systems fail by water and fixings: face-sealed render, EIFS and sheet trap water against the frame and rot or corrode it unseen; precast and stone fail at corroding hidden anchors. Combustible systems fail a different test: an immaculate panel with a polyethylene or EPS core is a regulated remediation item regardless of condition. Know how the system manages water and what it is made of before judging its face.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about cladding & wall systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Precast concrete, ACP, stone/brick veneer, terracotta, weatherboards, renders

sources.title: PAS 9980:2022 Fire risk appraisal of external wall construction

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Cladding is any external wall system hung on or fixed to a structure rather than built up from the ground as masonry: precast concrete panels, metal composite and solid aluminium panels, stone veneer on brackets, terracotta and ceramic rainscreen, fibre cement and render systems on framing, exterior insulation and finish systems (EIFS), insulated sandwich panels, and timber or fibre cement weatherboards. Masonry has its own page. The system is more than the face: it includes the support framing or brackets, fixings, any insulation, the sheathing or sarking behind, cavity barriers, and the joints and flashings that make it weathertight.

Every system manages rain in one of three ways, and the way it manages rain decides how it fails. Face-sealed (barrier) systems stop water at the outer surface and rely entirely on sealant joints; when a joint fails, water is inside with no way out. Most precast of the 1960s to 1990s, early EIFS and much render on sheet are face-sealed. Drained and ventilated (rainscreen) systems accept that water passes the face, and drain it down a cavity to flashings and weep points, with a sealed line behind. Most modern panel, terracotta and weatherboard systems work this way. Mass systems absorb and release water, as solid masonry and thick render on masonry do.

| System | Typical era and use | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precast concrete panels, face-sealed joints, cast-in fixings | 1960s to 1990s offices, apartments, institutions | Joint sealant at or past its third renewal; reinforcement corrosion where cover is low; concealed fixing corrosion |
| Stone veneer on dowels, cramps or brackets | 1970s to 2000s offices and retail podiums | Fixing corrosion in carbon steel; thin marble panels bowing; anchor holes cracking |
| Metal composite panels (ACP) with polyethylene core | About 1995 to 2018, apartments, offices, hotels, retail | Combustibility, not condition, is the issue: a regulated rectification item |
| EIFS and render on foam or sheet | 1980s to 2000s in the United States; 1990s to 2010s apartments in Australia and New Zealand | Face-sealed versions trap water against framing; hidden decay of timber or steel frame and sheathing |
| Fibre cement or render on timber or light steel frame, no cavity | 1990s to 2010s apartments and townhouses | Same water-trapping risk; cracking at sheet joints; leaks at windows and parapets |
| Insulated sandwich panels (EPS, PIR, mineral wool core) | 1970s onward, industrial, cool stores, retail sheds | EPS cores are combustible and drive insurance and fire risk; delamination where cores get wet |
| Terracotta and ceramic rainscreen on aluminium rails | 2000s onward, commercial and institutional | Clip and rail fixings; cracked tiles at clips; generally durable |
| Timber and fibre cement weatherboards | Houses throughout; townhouses | Paint cycle drives life; decay at ends and ground contact; cracking at fixings in fibre cement |

Building class shapes the risk. Apartments carry the combustibility and water-trapping legacy of the 1995 to 2018 period and are the focus of the cladding regimes in all three jurisdictions. Offices carry precast and stone with ageing fixings. Industrial buildings carry sandwich panels whose core type matters more than their appearance. Houses carry weatherboards and render, where the paint and the ground line decide the life.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precast concrete panel | Life of the building | Cover to reinforcement, carbonation, chloride exposure |
| Precast joint sealant (face-sealed) | 10 to 20 years | Exposure, joint design; see Sealants and Joints |
| Stone cladding | 50 to 100 years | Fixing material; thin marble bows; stone type |
| Carbon steel fixings and brackets | 30 to 60 years | Moisture at the fixing, coastal exposure |
| Stainless steel and aluminium fixings | Life of the building | Dissimilar metal contact, crevice corrosion in marine air |
| ACP and solid aluminium panel finish | 20 to 35 years | Coating type, UV, coastal exposure |
| EIFS and render on sheet | 20 to 30 years | Drained or face-sealed, impact, detailing at openings |
| Insulated sandwich panel | 25 to 40 years | Coating on the skins, cut-edge corrosion, core moisture |
| Timber weatherboards | 30 to 60 years with a maintained paint cycle | Paint cycle, ground clearance, end grain sealing |
| Fibre cement weatherboards and sheet | 40 to 60 years | Paint cycle, fixings, movement at joints |

What shortens life:

- Face-sealed detailing on any system with framing behind it: one failed joint wets the frame with no route out.
- Missing or reversed flashings at window heads, sills, floor lines and parapets; water directed into the wall rather than out of it.
- Coastal and industrial exposure, which consumes coatings and corrodes carbon steel fixings and cut edges.
- Dissimilar metals: aluminium rails on galvanised brackets, stainless fixings in aluminium without isolation, copper runoff.
- Impact at ground level and on balconies, which opens EIFS and render and exposes sandwich panel cores.
- Deferred sealant renewal on face-sealed systems.
- Ground and paving too close to the bottom of weatherboards, render and sheet.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Water trapped behind the face

Face-sealed EIFS, render on sheet and fibre cement without a cavity are only as good as their joints and their window details. When a sill or joint fails, water reaches the sheathing and frame and stays there. Timber frames rot; light steel frames corrode at the bottom track; oriented strand board and plywood sheathing delaminate. The face can look sound for years while the frame behind fails, which is how the leaky building crisis in New Zealand and the EIFS litigation in the United States unfolded.

### Fixing corrosion

Precast panels hang on cast-in ferrules, bearing angles and restraint fixings; stone hangs on dowels, cramps and kerf clips; panel systems hang on brackets and rails. Carbon steel fixings corrode where water reaches them. Expanding corrosion cracks the stone or concrete at the anchor and can release a section of panel. Section loss in hidden hangers is the most serious failure mode of heavy cladding because it gives little external warning.

### Reinforcement corrosion in precast

Thin precast panels often have little concrete cover over the reinforcement, especially at edges, ribs and returns. Once carbonation reaches the steel, or chlorides from coastal air do, the steel corrodes and spalls the concrete face, usually in lines that follow the bars.

### Stone bowing and delamination

Thin marble panels lose strength and bow permanently under repeated heating and cooling (thermal hysteresis), dishing outward or inward. Sandstone and some limestones delaminate when laid face-bedded. Bowed and delaminated stone cracks at its anchors.

### Combustibility

Metal composite panels with a polyethylene core, EPS-cored sandwich panels, some high-pressure laminates and timber, foam insulation in cavities, and missing or misplaced cavity barriers can carry fire up and across a façade. This is a design and compliance issue, not a condition issue: an immaculate panel can be the most serious item on the building.

### Panel and coating failure

Coated metal panels chalk and fade, then lose coating at edges and cut lines; composite panels can delaminate where skins debond from the core. Sandwich panels corrode from cut edges and fixings, and their cores degrade when wet. EIFS and render crack at sheet joints, around openings and from impact, and lose bond to the substrate.

### Weatherboard decay

Timber weatherboards decay where paint fails at end grain, at the ground line, and behind downpipes and gutters; boards cup and split as they cycle wet and dry. Fibre cement boards crack at fixings and lose coating; edges absorb water where unsealed.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Panel type and joint pattern: wide open joints suggest rainscreen; narrow sealed joints on every panel edge suggest face-sealed.
- Cracked, spalled or rust-stained precast, with staining in lines following reinforcement or at panel corners where fixings sit.
- Bowed stone panels visible in raking light; cracked stone at corners and anchor positions; missing or replaced panels in a different shade.
- Staining below window corners and sills on render and EIFS; cracks running from window corners; patched areas.
- Faded, chalked or peeling panel coatings; rust at sandwich panel laps and cut edges; dented panels at ground level.
- Weatherboards with peeling paint, split boards, decay at ends and at ground line; boards close to or below paving.
- Netting, hoarding or temporary covers on a façade, which mean someone has already found something.

### Close up on site

- Soft or bulging render and EIFS when pressed; hollow sound when tapped; cracks at sheet joints.
- Moisture readings and soft spots in framing behind sheet systems, taken at sills, the bottom plate and below windows.
- Movement of stone or precast panels when pushed; cracking at anchor positions; rust bleeding from joints.
- Panel labels or markings on the back of composite panels where a panel can be removed; the core visible at cut edges.
- Cavity barriers present or absent at floor lines and around openings, where a panel can be lifted.

### Inside the building

- Damp, mould and swelling at window reveals, at skirtings on external walls and at the base of walls under sills.
- Stained ceilings below parapets and at slab edges; corrosion at exposed light steel framing in plant rooms or ceilings.
- Musty smell in apartments with framed external walls, a common early sign of hidden decay.

### In the records

- Cladding audit, fire engineer report, regulator correspondence or registration on a state or national cladding programme.
- Insurance exclusions or loadings referring to the external walls or panel cores.
- Defect claims, expert reports and rectification orders on apartment buildings.
- Repeated leak repairs at the same windows or elevations; sealant renewal history.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staining and cracking below window corners on render or EIFS; damp at reveals inside | Water entry at window perimeter in a face-sealed system | No head or sill flashing; moisture readings high at the sill and bottom plate; decay found on opening up |
| Rust staining from precast joints; cracking at panel corners | Corrosion of concealed fixings | Staining at fixing positions per the panel drawings; cracks radiating from corners; openings expose corroded ferrules or angles |
| Spalling in lines across precast faces | Reinforcement corrosion from low cover | Covermeter shows low cover along the line; carbonation depth reaches the steel |
| Dished or bowed stone panels, cracks at anchors | Thermal bowing of thin marble, or anchor failure | Bowing uniform across panels of the same stone: hysteresis; local cracking at one anchor: anchor corrosion or overstress |
| Layers of stone flaking parallel to the face | Face-bedded stone, or salt crystallisation | Bedding planes parallel to the face; salts in the debris |
| Immaculate composite panels on an apartment block of the 1995 to 2018 era | Possible combustible core; no condition defect | Product identified from records, panel labels or a core sample |
| Sandwich panel skins rusting from laps and cut edges, panels bulging | Cut-edge corrosion; wet or degraded core | Corrosion starts at edges and fixings; panel soft or delaminated when pressed |
| Peeling paint and decay concentrated at weatherboard ends and the bottom courses | End grain moisture and ground-line wetting | Ends unsealed; boards within a short distance of paving or soil; sound boards higher up |

> A sound-looking face-sealed system can hide a failed frame. Where the system is face-sealed, sits on timber or light steel framing, and was built in the period of known failures, condition of the frame is unknown until it is probed or opened.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, cracked or displaced panel or stone over a footpath, entry or occupied area; anchor visibly failed | safety | Make safe immediately: remove, net or hoard; engineer within days |
| Combustible cladding identified where a regulator, scheme or order sets a remediation date | deadline | Timing set by the regulator; interim fire safety measures until done |
| Combustible cladding identified with no order yet | check | External wall fire risk assessment by a fire engineer sets whether and how soon it must be remediated |
| Decay or corrosion found in framing or sheathing behind a face-sealed system | failure | Remediation now; extent from opening up, often elevation by elevation |
| Spalling precast from reinforcement corrosion; fixing corrosion without displacement; leaks at windows | condition | Programme repair in the near term; extent from investigation |
| Coating faded and chalked; weatherboards due for repaint; sealant at age on a sound system | lifecycle | Renewal on cycle |
| Face-sealed system on framing of the at-risk era with no investigation on record | check | Probe and open up before sizing works |
| Isolated hairline cracks in render; minor coating wear | nil | Routine care |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer leads on panel and stone systems; a building surveyor can lead on houses and low-rise weatherboard and render. Combustibility is assessed by a fire engineer, and in Britain by an assessment under PAS 9980 for residential buildings in scope.

- Desk review of drawings, product certificates and any audit, to identify the system and its fixings before going on site.
- Close-up survey from rope access or a platform, every elevation over public areas, a representative sample elsewhere.
- Opening up at representative locations: sills and heads of windows, floor lines, parapets and the base of walls on framed systems; panel removal on rainscreen to see brackets, rails, insulation and cavity barriers; fixings exposed on precast and stone.
- Moisture probing of framing behind sheet and EIFS systems at the high-risk points, with probes left in place for monitoring where the wall will not be stripped.
- Concrete testing on precast: cover survey, carbonation depth, chloride content at the depth of the steel.
- Fixing testing: pull-out tests on stone anchors and remedial fixings; section loss measured on exposed hangers.
- Core identification of composite and sandwich panels by sample and laboratory test where records do not settle it.
- Water testing of windows and joints to locate leak paths before remedial design.

The report should state the system and how it manages water, what was found behind it, fixing condition, combustibility status, and remedial scope by elevation with measured extents.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Local repair: reseal joints, repair precast concrete to a recognised repair standard, replace individual panels and boards, repair render and recoat.
- Fixing remediation: supplementary stainless anchors drilled through panels or stone into the structure; replacement of corroded hangers, which can require panels to be removed and rehung.
- Recladding: removal of the system and replacement with a drained and ventilated system, including new sheathing, membrane and flashings, and frame repair where decayed. This is the usual answer for failed face-sealed systems on framing and for combustible panels.
- Overcladding: a new rainscreen fixed over an existing sound wall, used on precast and masonry where the substrate is sound and the joints are not worth renewing.
- Combustible cladding: replacement with non-combustible panels and insulation, reinstatement of cavity barriers, and interim measures (fire watch, alarms, changed evacuation strategy) until complete.
- Weatherboards: replace decayed boards, seal ends, restore ground clearance, repaint on cycle.

Interactions: recladding carries window, sealant, flashing and balcony work with it; scaffolding or access dominates; on occupied apartment buildings the programme is often elevation by elevation; heritage listing can restrict materials.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with rates per opening, test and sample. Recladding and overcladding are measured by façade area, with separate lines for windows, flashings and frame repair found on opening up. Fixing remediation is priced per anchor or per panel. Panel replacement and board replacement are rate-based. Access is often the largest single component.

Combustible cladding rectification is a lump-sum project with consultant, approval and interim measure costs, coded as code compliance with its timing driven by the regulator. Recladding of a failed face-sealed system is lifecycle or repairs, with the frame repair a conditional line sized from opening up. The usual register shape is two-part: investigation first, then a conditional works envelope.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code requires external walls of Type A and Type B construction to be non-combustible, tested to AS 1530.1, with performance solutions tested to AS 5113. State regimes act on combustible cladding: Cladding Safety Victoria administers rectification of high-risk buildings, New South Wales bans aluminium composite panels with more than 30 per cent polyethylene core on certain buildings under the Building Products (Safety) Act 2017 and runs Project Remediate, and Queensland ran a combustible cladding checklist programme. On strata buildings, cladding is common property; rectification and defect claims sit with the owners corporation.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B and regulation 7(2) prohibit combustible materials in the external walls of relevant buildings 18 m and over; the Building Safety Act 2022 places duties on accountable persons for higher-risk buildings, creates remediation orders and protects many leaseholders from remediation costs. PAS 9980:2022 sets the method for fire risk appraisal of external walls. The Cladding Safety Scheme and Building Safety Fund fund remediation of eligible buildings; lenders rely on EWS1 forms.
- United States. International Building Code Chapter 14 governs exterior walls, with NFPA 285 testing required for combustible components on most buildings of Types I to IV construction; EIFS follows ASTM E2568. Façade ordinances in New York, Chicago, Boston, San Francisco and others require periodic critical examination of cladding on taller buildings; New York's Cycle 10 runs from February 2025 to February 2029.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Façade drawings, specifications and product certificates naming each system, panel core and insulation.
- Any cladding audit, fire engineer report, PAS 9980 assessment, EWS1 form, regulator correspondence or order.
- Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings.
- Records of panel replacement, fixing remediation, recladding or overcladding.
- Leak logs, defect claims and expert reports on framed systems.
- Insurance terms referring to external walls.
- Repaint history for weatherboards and render.

pages.title: Commercial Kitchens
pages.question: How do commercial kitchens fail, and which kitchen findings are fire and life-safety risks?
pages.answer: Kitchens fail on fire first: grease builds in hoods and ducts when cleaning is missed, suppression no longer covers moved appliances, and gas interlocks are bypassed. Exhaust without make-up air backdraughts gas appliances and produces carbon monoxide. Wet floors cause slips and leak into floors below; cool room releases fail and trap workers; damaged linings fail food inspections. Clean ducts to the cooking demand and keep suppression matched to the layout.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about commercial kitchens; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, equipment integration, ventilation, hygiene installations

sources.title: NFPA 96 Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Commercial kitchens prepare food in restaurants, hotels, hospitals, aged care, schools, staff canteens and food courts. They concentrate hazards in one room: open flames and hot oil under grease-laden exhaust hoods, gas, wet slippery floors, heavy electrical loads, cool rooms that people can be trapped in, and food safety requirements for every surface. Functionally the kitchen must cook safely, exhaust heat, smoke and grease, stay hygienic and pass inspection. Whether the operator or the building owner is responsible varies: in leased restaurants the tenant usually owns the fit-out but the building carries the exhaust riser, grease waste and gas supply.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust hoods and ducts | Canopy hoods, grease filters, ducts to roof, exhaust fan | Capture; grease accumulation; fire |
| Fire suppression | Wet chemical systems over cooking appliances; extinguishers and blankets | Coverage of current appliances; servicing |
| Make-up air | Supply air to replace exhaust | Negative pressure, draughts, combustion problems |
| Gas | Supply, isolation valves, interlocks to exhaust | Shut-off when exhaust fails or fire |
| Floors and drainage | Non-slip floors falling to drains, floor wastes, grease arrestor | Slips; leaks; grease |
| Wall and ceiling finishes | Smooth, impervious, cleanable surfaces | Food safety; pest harbourage |
| Cool rooms and freezers | Insulated panels, doors, refrigeration | Entrapment release; ice; seals |
| Electrical | Heavy power supply, RCD protection | Capacity; wet environment |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen fit-out and finishes | 10 to 15 years | Use; cleaning; operator changes |
| Exhaust hoods and filters | 15 to 25 years; filters cleaned weekly | Grease; cleaning |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Grease; run hours |
| Cooking equipment | 8 to 15 years | Use; maintenance |
| Cool room panels and refrigeration | 15 to 25 years; refrigeration 10 to 15 | Ice damage; refrigerant rules |
| Floors | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; chemicals; water |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Grease in hoods, ducts and fans when cleaning is missed.
- Water and chemicals attacking floors, junctions and substrates.
- Menu and equipment changes outgrowing the exhaust, suppression and power.
- Electrification of cooking replacing gas with heavier electrical loads.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Grease duct fires

Grease builds up in filters, hoods, ducts and exhaust fans. A flare-up ignites it, and fire travels along the duct, sometimes through floors to the roof. Infrequent cleaning, missing access panels and ducts without fire-rated enclosures turn kitchen fires into building fires.

### Suppression mismatch

Wet chemical suppression is designed for a set appliance layout. When fryers and ranges are moved or added, nozzles no longer cover them; fusible links not replaced and gas interlocks bypassed stop the system working.

### Make-up air and combustion

Exhaust without adequate make-up air puts the kitchen under negative pressure: doors slam, draughts pull smoke out of hoods, and gas appliances and flues backdraught, producing carbon monoxide.

### Slips and floor failures

Wet, greasy floors cause slips. Floors without falls to drains hold water; failed floor junctions and wastes leak into substrates and floors below, rotting timber and corroding steel.

### Cool room hazards

Cool room doors must open from inside; failed internal releases have trapped workers. Ice build-up damages panels, failed door seals waste energy and corrupt food safety, and refrigeration faults lose stock.

### Hygiene and pests

Damaged wall linings, open joints, gaps around services and dead spaces behind equipment harbour pests and fail food safety inspections.

Equipment changes are the usual trigger: a new fryer bank, wok station or charcoal grill changes exhaust, suppression, power and gas loads all at once.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Grease on hood surfaces, filters and duct access panels; cleaning certificates and dates.
- Suppression nozzles against current appliance positions; service tags.
- Doors slamming or hard to open; smoke escaping hoods.
- Ponding water; cracked tiles and failed grout; floor wastes blocked.
- Cool room internal release present and working; ice on panels; damaged seals.
- Gaps around services; damaged linings; pest evidence.

### In the records

- Exhaust cleaning certificates.
- Suppression system service records.
- Gas interlock tests.
- Food safety inspection reports.
- Trade waste and grease arrestor records.
- Leak history below the kitchen.

- Charcoal, wok or high-volume frying equipment added since the kitchen was designed.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke escaping canopies at busy times | Exhaust capacity or make-up air shortfall | Airflow measurements |
| Doors slamming, flues backdraughting | Negative pressure | Pressure and CO measurement |
| Suppression nozzles over empty bench | Appliances moved since design | Layout against design |
| Stains below the kitchen | Floor membrane or waste failure | Flood test |
| Food safety non-compliances for linings | Damaged or unsuitable finishes | Inspection report |

> Grease in exhaust ducts, suppression that no longer covers the appliances, and gas without interlocked shut-off are fire and life-safety findings.

Most kitchen findings trace to a mismatch between the kitchen as designed and the cooking it now does.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease build-up in ducts; suppression not covering appliances; gas interlocks bypassed; cool room releases failed; CO from backdraught | safety | Rectify before cooking continues |
| Exhaust or refrigeration failed | failure | Repair now |
| Duct cleaning, suppression servicing or food inspection due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Floor, lining and drainage defects | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Fit-out and equipment at end of life | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Services capacity unknown for the current menu | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer experienced in kitchen ventilation leads, with the suppression and gas contractors, a hydraulic engineer for floors and drainage, and the operator's food safety lead.

- Exhaust inspection: hoods, filters, ducts from hood to fan and the fan itself, with grease depth measured at access points and the duct route checked for access panels and fire-rated enclosure through floors.
- Airflow measurement of hood capture and make-up air, and observation at peak cooking.
- Suppression review: nozzle positions against the appliances now installed, service tags, link replacement dates, manual release, and gas and power shut-off on discharge.
- Gas safety check: appliances, connections, isolation, interlock to exhaust, and carbon monoxide levels with appliances running.
- Floor and drainage inspection with flood tests and checks below the kitchen for leaks.
- Cool room safety check: internal releases, alarms, lighting, panels and seals.
- Food safety review against recent inspection findings.

The report should list fire and life safety items first, then capacity against the current menu and equipment, and a refurbishment plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Exhaust cleaning at a frequency matched to the cooking type (heavy frying and charcoal need far more frequent cleaning), with access panels added so the whole duct can be cleaned.
- Duct fire protection: fire-rated enclosures where ducts pass through other floors and spaces.
- Suppression redesigned to the current appliance layout, serviced and interlocked to gas and power.
- Make-up air balanced to exhaust so the kitchen is slightly negative but not starved.
- Floors: falls to drains, slip-resistant finishes, coved junctions and new membranes where leaks occur.
- Linings: impervious, cleanable surfaces with sealed penetrations to deny pests harbourage.
- Cool rooms: internal releases, alarms, seals, panels and refrigeration on cycle.
- Electrification planning: power capacity for induction and electric equipment where gas is being phased out.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Exhaust cleaning and suppression servicing recur, and are often the operator's cost. Exhaust, make-up air and duct fire protection upgrades are lump sums. Kitchen refurbishment is a lump sum including closure time, which in hotels and hospitals needs temporary kitchens. Floors and linings are priced by area. In leased premises, the lease decides who pays for base-building items such as the exhaust riser and grease waste.

Fire safety items are immediate; servicing is recurring compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 1668.1 and AS 1668.2 cover kitchen exhaust and fire requirements; AS 4674 covers the design and fit-out of food premises; the Food Standards Code sets premises requirements; gas installations follow AS/NZS 5601.1.
- United Kingdom. BESA DW/172 sets kitchen ventilation specification and TR19 Grease sets duct cleaning practice; food hygiene regulations apply; gas interlocks follow BS 6173.
- United States. NFPA 96 governs commercial cooking ventilation, including duct cleaning frequencies; UL 300 lists wet chemical suppression; the FDA Food Code and state health codes govern food premises.

Insurers in all three countries commonly require evidence of exhaust cleaning and suppression servicing, and may decline claims for kitchen fires without it.

Health authorities can close premises that fail food safety inspections.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Exhaust and duct cleaning certificates.
- Suppression system service records.
- Gas compliance and interlock test records.
- Food safety inspection reports.
- Leak history below the kitchen.
- Lease allocation of kitchen responsibilities.

- Equipment schedule and layout as currently installed.
- Insurance requirements for kitchen fire protection.

- Pest control contract and reports.

pages.title: Commercial Office Areas (Base-Build)
pages.question: How do office floors fail as working space, and how do you tell base-building problems from fit-out drift?
pages.answer: An office floor fails as a workplace before its parts wear out. Built-in limits (low ceilings, deep plates, few toilets) cap how far it can be repositioned; comfort fails where zoning no longer matches partitions, outside air is low, or the perimeter overheats; repeated fit-outs leave abandoned services and break sprinkler, detection and egress coverage. Separate base-building performance from tenant drift: the remedies and who pays differ. Time refurbishment to lease expiry.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about commercial office areas (base-build); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Ceiling systems, lighting, flooring, core services integration

sources.title: A Guide to Office Building Quality
Office building class definitions and floor measurement standards

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Commercial office areas are the lettable floors where tenants work: the open floor, ceilings, lighting, floor finishes, the air conditioning outlets and controls, power and data distribution, and the core services that reach each floor. As a functional space, an office floor is judged on whether it does its job for a tenant and holds its place in the market, not only on the condition of its parts. A floor can be in good condition and still fail if its ceiling is too low for current services, its air supply is below current expectations, its lighting is uneven, its toilets are too few for modern densities, or its energy rating keeps tenants away.

Responsibility is split, and the split decides who pays. The base building (sometimes called shell and core, or in Britain Category A fit-out) is the owner's: raised floors or slab finishes, suspended ceilings, base lighting, air conditioning to the floor, fire services, core toilets and amenities. The tenant fit-out (Category B in Britain) is the tenant's: partitions, meeting rooms, kitchens, joinery, specialist lighting and supplementary cooling. At lease end, make-good clauses decide what returns to base build and at whose cost.

| Element group | Typical base-building provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceilings | Suspended grid with tiles, or exposed soffits in newer and refurbished floors | Height, acoustic performance, access to services, appearance |
| Lighting and controls | LED panels or older fluorescent troffers on a regular grid, with controls | Even light at the desk, glare, energy, flexibility for layouts |
| Air conditioning outlets | VAV boxes, fan coils or chilled beams with diffusers and zones | Outside air, temperature control by zone, noise, draughts |
| Floor finishes | Carpet tiles on raised floor or screed; some exposed concrete | Wear, acoustic performance, flexibility for cabling |
| Power and data | Floor boxes, raised floor cabling, or ceiling and pole distribution | Capacity and flexibility for tenant layouts |
| Fire and life safety | Sprinklers, detection, warning, emergency lighting, exit signs | Coverage that follows the fit-out |
| Amenities | Core toilets, showers and end-of-trip facilities, tea points | Ratios for current occupancy; quality |
| Façade interface | Perimeter glazing, blinds, perimeter heating or cooling | Glare, heat gain, daylight, comfort at the perimeter |

Market grading formalises fitness for purpose. In Australia the Property Council's guide to office building quality grades buildings from Premium to D against floor plate, services, amenities and sustainability; in Britain the British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations; in the United States, buildings are commonly classed A, B or C. These grades move: a floor that was A grade at completion can slide as expectations for air, light, amenities and energy rise.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant fit-out | 7 to 12 years, usually a lease term | Lease events; tenant needs; workplace trends |
| Base-building carpet tiles | 10 to 15 years | Traffic; quality; make-good practice |
| Suspended ceiling tiles and grid | 20 to 30 years; tiles sooner where damaged | Water leaks; services works; appearance |
| Base-building lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED; fluorescent now obsolete | Technology; energy rating |
| Terminal units and diffusers | 15 to 25 years | Air conditioning page; controls |
| Base-building refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years for a major floor refurbishment | Market grade; vacancy; energy targets |
| Market grade | Drifts down a grade over 15 to 25 years without investment | Competing stock; rising expectations |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Rising market expectations for outside air, daylight, amenities, end-of-trip facilities, wellness ratings and energy performance, which age a floor faster than its materials wear.
- Repeated fit-outs that leave behind abandoned cabling, patched ceilings, unbalanced air systems and fire services altered piecemeal.
- Higher occupant densities than the floor was designed for, overloading air conditioning, toilets and lifts.
- Water leaks from above that stain ceilings and damage carpets.
- Energy and emissions rules that push older floors below letting or rating thresholds.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Functional obsolescence

Some limits are built in: floor-to-ceiling height that leaves little room for modern services and lighting, deep floor plates with poor daylight away from the façade, close column grids that constrain layouts, and cores with too few toilets or lifts for today's densities. These cannot be fixed by refurbishing finishes and decide how far a floor can be repositioned.

### Comfort failures

Hot and cold complaints concentrated at the perimeter, in meeting rooms and in corner offices point to zoning that no longer matches the layout, failed terminal units, or façade heat gain and glare. Stuffiness and afternoon fatigue point to low outside air. Uneven light and glare follow fit-outs that moved desks without moving fittings.

### Fit-out residue and drift

Each tenancy leaves traces: cabling abandoned in ceilings and floors, ceiling tiles cut and patched, diffusers capped, sprinkler heads moved, detectors added or removed, and air systems rebalanced for a layout that no longer exists. Over several tenancies the base building no longer matches its design or drawings, and services perform poorly even though each component works.

### Compliance drift after fit-outs

Fit-outs create new rooms and paths that must still meet egress travel distances, fire detection and sprinkler coverage, emergency lighting, exit signs and accessibility. Compliance problems on office floors almost always trace back to fit-out changes.

### Wear and damage

Carpet tiles wear in traffic routes and fray at edges; ceiling tiles sag, stain and crack; grid bends where services workers lean on it; corner protection and wall finishes in corridors are damaged. Wear matters most in multi-tenant floors and common areas where the owner is responsible.

### Energy and rating decline

Floors with fluorescent lighting, poor controls, old terminal units and single glazing drag down whole-building ratings, which affect leasing and in some places the right to let.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On a floor walk

- Ceiling height and how crowded the ceiling void is with ducts, cables and abandoned services when tiles are lifted.
- Stained, sagging, cut or mismatched ceiling tiles, showing leaks and repeated fit-out changes.
- Lighting type and evenness; dark patches or glare at screens; fluorescent fittings remaining.
- Diffusers capped, blocked by partitions or blowing onto desks; supplementary split systems added by tenants.
- Carpet worn in traffic routes, frayed at tile edges, or patched with mismatched tiles.
- Partitions or joinery cutting across sprinkler and detector coverage; exit signs not visible from new rooms.
- Toilet and end-of-trip provision against apparent occupancy.
- Blinds closed all day at the perimeter, a sign of glare and heat problems.

### In the records

- Comfort complaint logs by floor and zone.
- Fit-out approvals and as-built drawings for each tenancy.
- Make-good schedules and lease terms.
- Air and light measurements from commissioning or audits.
- Energy and indoor environment ratings.
- Vacancy and leasing feedback.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complaints at the perimeter in afternoons, blinds always down | Façade heat gain and glare | Orientation; glazing type; perimeter temperatures |
| Complaints in meeting rooms and enclosed offices | Zoning that no longer matches partitions | Terminal unit zoning against layout |
| Stuffiness and complaints after lunch | Low outside air or high density | CO₂ readings; outside air measurement |
| Ceiling void crowded with abandoned cabling and capped ducts | Fit-out residue from previous tenancies | Ceiling inspection |
| Stained tiles in a line | Leak from services or the floor above | Trace the line to a pipe, riser or wet area |
| Floor hard to lease despite good condition | Market grade drift or functional limits | Grade assessment; leasing feedback |
| Rooms without sprinkler or detector coverage | Fit-out compliance drift | Survey against the layout |

> Separate what the base building must fix from what the tenant changed. Most office-floor problems are either base-building performance (air, light, amenities, energy) or fit-out drift (coverage, zoning, residue); the remedy and who pays are different.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rooms without required sprinkler, detection, emergency lighting or exit coverage; egress paths blocked by the fit-out | safety | Rectify before occupation continues |
| Leaks damaging finishes and services; air conditioning failed on a floor | failure | Repair now |
| Rating, letting standard or lease obligation requiring upgrade by a date | deadline | By the required date |
| Comfort complaints; worn finishes in common areas; fit-out residue affecting services | condition | Repair or rebalance in the near term |
| Floor at the end of its refurbishment cycle; market grade sliding | lifecycle | Plan a base-building refurbishment, ideally at lease expiry |
| Grade, air, light and amenities never assessed against the market | check | Assess fitness for purpose |
| Normal tenant wear within a lease | nil | Recovered through make-good |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or leasing-focused building consultant leads, with a services engineer for air, light and controls and an access and fire consultant where fit-outs have changed layouts.

- Floor walk of every floor, recording base-building elements, condition, fit-out residue and compliance coverage, with ceiling tiles lifted at representative points.
- Fitness-for-purpose assessment against the relevant market guide: floor-to-ceiling height, floor plate depth and daylight, column grid, lighting, outside air, zoning, density capacity, amenities and end-of-trip ratios, and energy rating.
- Environmental measurements: temperature by zone over a working day, CO₂ as a proxy for outside air, light levels at desks, and noise from services.
- Coverage check of sprinklers, detection, emergency lighting and exit signs against the current layout, and egress distances.
- Base-build versus fit-out split from leases, fit-out approvals and make-good schedules, so findings are allocated correctly.
- Services integration review: terminal unit zoning, controls, power and data capacity per floor.
- Leasing evidence: vacancy, feedback from agents and tenants, and competing stock.

The report should grade each floor for condition, compliance and market fitness, separate base-building items from tenant obligations, and set out a floor-by-floor programme timed to lease events.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Compliance rectification after fit-outs: add or relocate sprinklers, detectors, emergency lights and exit signs; correct egress paths.
- Rebalance and rezone air conditioning to the current layout; replace failed terminal units and controls.
- Outside air upgrades where measured rates fall below current standards or market expectations.
- Lighting upgrade to LED with daylight and occupancy controls, designed for even desk light and low glare.
- Ceiling works: remove abandoned services, replace damaged tiles, or open up to exposed soffits where height is limited and acoustics can be managed.
- Floor finishes: carpet tile replacement in common areas and at refurbishment; make-good recovery for tenant areas.
- Amenities and end-of-trip upgrades to current ratios and expectations.
- Base-building refurbishment (Category A) at lease expiry, often with speculative fitted suites to attract smaller tenants.
- Façade and solar control: blinds, films or glazing upgrades where perimeter comfort fails.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Office floor costs are usually measured by lettable area per floor. Compliance rectification is itemised per device. Rebalancing and controls are lump sums per floor. Lighting and ceiling replacement are priced by area, usually done together. Carpet is by area. Base-building refurbishment is a lump sum per floor or by area, and is most economical on vacant floors at lease expiry. Amenities upgrades are lump sums per core or per floor.

Make-good recoveries from outgoing tenants offset some costs, and lease incentives, rather than capital works alone, often decide leasing outcomes. Compliance items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle or repositioning capital; tenant-caused damage is recoverable; rating-driven upgrades can carry deadlines.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The Property Council's guide to office building quality sets market grading; fit-outs need building approval under the National Construction Code, which governs egress, fire services and access; AS 1668.2 sets ventilation and AS/NZS 1680 lighting; NABERS Energy and Indoor Environment ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure affect leasing; leases commonly include make-good and green lease clauses.
- United Kingdom. The British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations and the Category A and B fit-out convention; fit-outs need building regulations approval and must keep fire safety and access; the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 set minimum standards for workplaces; EPC minimum standards apply to letting; dilapidations practice governs lease-end obligations.
- United States. Buildings are commonly classed A, B or C by market convention, and floor area is measured to BOMA standards; tenant improvements need permits under the International Building Code and must meet the 2010 ADA Standards; ASHRAE 55 and 62.1 set comfort and ventilation; city benchmarking and building performance standards affect older office stock.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Floor-by-floor tenancy schedule with lease expiries and make-good terms.
- Fit-out approvals and as-built drawings for each tenancy.
- Comfort complaint logs and any indoor environment measurements.
- Energy and indoor environment ratings and certificates.
- Base-building specification and any market grade assessment.
- Records of base-building refurbishments by floor.
- Leasing agent feedback and vacancy history.
- Fire services and egress certification after the latest fit-outs.

pages.title: Common Circulation Areas
pages.question: How do corridors and lift lobbies fail, and when do they stop being safe escape routes?
pages.answer: Corridors are escape routes first. They fail when stored furniture, bins and bikes narrow them, when fire and smoke doors are wedged open or apartment doors replaced with unrated ones, when smoke vents do not open, and when emergency lighting or exit signs fail. Then wear: trolleys gouge walls, carpets wear in traffic paths, odours spread through poorly ventilated corridors. Storage and doors that do not close are safety findings, not housekeeping.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about common circulation areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, wall protection, wayfinding, lighting in corridors and lift lobbies

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Common circulation areas are the corridors, lift lobbies and passages on each floor that connect lifts, stairs, tenancies, apartments and amenities. Functionally they are escape routes as much as access routes: they must stay clear, lit, signed and protected from smoke, while taking constant wear from people, trolleys, cleaning machines and furniture moves. In apartment buildings they are common property and among the most visible indicators of how a building is managed.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor finishes | Carpet, vinyl, tiles, timber | Wear, trips, cleaning, acoustics |
| Wall finishes and protection | Paint, wall coverings, corner guards, kick plates | Damage from trolleys and moves |
| Doors | Fire and smoke doors, apartment entry doors, hold-open devices | Closing, sealing, fire rating |
| Lighting | Corridor lighting with emergency lighting | Levels, controls, emergency coverage |
| Signage and wayfinding | Exit signs, floor numbers, unit numbers | Egress and finding destinations |
| Ventilation | Corridor supply, smoke vents in residential corridors | Odour, smoke control |
| Ceilings and services | Suspended ceilings carrying services | Access, fire rating where required |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridor carpet | 8 to 15 years | Traffic; quality; cleaning |
| Vinyl and hard floors | 15 to 25 years | Traffic; maintenance |
| Paint and wall coverings | 5 to 10 years | Damage; style |
| Fire and smoke door hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use; abuse |
| Corridor refurbishment | 10 to 20 years | Wear; market |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Furniture moves and trolleys damaging walls and corners.
- Storage and bins left in corridors.
- Door abuse: wedging, propping, slamming.
- Fit-outs that change corridor layouts.

Corridors look worn long before any element fails, because they take every trip people and goods make through the building. Their fitness for purpose is mostly about escape safety and presentation rather than material life.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Obstructed escape routes

Corridors fill with stored furniture, bins, bicycles, prams and deliveries, narrowing escape widths and adding fire load. In apartment buildings, residents' items in corridors are a persistent fire safety problem.

### Fire and smoke door failures

Corridor fire and smoke doors are wedged open, closers fail, hold-open devices are not linked to the alarm, and seals are damaged. Apartment entrance doors, which protect the corridor from a flat fire, are replaced or altered by residents. Each failure lets smoke into the escape route.

### Wear and damage

Carpets wear in traffic paths and at lift lobbies; walls and corners are gouged by trolleys and moves; doors and frames are chipped. Damage accumulates quickly in hotels, aged care, hospitals and apartment buildings.

### Lighting and signage

Dark corridors from failed or poorly controlled lighting, emergency lights not working, and exit signs hidden or wrong after layout changes compromise both daily use and escape.

### Smoke ventilation

In residential buildings, corridor smoke vents and shaft systems must open on alarm; failed actuators and blocked vents leave corridors filling with smoke.

### Layout changes and dead ends

Fit-outs and reconfigurations can create dead-end corridors longer than permitted or remove alternative escape routes.

### Odour and air quality

Poor corridor ventilation spreads cooking and garbage odours in apartment buildings and hotels.

In mixed-use and hotel buildings, corridors also carry trolleys and housekeeping, multiplying wear and door damage.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On a walk-through

- Items stored in corridors and lift lobbies.
- Fire doors wedged or propped; doors not closing fully; seals damaged.
- Apartment entrance doors of mixed designs or with added hardware.
- Worn carpet paths; gouged walls and corners.
- Dark spots; emergency lights or exit signs failed.
- Smoke vents blocked or closed.
- Dead-end corridors created by new partitions.

### In the records

- Fire door inspection records.
- Fire safety statements.
- Complaints about storage and odours.
- Refurbishment history.
- Strata or building rules on corridor use.

- Hold-open devices on fire doors, and whether they release when the alarm is tested.
- Lift lobby finishes worn at the lift doors, where traffic concentrates.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors wedged open on every floor | Doors used for convenience; no hold-open devices | Inspection; use patterns |
| Smoke spread in a minor fire or alarm test | Failed doors, seals or vents | Door survey; smoke vent test |
| Walls damaged at a consistent height | Trolleys or bins | Wall protection review |
| Corridors cluttered on residential floors | Storage shortage or poor management | Building rules; storage provision |
| Odours along corridors | Inadequate ventilation or unbalanced pressure | Airflow check |

> A corridor is an escape route. Storage in it and fire doors that do not close are safety findings, not housekeeping issues.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Obstructed escape routes; fire doors not closing; failed emergency lighting; smoke vents not opening | safety | Rectify now |
| Corridor lighting failed | failure | Repair now |
| Fire door checks and certification due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn finishes; wall damage; odours | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Corridors at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| No fire door register; layout changes unreviewed | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a fire safety consultant.

- Floor-by-floor walk recording obstructions, door condition, finishes, lighting and signage.
- Fire door survey of every corridor and apartment entrance door.
- Egress review: widths, dead ends and alternative routes against the current layout.
- Smoke vent and ventilation test.
- Lighting and emergency lighting check.
- Management review: rules, storage provision and enforcement.

The report should list safety items by floor, door defects, and a refurbishment plan.

A building surveyor leads, with a fire safety consultant for doors, egress and smoke systems, and the building manager for use and rules.

- Floor-by-floor walk at different times of day, recording obstructions, stored items, door positions, finishes, lighting and signage.
- Fire door survey of every corridor, lobby and apartment entrance door: closing from fully open, gaps, seals, hardware, glazing, labels.
- Egress review: corridor widths, travel distances, dead ends and alternative routes against the current layout and fire strategy.
- Smoke vent and ventilation test in residential corridors, triggered from the fire alarm.
- Lighting check: levels, controls and emergency lighting coverage.
- Management review: building rules, storage provision and how breaches are dealt with.

The report should give safety items floor by floor, a fire door defect register, and a refurbishment and management plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Clear and manage: remove stored items, provide storage, and enforce rules.
- Fire doors: repair closers and seals; fit hold-open devices linked to the alarm; replace non-compliant apartment doors.
- Wall protection: corner guards, rails and impact-resistant finishes where damage concentrates.
- Floor finishes: replace worn carpet with durable products suited to traffic.
- Lighting: LED with occupancy dimming that never leaves corridors dark.
- Smoke vents: repair and test.
- Refurbishment of finishes and signage.

- Storage provision: resident and tenant storage cages, bin rooms and bike parking so items have somewhere to go besides corridors.
- Signage and wayfinding renewed with layout changes, including exit signs visible from every point.
- Acoustic and odour control: corridor ventilation rebalanced and door seals renewed.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Corridor works are usually priced per floor. Fire door works are per door. Finishes by area. Lighting per fitting. Refurbishment per floor, often staged. Management measures are operating costs. Safety items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle.

Fire door remediation in apartment buildings can be large because every flat entrance door may need replacement or upgrading, often with owners sharing costs. Corridor refurbishments are best staged floor by floor to keep the building in use, with access to apartments and tenancies coordinated. Management measures such as storage and rule enforcement cost little and fix the most common safety problem.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets egress widths and travel distances, and fire and smoke door requirements; fire doors are inspected under AS 1851; strata by-laws control corridor use.
- United Kingdom. The Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual checks of flat entrance doors in residential buildings over 11 metres; Approved Document B sets requirements.
- United States. NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code require egress paths kept clear and fire doors maintained, with NFPA 80 inspection.

In strata and condominium buildings in all three countries, corridors are common property and their fire safety is the owners corporation's duty, while flat entrance doors may belong to individual owners, which complicates remediation.

Hotel and aged care corridors carry additional operator and accreditation requirements.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire door register and inspection records.
- Fire safety statements.
- Building or strata rules on corridors.
- Complaints and incident records.
- Refurbishment history.

- Flat entrance door ownership and replacement records in apartment buildings.
- Smoke vent test records.
- Egress and layout drawings after fit-outs.

- Records of items removed from corridors and notices issued.

pages.title: Common Internal Areas
pages.question: How do shared areas in apartment buildings fail, and what makes them a collective risk?
pages.answer: Residential common areas fail through residents' alterations, storage and deferred decisions. Flat entrance doors replaced or stripped of closers compromise the corridor escape route; bikes, furniture and charging e-bikes fill corridors, stairs and storerooms; intercoms and lift phones stop when networks are switched off; moves damage walls and lifts. Collective funding delays refurbishment until defects or orders force it. A funded capital works plan and enforced by-laws are the main controls.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about common internal areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Lobby, corridors, stairwells, entry intercom and security to shared residential common property

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Common internal areas are the shared interior spaces of apartment buildings: the entrance lobby with mailboxes and intercom, corridors and lift lobbies on each floor, stairs, and shared rooms such as bike stores, parcel rooms, gyms and residents' lounges. They are common property, owned and maintained collectively through the owners corporation, body corporate, residents' management company or landlord, and funded from levies or service charges. Functionally they must give residents safe, secure access and escape, present the building well, and stay affordable to maintain. This page draws together the residential aspects; the entrance, corridors and stairs each have their own space page.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry and intercom | Entry doors, intercom panel, access control, mailboxes, parcel lockers | Security; reliability; network dependence |
| Corridors and lift lobbies | Finishes, lighting, fire doors, smoke vents | Escape route; appearance; wear |
| Stairs | Fire-isolated or open stairs | Escape; storage; propped doors |
| Shared rooms | Bike stores, gyms, lounges, bin rooms | Fire load; batteries; hygiene; misuse |
| Fire and life safety | Detection, warning, emergency lighting, sprinklers, flat entrance doors | Compliance; resident alterations |
| Security | CCTV, fobs, access control to car parks and floors | Obsolescence; privacy; lost fobs |

Because costs are shared, decisions are collective and often deferred. Many owners corporations have long-term maintenance or capital works plans that are not followed, or none at all, and common areas then deteriorate until a defect or compliance order forces action.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridor carpet | 8 to 15 years | Traffic; moves |
| Paint and wall finishes | 7 to 12 years | Damage from moves |
| Intercom and access control | 10 to 15 years | Technology; network shutdowns; vendor support |
| Lobby refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Market; wear |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |
| CCTV | 7 to 10 years | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Furniture moves without protection, damaging walls, doors and lifts.
- Resident storage in corridors, stairs and bike rooms.
- Network changes: older intercoms, lift phones and alarm diallers depended on networks that have been switched off, such as Australia's 3G networks in late 2024 and copper lines being retired in Britain and the United States.
- Deferred maintenance from collective decision-making.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Flat entrance doors and resident alterations

Each flat's entrance door protects the corridor escape route from a fire in that flat. Residents replace doors with non-rated ones, remove closers, add cat flaps and letterboxes, and fit hardware that defeats the seals. Responsibility for these doors is often contested between owners and the building.

### Storage and battery fire risk

Bikes, prams, furniture and e-bikes left in corridors, stairs and lobbies obstruct escape and add fire load; e-bikes and scooters charging in common areas and storage rooms are a growing fire source.

### Intercom and access control obsolescence

Intercoms and access systems depending on retired mobile networks or copper lines stop working; proprietary fob systems tie buildings to one supplier; lost fobs compromise security.

### Wear and damage
