Moves, deliveries and heavy use damage lobbies, corridors, lift cars and doors; damage is often not recovered from residents.

### Security failures

Doors that do not close and latch, tailgating, and unmonitored CCTV allow intrusions, parcel theft and vandalism.

### Underfunding and deferral

Without a funded long-term plan, common area refurbishments and compliance works are deferred until they become urgent and more costly.

### Building defects in newer buildings

Newer apartment buildings often carry construction defects in common areas, such as waterproofing, fire separation and façade issues. Owners corporations must pursue them within statutory warranty periods, and the funds and expertise to do so are often lacking.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On a walk-through

- Items stored in corridors, stairs and lobbies; e-bikes charging in common areas.
- Flat entrance doors of mixed designs, without closers, or with added openings.
- Intercom panels faulty or replaced piecemeal; parcels piled in lobbies.
- Entry doors not closing or latching.
- Damaged walls, doors and lift interiors from moves.
- Worn carpets and dated lobbies.

### In the records

- Capital works or maintenance plan and fund balance.
- Annual fire safety certification.
- By-laws on storage, moves and alterations.
- Defect reports and claims.
- Intercom and access control contracts.

- Notices about defects, special levies or compliance orders on lobby noticeboards.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat doors without closers | Resident alterations | Door survey; by-law enforcement |
| Intercom stopped working | Network shutdown or obsolete equipment | Network type; vendor |
| Storage throughout corridors | Insufficient storage and weak enforcement | Storage provision; enforcement records |
| Common areas dated despite sound fabric | Deferred refurbishment | Capital works plan; fund balance |

> Flat entrance doors that do not self-close and seal, and storage or battery charging in corridors and stairs, are fire safety findings for the whole building.

Separate common property defects from resident behaviour: the first needs funding and works, the second needs by-laws and enforcement. Many common area problems combine both.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-compliant flat entrance doors; storage and charging in escape routes; failed emergency lighting | safety | Rectify now |
| Intercom or entry security failed | failure | Restore now |
| Fire safety certification or capital works plan due | deadline | As required |
| Worn finishes; security weaknesses | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Lobby and corridors at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish from the capital works fund |
| No capital works plan or door survey | check | Prepare |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with fire safety and security specialists, working through the strata manager, managing agent or landlord so residents can be notified and flats accessed.

- Common area walk-through of every floor, stair, lobby and shared room at different times, recording storage, doors, finishes, lighting, signage and security.
- Flat entrance door survey of every door: rating labels, closers, seals, gaps, hardware, glazing and alterations, with ownership noted.
- Intercom and access control review: technology, the network it depends on, vendor support, fob management and integration with lifts and car park gates.
- Storage and battery review: where residents store bikes and e-bikes, where they charge them, and what rooms exist for this.
- Capital works plan review: whether the plan reflects actual condition and whether the fund can pay for what is due.
- By-law and enforcement review: rules on storage, moves, door alterations and renovations, and how breaches are dealt with.

The report should list safety items, a funded refurbishment and compliance plan, and recommended by-law changes.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Flat entrance doors: complete a survey, enforce by-laws on alterations, and replace non-compliant doors, settling cost allocation between owners and the building first.
- Storage and charging rules with designated bike and storage rooms, battery charging rooms with detection, and enforcement.
- Intercom and access upgrades to supported systems using current networks or the internet, with open fob formats so the building is not locked to one vendor.
- Move management: booking, lift and wall protection, and recovery of damage costs from residents.
- Security: door closers and latches restored, CCTV reviewed, parcel lockers to reduce theft.
- Refurbishment of lobbies and corridors funded and scheduled through the capital works fund.
- Capital works plan prepared from a condition survey and reviewed regularly.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Common area works are paid for by levies or service charges and, for larger items, special levies. Flat entrance doors are priced per door, often the largest compliance cost in older apartment buildings. Intercom and access control upgrades are lump sums per building. Refurbishment is priced per floor or for the lobby. Planning and surveys are modest costs that reduce the risk of sudden special levies.

Safety items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle and the core of the capital works plan.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. State strata legislation requires owners corporations to maintain and repair common property, with New South Wales requiring a ten-year capital works fund plan and Victoria requiring maintenance plans for larger owners corporations; annual fire safety certification applies to essential safety measures; by-laws control storage, moves and alterations.
- United Kingdom. The Building Safety Act 2022 creates duties for higher-risk residential buildings, and the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual checks of flat entrance doors in buildings over 11 metres; leasehold law and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 govern service charge consultation.
- United States. State condominium and homeowners association laws govern common elements and reserves; Florida requires milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominium buildings of three or more storeys; local fire codes require corridors and stairs kept clear.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Capital works or maintenance plan and current fund balance.
- Annual fire safety certification and any orders.
- By-laws and records of enforcement.
- Defect reports and claims.
- Intercom and access control contracts and network details.
- Flat entrance door survey results.
- Minutes of owners corporation meetings on major works.

pages.title: Communications, Security & Specialist Systems
pages.question: How do communications, security and specialist building systems fail, and which failures are safety issues?
pages.answer: These systems turn over faster than buildings. The urgent issue is copper line retirement: lift emergency phones, alarm diallers and intercoms on copper lines can go silent, and Britain's network is retired on 31 January 2027. Access-controlled escape doors that do not release on fire alarm are a life-safety failure. Analogue CCTV and proprietary access control lose support; internet-exposed cameras are compromised; nurse call gaps put residents at risk.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about communications, security & specialist systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: CCTV, Access Control, Intercom, MATV, AV, Nurse Call

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
This element covers the low-voltage building systems that connect, secure and serve occupants: structured cabling and communications rooms; the incoming carrier and fibre connections; CCTV; access control and intercoms; master antenna and satellite television (MATV); audio-visual systems; public address; in-building mobile and emergency services radio coverage; and specialist systems such as nurse call in healthcare and aged care, and lift emergency telephones. Fire detection and warning systems have their own page.

| System | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structured cabling and comms rooms | All commercial and multi-residential buildings | Obsolete cabling categories; congested risers; undocumented patching; hot rooms |
| Carrier lead-in (fibre, copper) | All buildings | Copper networks being switched off; single lead-in with no diversity |
| CCTV (analogue and IP) | Commercial, residential, retail, car parks | Analogue obsolescence; poor coverage; cyber exposure; privacy compliance |
| Access control | Commercial and residential entries, car parks, lifts | Proprietary lock-in; controller obsolescence; failure to release on fire alarm |
| Intercoms | Apartment entries, car parks, lifts | Analogue systems failing; dependence on copper lines |
| MATV and satellite | Apartments, hotels, hospitals | Amplifiers and distribution ageing; changing broadcast standards |
| Lift emergency telephones and alarm diallers | Every lift; alarm monitoring | Copper line switch-off leaves them silent |
| In-building coverage (DAS, emergency radio) | Large and below-ground buildings | Coverage gaps; required for emergency services in some jurisdictions |
| Nurse call | Hospitals, aged care | Life safety for residents; obsolescence; coverage gaps |
| Audio-visual and public address | Commercial, education, assembly | Technology obsolescence |

These systems turn over faster than the building fabric: technology changes, vendors withdraw support, and the networks they rely on change. The biggest current change is the retirement of copper telephone networks, which affects every device that still dials out over a copper line.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structured cabling (copper) | 15 to 25 years | Category standards; bandwidth needs |
| Fibre backbone | 25 years and more | Physical damage |
| Network switches and comms equipment | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support |
| IP CCTV cameras and recorders | 7 to 10 years | Technology; firmware support |
| Analogue CCTV | At end of life | Replace |
| Access control controllers | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Intercoms | 10 to 15 years | Technology; line dependence |
| MATV amplifiers and distribution | 10 to 20 years | Standards changes |
| Nurse call systems | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |

What shortens life:

- Vendor end of support, especially for proprietary access control and nurse call.
- Network changes: copper switch-off, new broadcast standards.
- Cyber security requirements that retire insecure devices early.
- Hot, undocumented comms rooms.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Copper network retirement

Copper telephone networks are being retired: Britain's analogue network is retired on 31 January 2027, Australia has largely replaced copper with the NBN, and United States carriers are retiring copper lines. Lift emergency telephones, alarm and fire monitoring diallers, intercoms, door entry systems and some building management connections that depend on copper lines can go silent without warning. Lift emergency phones are the most serious: people trapped in a lift must be able to call for help.

### Technology and vendor obsolescence

Analogue CCTV, proprietary access control and older nurse call systems lose spare parts and support; a single controller failure can disable a system. Proprietary access control ties the building to one integrator for cards, readers and changes.

### Cyber exposure

IP cameras, access controllers and intercoms connected to the internet with default passwords and unpatched firmware are commonly compromised. Governments in all three countries have restricted certain camera and equipment manufacturers in government facilities, which affects buildings with government tenants.

### Fire interface failures

Access-controlled doors on escape routes must release on fire alarm or power failure; interfaces broken by upgrades or rewiring can lock people in. Lifts with access control must still respond to fire service controls.

### Coverage gaps

CCTV blind spots after fit-outs; access control bypassed by propped doors; weak mobile and emergency radio coverage in basements and large buildings; nurse call points missing in new rooms.

### Cabling and comms room problems

Older cabling categories cannot carry modern bandwidth or power-over-Ethernet loads; risers fill with abandoned cable; comms rooms overheat; patching is undocumented, so faults take days to trace.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Analogue cameras (coaxial cable) and old recorders; cameras pointing at walls or obscured.
- Access control readers of an old proprietary type; doors propped open.
- Lift car emergency phones; label or test showing the line type.
- Comms rooms: temperature, cable congestion, labelling, equipment age.
- Intercom panels faded or failing.
- Weak mobile reception in basements and cores.

### In the records

- Lift emergency phone and alarm monitoring line types and test records.
- Access control and CCTV vendor, version and support status.
- Fire interface test records for access-controlled doors.
- Cabling test results and documentation.
- Privacy policies and signage for CCTV.
- Nurse call test and maintenance records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lift phone silent on test | Copper line retired or disconnected | Line type; carrier notice |
| Alarm monitoring signals not received | Dialler on a retired line | Monitoring centre test |
| Doors stay locked in a fire alarm test | Broken fire interface | Interface test |
| Only one company can add a card | Proprietary access control | Vendor; licensing |
| Cameras visible from the internet | Insecure configuration | Security assessment |
| Network faults take days to trace | Undocumented cabling and patching | Documentation |

> Lift emergency telephones and alarm diallers on copper lines must be checked before the line is retired. A lift phone that cannot call out is a life-safety failure.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lift emergency phones or alarm diallers not working; access-controlled escape doors not releasing; nurse call failures | safety | Rectify now |
| Copper line retirement scheduled for devices still on copper | deadline | Migrate before the switch-off date |
| System failed (CCTV, access control, intercom) | failure | Repair now |
| Unsupported systems; cyber exposure; coverage gaps | condition | Upgrade in the near term |
| Systems at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| Line types unknown; no security assessment | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A communications and security systems consultant, with the lift contractor for emergency phones and a cyber security specialist.

- Inventory of every system with vendor, model, version, age and support status.
- Line audit: every device that dials out (lift phones, alarm diallers, intercoms, BMS modems) and the line type it uses.
- Testing: lift phones, alarm monitoring, nurse call, intercoms.
- Fire interface testing of access-controlled doors and lifts.
- Coverage review: CCTV, access control, mobile and emergency radio.
- Cyber security assessment of IP devices and remote access.
- Cabling and comms room survey: categories, capacity, documentation, cooling.
- Compliance review: privacy for CCTV, emergency radio coverage where required, procurement restrictions for government tenants.

The report should give the inventory, the copper migration list, safety failures, support status, security risks and a replacement programme.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Migrate devices off copper: lift phones and diallers to 4G/5G or IP with battery backup and monitoring.
- Fix fire interfaces and test them.
- Replace analogue CCTV with IP systems, designed for coverage and privacy.
- Replace proprietary access control with open-standard systems, with the owner holding licences and databases.
- Harden cyber security: segregated networks, changed credentials, firmware updates, removal of restricted equipment where required.
- Improve coverage: distributed antenna systems or emergency responder radio systems.
- Upgrade cabling and comms rooms; remove redundant cable; document patching.
- Replace nurse call systems with supported ones and full coverage.

- Battery backup for digital lift phones and diallers so they work during power failures.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Copper migration is priced per device with monitoring contracts recurring. CCTV, access control and intercom replacement are priced per device plus head end. Cabling upgrades are per outlet or per floor. In-building coverage systems are lump sums. Nurse call is per bed or room.

Safety rectification and copper migration are code compliance or deadline-driven; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance contracts recur.

Digital line migration often needs new equipment in lift cars and panels as well as a new service.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Cabling work requires registered cablers under the communications cabling rules; AS/NZS 3080 and related standards cover structured cabling; lift emergency communication requirements follow the lift standards; state privacy and surveillance laws govern CCTV; the copper network has largely been replaced by the NBN.
- United Kingdom. The analogue telephone network is retired on 31 January 2027, with all users to be migrated by then, affecting lift phones, alarm diallers and telecare; BS EN 81-28 covers remote alarms on lifts; UK GDPR and the Surveillance Camera Code govern CCTV.
- United States. Carriers are retiring copper lines under FCC rules; ASME A17.1 requires two-way communication in lifts; the International Fire Code and NFPA 1225 require emergency responder radio coverage in many buildings; federal procurement rules restrict certain telecommunications and video equipment.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Inventory of systems with vendors, versions and support status.
- Line types for lift phones, alarm diallers and intercoms, and carrier notices.
- Fire interface test records.
- Cabling documentation and test results.
- CCTV privacy policy and signage.
- Nurse call test records.
- Any cyber security assessment.

- Lift emergency phone test records.

pages.title: Disabled Access (DDA)
pages.question: How do buildings fall short on access, and which access findings create safety or discrimination risk?
pages.answer: Access findings fall into three kinds. Older buildings predate current requirements: steps at entries, narrow doors, no accessible toilets or lifts. Alterations can trigger upgrades to the path of travel the owner did not plan for. And features fail in use: tactile indicators lift into trip hazards, closers make doors too heavy, accessible toilets become storerooms, lifts stay out of service. Missing evacuation provision for people with disability is a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about disabled access (dda); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Ramps, handrails, tactile indicators, accessible amenities

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Disabled access covers the features that let people with disability reach, enter, use and leave a building: a continuous accessible path of travel from the street and car park, ramps and step-free entries, doors that are wide enough and light enough to open, lifts, accessible toilets and showers, handrails, tactile ground surface indicators that warn of hazards, luminance contrast so edges and doors can be seen, signage in braille and tactile form, hearing augmentation, accessible parking, and provision for evacuation. Requirements depend on the building's use and age, and on whether it is being altered.

| Provision | Where it applies | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accessible path of travel and entry | Public and commercial buildings, apartment common areas | Steps at entries; steep ramps; gaps and level changes |
| Ramps, kerb ramps and landings | Entries and changes of level | Too steep; no landings; no handrails; slippery |
| Doors and doorways | Throughout the accessible path | Too narrow; too heavy; poor circulation space; thresholds |
| Accessible toilets and showers | Public and commercial buildings | Wrong dimensions; used as storage; fittings missing |
| Tactile ground surface indicators | Stairs, ramps, kerbs, platform edges | Lifting and missing; wrong placement |
| Luminance contrast and signage | Doors, edges, stairs, wayfinding | Faded; missing braille and tactile signs |
| Hearing augmentation | Meeting rooms, auditoria, counters | Absent or not working |
| Accessible lifts and platform lifts | Multi-level buildings | Out of service; not compliant |
| Accessible parking | Car parks | Wrong size; no shared zone; not signed |

Era is a strong guide. Australian buildings designed before the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards took effect in 2011, British buildings before Approved Document M was extended in the 1990s and 2000s, and American buildings before the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) often fall well short of current requirements, and alterations to them can trigger upgrades.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ramps and paths | 30 to 50 years | Surface wear; settlement |
| Tactile indicators (adhesive or discrete) | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; adhesive failure; cleaning |
| Accessible toilet fittings | 15 to 25 years | Use; vandalism |
| Door closers and automatic door operators | 10 to 15 years | Use; adjustment |
| Hearing augmentation systems | 10 to 15 years | Technology; maintenance |
| Signage | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage |

What shortens life, or effectiveness:

- Heavy traffic lifting and wearing tactile indicators.
- Door closers adjusted too strong for fire or security, making doors too heavy to open.
- Fit-outs that block circulation space or remove features.
- Poor management: accessible toilets used for storage, ramps blocked, lifts left out of service.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Built before current requirements

Older buildings have steps at entries, narrow doors, no accessible toilets, no lift between levels, and no tactile or contrast provisions. These are not defects in the ordinary sense, but they expose owners and occupiers to discrimination complaints and limit who can use the building.

### Alterations that trigger upgrades

New work must generally meet current requirements, and in Australia and the United States, alterations can extend obligations to the path of travel serving the altered area. A fit-out or refurbishment can therefore bring an access upgrade obligation the owner did not plan for.

### Wear and loss of features

Tactile indicators lift and become trip hazards or are removed; luminance contrast strips fade; signage is damaged; handrails loosen; ramp surfaces become slippery.

### Door operating forces

Doors on accessible routes must be openable by people with limited strength. Closers set strong for fire, smoke or wind, and heavy external doors without automatic operators, make doors effectively impassable.

### Management failures

Accessible toilets used as storerooms or cleaners' rooms, ramps and accessible parking obstructed, lifts and platform lifts out of service for long periods, and hearing loops not switched on all remove access that exists on paper.

### Evacuation of people with disability

Many buildings provide accessible entry but no plan for getting people with disability out in an emergency: no refuges, evacuation lifts, communication systems or personal evacuation plans.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Steps or steep ramps at entries; level changes along routes.
- Doors that are narrow, heavy, or have high thresholds.
- Accessible toilets cluttered, locked or used as storage; missing grab rails or wrong layouts.
- Tactile indicators lifted, missing or in the wrong places; worn contrast strips.
- Signs without braille or tactile lettering where required.
- Lifts and platform lifts out of service.
- No hearing augmentation signage in meeting rooms and auditoria.

### In the records

- Access audits.
- Building approvals for alterations, with access reports.
- Complaints and discrimination claims.
- Personal emergency evacuation plans.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps at the only entry | Building predates access requirements | Era; approvals |
| New fit-out with an accessible toilet but steps at the entry | Path of travel not upgraded with the alteration | Approval documents; access report |
| Tactile indicators lifting at stairs | Adhesive failure from traffic and cleaning | Inspection |
| Doors that people in wheelchairs cannot open | Closer force too high or no automatic operator | Door force measurement |
| Accessible toilet full of boxes | Management practice | Observation |
| No refuge or evacuation plan | Egress for people with disability not addressed | Fire strategy; plans |

> Access findings divide into three kinds: wear and management issues that can be fixed quickly, non-compliance triggered by recent alterations, and historic shortfalls that carry discrimination risk. The kind decides urgency and who pays.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifted tactile indicators or damaged ramps creating trip hazards; no means of evacuation for people with disability | safety | Rectify now |
| Only accessible route unavailable (lift out of service, ramp blocked) | failure | Restore now |
| Upgrade required by an alteration approval or a complaint resolution | deadline | By the required date |
| Heavy doors, faded contrast, missing signage, accessible toilets misused | condition | Fix in the near term |
| Access features at end of life | lifecycle | Renew |
| No access audit; alterations planned | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An accredited access consultant leads; in California, a Certified Access Specialist.

- Access audit against current requirements, covering the path of travel from the boundary and car park through entries, circulation, lifts, sanitary facilities, signage and egress.
- Measurements: ramp gradients, door widths and opening forces, circulation spaces, toilet layouts, luminance contrast.
- Alteration review: which areas have been altered since access requirements took effect and what obligations followed.
- Management review: how accessible facilities are kept available.
- Egress review with the fire strategy for people with disability.

The report should separate safety items, compliance obligations triggered by alterations, discrimination risks, and good-practice improvements, with priorities.

- User consultation where practicable: people who use the building can identify barriers that measurements miss, such as confusing wayfinding or doors that only staff can unlock.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Entries: ramps, platform lifts or regraded paths; automatic doors.
- Doors: closer adjustment, automatic operators, wider doors, threshold ramps.
- Accessible sanitary facilities: new or upgraded rooms; clearing storage.
- Tactile indicators and contrast: replace lifted indicators, renew contrast strips.
- Signage in braille and tactile form; wayfinding.
- Hearing augmentation in meeting rooms and service counters.
- Lifts: reliability and accessibility upgrades.
- Evacuation provisions: refuges, communication, evacuation plans.
- Management: procedures to keep features available.

- Accessible parking resized and marked with shared zones and signage, close to the accessible entry.
- Wayfinding: consistent signage, contrast and lighting so people with low vision can find entries, lifts and toilets.
- Staged programme: where full compliance is impractical, an access action plan setting priorities and dates, which in Australia can be lodged with the Human Rights Commission and helps manage discrimination risk.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Minor works (tactile indicators, signage, closers) are itemised. Ramps and automatic doors are lump sums per entry. New accessible toilets are lump sums per room. Lifts are major projects. Path of travel upgrades triggered by alterations sit with the alteration project.

Safety items are immediate; alteration-triggered upgrades are code compliance; discrimination risk reduction is a strategic choice; renewals are lifecycle.

An access action plan spreads cost over time while showing commitment, which matters in discrimination disputes.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 and the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010 apply to new work and to the affected part and path of travel in alterations; the National Construction Code sets access requirements, calling up AS 1428.1 and related parts including tactile indicators.
- United Kingdom. The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments to remove barriers; Approved Document M sets access for new and altered buildings; BS 8300 sets design guidance for accessible buildings.
- United States. The Americans with Disabilities Act and 2010 ADA Standards apply, with existing public accommodations required to remove barriers where readily achievable and alterations required to improve the path of travel up to a proportion of the alteration cost; the Fair Housing Act covers multifamily housing; ICC A117.1 is adopted in building codes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Access audits and access reports for approvals.
- Building approvals for alterations, with access conditions.
- Complaints and discrimination claims.
- Personal emergency evacuation plans.
- Lift and platform lift downtime records.
- Management procedures for accessible facilities.

- Any access action plan.
- Accessible parking layout and signage records.

- Door opening force measurements on the accessible route.

pages.title: Dock Levellers & Goods Hoists
pages.question: How do dock levellers and goods hoists fail, and which faults put people at risk?
pages.answer: Dock equipment fails by overload, impact and lost safety devices. Heavier battery-electric forklifts overload levellers rated for older machines, cracking lips and decks; worn bumpers let trailers hit the building; hydraulic leaks let decks sink. The dangerous failures are free-fall protection that does not stop a deck when a trailer pulls away, trailers creeping without restraints, open dock edges, and goods hoist doors that open with no car behind them.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about dock levellers & goods hoists; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Platforms, hydraulic systems, controls

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Dock levellers bridge the gap and height difference between a loading dock floor and a truck bed, so forklifts and pallet jacks can drive between them. Goods hoists and service lifts move goods, not people, between levels: dumbwaiters in kitchens and hospitals, material hoists in retail and industrial buildings, and scissor lift tables at docks. Dock equipment works with dock doors, seals and shelters, vehicle restraints, bumpers, dock lighting and the dock edge itself, and its failures injure people and damage buildings and vehicles.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydraulic dock leveller | Logistics, retail, industrial docks | Hydraulic cylinders raise the deck and extend the lip; velocity fuses stop free fall |
| Mechanical (spring) dock leveller | Older and lighter-duty docks | Springs and hold-downs; more manual adjustment and wear |
| Air-bag dock leveller | Some logistics docks | Air bag lifts the deck; fan and bag condition |
| Edge-of-dock leveller | Light-duty docks | Small height range; mounted at the dock face |
| Vehicle restraints | Busy docks | Hold the trailer to the dock so it cannot creep or drive away during loading |
| Scissor lift tables | Docks without raised floors, mezzanines | Hydraulic scissor mechanism; pinch points |
| Goods hoists and dumbwaiters | Retail, hospitals, kitchens, warehouses | Small lifts for goods only; door interlocks critical |

Loading docks are among the most dangerous areas of logistics and retail buildings: trailers creep away from docks under forklift braking, people fall from open dock edges, forklifts fall through gaps, and levellers drop under load. Equipment condition, the surrounding dock structure and site management together decide the risk.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydraulic dock leveller | 15 to 25 years | Cycles; load ratings; impact |
| Mechanical dock leveller | 10 to 20 years | Spring and hinge wear |
| Hydraulic power packs and cylinders | 10 to 15 years | Seals; contamination |
| Lip hinges and deck plates | 10 to 20 years | Impact; fatigue cracking |
| Vehicle restraints | 10 to 15 years | Impact; controls |
| Dock seals and shelters | 5 to 10 years | Abrasion; UV |
| Dock bumpers | 3 to 8 years | Truck impacts |
| Goods hoists | 20 to 30 years; controls 15 to 20 | Duty; door abuse |

What shortens life:

- Overload: forklifts heavier than the leveller rating, especially with battery-electric forklifts that weigh more than older models.
- Impact from trailers backing into docks without bumpers, and from forklifts dropping onto lips.
- Lack of planned maintenance, with repairs only after breakdown.
- Weather at external docks, corroding pits, hinges and hydraulics.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Uncontrolled descent

If a trailer pulls away while the leveller lip rests on it, the deck drops. Velocity fuses in hydraulic levellers and safety legs or stops in mechanical levellers are meant to catch it; when they fail or are adjusted out, the deck falls with a forklift on it. This is the most serious leveller failure.

### Trailer creep and early departure

Trailers move away from the dock under the braking forces of forklifts, or drivers pull away before loading is finished. Without vehicle restraints or interlocks, forklifts fall into the gap.

### Structural cracking

Deck plates, lip hinges and support beams crack from fatigue and overload. Cracks start at welds and hinge points and grow until lips fail or decks deform.

### Hydraulic failures

Seals leak, oil contaminates, power packs fail and cylinders drift, so levellers do not rise, lips do not extend, or decks sink under load.

### Pit and dock edge damage

Pit edges and curb angles break up under repeated impact; bumpers wear away, letting trailers strike the building; dock walls and slabs crack.

### Open edges and falls

Docks without doors closed, without edge barriers, or with levellers left raised leave drops of over a metre where people and forklifts can fall.

### Goods hoist door interlocks

Goods hoists and dumbwaiters rely on landing door interlocks so a door cannot open unless the car is there. Failed or bypassed interlocks expose people to falls into the shaft and crushing; people riding goods-only hoists face the same risk.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Cracks at deck welds, lip hinges and beams; lips that do not extend fully or sit flat.
- Oil under levellers and around power packs; decks that drift down.
- Velocity fuses and safety legs present and working, and maintenance stands used.
- Bumpers worn, missing or loose; impact damage to dock walls and doors.
- Vehicle restraints present, working, and interlocked with doors or levellers where fitted.
- Broken pit edges and curb angles; trip hazards.
- Goods hoist landing doors that open without the car present; signs prohibiting riders.

### In the records

- Maintenance and service records for each leveller and hoist.
- Incident and near-miss reports at docks.
- Forklift weights and leveller ratings.
- Plant registration and inspection records for hoists.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deck sinks slowly under load | Hydraulic leak or failed holding valve | Drift test; oil leaks |
| Cracks at lip hinges and deck welds | Fatigue and overload | Inspection; forklift weight against rating |
| Deck does not stop when tested for free fall | Failed velocity fuse or safety leg | Free-fall test |
| Trailers moving during loading | No vehicle restraints or poor procedures | Observation; incident reports |
| Dock walls and doors damaged | Bumpers worn or missing | Inspection |
| Goods hoist door opens without car | Interlock fault or bypass | Interlock test |

> A dock leveller that does not stop when its lip loses support, or a goods hoist door that opens with no car behind it, is a life-safety failure. Take it out of use until repaired.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed free-fall protection; failed hoist door interlocks; cracked lips or decks; open dock edges without protection | safety | Take out of use now |
| Leveller or hoist inoperable at an operational dock | failure | Repair now |
| Hoist registration or inspection due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Hydraulic leaks, worn bumpers, broken pit edges | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Equipment at end of life or underrated for current forklifts | lifecycle | Replace |
| No maintenance records; forklift weights unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A dock equipment specialist or mechanical engineer, with a lift consultant for goods hoists.

- Inventory of every leveller, restraint, seal, bumper and hoist, with ratings and ages.
- Rating check: current forklift weights, including battery-electric models, against leveller capacity.
- Structural inspection of decks, lips, hinges, beams and pit frames for cracks.
- Function tests: raise, lip extension, free-fall protection, restraint engagement and interlocks.
- Hydraulic inspection: leaks, drift, oil condition.
- Dock structure: pit edges, walls, bumpers, doors and lighting.
- Goods hoists: door interlocks, controls, signage, registration.
- Operations review of incidents and loading procedures with the site operator.

The report should list each dock with its safety status, condition, rating adequacy and recommended works.

Inspections are best scheduled with the operator so docks can be taken out of service in turn without stopping operations.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Free-fall protection: replace velocity fuses, safety legs and stops; train staff in maintenance stands.
- Structural repair of cracked lips and decks, or leveller replacement with higher ratings.
- Vehicle restraints with interlocks to dock doors or levellers, and signal lights for drivers.
- Bumper replacement on a cycle, with steel-faced bumpers at heavy-use docks.
- Pit edge repair with new curb angles and concrete.
- Hydraulic overhaul: seals, power packs, oil.
- Dock seals and shelters renewed to reduce energy loss and weather.
- Goods hoist interlock repair or modernisation, with clear prohibition of riders.

- Edge protection: barriers or gates at docks without trucks, and procedures so levellers are stored level and dock doors are closed when not loading.
- Dock lighting inside trailers and at the dock edge so forklift drivers can see the gap and the lip.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Bumpers and seals are recurring replacements. Leveller replacement is per dock, including pit frame repairs, and needs the dock out of service. Vehicle restraints are per dock with electrical and control work. Pit edge repairs are per dock. Goods hoist modernisation is a lump sum per hoist.

Safety rectification is code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; bumpers, seals and repairs are repairs and maintenance. In logistics leases, tenants commonly maintain dock equipment and owners replace it at end of life.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Dock equipment and goods hoists are plant under the work health and safety regulations, which require risk management, maintenance and, for some hoists, registration; Safe Work Australia and state regulators publish guidance on loading dock and forklift safety.
- United Kingdom. PUWER 1998 requires work equipment to be maintained and inspected, and LOLER 1998 requires thorough examination of goods hoists; BS EN 1398 covers dock levellers; the HSE publishes guidance on loading bay safety and vehicle movement.
- United States. OSHA requires dock boards and levellers to be strong enough for their loads and secured, and requires measures against trailer movement; ANSI MH30.1 covers dock leveling devices; ASME A17.1 covers dumbwaiters and material lifts.

In all three jurisdictions, landlords and tenants should agree in the lease who maintains and inspects dock equipment.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Maintenance and service records for each dock leveller and hoist.
- Leveller ratings and current forklift weights.
- Incident and near-miss reports at docks.
- Goods hoist registration and inspection certificates.
- Lease terms allocating dock equipment maintenance and replacement.
- Loading procedures, including vehicle restraint use.

- Forklift fleet details, including weights of battery-electric models.

pages.title: Ductwork & Air Distribution
pages.question: How does ductwork fail, what are the warning signs, and when is it a fire safety issue?
pages.answer: Ductwork lasts decades, but what is attached to it does not. Torn vapour barriers on chilled ducts sweat and drip; joints leak; dirt accumulates and grows microbes; flexible ducts kink and sag; fit-outs unbalance the system. The serious finding is fire and smoke dampers missing, obstructed, painted shut, never connected or untested: they are life-safety devices on fixed testing regimes, and an untested damper should be treated as non-functional.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ductwork & air distribution; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Insulated ductwork, grilles, diffusers

sources.title: NFPA 80 Fire Doors and Other Opening Protectives

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Ductwork carries air between air handling units, fans and the spaces they serve: supply, return, outside air and exhaust. Air distribution includes the grilles, registers and diffusers at each end, the balancing dampers that set airflows, the flexible connections to terminal units, the insulation and vapour barrier on chilled ducts, internal acoustic lining, and the fire and smoke dampers where ducts pass through fire-rated walls and floors.

| Form | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised sheet steel, rectangular and spiral | Most commercial and institutional buildings | Long-lived; joints and seals age; corrodes in wet or chemical exhaust |
| Stainless steel | Kitchen exhaust, laboratories, wet areas | Durable; welded for grease ducts |
| Fibreglass ductboard | Some commercial and residential systems | Self-insulated; fibres erode; hard to clean |
| Flexible duct | Final connections to diffusers; houses | Kinks, sags and tears; short life |
| Internally lined duct | Acoustic sections near fans | Lining erodes and harbours dirt and microbes |
| Pre-insulated panel duct | Some modern commercial systems | Light; joints and damage |
| Builder's work shafts | Older buildings, risers | Masonry or plaster ducts; leaky and dirty |

Fire and smoke dampers close when heat or a fire alarm signal is detected, to stop fire and smoke travelling through the ductwork. They are life-safety devices with their own inspection and testing regimes, and they are commonly found missing, painted shut, obstructed or never connected to the fire alarm.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised ductwork | 30 to 50 years and more | Moisture; corrosive exhaust |
| Duct sealants and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | Temperature; age |
| Flexible duct | 15 to 20 years | Damage; UV in roof spaces |
| External insulation and vapour barrier | 20 to 30 years | Damage; condensation |
| Internal lining | 15 to 25 years | Air velocity; moisture |
| Grilles and diffusers | 20 to 30 years | Fit-out changes |
| Fire dampers | 20 to 30 years with testing | Corrosion; obstruction; fusible link age |

What shortens life:

- Torn vapour barriers on chilled ductwork.
- Corrosive and greasy exhausts.
- Fit-outs that cut, reroute and kink ductwork without rebalancing.
- Poor filtration upstream, which loads ducts with dust.
- Rodents and pests in older systems.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Air leakage

Joints and seams leak as sealants age, wasting fan energy and delivering less air than designed. Leaky return ductwork in ceilings draws in dust and fibres.

### Condensation on chilled ductwork

Supply ducts carrying cold air sweat if their insulation or vapour barrier is torn, compressed or missing. Water wets the insulation, drips onto ceilings, and corrodes the duct and its supports.

### Dirt accumulation and hygiene

Dust, debris and construction residue accumulate inside ducts, particularly where filtration has been poor. In humid conditions, microbes grow on the dirt. Internal acoustic lining erodes and sheds fibres into the airstream.

### Flexible duct problems

Long, sagging, kinked or crushed flexible duct restricts airflow; it tears and leaks; in roof spaces it degrades with heat.

### Loss of balance

Fit-outs add, remove and relocate diffusers and adjust dampers without rebalancing. Some areas get too much air, others too little, and the system no longer matches its design.

### Fire and smoke damper failure

Dampers corrode, seize, are obstructed by cables or debris, are painted or taped shut, or were never installed or connected. A damper that does not close lets fire and smoke through a fire-rated wall or floor.

### Hazardous materials

Older ductwork can contain asbestos in flexible connectors, gaskets, duct lagging and some insulation.

### Noise and draughts

High air velocities, throttled dampers near outlets and poorly selected diffusers generate noise and dump cold air onto occupants. Fit-outs that move partitions without moving diffusers create draughty and stuffy spots.

### Corrosion in wet and chemical exhausts

Exhausts from pools, laundries, kitchens and laboratories carry moisture and chemicals that corrode galvanised ductwork from the inside; corrosion shows first at the lowest points and joints where condensate collects.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In ceiling voids and risers

- Torn or missing insulation; wet insulation; condensation drips; rust on ducts and hangers.
- Flexible ducts sagging, kinked, crushed or disconnected.
- Dust and debris visible inside open ducts and at grilles.
- Fire dampers: access panels, fusible links, obstruction, painted blades.
- Older materials: flexible connectors and lagging of the asbestos era.

### In occupied spaces

- Dust streaks around supply diffusers.
- Draughts, noise, whistling.
- Hot and cold spots after fit-outs.
- Water stains from condensation on ceilings.

### In the records

- Test and balance reports.
- Duct cleaning and hygiene inspection reports.
- Fire damper inspection and test records.
- Fit-out records.
- Asbestos register.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water stains on ceilings along duct runs, in summer | Condensation from torn vapour barrier | Insulation inspection |
| Dust streaks around diffusers | Dirty ductwork or poor filtration | Duct inspection; filter condition |
| Zones short of air after a fit-out | Loss of balance or kinked flex | Airflow measurement |
| Fire damper blades painted or obstructed | Poor installation or maintenance | Inspection |
| Fibres at diffusers | Eroding internal lining or fibreglass ductboard | Inspection |

> Fire and smoke dampers are life-safety devices. A damper that has not been tested, cannot be accessed, or is obstructed should be treated as non-functional until tested.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire or smoke dampers missing, obstructed, failed or untested; deteriorating asbestos in duct materials | safety | Rectify now; fire engineer and licensed asbestos removal |
| Fire damper testing due | deadline | At the interval the standard sets |
| Condensation damaging ceilings; disconnected ducts | failure | Repair now |
| Dirty ductwork, poor balance, torn insulation | condition | Clean, rebalance and repair in the near term |
| Ductwork, insulation and flex at end of life | lifecycle | Replace with major plant or fit-out works |
| No hygiene inspection; fire damper register incomplete | check | Inspect |
| Minor dust | nil | Routine cleaning |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a ventilation hygiene specialist and a fire damper inspector.

- Visual inspection of a representative sample of ductwork, insulation, vapour barrier, flexible connections and supports, prioritising risers, plant rooms and areas with complaints.
- Hygiene inspection by camera and access panels, with dust samples, to AS/NZS 3666, BESA TR/19 or NADCA ACR practice, to decide whether cleaning is needed.
- Airflow measurement at a sample of diffusers and grilles against design, and a review of the latest test and balance report.
- Fire and smoke damper survey: location against every fire-rated wall and floor the ductwork passes, access panel present, blade and spring condition, fusible link, release and drop test, connection to the fire alarm where required.
- Leakage testing of sections to DW/143 or SMACNA methods where energy use or airflow shortfalls warrant.
- Asbestos sampling of flexible connectors, gaskets, lagging and older insulation.
- Noise survey where complaints exist.

The report should give a fire damper register with location, type, access and test result for every damper; hygiene condition; airflow and balance findings; insulation condition; hazardous materials; and prioritised works.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Fire and smoke dampers: install missing dampers, replace failed or corroded units, remove obstructions and paint, fit access panels, connect motorised dampers to the alarm, and test and register every damper.
- Cleaning by brushing, air washing and vacuum to the hygiene standard; cleaning is pointless without fixing the filtration or moisture problem that dirtied the ducts.
- Lining replacement: replace eroding internal lining with faced or perforated-metal-faced lining, or move attenuation to dedicated attenuators.
- Insulation and vapour barrier repair on chilled ductwork, sealing every joint.
- Flexible duct replacement: short, straight, supported runs.
- Sealing: reseal joints; aerosol internal sealing for inaccessible sections.
- Rebalancing after fit-outs, with diffusers relocated to suit partitions.
- Corrosion: replace corroded wet-exhaust sections in stainless steel with drainage at low points.
- Asbestos removal by licensed contractors.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and testing are lump sums with rates per damper tested. Fire damper rectification is priced per damper, with access panels and ceiling and wall making good, which can exceed the damper cost. Cleaning is priced by length or per system. Insulation repair is by length. Rebalancing is per floor or per system. Replacement of ductwork is usually carried in a fit-out or major plant project.

Fire damper works and testing are code compliance and recur; cleaning and repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle; asbestos removal is code compliance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4254.1 and 4254.2 cover flexible and rigid ductwork; AS 1668.1 covers fire and smoke control in ductwork; fire dampers are inspected and tested under AS 1851 as essential safety measures; AS/NZS 3666 covers hygiene.
- United Kingdom. BESA DW/144 specifies sheet metal ductwork; BESA TR/19 sets hygiene; fire dampers follow BS EN 15650 and are tested at least annually under BS 9999 guidance; Approved Document B.
- United States. SMACNA standards for ductwork; NFPA 90A for air conditioning systems; NFPA 80 and NFPA 105 require fire and smoke dampers to be tested one year after installation and then every four years (six in hospitals); NADCA ACR for duct cleaning.

Fire damper testing is commonly an annual certification item in all three countries.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire and smoke damper register with test records and dates.
- Annual essential safety measures or fire safety statements covering dampers.
- Test and balance reports, original and after recent fit-outs.
- Duct hygiene inspection and cleaning records.
- Asbestos register.
- Mechanical as-built drawings showing ductwork and damper locations.
- Fit-out records showing changes to ductwork.

pages.title: Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging
pages.question: How does EV charging fail in existing buildings, and what limits how many chargers a building can take?
pages.answer: EV charging in existing buildings is mostly a capacity problem. A few uncontrolled chargers can overload a car park board or the main supply, so load management or a supply upgrade comes first. Faults come from shared circuits, missing protection and poor terminations; extension-lead charging is a fire and shock risk. Unmetered charging on common supply causes disputes, and proprietary software can strand chargers. Enclosed car parks raise fire questions regulators are still settling.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about electric vehicle (ev) charging; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Charging infrastructure installation

sources.title: Approved Document S: infrastructure for charging electric vehicles

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Electric vehicle charging infrastructure supplies power to vehicles parked at a building: wall-mounted and pedestal AC chargers for overnight and workplace charging, DC fast chargers for rapid top-ups, the cabling and distribution boards that feed them, load management systems that share limited supply between chargers, and the software, payment and billing systems that run them. It is increasingly expected by tenants and residents and required for new buildings in some places, and retrofitting it into existing buildings is mostly an electrical capacity and cost-allocation problem.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-phase AC wall chargers | Houses, apartment car spaces, workplaces | Slow overnight charging; modest load each |
| Three-phase AC chargers | Workplaces, apartments, commercial car parks | Faster; higher load; needs three-phase supply |
| DC fast chargers | Retail, service stations, fleet depots | High power; large supply upgrades; cooling |
| Load-managed networks | Apartment and office car parks | Share available capacity among many chargers |
| Shared-bay or common chargers | Apartments without individual circuits | Billing and booking systems |

In apartment buildings, the questions are as much legal as technical: who owns the car spaces and the cabling routes, how capacity is shared, who pays for the backbone, and how each user is billed. Strata and condominium law in several jurisdictions has been changed recently to make approval easier.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AC chargers | 8 to 12 years | Use; weather; software support |
| DC fast chargers | 8 to 12 years; modules sooner | Heat; use; manufacturer support |
| Cabling and distribution | 25 to 40 years | Installation quality; loading |
| Load management systems | 8 to 12 years | Software and communications support |
| Charger software and back-end services | Depends on vendor | Protocol support; vendor viability |

What shortens life:

- Weather and vandalism at external and public chargers, damaging cables and connectors.
- Vendor failure: networked chargers can be stranded if the operator or software platform disappears, unless they use open protocols.
- Heat in enclosed car parks and around high-power DC chargers.
- Poor installation, which causes nuisance tripping and earth faults.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Electrical capacity

Each charger is a large continuous load. A few uncontrolled chargers can exceed the spare capacity of a car park distribution board or the building's main supply. Without load management or a supply upgrade, adding chargers causes tripping, overheating and, at worst, overloaded cables. Capacity, not chargers, is usually the limiting factor.

### Installation faults

Chargers need dedicated circuits, correct earthing and protection against specific faults such as loss of the supply neutral and DC fault currents. Chargers installed on shared circuits, without the required protection, or with poor terminations overheat, trip and create shock risks.

### Software, protocols and stranded assets

Networked chargers depend on back-end software for access, billing and load management. Proprietary systems can strand chargers if the vendor fails or ends support; open protocols allow switching providers.

### Billing and fairness

In shared buildings, chargers on common supply without metering shift costs to other owners; disputes follow. Sub-metering and billing systems solve this but must meet legal metrology rules where users are charged.

### Fire safety concerns

Electric vehicle fires are not more frequent than petrol vehicle fires on current evidence, but they burn differently, can reignite and are harder to extinguish. In enclosed and basement car parks, location of chargers, detection, ventilation and fire brigade access are under active review by regulators.

### Damage and wear

Cables run over, connectors dropped and damaged, and chargers struck by vehicles cause faults and hazards.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Chargers on circuits shared with other loads; distribution boards with no spare capacity.
- Damaged cables and connectors; chargers out of service.
- Extension leads running from outlets to vehicles in car parks, an unsafe workaround where chargers are not available.
- Chargers without bollards or wheel stops in vehicle paths.
- Chargers located near exits or fire stairs in enclosed car parks.

### In the records

- Electrical capacity study and maximum demand data.
- Charger installation certificates and test results.
- Load management settings.
- Strata by-laws or agreements for EV charging.
- Charger fault and downtime logs.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chargers trip when several vehicles charge | Capacity exceeded or no load management | Load measurement; maximum demand |
| Charger warm at terminals, faults recorded | Poor terminations or undersized cabling | Thermography; inspection |
| Residents charging from general outlets with extension leads | Lack of approved charging | Observation |
| Chargers offline and unusable | Back-end or communications failure | Network status; vendor |
| Disputes over electricity costs | Unmetered charging on common supply | Metering arrangement |

> Charging from general-purpose outlets with extension leads, and chargers added without a capacity check, are fire and shock risks. Stop the practice and assess capacity before adding more chargers.

A capacity problem shows when many vehicles charge at once (evenings in apartments, mornings at workplaces); an installation problem shows at one charger regardless of how many are in use.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overloaded circuits or boards; unsafe installations; extension-lead charging | safety | Isolate and rectify now |
| Chargers out of service | failure | Repair |
| New-building or approval requirements for EV provision | deadline | As required |
| Unmetered charging; poor load management; ageing chargers | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Chargers at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No capacity study; tenant or resident demand rising | check | Assess capacity |
| Working, metered, managed | nil | Routine |

Most EV findings in existing buildings are capacity and fairness issues rather than defects; the safety grade is reserved for overloaded circuits, missing protection and informal charging.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer leads, with an EV infrastructure specialist and, for strata buildings, advice on by-laws and cost sharing.

- Capacity study: measured maximum demand against supply and car park board ratings, and the number of chargers that can be supported with and without load management.
- Installation inspection of existing chargers: circuits, protection, earthing, terminations and test results.
- Demand forecast: likely uptake among residents, tenants or fleet, and charger types needed.
- Layout and fire review: charger locations, vehicle protection, ventilation, detection and brigade access in enclosed car parks.
- Metering and billing review: how energy is measured and charged.
- Software review: protocols, vendor support and data access.

The report should give a staged infrastructure plan from current capacity to future demand, safety rectification, and cost allocation options.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Backbone infrastructure: a dedicated distribution board and cable tray serving the car park, sized for future chargers, so individual chargers can be added cheaply later.
- Load management sharing available capacity dynamically among chargers, often avoiding a supply upgrade.
- Supply upgrade where demand exceeds what load management can handle, coordinated with the network.
- Rectification of unsafe installations: dedicated circuits, correct protection and earthing, new terminations.
- Metering and billing for each charger or user.
- Open-protocol chargers so the building is not tied to one operator.
- Vehicle protection: bollards and wheel stops at chargers.
- Fire safety measures in enclosed car parks as guidance requires: location away from exits, detection and ventilation reviews.
- Strata by-laws setting standards, approval processes and cost sharing.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Capacity studies are lump sums. Backbone infrastructure is a lump sum per car park level; individual chargers are priced per charger with connection to the backbone. Load management is a lump sum plus subscription. Supply upgrades are large lump sums with network contributions and long lead times. Software, billing and maintenance are recurring.

Safety rectification is immediate; new-building requirements are code compliance; backbone and chargers are improvements often funded by users or tenants; replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. EV charging installations follow AS/NZS 3000 and the charging equipment standards; the Australian Building Codes Board has published advice on EV charging in buildings; New South Wales and other states have amended strata law to ease approval of charging in apartment buildings; some planning schemes require EV-ready car parks.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document S requires charge points or cable routes in new and majorly renovated residential and non-residential buildings with parking; BS 7671 Section 722 sets installation requirements, including protection against loss of the supply neutral; the IET Code of Practice guides installation; smart charge point regulations apply.
- United States. NFPA 70 Article 625 governs EV charging installations; several states and cities require EV-ready parking in new buildings; federal funding programmes set standards for public chargers; accessibility guidance applies to accessible charging spaces.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Electrical capacity study and maximum demand data.
- Charger installation certificates and test results.
- Load management system details and settings.
- Metering and billing arrangements.
- Strata by-laws or lease clauses on EV charging.
- Charger fault and downtime records.
- Vendor and software contracts.

- Records of any EV-related incidents or fire brigade advice for the car park.
- Network operator correspondence on supply upgrades.

pages.title: Electrical & Communications Risers
pages.question: How do service risers fail, and why are they a fire safety and capacity issue?
pages.answer: Risers fail at the floors and in their capacity. Every cable and pipe added breaks the fire stopping unless reinstated, so older risers often let fire and smoke reach every floor. Trays fill with abandoned cables, leaving no room for new services and adding fire load; enclosed risers overheat; water reaches electrical equipment; riser cupboards become storerooms. Open riser penetrations are a safety finding; exhausted capacity limits tenants and electrification.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about electrical & communications risers; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Access provisions, cable management, ventilation, safety

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Risers are the vertical shafts and cupboards that carry services between floors: electrical risers with sub-mains, busducts and distribution boards; communications risers with backbone cabling, fibre and carrier equipment; and hydraulic and mechanical shafts with pipes and ducts. Functionally a riser must give services a protected route, give maintenance staff safe access, keep fire and smoke from spreading between floors, stay cool and dry, and have room for future services. Risers are where capacity for new tenants, electrification and EV charging is decided, and where fire separation between floors most often breaks down.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access doors | Fire-rated doors or panels on each floor | Rating, locking, signage |
| Floor fire stopping | Fire-stopped slab penetrations at every floor | Integrity after every new cable |
| Cable support | Trays, ladders, conduits, busducts | Capacity, segregation, support |
| Distribution equipment | Floor distribution boards, comms racks, carrier equipment | Clearance, heat, labelling |
| Ventilation | Natural or mechanical cooling | Heat build-up from equipment |
| Lighting and power | Lighting and outlets for maintenance | Safe work |
| Spare capacity | Space on trays and in the shaft | Future services |

Because risers are behind locked doors, their condition is often unknown to owners and only discovered when a fire engineer or new tenant opens them.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Riser structure and doors | Life of the building; door hardware 10 to 20 years | Use; alterations |
| Fire stopping | Until next disturbed | Every new cable or pipe |
| Cable trays and support | 30 to 50 years | Overloading |
| Communications cabling | 15 to 25 years | Technology |
| Spare capacity | Consumed by each tenancy and upgrade | Demand growth |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Abandoned cables left in place when tenants and carriers change.
- New services squeezed in without fire stopping or support.
- Storage in riser cupboards.
- Demand growth from electrification, data and EV charging.

Risers are long-lived structurally; their usefulness is consumed by each tenancy, carrier and upgrade that adds services without removing old ones.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Broken fire stopping

Every cable or pipe added through a riser floor breaks the fire stopping unless it is reinstated with a tested system. Over years, riser floors become a series of holes packed with foam, mineral wool or nothing, letting fire and smoke travel between all floors. This is one of the most common serious fire defects in existing buildings.

### Congestion and abandoned cabling

Cable trays fill with abandoned cables that nobody dares remove, leaving no space for new services, overloading supports, adding fire load and smoke from burning insulation, and making tracing faults slow.

### Heat

Distribution boards, busducts and comms equipment in enclosed risers generate heat; without ventilation, temperatures rise, shortening equipment life and causing faults.

### Water ingress

Risers next to plumbing shafts and wet areas, or below roof penetrations, get water on electrical and communications equipment.

### Access, security and labelling

Riser doors left unlocked, used as cleaners' cupboards or storage, or locked with keys no one can find; equipment unlabelled so isolations are unsafe.

### Capacity exhaustion

Risers without spare space or electrical capacity limit what tenants and new uses can do; adding a new riser later is expensive.

### Unknown circuits and unsafe isolation

When boards and cables in risers are unlabelled or labels are out of date after fit-outs, electricians cannot be sure what they are isolating. Work on live circuits and accidental outages to other tenants follow.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On a riser walk, every floor

- Open or poorly sealed slab penetrations; foam around cables.
- Overfull trays; cables hanging free; abandoned cables.
- Storage and rubbish in riser cupboards.
- Warm air on opening the door; equipment fans running hard.
- Water staining, drips or corrosion.
- Unlabelled boards and cables; doors unlocked or without fire rating labels.

### In the records

- Riser drawings and capacity schedules.
- Fire stopping records with photographs.
- Cabling records and carrier agreements.
- Maximum demand data per riser.

- Riser doors without fire rating labels or closers.

- Carrier equipment installed without approval or records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Light visible through slab penetrations | Fire stopping missing | Inspection from both sides |
| Trays bowed or collapsed | Overloading with cables | Inspection |
| Equipment faults on hot days | Riser overheating | Temperature logging |
| New tenant cannot connect | Space or capacity exhausted | Capacity survey |
| Corrosion on boards | Water ingress | Leak tracing |

> Open penetrations in riser floors let fire and smoke reach every floor. Treat them as safety findings and reinstate fire stopping with tested systems.

Fire stopping failures are almost always cumulative: each contractor breaks a little and nobody reinstates it.

Distinguish missing capacity (no space or electrical headroom) from wasted capacity (abandoned cables, poorly organised trays); the second is far cheaper to fix.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsealed riser floors; storage in risers; water on electrical equipment | safety | Rectify now |
| Riser equipment failed from heat or water | failure | Repair now |
| Fire stopping certification due with annual statements | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Congestion; overheating; poor labelling | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Capacity exhausted for planned uses | lifecycle | Plan new capacity |
| No capacity or fire stopping records | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

A single riser floor without fire stopping can compromise compartmentation for the whole building, so riser findings should be graded on what they connect, not how small the gap looks.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical and communications engineer leads, with a passive fire specialist for penetrations and the carriers for their equipment.

- Riser walk on every floor: penetrations through slabs and walls, fire stopping type and condition, doors and their ratings and locks, trays and supports, distribution equipment, labelling, housekeeping, water and temperature, with photographs.
- Capacity survey: free space on trays and in the shaft, electrical capacity of submains and busducts against maximum demand, and fibre and copper backbone capacity.
- Abandoned cable identification by tracing and carrier records, to free space and reduce fire load.
- Temperature logging in risers holding active equipment through a hot period.
- Records review: riser drawings, fire stopping records and carrier agreements.

The report should list fire stopping defects floor by floor, capacity remaining for planned uses, and works needed.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Fire stopping with tested systems at every floor and wall penetration, recorded with photographs and product details so the next contractor can see what was done.
- Abandoned cable removal, which frees space, reduces fire load and makes faults easier to trace.
- Cable management: new or additional trays and supports, segregation of power and data, and labelling of every cable and board.
- Ventilation or cooling where equipment heat builds up.
- Water protection: drip trays, upstands and relocation of pipes away from electrical equipment.
- Access control and housekeeping: locked doors with managed keys and no storage.
- Penetration permits so every new service is fire stopped and recorded.
- New capacity: additional risers, busducts or backbone where demand will exceed what exists.

- Riser register: a floor-by-floor record of services, capacity and fire stopping, updated after every job.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown: Fire stopping is priced per penetration or per riser floor, and a whole-building remediation can be substantial in older buildings. Cable removal is priced per riser. Trays by length. Cooling per riser. New risers are major projects involving slab penetrations on every floor, so preserving and recovering capacity in existing risers is usually far cheaper. Fire stopping is code compliance; capacity is lifecycle or tied to the project needing it.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia.
