The National Construction Code requires service penetrations through fire-rated floors and walls to be protected, with AS 4072.1 setting penetration systems and AS 1530.4 testing; fire stopping is an essential safety measure in annual certification; communications cabling must be done by registered cablers; AS/NZS 3000 governs electrical installations in risers.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B requires fire stopping of penetrations through compartment floors and walls; BS 7671 governs electrical installations; the Building Safety Act 2022 adds golden thread information duties for higher-risk buildings, including records of fire stopping.
- United States. The International Building Code and NFPA 101 require fire-rated shafts and tested firestop systems; NFPA 70 governs electrical installations and requires removal of accessible abandoned communications cables in many cases; local fire marshals inspect firestopping.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Riser drawings and capacity schedules.
- Fire stopping records with photographs and products.
- Cabling records and carrier agreements.
- Maximum demand data by riser.
- Riser temperature records.
- Penetration permit records.

- Fire safety certification noting riser fire stopping.
- Records of electrical and communications works by tenants and carriers, with approvals.
- Planned loads such as EV charging and electrification that will use riser capacity.

pages.title: Emergency Lighting
pages.question: How does emergency lighting fail, how do you test it, and when is it a life-safety defect?
pages.answer: Emergency lighting fails at the battery: fittings that light on a quick test go dark before the rated duration. Fit-outs cause the other failures: fittings rewired to the wrong circuit so they stay dark when local lights fail, new corridors without coverage, exit signs pointing to doors that no longer lead out. Self-test systems help only if someone reads their reports. It is a life-safety system, and its test records establish its position.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about emergency lighting; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Central battery systems and self-contained units

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Emergency lighting lights the way out when normal lighting fails. It has three jobs: escape route lighting along corridors, stairs and to final exits; open-area (anti-panic) lighting in large rooms so people can reach a route; and high-risk task lighting where a process must be shut down safely. Exit signs, lit at all times or photoluminescent, show the direction to exits. It is a life-safety system with prescribed design, testing and record-keeping in all three jurisdictions.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-contained luminaires and exit signs | Most buildings | Battery, charger and lamp in each fitting; every fitting must be tested |
| Central battery systems | Larger buildings, hospitals, theatres, some towers | Batteries and inverter in one room; sub-circuit monitoring; wiring must survive fire |
| Monitored or addressable systems | Larger buildings from the 2000s | Fittings test themselves on schedule and report faults to a panel or software |
| Maintained fittings | Exit signs; theatres, cinemas, public spaces | Lit at all times, and stay lit in a failure |
| Non-maintained fittings | Most escape lighting | Off normally, on when the local supply fails |
| Photoluminescent signs and markings | Stairs and exit signs where permitted | Glow after charging by normal light; no wiring |

Fittings must be placed at every exit door, every change of direction and intersection, on every stair flight, near fire alarm call points and fire-fighting equipment, and outside final exits, with enough light along the route. Fittings must also sense the failure of the local lighting circuit they serve: a fitting wired to a different circuit will not come on when the lights around it fail.

Era tells you the likely state. Fluorescent self-contained fittings with nickel-cadmium batteries dominate installations of the 1980s to 2000s and are at end of life; LED fittings with nickel-metal hydride or lithium iron phosphate batteries are the current generation, often with self-test.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries | 4 to 6 years | Heat in ceiling spaces; charging |
| Lithium iron phosphate batteries | 8 to 10 years | Heat; battery management |
| LED emergency luminaires and exit signs | 15 to 20 years | Driver and charger; heat |
| Fluorescent emergency fittings | 10 to 15 years | Lamp availability ending |
| Central battery systems | 15 to 20 years; batteries 5 to 10 | Battery room temperature |
| Monitoring panels and software | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Photoluminescent signs | 20 to 25 years | Fading; charging light levels |

What shortens life:

- Heat: fittings in hot ceiling spaces, near plant or in roof spaces lose battery life fastest.
- Missed testing: batteries never discharged lose capacity unnoticed.
- Fit-outs that disconnect fittings, rewire them to the wrong circuits, or hide them behind new partitions.
- Damage in car parks, plant rooms and stairs.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Battery capacity loss

Batteries are the commonest failure. They lose capacity with age and heat until the fitting cannot run for its rated duration: typically 90 minutes in Australia and the United States, and often three hours in Britain where premises may be re-occupied straight after a failure. A fitting that lights on a quick switch test can fail a full-duration test, which is why the duration test is required.

### Charger and lamp failure

Chargers fail and leave batteries flat; fluorescent tubes and early LED modules fail; indicators fail so faults are not seen.

### Wiring faults from alterations

Non-maintained fittings must be fed from the same unswitched circuit as the normal lighting in that area so that they detect its failure. Fit-outs often rewire them to another circuit or to a switched supply; the fitting then stays dark when the local lights fail, or drains its battery every time the lights are switched off.

### Coverage gaps

New partitions create corridors, dead ends and changes of direction the original layout did not cover; exit signs end up pointing to doors that no longer lead out, or are hidden behind signage and joinery.

### Central battery failures

Central battery systems fail as one: a battery, inverter or changeover fault darkens a whole area. Sub-circuit monitoring must detect local lighting failures, and wiring to fittings must be fire-resisting so it survives long enough to be useful.

### Silent monitoring failures

Self-test and addressable systems only help if someone reads their reports. Communication faults, unsupported software and disabled schedules leave a building believing it is tested when it is not.

### Photoluminescent limitations

Photoluminescent signs need enough normal light to charge; in dim stairs and plant areas they may not glow brightly enough when needed.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Charge indicators off on fittings; exit signs unlit or dim.
- Fittings damaged, missing, painted over or hidden by fit-out.
- Escape routes, stairs, changes of direction and final exits without fittings.
- Exit signs pointing the wrong way, or to doors now locked or removed.
- Test labels and dates on fittings; key switches for testing.
- Central battery room: temperature, battery condition, alarms.

### In the records

- Test logbook with each fitting, its result and date.
- Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report.
- Monitoring system reports and fault lists.
- Battery replacement records.
- Emergency lighting layout drawings against the current fit-out.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fittings pass a short test but go dark within the duration | Battery capacity lost | Full-duration discharge test |
| Charge indicators off | Charger, supply or indicator failure | Inspection and test |
| Fitting works on test switch but stays dark when local lights fail | Wired to the wrong circuit | Circuit check against local lighting |
| Batteries flat each morning | Fed from a switched supply | Circuit check |
| Dark sections of escape routes after a fit-out | Coverage gap | Layout review against current partitions |
| Monitoring shows no faults for years | Monitoring not working or not testing | Manual test of a sample |

> Emergency lighting that fails its duration test, is wired so it will not operate, or is missing from escape routes is a life-safety defect. Buildings cannot be certified for their annual fire safety obligations until it is fixed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Escape routes, stairs or exits without working emergency lighting or exit signs; fittings that will not operate on local failure | safety | Rectify now |
| Periodic testing due | deadline | Six-monthly duration test in Australia; monthly functional and annual duration tests in Britain and the United States |
| Batteries failing duration tests across the installation | condition | Replace batteries or fittings in the near term |
| Fluorescent fittings and old batteries at end of life | lifecycle | Replace with LED, ideally with self-test |
| No test records; layout not checked after fit-outs | check | Test every fitting and review coverage |
| Isolated faults found and fixed at testing | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical contractor licensed for fire safety systems carries out testing; a lighting designer or fire engineer reviews coverage where layouts have changed.

- Full-duration test of every fitting by simulating failure of the normal supply, recording each result.
- Circuit check that each non-maintained fitting is fed from the local lighting circuit it protects.
- Coverage survey against the current layout: every exit, change of direction, stair flight, call point and final exit; light levels along routes where doubtful.
- Exit sign review: visibility, direction, legibility, correct pictograms.
- Central battery inspection: batteries, charger, inverter, changeover, sub-circuit monitoring, room ventilation and temperature, fire-resisting wiring.
- Monitoring check: manual test of a sample against what the system reports.
- Records review: logbooks, annual statements, battery dates.

The report should list every fitting with its result, coverage gaps, wiring faults, and the works needed to certify the system.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Battery replacement programme: replace all batteries of an age together rather than fitting by fitting.
- Fitting replacement with LED fittings and long-life batteries, which cuts energy and maintenance.
- Self-test or addressable monitoring, so testing is automatic and faults are reported, with someone responsible for reading the reports.
- Rewiring of fittings fed from the wrong circuits.
- Coverage additions after fit-outs, designed to the standard.
- Exit sign updates to current pictograms and positions.
- Central battery refurbishment: batteries, chargers, monitoring, or replacement with distributed fittings.

- Records: a logbook or digital record for every fitting, with test dates, results and actions.
- Escape route lighting design verified by measurement after major fit-outs.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing is a recurring contract at the prescribed interval. Battery replacement is priced per fitting and recurs on battery life. Fitting replacement is priced per fitting, with ceiling access in occupied areas. Monitoring systems are priced per fitting plus a panel. Coverage additions are per fitting with design. Central battery refurbishment is a lump sum.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; battery replacement is repairs and maintenance on a cycle; fitting replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code requires emergency lighting and exit signs (Part E4); AS/NZS 2293.1 covers design, AS/NZS 2293.3 luminaires and exit signs, and AS/NZS 2293.2 inspection and maintenance, including a six-monthly discharge test for at least the rated duration. Emergency lighting is an essential safety measure under state building regulations, certified annually.
- United Kingdom. BS 5266-1 sets the code of practice, with BS EN 1838 for lighting levels and BS EN 50172 for systems: monthly functional tests and an annual full-duration test, with a logbook. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 places the duty on the responsible person.
- United States. NFPA 101 Section 7.9 requires emergency lighting with monthly 30-second tests and an annual 90-minute test, or approved self-testing equipment; Section 7.10 covers exit marking; UL 924 lists equipment; the International Building and Fire Codes adopt equivalent requirements.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Emergency lighting test logbook with every fitting and result.
- Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report.
- Monitoring system reports and fault history.
- Battery replacement records and dates.
- Emergency lighting and exit sign layout drawings.
- Fit-out records since the last layout review.

- Monitoring system access and reports.

pages.title: Emergency Power
pages.question: How do standby generators and UPS systems fail, and how do you know they will work in an outage?
pages.answer: Emergency power fails when it is needed. Generators most often fail to start: flat batteries, failed chargers or heaters, contaminated fuel. Diesels run unloaded in weekly tests wet stack and lose power. UPS batteries fail silently and drop the load the instant mains fails. Loads added over the years can exceed capacity, stalling the generator when fire pumps start. A generator not tested under load recently is unproven.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about emergency power; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Standby generators, fuel systems, UPS systems

sources.title: NFPA 110 Emergency and Standby Power Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Emergency power keeps essential loads running when the normal supply fails: standby generators with their fuel systems, automatic transfer switches and exhaust; uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) with their batteries; and the distribution that carries emergency power to the loads. Some loads are life safety (fire pumps, smoke control fans, fire-fighting lifts, emergency lighting central systems); others are business continuity (data rooms, refrigeration, critical tenants). Healthcare buildings combine both, with the strictest requirements.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diesel standby generator | Supply essential loads after a mains failure | Fails to start (batteries, fuel, heaters); fails under load; wet stacking from light running |
| Gas generator | As above, on mains gas | Gas supply may fail in the same event |
| Fuel system: bulk tank, day tank, pumps, pipework | Store and deliver fuel | Fuel degradation, water and microbial growth; leaks; bund failures |
| Automatic transfer switch (ATS) | Switch loads between mains and generator | Mechanism failure; incorrect settings |
| Static UPS | Bridge the gap until the generator starts; condition power | Battery failure; capacitor and fan ageing |
| UPS batteries (VRLA, lithium) | Stored energy | Short life; heat sensitivity; thermal runaway in some chemistries |
| Load bank connection | Testing under load | Absent, so generators are never properly tested |

The question that matters is not whether a generator exists but which loads it actually supports, whether it can carry them, and whether it has been proven to start and run under load recently. Load growth, tenant additions and changes to fire systems often put loads on the emergency supply that the generator was never sized for.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diesel generator set | 25 to 30 years (or by run hours) | Maintenance; exercising under load |
| Starting batteries | 3 to 5 years | Heat; charger condition |
| Automatic transfer switches | 20 to 30 years | Operation; maintenance |
| Static UPS | 10 to 15 years | Heat; capacitor and fan replacement |
| VRLA batteries | 3 to 7 years | Temperature; cycling |
| Lithium batteries | 10 to 15 years | Temperature; management system |
| Fuel tanks | 20 to 40 years | Corrosion; water; bund integrity |
| Stored diesel fuel | 1 to 2 years without treatment | Water; microbial growth; oxidation |

What shortens life:

- Running unloaded during weekly tests, which causes wet stacking in diesels.
- Hot battery rooms: every 10 °C above about 20 to 25 °C roughly halves lead-acid battery life.
- Water in fuel from condensation and tank breathing.
- Lack of exercise: generators that never run under load fail when needed.
- Deferred battery replacement.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Failure to start

The commonest reason a generator fails in an emergency is that it does not start: flat or failed starting batteries, failed charger, failed coolant heater in cold climates, air in the fuel system, or a fault in the controller. Each is cheap to prevent and invisible without testing.

### Wet stacking

Diesels run at light load do not reach operating temperature; unburnt fuel and carbon build up in the exhaust and cylinders. The engine then smokes, loses power and may fail when asked to take full load. Weekly no-load runs cause it; regular load bank testing prevents it.

### Fuel degradation

Diesel stored for long periods takes up water, grows microbes at the fuel-water interface (diesel bug), oxidises and forms sludge. Filters block in the first hours of running, exactly when the generator is needed. Biodiesel blends degrade faster.

### Transfer switch faults

Transfer switches that are rarely operated can stick, and settings changed during maintenance can stop them transferring or prevent return to mains. A transfer switch failure looks like a generator failure to the building.

### UPS failures

UPS batteries fail first, usually without warning unless monitored; a UPS with failed batteries drops its load the instant the mains fails. Capacitors and cooling fans age and need replacement at mid-life. Lithium battery systems introduce fire risks that need separation and detection.

### Capacity and load mismatch

Loads added to emergency boards over the years can exceed the generator's capacity; large motor loads such as fire pumps and smoke fans starting together can stall it. Life-safety loads must be given priority and the generator must carry them.

### Exhaust, ventilation and noise

Generator rooms need combustion and cooling air; blocked louvres and recirculated exhaust cause overheating. Exhaust discharge near air intakes and windows brings fumes into the building. Noise and air emission limits constrain where and how long generators can run.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the generator and UPS rooms

- Nameplates: rating, year, run hours.
- Battery dates and condition; charger status.
- Coolant heater working (engine block warm).
- Fuel tank level, gauges, water in sight glasses; bund condition and contents.
- Exhaust soot and oil leaks.
- Louvres clear; room temperature.
- UPS alarms; battery room temperature.

### In the records

- Test logs: weekly or monthly runs, with load and duration.
- Load bank test reports.
- Fuel test results.
- Battery test and replacement records.
- Transfer switch tests.
- List of loads on emergency supply and the load study.
- Records of real outages and how the system performed.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black smoke and oil at exhaust joints | Wet stacking | Test logs showing no-load running |
| Generator failed to start in a test or outage | Batteries, charger, fuel or heater | Battery test; charger output; fuel filters |
| Filters blocking during runs | Fuel contamination | Fuel sample |
| UPS dropped load on mains failure | Failed batteries | Battery test |
| Generator stalls when fire systems start | Capacity or load sequencing | Load study |
| Fumes inside the building during tests | Exhaust re-entry | Discharge location |

> A standby generator that has not been tested under load recently should be treated as unproven. Weekly no-load runs do not show whether it will carry the building.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Generator serving life-safety loads fails to start or carry load; fuel leak; lithium battery fire risk without separation | safety | Rectify now; interim measures |
| Generator or UPS failed | failure | Repair now |
| Mandatory testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Batteries at end of life; fuel contaminated; wet stacking; capacity tight | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Generator or UPS at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No load bank test or load study | check | Test and study |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer leads, with the generator and UPS maintenance contractors.

- Records review: test logs, load bank reports, fuel analysis, battery records, maintenance, outage history.
- Inspection of generator, fuel system, transfer switches, UPS and batteries, rooms and exhaust.
- Load bank test at or near rated load for a sustained period.
- Black-start test: simulated mains failure with transfer of real loads.
- Fuel sampling for water, microbes and contamination.
- Battery testing by impedance or discharge.
- Load study: what is on emergency supply, life-safety priority, starting sequence, capacity.

The report should state whether the system is proven to carry its loads, the life-safety position, condition and remaining life, and works needed.

- Transfer switch test: transfer, retransfer and timing, with settings recorded.

Tests are planned with the building so critical tenants and life-safety systems are covered throughout.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Testing regime: exercise generators monthly under meaningful load, run periodic load bank tests at or near rated load, and run full black-start tests transferring real loads; record every test.
- Starting system: replace starting batteries on a fixed cycle, check chargers and coolant heaters, and fit monitoring that alarms on battery or charger faults.
- Fuel management: test fuel periodically; polish and treat it; remove water; turn fuel over; maintain tanks, bunds, vents and leak detection.
- Generator overhaul at run-hour or age intervals, or replacement where parts and controls are no longer supported.
- UPS maintenance: replace batteries on a cycle with monitoring; replace capacitors and fans at mid-life; replace the UPS at end of life.
- Load management: remove non-essential loads from emergency boards, sequence the starting of large motors such as fire pumps and smoke fans, and increase capacity where the life-safety load needs it.
- Load bank connection point so testing can be done without disconnecting the building.
- Room and exhaust works: clear louvres, extend exhaust away from intakes, add acoustic treatment.
- Battery safety: separation, ventilation and detection for lithium and large lead-acid installations.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing, fuel management and maintenance are recurring contracts; load bank tests and fuel polishing are recurring lump sums. Starting and UPS batteries are replaced on a cycle and are best carried as recurring allowances. Generator replacement is a lump-sum project including the generator set, crane lift, fuel system, exhaust and acoustic works, switchboard and transfer switch changes, and commissioning, with temporary generation where life-safety loads must remain covered. UPS replacement is similar.

Life-safety testing and rectification are code compliance; batteries and fuel management are repairs and maintenance on a cycle; replacement is lifecycle; capacity increases sit with the project that adds load.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3010 covers generating sets, AS/NZS 3009 emergency power in hospitals, and AS 1940 fuel storage; generators supporting fire systems are maintained as essential safety measures.
- United Kingdom. BS 7698 and BS ISO 8528 cover generating sets; BS 9999 and BS 5839 set life-safety supply requirements; healthcare follows HTM 06-01.
- United States. NFPA 110 sets testing for emergency and standby power systems, including monthly exercise under load for at least 30 minutes and a four-hour test every three years for Level 1 systems; NFPA 111 covers stored energy systems; NFPA 70 Articles 700, 701 and 702 cover emergency, legally required and optional standby systems.

Environmental permits also apply in all three jurisdictions to larger diesel generators, limiting running hours and emissions, which affects testing regimes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Generator and UPS test logs with load and duration.
- Load bank test reports.
- Fuel analysis results and fuel management records.
- Starting and UPS battery test and replacement records.
- Load study and the list of loads on each emergency board.
- Outage history and how the system performed.
- Maintenance contracts and service reports.
- Generator run hours, installation date and overhaul history.
- Environmental permits for the generator where required.

pages.title: Energy Efficiency Upgrades
pages.question: How do energy efficiency upgrades underperform, and when does efficiency become a compliance deadline?
pages.answer: Energy upgrades fail in operation more than equipment: drives bypassed, LED without controls, efficient plant sequenced badly, recommissioning savings drifting back within a few years. Fabric upgrades without moisture control cause condensation and mould; electrification hits supply and emitter limits. Ratings, minimum letting standards and building performance limits now turn efficiency into a deadline and value issue regardless of physical condition. Measure, or savings disappear.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about energy efficiency upgrades; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: LED retrofits, VSD installations, high-efficiency plant

sources.title: Non-domestic private rented property: minimum energy efficiency standard

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Energy efficiency upgrades are works that cut a building's energy use and emissions: LED lighting and controls, variable speed drives on fans and pumps, high-efficiency chillers, boilers and heat pumps, building management system tuning, insulation and glazing improvements, air sealing, heat recovery, and on-site renewable generation. They are increasingly driven by regulation and the market rather than by savings alone: ratings and disclosure schemes affect leasing and value, minimum standards restrict letting in some places, and building performance standards set emissions limits with penalties.

| Upgrade | Typical effect | Watch points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED lighting with controls | Large cut in lighting energy | Driver quality; controls commissioning |
| Variable speed drives on fans and pumps | Large cut in fan and pump energy at part load | Harmonics; drives bypassed; poor sequencing |
| High-efficiency chillers and boilers | Lower plant energy | Sizing to current load; low delta T; return temperatures |
| Heat pumps replacing gas | Electrification; lower emissions | Flow temperatures; emitters; electrical capacity |
| BMS recommissioning and analytics | Often the cheapest saving | Overrides creeping back |
| Insulation, glazing and air sealing | Lower heating and cooling loads | Condensation; ventilation |
| Heat recovery ventilation | Lower ventilation energy | Maintenance; cross-leakage |
| Solar PV and batteries | On-site generation | Roof; connection limits |

The market tools differ by country: NABERS ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure in Australia; Energy Performance Certificates, the minimum energy efficiency standards and Display Energy Certificates in Britain; ENERGY STAR benchmarking and city building performance standards in the United States.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Upgrade | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED fittings | 15 to 20 years | Drivers; heat |
| Variable speed drives | 10 to 15 years | Heat; harmonics |
| Heat pumps and efficient plant | 15 to 25 years | Maintenance; sizing |
| BMS recommissioning savings | 2 to 5 years before drift | Overrides; staff changes |
| Insulation and glazing upgrades | Life of the building | Moisture; installation |
| Solar PV | 25 to 30 years; inverters 10 to 15 | Inverters; roof |

What shortens the life of savings:

- Drift: controls overridden, schedules lost, setpoints changed.
- Poor commissioning so upgrades never deliver their designed savings.
- Load growth and longer hours offsetting savings.
- Lack of measurement, so nobody notices when savings disappear.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### The performance gap

Upgrades often save less than predicted: drives installed but bypassed, LED retrofits without controls, efficient chillers sequenced badly, heat pumps undersized. The gap between predicted and actual savings is usually commissioning and operation, not equipment.

### Savings drift

Savings from recommissioning and controls fade over two to five years as overrides accumulate and staff change. Without monitoring, buildings slide back to old performance.

### Regulatory obsolescence

Rising minimum standards and emissions limits can make a building unlettable or liable to penalties regardless of its physical condition, turning efficiency into a compliance and value issue.

### Unintended consequences

Insulation and air sealing without ventilation and moisture control cause condensation and mould; electrification without electrical capacity planning hits supply limits; heat pumps on emitters sized for boilers leave buildings cold.

### Product and installation quality

Low-quality LED drivers, drives with harmonic problems, and poorly installed insulation fail early or underperform.

### No measurement and verification

Without sub-metering and a baseline, savings cannot be proved, incentives cannot be claimed, and failures go unnoticed.

### Split incentives

In leased buildings, owners pay for upgrades while tenants often receive the savings, and tenants control lighting, equipment and hours. Without green lease clauses and shared data, worthwhile upgrades are not made and savings are not sustained.

### Rebound and load growth

Savings are eroded when buildings run longer hours, add equipment, densify occupancy or add data and EV charging loads, which can make an upgrade appear to have failed when it is working.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site and in data

- Energy use not falling after upgrades, or rising again after a year or two.
- Drives in bypass or hand mode; plant running at night.
- LED lighting on in empty spaces.
- Condensation and mould after fabric upgrades.
- Ratings below market expectations or legal minimums.

### In the records

- Energy bills and interval data.
- Ratings and certificates with expiry dates.
- Energy audits and upgrade business cases.
- Measurement and verification reports.
- Building performance standard filings.

- Ratings drifting down at each renewal despite upgrades, a sign of operational drift or load growth.
- Tenants unaware of the building's rating or their own consumption.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No saving after a drive retrofit | Drive bypassed or controls not changed | Drive status; trend data |
| Savings fading after recommissioning | Overrides and drift | BMS overrides; trend data |
| Condensation after insulation upgrade | No vapour control or ventilation | Inspection; humidity |
| Heat pump building cold in winter | Undersized heat pump or emitters | Heat loss vs output |
| Rating below the letting minimum | Regulatory shortfall | Certificate |

> The cheapest energy saving is usually in the controls and operation of what is already installed. Check those before buying new equipment.

Normalising for weather and occupancy is essential before judging an upgrade: raw bills mislead when the climate or use of the building has changed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fabric upgrade causing condensation and mould affecting health | safety | Rectify now |
| Building below a legal minimum for letting or facing performance standard penalties | deadline | By the regulatory date |
| Upgrades underperforming; savings drifting | condition | Recommission in the near term |
| Plant at end of life: an opportunity to upgrade | lifecycle | Replace with efficient, low-emission plant |
| No audit; ratings unknown | check | Audit |
| Upgrades performing | nil | Monitor |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An energy auditor or building services engineer leads, with the controls contractor and, for fabric work, a building physics specialist.

- Energy audit to a recognised standard (AS/NZS 3598 in Australia, ESOS requirements in Britain for large organisations, ASHRAE 211 in the United States), breaking consumption down by end use and identifying measures with costs and savings.
- Interval data analysis: base load, night and weekend consumption, start-up times and weather response, which reveal waste faster than any site visit.
- Ratings and compliance review: current ratings and certificates, their expiry, legal minimums for letting or sale, and any building performance standard limits and dates that apply.
- Controls review: overrides, schedules, setpoints, sequences and drives in bypass.
- Verification of past upgrades: whether installed measures are operating as designed.
- Electrification and capacity review: electrical supply headroom for heat pumps and EV charging.
- Fabric and moisture review before insulation, glazing or air sealing work.

The report should rank measures by cost and saving, state regulatory deadlines and exposure, and include a measurement and verification plan so savings can be proved and held.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Recommissioning: remove overrides, restore schedules, reset setpoints and tune sequences, usually the best value measure.
- LED with controls installed together, so light is both efficient and switched off when not needed.
- Variable speed drives on fans and pumps, with control sequences changed so they actually vary speed.
- Plant replacement at end of life with efficient, right-sized and lower-emission plant, including heat pumps where the building and supply suit them.
- Fabric upgrades: insulation, glazing and air sealing designed with vapour control and ventilation.
- Heat recovery on ventilation systems with high outdoor air rates.
- On-site generation and storage where roof, connection and tariffs suit.
- Monitoring and analytics: sub-metering and automated fault detection so drift is caught early.
- Tenant engagement through green lease clauses and shared data, since tenants control much of the energy use.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and recommissioning are lump sums with quick paybacks. Equipment upgrades are lump sums per measure, often timed with end-of-life replacement so only the efficiency premium is attributed to energy. Fabric upgrades are larger and slower to pay back but can be essential for ratings. Monitoring and analytics are recurring subscriptions. Incentives can offset costs, such as state energy saving schemes in Australia and federal tax incentives for efficient commercial buildings in the United States.

Upgrades required to meet letting minimums or performance standards carry deadlines and penalties; otherwise they are lifecycle or improvement items justified by savings, value and tenant demand.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. NABERS ratings are widely used in commercial leasing; Commercial Building Disclosure requires a current energy certificate when offices of 1,000 m² or more are sold or leased; the National Construction Code Section J sets energy efficiency for new and altered work; state schemes in Victoria and New South Wales fund many upgrades.
- United Kingdom. Energy Performance Certificates are required on sale and letting, and let non-domestic property must meet a minimum EPC rating of E, with proposals to raise the minimum further; large organisations must carry out ESOS assessments; Approved Document L governs work to existing buildings; Display Energy Certificates apply to larger public buildings.
- United States. Many cities and states require energy benchmarking through ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager; building performance standards such as New York City's Local Law 97 set emissions limits with penalties; ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC govern new work; federal tax incentives support efficient commercial buildings.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Energy bills and interval data for at least two years.
- Current ratings, certificates and their expiry dates.
- Energy audits and upgrade business cases.
- Measurement and verification reports for past upgrades.
- Building performance standard filings and any penalties.
- Green lease clauses and tenant energy data.
- Electrical capacity information for electrification.

pages.title: Escalators & Moving Walks
pages.question: How do escalators and moving walks fail, and which faults are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Escalators wear at step chains, drives and handrails, and fail most dangerously at the edges: broken comb teeth and skirt gaps trap feet and fingers, handrails running at a different speed from the steps cause falls, brakes that stop too hard throw passengers, and safety devices bypassed in maintenance remove protection. Controllers lose support like lift controllers, and units are usually modernised or replaced whole.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about escalators & moving walks; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Drive motors, step chains, handrails, control systems

sources.title: ASME A17.1 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Escalators and moving walks carry large numbers of people between levels or along concourses in shopping centres, transport interchanges, airports, offices and institutions. Each comprises a steel truss, a drive machine and brake, step or pallet chains carrying steps or pallets, handrails driven in step with the treads, comb plates where people step on and off, skirt panels beside the steps, and a set of safety devices that stop the unit when something goes wrong.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial escalator | Shopping centres, offices | Designed for moderate duty cycles |
| Heavy-duty (public service) escalator | Transport interchanges, airports, stadiums | Designed for continuous heavy use; heavier components |
| Moving walk (pallet type) | Airports, large retail | Flat or inclined pallets; trolley use in retail |
| Outdoor escalator | Transport and public realm | Weather exposure; drainage; corrosion |

Escalators are among the most heavily used and most injury-prone pieces of building equipment; most injuries involve falls, often linked to handrail speed mismatches, abrupt stops or passenger behaviour, and entrapments at comb plates and skirts.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Truss | 40 years and more | Corrosion; water |
| Drive machine and gearbox | 20 to 30 years | Duty; lubrication |
| Step chains | 15 to 25 years | Load; lubrication; wear |
| Steps and pallets | 20 to 30 years | Damage; wear |
| Handrails | 5 to 10 years | UV; cracking; tension |
| Controllers | 15 to 20 years | Manufacturer support |
| Comb plates | Replaced as teeth break | Damage |

What shortens life:

- Duty beyond what the unit was designed for.
- Outdoor exposure.
- Poor lubrication.
- Trolleys and luggage.

The duty an escalator was designed for matters as much as its age. A commercial escalator moved into a transport interchange, or a shopping centre escalator running longer hours than designed, wears through chains, steps and drives years early. Heavy-duty units built for public transport have heavier components and longer intervals between major overhauls.

- Excess duty: more hours, more passengers or heavier loads than designed.
- Outdoor and semi-outdoor exposure: rain, dust and salt corrode trusses, chains and steps, and water collects in the pit.
- Poor lubrication of chains and drives, which accelerates wear and noise.
- Trolleys, prams and luggage on units not designed for them, which damage steps and combs.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Step chain and drive wear

Step chains elongate and their rollers wear, so steps run unevenly, gaps open between steps, and noise and vibration grow. Drive chains and gearboxes wear with heavy duty and poor lubrication. A broken step chain or drive chain without working protection devices can let steps run back.

### Comb plate and skirt entrapment

Broken comb teeth, excessive gaps between steps and skirts, and missing skirt deflectors create entrapment points for shoes, fingers and clothing, particularly for children.

### Handrail faults

Handrails crack, stretch, slip and run at a different speed from the steps; passengers holding a lagging or leading handrail lose balance. Handrail inlets where the rail enters the balustrade are a finger entrapment point.

### Brake and stopping faults

Brakes that stop too abruptly throw passengers; brakes that stop too slowly do not hold a loaded escalator. Stopping distances are tested against limits.

### Safety device failure

Comb plate switches, handrail inlet switches, missing step detectors, overspeed and reversal protection, and emergency stops must all work. Devices bypassed during maintenance and not reinstated are a serious hazard.

### Step damage

Cracked or broken steps, missing demarcation lines, and damaged cleats cause trips and entrapments.

### Controller obsolescence

Controllers lose manufacturer support like lift controllers; escalators are usually replaced or modernised as a whole rather than in many small stages.

Water and debris in the lower pit also corrode chains and drive components and can short electrical equipment, especially on outdoor and semi-outdoor units.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Comb plates: broken or missing teeth, and the gap between comb and step.
- Gaps between steps and skirt panels along the incline; skirt deflector brushes present and intact.
- Handrail speed against step speed, cracks and gloss loss on the handrail, and inlet guards where the rail enters the balustrade.
- Noise, vibration and uneven running of steps, felt by standing on the unit.
- Step condition: cracks, broken cleats, missing yellow demarcation lines.
- Emergency stop buttons at both landings, accessible and labelled.
- Water, debris and corrosion visible in the upper and lower landing pits during maintenance.

### In the records

- Breakdown, entrapment and injury records, with causes.
- Maintenance logs and safety device test records.
- Periodic inspection certificates.
- Modernisation or replacement history, and duty data where monitored.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps running unevenly with noise | Step chain and roller wear | Chain elongation measurement |
| Passengers stumbling at the top | Handrail speed mismatch | Speed measurement |
| Broken comb teeth | Impact from objects or wear | Inspection |
| Unit stops abruptly | Brake or safety device fault | Stopping distance test |
| Rising breakdowns and long parts waits | Controller obsolescence | Parts support status |

> Broken comb teeth, excessive skirt gaps and bypassed safety devices are entrapment and fall hazards. Stop the unit until fixed.

Falls usually point to handrail speed, abrupt stopping or step irregularities; entrapments point to combs, skirts and inlets. Recording the location and cause of each incident shows which component needs attention.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken combs; skirt gaps; bypassed safety devices; brake faults | safety | Stop until fixed |
| Unit out of service | failure | Repair now |
| Periodic inspection due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Chain wear; handrail wear; noisy drives | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Unit at end of life | lifecycle | Plan replacement or modernisation |
| No audit or injury analysis | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An independent lift and escalator consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor operating the unit; testing needs the unit out of service and landings protected.

- Records review: breakdowns, entrapments and injuries over several years, maintenance hours and scope, inspection findings.
- Component inspection with steps removed: step chains and rollers (elongation measured), steps and pallets, drive chain and machine, brake, truss, tracks and lubrication.
- Safety device testing: comb plate, handrail inlet, missing step, overspeed and reversal protection, emergency stops, skirt switches.
- Stopping distance tests against the limits for the unit, unloaded and where possible loaded.
- Handrail speed measured against step speed on both sides.
- Gap measurements between steps, skirts and combs.
- Duty assessment of current traffic against design, and controller parts support.

The report should state safety defects, component condition and remaining life, whether the unit suits its duty, and whether to repair, modernise in the existing truss or replace.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Comb plate and step replacement wherever teeth are broken or steps damaged, with demarcation lines renewed.
- Handrail replacement on its cycle, with drive adjustment so speed matches the steps.
- Step chain replacement when elongation reaches the limit, often with step rollers and tracks.
- Safety upgrades: skirt deflectors, handrail inlet guards, missing step detection and other devices required by current standards.
- Modernisation in the existing truss: new drive, brake, controller, chains, steps and handrails, which avoids removing the truss.
- Full replacement where the truss is corroded, the unit is unsuited to its duty, or modernisation is uneconomic.
- Weather protection and pit drainage for outdoor units.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance is a recurring contract, and handrails, combs and steps are replaced as recurring repairs. Modernisation in the truss is a lump sum per unit with a planned outage of several weeks. Full replacement is a larger lump sum that includes removal and installation through building openings or by crane, structural and finishes works, and a longer outage; in shopping centres and stations the disruption cost to tenants and operators often shapes timing.

Modernisation and replacement are lifecycle; safety upgrades are code compliance; component replacement is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Escalators and moving walks are registered plant under state work health and safety regulations, with design and modernisation to the AS 1735 series (now aligned with EN and ISO standards) and periodic inspection where state rules require it.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 115-1 governs design and installation, and BS EN 115-2 the improvement of safety of existing units; PUWER 1998 requires maintenance and inspection, and the HSE has issued guidance on escalator safety.
- United States. ASME A17.1 governs escalators and moving walks, with periodic inspections and tests (including brake tests) set by state and city elevator authorities, and A17.3 for existing units.

Accessibility rules in all three jurisdictions do not treat escalators as an accessible route, so a lift must be available wherever an escalator links levels; taking a lift out of service at the same time as an escalator modernisation can break that requirement.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Breakdown, entrapment and injury records with causes.
- Maintenance contract, scope and hours.
- Periodic inspection certificates and outstanding defects.
- Safety device and stopping distance test records.
- Modernisation or replacement history and recommendations.
- Manufacturer parts support advice for the controller and drive.
- Traffic and duty data where available.

pages.title: External Coating Systems
pages.question: How do external paints, renders and protective coatings fail, what does each failure mean, and when does it matter beyond appearance?
pages.answer: Most coating failures are water or preparation problems, not product problems. Peeling to bare substrate at sills and wall bases means moisture behind; peeling between coats means poor preparation or incompatible layers; chalking is normal ageing and the cue to recoat. What matters most is what the coating protects: rust stains through a concrete coating mean the reinforcement is already corroding, and hollow render over a footpath is a falling hazard. Old layers may contain lead.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about external coating systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Paint systems on concrete, masonry, metal substrates; adhesion, weathering, protective function

sources.title: AS/NZS 2311:2017 Guide to the painting of buildings
Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting Program

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
External coating systems are the paints, renders, texture coatings and protective coatings on the outside of a building. Some are decorative, but most do a job: keeping water out of masonry and render, stopping carbonation reaching reinforcement in concrete, protecting steel from corrosion and timber from decay. When a protective coating fails, the element beneath starts to fail.

| Coating | Where it is used | What it protects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acrylic paint | Render, masonry, fibre cement, timber | Appearance; water shedding; timber and sheet substrates |
| Alkyd and oil-based enamel | Older timber joinery and metalwork | Timber and steel; becomes brittle with age |
| Texture and membrane coatings | Render, fibre cement, concrete, apartments from the 1980s | Water resistance; bridging fine cracks |
| Elastomeric coatings | Concrete and render prone to cracking | Crack bridging and water resistance |
| Anti-carbonation coatings | Concrete frames and precast | Slowing carbonation to protect reinforcement |
| Mineral (silicate) paints and limewash | Masonry, heritage render | Breathable protection compatible with lime and stone |
| Cement and polymer renders | Masonry walls, sheet systems | Weather barrier and finish; see Cladding and Wall Systems for render on sheet |
| Protective coatings on steel | Exposed steel frames, balustrades, awnings, plant | Corrosion protection, often over galvanising |

Older buildings carry many layers. In Australia, paint applied before about 1970 commonly contains lead; in the United States, the cut-off for housing is 1978; in Britain, lead paint was common until the 1960s and in some uses later. Thick stacks of old paint crack and peel as a unit, and their removal is a hazardous materials operation.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Coating | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acrylic on masonry and render | 8 to 15 years | Exposure; preparation; colour (dark colours age faster) |
| Paint on timber | 5 to 10 years | Exposure; end grain sealing; timber movement |
| Texture and elastomeric coatings | 10 to 20 years | Film thickness; substrate movement |
| Anti-carbonation coatings | 10 to 20 years | Product; film thickness; UV |
| Mineral paints and limewash | 10 to 20 years (limewash 3 to 7 years) | Exposure; substrate |
| Render | 30 to 60 years | Bond to substrate; cracking; water from above |
| Protective coatings on steel | 10 to 25 years to first major maintenance | Corrosivity of the site; system specification |

What shortens life:

- Preparation: coating applied over dust, chalk, mould, loose old paint or damp substrates fails early, whatever the product.
- Exposure: UV on north and west elevations in Australia, wind-driven rain, coastal salt, industrial atmospheres.
- Moisture behind the coating: rising damp, leaking gutters, failed flashings and sills.
- Incompatible layers: acrylic over gloss enamel without preparation; impermeable paint over lime render or soft brick.
- Substrate movement: cracking sheet joints, moving timber, cracking concrete.
- Too many coats: thick stacks crack and peel as a unit.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Chalking and fading

UV breaks down the binder at the surface, leaving loose pigment that wipes off as a powder. It is the normal ageing of exterior paint and the usual cue for a recoat.

### Loss of adhesion

Paint peels from the substrate when moisture builds up behind it or it was applied over a poor surface; it peels between coats when a new coat was applied over a glossy, dirty or incompatible older coat.

### Blistering

Blisters form when moisture vapour from inside the wall pushes against an impermeable film, or when solvent or water is trapped during application. Blisters full of water point to moisture behind.

### Cracking

Brittle old alkyd and oil paints crack in a fine pattern as they age (checking, alligatoring). Coatings crack along lines that follow joints in sheet substrates and cracks in concrete or render below.

### Render debonding and cracking

Render loses its bond to masonry when water gets behind it or when it is stronger than the backing; it sounds hollow, bulges and falls. Fine map cracking is drying shrinkage; cracks along regular lines follow the substrate.

### Coating failure on concrete

Where an anti-carbonation or protective coating fails, carbonation advances to the reinforcement, which corrodes and spalls the concrete. Rust staining through a coating is the sign that it is already happening.

### Breakdown on steel

Coatings on steel break down at edges, welds, bolts and damage points first, then rust spreads under the film. Galvanising under the coating extends life until it too is consumed.

### Lead paint deterioration

Deteriorating lead paint chalks, flakes and sheds lead dust and chips onto the ground and into interiors, which is a health hazard, particularly to children.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Faded and patchy colour; mismatched patches from local repairs.
- Peeling and flaking, worst at sills, the base of walls, under gutters and on the most exposed elevations.
- Cracked and bulging render; missing render patches exposing the masonry.
- Rust staining through coatings on concrete; rust at edges and fixings of coated steel.
- Mould, algae and dark staining on shaded elevations.

### Close up on site

- Chalk on a finger wiped across the surface.
- Peeling to bare substrate or between coats; thickness of the paint stack at a peeled edge.
- Blisters: dry or water-filled.
- Hollow sound of render when tapped; cracks following sheet joints.
- Coating cracks tracking cracks in the concrete beneath; spalling under coatings.

### Inside the building

- Damp at the inside face of walls with failed coatings, and blistering of internal paint on external walls.

### In the records

- Repaint history with dates, products and preparation specifications.
- Hazardous materials register and lead testing.
- Coating warranties and concrete repair records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powder on the finger, colour faded | Normal UV ageing | Even across the elevation; worst on the sunniest faces |
| Peeling to bare substrate at sills, wall bases and under gutters | Moisture behind the coating | Source of water at that location; damp readings behind |
| Peeling between coats in sheets | Intercoat adhesion failure: incompatible or poorly prepared coats | Cross-cut adhesion test fails between layers; glossy layer beneath |
| Water-filled blisters | Moisture vapour or water from behind | Damp substrate; impermeable coating on a wall that needs to breathe |
| Fine crazing in a mud-crack pattern on old paint | Embrittled thick alkyd or oil paint | Paint stack thick; age |
| Cracks in straight lines at regular spacing | Substrate joints in sheet or panel | Joint locations match |
| Hollow, bulging render | Render debonded from masonry | Tapping; render lifts at the edges |
| Rust staining through a coating on concrete | Reinforcement corrosion beneath | Cover survey; carbonation depth at the steel |

> A fresh coat of paint hides what is underneath. On concrete, an apparently sound coating with rust stains emerging, or on render, a sound surface that sounds hollow, means the problem is in the substrate.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose render over a public or occupied area; deteriorating lead paint where children live or play | safety | Remove loose render and protect below; stabilise lead paint under controls immediately |
| Coating failure with concrete spalling and exposed reinforcement | failure | Concrete repair and recoat now |
| Widespread peeling, blistering or render debonding without loss; coating failure on steel with spreading rust | condition | Repair and recoat in the near term |
| Chalking and fading; coating at the end of its cycle | lifecycle | Recoat on cycle |
| Lead-safe work requirements on pre-1978 housing in the United States before works | deadline | Works must follow the rule; timing set by the works |
| Pre-1970 paint layers with unknown lead content; coating on concrete with unknown carbonation depth | check | Test before specifying works |
| Isolated scuffs, minor mould on shaded walls | nil | Clean and touch up |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A coatings inspector or building surveyor leads; a concrete repair specialist joins where reinforcement corrosion is suspected.

- Condition rating of chalking, cracking, flaking, blistering and rusting against the ISO 4628 series.
- Adhesion testing by cross-cut (ISO 2409 or ASTM D3359) or pull-off (ISO 4624 or ASTM D4541).
- Film thickness measurement on steel and on concrete coatings.
- Render tapping survey to map hollow areas.
- Carbonation depth testing with phenolphthalein, and cover survey, on coated concrete.
- Lead testing by laboratory analysis of paint chips or by XRF on buildings of the relevant era.
- Moisture investigation where peeling or blistering points to water behind.

The report should state the coating system and its condition, the cause of failures, substrate repairs needed, hazardous content, and a specification for preparation and recoating.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Wash and recoat where the coating is chalked but sound.
- Spot preparation and recoat where failure is local.
- Full removal and recoat where the stack has failed or is incompatible; under lead controls where lead is present.
- Fix the water first: gutters, sills, flashings and damp sources, or the new coating will fail the same way.
- Render: cut out and replace debonded areas, or strip and re-render, with a mix compatible with the substrate.
- Concrete: repair spalls and treat reinforcement to a recognised concrete repair standard, then apply an anti-carbonation coating.
- Steel: blast or mechanically clean, then apply a protective system specified for the site corrosivity category.
- Heritage masonry: remove impermeable paints and use mineral paints or limewash.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Recoating is priced by area with preparation rated separately; substrate repairs (render, concrete) are priced by area or per repair. Access often dominates on multi-storey buildings. Lead removal adds containment, waste disposal and clearance testing. Recoating recurs on a cycle set by the coating and exposure.

Recoating is lifecycle; patching is repairs and maintenance; lead management is code compliance; concrete repair before recoating is repairs or lifecycle depending on extent.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 2311 guides the painting of buildings, AS/NZS 2312 the protection of structural steel, and AS 4361.2 the management of lead paint in residential, public and commercial buildings. On strata buildings, external repainting is common property and a regular sinking-fund item.
- United Kingdom. BS 6150 guides the painting of buildings, BS EN ISO 12944 the protection of steel, BS EN 1504 concrete repair and protection, and BS EN 13914-1 external render. The Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002 govern work on lead paint.
- United States. The EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule (40 CFR Part 745) requires lead-safe work practices on housing and child-occupied facilities built before 1978; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.62 covers worker exposure. AMPP (formerly SSPC and NACE) standards govern protective coatings on steel.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Repaint history with dates, products and specifications.
- Coating warranties.
- Hazardous materials register and lead test results.
- Concrete repair and carbonation testing records for coated concrete.
- Records of damp and leak repairs on affected walls.

- Colour and product schedule for the current coating.
- Heritage constraints on colours and materials.

pages.title: Fencing, Gates & Signage
pages.question: How do fences, powered gates and signs fail, and which failures put lives at risk?
pages.answer: The life-safety risks here are powered gates and pool barriers. Powered sliding and swing gates crush and trap people when force limitation, safety edges and beams fail or are set wrongly, and gates that leave their tracks can fall. Pool gates that do not self-close and latch, gaps and climbable objects defeat child barriers. Fences rot at their posts and boundary walls lean. Exit and safety signs that are missing or wrong mislead people.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fencing, gates & signage; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Perimeter fencing, gates (including operators), wayfinding, statutory signage

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Fencing, gates and signage cover the boundary and security elements of a site and the signs that guide and warn people: perimeter fences and walls, pool and play area fencing, security fencing, pedestrian and vehicle gates, powered sliding and swing gates, boom gates and bollards, and wayfinding, statutory, safety and accessibility signs. The serious risks are in powered gates and barriers, which have killed and injured people, and in safety barriers such as pool fences, where a failure lets children reach water.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber, steel and masonry boundary fences | All sites | Decay, corrosion, lean; boundary responsibility |
| Pool and play area fences | Residential, hotels, schools, childcare | Gates not self-closing and latching; gaps; climbable objects |
| Security fencing | Industrial, commercial, utilities | Damage; breaches; corrosion |
| Powered sliding and swing gates | Apartments, commercial and industrial sites | Crushing and impact hazards; safety device failure |
| Boom gates and barriers | Car parks | Impact on people and vehicles |
| Bollards | Building frontages, car parks | Impact damage; inadequate protection |
| Statutory and safety signs | All buildings | Missing, faded or inaccurate signs; non-compliance |
| Wayfinding and accessibility signs | Larger buildings and public sites | Legibility, tactile and braille requirements |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber fences | 15 to 25 years | Post decay; treatment |
| Steel and aluminium fences | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; coastal exposure |
| Masonry boundary walls | 50 years and more | Foundations; roots; lean |
| Gate operators and controls | 10 to 15 years | Use; weather; maintenance |
| Gate safety devices (photo-eyes, edges) | 5 to 10 years | Damage; alignment; weather |
| Boom gates | 10 to 15 years | Use; impact |
| Signs | 10 to 20 years | UV fading; vandalism |

What shortens life:

- Ground contact at post bases.
- Vehicle impact on gates, barriers and fences.
- Heavy use of powered gates without maintenance.
- UV fading signs and degrading plastics.
- Tree roots pushing over boundary walls.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Powered gate crushing and impact

Powered sliding and swing gates and barriers create crushing points at closing edges, shearing points where gates pass posts, and drawing-in points at rollers and racks. Gates without working force limitation, safety edges and photoelectric beams, or with them set wrongly, can crush people, especially children. Gates that come off their tracks or hinges can fall. Deaths and serious injuries have led to specific safety standards in all three countries.

### Pool and play fence failures

Pool gates that do not self-close and self-latch from any open position, gaps under or through fences, and climbable objects such as chairs, pot plants and barbecues placed next to fences defeat the barrier. Most child drownings in home and apartment pools happen where barriers have failed or been propped open.

### Decay and corrosion

Timber fence posts rot at ground level and fences lean or fall in wind; steel corrodes at bases and welds; masonry walls crack and lean from tree roots, poor foundations and retained soil.

### Signage failures

Exit, fire, safety and accessibility signs go missing, fade, become hidden behind fit-outs, or point the wrong way after layout changes. Car park signs for height clearance and speed are damaged. Signs that are wrong are worse than none, because people rely on them.

### Security breaches

Damaged fences and gates that do not close or lock leave sites open; access control on gates fails or is bypassed.

### Boundary disputes and responsibility

Fences and walls on boundaries are often shared, and responsibility for repair or replacement depends on law and agreement; leaning walls toward a neighbour create liability.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Powered gates: safety edges, photoelectric beams, force settings, warning signs, manual release, tracks and stops.
- Pool gates: self-closing and latching from any position; latch height; gaps; climbable objects within the non-climbable zone.
- Fences leaning, posts rotted or loose, panels missing.
- Boundary walls cracked or leaning.
- Bollards and barriers damaged by vehicles.
- Signs: present, legible, correct and visible.

### In the records

- Gate maintenance and safety test records.
- Pool barrier certificates and registration.
- Boundary agreements and surveys.
- Signage schedules.

- Children or the public able to reach powered gate mechanisms, rollers and racks without guards.
- Signs for car park height clearance that do not match the actual lowest point.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gate does not reverse when it meets an obstruction | Force limitation or safety edge failure | Force measurement; device test |
| Gate jerks, jumps or leaves the track | Worn rollers, track or stops | Inspection |
| Pool gate stays open from some positions | Hinge tension or latch fault | Test from several open positions |
| Fence leaning in sections | Post base decay | Probe posts |
| Boundary wall leaning with a tree nearby | Root pressure or foundation movement | Inspection; engineer |
| Exit signs pointing to a removed door | Layout changed without updating signs | Walkthrough against plans |

> A powered gate that does not stop and reverse on contact, or a pool gate that does not self-close and latch, is a life-safety failure. Disable the gate or close the pool until fixed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gate safety devices failing; pool barrier non-compliant; boundary wall leaning toward a public area; exit signs wrong or missing | safety | Disable, close or rectify now |
| Gate or fence failed; site insecure | failure | Repair now |
| Pool barrier inspection or registration due | deadline | By the required date |
| Decay, corrosion, worn operators, faded signs | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Fences and operators at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No gate safety test records; signage not reviewed after changes | check | Inspect |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A gate and automation specialist for powered gates; a pool barrier inspector where required; a building surveyor for fences, walls and signage.

- Powered gate safety assessment: identify crushing, shearing and drawing-in points; test force limitation with a force meter; test safety edges, photoelectric beams, stop and reverse functions, manual release and warning devices.
- Pool barrier inspection against the applicable standard: height, gaps, gates and latches, non-climbable zones and nearby objects.
- Fence and wall survey: lean, post condition, corrosion, foundations and tree influence.
- Boundary check: position against title and survey, and any agreements with neighbours.
- Signage audit against the current layout, fire strategy and accessibility requirements.
- Bollard and barrier check for damage and adequacy where vehicles approach buildings and pedestrians.

The report should give the safety status of gates and barriers, required rectification, and a renewal plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Powered gate safety upgrades: force limitation, safety edges, photoelectric beams at the right heights, guards over rollers and racks, end stops and anti-derailment, warning lights, manual release, and a documented risk assessment.
- Gate operator replacement at the end of life, with controls meeting current standards.
- Pool barrier rectification: gate hardware, latch heights, gap closures, removal of climbable objects, and certification.
- Fence repairs: replace posts with galvanised stirrups or steel, replace panels, or rebuild.
- Boundary wall repairs or rebuilding, with neighbour agreement.
- Bollards to protect entrances, gates and pedestrians from vehicles.
- Signage renewal to current standards, including tactile and braille signs where required.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Gate maintenance and safety testing recur. Safety upgrades are lump sums per gate. Operator replacement is per gate. Fences are priced by length. Boundary walls by length and height, often shared with neighbours. Pool barrier rectification is usually a modest lump sum. Signage is priced per sign or as an audit-based package.

Safety rectification is code compliance and immediate; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

Disabling an unsafe powered gate has an operational cost in security and access that should be weighed against the speed of repair.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Powered gates follow AS/NZS 60335.2.103 for drives and manufacturer safety requirements; pool barriers follow AS 1926.1 with state registration and certification; fencing disputes follow state dividing fences legislation; exit and safety signs follow the National Construction Code and AS 1319.
- United Kingdom. Powered gates follow BS EN 12453 and BS EN 12604, and the Machinery Directive principles under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations; the Health and Safety Executive has issued alerts on powered gate deaths; party wall and boundary law apply; safety signs follow the Health and Safety (Safety Signs and Signals) Regulations 1996.
- United States. Gate operators follow UL 325 and gate construction ASTM F2200; pool barriers follow the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code and local codes; exit signs follow NFPA 101 and the International Building Code; accessible signage follows the 2010 ADA Standards.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Powered gate risk assessments, maintenance and safety test records.
- Gate operator make, model and age.
- Pool barrier certificates and registration.
- Boundary surveys and fencing agreements with neighbours.
- Signage schedule and records of signage updates after fit-outs.
- Incident records involving gates and barriers.

- Pool barrier inspection reports and records of gate hardware replacement.

pages.title: Fire Detection & Alarm Systems
pages.question: How do fire detection and alarm systems fail, when are they at the end of their life, and which findings leave a building unprotected?
pages.answer: Detection systems pass their tests until they cannot be supported. An unsupported panel is end of life because the next fit-out cannot be programmed in. The dangerous failures are quieter: zones isolated after works or nuisance alarms, detectors left covered, fit-outs without coverage, interfaces to lifts, doors and smoke control that no longer work, and signalling that stops when copper lines are retired. Isolations and failed interfaces mean the building is unprotected now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fire detection & alarm systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: FIP, smoke/heat detectors, occupant warning (EWIS)

sources.title: NFPA 72 National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A fire detection and alarm system detects fire, warns occupants, calls the fire brigade and drives the building's fire responses. It comprises detectors and manual call points; the fire indicator or control panel; occupant warning, from simple sounders to emergency warning and intercommunication systems (EWIS) with voice messages and wardens' phones; alarm signalling to a monitoring centre or brigade; and the interfaces that shut down or switch air handling to fire mode, home lifts, release doors, start smoke control and signal sprinkler and suppression status.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Photoelectric point smoke detector | Most occupied spaces | Best for smouldering fires; affected by dust and steam |
| Ionisation smoke detector | Older installations | Contains a small radioactive source; being replaced; disposal rules apply |
| Heat detector (fixed or rate-of-rise) | Kitchens, car parks, plant rooms, dusty areas | Slower; used where smoke detectors would false alarm |
| Multi-sensor detector | Modern offices, hotels | Combines smoke and heat to reduce false alarms |
