| Optical beam detector | Atria, warehouses, large open volumes | Needs stable mounting and alignment |
| Aspirating smoke detection | Data rooms, heritage buildings, high ceilings, prisons | Very sensitive; pipe network must stay clear |
| Flame detector | Fuel stores, hangars, industrial | Line of sight to the hazard |
| Domestic smoke alarms | Houses and apartments | Self-contained or interconnected, mains or long-life battery; 10-year life |

Systems are conventional (detectors grouped in zones, so the panel knows only the zone) or addressable (each device reported individually, with drift compensation and fault reporting). Large buildings network several panels. What a system must include depends on building class and height under each jurisdiction's building code; what it must do in an alarm is set out in the cause-and-effect matrix, which is the document most often out of date.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control and indicating panel | 15 to 20 years before manufacturer support ends | Vendor support; programming tools |
| Point smoke and heat detectors | 10 to 15 years | Contamination; environment; manufacturer advice |
| Domestic smoke alarms | 10 years | Built-in end of life |
| Aspirating systems | 15 to 20 years; filters and fans sooner | Pipe condition; environment |
| Beam detectors | 10 to 15 years | Mounting stability |
| EWIS amplifiers and speakers | 15 to 20 years | Heat; vendor support |
| Standby batteries | 3 to 5 years | Temperature; charger |
| Fire-rated cabling | Life of the building | Damage; alterations |

What shortens life:

- Contamination: dust, steam, insects and construction dust drift detectors toward false alarms.
- Fit-outs that cover, remove, relocate or add detectors and change zones without reprogramming.
- Panel obsolescence that stops the system being extended or reprogrammed.
- Neglected batteries in panels and EWIS.
- Building works during which detectors are covered or zones isolated and never restored.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Panel obsolescence

A panel keeps passing its routine tests until the day it cannot be repaired, extended or reprogrammed because its maker no longer supports it. That day usually comes with a tenancy change: a fit-out needs new devices and new cause-and-effect programming, and the panel cannot take them. Unsupported panels are therefore end of life whatever their test results.

### False and unwanted alarms

Contaminated detectors, the wrong detector type for the space (smoke detectors in kitchens and near showers), cooking, steam, dust from works, and insects cause unwanted alarms. Brigades charge for repeated unwanted alarms in many jurisdictions; occupants learn to ignore alarms; and the response to repeated false alarms is often to isolate zones, which leaves areas unprotected.

### Isolations and covered detectors

Detectors are covered and zones isolated during building works and cleaning, then forgotten. A building can run for months with floors effectively unprotected. Addressable panels show isolations; the question is whether anyone reads them.

### Coverage gaps

Fit-outs add rooms, partitions, ceilings and voids without adding detectors; concealed spaces above ceilings and below floors are left unprotected where required; detectors end up too close to air supply diffusers, which blow smoke away from them.

### Cause-and-effect drift

Over the years the interfaces the panel drives change: air handling units replaced, lifts modernised, access control upgraded, smoke control added. Unless the cause-and-effect matrix and interfaces are updated and tested together, lifts do not home, doors do not release, and smoke control does not start in a real fire.

### Occupant warning failures

Sounders and speakers that are inaudible in parts of the building, EWIS amplifiers with failed batteries, and messages that are unintelligible in noisy or reverberant spaces leave occupants unwarned.

### Alarm signalling failures

Alarm signalling equipment that dials out over a copper line stops working when the line is retired; monitoring contracts lapse; dual-path signalling is reduced to one path. The panel alarms locally but nobody is called.

### Domestic alarm failures

Smoke alarms in dwellings are removed, painted over, disconnected after nuisance alarms, or simply past their ten-year life; interconnection between alarms fails; tenancies change without checks.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### At the panel

- Panel make, model and age; vendor support status.
- Faults, isolations and disabled devices on the display or event log.
- Battery dates; standby charge indication.
- Zone block plan or graphics matching the building as it now is.
- Logbook entries for tests, faults and false alarms.

### In the building

- Detectors covered with caps, bags or tape; painted detectors.
- Rooms and voids without detectors; detectors next to supply diffusers.
- Smoke detectors in kitchens, bathrooms and dusty areas.
- Call points obstructed or missing at exits.
- Sounders and speakers absent from new rooms.
- Domestic alarms missing, beeping or dated more than ten years ago.

### In the records

- Routine service records at each required frequency.
- Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report.
- Unwanted alarm history and brigade charges.
- Cause-and-effect matrix and the last full interface test.
- Alarm signalling contract and the line or network it uses.
- Fire engineering report or fire strategy.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated unwanted alarms from one area | Wrong detector type or contamination | Event log; detector type against the space |
| Zones isolated for weeks | Isolation after works or nuisance alarms | Event log; works records |
| New tenancy cannot be connected | Panel unsupported or at capacity | Vendor advice; panel loading |
| Lifts did not home or doors did not release in a test | Interface or cause-and-effect fault | Interface test; matrix review |
| Brigade not called in a test | Signalling failure, often a retired line | Monitoring centre test; line type |
| Alarm inaudible in parts of the building | Insufficient sounders or speakers after fit-outs | Sound level and intelligibility test |

> A current annual statement establishes compliance at its date; it does not establish remaining life. A compliant system on an unsupported panel is at the end of its life, and isolated zones mean parts of the building are unprotected regardless of what the paperwork says.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zones isolated or detectors covered in occupied areas; alarm signalling not reaching the brigade; inaudible warning; failed interfaces to lifts, doors or smoke control | safety | Restore protection now; fire watch until done |
| Panel failed or out of service | failure | Restore now with interim fire watch |
| Routine service, annual certification or domestic alarm requirements due | deadline | At the prescribed interval or date |
| Contaminated or aged detectors; repeated unwanted alarms; coverage gaps; matrix out of date | condition | Repair and recommission in the near term |
| Unsupported panel; detectors at end of life | lifecycle | Plan replacement before the next tenancy change |
| No interface test on record; system not reviewed after fit-outs | check | Audit and full integrated test |
| Isolated faults found and fixed at service | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer or fire safety consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor and, for complex buildings, a fire engineer.

- Records review: service records against the required frequencies, annual statements, event logs, unwanted alarm history, cause-and-effect matrix, fire strategy and any performance solutions.
- Panel inspection: make, model, firmware, vendor support, spare capacity, isolations, faults, battery age and standby test.
- Coverage survey against the current layout, including ceiling and floor voids where detection is required, detector types against spaces, and call points at exits.
- Detector sampling: sensitivity and contamination readings from the panel for addressable systems; functional tests of a sample.
- Occupant warning test: sound levels and, for voice systems, speech intelligibility in representative spaces.
- Signalling test end to end with the monitoring centre, and identification of the communication path.
- Full integrated test of the cause-and-effect matrix with every interface operating: air handling, smoke control, lifts, doors, sprinkler and suppression signals.
- Domestic alarms: type, power, interconnection and age in a sample of dwellings, or all where the law requires.

The report should state compliance, coverage gaps, unwanted alarm causes, interface results, signalling path, panel support status, and a plan for repair or replacement.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restore protection: remove covers, clear isolations, and manage future isolations through a permit and daily check.
- Reduce unwanted alarms: right detector for each space (heat or multi-sensor in kitchens and near bathrooms), clean or replace contaminated detectors, relocate detectors away from diffusers, and manage hot works.
- Coverage additions after fit-outs, designed to the standard, with the zone plan and graphics updated.
- Cause-and-effect update and full integrated testing whenever any interfaced system changes.
- Panel replacement with a supported addressable system, reusing compatible cabling where possible, with temporary protection during changeover.
- Detector replacement programme on age, by floor or zone.
- Occupant warning upgrade: additional sounders or speakers, or a voice system where intelligibility is required.
- Signalling upgrade to supported, preferably dual-path, communications before copper lines are retired.
- Domestic alarms: interconnected photoelectric alarms, hard-wired or with ten-year sealed batteries, where required.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and annual certification are recurring contracts. Detector replacement is priced per device. Coverage additions per device, with design and reprogramming. Panel replacement is a lump-sum project including the panel, reprogramming, interfaces, commissioning and full integrated testing, with temporary fire watch or temporary panels during changeover. Signalling upgrades are a lump sum plus a recurring monitoring fee. Unwanted alarm charges are an operating cost that the remedies reduce.

Servicing, rectification and signalling are code compliance; detector and panel replacement are lifecycle; the integrated test is the check line that sizes the rest.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets required detection and warning by building class; AS 1670.1 covers detection system design, AS 1670.4 emergency warning and intercommunication, and AS 1851 routine service at monthly, six-monthly and yearly frequencies. Systems are essential safety measures with annual certification (the Annual Fire Safety Statement in New South Wales and the annual essential safety measures report in Victoria). Brigades charge for unwanted alarms. Queensland requires interconnected photoelectric smoke alarms in all dwellings by 1 January 2027.
- United Kingdom. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 places duties on the responsible person; BS 5839-1 covers non-domestic systems (weekly call point tests and periodic servicing, with every device tested annually), BS 5839-6 dwellings and BS 7273 interfaces; the Building Safety Act 2022 and Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 add duties for higher-risk residential buildings. Rented homes must have smoke alarms under the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm regulations.
- United States. NFPA 72 governs installation, inspection and testing, including annual functional testing of initiating devices and periodic smoke detector sensitivity testing; NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code set where systems are required; NFPA 4 covers integrated system testing; many jurisdictions charge for false alarms.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Routine service records for the last twelve months against the required frequencies.
- Current annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report, with any qualifications.
- Panel make, model, firmware and vendor support status.
- Event log extract showing faults, isolations and unwanted alarms.
- Cause-and-effect matrix and the latest full integrated test report.
- Alarm signalling contract and communication path.
- Zone block plan and as-built drawings.
- Fire strategy or fire engineering report, and any performance solutions.
- Domestic smoke alarm records for residential buildings.

pages.title: Fire Pumping Systems
pages.question: How do fire pumps fail, how do you prove a pump will deliver in a fire, and which findings leave sprinklers and hydrants without enough water?
pages.answer: Fire pumps fail to start (flat diesel batteries, fuel problems, controllers left in manual, power isolated) or fail to deliver (worn impellers, blocked strainers, falling town main pressure). Only an annual flow test against the pump curve proves performance; many pumps have no usable test arrangement. A jockey pump starting constantly is masking a leak. Electric pumps fed after the main switch can lose power when the building is isolated in a fire.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fire pumping systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Electric and diesel fire pumps, controllers

sources.title: NFPA 20 Installation of Stationary Pumps for Fire Protection

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Fire pumps boost water pressure and flow to sprinklers, hydrants and hose reels where the town main cannot supply enough on its own. A pumpset comprises one or more duty pumps driven by electric motors or diesel engines, a small jockey (pressure maintenance) pump that keeps the system pressurised, controllers that start pumps automatically when pressure falls, test and flow measurement arrangements, and the suction supply from the main or from storage tanks. Diesel pumps also have fuel, batteries, cooling and exhaust systems.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electric duty pump and controller | Primary fire pump in many buildings | Supply not protected; controller faults; motor failure |
| Diesel duty pump | Independent of mains power; standby or duty | Fails to start (batteries, fuel); cooling; exhaust |
| Jockey pump | Keeps pressure up so duty pumps start only in a real demand | Runs constantly when the system leaks; masks leaks |
| Controllers | Start and supervise pumps; report to fire panel | Electronics; settings; obsolescence |
| Suction supply: town main, break tank, storage tanks | Water source | Low main pressure; tank sediment, corrosion, failed level controls |
| Test header and flow meter | Annual performance testing | Absent or unusable, so pumps are never flow tested |
| Pump room | Housing | Freezing; flooding; ventilation; access |

The power supply to an electric fire pump must keep it running in a fire: it is connected ahead of the main switch or from a protected supply, and its cables are fire-rated, so isolating the building does not stop the pump. Pump rooms are often separately fire-rated, with access for the brigade.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire pumps (casing and impeller) | 25 to 35 years | Water quality; run time; cavitation |
| Electric motors | 20 to 30 years | Run time; damp |
| Diesel engines | 25 to 30 years | Exercise; maintenance |
| Controllers | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Jockey pumps | 10 to 15 years | Cycling |
| Starting batteries | 3 to 5 years | Temperature; charger |
| Steel tanks | 20 to 30 years | Internal corrosion; coatings |
| Concrete tanks | 40 years and more | Joints; leaks |

What shortens life:

- Missed weekly runs, which leave seals dry, batteries flat and faults undetected.
- A leaking system that makes the jockey pump cycle constantly.
- Cold pump rooms in winter.
- Water quality and sediment drawn from tanks.
- Cavitation from poor suction conditions.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Failure to start

Diesel pumps fail to start for the same reasons as standby generators: flat batteries, failed chargers, fuel problems, failed engine heaters. Electric pumps fail to start when their supply has been isolated, a controller fault is present, or settings have changed. A pump that does not start on a pressure drop leaves the sprinklers and hydrants on town main pressure alone.

### Performance decline

Impellers wear and erode, wear rings open up, and suction strainers block; the pump delivers less flow and pressure than its rating. Only an annual flow test against the pump's rated curve shows the decline. Pumps whose test arrangements were never installed or have become unusable are often never flow tested.

### Water supply problems

Town main pressures fall as utilities manage networks; break tanks and storage tanks lose capacity to sediment, corrosion and failed inlet valves; suction pipes blocked or undersized cause cavitation. The pump can only boost what reaches it.

### Jockey pump cycling

A jockey pump that starts frequently is replacing water lost through a leak or a passing valve. It wears out quickly, and the leak it masks may be corroding pipework or wasting water.

### Power supply vulnerability

Electric fire pumps connected after the main switch, or with non-fire-rated cabling, can lose power when the building is isolated in a fire, or when the cable burns. This is a design defect found in older buildings and after switchboard replacements.

### Pump room conditions

Pump rooms freeze in cold climates, flood in basements, overheat in summer, and are used for storage. Diesel exhaust leaks and fuel spills create further hazards.

### Relief valves and churn overheating

Pumps running against closed outlets (churn) heat the water in the casing; circulation relief valves and pressure relief valves prevent damage and over-pressure. Stuck or wrongly set relief valves either waste water continuously or let pressures exceed what pipework and fittings are rated for.

### Controller settings and modes

Controllers left in manual or off after maintenance, start pressures set wrongly, and pumps set to stop automatically when they should run until manually stopped are common findings after service visits. The controller's status should be supervised by the fire alarm panel.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the pump room

- Nameplates: rating, year; pump curve displayed.
- Controllers showing alarms or manual mode; selector switches in off.
- Diesel batteries, fuel level, engine heater, exhaust condition.
- Packing gland or seal leaks; corrosion; vibration.
- Jockey pump run counter; frequent starts.
- Pressure gauges; test header and flow meter presence.
- Room temperature, ventilation, flooding signs, storage.

### In the records

- Weekly run test records.
- Annual flow test results plotted against the pump curve.
- Diesel battery and fuel records.
- Tank inspection and cleaning records.
- Water authority pressure and flow information.
- Power supply arrangement for electric pumps.

- Controller status signalled to the fire panel.
- Relief valve discharge during weekly runs.
- Pump room access for the brigade and its signage.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow test below the rated curve | Impeller wear, blocked strainer, or suction restriction | Suction pressure during test; strainer inspection |
| Jockey pump starts every few minutes | System leak or passing valve | Pressure decay test with pumps isolated |
| Diesel slow to start or fails | Batteries, fuel or heater | Battery test; fuel sample |
| Cavitation noise during tests | Low suction pressure or blocked suction | Suction gauge; tank level |
| No flow tests on record | No usable test arrangement | Inspection |
| Pump supply after the main switch | Design defect | Single-line diagram |

> A fire pump that has not been flow tested against its rating is unproven. A pump that starts and runs on weekly tests can still be unable to deliver the flow the sprinklers and hydrants need.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pump fails to start; controller in off or manual; pump supply unprotected; performance well below design | safety | Restore now; fire watch and brigade notification |
| Pump failed or out of service | failure | Repair now with impairment management |
| Weekly runs and annual flow tests due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Performance decline; jockey cycling; battery or fuel issues; tank deterioration | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Pumps or controllers at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No flow test record; town main pressure not checked recently | check | Flow test and supply check |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer with the pump maintenance contractor.

- Records review: weekly run logs, annual flow tests, battery and fuel records, tank inspections.
- Inspection of pumps, motors, engines, controllers, jockey pump, pipework, valves, tanks and pump room.
- Flow test at churn, rated flow and peak flow, plotted against the manufacturer's curve and the system's design requirement.
- Supply check: town main pressure and flow, tank capacity and condition.
- Power supply review for electric pumps: connection point and cable rating.
- Leak investigation where the jockey pump cycles frequently.

The report should state whether pumps deliver the required performance, the reliability of starting and power, the adequacy of the water supply, and works needed.

- Controller testing: automatic start on pressure drop, alarm signals to the fire panel, and phase reversal and power failure alarms on electric controllers.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Overhaul: impeller and wear ring replacement, seals, bearings, alignment.
- Starting reliability: battery replacement cycle, chargers, engine heaters, fuel management.
- Controller replacement.
- Test arrangements: install a flow meter or test header so annual testing is possible.
- Power supply correction: reconnect ahead of the main switch with fire-rated cable.
- Leak repair to stop jockey pump cycling.
- Tank works: clean, recoat, reline or replace; repair level controls.
- Pump replacement where performance cannot be restored, sized to current design requirements.
- Pump room: heating, drainage, ventilation, clearance.

- Relief valves: reset or replace circulation and pressure relief valves, and pipe discharges to drain.
- Supervision: signal controller mode, pump running and power failure to the fire panel so faults are seen.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Weekly and annual testing are recurring. Overhauls are lump sums per pump. Controller and pump replacement are lump-sum projects with temporary measures during the outage. Power supply correction is a lump sum. Tank cleaning recurs; relining and replacement are lump sums.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; overhaul and replacement are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Pump room works and tank relining often require the system to be impaired; temporary pumps, fire watches and brigade notification are part of the project cost.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 2941 governs fire pump installations; AS 1851 sets routine service, including weekly pumpset tests and annual flow tests; fire pumps are essential safety measures with annual certification; water authorities publish main pressure information for design.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 12845 and the LPC Rules set sprinkler pump requirements, including weekly automatic start tests; BS 9990 covers wet rising mains; insurers often set additional pump testing requirements.
- United States. NFPA 20 governs installation; NFPA 25 sets testing, including weekly no-flow runs for diesel pumps, monthly for electric pumps (or weekly where required), and annual flow tests against the pump curve.

In all three jurisdictions, insurers and the fire brigade commonly need notice before a fire pump is taken out of service, and impairment procedures apply until it is restored.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Weekly pump run records.
- Annual flow test reports plotted against the pump curve.
- Diesel battery and fuel records.
- Tank inspection and cleaning records.
- Single-line diagram showing the fire pump power supply.
- Pump and controller installation dates.
- Water supply pressure and flow data.

- Controller alarm and supervision test records.
- Impairment records for pump outages.

pages.title: Fireplaces
pages.question: How do fireplaces and heaters fail, and which findings mean stop using them?
pages.answer: The main risks are carbon monoxide and fire. Flued gas heaters with cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues, and fires that spill under negative pressure, put carbon monoxide into homes; unflued heaters release combustion products indoors. Wood heaters too close to combustibles or on small hearths ignite surroundings; creosote causes flue fires. Any sign of spillage or carbon monoxide means stop use until tested; service gas heaters regularly and fit carbon monoxide alarms.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fireplaces; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Ornamental, decorative and functional fireplaces \u2014 period-stock feature element

sources.title: NFPA 211 Chimneys, Fireplaces, Vents, and Solid Fuel-Burning Appliances

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Fireplaces and heaters with flues include open masonry fireplaces, enclosed wood heaters (slow combustion stoves), gas log fires and flued gas space heaters. They combine fire, combustion products and a flue, so their risks are fire spreading to the building, carbon monoxide entering living spaces, and smoke and emissions. Chimneys and flues are covered on their own page; this page covers the appliance, hearth, surrounds and the room.

| Type | Where it is found | Main risks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open fireplaces | Older houses | Sparks and embers; poor draw; heat loss |
| Wood heaters | Houses, especially rural | Clearances to combustibles; flue fires; emissions |
| Gas log fires | Houses and apartments | Flue spillage; servicing |
| Flued gas space heaters | Houses | Carbon monoxide from cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues |
| Unflued gas heaters | Older homes | Combustion products indoors; banned or restricted in some places |
| Decorative and ethanol fireplaces | Apartments | Fuel handling fires |

Many older homes have fireplaces that are no longer used but remain open to the flue, while others have been converted to gas or fitted with inserts; the condition of each, and whether the flue still suits the appliance, is often unknown.

For assessment, fireplaces are graded by the risk they pose to occupants as much as by their condition; a sound-looking heater can still spill carbon monoxide.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Item | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wood heaters | 15 to 25 years | Use; firebox wear |
| Gas heaters and log fires | 10 to 20 years | Servicing |
| Hearths and surrounds | Life of the building | Cracking; alterations |
| Door seals and glass | 5 to 10 years | Heat |

What shortens life:

- No servicing of gas heaters.
- Burning wet or treated timber.
- Alterations that bring combustible materials close.

Appliance life depends heavily on use and servicing. Gas heaters that are serviced regularly last much longer and stay safer than those left for years; wood heater fireboxes, baffles and bricks wear with heavy use and wet fuel. Hearths and surrounds last as long as the building unless cracked by heat or altered. The useful life of wood heating is also being shortened by emissions rules and by electrification, which make replacement with heat pumps more attractive than like-for-like renewal.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Carbon monoxide

Gas space heaters with cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues, and fires whose flues spill under negative pressure from exhaust fans, put carbon monoxide into homes. Deaths from unserviced gas heaters have led to safety campaigns and servicing advice.

### Clearances to combustibles

Wood heaters and fireplaces installed too close to timber framing, linings, furniture or mantels, or on inadequate hearths, ignite nearby materials over time.

### Flue fires and blockages

Creosote from slow-burning wet wood builds up and ignites in flues; nests and debris block flues; see the chimney page.

### Smoke and emissions

Wood heaters produce fine particle pollution indoors and outdoors; regulations restrict emissions and, in some areas, use.

### Unflued appliances

Unflued gas heaters release combustion products and moisture into rooms; they are restricted in schools and some jurisdictions.

### Negative pressure and spillage

Kitchen rangehoods, bathroom fans and clothes dryers depressurise tightly sealed homes, pulling combustion products down flues and into rooms. Spillage is worst when several fans run together, which is why testing must be done under worst-case conditions.

### Alterations around appliances

Renovations bring new timber mantels, shelving, cabinetry and wall linings close to fireplaces and heaters, often without anyone checking clearances, and new airtightness reduces the combustion air an appliance needs.

### Conversions and inserts

Gas log fires and inserts fitted into old masonry fireplaces depend on flues that may be cracked or unsuited, and on correct flue liners and terminations.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Soot staining above fireplaces or heaters.
- Heaters close to combustible walls or mantels; small hearths.
- Gas heaters without service tags; yellow flames.
- No carbon monoxide alarm.
- Cracked fireboxes and door glass.

### In the records

- Gas heater service records.
- Installation certificates.
- Chimney sweeping records.

- Doors and windows sealed tightly in a home with an open fireplace or gas heater, limiting combustion air.
- Exhaust fans near heaters, which can cause spillage.
- Timber mantels and shelving installed close to fireboxes.
- Smoke smell in the house after the fire has burned down.
- Heaters with dated or missing compliance plates.

- Wet or painted timber stored for burning, which builds creosote quickly.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soot above a gas heater | Incomplete combustion or spillage | Service; CO test |
| Headaches when the heater runs | Carbon monoxide | CO test |
| Scorched timber near a wood heater | Inadequate clearance | Measurement |
| Smoke into the room | Poor draw or blocked flue | Flue inspection |

> Any sign of carbon monoxide or flue spillage means stop using the appliance until a licensed gas fitter has tested it.

Separate appliance faults (servicing, cracked heat exchangers, worn seals) from installation faults (clearances, flues, combustion air) and from house effects (negative pressure from fans and airtightness), because each needs a different fix.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon monoxide or spillage; inadequate clearances; unflued heaters in bedrooms | safety | Stop use now |
| Appliance failed | failure | Repair or replace |
| Gas safety checks due in rented homes | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn seals and glass | condition | Repair |
| Appliance at end of life | lifecycle | Replace or decommission |
| Service history unknown | check | Service and test |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Carbon monoxide findings are always graded as safety regardless of how old or new the appliance is, because the consequence is death; clearance and flue defects follow closely because they cause house fires.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed gas fitter for gas appliances and a qualified installer or chimney sweep for solid fuel, with the building surveyor.

- Gas appliance service with carbon monoxide spillage testing under worst-case conditions (exhaust fans running, doors closed).
- Clearance check of wood heaters and fireplaces to combustible materials and hearth size against the installation standard.
- Flue inspection and sweeping.
- Carbon monoxide alarm check.
- Compliance check of installation certificates and emissions ratings.

The report should state whether each appliance is safe to use, and repairs, replacement or decommissioning.

Testing should be repeated after any renovation that changes airtightness or adds exhaust fans.

- Occupant interview: symptoms when appliances run, smoke or smells, and how often appliances are used and serviced.

Record results for each appliance separately.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Service gas heaters at the recommended interval, commonly every two years.
- Replace cracked or unsafe appliances, including older flued gas heaters that fail testing.
- Correct clearances with heat shields, larger hearths or relocation.
- Sweep flues and fit bird guards.
- Carbon monoxide alarms in rooms with fuel-burning appliances.
- Remove unflued heaters from bedrooms and sensitive buildings.
- Decommission unused fireplaces and seal and ventilate their flues, or convert to electric heating as part of electrification.

- Combustion air: provide dedicated air supply to appliances in airtight homes, or replace with room-sealed appliances.
- Spillage controls: interlock or balance exhaust fans in homes with open-flued appliances.

- Owner guidance on dry firewood, flue cleaning intervals and never running unflued heaters in closed bedrooms.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing and sweeping recur. Appliance replacement is per unit. Clearance corrections are itemised. Decommissioning is a small lump sum per fireplace.

Safety items are immediate; servicing is recurring; replacement is lifecycle.

Carbon monoxide alarms and servicing are inexpensive compared with the risk they control. Replacing an older flued gas heater or wood heater with a heat pump may cost more up front but removes the carbon monoxide and flue risks, and often qualifies for energy incentives.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 2918 covers installation of solid fuel heating appliances; AS/NZS 4012 and 4013 set wood heater efficiency and emissions; AS/NZS 5601.1 covers gas appliances; state gas regulators recommend regular servicing of gas heaters.
- United Kingdom. The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require annual gas safety checks in rented homes; Approved Document J covers combustion appliances; smoke control areas and Ecodesign rules restrict wood burning; carbon monoxide alarms are required with fixed combustion appliances in many homes.
- United States. NFPA 211 covers chimneys, fireplaces and vents; the EPA sets new wood heater emissions standards; the International Residential and Fuel Gas Codes cover installation; many states require carbon monoxide alarms.

Rental minimum standards in several places also set heater requirements.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Gas heater service records.
- Installation certificates.
- Chimney sweeping records.
- Carbon monoxide alarm details.
- Emissions ratings of wood heaters.

- Records of renovations near heaters or fireplaces.
- Electrification or heater replacement plans.
- Any incidents involving smoke, soot or carbon monoxide.

- Wood heater emissions compliance plates and model details.

pages.title: Flooring
pages.question: How do floor finishes fail, and which flooring findings are safety or neighbour issues?
pages.answer: Flooring fails mostly from moisture and movement. Slabs without vapour barriers or not dried debond vinyl and resin and cup timber; tiled floors without movement joints crack and tent; hard floors in apartments without acoustic underlays cause noise disputes. Polished and glazed floors become slippery when wet, and lifted tiles and carpet edges trip people. Test older vinyl tiles for asbestos before removing them.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about flooring; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Timber boards, engineered timber, carpet, tiles and floor coverings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Flooring is the finish layer people walk on: carpet, vinyl sheet and tiles, timber (solid, engineered and parquet), laminate, ceramic and stone tiles, polished concrete and resin floors, laid over screeds, underlays and the structural floor. Flooring is judged on wear and appearance, but its failures also include slips and trips, acoustic complaints between apartments, moisture-driven failures that start in the slab below, and hazardous materials in older vinyl tiles and adhesives.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carpet | Offices, apartments, hotels | Wear, stains, trips at joins |
| Vinyl sheet and tiles | Healthcare, kitchens, apartments | Moisture debonding; seams; older tiles may contain asbestos |
| Solid and engineered timber | Homes, apartments, offices | Cupping and gapping from moisture; acoustic complaints |
| Laminate | Homes and apartments | Swelling at joints; acoustic |
| Ceramic and stone tiles | Entries, wet areas, kitchens | Cracking, tenting, slips when wet |
| Polished concrete and resin | Commercial and modern homes | Cracking; slips; coating wear |

In offices the base-building floor finish usually belongs to the owner and tenant flooring to the tenant; in apartments flooring is usually the owner's, with by-laws controlling changes.

The engine should treat flooring by space: the same finish can be fine in a bedroom and a hazard in a wet entry.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Type | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial carpet tiles | 10 to 15 years | Traffic; quality |
| Residential carpet | 8 to 12 years | Use; tenancy turnover |
| Vinyl | 15 to 25 years | Traffic; moisture below |
| Timber | 30 to 50 years with refinishing | Moisture; wear |
| Laminate | 10 to 20 years | Moisture |
| Ceramic and stone tiles | 30 to 50 years | Movement; installation |

What shortens life:

- Moisture from slabs without vapour barriers, leaks and wet cleaning.
- Missing movement joints in tiled floors.
- Heavy traffic and grit.
- Poor substrate preparation.

Floor life depends on traffic, grit control at entries, cleaning practices and moisture in the substrate. A good floor laid on a damp slab can fail within months, while a modest floor on a dry, well-prepared substrate with good matting can last decades.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Moisture from below

Moisture rising through concrete slabs debonds vinyl and resin, swells and cups timber, and causes adhesives to fail; old slabs without vapour barriers and new slabs not dried before flooring are the usual causes. Timber also cups from leaks and humidity.

### Tile cracking and tenting

Tiled floors laid without movement joints at perimeters and across large areas crack, debond and lift in a ridge (tenting) as the slab and tiles move with temperature and shrinkage.

### Impact noise

Hard floors in apartments, especially timber and tile laid over carpet areas without acoustic underlays, transmit footsteps to the unit below, generating complaints and by-law disputes.

### Slips and trips

Polished and glazed surfaces become slippery when wet; lifted tiles, curled carpet edges and changes in level trip people.

### Wear

Traffic paths wear carpet, scratch timber and wear through coatings; grit tracked in accelerates wear.

### Hazardous materials

Older vinyl floor tiles and their adhesives commonly contain asbestos; they are safe in place but release fibres when broken up or sanded.

### Substrate failures

Self-levelling compounds that crack or debond, screeds that are weak or uneven, and timber subfloors that move transmit their defects through the finish: cracks reflect through vinyl and tiles, and uneven substrates cause trips and premature wear.

### Cleaning damage

Wrong cleaning chemicals strip coatings, polish stone, soften adhesives and leave slippery residues.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Timber boards cupped or gapped; vinyl bubbling or lifting.
- Tiles cracked, hollow-sounding or ridged.
- Worn carpet paths and frayed tile edges.
- Hard floors in upper apartments with complaints below.
- Older vinyl tiles of small square formats.
- Slippery entries and wet areas.

### In the records

- Moisture test results before flooring.
- Strata approvals and by-laws for hard floors.
- Asbestos register.
- Slip incidents.

- Cracks in vinyl or tiles following a straight line, reflecting a joint or crack in the slab below.
- Dark discolouration or adhesive bleeding at vinyl seams, signs of moisture.
- Gaps between timber boards widening in dry weather and closing in wet.

- Grit and water tracked inside entries, wearing and dulling floors.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vinyl or resin lifting across a slab | Moisture vapour from the slab | In-situ relative humidity test |
| Timber cupping | Moisture from below or a leak | Moisture readings |
| Tiles ridging along a line | No movement joints | Joint inspection |
| Noise complaints after a renovation | Hard floor without acoustic underlay | Floor construction; acoustic test |
| Slips on entry tiles | Low wet slip resistance | Slip test |

> Do not sand, grind or rip up older vinyl tiles and adhesives until they have been tested for asbestos.

Flooring failures concentrated near external walls, wet areas or at ground level point to moisture; failures across the whole floor point to substrate preparation or the product.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip hazards; slippery floors with incidents; damaged asbestos-containing tiles | safety | Make safe now |
| Floor failed (lifting, tenting) | failure | Repair now |
| By-law or tribunal orders on noise | deadline | As required |
| Wear; minor cupping; stains | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Flooring at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Moisture or asbestos status unknown | check | Test before works |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Flooring findings rarely reach safety grade except for trip and slip hazards and disturbed asbestos tiles; most are condition and lifecycle items, but moisture-driven failures recur until the cause is fixed.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or flooring specialist leads, with an asbestos assessor for older floors and an acoustic consultant where noise is the issue.

- Condition survey of flooring by area: wear, lifting, cracking, cupping and trip edges.
- Moisture testing of slabs by in-situ relative humidity probes before new flooring, and of timber floors where cupping occurs.
- Tile inspection: tapping for hollow tiles, checking for movement joints.
- Slip resistance testing of floors at entries, wet areas and ramps.
- Acoustic testing of impact sound between apartments where complaints exist.
- Asbestos sampling of older vinyl tiles and adhesives before removal.

The report should give causes of failure, safety items, and replacement or repair recommendations.

Before replacing a failed floor, establish the cause, or the replacement will fail the same way.

For apartment noise disputes, test the floor as built rather than relying on product data, because installation details such as perimeter isolation decide the result.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Moisture mitigation with surface membranes or proper drying before new flooring.
- Movement joints cut into tiled floors, with lifted tiles relaid.
- Acoustic underlays under hard floors in apartments, required by by-laws.
- Slip treatments or replacement finishes in wet and entry areas, with entry matting.
- Trip hazard repair: relay lifted tiles, restretch or replace carpet, fit transition strips.
- Refinishing timber floors rather than replacing them.
- Licensed removal of asbestos-containing tiles and adhesives, or leaving them encapsulated under new flooring.
- Replacement on cycle with products suited to the traffic and moisture conditions.

- Substrate repair: remove failed screeds and levelling compounds before new flooring.

- Entry matting long enough to remove grit and water, protecting floors throughout the building.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Flooring is priced by area. Moisture membranes add to the cost of new flooring but prevent repeat failures. Acoustic underlays add modestly. Asbestos removal adds licensed removal and clearance. Replacement in occupied buildings is staged, with furniture moves.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; tenant-caused damage is recoverable.

Investigating moisture costs little compared with replacing a floor that fails twice.

Replacement in rental and hotel stock is timed with vacancies.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Slip resistance classification follows AS 4586 with guidance in Standards Australia handbook HB 198; resilient flooring installation follows AS 1884; strata by-laws commonly require approval and acoustic underlays for hard floors; the National Construction Code sets sound insulation for apartment floors.
- United Kingdom. BS 8203 covers resilient floor coverings and BS 8204 screeds; Approved Document E covers sound insulation; the HSE slip assessment approach guides floor safety.
- United States. ASTM F2170 sets slab moisture testing; ANSI A326.3 slip resistance; the International Building Code sets impact insulation class for floors between dwellings; condominium rules often regulate hard floors.

In all three countries, apartment by-laws or rules often require owners to obtain approval and use acoustic underlays before laying hard floors.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Moisture test results for recent flooring.
- Strata approvals and by-laws on hard flooring.
- Asbestos register covering floor tiles.
- Slip and trip incident records.
- Flooring warranties.

- Cleaning specifications.
- Substrate preparation records.
- Noise complaints from neighbours.

- Moisture records for the substrate.
- Records of leaks affecting floors.

- Product data for installed floors.

pages.title: Foundations
pages.question: How do foundations fail, how do you tell subsidence from heave or settlement, and when is underpinning needed?
pages.answer: Foundations rarely wear out; the ground moves them. Trees drying clay cause subsidence, worst at the corner nearest the tree and seasonal at first; tree removal and leaks cause heave; leaking drains wash soil away; timber piles rot when groundwater falls; stumps decay. Read the crack taper and distortion, then monitor for a full wet and dry season: progressive movement matters more than width. Remove the cause before underpinning.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about foundations; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Concrete footings, piles, pile caps, slabs, strip footings, pad foundations

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Foundations transfer the building's weight to the ground. Their form depends on the soil and the load: strip footings under walls, pad footings under columns, raft slabs over the whole footprint, piles taken down to firmer strata, and in older Australian houses, timber or concrete stumps supporting suspended floors. A foundation's behaviour is governed as much by the ground as by the concrete: reactive clays that swell and shrink with moisture, fill, soft alluvium, groundwater, mine workings and earthquakes all move foundations that are themselves sound.

| Type | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strip and pad footings | Most low-rise buildings of all eras | Shallow; affected by soil moisture change, trees and leaking drains |
| Raft and stiffened raft slabs | Houses and low-rise on reactive clays (Australia, parts of the US) | Edge movement and dishing or doming with soil moisture |
| Bored and driven piles | Larger buildings, poor ground | Defects at construction; corrosion; negative skin friction in settling fill |
| Timber piles | Older buildings in waterfront cities (Boston, parts of Europe) | Decay where the water table drops and exposes the timber |
| Timber and concrete stumps | Australian houses with suspended floors | Timber stumps rot and sink; concrete stumps crack and lean |
| Screw piles and mini-piles | Underpinning and light structures | Corrosion; installation quality |

In Australia, sites are classified by soil reactivity under AS 2870, from stable sand and rock through moderately, highly and extremely reactive clays to problem sites; the classification sets how much movement a house footing must tolerate. In Britain, shrinkable clays in the south-east and trees drive most subsidence. In the United States, expansive soils in Texas, Colorado and California, and seismic hazard on the west coast, dominate.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete footings and piles | Life of the building | Soil movement; sulfates; construction quality |
| Timber piles below the water table | Indefinite while saturated | Exposure when groundwater falls |
| Timber stumps | 30 to 60 years | Moisture, termites, species, treatment |
| Concrete stumps | 50 years and more | Reinforcement corrosion; lean |
| Underpinning | Life of the building if the cause is addressed | Recurrence of the original cause |

Foundations rarely wear out; they move. What shortens their effective life is a change in the ground around them:

- Trees drawing moisture from clay, which shrinks and lets footings drop, most in dry seasons and droughts.
- Tree removal, which lets clay rewet and swell over years (heave).
- Leaking drains and water pipes, which soften soil and wash fines away.
- Poor site drainage: water ponding against footings, downpipes discharging at the wall base.
- Excavation nearby: neighbouring basements, trenches and dewatering.
- Falling groundwater, which exposes timber piles to decay.
- Mine workings collapsing below the site.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Subsidence from clay shrinkage

Clay soils lose volume as they dry. Tree roots and drought dry the soil beneath part of a building, which then drops relative to the rest. Movement is seasonal at first, opening in summer and closing in winter, and can become progressive as the tree grows. Damage concentrates at the corner or side nearest the tree.

### Heave

Clay swells as it wets. Removing large trees, leaking pipes and changed drainage let clay rewet under a building; the affected part rises, sometimes over many years. Heave lifts floors and cracks walls in patterns opposite to subsidence.

### Settlement

New loads compress the ground beneath them. Most settlement happens early in a building's life; continuing settlement points to fill that is still consolidating, soft soils, or an extension on a shallower foundation pulling away from the original.

### Washout and erosion

Leaking drains and broken stormwater pipes wash fine soil from beneath footings, leaving voids that let them drop locally, often suddenly.

### Timber pile and stump decay

Timber piles last as long as they stay saturated. When groundwater falls, through dewatering or changed drainage, the tops dry and rot, and the structure above settles. Timber stumps rot at ground level and are attacked by termites, and the floor sinks unevenly.

### Chemical attack

Sulfates in soil and groundwater attack concrete; acid sulfate soils and contaminated land corrode reinforcement and steel piles.

### Earthquake and liquefaction

Earthquakes can cause loose saturated sands to liquefy, so foundations lose support. Older foundations not designed for seismic loads can fail to hold buildings together in a quake.

### Mine subsidence

Collapse of old coal and mineral workings beneath a site produces settlement troughs and tilt. Mining regions in New South Wales, Britain and parts of the United States carry this risk and have notification or compensation schemes.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### Outside

- Tapering diagonal cracks in masonry, usually starting at openings and running through bricks and mortar.
- Distorted window and door heads; gaps between frames and walls.
- Cracks continuing below the damp-proof course into the footing.
- Trees within a distance of the building comparable to their height, especially on clay.
- Paths and paving sloping toward walls; downpipes discharging at the wall base.
- Gaps opening between extensions and the original building.

### Inside

- Doors and windows sticking or swinging open; floors sloping noticeably.
- Cracks at the corners of openings and between walls and ceilings.
- Skirting boards pulling away from floors; tiled floors cracking along a line.

### In the records

- Soil and site classification; geotechnical reports.
- Previous underpinning or restumping.
- Insurance subsidence claims.
- Crack monitoring data.
- Drain CCTV surveys.
- Mine subsidence or coal mining reports.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diagonal cracks widening toward the top at one corner, near a large tree | Subsidence from clay shrinkage | Seasonal crack opening; soil moisture and root analysis |
| Cracks widening in summer and closing in winter | Seasonal clay movement | Twelve months of crack monitoring |
| Floors lifting in the middle, cracks wider at the top of internal walls | Heave after tree removal or leaks | Level survey; history of tree removal |
| Sudden local drop near a drain run | Washout from a leaking drain | Drain CCTV; void detection |
| Crack between extension and original building | Different foundations moving differently | Foundation depths; level survey |
| Uneven floors in a house on timber stumps | Decayed or sunken stumps | Sub-floor inspection |
| Building tilting slowly over a wide area | Mine subsidence or regional settlement | Mining records; survey |

> Width alone does not decide severity. Progressive movement is more serious than a wide crack that has stopped. Twelve months of monitoring, covering a full wet and dry season, is usually needed to tell them apart on reactive clay.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid or large movement with wide cracks, distorted openings that threaten egress, or loss of bearing to walls and columns | safety | Prop and engineer now |
| Progressive movement with cracks of 5 to 15 mm or more | failure | Stabilise now: fix the cause and underpin where needed |
| Seasonal movement causing repeated cracking; decaying stumps | condition | Address causes and repair in the near term |
| Mine subsidence or heritage obligations requiring action by a date | deadline | By the required date |
| Cracks of unknown cause; trees near a building on clay | check | Monitor for twelve months and investigate |
| Hairline cracks shown stable | nil | Cosmetic repair |

Crack widths map to damage categories under BRE Digest 251 in Britain and Appendix C of AS 2870 in Australia; see the masonry page. A lifecycle grade rarely applies to foundations themselves; it applies to stumps and other replaceable elements.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural or geotechnical engineer leads, with an arborist where trees are involved and a drainage contractor for drain surveys.

- Crack mapping and monitoring: record every crack with width and taper, fit tell-tales or gauge studs, and read them monthly for at least a year.
- Level survey of floors and brick courses to show the shape of movement.
- Drain investigation: CCTV and pressure testing of drains and water pipes near the affected area.
- Trial pits and boreholes: foundation type and depth, soil type, moisture content and plasticity, roots.
- Tree survey: species, height, distance and water demand; root identification from samples.
- Groundwater monitoring where timber piles or dewatering are involved.
- Records review: original foundation design, previous repairs, insurance claims, mining reports.

The report should identify the cause of movement with the evidence for it, whether movement is seasonal or progressive, and the remedy, starting with removing the cause.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Remove the cause first: repair leaking drains and pipes, fix site drainage, manage or remove trees (with heave risk assessed before removal), and stop downpipes discharging at the wall base.
- Monitor after removing the cause; many buildings stabilise and need only crack repair.
- Underpinning where movement continues: mass concrete underpinning, mini-piles, screw piles, or resin injection to stiffen and lift soils, selected for the ground and access.
- Restumping of houses on decayed timber stumps with concrete or steel stumps, with re-levelling of floors.
- Root barriers between trees and buildings where trees must stay.
- Crack repair after stabilisation: stitching with helical bars, repointing, and replacement of damaged bricks.
- Heave precautions where trees are removed from clay sites: phased removal, monitoring and flexible repairs.
- Pile remediation for decayed timber piles: underpinning to new piles, or raising groundwater where possible.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Monitoring and investigation are lump sums spread over a year. Drain repairs are priced by length or per defect. Underpinning is priced per metre of wall or per pile, with access, excavation and reinstatement of floors and finishes inside often doubling the cost. Restumping is priced per stump or per house. Crack repairs are itemised after stabilisation.

Underpinning and restumping are lifecycle or major repair items; drain and drainage works are repairs and maintenance; monitoring is the check line that decides whether underpinning is needed at all. In Britain, subsidence is commonly an insurance matter, and insurers manage the investigation and repair.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 2870 governs residential slabs and footings, including site classification and damage categories; AS 2159 covers piling; the National Construction Code calls these up. In New South Wales, Subsidence Advisory NSW manages mine subsidence districts and compensation. Restumping and underpinning need building approval.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document A governs structure; BS 8004 and BS EN 1997 cover foundations; NHBC Standards Chapter 4.2 sets building near trees; the Coal Authority provides mining reports. Subsidence is usually handled through buildings insurance, and underpinning needs building regulations approval and often party wall notices.
- United States. The International Building and Residential Codes (Chapter 18 of the IBC) govern foundations, with special provisions for expansive soils; ASCE 7 sets seismic design; the International Existing Building Code governs repairs. Boston's Groundwater Conservation Overlay District protects timber piles from falling groundwater.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Geotechnical reports and the site or soil classification.
- Foundation drawings and design.
- Crack monitoring records and engineer's reports on movement.
- Underpinning, restumping or previous repair records, with warranties.
- Insurance claims for subsidence or heave.
- Drain CCTV surveys and repair records.
- Tree removal records and arborist reports.
- Mine subsidence or mining reports where relevant.

pages.title: Gas Services
pages.question: How do building gas services fail, and when do they become a safety or decommissioning question?
pages.answer: Gas services fail by leaks, corrosion and alteration. Joints and regulators leak; buried and damp steel corrodes; pipes in car parks are struck; appliances removed without capping leave live open ends; emergency shut-offs seize or lose their interfaces. Any smell of gas is a leak until proven otherwise. Gas restrictions and electrification mean many installations now face decommissioning within the building's life, which changes repair decisions.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about gas services; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Supply pipework, metering

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Gas services bring natural gas or LPG from the network or storage to appliances: the meter and regulator set, consumer piping through the building, isolation valves, emergency shut-off valves, and connections to boilers, water heaters, cookers, kitchens and process equipment. LPG installations add cylinders or bulk tanks with their own separation and safety rules. Appliances, flues and combustion air are covered on their own pages.

| Material | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black or galvanised steel | Older commercial and residential piping, risers | Corrosion, especially where buried or in damp areas; thread leaks |
| Copper | Residential and light commercial, especially Australia and Britain | Mechanical damage; leaks at joints |
| Polyethylene | Buried service and site mains | Third-party damage; must be protected where it emerges |
| Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) | US houses and light commercial | Lightning can perforate it unless bonded |
| Multilayer composite | Newer installations | Correct fittings and tools essential |

Gas policy is changing what these systems are worth. Victoria bars gas connections to new homes needing planning permits from 2024, the ACT bars new gas network connections, Britain is moving buildings off fossil-fuel heating, and New York City requires new buildings to be all-electric. Existing gas services may face decommissioning within the life of the building, which changes whether to repair or retire them.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel piping above ground | 40 to 60 years | Damp; coating |
| Buried steel | 20 to 40 years | Soil corrosivity; cathodic protection |
| Copper piping | 50 years and more | Damage |
| Polyethylene | 50 years and more | Third-party damage |
| Regulators | 15 to 25 years | Network conditions; debris |
| Emergency shut-off valves | 15 to 25 years | Testing |
| LPG tanks | 20 to 30 years with periodic inspection | Corrosion; certification |

What shortens life:

- Damp and buried environments without protective coatings or cathodic protection.
- Mechanical damage in car parks, loading docks and plant rooms.
- Unauthorised alterations by unlicensed people.
- Lightning on unbonded CSST.

Gas piping rarely wears out above ground in dry conditions; its life is set by corrosion where it is buried or damp, by damage, and increasingly by whether the building will keep using gas at all.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Leaks

Leaks occur at threaded joints, unions, valves and where pipes have been damaged or corroded. Small leaks waste gas and can be found by smell or tightness testing; larger leaks in confined spaces create explosion risk. Gas detectors in plant rooms and kitchens give warning only if they work.

### Corrosion

Buried steel without coating or cathodic protection corrodes, particularly in wet or aggressive soils; above-ground steel corrodes where it passes through walls and floors, where condensation sits, or in coastal air.

### Mechanical damage

Gas pipes in car parks and loading docks are struck by vehicles; pipes in plant rooms are used as supports or damaged during works. Unprotected meters and regulators at ground level are vulnerable.

### Unauthorised alterations and redundant pipework

Pipes extended to new appliances by unlicensed people, redundant pipes left live, or open ends left uncapped when appliances were removed create direct leak paths.

### Emergency shut-off failures

Kitchens and plant rooms need accessible manual isolation and often automatic shut-off on fire alarm or loss of ventilation. Valves that are seized, inaccessible or disconnected from their controls do not stop gas in an emergency.

### CSST and lightning

In the United States, corrugated stainless steel tubing can be perforated by nearby lightning strikes, causing fires, unless it is bonded as its manufacturers and codes require.

### LPG storage

LPG cylinders and tanks must be separated from openings, drains, ignition sources and boundaries; LPG is heavier than air and collects in low places. Encroachment by later buildings, fences and drains often breaks separation distances.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Smell of gas around meters, regulators, plant rooms and appliances.
- Corrosion on steel pipe, especially at penetrations and near the ground.
- Pipes in vehicle areas without impact protection.
- Capped and uncapped open ends; redundant pipework.
- Emergency shut-off valves: location, labelling, accessibility.
- Gas detectors in plant rooms and kitchens, and their test labels.
- LPG cylinders and tanks: separation, signage, condition.

### In the records

- Gas compliance certificates for installations and alterations.
- Gas safety records for rented homes.
- Tightness test results.
- Gas consumption data.
- Network or supplier notices.

- Appliances with yellow or sooty flames, scorching around burners, or condensation and staining near flues, which point to combustion problems rather than piping, but share the same inspection.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas smell near the meter | Leaking regulator or meter connection | Leak detection |
| Gas consumption with appliances off | Leak in consumer piping | Tightness test |
| Rust and pitting at wall penetrations | Corrosion where moisture is trapped | Inspection |
| Kitchen gas not cutting off on alarm test | Shut-off valve or interface fault | Function test |
| Uncapped pipe ends | Appliances removed without capping | Inspection |

> Any smell of gas is treated as a leak until proven otherwise: isolate the supply, ventilate, avoid ignition sources and call the gas network or a licensed gas fitter.

Distinguish a supply problem from an installation problem: low pressure across all appliances points to the regulator or network; a problem at one appliance points to its branch, valve or the appliance itself.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leak; uncapped live pipe; failed emergency shut-off; LPG separation breached | safety | Isolate and rectify now |
| Supply disconnected by the network for safety | failure | Repair and recommission now |
| Landlord gas safety checks or periodic inspections due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Corrosion; unprotected pipes; redundant pipework | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Piping at end of life; gas phase-out planned | lifecycle | Replace or decommission |
| Installation never tested; alterations unrecorded | check | Tightness test and inspection |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed gas fitter or gas engineer; for large and commercial installations, a gas engineer with the relevant competence.

- Tightness test of the installation, and pressure tests after alterations.
- Visual inspection of meters, regulators, piping, supports, penetrations, isolation and shut-off valves.
- Function test of emergency shut-off valves and their interfaces with fire alarms and ventilation.
- Gas detector test in plant rooms and kitchens.
- Bonding check of CSST in the United States and of metallic gas piping generally.
- LPG separation review.
- Consumption review and decommissioning options.

The report should state safety defects, the tightness test result, condition of piping and valves, compliance, and whether to repair, replace or decommission.

- Ventilation check of plant rooms, kitchens and meter enclosures, since gas safety depends on combustion air and on dispersing small leaks.
- Records reconciliation: compare compliance certificates with the appliances and pipework actually present to find unrecorded alterations.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Leak repairs and recommissioning by licensed gas fitters.
- Pipe replacement of corroded sections, with coatings or replacement materials suited to the environment.
- Impact protection of pipes, meters and regulators in vehicle areas.
- Capping and removal of redundant pipework.
- Emergency shut-off upgrades with interfaces to fire alarms and kitchen ventilation.
- Gas detection in plant rooms and commercial kitchens.
- CSST bonding.
- Decommissioning with electrification, including safe disconnection and removal of meters by the network.

- Meter and regulator relocation out of enclosed spaces, car parks or vehicle paths, arranged with the network operator.
- Labelling of isolation valves and pipework so emergency services and maintenance staff can find and shut off gas quickly.
- Ventilation upgrades to plant rooms and kitchens where combustion air or leak dispersal is inadequate.
- Network coordination: when decommissioning, have the network remove the meter and disconnect the service so no live gas remains at the property boundary.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections and gas safety checks recur. Repairs are itemised. Pipe replacement is by length with access. Shut-off and detection systems are lump sums per area. Decommissioning is a lump sum, usually part of an electrification project that also carries appliance replacement and electrical upgrades.

Safety rectification and inspections are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; decommissioning sits with electrification.

Work on gas services must be done by licensed or registered gas fitters and certified, so even small items carry call-out, testing and certification costs. Network charges apply to meter relocation and disconnection.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 5601.1 governs gas installations and AS/NZS 1596 LPG storage; gas fitters are licensed and issue compliance certificates; state gas safety regulators oversee installations; Victoria and the ACT restrict new gas connections.
- United Kingdom. The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require Gas Safe registered engineers, annual landlord gas safety checks in rented homes, and maintenance; IGEM standards cover non-domestic installations.
- United States. NFPA 54 (the National Fuel Gas Code) and the International Fuel Gas Code govern installations, including CSST bonding; NFPA 58 covers LPG; local jurisdictions and utilities set permits and inspection; some cities require all-electric new construction.

In strata, condominium and leasehold buildings in all three jurisdictions, common gas piping is usually the owners corporation's or landlord's responsibility up to each dwelling's meter or isolation valve, with appliances and internal piping the occupant's; responsibility for decommissioning shared gas supplies needs to be settled before electrification projects start.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Gas compliance certificates for the installation and alterations.
- Landlord gas safety records for rented homes.
- Tightness test results.
- Emergency shut-off and gas detector test records.
- Gas consumption data.
- LPG installation and inspection records.
- Electrification plans affecting gas.

- Ventilation design for plant rooms and kitchens.
- Network operator correspondence about the supply and meters.

pages.title: Glazing Systems
pages.question: How do windows, curtain walls and glazed façades fail, what does each failure look like, and when is it urgent?
pages.answer: Glazing fails at seals, drainage and glass before frames. IGUs fog when edge seals fail, usually where water sits in blocked sills; leaks recur at predictable joints: sill ends, curtain wall splices, stack joints. Toughened glass can break with no impact from nickel sulphide inclusions, which at height is a safety issue. Structural silicone holds glass on and must be tested, not trusted. Frames usually outlast all of these.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about glazing systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Curtain walls, window walls, punched windows, IGUs, traditional framed windows

sources.title: Centre for Window and Cladding Technology

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Glazing systems are the framed and frameless glass in a building's envelope: windows, sliding and hinged doors, shopfronts, window walls, curtain walls, structural silicone glazing and point-fixed glass. Skylights and atrium roofs have their own page. A system is the glass, the frame, the gaskets and seals that hold the glass and keep water out, the internal drainage, the anchors to the structure, and the perimeter seal to the surrounding wall.

| System | Where it is used | How it keeps water out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Framed windows: timber, steel, aluminium, uPVC | Houses, older apartments and offices, institutions | Frame seals and drained sill; perimeter sealant and flashing to the wall |
| Window wall (slab to slab) | Apartments from the 1990s | Units span floor to floor, set on the slab edge; depends on sill drainage, end dams and the perimeter seal |
| Stick curtain wall | Offices, 1960s onward | Mullions and transoms assembled on site; pressure-equalised drainage; splice and transom joints are the weak points |
| Unitised curtain wall | Offices and towers from the 1990s | Factory-made units with interlocking stack and mullion joints; quality more consistent, joints still critical |
| Structural silicone glazing (SSG) | Offices from the 1980s | Glass bonded to the frame with silicone instead of caps; adhesion is the structural fixing |
| Point-fixed (spider) and fin glazing | Entrances, atria, retail | Bolted fittings through holes in toughened or laminated glass; weather seal is sealant between panes |
| Shopfronts | Retail at ground level | Simple frames and large panes; impact and security dominate |

Glass type matters to safety and to how glass breaks. Annealed (float) glass breaks into large sharp shards. Heat-strengthened glass is about twice as strong and breaks into larger pieces that tend to stay in the frame. Toughened (tempered) glass is four to five times as strong and breaks into small cubes; it can break spontaneously from nickel sulphide inclusions unless heat-soak tested. Laminated glass holds together when broken. Insulated glass units (IGUs) are two or three panes sealed around the edge with a dry air or gas space; the edge seal is their life.
