Double glazing became standard in British housing from the 1980s, in Australian commercial work through the 2000s, and more widely in Australian housing after the energy provisions tightened.

Era tells the story: steel windows with putty glazing in pre-war and mid-century buildings; single-glazed aluminium in Australian and American stock of the 1960s to 1990s; stick curtain walls with captured glass in offices of the 1970s and 1980s; four-sided SSG in the late 1980s and 1990s; unitised systems and IGUs from the 2000s.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aluminium framing | 40 to 60 years | Anodising or powder coat condition; coastal exposure; thermal breaks |
| Steel windows | 60 years and more with maintenance | Paint cycle; rust jacking at glass and in masonry |
| Timber windows | 30 to 60 years | Paint cycle; sill decay |
| uPVC windows | 25 to 35 years | UV, hardware |
| IGU edge seal | 20 to 30 years | Water standing in the glazing rebate; sealant quality; UV on exposed seals |
| EPDM gaskets | 20 to 30 years | UV; shrinkage at corners |
| Wet perimeter and cap seals | 10 to 20 years | Exposure; joint design |
| Structural silicone | 25 years and more | Original adhesion and cure; never assumed without testing |
| Hardware: hinges, stays, rollers, locks | 10 to 25 years | Use; coastal corrosion |

What shortens life:

- Water held in the glazing rebate because weep holes are blocked or omitted, which destroys IGU edge seals from below.
- West and north elevations in Australia (west and south in the northern hemisphere), where UV and thermal cycling age seals and gaskets fastest.
- Coastal air on aluminium finishes, steel anchors and stainless fittings.
- Missing sill flashings and end dams on window walls, sending water into the slab edge and the unit below.
- Frame deflection under wind and building movement on long spans, which works seals loose.
- Poor cleaning practice: abrasive cleaning and scrapers scratch glass and damage coatings and seals.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Water infiltration

Glazing leaks at a small number of predictable places: the perimeter seal between frame and wall, the sill where it meets the slab or opening below, end dams at sill ends, splice joints in stick curtain wall mullions, transom-to-mullion joints, stack joints in unitised systems, and glazing pockets that cannot drain. Most systems are designed to let some water past the outer seal and drain it out again; leaks occur when the drainage path is blocked, missing or overwhelmed.

### IGU edge seal failure

Moisture enters the cavity of an insulated unit through a failed edge seal. The first sign is fogging or condensation between the panes, then a white bloom or residue on the inner faces, and on low-emissivity units, a hazy or corroded coating. Thermal performance falls and the unit cannot be repaired, only replaced.

### Gasket shrinkage and seal ageing

Dry gaskets shrink back from corners, leaving gaps where water enters the glazing pocket. Wet seals harden and lose adhesion. On capped systems, the cap can loosen as pressure plates relax.

### Glass breakage

Thermal stress breaks annealed and some heat-strengthened glass when part of a pane heats faster than the rest: shading from deep frames, internal blinds close to tinted glass, and edge damage concentrate the stress. Nickel sulphide inclusions break toughened glass spontaneously, often years after installation and without any load; non-heat-soaked toughened glass at height can release a whole pane of fragments. Impact and edge damage from installation or building movement account for most other breaks.

### Structural silicone adhesion loss

On SSG, the silicone bond is what holds the glass on. Poor surface preparation, incompatible materials, inadequate bite (bond width) or cure at installation can leave bonds that pass a visual check but have little strength. Loss of adhesion lets glass move, leak and in the worst case detach.

### Anchor and bracket corrosion

Curtain wall and window wall anchors fix the system to the slab edge. Water reaching them through failed perimeter seals or slab edge joints corrodes carbon steel components, and dissimilar metal contact corrodes aluminium. They are concealed behind ceiling and floor finishes.

### Steel window corrosion

Steel windows rust where paint fails, and rust at the glazing rebate jacks the glass and cracks it. Steel frames built into masonry rust at the sill and jamb and crack the surrounding brick or stone.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Misted or hazy panes in a pattern across an elevation: IGU seal failure, often concentrated on the most exposed faces.
- Replaced panes visible as a different tint or reflection, a record of breakage or seal failure.
- Broken or taped panes; netting or protection below a curtain wall.
- Gaskets visibly shrunk at corners, caps missing or displaced, black streaking below gaskets.
- Staining or efflorescence at sills and on the slab edge below window walls.
- Rusting steel windows with cracked panes; cracked masonry at window jambs.

### Close up on site

- Blocked or absent weep holes in sills and transoms.
- Wet seals hard, cracked or peeling; gaps at gasket corners; gaps at the perimeter seal.
- On SSG, a visible change in the silicone line, staining behind glass, or glass that moves when pressed.
- Glass type markings in the corner of each pane (toughened, laminated, heat-soak); absence of markings on panes required to be safety glass.
- Hardware loose, corroded or failing; doors and sashes not closing.

### Inside the building

- Water staining, swollen floor finishes and mould at sills and at the base of window walls.
- Condensation on frames and glass on cold days, more than the glass type should allow; draughts at sashes and joints.
- Corrosion at accessible anchors in ceiling voids at the slab edge.

### In the records

- Breakage log, especially repeated spontaneous breakage of toughened glass.
- Leak logs that recur at the same floor or the same mullion line.
- Glass schedule, heat-soak certificates, SSG adhesion test records and warranties.
- Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fogging or white bloom between panes | IGU edge seal failure | Cannot be wiped from either face; units at the bottom of the elevation or with blocked weeps worst affected |
| Break in toughened glass with no impact, small fragments, a characteristic butterfly-shaped pair of fragments at the origin | Nickel sulphide inclusion | Origin inside the pane, not at an edge; glass not heat-soaked; other spontaneous breaks in the same batch |
| Single crack starting at an edge at right angles, wandering across the pane | Thermal stress in annealed or heat-strengthened glass | Edge damaged or partly shaded; blinds or film close to the glass; tinted or coated glass |
| Cracks radiating from a point | Impact | Point of contact visible; often at low level |
| Leak at the same mullion on every floor | Splice or stack joint failure in the curtain wall | Water test at the joint reproduces the leak |
| Leak at sill ends and at the slab below window walls | Missing or failed end dams and sill flashing | Water test at sill ends; water found on the slab edge on opening up |
| Leak only in heavy wind-driven rain | Overwhelmed drainage or pressure equalisation failure | Weep holes blocked or baffles missing; water rises in the sill under pressure |
| Glass loose or moving on an SSG façade | Structural silicone adhesion loss | Hand pull adhesion test fails at the substrate; bond width less than design |
| Cracked glass and rust at steel windows | Rust jacking at the glazing rebate | Rust visible at the rebate; putty or glazing compound failed |

> Spontaneous breakage of toughened glass at height is a safety matter, not a maintenance one. A building with non-heat-soaked toughened glass over public areas and a history of breakage needs an assessment of the remaining risk, not just replacement of the broken pane.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken or loose glass at height over a public or occupied area; SSG glass moving; spontaneous breakage of non-heat-soaked toughened glass above a footpath | safety | Make safe immediately: remove, protect below, restrict access; engineer and glazier within days |
| Active leaks damaging slab edges, finishes or units below; corroded anchors with displacement | failure | Repair now; locate the leak path by water testing first |
| Widespread gasket shrinkage, failed perimeter seals, IGU failure across an elevation, hardware failing | condition | Programme repair or replacement in the near term |
| Seals and IGUs at age without failure; single-glazed system below current energy expectations | lifecycle | Plan renewal or upgrade, often combined with a façade programme |
| Façade ordinance finding of unsafe or safe with repair | deadline | Timing set by the ordinance |
| SSG with no adhesion test record; toughened glass at height with no heat-soak record; recurring leaks of unknown path | check | Test before sizing works |
| Isolated misted unit; minor hardware wear | nil | Replace or adjust in routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer leads; a glazier assists with glass identification and opening of glazing pockets.

- Visual survey of every elevation, close up from building maintenance units or rope access where defects are suspected, recording broken, misted and replaced units and seal condition.
- Glass identification from markings and with a polarising filter or edge-stress viewer to confirm toughened glass; heat-soak status from records.
- Field water testing to locate leak paths: a nozzle test under AAMA 501.2 or a chamber test under ASTM E1105 in the United States, and test methods under AS/NZS 4284 practice in Australia, done before any remedial design.
- Adhesion testing of sealants and structural silicone by the hand pull method in ASTM C1521, with bond width and depth measured.
- Opening up of glazing pockets, sill drainage and a sample of slab-edge anchors behind ceilings and floor finishes.
- Thermography to show air leakage, failed IGUs and thermal bridging at frames.

The report should identify the system and glass types, leak paths found by testing, IGU and seal condition by elevation, SSG adhesion results, anchor condition, and any glass that must be made safe.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Drainage restoration: clear weeps, reinstate baffles and end dams, which often stops leaks without resealing.
- Reseal and regasket: replace perimeter seals, cap seals and gaskets; on stick curtain walls a wet-sealed overlay of joints can extend life.
- IGU replacement unit by unit, or reglazing of whole elevations where failure is widespread.
- SSG remediation: supplementary mechanical retention (toggles or caps) where adhesion is doubtful, or full reglazing.
- Toughened glass risk: replace with heat-soaked or laminated glass where breakage history or location warrants; interim protection below.
- Anchor repair: replace or supplement corroded anchors, which requires access through finishes.
- Replacement or overclad: full replacement of the system, or a new system over the old on curtain walls, when frames, seals and glass are all at end of life or an energy upgrade is wanted.
- Steel windows: strip, treat and repaint, reglaze with matching sections, or install secondary glazing on heritage frames.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with rates per water test and adhesion test. Resealing and regasketing are measured by linear metre; IGU replacement per unit; reglazing and replacement by façade area. Access by building maintenance unit, rope access or swing stage, and out-of-hours work in occupied buildings, are often the largest components.

Two-part lines are normal: testing first, then works sized from the results. Reseal and regasket are repairs and maintenance; IGU and system replacement are lifecycle; safety glazing upgrades and ordinance findings are code compliance; make-safe is immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 1288 for glass selection and installation and AS 2047 for windows and external glazed doors; insulated glass units are made to AS/NZS 4666, and Section J sets energy performance for glazing. On strata buildings, windows are commonly lot property and the façade common property, which complicates whole-building replacement.
- United Kingdom. Approved Documents K (safety glazing and protection from impact), L (energy), B (fire) and Q (security in dwellings) apply; glazing follows the BS 6262 series, curtain walling BS EN 13830, toughened glass BS EN 12150, heat-soaked toughened glass BS EN 14179 and insulating glass units BS EN 1279. The Centre for Window and Cladding Technology publishes the working standards for curtain walling.
- United States. International Building Code Chapter 24 governs glass and glazing; ASTM E1300 sets load resistance, ASTM C1048 heat-treated glass, ASTM E2190 insulating glass units and ASTM C1401 structural sealant glazing; safety glazing follows 16 CFR 1201. Façade ordinances include windows and curtain walls in the periodic examination; New York's Cycle 10 runs from February 2025 to February 2029.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Shop drawings and the glass schedule, with glass types by location.
- Heat-soak certificates for toughened glass, and SSG adhesion test and compatibility records.
- Breakage log and leak log by location.
- Previous water testing, façade inspection reports and ordinance filings.
- Warranties for IGUs, sealants and systems, with dates.
- Window maintenance and hardware service records.
- Façade access strategy and the certification of the equipment that serves it.

pages.title: Hazardous Materials
pages.question: Which hazardous materials should be presumed in a building, and when do they become a safety or capital issue?
pages.answer: Hazardous materials are mostly safe while sound and undisturbed; the risk is works and deterioration. Asbestos is presumed in buildings of the relevant era until a register says otherwise, and a register that did not inspect an area clears nothing there. Weathered asbestos cement, damaged friable lagging, flaking lead paint and leaking PCB capacitors are safety findings. Removal is usually costed with the works that will disturb the material.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hazardous materials; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Management/removal of asbestos, lead paint, synthetic mineral fibres

sources.title: Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials are building materials and components that can harm people when they deteriorate or are disturbed: asbestos, lead paint, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), synthetic mineral fibres, mercury in lamps and controls, ozone-depleting substances in plant, and ground hazards such as radon and contaminated land. Most are not a hazard while sound and undisturbed. They become a capital issue when they deteriorate, when works disturb them, and when the building is refurbished or demolished.

| Material | Typical era and use | Hazard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos (cement sheet, vinyl tiles, insulation, lagging, sprayed coatings, gaskets, textured coatings) | Buildings before about 1990 in Australia and Britain (banned 2003 and 1999); US legacy materials of similar eras | Fibres cause mesothelioma, lung cancer and asbestosis when disturbed |
| Friable asbestos (sprayed insulation, lagging, loose fill) | Commercial buildings, plant rooms, some houses | Releases fibres readily; highest risk |
| Lead paint | Buildings painted before about 1970 (Australia), the 1960s (Britain), 1978 (US housing) | Lead poisoning from dust and chips, especially children |
| PCBs | Fluorescent light capacitors, transformers, sealants, 1950s to 1980 | Toxic and persistent; contaminate surroundings |
| Synthetic mineral fibres | Insulation, ceiling tiles, from mid-century | Skin and respiratory irritation; older types more hazardous |
| Mercury | Fluorescent lamps, thermostats, switches | Toxic if broken or disposed of incorrectly |
| Ozone-depleting substances | Halon fire systems, older refrigerants | Regulated; require recovery |
| Radon and ground gases | Buildings on certain geologies and contaminated land | Lung cancer; explosion risk from methane |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Material | What happens over time | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bonded asbestos cement | Weathers, erodes and cracks; becomes friable at the surface | Exposure; lichen; impact |
| Friable asbestos | Deteriorates and releases fibres | Vibration; water; disturbance |
| Vinyl tiles and adhesives | Stable unless sanded or removed | Works |
| Lead paint | Chalks, flakes and peels | Weather; friction at windows and doors |
| PCB capacitors | Leak as they age | Age; heat |
| Asbestos registers | Become outdated after works and with time | Review cycles |

What drives risk:

- Works: refurbishment, services installation, drilling and demolition disturbing materials that were stable.
- Deterioration from weather, water and vibration.
- Out-of-date registers that do not reflect what is there.
- Contractors who are not told what they may disturb.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Disturbance during works

Most exposure happens when trades drill, cut, sand or remove materials without knowing they contain asbestos or lead: electricians in ceiling voids, plumbers in risers, painters preparing old surfaces, flooring contractors lifting tiles. The register exists to prevent this, and the refurbishment survey before works is the critical step.

### Deterioration in place

Weathered asbestos cement roofs and walls shed fibre and cannot be safely cleaned or coated; friable lagging and sprayed insulation deteriorate with vibration and water; lead paint flakes and chalks around windows and doors, contaminating soil and interiors.

### Register failures

Registers that are out of date, incomplete, marked "not accessed" for large areas, or not shown to contractors give false assurance. A register that says "no asbestos detected" in areas that were never inspected is a common trap.

### PCB leaks

Capacitors in old light fittings and transformers leak oily PCB fluid as they age, contaminating fittings, ceilings and the surrounding fabric.

### Cost on refurbishment and demolition

Hazardous materials turn refurbishments and demolitions into licensed removal projects, often with significant cost and programme effects, especially where friable asbestos is extensive.

### Ground hazards

Radon enters buildings through floors in affected areas; contaminated land and landfill gas affect basements and ground floors.

### Fire and storm damage

Fire, storms and impact can break asbestos materials and spread debris across a site and neighbouring land, turning a managed material into an emergency clean-up.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Grey cement sheeting on roofs, eaves, walls and fences in buildings of the relevant era.
- Lagged pipework and boilers in plant rooms; sprayed coatings on steel and soffits.
- Vinyl floor tiles of older sizes and patterns; textured ceiling coatings.
- Asbestos labels or warning stickers; areas marked "not accessed" in registers.
- Flaking paint on older window frames, doors and railings.
- Old fluorescent fittings with capacitors; oily residue.

### In the records

- Asbestos register and management plan with dates.
- Refurbishment and demolition surveys.
- Removal and clearance certificates.
- Lead and PCB test results.
- Radon results in affected areas.

- Debris, dust or broken fragments of suspect materials on floors, in ceiling voids or around plant, a sign that materials have already been disturbed.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cement sheet roof weathered with exposed fibres | Asbestos cement weathering | Sampling; register |
| Damaged lagging in a plant room | Friable asbestos deteriorating | Sampling; air monitoring |
| Register shows large areas not accessed | Incomplete survey | Register review |
| Flaking paint on a pre-1970 building | Possible lead paint | Paint testing |
| Oily residue in old light fittings | Leaking PCB capacitors | Sampling |

> Never assume a material is free of asbestos because it is not on the register. If the register did not inspect an area, treat suspect materials there as asbestos until sampled.

Treat the register as a starting point, not a conclusion: its age, scope and any areas not accessed decide how much reliance it deserves.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Damaged friable asbestos in accessible areas; deteriorating lead paint where children are present; leaking PCBs | safety | Isolate and remediate now |
| Asbestos released by works | failure | Stop work, decontaminate and clear now |
| Register review or management plan update due; no register in a workplace of the relevant era | deadline | At the required interval |
| Bonded asbestos weathering; lead paint flaking | condition | Manage or remove in the near term |
| Removal planned with refurbishment or replacement | lifecycle | Plan with the works |
| Areas not accessed; refurbishment planned | check | Survey before works |
| Sound and managed materials | nil | Manage in place |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed or accredited asbestos assessor or surveyor; lead and PCB specialists as needed.

- Management survey to identify accessible materials for the register.
- Refurbishment and demolition survey, intrusive, before any works that will disturb the fabric.
- Sampling and laboratory analysis of suspect materials.
- Condition assessment and risk scoring of each material.
- Lead paint testing by laboratory or XRF.
- PCB identification of capacitors and sealants.
- Air monitoring where release is suspected.
- Radon testing in affected areas.

The report should give a register with locations, materials, condition and risk, actions, and the removal scope linked to planned works.

Surveys must be matched to purpose: a management survey supports day-to-day safety but is not enough for refurbishment or demolition, which needs intrusive sampling of the areas to be disturbed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Manage in place: label, protect from damage and inspect sound materials on a schedule, recording condition in the register.
- Encapsulation of sound bonded materials with sealants or enclosures where removal is not yet needed.
- Licensed removal with enclosures, air monitoring, decontamination, disposal and clearance certificates.
- Lead paint: stabilise or remove under lead-safe work practices, with clean-up and clearance testing.
- PCB removal of capacitors, transformers and sealants as hazardous waste, with cleaning of contaminated fabric.
- Register updates after every removal or change, with the management plan reviewed.
- Contractor controls: permits requiring register checks before any work that drills, cuts or removes materials.
- Radon mitigation by sealing and sub-floor depressurisation where tests exceed action levels.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys and register reviews recur. Removal is priced per area or per item, with containment, air monitoring, disposal and clearance. Friable removal costs much more than bonded. Removal is usually carried in the works line that disturbs it.

Register, management and safety items are code compliance; removal with refurbishment is lifecycle; emergency remediation is immediate.

Removal discovered mid-project costs far more than removal planned from a refurbishment survey, through delays, re-sequencing and decontamination.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The model work health and safety regulations require an asbestos register and management plan for workplaces built before the end of 2003, reviewed at least every five years and after works; licensed removal; the Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency coordinates national strategy; AS 4361.2 covers lead paint.
- United Kingdom. The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 impose a duty to manage asbestos in non-domestic premises; HSG264 sets survey practice; the Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002 apply.
- United States. OSHA regulates asbestos exposure; EPA rules govern renovation and demolition notification and, since 2024, ban ongoing uses of chrysotile asbestos; the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule governs lead in pre-1978 housing.

Disclosure obligations at sale and lease vary but commonly include known asbestos in all three countries.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Asbestos register and management plan.
- Refurbishment and demolition surveys.
- Removal and clearance certificates.
- Lead paint and PCB testing.
- Radon results.
- Contractor permit procedures.

- Air monitoring results after removals.
- Records of incidents involving disturbed materials.
- Lead paint disclosure documents for residential property.
- Hazardous waste disposal records.

pages.title: Heat Rejection Plant
pages.question: How do cooling towers, dry coolers and condensers fail, and what makes a cooling tower a public health item?
pages.answer: Cooling towers are first a public health item: Legionella grows in warm, dirty, stagnant water and towers spread it as aerosols, so registration, risk management, sampling and prescribed responses are law in all three jurisdictions. Mechanically, towers scale, corrode and foul; fill collapses under deposits; fans and gearboxes wear. Dry coolers and air-cooled condensers lose capacity to coil corrosion near the coast and to hot air recirculating behind screens and walls.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about heat rejection plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cooling towers, dry coolers, condensers

sources.title: Legionnaires' disease: the control of legionella bacteria in water systems (L8)
Legionella control in cooling water systems
Cooling towers
sources.publisher: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Heat rejection plant takes heat out of a building's cooling system and releases it to the outside air. Water-cooled chillers reject heat through cooling towers or dry coolers; air-cooled chillers and refrigeration plant reject it through condenser coils on the machine itself. The choice of system decides the risks: cooling towers are efficient but carry a Legionella risk that is regulated in all three jurisdictions; dry and air-cooled systems avoid that risk but are larger, noisier and lose capacity on hot days.

| Type | How it works | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open-circuit cooling tower | Condenser water sprayed over fill; part evaporates, cooling the rest | Legionella; scale, corrosion and biofouling; structural corrosion |
| Closed-circuit cooler (fluid cooler) | Condenser water stays in a coil; a separate spray circuit evaporates over it | Legionella in the spray circuit; coil corrosion |
| Evaporative condenser | Refrigerant condenses in a coil wetted by spray | Legionella; coil corrosion; refrigerant leaks |
| Dry cooler | Water or glycol through finned coils, fans blowing air across | Coil corrosion; reduced capacity in heat |
| Adiabatic cooler | Dry cooler with pre-cooling pads or sprays used on hot days | Water quality in pads and sprays; pad decay |
| Air-cooled condenser (on chillers and split plant) | Refrigerant condenses in finned coils | Coil corrosion; hot air recirculation |

Towers sit on roofs or at ground level and are built in galvanised steel, stainless steel, fibreglass or concrete. Inside are the fill (the surface over which water spreads), drift eliminators (which catch water droplets before they leave), the basin, distribution system, fans with motors and gearboxes or belts, and the water treatment and bleed equipment.

Every cooling tower has a water treatment system that is as important as the tower: chemical dosing (corrosion and scale inhibitors, biocides), controlled bleed-off to limit how far dissolved solids concentrate, often side-stream filtration, and monitoring. Treatment is usually provided by a specialist contractor under a service agreement, and the regulated records are theirs to keep but the owner's to hold.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised steel cooling tower | 15 to 20 years | Water treatment; white rust; basin corrosion |
| Stainless or fibreglass cooling tower | 20 to 30 years | UV on fibreglass; structural supports |
| Concrete tower | 30 to 40 years | Concrete deterioration |
| Fill | 10 to 15 years | Fouling; collapse under weight of deposits |
| Drift eliminators | 10 to 15 years | UV; damage; fouling |
| Fans, motors, gearboxes | 15 to 20 years | Vibration; lubrication |
| Dry coolers | 20 to 25 years | Coil corrosion; fan motors |
| Air-cooled condenser coils | 15 to 20 years; 5 to 10 unprotected near the coast | Salt air; coating |

What shortens life:

- Water treatment failures: scale, corrosion and biofouling all follow.
- Coastal and industrial air on coils and steel.
- Debris and nearby sources: leaves, dust from construction, exhausts drawn into towers.
- Poor siting: towers and condensers too close to walls or screens, so hot air recirculates.
- Intermittent operation with stagnant water.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Legionella growth

Legionella bacteria multiply in warm water with sediment, biofilm and stagnation, and cooling towers produce aerosols that can carry them to people nearby. Outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease have been traced to towers in all three countries, which is why towers are registered, risk-managed and tested by law. Risk rises with poor water treatment, dead legs and stagnant pipework, damaged drift eliminators, intermittent operation, and dirty fill and basins.

### Scale

As water evaporates, dissolved minerals concentrate. Without enough bleed-off and treatment, they deposit as scale on fill and in condenser tubes, cutting heat transfer and raising chiller energy use.

### Corrosion

Galvanised towers develop white rust when the zinc is attacked by poorly balanced water, especially in the first months; steel basins and supports then corrode. Fibreglass degrades under UV. Coils on dry coolers and condensers corrode, especially aluminium fins in salt air.

### Biofouling and fill collapse

Biofilm and sediment build up on fill, adding weight until the fill sags and collapses, and providing habitat for Legionella.

### Mechanical failures

Fan blades crack, gearboxes leak and wear, belts slip, motors fail, and vibration switches fail to act. A fan or gearbox failure takes a cell out of service.

### Hot air recirculation

Air-cooled condensers and dry coolers placed too close together, against walls or behind solid plant screens, draw in their own hot discharge air. Capacity falls on hot days and head pressures rise.

### Stagnation and dead legs

Towers that run intermittently, standby cells left full, and pipework branches that no longer carry flow hold warm stagnant water where biofilm and Legionella grow. Plant changes over the years often leave dead legs behind.

### Drift and siting

Drift eliminators catch water droplets before they leave the tower. Damaged, displaced or poorly fitted eliminators release more aerosol, and towers placed near air intakes, openable windows, roof terraces or public areas expose people to it.

### Water consumption

Towers consume water through evaporation, drift and bleed. Uncontrolled bleed, overflowing basins and leaks waste water and dilute treatment chemicals.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From aerial imagery and the roof

- Tower type and material; visible corrosion and staining.
- Drift and staining on surrounding roof and plant.
- Proximity of towers to air intakes, windows and occupied areas.
- Condensers boxed in by walls or screens.

### On site

- Scale and biofilm on fill and basin; sludge in basins.
- Damaged or missing drift eliminators.
- Corrosion of basin, casing and supports; white rust.
- Fan and gearbox noise, oil leaks, vibration.
- Water treatment dosing equipment working, chemicals in date.
- Coil fins corroded, flattened or blocked.

### In the records

- Tower registration and risk management plan.
- Legionella and bacterial count sampling results.
- Water treatment reports.
- Independent audit reports where required.
- Maintenance and cleaning records.

- Basin overflowing or make-up valve running constantly.
- Algae on exposed wet surfaces in sunlight.
- Visible plume or drift wetting nearby surfaces.
- Standby cells left full and stagnant; isolated pipework branches.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rising condenser approach on the chillers | Scaled or fouled tower and tubes, or tower capacity lost | Tower inspection; water treatment records |
| White powder on galvanised surfaces | White rust from unbalanced water | Water chemistry |
| Fill sagging or collapsed | Biofouling and deposits | Visual; fill weight |
| High bacterial counts | Treatment failure, dead legs, stagnation | Records; system inspection |
| Head pressure high on hot days, air-cooled plant | Hot air recirculation or fouled coils | Temperature at coil inlet higher than ambient |

> A positive Legionella result above regulatory action levels requires the response the regulation prescribes, typically immediate disinfection, re-testing and notification. It is not a maintenance item.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella above the action levels in the regulation; tower near air intakes or public areas with damaged drift eliminators | safety | Disinfect and follow the prescribed response now |
| Tower not registered, no risk management plan, sampling or audit overdue | deadline | Comply immediately |
| Tower out of service; fill collapsed; fan failure | failure | Repair now |
| Corrosion, scale, worn mechanicals | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Tower at end of life | lifecycle | Replace; consider dry or adiabatic alternatives |
| Condenser capacity in doubt on hot days | check | Assess |
| Normal wear | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer and the water treatment contractor; an independent auditor where regulation requires one.

- Records review: registration, risk management plan, sampling results and trends, treatment logs, cleaning and disinfection records, audit reports.
- Tower inspection with the tower drained and isolated: fill, eliminators, distribution, basin, casing, structure, access.
- Water sampling for Legionella (laboratory culture to AS/NZS 3896 in Australia, or an equivalent accredited method) and heterotrophic plate count, with chemistry for conductivity, pH, inhibitor and biocide levels.
- System survey for dead legs, stagnant branches and standby cells.
- Siting review: distance to air intakes, windows and occupied areas; recirculation around condensers.
- Mechanical checks: fan, gearbox and motor vibration, oil condition, belt tension.
- Capacity check: the tower's ability to deliver design condenser water temperature on a hot day, against the chillers' needs; a performance test to the Cooling Technology Institute method where capacity is in doubt.
- Structural check of supports and the roof under the tower.

The report should state compliance status, the Legionella risk position, tower condition and remaining life, capacity, siting risks, and whether to refurbish, replace like for like, or move to a dry or adiabatic system.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Compliance: register, write or update the risk management plan, restore sampling and audit schedules, keep records.
- Clean and disinfect on the regulated schedule and after positive results.
- Water treatment: automatic dosing and conductivity-controlled bleed, side-stream filtration, and monitoring.
- Remove dead legs and drain standby cells or circulate them.
- Replace fill and drift eliminators; high-efficiency eliminators where the tower is near people.
- Mechanical repairs: fans, gearboxes, motors, variable speed drives.
- Basin and casing repair: coatings, stainless basins, structural repairs.
- Relocation or screening away from intakes and occupied areas.
- Replacement with a new tower in stainless or fibreglass, or with dry or adiabatic coolers.

| Option | Advantages | Trade-offs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New cooling tower | Most efficient chiller operation; compact | Legionella regime continues; water use |
| Dry cooler | No Legionella regime; no water use | Larger, heavier, noisier; chiller efficiency lower on hot days |
| Adiabatic cooler | Near tower efficiency on hot days with much less water; lower Legionella risk | Pads and sprays need water management; still regulated in some jurisdictions |
| Air-cooled chillers replacing water-cooled plant | Removes the tower and condenser water system | Lower efficiency; space and noise on the roof |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Water treatment, sampling and audits are recurring contracts and compliance costs. Fill and eliminator replacement are lump sums per cell. Mechanical repairs are itemised. Tower replacement is a lump-sum project including crane lift, structural works, pipework and electrical connection, controls, water treatment equipment and commissioning, with temporary heat rejection where the building cannot be without cooling.

Moving to dry or adiabatic cooling can change chiller selection and roof structure, and is usually part of a wider plant strategy rather than a like-for-like line.

Legionella compliance is code compliance and recurs; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; a positive result is immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. States regulate cooling towers under public health legislation, typically requiring registration, a risk management plan, independent audit and routine Legionella and heterotrophic plate count sampling with prescribed responses (for example the Public Health and Wellbeing Regulations 2019 in Victoria and the Public Health Regulation 2022 in New South Wales). AS/NZS 3666 sets design, maintenance and performance-based maintenance of cooling water systems.
- United Kingdom. The Notification of Cooling Towers and Evaporative Condensers Regulations 1992 require towers to be notified to the local authority; the HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 and HSG274 Part 1 set the control regime.
- United States. ASHRAE 188 sets the risk management standard for building water systems; New York City's Local Law 77 requires cooling tower registration, inspection and Legionella sampling; the Cooling Technology Institute publishes standards for tower performance and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Tower registration and the current risk management plan.
- Legionella and heterotrophic plate count results for at least two years, with the responses taken to any positive results.
- Water treatment service reports and chemical dosing records.
- Cleaning and disinfection records.
- Independent audit reports where required.
- Maintenance records for fans, gearboxes and motors.
- Installation date and materials of the tower.
- Drawings showing tower location relative to air intakes and occupied areas.

pages.title: Hot & Warm Water Plant
pages.question: How do hot water systems fail, and how do you balance Legionella risk against scalding?
pages.answer: Hot water plant sits between two hazards: water must be stored at 60 °C and kept hot through the loop to control Legionella, yet delivered cool enough not to scald. Failures sit at both ends: cool storage, failed circulation pumps, dead legs and little-used outlets grow Legionella; failed or bypassed TMVs scald vulnerable people. Tanks corrode when anodes are spent; relief valves seize. Electrification is reshaping replacement choices.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hot & warm water plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Water heaters (gas/electric, storage/instantaneous), TMVs

sources.title: Legionnaires' disease: technical guidance HSG274 Part 2

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Hot and warm water plant heats water for washing, bathing and kitchens: storage water heaters (gas, electric, heat pump, solar), continuous-flow (instantaneous) heaters, central plant with calorifiers or plate heat exchangers and a heated flow-and-return loop, and the thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) and tempering valves that limit outlet temperatures to prevent scalding. It sits between two hazards that pull in opposite directions: water must be kept hot enough to control Legionella, and delivered cool enough not to scald.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas storage water heater | Houses, small commercial | Anode protection, burner and flue; 8 to 12 year life |
| Electric storage water heater | Houses and apartments | Element and thermostat; anode; off-peak operation |
| Heat pump water heater | Houses and apartments, electrification retrofits | Lower storage temperatures; boost cycles for Legionella control |
| Solar water heater | Houses in sunny climates | Collectors on roof; frost and overheating protection; booster |
| Continuous-flow (instantaneous) gas or electric | Houses, apartments, small commercial | No storage; flow and pressure dependent |
| Central plant with flow and return loop | Apartments, hotels, hospitals, offices | Calorifiers or heat exchangers, circulating pumps, balancing valves |
| Thermostatic mixing valves | Healthcare, aged care, childcare, schools, accessible bathrooms | Blend hot and cold to a safe temperature at the outlet; need annual testing |

Required temperatures differ by jurisdiction but follow the same logic: store at 60 °C or more; keep circulating water hot throughout the loop; deliver to outlets at a temperature that will not scald, lower still in buildings for children, the elderly and people with disabilities. Fuel policy is changing hot water as it is changing heating: gas restrictions and electrification push heat pump and electric systems.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Storage water heaters | 8 to 15 years | Anode replacement; water hardness; temperature |
| Heat pump water heaters | 10 to 15 years | Compressor; coastal exposure |
| Solar collectors | 15 to 25 years | Frost; overheating; seals |
| Continuous-flow heaters | 10 to 15 years | Scale; flow |
| Calorifiers | 20 to 25 years | Water quality; inspection |
| Circulating pumps | 10 to 15 years | Run hours; scale |
| Thermostatic mixing valves | 10 to 15 years with annual service | Scale; debris; maintenance |
| Copper hot water pipework | 40 to 60 years | Water chemistry; velocity |

What shortens life:

- Hard water, which scales heat exchangers, elements and valves and reduces efficiency.
- Neglected anodes: once the sacrificial anode is consumed, the tank corrodes from inside and fails.
- High velocity in hot water pipes, which erodes copper at bends.
- Poor maintenance of TMVs, which drift and fail.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Legionella growth

Legionella grows between about 20 and 45 °C. Storage that runs cool to save energy, stratified tanks with cold water at the base, loops that fall below temperature at their far ends, dead legs, and little-used outlets all create growth sites. Showers then aerosolise the bacteria. Healthcare and aged care buildings, with vulnerable occupants, carry the highest risk.

### Scalding

Water at storage temperatures causes serious burns within seconds, especially to children, the elderly and people with reduced sensation. TMVs that fail, drift or are removed, and tempering valves missing from outlets that need them, expose occupants to scalding.

### Tank corrosion and leaks

Storage tanks are protected by sacrificial anodes. When anodes are spent, tanks rust through and leak, often without warning, causing water damage in roof spaces, cupboards and ceilings.

### Relief valve failure

Temperature and pressure relief valves protect tanks from explosion. Valves that are never operated seize, and discharge pipes that are blocked, run to unsafe places or are missing put people and buildings at risk.

### Circulation and balancing faults

Central systems depend on circulating pumps and balancing valves to keep the whole loop hot. Failed pumps, seized or unbalanced valves, and branches added in fit-outs leave parts of the system cool, wasting water while people run taps and growing Legionella.

### TMV failure

TMVs scale and foul and their thermostatic elements drift. They can fail hot (scald risk) or cold. They must be tested and serviced, typically annually, and after any work on the system.

### Gas heater combustion faults

Gas water heaters in poorly ventilated cupboards or with blocked flues can produce carbon monoxide; flues disconnected in renovations are a recurring finding.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Water heater nameplates, ages and anode service tags.
- Rust and water staining at the base of tanks; damp in cupboards and ceilings below roof-space heaters.
- Relief valve drain lines: present, discharging, terminating safely.
- Thermometers at calorifier outlets and returns; temperature at the far end of the loop.
- TMV locations, service tags and dates.
- Long waits for hot water at outlets; very hot water at sinks in sensitive areas.
- Gas heater flues and cupboard ventilation.

### In the records

- Water temperature monitoring records.
- Legionella risk assessment and test results.
- TMV service records.
- Heater replacement history.
- Scald incident reports.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return loop below 50 °C | Circulating pump failure or imbalance | Temperature mapping; pump status |
| Long waits for hot water at certain outlets | Dead legs or loop not reaching that branch | Temperature at outlet over time |
| Very hot water at basins in an aged care home | Failed or bypassed TMV | TMV test |
| Water under a storage tank | Tank corroded through or relief valve discharging | Inspection |
| Relief valve discharging continuously | Thermostat failure or high mains pressure | Temperature and pressure checks |
| Positive Legionella result | Low storage or loop temperatures, stagnation | Temperature records; outlet use patterns |

> A failed TMV in a building for vulnerable people is a scald risk, and a hot water system that cannot keep its loop above 50 °C is a Legionella risk. Both are safety findings, not maintenance items.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed TMVs in healthcare, aged care, childcare or accessible bathrooms; positive Legionella; relief valve blocked; gas heater flue spillage | safety | Isolate, disinfect or rectify now |
| Heater failed; no hot water | failure | Replace now |
| TMV servicing and Legionella testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Loop below temperature; scale; corroding tanks | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Heaters at end of life | lifecycle | Replace, considering electrification |
| No risk assessment or temperature records | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber, with a water hygiene specialist for Legionella risk.

- Legionella risk assessment of the whole system: storage, loop, dead legs, little-used outlets, vulnerable occupants.
- Temperature mapping at storage outlets, loop returns and sentinel outlets nearest and furthest from the plant, recorded over at least a day.
- TMV testing of a sample or all valves in sensitive buildings: outlet temperature, fail-safe on cold supply loss, condition of strainers and checks.
- Heater inspection: age, anode, relief valves and drains, flues, ventilation, scale.
- Water sampling for Legionella where risk or history warrants.
- Circulation check: pumps, balancing valves and their settings.
- Energy review: heat loss from loops, fuel type and electrification options.

The report should state Legionella and scald risks, temperature performance, plant condition and remaining life, and an upgrade or replacement plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Temperature control: restore storage to at least 60 °C, fix circulation, rebalance loops, add pipe insulation.
- Dead leg removal and flushing regimes for little-used outlets.
- TMV servicing annually, with replacement of failing valves and installation where codes now require them.
- Anode replacement to extend tank life; tank replacement on failure or age.
- Relief valve testing and discharge pipe correction.
- Disinfection after positive results: thermal or chemical, followed by re-testing.
- Electrification: heat pump water heaters or electric systems replacing gas, with boost cycles for Legionella control and electrical capacity checked.
- Water treatment for scale in hard water areas.

- Point-of-use heating for remote outlets that the loop cannot keep hot economically.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
TMV servicing and Legionella testing recur annually. Heaters are replaced per unit, often on a recurring allowance in residential buildings. Central plant replacement is a lump sum with temporary hot water. Loop rebalancing and dead leg removal are lump sums. Electrification adds electrical capacity, space and possibly roof or external plant locations.

Safety and testing are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; repairs and anode replacement are repairs and maintenance.

Legionella remediation after a positive result carries disinfection, re-testing and sometimes temporary closures.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3500.4 governs heated water, requiring storage at 60 °C and delivery to personal hygiene outlets at no more than 50 °C, or 45 °C in healthcare, aged care, childcare and similar buildings; TMVs are maintained to AS 4032.3; state health departments regulate Legionella in some building types; gas appliances follow AS/NZS 5601.1.
- United Kingdom. The HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 and HSG274 Part 2 require storage at 60 °C and distribution at 50 °C (55 °C in healthcare) within a minute, with monthly temperature checks; TMVs to TMV2 or TMV3 schemes in care settings; Approved Document G sets safety requirements for hot water systems.
- United States. ASHRAE 188 sets a risk management standard for Legionella in building water systems, and many healthcare facilities are required to have water management programmes; plumbing codes require mixing valves listed to ASSE standards at certain fixtures.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Legionella risk assessment and water management plan.
- Temperature monitoring records.
- Legionella test results and actions taken.
- TMV register and service records.
- Water heater register with ages and service records.
- Scald incident reports.
- Gas compliance certificates for gas heaters.

- Records of outlet flushing for little-used fixtures.
- Drawings of the hot water loop showing balancing valves.

pages.title: Hydrant & Hose Reel Systems
pages.question: How do hydrant, rising main and hose reel systems fail, and when are they unusable by fire-fighters?
pages.answer: Hydrant systems fail where fire-fighters meet them. Boosters and hydrants are hidden by planting, parking and hoardings; caps go missing and valves seize. Flow and pressure at remote outlets fall as mains pressures drop and pipes corrode, which only a flow test shows. Dry risers leak when charged. Hose reels crack and leak. A booster the brigade cannot find or connect to is a failed system however well it was built.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hydrant & hose reel systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Hydrant outlets, hose reels, pipework

sources.title: NFPA 14 Installation of Standpipe and Hose Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Hydrant systems give fire-fighters water at the building: external hydrants in the grounds, internal hydrant landing valves in stairs and on floors, rising mains (wet or dry) that carry water up tall buildings, and a booster or fire brigade inlet where fire appliances can pump into the system. Hose reels are fixed hoses for occupants to tackle small fires. In the United States the equivalent internal system is the standpipe, in Classes I to III.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| External pillar or below-ground hydrants | Sites, campuses, industrial estates | Must be accessible and visible to fire appliances |
| Internal hydrant landing valves | Fire stairs and floors of larger buildings | Valves, outlets and caps; fire-fighters bring hoses |
| Booster assembly or brigade inlet | Building frontage | Where appliances connect; must be accessible and signed |
| Dry rising main | Mid-rise buildings, especially in Britain | Empty pipe charged by fire appliances |
| Wet rising main | Tall buildings | Permanently charged, usually with pumps |
| Hose reels | Australian commercial and industrial buildings; less common elsewhere | Occupant use; hose and nozzle deteriorate |
| Standpipes (US) | US multi-storey buildings | Class I for fire service; II and III with occupant hose |

In tall buildings the system is divided into pressure zones, with pumps, intermediate tanks or pressure-reducing valves keeping outlet pressures within the range fire-fighters' hoses and nozzles can handle. Booster assemblies carry a block plan showing the system, zones and pressures for the brigade. The system must suit the local brigade's couplings and procedures, which differ between jurisdictions and sometimes between brigades.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrant valves and landing valves | 20 to 30 years | Operation; corrosion; vandalism |
| Booster assemblies | 25 to 40 years | Damage; corrosion; caps stolen |
| Galvanised pipework | 30 to 50 years | Internal corrosion; MIC |
| Dry riser inlets and valves | 20 to 30 years | Vandalism; corrosion |
| Hose reel hoses | 10 to 15 years | UV; abrasion |
| Hose reel units | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; damage |

What shortens life:

- Vandalism and theft: caps, couplings and brass fittings.
- Seldom operated valves that seize.
- Landscaping, parking and construction that obstruct access.
- Freezing of exposed wet pipework.
- Internal corrosion.

Hydrant systems are rarely used in earnest, so their condition is established only by testing; a valve that has not been operated for years is likely to stick when the brigade needs it.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Obstructed access

Hydrants and boosters must be reachable by fire appliances and visible on arrival. Planting, parking bays, bins, fences and construction hoardings block them; signage fades or is removed; booster cabinets are locked with the wrong key.

### Valve failures

Hydrant and landing valves seize, leak or are vandalised; caps and blank flanges go missing, letting debris in; dry riser inlets are damaged; non-return valves stick.

### Inadequate flow and pressure

Hydrant systems must deliver a set flow at a set pressure at the most remote outlets. Falling town main pressures, corroded or partly blocked pipes, failed pumps and closed valves leave outlets short. Only a flow test shows it.

### Dry riser failures

Dry risers leak when charged because joints, valves and drain valves have deteriorated unseen; inlets and landing valves are vandalised; air release valves stick.

### Hose reel failures

Hoses crack and leak from UV and age; nozzles go missing; reels jam; isolating valves are closed; reels are obstructed by storage.

### Backflow prevention

Backflow prevention devices protect drinking water from fire system water; they need annual testing and can restrict flow if poorly selected or failing.

### Pressure-reducing valve failures

Pressure-reducing valves at landing valves or zone boundaries in tall buildings drift, stick or are adjusted wrongly. Outlets then deliver pressure too high for fire-fighters to control a hose safely, or too low to fight a fire. Their settings are only proven by flow testing at each zone.

### Internal corrosion and blockage

Galvanised and black steel hydrant mains corrode internally; microbiologically influenced corrosion causes pinhole leaks; corrosion products and debris block valves and reduce flow at remote outlets.

### Freezing

Wet pipework in unheated car parks, external areas and roof spaces freezes and splits in cold climates; dry systems are used in these locations for that reason.

### Coverage after extensions

Building extensions, new mezzanines and subdivided tenancies put parts of the building beyond hose reach from existing outlets; the original design no longer covers the building.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Booster and hydrants visible and accessible from the street; signage; caps present.
- Landing valves in stairs: caps, wheels, leaks, signage.
- Dry riser inlets: doors, caps, damage.
- Hose reels: hose condition, nozzle, isolating valve open, obstruction.
- Corrosion and leaks on pipework.

### In the records

- Routine service records.
- Flow and pressure test results.
- Dry riser pressure test records.
- Backflow device test records.
- Block plan at the booster.

- Pressure-reducing valve settings and tags at landing valves in tall buildings.
- Booster block plan present, legible and matching the building.
- Areas of extensions without hydrant or hose reel coverage.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow test below requirement at remote outlets | Supply decline, corrosion or closed valves | Pressure readings along the system |
| Dry riser loses pressure on test | Leaking valves or joints | Pressure test and inspection |
| Booster hidden from the street | Access obstruction | Site inspection |
| Hose reel leaks when pressurised | Aged hose | Inspection |

> A booster or hydrant that fire-fighters cannot find, reach or connect to is a failed system, however well it was built.

Two patterns are often confused. Low pressure at every outlet points to the supply or pumps; low pressure only at remote outlets or one zone points to pipework, valves or a pressure-reducing valve in that part of the system.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster or hydrants inaccessible or inoperable; dry riser failing pressure test; flow well below requirement | safety | Restore now; notify the brigade |
| Routine service and flow testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Leaks; seized valves; missing caps; aged hoses | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Pipework and valves at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No flow test on record | check | Flow test |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer or the hydrant maintenance contractor, coordinated with the brigade where its equipment is used for testing.

- Access and signage inspection from the brigade's arrival point: booster and hydrant visibility, clear hardstand, signage, lighting, block plan, cabinet keys.
- Coverage check of every part of the building against hose reach from the outlets, especially after extensions and fit-outs.
- Valve inspection and operation: hydrant valves, landing valves, isolating valves (open and secured), non-return valves, caps and couplings.
- Flow and pressure test at the most hydraulically remote outlets, and at each pressure zone in tall buildings, against the design requirement; pressure-reducing valve settings confirmed under flow.
- Dry riser pressure test and inlet, valve and drain inspection.
- Hose reel test: flow, hose condition, nozzle, reel operation.
- Backflow device test.
- Pipework inspection for corrosion, leaks, supports and frost protection.

The report should state whether the system delivers required flow and pressure at every outlet and zone, whether the brigade can find and connect to it, coverage gaps, and failed components.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Clear and protect access: relocate parking, bins and planting; bollards against vehicle damage; signage and lighting; updated block plans.
- Replace valves, caps and couplings, with anti-theft and anti-vandal fittings where theft is common.
- Recalibrate or replace pressure-reducing valves and confirm by flow test.
- Restore performance: clear blockages, replace corroded pipe, add or upgrade pumps, increase supply connections.
- Dry riser repairs: inlet boxes, valves, drains, joints, air release valves.
- Extend coverage with additional outlets after extensions.
- Hose replacement and reel servicing.
- Frost protection of exposed wet pipework.
- Booster relocation where it cannot be made accessible.

- Cabinet keys standardised to brigade keys and cabinets left unlocked where permitted.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and flow testing recur; dry riser pressure tests recur annually where required. Valve, coupling and hose replacement are priced per item. Pipework replacement is by length, with access and making good. Pressure-reducing valve replacement is per valve. Additional outlets are priced per outlet with pipework. Booster relocation is a lump sum with civil works.

Testing, access and safety rectification are code compliance; pipework and valve replacement at end of life is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 2419.1 governs hydrant installations and AS 2441 hose reels; AS 1851 sets routine service and flow testing; AS 2845 covers backflow prevention; essential safety measures with annual certification.
- United Kingdom. BS 9990 covers rising mains, including six-monthly inspection and annual pressure testing of dry risers; Approved Document B sets requirements for fire-fighting access and water.
- United States. NFPA 14 governs standpipes and NFPA 25 their inspection and testing, including periodic flow tests and hydrostatic tests of dry standpipes; NFPA 24 covers private hydrants and mains.

Brigade requirements also apply in all three jurisdictions: couplings, booster locations and block plans must suit the local fire service, which may inspect and comment on hydrant arrangements during approvals and after changes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Routine service records and annual certification.
- Flow and pressure test reports for remote outlets and each pressure zone.
- Dry riser pressure test records.
- Pressure-reducing valve settings and test records.
- Backflow prevention device test records.
- Booster block plan and hydrant system drawings.
- Records of extensions and fit-outs since the system was designed.

pages.title: Insulation
pages.question: How does roof insulation fail, how do you tell condensation from a leak, and which insulation findings are hazards?
pages.answer: Insulation fails by gaps, wetting and condensation. Drips across a ceiling in cold weather with no rain are condensation, not a leak; mould in lines follows thermal bridges at framing. Wet insulation in a warm flat roof must come out. Some findings are hazards rather than performance problems: batts over downlights, foil on damaged wiring, loose-fill asbestos and vermiculite. Spray foam on rafters hides the structure and can trap moisture.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about insulation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Thermal and acoustic performance and condition

sources.title: Protect your family from exposures to asbestos: vermiculite

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Roof and ceiling insulation limits heat flow through the roof. It is bulk (glasswool, rockwool, polyester, cellulose, natural wool), reflective (foil laminates and foil-faced blankets), rigid board (PIR, PUR, XPS, EPS, mineral fibre) or sprayed foam. It works with vapour control layers, sarking, ventilation and the airtightness of the ceiling to manage condensation.

| Arrangement | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batts or loose fill on the ceiling, ventilated roof space | Houses and low-rise | Gaps, compression, displacement by trades; downlight clearances |
| Blanket under metal sheeting | Industrial and commercial sheds; Australian houses | Condensation where the blanket and foil are damaged |
| Warm flat roof: boards above the deck, under the membrane | Commercial and apartment flat roofs | Saturation by leaks; combustibility of boards on tall buildings |
| Inverted roof: boards above the membrane under ballast | Commercial roofs and podiums | Rainwater cooling below the boards; ballast displaced |
| Cold flat roof: insulation between joists below the deck | Older flat roofs, extensions | Interstitial condensation and deck decay |
| Spray foam to the underside of roof sheeting or rafters | Retrofits, especially in Britain from the 2010s | Hides the roof structure; condensation and decay behind it; lender acceptance |

Some older insulation is hazardous: loose-fill asbestos (the Mr Fluffy homes in the ACT and New South Wales), vermiculite that may contain asbestos, and foil laminates stapled over live wiring under the 2009 and 2010 Australian Home Insulation Program.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Insulation | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk batts and blankets, dry and undisturbed | 30 to 50 years | Compression, wetting, vermin |
| Loose fill | 20 to 40 years | Settlement; displacement |
| Rigid boards in warm roofs | 25 to 50 years | Water from leaks |
| Reflective foil | 20 to 40 years | Dust on the reflective face; damage |
| Spray foam | 30 years and more | Adhesion; shrinkage; what it hides |

What shortens life:

- Disturbance by trades running cables, ducts and downlights.
- Leaks and condensation.
- Poor vapour control on the warm side.
- Vermin nesting in batts.
- Dust on foil, which defeats its reflectivity.

Performance falls long before the material wears out. Batts compressed to half their depth lose much of their insulating value; foil covered in dust loses most of its reflective benefit; loose fill settles and blows into drifts. A roof can have insulation throughout and still deliver a fraction of the labelled value.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Gaps, compression and displacement

Small gaps cut performance out of proportion to their area. Batts pushed aside by trades, compressed under boards and storage, or cut back from downlights leave cold spots, mould on ceilings and higher energy use.

### Condensation

Warm moist air from below reaches a cold surface: the underside of metal sheeting, the deck of a cold flat roof, or sarking with low vapour permeability. Water forms, wets the insulation, drips on ceilings, corrodes metal and decays timber. Tightly sealed modern roofs in cold and alpine climates are more prone than older draughty ones, which is why codes now include condensation provisions.

### Wetting from leaks

Bulk insulation that gets wet loses most of its value and holds water against the ceiling and structure. In warm flat roofs, wet boards spread water across the roof and must be removed.

### Thermal bridging

Rafters, purlins, steel framing and slab edges carry heat past the insulation; they show as lines on thermal images and as pattern staining on ceilings.

### Fire and electrical hazard

Batts over downlights and transformers can overheat and ignite; foil laminates in contact with damaged wiring can become live. Combustible boards in roof build-ups on tall buildings are restricted.

### Spray foam

Foam applied to the underside of roof coverings or rafters makes the structure impossible to inspect, can trap moisture against timber, and makes covering repairs harder. In Britain, many lenders and surveyors will not accept it without evidence it was correctly specified and installed.

### Inverted roof faults

In inverted roofs, rainwater running under the insulation boards cools the membrane and reduces performance; boards float or blow away where ballast is light; boards absorb water over time if not closed-cell.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the roof space

- Gaps, displaced and compressed batts; insulation missing over areas.
- Batts over or against downlights and transformers.
- Wet, stained or mouldy insulation; water marks on the underside of sheeting.
- Foil laminates sagging onto wiring.
- Loose fluffy grey-blue material or granular vermiculite.
- Spray foam on the underside of the covering or rafters.

### Inside the building

- Mould spots on ceilings, often in a pattern following framing or near external walls.
- Water drips on ceilings in cold weather with no rain.
- Rooms under the roof much hotter or colder than others.

### In the records

- Insulation type and R-values; installation certificates.
- Energy ratings: NABERS, EPC, ENERGY STAR.
- Mr Fluffy register (ACT and New South Wales) and asbestos register.
- Spray foam installation records and manufacturer documentation.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water drips across a ceiling in cold weather with no rain | Condensation | Uniform pattern; underside of sheeting wet; humid space below; no vapour control |
| Water stain under one point after rain | Leak | Defect in the covering above |
| Mould on ceilings in lines | Thermal bridging at framing | Lines follow joist or rafter spacing |
| Mould near external walls and corners | Missing insulation at the ceiling edge | Insulation stops short of the wall plate |
| Hot or cold rooms | Gaps or missing insulation | Thermal imaging |

> Loose grey or blue fluffy material in an Australian roof space, especially in the ACT or New South Wales, may be loose-fill asbestos. Do not disturb it; it requires immediate expert assessment.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose-fill asbestos; foil over damaged wiring; batts over downlights or transformers | safety | Isolate and assess now; do not disturb |
| Saturated insulation; active condensation decaying the structure | failure | Remove wet insulation and fix the cause now |
| Gaps and compression across large areas; condensation without damage yet | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Insulation below current standards, triggered for upgrade by roof works | deadline | Upgrade with the works |
| Possible vermiculite or spray foam with no records | check | Identify and assess first |
| Small gaps | nil | Top up in routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or energy consultant leads, with a hygrothermal assessment where condensation is suspected.

- Roof space inspection of coverage, depth, condition and clearances.
- Thermal imaging from inside in cold weather.
- Core samples through flat roof build-ups.
- Condensation risk analysis of the build-up (BS EN ISO 13788 or dynamic modelling).
- Sampling of suspect materials for asbestos.
- Electrical inspection where foil is near wiring.

The report should state insulation type, coverage and depth, any wet areas, condensation risk in the build-up, any hazardous materials, and what an upgrade would require.

- Depth and coverage measured on a grid across the roof space and compared with the labelled R-value.
- Sarking and membrane identification from labels or product data, to establish vapour permeability.
- Ventilation check: eaves, ridge and gable openings, and whether insulation blocks them.
- Hygrothermal modelling before retrofitting insulation into cold or tightly sealed roofs.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Top up and refit batts; install downlight covers or replace downlights with insulation-contact rated fittings.
- Remove and replace wet insulation; fix the leak or condensation source first.
- Vapour control and ventilation: add a vapour control layer on the warm side, ventilate roof spaces, use vapour-permeable sarking.
- Convert cold flat roofs to warm roofs when the roof is renewed.
- Remove spray foam where it is hiding decay or causing condensation, and reinstate a ventilated build-up.
- Licensed removal of asbestos-containing insulation.

- Loose-fill top-ups with depth markers so coverage can be checked later.
- Eaves baffles to keep ventilation paths open over the insulation.
- Confirmed loose-fill asbestos: licensed assessment and, in the ACT and New South Wales, the government purchase and demolition programmes.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a lump sum. Top-up and replacement are priced by area. Wet insulation removal adds strip-out and disposal. Asbestos removal is licensed, with clearance testing. Upgrades triggered by roof works are carried in the roof line.

Upgrades triggered by works are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; top-ups are repairs and maintenance; hazardous insulation is code compliance.

Top-ups are inexpensive where access is easy; costs rise sharply in low or obstructed roof spaces and where downlights and cabling must be made safe first. Flat roof insulation upgrades are carried in the membrane replacement line, not separately.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets energy requirements in Section J and the Housing Provisions, and condensation management for houses; insulation materials follow AS/NZS 4859.1 and installation AS 3999; downlight clearances follow AS/NZS 3000. The ACT and New South Wales maintain registers of loose-fill asbestos (Mr Fluffy) homes.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document L sets thermal requirements and triggers upgrades on renovation; Approved Document C and BS 5250 govern moisture and condensation; RICS has published guidance on spray foam insulation.
- United States. The International Energy Conservation Code and ASHRAE 90.1 set requirements; International Building Code Section 1202 covers attic ventilation and Chapter 26 foam plastics. The EPA publishes guidance on vermiculite that may contain asbestos.

Insurance and lending can turn on insulation type in all three markets: spray foam on rafters and asbestos-containing products affect mortgage, insurance and sale decisions.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Insulation type, R-value and installation records.
- Energy ratings.
- Asbestos register; loose-fill asbestos register status in the ACT and New South Wales.
- Spray foam installation documentation.
- Records of condensation, mould and leaks under the roof.

- Photographs of the roof space.
- Any hygrothermal or condensation assessment.
- Electrical safety inspection of the roof space where foil insulation is present.

pages.title: Integrated Building Systems
