pages.question: How do the interfaces between building systems fail, and why can a building pass every test and still fail in a fire?
pages.answer: Critical functions live in the interfaces: fire alarms shutting down air handling, starting smoke control, homing lifts, releasing doors and cutting gas. Each system passes its own tests while the links between them go untested, and every new fire panel, lift controller or BMS can break them. Documentation is lost, proprietary gateways lock buildings in, and shared networks expose systems to attack. Only full integrated testing proves a building in a fire.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about integrated building systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: MEP interfaces across functional spaces

sources.title: NFPA 4 Integrated Fire Protection and Life Safety System Testing

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Integrated building systems are the interfaces between services: the links that make the fire alarm shut down air handling, start smoke control, release doors and home lifts; the building management system reading meters and controlling plant; access control talking to lifts and car park gates; and the networks that now carry most of this data. Each system has its own page; this page covers what happens between them. In modern buildings, many critical functions exist only in the interfaces, so a building can have every system working on its own and still fail in a fire or an outage.

| Interface | What it does | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire alarm to air handling and smoke control | Shut down or switch AHUs; start fans and dampers | Interfaces broken by upgrades; cause-and-effect out of date |
| Fire alarm to lifts | Home lifts; enable fire-fighter control | Lift modernisation without re-testing |
| Fire alarm to access control and doors | Release locks; close fire doors | Locks that stay locked |
| Fire alarm to gas and kitchen systems | Shut off gas; stop exhaust or start suppression | Bypassed interlocks |
| BMS to plant and meters | Control, schedule and monitor | Overrides; lost points; unsupported software |
| Access control to lifts and car parks | Floor and gate access by credential | Vendor lock-in; failed integration after upgrades |
| Building networks | Carry BMS, security, lighting and metering data | Cyber exposure; no ownership; flat networks |

The record of how these systems are supposed to work together (the cause-and-effect matrix, the integration specification and the network design) is often the first document lost, and the last one updated.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Item | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause-and-effect matrix | Valid until any connected system changes | Upgrades, fit-outs, modernisations |
| Interface hardware (relays, modules, gateways) | 10 to 20 years | Panel and system replacement |
| Integration software and protocols | 5 to 15 years | Vendor support; security updates |
| Network equipment | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support; security |
| Documentation | Out of date at the first change | Discipline of updating |

What shortens validity:

- Replacing one system (fire panel, lift controller, BMS) without re-testing the others connected to it.
- Fit-outs that add zones, doors and plant without updating the matrix.
- Proprietary protocols that stop working when one vendor changes.
- Unmanaged networks that no one owns.

Integration lasts only as long as every connected system stays unchanged.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Untested interfaces

Systems are routinely tested on their own: fire alarms, smoke fans, lifts and locks each pass their checks. The interfaces between them are tested only in full integrated tests, which are often skipped. Faults then appear only in a real fire: air handlers keep running, lifts do not home, doors stay locked.

### Changes without re-testing

A new fire panel, lift controller, access control system or BMS breaks interfaces unless every connected function is re-tested. Each modernisation is a point of failure for the others.

### Lost documentation

Without a current cause-and-effect matrix and integration records, nobody knows what the building should do in a fire or outage, so faults cannot be recognised.

### Vendor lock-in and obsolescence

Integrations built on proprietary gateways depend on vendors who may withdraw support, raise prices or disappear, leaving the building unable to change any one system without disturbing the rest.

### Cyber exposure

Building systems connected to shared or internet-facing networks, with default passwords and unpatched software, can be attacked, and an attack on one system can reach others. Building networks often have no owner and no security monitoring.

### Unclear ownership

Interfaces cross the responsibilities of several contractors; each maintains its own system and none owns the links. Faults fall between them.

Interfaces are also lost quietly during routine maintenance, when relays are bypassed to stop nuisance shutdowns and never restored.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Systems of very different ages and vendors connected together.
- BMS graphics or alarms showing communication failures with other systems.
- Interface panels and relays without labels.
- Building network equipment in unsecured cupboards; no network diagram.

### In the records

- Cause-and-effect matrix and its date.
- Full integrated test reports.
- Integration specifications and protocols.
- Network diagrams and access controls.
- Cyber security assessments.

- Bypass switches or disabled outputs on fire panels for air handling, lifts or doors.

- Contractors who each say an interface is someone else's responsibility.
- Fire drills where some systems responded and others did not.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifts did not home in a real alarm | Interface broken after lift or fire panel change | Integrated test |
| Doors stayed locked in a drill | Access control interface failure | Interface test |
| BMS shows plant offline | Gateway or protocol failure | Network diagnostics |
| No one can say what the building does in a fire | Matrix lost or out of date | Records review |
| Unknown devices on the building network | Unmanaged network | Network audit |

> A building whose fire interfaces have not been proven by a full integrated test since its last major change should be treated as unproven in a fire, even if every system passes its own checks.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire interfaces failing (AHUs, smoke control, lifts, doors, gas) | safety | Rectify now; fire watch if needed |
| Integration failure stopping plant or access | failure | Restore now |
| Integrated testing due under standards or certification | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Cyber exposure; poor documentation | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Integration platforms unsupported | lifecycle | Plan replacement |
| No integrated test since major changes | check | Test |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer experienced in systems integration leads, with the fire, mechanical, lift, security and controls contractors present and a cyber security specialist for networks.

- Records review: cause-and-effect matrix, integration specifications, protocols, network diagrams, and the dates of every change to connected systems.
- Full integrated test of fire functions: initiate alarms by zone and confirm every connected response, including air handling, smoke control, lifts, doors, gas and suppression.
- BMS and access integration check: communications, points, and functions across systems.
- Network and cyber review: segmentation, remote access, credentials, patching and ownership.
- Responsibility map: who maintains each interface.

The report should state which interfaces work, which fail, who owns each, and what must be fixed or documented.

The integrated test is the single most informative check of a building's life-safety systems, and it is usually the one most overdue.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Rectify failed interfaces and re-test every connected function, not just the one that failed.
- Update the cause-and-effect matrix and integration records, and make updating them a condition of every contract that touches a connected system.
- Integrated testing at least annually and after any change to the fire panel, smoke control, lifts, access control or BMS, with all contractors present.
- Open protocols in new integrations, so systems can be replaced independently.
- Network segmentation: separate building systems from corporate and guest networks, control remote access, change default credentials and patch.
- Single point of responsibility: appoint one contractor or engineer to own the interfaces and coordinate testing.
- Golden thread of information: a maintained record of how systems connect, kept with the building.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Full integrated testing is a recurring lump sum, larger than the sum of individual tests because several contractors must attend together out of hours. Interface repairs are itemised and usually modest. Replacing an integration platform is a lump sum that should be timed with the replacement of a major connected system. Network security works are lump sums with recurring monitoring. Documentation is a small cost that saves large ones.

Fire interface items are code compliance; integration platforms are lifecycle; cyber measures are risk management.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 1851 sets routine service of fire protection systems and their interfaces, and AS 1670.1 and AS 1668.1 define fire alarm and smoke control interfaces; annual fire safety certification depends on those interfaces working; performance solutions often rely on them.
- United Kingdom. BS 7273 covers the interface between fire detection and other systems such as door locks and gas shut-off; BS 9999 sets testing; the Building Safety Act 2022 requires a golden thread of accurate building information, including how systems connect, for higher-risk buildings.
- United States. NFPA 4 sets integrated testing of fire protection and life safety systems, including after changes; NFPA 72 covers interfaces; local fire codes and authorities having jurisdiction require re-acceptance testing after modifications.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Current cause-and-effect matrix with its date and author.
- Full integrated test reports since the last major change.
- Integration specifications, protocols and gateway details.
- Network diagrams and remote access arrangements.
- Cyber security assessments.
- Contracts showing who maintains each interface.

- Records of bypassed or disabled fire panel outputs.

pages.title: Internal Doors & Hardware
pages.question: How do internal doors and hardware fail, and which door findings are life-safety failures?
pages.answer: Doors usually outlast their hardware. Closers leak and lose adjustment so fire doors stay open or doors become too heavy for people with disability; hinges wear and frames distort so doors bind and do not latch; seals are painted over or lost. The life-safety failures are on escape routes: keyed locks and chains on exit doors, wrong exit devices, and electronic locks that do not release on fire alarm or power loss.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal doors & hardware; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fire ratings, access control integration, finish coordination; residential internal doors, architraves, skirtings, built-in robes and joinery

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Internal doors and hardware control movement, privacy, security, sound and fire between spaces: the door leaves and frames, and the hardware that makes them work, including hinges, locks and latches, handles, closers, exit devices (panic bars), door stops, seals, electric strikes and magnetic locks for access control, and hold-open devices. Doors occur in every space, and their failures cut across fire safety, security, accessibility and acoustics. Fire doors are covered in detail on the passive fire protection page; this page covers doors and hardware generally.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hollow-core timber doors | Residential and light commercial | Damage; poor sound and fire performance |
| Solid-core timber doors | Offices, apartments, fire and acoustic doors | Swelling, binding, seal loss |
| Steel doors and frames | Plant rooms, stairs, back-of-house | Corrosion; frame damage |
| Glazed doors | Offices, lobbies, meeting rooms | Unsafe glass; missing manifestation |
| Door closers | Fire doors, entry doors, corridors | Oil leaks; wrong force settings |
| Exit devices and egress hardware | Exit doors, stairs, assembly areas | Wrong type; locked without release |
| Electronic locking | Access-controlled doors | Fail-secure on egress routes; interface faults |
| Hinges, locks and handles | All doors | Wear; sagging; non-accessible handles |

Hardware wears much faster than doors. A building with sound doors can still fail on egress, accessibility and fire safety because of its closers, locks and exit devices.

For the engine, doors are best assessed by function rather than by count: a building with a few non-compliant exit doors has a more serious finding than one with many worn but compliant internal doors.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door leaves | 25 to 50 years | Use; damage; moisture |
| Frames | Life of the building if undamaged | Impact; movement |
| Closers | 10 to 15 years | Cycles; adjustment |
| Hinges | 15 to 30 years | Door weight; cycles |
| Locks and latches | 10 to 20 years | Cycles; abuse |
| Exit devices | 15 to 20 years | Use |
| Electronic locks | 10 to 15 years | Electronics; vendor support |
| Seals | 5 to 15 years | Damage; painting |

What shortens life:

- High traffic in corridors, entries and amenities.
- Abuse: doors kicked, wedged, slammed and struck by trolleys.
- Moisture swelling timber doors near wet areas and entrances.
- Building movement that distorts frames.

Hardware on high-traffic doors may need replacing several times within the life of the door.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Egress hardware failures

Doors on escape routes must open easily in the direction of travel without keys or special knowledge. Keyed deadlocks on exit doors, magnetic locks that do not release on fire alarm or power loss, chained doors, and exit devices of the wrong type for the occupancy trap people.

### Closer failures

Closers leak oil, lose adjustment, and are disconnected or removed. Fire and smoke doors then stay open; entry doors slam; doors set too strong cannot be opened by people with limited strength.

### Binding and sagging

Heavy doors on worn hinges sag, frames distort from building movement, and timber swells, so doors bind, do not latch, and are left open.

### Accessibility failures

Round knobs, high opening forces, narrow clear widths, high thresholds and insufficient space beside the door make doors impassable for many people with disability.

### Security failures

Worn locks, lost master keys and unmanaged key systems, and access-controlled doors that do not latch compromise security.

### Acoustic and smoke seal loss

Seals painted over, damaged or removed let sound and smoke through, undermining meeting room privacy and smoke compartments.

### Automatic door faults

Automatic swing and sliding doors inside buildings, common at accessible entries and amenities, fail when sensors drift or operators wear, either closing on people or refusing to open.

### Alterations by occupants

Tenants and residents replace hardware with decorative or non-compliant items, add bolts and chains, fit kick-down stops to hold fire doors open, and remove closers they find inconvenient.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Doors propped, wedged or not closing; closers leaking oil or disconnected.
- Doors binding, sagging or not latching; worn hinges.
- Keyed locks or chains on exit doors; magnetic locks on escape routes.
- Round knobs and heavy doors on accessible routes.
- Damaged leaves and frames; missing seals.
- Glazed doors without manifestation.

### In the records

- Door and hardware schedule.
- Fire door inspection records.
- Access control and fire alarm interface tests.
- Keying and master key records.
- Access audit.

- Kick-down stops, hooks or wedges on fire doors.
- Decorative hardware on doors that need certified fire-rated hardware.
- Automatic doors reopening repeatedly or closing too fast.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors not closing fully | Closer adjustment or failure, or binding | Test from fully open |
| Door hard to open | Closer set too strong or stack effect | Opening force measurement |
| Exit door locked when the alarm sounds | Electronic lock not released | Interface test |
| Door rubs at the head on the lock side | Hinge wear or frame distortion | Inspection |
| Noise through meeting room doors | Missing or damaged seals | Inspection |

> Any door on an escape route that cannot be opened from the inside without a key, or that stays locked in a fire alarm or power failure, is a life-safety failure.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exit doors locked or with wrong hardware; electronic locks not releasing; fire doors not closing | safety | Rectify now |
| Doors failed or security breached | failure | Repair now |
| Fire door and egress hardware inspections due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn hardware, binding doors, heavy doors on accessible routes | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Hardware at end of life; obsolete keying | lifecycle | Replace |
| No door schedule or interface test | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A door hardware specialist or building surveyor, with fire, access and security consultants.

- Door survey of doors on escape routes, fire doors, accessible routes and secure areas: leaf, frame, hardware, operation, closing, latching and seals.
- Egress hardware check: type and operation of exit devices and locks against the occupancy.
- Interface testing of electronic locks with the fire alarm and on power failure.
- Opening force measurement on accessible routes.
- Keying review.

The report should give a door schedule with defects and a hardware replacement plan.

Doors are best surveyed with a hardware schedule in hand, so each door's function (fire, egress, access, security, acoustic) is known before it is judged.

- Automatic door safety check of sensors, speeds and forces.

Check doors in both directions of travel.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Egress hardware: replace keyed locks on exit doors with compliant exit devices; fail-safe electronic locks on escape routes.
- Closers replaced and adjusted to balance closing and opening force.
- Hinges and frames repaired so doors close and latch.
- Accessible hardware: lever handles, lower forces, automatic operators.
- Seals replaced.
- Keying system renewed with key control.
- Door protection where trolleys strike doors.

- Remove hold-open hooks and wedges, replacing them with hold-open devices that release on alarm where doors need to stay open.
- Hardware standards for tenants and residents so replacements comply.
- Automatic door servicing to the standard.

- Door protection plates and frame guards where trolleys and bins strike doors.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Hardware is priced per door and per item, and most hardware renewal is far cheaper than door replacement. Door replacement is priced per door, more for fire-rated and acoustic doorsets with frames and certification. Keying systems are priced per building. Automatic operators are priced per door with power and controls. Interface works for electronic locks are lump sums with fire alarm programming.

Egress and fire door items are code compliance; hardware renewal is lifecycle; adjustments and repairs are repairs and maintenance. Accessibility upgrades may be triggered by alterations.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets egress door hardware and swing requirements; AS 1905.1 covers fire doors; AS 1428.1 sets accessible door requirements; AS 5007 covers powered doors.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 1125 covers panic exit devices and BS EN 179 emergency exit devices; BS EN 1154 covers closers; Approved Documents B and M and BS 8300 apply.
- United States. NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern egress doors and locking; NFPA 80 covers fire doors; ANSI/BHMA A156 standards cover hardware; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessible door requirements.

In all three countries, a single non-compliant lock on an exit door can lead to orders or prosecution after an incident, so egress hardware is a priority in any audit.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Door and hardware schedule with fire ratings.
- Fire door inspection records.
- Access control and fire alarm interface test records.
- Keying and master key records, including lost keys.
- Access audit covering doors on accessible routes.
- Records of door replacements by tenants or residents.

- Automatic door service records.

pages.title: Internal Stairwells
pages.question: How do stairwells fail as daily stairs and escape routes, and which findings are life-safety failures?
pages.answer: Stairs fail in daily use through falls: worn and slippery nosings, edges that cannot be seen, uneven risers, missing handrails, dark landings. As escape routes they fail when doors are propped or closers broken, when storage fills the enclosure, when security locks doors without release or re-entry, when emergency lighting fails, and when final exits are blocked. Propped doors, storage, failed emergency lighting and locked exits are life-safety failures.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal stairwells; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Treads, risers, handrails, balustrades, wall finishes, lighting, safety systems

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Internal stairwells are the vertical escape routes and everyday stairs of a building: fire-isolated stairs enclosed in fire-rated construction, open stairs between floors, and feature stairs in lobbies and atria. Functionally a stair must be safe to use every day (even risers, slip-resistant nosings, handrails, good light), and, if it is an escape stair, must stay clear, protected from fire and smoke, lit when the power fails, and lead people out to safety. Fire-isolated stairs are the most important life-safety space in a multi-storey building and the one most often misused for storage, smoking and shortcuts.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treads, risers and nosings | Concrete, steel or timber stairs with nosings | Even geometry; slip resistance; visible edges |
| Handrails and balustrades | Handrails on one or both sides; balustrades at open sides | Height, continuity, grip, openings |
| Enclosure and doors | Fire-rated walls and self-closing fire doors | Fire and smoke separation |
| Smoke control | Stair pressurisation or vents in taller buildings | Keeping smoke out |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Lighting on every flight and landing | Visibility when power fails |
| Signage | Exit signs, floor level identification, re-entry signs | Orientation in an emergency |
| Discharge | Exit to open space or a protected route | Clear path to safety |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair structure | Life of the building | Corrosion of steel stairs; alterations |
| Nosings | 10 to 25 years | Traffic; product |
| Floor finishes on treads and landings | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Fire door hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use; abuse |
| Paint and wall finishes | 7 to 15 years | Damage; appearance |
| Stair lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Use as storage, smoking areas or shortcuts, with doors propped open.
- Worn nosings that become slippery and hard to see.
- Security measures that lock stair doors without proper release.
- Penetrations by services through stair walls.

Stair condition is less a matter of age than of how the stair is used.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Falls

Falls on stairs are among the most common serious injuries in buildings. Worn or slippery nosings, edges that cannot be seen, uneven risers, missing handrails, poor lighting and wet treads from leaks all contribute. Older stairs often have handrails on one side only and nosings without contrast.

### Fire doors propped or failing

Stair doors are propped for convenience, ventilation or deliveries, and closers and latches fail. A propped stair door lets smoke into the escape route for every floor above and defeats stair pressurisation.

### Storage and obstruction

Furniture, boxes, bicycles and rubbish stored in stairs, especially under the lowest flight, narrow the route and add fire load inside the protected enclosure.

### Locking and re-entry

Security often locks stair doors from the stair side to stop people moving between floors. Rules in each jurisdiction allow this only under conditions such as release on fire alarm or re-entry floors, so that people in a smoke-filled stair can leave it. Locks fitted without those conditions can trap people.

### Loss of fire separation

Service penetrations, unrated access panels and glazing replaced with ordinary glass compromise the stair enclosure.

### Smoke control failure

Pressurisation that has failed or is unbalanced either lets smoke in or makes doors too hard to open; see the smoke management page.

### Blocked discharge

Stairs that discharge into car parks, loading docks or locked yards, or whose final exit doors are blocked or chained, fail at the last step.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site, flight by flight

- Doors propped, wedged or held by hooks; closers and latches not working.
- Storage, bikes or rubbish in stairs and under flights.
- Worn, polished or loose nosings; no contrast strips.
- Handrails missing, loose or on one side only.
- Dark landings; emergency lights failed.
- Floor level signs missing.
- Locked stair doors with no indication of release.
- Final exits blocked or locked.

### In the records

- Fire door inspection records.
- Annual fire safety certification.
- Fall incidents on stairs.
- Smoke control test records.
- Security locking arrangements and fire alarm interfaces.

- Cigarette butts and furniture on landings, a sign the stair is used as a break area.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Falls on one flight | Uneven risers, worn nosings or poor light | Riser measurement; nosing condition |
| Doors propped on several floors | Stair used for circulation between floors | Use patterns |
| Smoke in the stair during a drill | Doors propped or pressurisation failed | Door survey; smoke test |
| People unable to leave the stair on a floor | Locked re-entry without release | Security interface test |
| Water on treads | Roof or services leak into the stair | Leak tracing |

> Fire-isolated stairs must stay clear, closed, lit and able to discharge to safety. Storage, propped doors, failed emergency lighting and locked final exits are life-safety failures.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propped or failed stair doors; storage in stairs; failed emergency lighting; locked final exits; unsafe locking | safety | Rectify now |
| Stair unusable through damage or leaks | failure | Repair now |
| Fire door and emergency lighting checks due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn nosings; missing handrails; dark landings | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Finishes at end of life | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| No review of locking and re-entry | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Most stair findings are cheap to fix, so there is rarely a reason to defer them.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a fire safety consultant; a security consultant where stairs are locked.

- Flight-by-flight inspection of every stair: doors, closers and latches, storage, treads and nosings, handrails, lighting, signage, enclosure penetrations and discharge.
- Riser and going measurement where falls occur or stairs look irregular.
- Slip resistance testing of nosings and landings.
- Locking and re-entry test: security doors released by the fire alarm and on power failure.
- Smoke control and emergency lighting tests.
- Use review: why doors are propped and stairs used for storage.

The report should list life-safety items by stair and floor, and stair improvements.

Stairs are best inspected at different times of day, because propped doors and storage often appear outside business hours.

Night and weekend checks are often revealing.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Door repair: closers, latches and seals restored so every stair door closes and latches from fully open; hold-open devices linked to the fire alarm where stairs are genuinely used for circulation between floors.
- Clear storage from every stair and enforce building rules, with regular checks recorded.
- Nosings: slip-resistant nosings with contrasting edges on every tread and landing edge, so each step can be seen and gripped.
- Handrails on both sides where required, continuous through landings, at the right height and graspable.
- Lighting: even lighting on every flight with emergency lighting tested to the standard, and occupancy-dimmed lighting that never leaves a flight dark.
- Locking: bring security locking into line with release-on-alarm and re-entry rules, with signage on the stair side.
- Fire stopping of service penetrations and replacement of any unrated panels or glazing in the enclosure.
- Final exits kept clear and openable without keys, with signage outside to stop obstruction.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Stair works are priced per flight or per stair. Nosings and handrails are priced by length; door works per door; lighting per fitting; locking changes per door with fire alarm interface. Most items are code compliance and low in cost relative to their safety value; the main cost driver is doing the work without closing escape routes, which usually means one stair at a time and out-of-hours work.

Keeping stairs clear costs only management time.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets stair geometry, handrails, fire-isolated stairs and door requirements, with fire doors maintained under AS 1851; slip resistance follows AS 4586; strata and building rules prohibit storage in stairs.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B governs escape stairs and Approved Document K stair geometry and guarding; the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require checks of fire doors in residential buildings; the responsible person must keep escape routes clear.
- United States. NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern exit stairs, including re-entry rules for locked stair doors; NFPA 80 covers stair door inspection; OSHA requires exit routes kept clear.

Insurers and fire services in all three countries treat obstructed or compromised escape stairs as serious breaches and can require immediate action or issue orders.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire door inspection records for every stair door.
- Annual fire safety certification and any qualifications on stairs.
- Stair fall incident records.
- Security locking and fire alarm interface test records.
- Smoke control and emergency lighting test records.
- Building rules on stair use and storage, with records of enforcement.

pages.title: Internal Wall & Ceiling Finishes
pages.question: How do wall and ceiling finishes fail, and when is a ceiling dangerous?
pages.answer: Most finish failures are cosmetic, but some are not. Old lath and plaster ceilings lose their keys and sag, and plasterboard ceilings with failed fixings or soaked by leaks bow and can fall without warning. Textured coatings and older plasters may contain asbestos and older paints lead, which are safe until disturbed. Hairline cracks at joints are normal; tapering and recurring cracks can signal structural movement. Mould points to condensation.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal wall & ceiling finishes; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Plaster, linings, paint, cornices, decorative plasterwork to walls and ceilings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Internal wall and ceiling finishes are the visible surfaces of rooms: lath and plaster in older buildings, plasterboard on timber or steel framing, suspended ceiling grids and tiles in commercial buildings, paint, wall coverings, textured coatings, timber panelling, wall tiles and acoustic panels. They are judged on appearance, but some failures are structural in effect: old lath and plaster ceilings and poorly fixed plasterboard ceilings can collapse, and textured coatings and paints in older buildings may contain asbestos or lead.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lath and plaster | Houses and buildings before about 1940 | Plaster keys break and ceilings sag and fall |
| Plasterboard | Most buildings since the 1950s | Cracks at joints, nail pops, sagging ceilings, water damage |
| Suspended ceilings | Commercial buildings | Stained and sagging tiles; grid damage; missing tiles |
| Textured coatings | Ceilings and walls from the mid twentieth century | May contain asbestos in older buildings |
| Paint | Everywhere | Flaking; lead in older paint; mould |
| Wall tiles | Wet areas, kitchens | Cracking, debonding, grout failure |
| Wall coverings and panelling | Offices, hotels, older homes | Peeling, damage, fire performance |

Finishes are assessed by space, since ceilings over beds, desks and corridors carry more consequence if they fall than those over storage.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Finish | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Wear; moisture; style |
| Plasterboard | Life of the building if dry and well fixed | Water; movement; fixing |
| Lath and plaster | 80 to 120 years | Vibration; water; loss of key |
| Suspended ceiling tiles | 15 to 25 years | Water; services works; appearance |
| Suspended ceiling grid | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Wall coverings | 10 to 15 years | Damage; style |

What shortens life:

- Water from leaks and condensation.
- Building movement cracking joints and cornices.
- Services works that cut and patch ceilings.
- Vibration and roof works loosening old plaster.

Ceilings in older buildings deserve particular attention because their age, not their appearance, often decides whether they are safe.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Ceiling sagging and collapse

Lath and plaster ceilings hang by plaster keys pushed through the laths; as keys break with age, vibration and water, the ceiling sags and can fall in large sections. Plasterboard ceilings fixed with failing adhesive, too few fasteners or undersized battens, or soaked by leaks, sag and can drop without warning. Sagging ceilings are a safety finding.

### Cracking

Cracks at plasterboard joints, cornices and corners come from timber shrinkage, seasonal movement and structural movement. Most are cosmetic; cracks that are wide, recurring or tapering may reflect foundation or structural movement.

### Water damage and mould

Leaks from roofs, wet areas and services stain, soften and collapse ceilings; condensation in bathrooms and cold rooms grows mould on ceilings and walls.

### Hazardous finishes

Textured coatings and some plasters, ceiling tiles and wall boards in older buildings contain asbestos; older paint contains lead. They are safe while intact but release fibres or dust when sanded, drilled or removed.

### Suspended ceiling problems

Tiles stain from leaks and sag from humidity; grids are bent by trades; tiles are left out after works, breaking fire, acoustic and smoke performance where the ceiling is part of a system.

Heavy fittings such as light fittings, fans and speakers hung from plasterboard without proper support also pull ceilings down over time.

Fire-rated ceilings lose rating when cut for services.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Ceilings sagging, bulging or with cracks running along battens; cornices pulling away.
- Nail pops and cracks at plasterboard joints.
- Stains, softness and mould on ceilings.
- Textured ceilings and walls in older buildings.
- Flaking paint on older surfaces.
- Missing, stained or sagging suspended ceiling tiles.

### In the records

- Asbestos register.
- Leak history.
- Previous ceiling repairs.

- Cracks running parallel at regular spacing on ceilings, following battens or joists.
- Ceiling fans and heavy fittings fixed to plasterboard alone.
- Patched and mismatched suspended ceiling tiles after services works.
- Bulges in ceilings below wet areas or roof leaks.

- Mould returning on ceilings soon after repainting.
- Old ceilings with fine cracks and slight bulges.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old ceiling sagging in the middle of the room | Lath and plaster keys failing | Inspection from above |
| Plasterboard ceiling bowing between battens | Fixing or adhesive failure, or water | Inspection from the roof space |
| Hairline cracks at joints and cornices | Normal shrinkage and movement | Pattern; stability |
| Tapering cracks above doors and windows | Structural or foundation movement | See foundations page |
| Mould on bathroom ceiling | Condensation from poor exhaust | Fan and humidity check |
| Stained suspended tiles in a line | Leak from services or the floor above | Trace the line |

> A sagging ceiling, particularly an old lath and plaster ceiling or a plasterboard ceiling bowing between supports, can fall without warning. Keep people out from under it until it is assessed.

Recurring mould after repainting means the moisture cause has not been fixed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sagging ceilings; damaged asbestos-containing finishes; flaking lead paint where children are present | safety | Exclude, make safe and remediate now |
| Ceiling collapsed or water-damaged | failure | Repair now |
| Asbestos register review due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Cracking, mould, stained tiles, worn paint | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Finishes at end of cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Hazardous content unknown in older finishes | check | Sample before works |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

A sagging ceiling is graded as safety even if it has not moved recently, because collapse gives little warning and falls on people below.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects, with a licensed asbestos assessor before any sampling or works on older finishes.

- Ceiling inspection from below and, where accessible, from the roof space or ceiling void, checking fixings, keys, battens and adhesives.
- Crack mapping with widths and patterns to separate cosmetic from structural cracking.
- Moisture and mould assessment where stains or mould appear.
- Hazardous materials sampling of textured coatings, older plasters, ceiling tiles and paints before work.
- Suspended ceiling survey where the ceiling forms part of a fire, smoke or acoustic system.

The report should identify any collapse risk, hazardous content, the cause of cracking and staining, and a repair or refurbishment plan.

Where ceilings are old and inaccessible from above, a small inspection opening can confirm their fixing.

Record which rooms sit under old or sagging ceilings, so that the most occupied rooms are made safe first and the others are scheduled.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Ceiling securing: refix plasterboard with additional fasteners, or replace sagging lath and plaster ceilings, after propping where needed.
- Crack repair after any movement is resolved, with flexible joints where movement will recur.
- Leak and moisture fixes before redecorating, then repair or replacement of damaged boards.
- Mould treatment and improved ventilation.
- Hazardous materials: leave intact asbestos-containing finishes undisturbed and recorded, or remove by licensed contractors before works; stabilise or remove lead paint safely.
- Suspended ceilings: replace stained and missing tiles and straighten grids; restore ceiling systems that form part of fire or acoustic designs.
- Redecoration on cycle.

- Support heavy fittings from framing, not plasterboard.

- Ventilation improvements in bathrooms and laundries so ceilings do not grow mould again after repainting.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Ceiling repairs and replacements are priced by area, with propping and access, and in occupied buildings the cost of temporary relocation. Hazardous materials removal adds licensed removal, air monitoring and clearance. Suspended tiles are priced per tile or by area. Redecoration is by area on a cycle.

Collapse risks are immediate; hazardous materials are code compliance when disturbed; redecoration and ceiling replacement are lifecycle.

Ceiling refixing is far cheaper than repairs after a collapse.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Plasterboard installation follows AS/NZS 2589; lead paint management follows AS 4361.2; asbestos-containing finishes are managed under work health and safety laws.
- United Kingdom. Plastering and drylining follow BS 8212 and BS EN 520; asbestos-containing textured coatings are managed under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012; lead paint follows HSE guidance.
- United States. Gypsum board application follows ASTM C840 and GA-216; lead-safe practices under the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule apply in pre-1978 housing; asbestos is regulated by OSHA and the EPA.

In all three countries, work that disturbs asbestos-containing finishes must follow asbestos rules, and in rental housing, landlords must keep ceilings and walls safe and free of hazards such as mould and lead dust under housing standards.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Asbestos register covering finishes.
- Lead paint test results for older buildings.
- Leak history and repairs.
- Previous ceiling repairs or replacements.
- Records of works that disturbed finishes.

- Mould complaints.
- Records of heavy fittings installed on ceilings.
- Building age and renovation history.

- Records of ceiling repairs after leaks.

pages.title: Kitchen
pages.question: How do residential kitchens fail, and which kitchen findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Kitchens are usually refurbished for style before they fail, but the real defects are hidden. Slow leaks under sinks and dishwashers swell cabinet bases and floors; aged flexible hoses burst and flood apartments below; recirculating or ceiling-ducted rangehoods leave moisture and combustion products indoors; gas cooktops too close to combustibles or fitted without certification are fire risks; new appliances overload old circuits. Replace hoses on a cycle and duct extraction outside.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about kitchen; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cabinetry, benchtops, appliances, joinery, butler\u2019s pantry

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
The residential kitchen is the room where water, gas or high electrical loads, heat, grease and heavy daily use come together: cabinetry and benchtops, sink and tapware, dishwasher and laundry connections where present, cooktop and oven, rangehood, refrigerator, splashbacks and the floor beneath. Functionally it must work, stay dry, extract cooking moisture and fumes, and be safe from fire, gas and electrical hazards. Kitchens are usually refurbished for style long before they fail, but hidden leaks under sinks and dishwashers, and gas and ventilation issues, are real defects.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cabinetry | Particleboard or MDF carcasses with laminate or two-pack doors | Moisture swelling, hinges, drawers |
| Benchtops | Laminate, stone, engineered stone, timber, stainless steel | Damage, joints, sealing at the sink |
| Sink and tapware | Sink, mixer, waste, under-sink connections | Leaks into cabinets and floors |
| Appliances | Cooktop, oven, dishwasher, rangehood, refrigerator | Age, safety, energy, connections |
| Rangehood and exhaust | Ducted to outside or recirculating | Moisture, grease and combustion products |
| Gas or electric cooking | Gas cooktop with flexible connection; induction or ceramic | Gas safety; electrical capacity |
| Splashback and clearances | Tiles, glass, stone | Heat clearances near burners |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years | Style; wear; leaks |
| Cabinetry | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; hardware |
| Laminate benchtops | 10 to 20 years | Heat; moisture at joints |
| Stone and engineered stone benchtops | 25 years and more | Impact; sealing |
| Cooktops and ovens | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Dishwashers | 8 to 12 years | Use; water quality |
| Rangehoods | 10 to 15 years | Grease; motors |
| Flexible hoses | 5 to 10 years | Burst risk with age |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Slow leaks under sinks and dishwashers swelling cabinetry and floors.
- Ageing flexible hoses that burst.
- Recirculating rangehoods that leave moisture and combustion products in the home.
- Heavy use in rented and shared homes.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Leaks under the sink and appliances

Waste connections, tap connections and braided flexible hoses leak slowly into the cabinet base, which swells, delaminates and grows mould; dishwasher inlet and outlet hoses leak into the floor. Burst flexible hoses flood whole apartments and the units below, and are a leading cause of residential water damage insurance claims.

### Inadequate extraction

Recirculating rangehoods or hoods ducted into the ceiling space leave moisture, grease and, with gas cooking, nitrogen dioxide and other combustion products indoors. Condensation and mould follow in poorly ventilated homes.

### Gas safety

Flexible gas connections deteriorate; burners placed too close to combustible splashbacks or cabinets are a fire risk; cooktops fitted by unlicensed people may leak.

### Fire

Cooking is the leading cause of house fires. Grease-laden rangehood filters, combustible materials near cooktops and the absence of fire blankets or alarms in kitchens of older homes raise the risk.

### Electrical capacity

Induction cooktops and more appliances need circuits older kitchens do not have; overloaded circuits and power boards trip or overheat.

### Benchtop and cabinet wear

Laminate swells at sink cut-outs and joints, stone chips and cracks at cut-outs, hinges and drawer runners fail. Engineered stone in place is not a hazard, but cutting it releases silica dust; Australia has banned new engineered stone installations.

In rented homes and shared housing, heavy use and slow reporting of leaks accelerate damage.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the kitchen

- Swollen, stained or soft cabinet bases under the sink and dishwasher.
- Flexible hoses that are kinked, rusted or past their date.
- Rangehood type and where it discharges; greasy filters.
- Gas cooktop clearances to splashbacks and cabinets.
- Power boards running appliances; tripping.
- Swollen laminate at joints; cracked stone at cut-outs.
- Mould on ceilings or in cupboards.

### In the records

- Gas compliance certificates.
- Appliance ages and warranties.
- Leak and insurance claims.
- Electrical certificates for renovations.

- No isolation valves under the sink, or valves that cannot be turned.
- Fire blanket and smoke alarm near the kitchen absent.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swollen cabinet base under the sink | Slow leak at waste or tap connections | Inspection with the cabinet emptied |
| Water on the floor in front of the dishwasher | Hose or door seal leak | Run a cycle and inspect |
| Condensation and mould after cooking | Rangehood recirculating or ducted into the ceiling | Duct route inspection |
| Scorch marks behind the cooktop | Clearance to combustible materials too small | Measurement against gas rules |
| Circuit trips when cooking | Overloaded circuit | Load assessment |

> Flexible hoses past their life, gas cooktops too close to combustible materials, and gas connections fitted without certification are safety findings.

Kitchens are judged mostly on what cannot be seen: the cabinet base under the sink, the hose behind the dishwasher and the duct above the rangehood. Open them before forming a view.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leaks or unsafe clearances; aged flexible hoses; overloaded circuits | safety | Rectify now |
| Active leaks damaging floors or units below | failure | Repair now |
| Tenancy or sale requirements for gas or electrical safety | deadline | As required |
| Swollen cabinetry; weak extraction; worn appliances | condition | Repair or replace in the near term |
| Kitchen at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Gas and electrical compliance unknown | check | Inspect |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or building inspector leads, with a licensed gas fitter for gas cooking and an electrician where circuits are in doubt; in apartments, access to the unit below helps trace leaks.

- Under-sink and appliance inspection with cabinets emptied: waste and tap connections, flexible hoses and their dates, isolation valves, cabinet bases and the floor beneath.
- Moisture readings in floors, walls and kickboards around the sink, dishwasher and refrigerator water connection.
- Dishwasher test: run a cycle and inspect for leaks at hoses, seals and the floor.
- Rangehood check: type, airflow, filter condition and where the duct actually discharges.
- Gas safety check by a licensed fitter: connection condition, leak test, burner clearances to splashbacks and cabinets.
- Electrical check: number and rating of circuits, RCD protection, use of power boards, tripping history.
- Condition survey of cabinetry, benchtops, splashbacks and appliances, with ages.

The report should list safety items, leaks and damage with their extent, and when the kitchen is due for renewal.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Flexible hose replacement on a cycle, with quality braided hoses and accessible isolation valves, a cheap measure against flooding.
- Leak repairs of wastes and connections, with replacement of swollen cabinet bases and kickboards and repair of damaged floors.
- Ducted extraction: a rangehood ducted to the outside, sized for the cooktop, with filters cleaned regularly.
- Gas safety works: certified connections and compliant clearances, or conversion to induction cooking where electrification is planned.
- Electrical upgrades: dedicated circuits for cooktops, ovens and dishwashers, with RCD protection.
- Fire safety: smoke alarms positioned to avoid nuisance alarms, and a fire blanket near the cooktop.
- Leak detection: water sensors under sinks and dishwashers, especially in apartments.
- Refurbishment on cycle, with moisture-resistant carcasses and sealed benchtop cut-outs.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Hose replacement, leak repairs and leak sensors are small items with large avoided costs. Rangehood ducting is a lump sum, harder in apartments where ducts must reach the façade. Electrical upgrades are lump sums, sometimes requiring switchboard work. Induction conversion is a lump sum including the appliance and circuit. Kitchen refurbishment is priced per kitchen and in rented stock timed with vacancies.

Safety items are immediate; refurbishment is lifecycle; leak repairs are repairs and maintenance. In strata, water damage to other units from kitchen leaks usually falls to the owner whose fittings failed.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 5601.1 sets gas appliance installation and clearances, and gas work must be done by licensed fitters with compliance certificates; the National Construction Code requires kitchen exhaust to discharge to the outside in newer homes; work health and safety law has banned new engineered stone installations since 1 July 2024; strata by-laws often control kitchen renovations.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document F sets extract ventilation rates for kitchens; the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require Gas Safe registered engineers and annual gas safety checks in rented homes; electrical work must comply with BS 7671 and Part P.
- United States. The International Residential Code covers range hoods, kitchen circuits and GFCI protection; the International Fuel Gas Code covers gas cooking appliances and clearances; some cities restrict gas in new buildings.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Gas compliance certificates for cooktops and ovens.
- Electrical certificates for kitchen renovations.
- Appliance ages and warranties.
- Leak and insurance claims, including damage to units below.
- Strata approvals for kitchen renovations.
- Records of flexible hose replacement.

- Records of any kitchen fires or near misses.
- Electrification plans affecting gas cooking.

pages.title: Landscaping & Irrigation
pages.question: How does landscaping affect the building, and which landscape findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Landscaping matters most where it meets the building. Trees drop limbs and fall, and their roots cause subsidence on clay, block drains and lift paving; podium and roof planters leak through membranes into car parks and apartments; irrigation sprays onto walls and lacks backflow protection; garden beds bridge damp-proof courses and termite barriers. Defective trees over occupied areas are a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about landscaping & irrigation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Hard and soft landscaping, retaining walls, irrigation systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Landscaping covers the planted and hard-landscaped external areas of a site: trees, garden beds, lawns, planters, podium and roof gardens, green walls, landscape walls and features, and the irrigation systems that water them. Landscaping interacts with the building more than its cost suggests: trees damage foundations, drains and pavements; planters on podiums and roofs load the structure and test waterproofing; irrigation leaks soak walls and membranes; and in bushfire areas vegetation sets fire risk.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trees | All sites | Limb and tree failure; roots affecting foundations, drains and paving |
| Planters on podiums and roofs | Apartments, offices, retail | Membrane leaks; root penetration; load |
| Green walls | Commercial buildings from the 2000s | Irrigation leaks; plant loss; fixings |
| Irrigation systems | Most landscaped sites | Leaks; overspray onto buildings; backflow; controllers |
| Garden beds against buildings | All buildings | Bridging damp-proof courses and termite barriers |
| Landscape walls and edging | All sites | Movement; drainage |

Landscape works also carry statutory and planning obligations: tree preservation controls, landscape conditions on development approvals, and bushfire vegetation management, all of which constrain what an owner can change.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trees | Decades to centuries | Species; site; maintenance |
| Shrubs and planting | 5 to 20 years | Species; care; water |
| Irrigation controllers | 8 to 12 years | Technology; weather |
| Irrigation pipework and emitters | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage; water quality |
| Green wall systems | 10 to 20 years; plants sooner | Irrigation; plant selection; maintenance |
| Podium planter waterproofing | 20 to 30 years | Root barriers; drainage |

What shortens life:

- Poor plant selection for the site: large trees near buildings, vigorous roots near drains.
- Lack of maintenance: unpruned trees, untended irrigation.
- Drainage failures in planters.
- Construction damage to tree roots.

Trees outlast most building elements but change constantly: a sapling planted near a wall becomes a large tree within the life of the building, and its effect grows with it.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Tree and limb failure

Trees with decay, cracks, weak forks, root damage or dieback drop limbs or fall in storms. Trees damaged by construction often decline years later. Failures over car parks, footpaths and play areas cause injuries and damage.

### Root damage to buildings and services

Roots draw moisture from clay soils, causing foundation subsidence; they enter and block drains through joints; they lift pavements and walls. Removing trees on clay can cause heave.

### Podium and roof planter leaks

Planters over occupied space depend on waterproofing, root barriers and drainage. Roots penetrate unprotected membranes, drains block with soil and roots, and leaks appear in car parks and apartments below. Saturated planters can also exceed the structure's design load.

### Irrigation faults

Irrigation leaks and overspray wet walls, footings and windows, causing damp, efflorescence and decay; systems run in rain; connections to drinking water lack backflow protection.

### Bridging damp-proof courses and termite barriers

Garden beds and mulch heaped against walls cover vents, bridge damp-proof courses and give termites hidden access over barriers.

### Vegetation and bushfire

In bushfire-prone areas, vegetation and mulch close to buildings carry fire to the walls, decks and roof gutters.

### Construction damage

Trenching, excavation, compaction and level changes within a tree's root zone kill roots and destabilise trees, often with decline appearing years later when the link is forgotten.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Trees with dead limbs, cracks, cavities, fungal fruiting bodies, lean or root lifting.
- Large trees close to buildings on clay soils.
- Leaks and staining under podium planters; plants growing from drainage outlets.
- Irrigation spraying onto walls, windows and paving; wet patches and leaks.
- Garden beds above damp-proof courses and vents; mulch against walls.
- Green walls with dead plants, leaks and staining below.

### In the records

- Arborist reports and tree management records.
- Landscape maintenance contracts.
- Irrigation drawings and backflow tests.
- Leak history under planters.

- Soil levels raised around tree trunks, or trenches cut close to trees, signs of root damage.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks in a car park under a planter | Membrane failure or blocked drainage | Flood test; drainage inspection |
| Cracks in a building near a large tree on clay | Subsidence from root moisture uptake | See foundations page |
| Repeated drain blockages near trees | Root intrusion | CCTV |
| Damp walls behind garden beds | Bridged damp-proof course or irrigation | Inspection |
| Dead branches in a tree crown | Decline, decay or root damage | Arborist assessment |

> A tree with significant defects over an occupied area, car park, road or footpath is a safety risk. Get an arborist's assessment and act on it.

Root problems are distinguished from other causes by position and timing: damage that follows the line of a tree's roots, worsens in dry seasons and is worst nearest the tree points to the tree; damage unrelated to tree positions points elsewhere.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defective trees over occupied areas; vegetation creating bushfire risk | safety | Prune, remove or exclude now |
| Planter leaks damaging structure or units | failure | Repair now |
| Irrigation backflow testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Roots affecting drains and paving; bridged damp-proof courses; irrigation overspray | condition | Address in the near term |
| Planting, irrigation and green walls at end of life | lifecycle | Renew |
| No tree risk assessment | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

Tree findings are graded by consequence as well as defect: the same decay in a tree over a car park, a footpath or a play area is a higher grade than in a tree in an unused corner of the site.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A qualified arborist for trees; a landscape architect or contractor for landscaping; a waterproofing specialist for planters.

- Tree risk assessment using a recognised method, prioritising trees near people and buildings.
- Root and foundation review where trees are near buildings on clay.
- Planter investigation: drainage, root barriers, membrane condition, saturated weight against design loads.
- Irrigation audit: leaks, overspray, controllers, backflow devices.
- Building interface check: beds, mulch and paving against walls, vents and barriers.
- Bushfire assessment where relevant.

The report should give tree risks, building interactions, planter and irrigation issues, and a maintenance and renewal plan.

Tree risk is judged by the likelihood of failure and the consequence: a defective tree over an empty field is less urgent than a sound-looking tree with a structural defect over a children's play area or a busy entrance.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Tree work: pruning, removal, cabling or replacement with suitable species, with heave assessed before removing trees near buildings.
- Root barriers between trees and buildings or drains.
- Planter rectification: new membranes with root barriers, drainage cells and clear outlets.
- Irrigation repair: redirect sprays, fix leaks, rain sensors, smart controllers, backflow devices.
- Clearances: lower beds and remove mulch from walls, vents and barriers.
- Vegetation management in bushfire areas.
- Green wall renewal.

- Tree protection during any works near trees, with fencing and root protection zones.
- Water-efficient landscaping: drought-tolerant planting and drip irrigation, reducing water use and leaks.
- Maintenance programme setting pruning, irrigation checks, planter drainage clearing and mulch control.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Landscape maintenance is a recurring contract. Arborist assessments recur. Tree work is per tree. Planter rectification is a lump sum with soil removal and reinstatement. Irrigation upgrades are lump sums.

Safety tree work is immediate; planter rectification is lifecycle or failure; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

Tree removal near buildings on clay can require phased work and monitoring to manage heave. Podium planter rectification usually means removing soil and plants by hand or crane, which often costs more than the waterproofing itself.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4970 covers protection of trees on development sites and AS 4373 pruning; tree preservation controls apply in many council areas; AS 3959 sets construction in bushfire-prone areas.
- United Kingdom. BS 5837 covers trees in relation to construction; tree preservation orders and conservation areas restrict work on trees; occupiers owe a duty of care for tree safety.
- United States. ANSI A300 sets tree care standards; local tree ordinances apply; wildland-urban interface codes set vegetation clearances in fire-prone areas.

In all three jurisdictions, landscape conditions attached to planning approvals can require planting to be kept or replaced, and trees on boundaries create shared liability with neighbours. Strata and condominium landscaping is common property, with by-laws on what owners may plant on balconies and in private courtyards over shared structures.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Arborist reports and tree management records.
- Tree preservation orders or controls.
- Landscape maintenance contracts.
- Irrigation drawings and backflow test certificates.
- Planter waterproofing records and leak history.
- Bushfire assessments.

- Planning approval landscape conditions.
- Records of works near trees.
- Strata by-laws on planting.

- Bushfire attack level assessments where relevant.

pages.title: Lift Cars & Machine Rooms
pages.question: How do lift cars, machine rooms and pits fail as spaces, and what does the building control?
pages.answer: Lift spaces fail through heat, water, wear and missing accessibility features. Hot machine rooms make controllers fail, so breakdowns cluster in hot weather; water in pits corrodes buffers and safety gear; car interiors are battered by goods and moves; older cars lack braille, tactile and audio features. Machine rooms become storerooms. The building usually controls these space issues even when the lift contractor maintains the machinery.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lift cars & machine rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Interior finishes, lighting, ventilation, architectural integration

sources.title: ASME A17.1 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Lift cars and machine rooms are the spaces of the lift installation: the car interior that passengers ride in, the landing entrances on each floor, the machine room or control space, and the shaft and pit. The machinery itself is on the lifts page; this page covers the spaces. Functionally the car must be safe, accessible, lit, ventilated and presentable; the machine room must keep equipment cool, dry, secure and reachable; and the pit and shaft must stay dry and clear.

| Space | Typical provision | What matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car interior | Wall panels, floor, ceiling, lighting, handrails, mirror, ventilation fan | Finish condition, accessibility, lighting, air |
| Car fixtures | Buttons, indicators, audio, emergency phone, CCTV | Accessibility, function, communication |
| Landing entrances | Door frames, sills, indicators and buttons on each floor | Damage, sill trip edges, fire rating |
| Machine room | Controller, drive, machine; ventilation, lighting, access | Temperature, security, housekeeping |
| Pit | Buffers, ladder, lighting, drainage or sump | Water, debris, access |
| Shaft | Fire-rated enclosure, venting where required | Fire separation, water ingress |

In buildings with several lifts, the condition of cars and landings is a daily signal of building quality to every occupant and visitor, and dated cars can undermine an otherwise refurbished lobby.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car interior finishes | 10 to 20 years | Use; goods carried in passenger lifts |
| Car flooring | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; trolleys |
| Landing door frames and finishes | 15 to 25 years | Impact; cleaning |
| Car ventilation fans and lighting | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| Machine room ventilation and cooling | 15 to 20 years | Heat load; maintenance |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Goods and furniture carried in passenger lifts without protective blankets.
- Hot machine rooms shortening controller life.
- Water in pits and shafts.
- Machine rooms used for storage.

Car interiors are usually refurbished with controls modernisation, so their timing is tied to the lift cycle.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Interior damage and wear

Car walls are dented and scratched by trolleys, furniture and building materials; floors wear at the entrance; handrails loosen; mirrors crack. The car interior is the lift's face to users and dates the building quickly.

### Accessibility shortfalls

Older cars lack braille and tactile buttons, audible announcements, handrails, adequate size for wheelchairs, and visual indicators; these are usually corrected at modernisation.

### Car ventilation and lighting

Failed car fans and lights make cars hot and dark, and trapped passengers distressed.

### Machine room overheating

Machine rooms without adequate ventilation or cooling overheat; electronic controllers and drives fail or trip, causing breakdowns concentrated in hot weather.

### Water in pits and shafts

Groundwater, failed sumps, cleaning water and leaks reach pits, corroding buffers, rails and safety gear and causing electrical faults; flooding can take lifts out of service for long periods.

### Storage and security

Machine rooms used as storerooms, left unlocked, or reached only by unsafe ladders and roofs expose workers and equipment to risk.

### Sill gaps and levelling at landings

Worn landing sills and poor levelling leave trip edges at entrances; see the lifts page for causes.

In machine-room-less lifts, the control equipment sits in a cabinet at a landing or in the shaft, so access and heat problems move into corridors and shafts.

Machine rooms on roofs also suffer roof leaks that drip onto controllers.

Lift lobbies and landing areas also suffer damage when goods are wheeled to the lift, so landing frames and nearby walls wear at the same rate as the car.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Car interiors dented, scratched or with protective blankets permanently fitted.
- Buttons without braille or tactile marking; no audible announcements.
- Hot, dark or stuffy cars.
- Machine rooms hot, unlocked, or used for storage.
- Water or oil in pits.
- Damaged landing frames and sills.

### In the records

- Lift breakdown records, especially in hot weather.
- Machine room temperature records.
- Pit inspection notes from the lift contractor.
- Modernisation history.

- Control cabinets at landings in machine-room-less installations, with their locks and ventilation.

- Roof leaks or staining in rooftop machine rooms.
- Trapped passenger incidents and how long they lasted.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakdowns cluster on hot days | Machine room overheating | Temperature logging |
| Corrosion of pit equipment | Water in the pit | Pit inspection; sump |
| Car walls repeatedly damaged | Goods and moves in passenger lifts | Protection practices |
| Complaints from vision-impaired users | Missing tactile and audio features | Accessibility audit |

> Separate space issues (heat, water, finishes, accessibility features) from machinery issues; the lift contractor handles the second but the building usually controls the first.

Water in a pit after every storm points to groundwater or a failed sump; water after cleaning points to washdown entering the shaft.

If breakdown records show controllers and drives failing mainly in summer, check machine room temperatures before replacing components; cooling is often the cheaper and lasting fix.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water in pits affecting safety equipment; machine rooms with unsafe access or storage | safety | Rectify now |
| Lifts out of service from heat or flooding | failure | Restore now |
| Statutory lift inspections | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn interiors; hot cars; accessibility gaps | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Interiors at end of life | lifecycle | Refurbish, ideally with modernisation |
| Machine room conditions unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Most findings in these spaces are building responsibilities that reduce breakdowns and entrapments when fixed, and they are often cheaper than the breakdowns they cause.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A lift consultant leads with the building surveyor, coordinating with the lift contractor for access to machine rooms, shafts and pits.

- Car inspection of every car: walls, floor, ceiling, lighting, ventilation fan, handrails, mirrors, fixtures, braille and tactile buttons, audible announcements and visual indicators.
- Machine room inspection: temperature against equipment limits, ventilation and cooling, lighting, access route and ladders, security, housekeeping, lifting beams and fire separation.
- Pit inspection with the contractor: water, sump and pump, debris, lighting, ladder.
- Landing survey on each floor: door frames, sills, indicators, buttons and fire rating labels.
- Records review: breakdowns by season and cause, inspection reports, modernisation history.

The report should separate building items (heat, water, finishes, access and housekeeping) from lift contractor items, and align refurbishment with modernisation.

Where the lift contractor has already reported building-side defects, start from their reports, which often list heat, water and access problems repeatedly over years.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Car refurbishment with durable, impact-resistant finishes, ideally timed with controls modernisation so accessibility features are upgraded at the same time.
- Protective pads and procedures for moves and deliveries in passenger lifts, or directing goods to a goods lift.
- Machine room cooling and ventilation sized to the equipment heat, with temperature alarms.
- Pit drainage and waterproofing, with sump pumps and alarms where groundwater is present.
- Accessible fixtures: braille and tactile buttons, audible and visual indicators, handrails.
- Machine room access and housekeeping: safe access routes, locks, lighting and removal of storage.
- Landing repairs to frames and sills.

- Roof and shaft waterproofing for rooftop machine rooms and shafts.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Car interiors are priced per car and are best done with modernisation to avoid two disruptions. Machine room cooling is a lump sum per room; pit works per pit; landing repairs per floor.
