Interior refurbishment is lifecycle; accessibility and access safety items are code compliance; heat and water works are condition items that cut breakdowns.

Heat and water fixes in machine rooms and pits are usually cheap relative to the breakdowns and damaged equipment they prevent, and should not wait for modernisation. In strata buildings, these spaces are common property and their costs fall to the owners corporation.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The AS 1735 series governs lifts and the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards set accessibility for new and upgraded lifts, including car size, controls and indicators; work health and safety laws govern safe access to machine rooms and pits.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 81-20 covers lift construction including machine spaces, and BS EN 81-70 accessibility; LOLER requires thorough examination; the Workplace Regulations and Work at Height Regulations govern access.
- United States. ASME A17.1 sets machine room and pit requirements, including temperature limits, lighting and access; the 2010 ADA Standards govern car accessibility; state elevator authorities inspect.

In all three countries, machine rooms and pits are restricted spaces that only authorised lift workers may enter.

Accessibility upgrades usually follow modernisation.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Breakdown records by season and cause.
- Machine room temperature records.
- Pit inspection notes and sump records.
- Accessibility audit of lifts.
- Modernisation history and plans.
- Car interior refurbishment history.

- Entrapment records with durations and causes.
- Lift contractor reports noting building-side defects such as heat, water and access.
- Records of roof or shaft leaks affecting lift equipment.

pages.title: Lighting Control System
pages.question: How do lighting control systems fail, and how do you tell if they are working?
pages.answer: Lighting controls fail by being defeated rather than broken. Sensors are covered, time clocks bypassed, daylight dimming disabled, and car parks lit at full output all night. Fit-outs leave sensors in the wrong places. Proprietary networked systems lose vendor support and programming tools. The test is simple: walk the building at night and read the interval meter. A good system that has been overridden saves nothing.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lighting control system; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: BMS integration, time clocks, motion/daylight sensors, networked systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A lighting control system decides when lights are on and how bright: time clocks and astronomical timers, photocells, occupancy and absence sensors, daylight sensors that dim lights near windows, switches and scene controllers, and networked systems that address each luminaire individually, such as DALI and proprietary wired and wireless platforms, often linked to the building management system. In common areas and car parks, controls cut most of the lighting energy; in offices they are part of how a tenancy works.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time clocks and contactors | Common areas, external lighting, older buildings | Simple; lose schedules after power failures or daylight saving changes |
| Photocells and astronomical timers | External and façade lighting | Photocells get dirty or shaded; timers need correct location |
| Occupancy and absence sensors | Corridors, stairs, toilets, car parks, offices | Placement and time delay decide success |
| Daylight dimming | Perimeter zones of offices and atria | Often never commissioned, or later disabled |
| DALI and DALI-2 | Offices and commercial from the 2000s | Open standard; needs programming, documentation and gateways |
| Proprietary networked and wireless systems | Offices, retail and campuses from the 2010s | Flexible; vendor lock-in; software support; cyber exposure |
| Integration with BMS, security and emergency lighting tests | Larger buildings | Interfaces break when either side changes |

Energy codes in all three jurisdictions require automatic controls in new and substantially altered buildings, and energy ratings reward them. A good system that has been overridden or never commissioned saves nothing.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time clocks and contactors | 15 to 20 years | Contact wear; battery backup |
| Occupancy and daylight sensors | 10 to 15 years | Technology; damage; dirt |
| DALI controllers and gateways | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Proprietary networked systems | 8 to 15 years | Vendor support; software and app support |
| Wall controllers and scene plates | 15 to 20 years | Use |

What shortens life:

- Vendor end of support for proprietary hardware, software and apps.
- Lost programming, passwords and documentation.
- Fit-outs that move partitions without moving sensors or regrouping fittings.
- Overrides left in place after complaints.

Software and apps age faster than hardware: a system with sound sensors can become unmanageable when the commissioning software stops running on supported computers.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Overrides and defeat

Occupants and facilities staff defeat controls that annoy them: sensors taped over, time clocks bypassed with a switch, lighting held on through the BMS. Car parks then run at full output 24 hours a day, and common areas stay lit all night.

### Poor commissioning and drift

Daylight dimming set too conservatively or switched off; time delays too short (lights going off on people) or too long (saving little); groups that no longer match the floor layout after fit-outs; time clocks that lost their schedule after a power failure or never adjusted for daylight saving.

### Sensor placement

Sensors behind partitions, too far from desks, aimed at corridors or above glazed walls switch lights off on occupants or on for passers-by. Car park sensors that cannot see along aisles leave drivers in the dark.

### Obsolescence and lock-in

Proprietary systems depend on the vendor's gateways, software and commissioning tools. When support ends, faults cannot be fixed and layouts cannot be changed without replacing the system.

### Integration failures

Links to the BMS, security system and automatic emergency lighting tests break when either side is upgraded; automated tests stop silently.

### Cyber exposure

Networked lighting systems on the building or corporate network, with default passwords or unpatched gateways, can be a route into other systems.

### Sensor drift and dirt

Daylight sensors drift and collect dust, so they read less daylight than there is and keep lights brighter than needed. Battery-powered wireless sensors stop reporting when batteries run flat, and systems may default to lights on.

### Emergency lighting test integration

Many DALI and networked systems run automatic emergency lighting tests and log results. When the integration breaks, tests stop running, but the building may still believe it is compliant.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Lights on in empty areas after hours; car parks at full output all night.
- Sensors covered, disconnected or missing; switches added to bypass controls.
- Perimeter lights at full output on bright days.
- Controllers and gateways in plant rooms with fault lights.
- Complaints of lights switching off in meeting rooms or toilets.

### In the records

- Programming backups, group schedules and documentation.
- Vendor, software and firmware versions; support status.
- Interval meter data showing night-time lighting load.
- Complaint records about lighting.

- Wireless sensors with flat or low battery warnings.
- Emergency lighting test logs that stop at a date.
- Time clocks showing the wrong time.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High night-time electricity use | Lighting not switching off | Interval meter data; night visit |
| Lights switching off on occupants | Short time delays or poor sensor placement | Settings; sensor locations against layout |
| Perimeter lights at full output in daylight | Daylight dimming disabled or never set up | Settings; light level measurement |
| No-one can change programming | Proprietary lock-in or lost tools and passwords | Vendor; documentation |
| Emergency lighting tests not running | Integration failure | Test logs |

> The fastest assessment of lighting controls is a walk through the building at night and a look at the interval meter. Both show whether the controls are doing anything.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stairs or egress paths left dark by sensor faults or settings | safety | Fix now |
| System failed, lights stuck on or off | failure | Repair now |
| Overrides, drift and poor commissioning | condition | Recommission in the near term |
| System unsupported or proprietary at end of life | lifecycle | Plan replacement, preferably open protocol |
| No documentation; energy data not reviewed | check | Audit |
| Minor adjustments | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical or lighting controls specialist.

- Night audit: walk the building after hours and note what is on and why.
- Interval meter analysis of lighting loads by time of day and day of week.
- Controls inventory: types, vendors, versions, gateways and support status.
- Sensor and setting review against current layouts: placement, time delays, daylight levels, groups.
- Safety check: stairs and egress paths stay lit when occupied.
- Integration testing with the BMS, security and emergency lighting test systems.
- Documentation and ownership review: programming backups, tools, passwords, who holds them.

The report should quantify energy wasted by poor control, list safety issues, give support status, and recommend recommissioning or replacement.

- Car park check: lighting levels in dimmed mode against the minimum for safe movement.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Recommissioning: reset schedules, time delays and daylight levels; regroup to current layouts; remove overrides. Usually the cheapest energy saving in the building.
- Sensor relocation and replacement to suit layouts.
- Car park controls: dim to a background level when unoccupied rather than switching off, so drivers are never in the dark.
- Replacement with an open-protocol system such as DALI-2, with programming, tools and passwords held by the owner.
- Integration repair with BMS and emergency lighting tests.
- Network security: segregate lighting networks and change default credentials.
- Documentation: groups, schedules, settings and backups.

- Training for facilities staff so settings are changed properly rather than overridden.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and recommissioning are lump sums and usually pay back quickly in energy. Sensor replacements are per unit. System replacement is per floor or per area, often combined with LED conversion so both are done once with ceilings open.

Recommissioning is repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle or an energy upgrade; safety fixes on egress paths are immediate.

Combining control upgrades with LED conversion avoids paying twice for ceiling access.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. NCC Section J requires automatic lighting controls in many spaces in new and altered buildings; NABERS Energy ratings reward effective control.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document L requires lighting controls in new and refurbished buildings; BS EN 15193 sets methods for lighting energy.
- United States. ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC set mandatory controls (occupancy, daylight, scheduling); California Title 24 adds further requirements.

Energy rating and disclosure schemes in all three countries make lighting energy a lettability and compliance issue: NABERS and Commercial Building Disclosure in Australia, Energy Performance Certificates and minimum standards in Britain, and building performance standards in several United States cities. Controls are usually the cheapest way to improve these ratings.

Where controls dim or switch egress lighting, the minimum levels for safe movement in each jurisdiction still apply in every control state, including car parks and stairs.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Programming backups, group and schedule documentation.
- Vendor, software and firmware details and support status.
- Interval meter data for lighting.
- Complaint records.
- Who holds programming tools and passwords.

- Energy ratings and disclosure certificates.
- Records of fit-outs that changed lighting groups.
- Commissioning reports for the original installation.

pages.title: Lighting
pages.question: How do lighting installations fail, and when does obsolescence or safety force replacement?
pages.answer: Lighting is being pushed to LED: fluorescent, metal halide and other mercury lamps are being withdrawn and replacements are scarce. LED fittings fail at their drivers, from heat and surges. The safety findings are elsewhere: steel lighting columns corrode at the ground line and fall in wind, suspended fittings hang from corroded fixings, stairs and car parks are lit below standard, and pre-1980 fittings may hold leaking PCB capacitors.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lighting; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Luminaires for common, external, and specialty areas

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Lighting here covers the luminaires the building owner is responsible for: lobbies, corridors, stairs, toilets, car parks, plant rooms, loading docks, external areas, façade and landscape lighting, and lighting columns on site. Tenant lighting is usually part of fit-outs but may revert to the owner at lease end. Emergency lighting and lighting controls have their own pages.

| Type | Where it is found | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear fluorescent (T8, T5) with magnetic or electronic ballasts | Offices, car parks, corridors, plant rooms from the 1970s | Lamps being withdrawn under mercury rules; ballasts failing |
| Compact fluorescent | Downlights, common areas | Being withdrawn |
| Metal halide and high-pressure sodium | Car parks, external areas, warehouses, sports | Inefficient; slow to restrike; lamps and ballasts scarce |
| Halogen and incandescent | Downlights, displays, older common areas | Inefficient; hot; general lamps restricted in many markets |
| LED | Most new and retrofit installations since the 2010s | Long life; drivers fail first; early products varied in quality |
| Fluorescent fittings with PCB capacitors | Fittings made before about 1980 | Leaking capacitors are hazardous |
| Lighting columns (steel, aluminium, concrete) | Car parks, campuses, external areas | Base corrosion can fell a column |
| Suspended and high-bay fittings | Warehouses, atria, car parks | Fixing corrosion; falling fittings |

Required light levels vary by space: stairs, car parks and external paths have minimums for safe movement and security; offices and work areas have task levels. Many older car parks and stairs fall short because fittings have failed or been removed, lamps have depreciated, or layouts have changed.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED luminaires | 50,000 hours or more to 70 per cent output; 15 to 20 years | Heat; driver quality |
| LED drivers | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Fluorescent fittings | 20 to 25 years | Ballasts; lamp supply ending |
| External luminaires | 15 to 20 years | Ingress protection; coastal exposure |
| Steel lighting columns | 25 to 40 years | Base corrosion; impact |
| Aluminium columns | 30 to 50 years | Base corrosion in salt and soil |
| Concrete columns | 30 to 50 years | Reinforcement corrosion |

What shortens life:

- Heat in enclosed fittings and hot ceiling spaces.
- Water ingress where seals and glands fail.
- Coastal and road-salt exposure on fittings and columns.
- Surges from lightning and switching, especially on long external circuits.
- Vehicle impact in car parks and on columns.
- Poor-quality retrofits.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Lamp obsolescence

Fluorescent, compact fluorescent, metal halide and other mercury-containing lamps are being withdrawn under the Minamata Convention and related rules: most fluorescent tubes left the European Union and British markets in 2023, several United States states have banned them, and Australia is phasing mercury lamps out. Inefficient general-service lamps are also restricted. Buildings still lit by these lamps face rising lamp costs and scarcity and are converting to LED.

### LED driver and product quality

LED chips age slowly; their drivers fail from heat and surges. Early-generation and low-cost LED products suffered colour shift, flicker, poor dimming and early failure. Retrofit LED tubes in fluorescent fittings can be unsafe if the fitting was rewired incorrectly or the tube is unsuited to the ballast.

### Inadequate light levels

Stairs, car parks, loading docks and external paths lit below the required level create trip, vehicle and security risks. Causes include failed fittings left unreplaced, lamp depreciation, dirty or yellowed diffusers, fittings removed in fit-outs, and new layouts.

### Lighting column failure

Steel columns corrode from the inside and outside at and just below ground level, where water and salt collect, and at the access door opening, which weakens the section. They fall without warning in wind. Columns struck by vehicles are cracked or bent at the base. Concrete columns spall when reinforcement corrodes.

### Fixing failure

Suspended fittings in car parks and warehouses hang from fixings that corrode in damp, exhaust-laden air; fittings on façades and soffits corrode at their brackets. Falling fittings are a safety finding.

### PCB capacitors

Fluorescent and high-intensity discharge fittings made before about 1980 often contain capacitors filled with PCBs. As they age they leak an oily residue, and they must be removed and disposed of as hazardous waste.

### Glare, spill and planning conditions

External lighting that spills onto neighbours, the night sky or habitat can breach planning conditions and invite complaints; glare from poorly aimed floodlights reduces visibility rather than improving it.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Lamp and fitting types, counted by area; fittings out; flicker; colour mismatch between fittings.
- Dim stairs, car parks and paths; dark zones between fittings.
- Yellowed diffusers; water and insects inside external fittings.
- Corrosion at column bases, missing or loose access doors, cracked bases, leaning columns.
- Suspended fittings with corroded fixings; fittings hanging by cables.
- Old fluorescent fittings in plant rooms and car parks; oily residue at capacitors.

### In the records

- Lighting inventory and maintenance records; failure rates.
- Lux surveys.
- LED retrofit records and product data.
- Column inspection and testing records.
- Hazardous materials register.
- Energy data for common area lighting.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED fittings failing in clusters on one circuit | Driver failure from heat or surges | Driver type, location and circuit history |
| Fluorescent lamps hard or costly to source | Mercury lamp withdrawal | Supplier advice |
| Dark stairs or car park zones | Failed or removed fittings, or depreciation | Lux survey against the standard |
| Rust and section loss at a column base or door | Ground-line corrosion | Ultrasonic wall thickness test |
| Oily residue in old fittings | Leaking PCB capacitor | Sampling; date of manufacture |
| Flicker or colour shift in LED fittings | Driver or product quality | Product data; replacement history |

> A lighting column with visible corrosion or damage at its base, or a suspended fitting with corroded fixings, is a falling hazard. Treat it as unsafe until tested.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Columns corroded or damaged at the base; suspended fittings with failed fixings; leaking PCB capacitors | safety | Remove, secure or isolate now |
| Stairs, car parks or paths unlit | failure | Restore now |
| Widespread failures; levels below standard | condition | Repair and relamp in the near term |
| Fluorescent and HID lighting due for LED conversion | lifecycle | Plan conversion, often with controls |
| No column testing; PCB status unknown; no lux survey | check | Inspect and survey |
| Isolated failures | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical contractor or lighting engineer; a structural engineer or specialist for column testing.

- Inventory of luminaires by type, wattage, area and age, with failure counts.
- Lux survey on a grid in stairs, car parks, loading docks and external areas, against the relevant standard.
- Column inspection: visual check of base, door and foundation; ultrasonic wall thickness testing at the ground line; tests at intervals set by an inspection regime.
- Fixing inspection of suspended and façade fittings.
- Hazardous materials: identify pre-1980 fittings and sample capacitors where needed.
- Energy review: installed load and hours, savings from LED and controls.
- External lighting review against planning conditions and spill limits.

The report should give the inventory, light levels against standards, column and fixing safety, hazardous materials, and an LED conversion plan with energy savings.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- LED conversion with new fittings rather than retrofit tubes, designed to the required levels, usually combined with controls.
- Car park and stair upgrades to bring levels to standard.
- Column replacement, or base sleeving and repair where testing shows limited loss; impact protection in car parks.
- Fixing replacement with corrosion-resistant fixings; secondary safety chains on suspended fittings.
- PCB removal and disposal as hazardous waste.
- Surge protection on external lighting circuits.
- External lighting redesign to control spill and glare.

- Maintenance factor: design new lighting with realistic allowance for dirt and depreciation, and schedule cleaning.
- Car park protection: guards on low-mounted fittings exposed to vehicles.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
LED conversion is priced per fitting or per area, with access (high-bay and car park work), design, and disposal of old fittings. Columns are priced per column including foundation where needed. Fixing works are per fitting. PCB removal is per fitting with hazardous waste disposal. Lux surveys and column testing are lump sums, with testing recurring.

LED conversion is lifecycle or an energy upgrade with payback; column safety, levels below standard and PCB removal are code compliance; relamping and repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 1680 sets interior lighting, including safe movement in stairs and circulation; AS/NZS 1158 sets public and pedestrian area lighting, applied to car parks and external paths; NCC Section J limits lighting energy in new and altered work; Australia is a party to the Minamata Convention and is phasing out mercury lamps.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 12464-1 and 12464-2 set indoor and outdoor workplace lighting, BS 5489-1 road and public area lighting; the Institution of Lighting Professionals' TR22 sets inspection and testing of lighting columns; most fluorescent lamps were withdrawn from sale in 2023; Approved Document L limits energy.
- United States. Illuminating Engineering Society recommended practices set levels (including parking facilities); ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC limit lighting power; federal efficiency rules restrict inefficient general-service lamps, and several states have banned fluorescent lamps.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Lighting inventory and maintenance records.
- Lux surveys of stairs, car parks and external areas.
- Lighting column inspection and test records.
- LED retrofit records and product warranties.
- Hazardous materials register.
- Common area lighting energy data.
- Planning conditions on external lighting.

- Lighting design reports for recent upgrades.

pages.title: Lightning Protection
pages.question: How do lightning protection systems fail, and how do you know a system still protects the building?
pages.answer: Lightning protection fails by losing continuity and coverage rather than wearing out. Roof works detach conductors and nobody reinstates them; new plant, solar and antennas are left unbonded and outside the protected zone; copper is stolen at low level; earth resistance rises as electrodes corrode; surge protection devices are exhausted after storms. Only continuity and earth testing show whether the system still works. ESE terminals rely on coverage claims the main standards do not recognise.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lightning protection; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Air terminals, down-conductors, earthing systems

sources.title: NFPA 780 Installation of Lightning Protection Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A lightning protection system intercepts lightning strikes and conducts the current safely to earth, so it does not pass through the building fabric, start a fire or damage equipment. External protection comprises air terminals or a mesh of conductors on the roof, down conductors on the façade or within the structure, and an earth termination network. Internal protection comprises equipotential bonding of metal services and surge protection devices on power, data and communications lines.

| Component or type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional air terminals and roof mesh | Most protected buildings | Recognised by all main standards; coverage designed by the rolling sphere or mesh method |
| Down conductors | Façades, within columns, or using the steel frame | Must be continuous and bonded; test joints at the base |
| Earth electrodes and earth network | Below ground around the building | Corrode; resistance rises; disturbed by excavation |
| Bonding to metal roof plant, railings and services | Roofs and service entries | Lost when plant is added or replaced |
| Surge protection devices | Main boards, data and communications entries | Absorb surges and wear out |
| Early streamer emission (ESE) terminals | Some buildings, marketed as covering wider areas | The enhanced coverage claimed is not recognised by IEC and BS EN 62305, and NFPA 780 does not cover them |

Not every building needs a system; the decision comes from a risk assessment considering height, exposure, construction, contents, occupants and the consequence of a strike. Tall buildings, buildings on exposed sites, hazardous stores, heritage buildings, hospitals and buildings with sensitive electronics usually do.

Design follows a lightning protection level chosen from the risk assessment. Under IEC and BS EN 62305 there are four levels (I is the most demanding), each with its own rolling sphere radius (20, 30, 45 and 60 metres), mesh size and down conductor spacing. Natural components such as a continuous steel frame, reinforcing steel or a metal roof can form part of the system if they are electrically continuous and thick enough, which is common in modern framed buildings and must be confirmed rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copper and aluminium conductors | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; theft; dissimilar metals; coastal exposure |
| Air terminals | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; damage |
| Earth electrodes | 20 to 40 years | Soil corrosivity; excavation |
| Test joints and clamps | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; tampering |
| Surge protection devices | Until they absorb enough surges; often 5 to 15 years | Lightning activity; switching surges |

What shortens life:

- Roof works that detach conductors and do not reinstate them.
- New rooftop plant, solar arrays and antennas added without bonding or coverage.
- Copper theft of down conductors and earth tapes.
- Dissimilar metals: aluminium against copper or lead, causing corrosion at joints.
- Excavation that damages earth electrodes.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Loss of continuity

Conductors detach from their fixings, are cut during roof works, or are stolen. A break in the path means a strike looks for another way to earth: through the fabric, services or people.

### Rising earth resistance

Earth electrodes corrode, soil dries, and connections loosen. Higher resistance means higher voltages during a strike and a greater chance of side flashing to services.

### Coverage gaps

New plant, solar arrays, antennas, telecommunications masts and roof extensions sit outside the original protected zone or are left unbonded.

### Bonding failures

Metal pipes, cable trays, handrails and plant that are not bonded can flash over to the protection system or to each other, causing fire or damage.

### Surge protection exhaustion

Surge protection devices sacrifice themselves to protect equipment; after enough surges they no longer protect, often without obvious indication unless status indicators are checked.

### Side flashing and touch voltages

Where metal services, plant or people are too close to a down conductor, the strike current can jump across the gap (side flashing). Near down conductors at ground level, people can be exposed to dangerous touch and step voltages; insulation, barriers or bonding control this.

### Unverified natural components

Systems that rely on the steel frame or reinforcement as down conductors depend on continuity that was meant to be confirmed at construction. Later alterations, cut reinforcement and replaced roof sheeting can break that continuity without anyone noticing.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On the roof and façade

- Conductors loose, detached, cut or missing; fixings broken.
- Plant, solar and antennas without bonding connections.
- Corrosion at joints, especially between dissimilar metals.
- Test joints at the base of down conductors missing, damaged or painted over.
- Down conductors stolen at low level.

### In the records

- Design, risk assessment and drawings.
- Inspection and test reports with earth resistance readings.
- Records of roof works and plant additions.
- Surge protection device status checks.

- Burn marks or melted fixings near air terminals after storms.
- Equipment failures after storms.

- Air terminals bent or missing after roof works.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conductor ends hanging free near new plant | Roof works without reinstatement | Continuity test |
| Missing down conductors at low level | Theft | Inspection |
| High earth resistance readings | Corroded electrodes or dry soil | Test against previous readings |
| Equipment damage after storms | Surge protection absent or exhausted | Device status; coordination |
| ESE terminal with few down conductors | Design relying on unrecognised coverage claims | Design review against the standard |

After a strike, damage tells you where the current went: burns at joints and fixings point to poor connections; damage to equipment inside points to missing bonding or surge protection; damage to masonry points to side flashing or a broken conductor.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose conductors at height over public areas; protection missing on hazardous stores | safety | Secure or rectify now |
| System broken (continuity lost) | failure | Repair now |
| Inspection and testing due | deadline | At the interval the standard sets |
| High earth resistance; corrosion; unbonded plant | condition | Repair in the near term |
| System at end of life | lifecycle | Replace, often with re-roofing |
| No risk assessment; ESE system; no records | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A lightning protection specialist or electrical engineer.

- Risk assessment to confirm whether protection is required and to what level.
- Visual inspection of air terminations, conductors, fixings, joints, bonding and test points.
- Continuity testing of conductors and bonds.
- Earth resistance testing of each electrode and the whole network.
- Coverage check of new plant, solar and antennas against the design.
- Surge protection review: devices present, status, coordination.

The report should give the system status, test readings against previous results, gaps, and works needed.

Inspection intervals under BS EN 62305 depend on the protection level: for levels I and II, a visual inspection every year and a complete inspection every two years; for levels III and IV, every two and four years. Critical structures such as those with explosive or flammable contents are inspected more often. Earth resistance is measured by fall-of-potential or clamp methods and compared with previous readings rather than judged alone.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Reinstate and refix conductors; replace stolen sections with less attractive materials or concealed routes.
- Bond new plant, solar arrays and antennas.
- Extend coverage to new roof elements.
- Earth improvement: additional or replacement electrodes.
- Surge protection: replace exhausted devices and coordinate across boards and data entries.
- Redesign of ESE-based systems to a recognised standard where risk requires.
- Coordinate with re-roofing so the system is reinstated and tested.

Interactions: lightning protection must be bonded to new solar arrays, plant and antennas, coordinated with surge protection at the main switchboard, and reinstated after every re-roofing; heritage buildings may need conductor routes approved.

- Test joints reinstated at the base of every down conductor so future testing is possible.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and testing are recurring lump sums. Repairs are itemised by length of conductor or per bond. Earth improvements are per electrode. Full replacement is a lump sum, often carried with re-roofing. Surge protection is per device.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle.

Theft-prone sites may justify concealed or less valuable conductor materials despite higher installation cost. Inspections are best combined with roof access for other work.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 1768 sets lightning protection, including risk assessment, design and inspection; surge protection follows AS/NZS 1768 and AS/NZS 3000.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 62305 sets risk assessment, design and inspection, with visual inspection and full testing at intervals set by the protection level (more often for higher levels); BS 7430 covers earthing.
- United States. NFPA 780 sets installation requirements; UL 96A covers installation and certification; NFPA 70 covers surge protection devices.

Insurers in all three jurisdictions may require lightning protection for high-risk buildings and evidence of inspection. Heritage buildings often have historic systems that need repair rather than replacement, with routes agreed with heritage authorities.

Explosives and flammable stores carry stricter protection and inspection requirements in all three jurisdictions under their hazardous materials rules.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Risk assessment and design drawings.
- Inspection and test reports with earth resistance readings.
- Records of roof works and plant additions.
- Surge protection device schedule.

- Insurer requirements and inspection records.
- Records of strikes and storm damage.
- Heritage constraints on conductor routes.

- Records of plant, antennas and solar added to the roof since the last inspection.

pages.title: Load-Bearing Masonry
pages.question: How do load-bearing masonry walls fail, and when do alterations or bowing make them unsafe?
pages.answer: Load-bearing masonry rarely fails on its own; it fails when it loses support or restraint. Walls and chimney breasts removed without engineering, steel beams on inadequate bearings, floors not tied to walls so gables bow, rubble-cored stone faces separating, and rotted timber lintels behind arches are the common causes. Bowing walls and crushed bearings need urgent engineering. Unreinforced masonry is the most vulnerable construction in earthquakes.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about load-bearing masonry; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Solid brick, stone, or blockwork walls, lintels, arches

sources.title: Technical advice
sources.publisher: Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Load-bearing masonry walls carry floors and roofs as well as enclosing the building. They are solid brick, stone or blockwork, sometimes cavity walls where the inner leaf carries the load, with arches, lintels and piers over and between openings. Most pre-war houses, terraces, warehouses and institutional buildings in Australia, Britain and the United States are load-bearing masonry, as are many low-rise apartment blocks of later eras. The façade aspects of masonry (ties, pointing, spalling) are covered on the masonry and brickwork page; this page covers how masonry carries load and how that fails.

| Form | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid brick walls | Pre-war houses, terraces, warehouses | Removed walls and breasts; lack of restraint; settlement |
| Stone walls with rubble cores | Older buildings, especially in Britain and colonial Australia | Separation of faces from cores; bulging |
| Cavity walls with load-bearing inner leaf | Mid twentieth century onward | Ties; inner leaf alterations |
| Concrete blockwork | Low-rise residential and commercial | Shrinkage cracking; reinforcement where present |
| Unreinforced masonry in seismic regions | Older buildings in California and other seismic areas | Collapse in earthquakes |

Masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension and bending. It depends on being held in line by the floors and roof it supports, on arches and lintels spanning openings, and on not being weakened by holes and removed walls. Most structural failures in masonry buildings come from alterations or loss of restraint rather than from the masonry itself.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid brick and stone walls | Centuries if dry and restrained | Water; alterations; foundation movement |
| Lime mortar joints | 50 to 100 years | Exposure; hard repointing |
| Timber lintels and bond timbers | 50 to 150 years | Decay; insects |
| Steel lintels | 40 to 80 years | Corrosion |
| Brick arches | Life of the building | Spreading; abutment movement |
| Wall restraint straps and ties | 50 years and more | Corrosion |

What shortens life:

- Alterations: walls removed, openings widened, chimney breasts taken out.
- Loss of restraint: floors and roofs not tied to walls, or ties removed.
- Water washing out mortar and rotting embedded timbers.
- Foundation movement.
- Hard cement repairs and impermeable coatings.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Alterations

Load-bearing walls removed to open up rooms, openings widened, chimney breasts removed and walls chased for services remove support or concentrate load. Steel beams inserted without adequate bearings, padstones or engineering crush the masonry at their ends.

### Bowing and lack of restraint

Walls that are not tied to the floors and roof they support can bow outward, especially tall gable walls and walls where floor joists run parallel and so do not bear on them. Removal of internal walls that braced external ones has the same effect.

### Separation of rubble-cored walls

Stone walls with rubble cores separate as the core mortar washes out; the outer faces bulge and can collapse.

### Lintel and arch failure

Timber lintels behind arches and timber bond courses in old walls rot; steel lintels corrode; arches spread when their abutments move or when nearby openings remove their support. Masonry above drops and cracks.

### Overload

New loads such as storage, roof plant, added storeys and heavier roof coverings can exceed the capacity of slender or weakened walls, which crush, crack vertically or bow.

### Settlement

Foundation movement cracks masonry walls diagonally through openings; see the foundations page.

### Earthquake vulnerability

Unreinforced masonry is the most vulnerable common construction in earthquakes: walls fall outward, parapets and chimneys collapse, and floors pull out of their bearings. Seismic regions require or encourage retrofit.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Walls bowing outward or out of plumb, especially gables and tall walls.
- Cracks below beam ends; crushed or cracked masonry at bearings.
- Cracks and dropped brickwork over openings; arches cracked at the crown or separating at the springing.
- Bulging stone faces; loose stones.
- Rooms opened up by removing walls or chimney breasts, with new beams.
- Vertical cracking in piers between openings.

### In the records

- Building approvals and engineering for alterations.
- Previous structural reports.
- Restraint or strapping works.
- Seismic evaluations in seismic regions.

- Doors and windows in upper storeys that bind or have been planed repeatedly, often the first sign of a wall moving out of plumb.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall bowing outward with floors running parallel | Lack of restraint | Plumb survey; inspection of floor-to-wall connections |
| Cracks below the ends of a new beam | Inadequate bearing or padstone | Opening up at the bearing |
| Dropped brickwork over an opening | Failed lintel or spreading arch | Inspection of lintel or abutment |
| Bulging stone face with cracks | Separation from the rubble core | Tapping; endoscope into the core |
| Vertical cracks in a heavily loaded pier | Overload or crushing | Load review |
| Diagonal cracks through openings | Foundation movement | See the foundations page |

> Alterations to load-bearing walls without engineering are a common cause of structural failure in older buildings. Where walls or chimney breasts have been removed, find out what is now carrying the load.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walls bowing significantly; crushed bearings under beams; bulging stone faces; unreinforced masonry parapets in seismic areas | safety | Prop and engineer now |
| Failed lintels with dropped masonry; unsupported loads after alterations | failure | Support and repair now |
| Seismic retrofit required by ordinance | deadline | By the ordinance date |
| Early bowing; cracked arches; decaying lintels | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Lintels at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Alterations with no engineering on record | check | Assess |
| Stable minor cracks | nil | Monitor |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer experienced with masonry and, for heritage buildings, conservation.

- Plumb and bulge survey of walls, with monitoring where movement is suspected.
- Restraint check: how floors, roofs and walls are connected, by opening up at representative points.
- Alteration review: identify removed walls and breasts and check what supports the load, with approvals.
- Bearing inspection at beam ends and lintels.
- Wall construction: solid, cavity or rubble-cored, by endoscope or opening.
- Load review against current use.
- Seismic evaluation in seismic regions.

The report should state stability, the cause of movement, safety measures and repairs.

Movement is judged over time: fixed survey targets on bowing walls, read several times over a year, show whether a bow is historic and stable or still growing, which decides between monitoring and immediate restraint.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restraint: straps tying floors and roofs to walls, tie rods with pattress plates across buildings, and helical ties into walls.
- Bearings: padstones and spreader beams under beam ends.
- Lintel replacement and arch repair.
- Crack stitching with helical bars after the cause is addressed.
- Grouting of rubble cores and pinning of stone faces.
- Rebuilding of badly bowed or failed sections.
- Seismic retrofit: anchoring walls to floors, bracing parapets, adding frames or walls.
- Retrospective engineering and approval for past alterations.

- Temporary propping and shoring while permanent repairs are designed, so that a bowing wall or failed lintel cannot collapse in the meantime.
- Lime-based repairs in traditional masonry so repairs move and breathe with the original, avoiding the damage hard cement causes.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum. Restraint and stitching are priced per tie or per metre. Lintel replacement per opening with propping. Rebuilding by area. Seismic retrofit is a lump-sum project. Propping is an immediate cost.

Repairs to stop movement are condition items; ordinance retrofits are deadlines; safety items are immediate.

Propping and shoring can run for months while designs and approvals are prepared, and their hire is a recurring cost until the permanent repair is complete. Work to party walls adds surveyors' fees and agreement with neighbours. Heritage approval can extend programmes and require specialist materials and trades.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 3700 and AS 4773 govern masonry; AS 1170.4 sets earthquake actions; alterations to load-bearing walls need building approval; heritage controls often apply.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 1996 governs masonry; Approved Document A covers structure and restraint; alterations need building regulations approval and often party wall notices; heritage buildings need listed building consent.
- United States. TMS 402 governs masonry design; the International Existing Building Code Appendix A1 covers seismic strengthening of unreinforced masonry; several California cities require unreinforced masonry and soft-storey retrofits.

In all three jurisdictions, past alterations without approval can create disclosure, insurance and certification issues at sale or refinancing, and may require retrospective approval or rectification before a building can be certified. Strata and leasehold buildings treat load-bearing walls as common or landlord structure even where they sit within a unit, so owners cannot alter them without consent.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Building approvals and engineering for alterations.
- Previous structural reports.
- Restraint and strengthening records.
- Seismic evaluations and retrofit orders.
- Heritage listing.

- Records of chimney breast or wall removals, with what now supports the load.
- Monitoring data for bowing walls.
- Party wall awards for work to shared walls.
- Strata or landlord consents for alterations within units.

pages.title: Loading Docks & Goods Handling
pages.question: How do loading docks fail as working spaces, and which dock findings are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Docks fail first on safety: forklifts, reversing trucks and pedestrians mixing without segregation; roller shutters with failed springs or safety edges; open dock edges; fumes from idling vehicles entering the building. Then on condition and capacity: columns and doors struck repeatedly, slab joints broken by heavy forklifts, depressed docks flooding when pumps fail, and waste rooms overflowing with odour, vermin and fire risk.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about loading docks & goods handling; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Industrial finishes, safety systems, equipment integration

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Loading docks and goods handling areas are where vehicles deliver and collect goods and waste: truck bays and hardstand, dock levellers and doors, the dock floor, goods lifts and hoists, waste and recycling rooms, bin wash areas and the corridors that lead into the building. Functionally the dock must let vehicles, forklifts, trolleys and people move without colliding, keep weather and fumes out of the building, carry heavy loads, drain properly, and handle waste hygienically. In shopping centres, hospitals, hotels and mixed-use buildings it is shared by many tenants and operators and is often the most abused space in the building.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dock doors | Roller shutters, sectional doors, high-speed doors | Safe operation; weather and security |
| Dock levellers and restraints | Hydraulic levellers, vehicle restraints, bumpers | Free-fall protection; trailer creep |
| Dock floor and hardstand | Heavy-duty concrete, joints, drainage | Loads, joints, falls to drains |
| Traffic management | Line marking, barriers, pedestrian paths, mirrors, lighting | Segregation of people and vehicles |
| Waste and recycling rooms | Bin rooms, compactors, bin wash | Hygiene, vermin, fire, ventilation |
| Goods lifts and hoists | Goods lifts serving floors and tenancies | Reliability; door damage |
| Ventilation | Exhaust for vehicle fumes in enclosed docks | Diesel fumes and carbon monoxide |
| Impact protection | Bollards, column guards, wall protection | Protecting structure and services |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roller shutters and dock doors | 15 to 20 years; springs and motors sooner | Cycles; impact; maintenance |
| Dock levellers | 15 to 25 years | Loads; impact |
| Dock floor joints and surfaces | 10 to 20 years before major repair | Wheel loads; impact |
| Line marking and signage | 2 to 5 years | Traffic |
| Compactors and waste equipment | 10 to 15 years | Use; maintenance |
| Bollards and guards | 10 to 20 years | Impact |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Larger vehicles than the dock was designed for, scraping canopies and turning over kerbs.
- Heavier forklifts, including battery-electric models, overloading levellers and slab joints.
- More tenants and deliveries than the dock was sized for, causing congestion.
- Poor waste management that spills into circulation and drains.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Vehicle and pedestrian collisions

Docks mix reversing trucks, forklifts and pedestrians. Without segregated walkways, barriers, lighting and rules, people are struck; this is among the most serious workplace hazards in buildings with docks.

### Dock door failures

Roller shutters and sectional doors are struck by vehicles and forklifts; counterbalance springs and cables fail; safety edges and photo-eyes are damaged or bypassed. A door whose spring fails can drop suddenly.

### Falls from dock edges

Open dock edges without doors closed or barriers, and levellers left raised, create drops for people and forklifts. Trailers pulling away early or creeping are covered on the dock leveller page.

### Impact damage

Columns, walls, services, sprinkler pipes and door frames in docks are struck repeatedly; unprotected columns can be weakened, and struck sprinkler pipes flood docks.

### Drainage and flooding

Depressed truck docks drain to pits and pumps; blocked grates and failed pumps flood the dock in storms. Oil and waste wash into stormwater without interceptors.

### Waste room hygiene and fire

Overflowing bins, broken compactors and poor washdown attract vermin and odour; waste rooms are also a common fire origin when bins are stored against walls or under combustible linings.

### Fumes

Vehicles idling in enclosed docks fill them with diesel fumes and carbon monoxide that can be drawn into the building through doors and air intakes.

Congestion compounds every hazard: when more deliveries arrive than bays allow, trucks wait on access roads and footpaths and drivers take shortcuts.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Pedestrian routes absent or crossed by forklift paths; worn line marking; no barriers at doors.
- Damaged roller shutters, guide rails and safety edges; doors held open.
- Gouged columns and walls; missing bollards; damaged sprinkler pipes.
- Broken slab joints and potholes in the dock floor.
- Ponding and blocked grates; pump alarms.
- Overflowing waste rooms; odour; vermin evidence.
- Fumes in the dock and adjoining corridors.

### In the records

- Traffic management plan.
- Incident and near-miss reports.
- Door and leveller maintenance records.
- Waste contracts and complaints.
- Pump and drainage maintenance.

- Trucks queuing on public roads or footpaths waiting for a bay.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Near misses between forklifts and people | No segregation or traffic plan | Observation; incident records |
| Door damaged repeatedly at the same height | Vehicle or forklift impact | Door location against traffic paths |
| Canopy and services damaged at the dock entry | Vehicles taller than the dock was designed for | Clearance against vehicle fleet |
| Dock floods in storms | Blocked grates or failed pumps | Inspection; pump tests |
| Odour and vermin in the dock | Waste room management | Inspection; contract review |

> Vehicle-pedestrian segregation, dock door safety devices and dock edge protection are life-safety matters. Fix them before condition items.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No pedestrian segregation; dock doors with failed safety devices or springs; open edges; fumes entering the building | safety | Rectify now |
| Dock unusable through door, leveller or flooding failure | failure | Repair now |
| Statutory inspections of doors, lifts or equipment due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Impact damage; slab joints; waste hygiene | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Doors, levellers and finishes at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No traffic management plan or capacity review | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a workplace transport or safety specialist, the dock equipment and door contractors, and the centre or facilities manager who runs the dock.

- Operations observation at peak delivery times, recording vehicle movements and sizes, reversing manoeuvres, forklift and trolley paths, pedestrian routes, and where people wait.
- Traffic management review: whether there is a written plan, whether it matches what happens, and whether segregation, crossings, barriers, mirrors and lighting support it.
- Door and leveller safety checks: springs, cables, safety edges, photo-eyes, free-fall protection and restraints, against maintenance records.
- Impact damage survey of columns, walls, door frames, sprinkler pipes and services, with a structural engineer where columns are damaged.
- Floor, drainage and pump survey: joints, surface, falls, grates, pits, pumps and interceptors.
- Waste room review: capacity against tenants, equipment, washdown, vermin control, fire separation and sprinkler coverage.
- Air quality check for diesel fumes and carbon monoxide in enclosed docks and adjoining spaces.

The report should rank safety measures first, then capacity and condition, with a staged plan that keeps deliveries running.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Traffic management: physically segregated walkways with barriers, marked crossings, convex mirrors, good lighting and a written plan briefed to drivers and staff.
- Dock door safety: replace failed springs and cables, restore safety edges and photo-eyes, add guide protection and fast-acting doors where traffic is heavy.
- Impact protection: bollards at doors and corners, column guards, and protection for sprinkler pipes and services in vehicle paths.
- Floor and joint repair with armoured joints in forklift routes.
- Drainage: regular grate and pit cleaning, pump maintenance with alarms, oil interceptors where vehicles wash or leak.
- Waste rooms: right-sized rooms, compactors, washdown with drainage, vermin proofing, fire-rated enclosure and sprinkler coverage.
- Ventilation of enclosed docks, interlocked with carbon monoxide detection, and no-idling rules.
- Delivery scheduling where docks are congested, reducing conflicts without building works.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Traffic management works, bollards and guards are itemised and modest, and among the best value safety spending in a building. Doors and levellers are priced per bay; floor repairs by length of joint or area; waste room upgrades and ventilation are lump sums. Works in operating docks are usually done at night or in stages, adding cost. Tenants and operators often share dock costs through outgoings.

Safety items are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Work health and safety laws require traffic management where vehicles and people interact, with Safe Work Australia guidance on traffic management in workplaces; powered garage and industrial door drives follow AS/NZS 60335.2.95; waste room requirements are set by councils and the National Construction Code.
- United Kingdom. The Health and Safety Executive's workplace transport guidance and the Workplace Regulations 1992 require safe traffic routes; powered industrial doors follow BS EN 13241 and BS EN 12453; Approved Document H covers refuse storage.
- United States. OSHA requires safe walking-working surfaces, forklift operation and dock safety measures; industrial doors follow UL 325 for operators; local codes set waste room and ventilation requirements.

Planning approvals in all three countries often limit delivery hours and vehicle sizes, constraining how docks can operate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Traffic management plan.
- Incident and near-miss reports at the dock.
- Dock door and leveller maintenance and safety records.
- Waste contracts and complaint records.
- Drainage and pump maintenance records.
- Delivery schedules and vehicle sizes.

- Planning conditions on delivery hours and vehicle sizes.
- Records of structural damage from vehicle impacts.

pages.title: Lobbies & Atria
pages.question: How do lobbies and atria fail, and what makes a large open volume unsafe?
pages.answer: Atria are judged on what can fall, what can burn and what can be reached. Older overhead glass that is not laminated can fall; upper-level balustrades below current heights or with climbable rails create fall risks; smoke control fails when fans and make-up air fail or the volume is infilled. Then comfort and maintenance: atria stratify and overheat at the top, condense on cold glass, echo, and leave lights and detectors at height unmaintained for lack of access.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lobbies & atria; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Floor finishes, wall treatments, ceiling systems, lighting, architectural elements

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Lobbies and atria are the large internal volumes that organise a building: ground floor lobbies leading to lifts, and multi-storey atria that bring daylight into deep plans and connect floors visually. They combine architectural finishes, high-level glazing and lighting, open edges at upper levels, and in atria, smoke control systems that make the open volume safe in a fire. Functionally they must be safe to stand under and beside, comfortable, maintainable at height, and controllable in a fire.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overhead glazing and roofs | Glazed atrium roofs, skylights, clerestories | Overhead glass safety; leaks; heat gain; cleaning |
| Edges and balustrades | Balustrades on upper-level walkways and bridges | Fall protection; climbability; glass safety |
| Smoke control | Atrium smoke exhaust, make-up air, smoke curtains | Keeping smoke above people in a fire |
| Finishes | Stone floors, feature walls, high ceilings | Durability, slip, acoustics |
| High-level lighting and equipment | Feature lighting, speakers, detectors at height | Maintenance access |
| Climate control | Air conditioning, perimeter heating, natural ventilation | Stratification, solar gain, draughts |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finishes refurbishment | 15 to 25 years | Market; wear |
| Atrium glazing seals and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | UV; movement |
| Atrium glass | 25 to 40 years | Breakage; coatings |
| Smoke control equipment | 20 to 25 years | Testing; controls |
| High-level lighting | 15 to 20 years | Technology; access |
| Balustrades | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; code changes |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Maintenance access that was never designed, so high-level items are neglected.
- Solar gain and stratification that make atria hot at upper levels.
- Alterations that enclose or infill the volume and undermine smoke control.
- Acoustic problems as hard finishes reflect noise.

Atria are often the oldest-looking part of a refurbished building, because their height makes them the hardest and most expensive area to refresh.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Overhead glass and falling objects

Atrium roofs and high glazing overhang occupied floors. Overhead glass must hold together when broken; older monolithic toughened or wired glass can fall. High-level fittings, signs and decorations can also fall if fixings corrode or are disturbed.

### Falls from upper levels

Atria create open edges on every upper floor. Balustrades below current heights, with climbable rails or furniture placed against them, and glass panels that can break and fall, create fall risks to people above and impact risks to people below. Some buildings have needed screens to prevent deliberate falls.

### Smoke control failure

An atrium connects floors that would otherwise be separate compartments. In a fire, smoke rises into the atrium and must be exhausted fast enough to stay above people. Failed fans, blocked make-up air, enclosed floors and untested systems turn the atrium into a smoke chimney.

### Comfort and condensation

Atria stratify: hot air collects at the top, making upper walkways uncomfortable, while the ground floor is cold and draughty. Glazed roofs gain heat in summer and lose it in winter, and condensation drips from cold glass and frames.

### Acoustics

Large volumes with hard finishes echo, making announcements unintelligible and lobbies noisy.

### Inaccessible maintenance

Lights, detectors, speakers and glazing at height that can only be reached by scaffold or large lifts go unmaintained, and failed lights and detectors are left in place.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Balustrade heights and climbability at upper levels; furniture or planters against them.
- Glass type markings in atrium roofs and balustrades; cracked panes.
- Leak staining on atrium floors and walls; condensation marks.
- Failed high-level lights and fittings left in place.
- Upper walkways noticeably hotter than the ground floor.
- Smoke curtains, vents and fans present; obstructions around them.
- Infilled floors or new enclosures within the atrium.

### In the records

- Fire engineering report and atrium smoke control design.
- Integrated smoke control test reports.
- Glass schedules for roof and balustrades.
- Maintenance access strategy.
- Leak history.

- Furniture, planters or display stands placed against upper-level balustrades.
- Echo making announcements hard to understand.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drips onto the floor in cold weather without rain | Condensation on cold glass or frames | Weather correlation; humidity |
| Drips in rain | Glazing seal or gutter failure | Water test |
| Upper levels hot, ground floor draughty | Stratification and stack effect | Temperature profile |
| Many failed high-level lights | No practical maintenance access | Access strategy |
| Smoke test fails to clear the atrium | Exhaust or make-up air shortfall, or changed geometry | Integrated test; layout review |

> Any change that encloses, infills or alters an atrium can invalidate its smoke control design. Check the fire engineering basis before approving works within the volume.

Problems in atria are usually of three kinds: safety at the edges and overhead, smoke behaviour in a fire, and comfort and maintenance. Each needs its own specialist, and the smoke question is the one most often left untested after alterations.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-laminated overhead glass over occupied areas with breakage history; low or climbable balustrades at upper levels; smoke control failing tests | safety | Protect, restrict access or rectify now |
| Leaks damaging finishes; lights and detectors failed at height | failure | Repair now |
| Smoke control testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Comfort and acoustic problems; worn finishes | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Finishes and glazing seals at end of life | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Glass types and smoke design unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or façade engineer with a fire engineer and services engineer.

- Overhead glazing survey: glass types, seals, gutters, cracked or loose panes, from access equipment.
- Edge survey: balustrade heights, openings, climbability, glass type and fixings at every upper level.
- Smoke control review against the fire engineering report, with integrated testing.
- Comfort survey: temperature profile by level, draughts, solar gain, condensation.
- Acoustic assessment where announcements or noise are a problem.
- Maintenance access review: how every high-level item is reached.
- Alteration review: changes to the volume since design.

The report should state safety items, smoke control status, comfort and acoustic issues, and a maintenance access and refurbishment plan.

Inspection of high-level elements is best combined with scheduled glazing cleaning or smoke testing, when access equipment is already in place.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Overhead glass: replace with laminated glass or add protective screens; renew seals and gutters.
- Balustrades: raise heights, close climbable rails, replace monolithic glass, add screens where risk warrants.
- Smoke control: repair fans and dampers, restore make-up air, redesign after alterations.
- Comfort: high-level exhaust or destratification fans, solar control glazing or films, draught lobbies at entries.
- Acoustic treatment: absorptive panels, baffles and finishes.
- Maintenance access: gantries, monorails, winches for lights, or relocation of equipment to reachable positions.
- Refurbishment of finishes and lighting.

- Edge management: rules and fixings that keep furniture, planters and display items away from balustrades so they cannot be climbed.
- Condensation control: thermally broken frames, warm air washes over glazing, or humidity control where drips recur.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
High-level work in atria is dominated by access: scaffolds over occupied floors, specialist lifts and out-of-hours work. Glazing and balustrade works are per pane or per metre plus access. Smoke control works and redesign are lump sums. Maintenance access installations are lump sums that reduce future costs. Refurbishment is a lump sum.

Safety items are immediate or code compliance; smoke testing recurs; refurbishment is lifecycle; access installations are improvements with operating savings.

Because access is the main cost, inspection, cleaning, lamp replacement and glazing repairs should be bundled into a single high-level campaign every few years rather than done piecemeal.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code treats atria as a special case, with smoke hazard management, sprinklers and separation requirements; AS 1288 governs overhead and barrier glass and AS 1668.1 smoke control; changes to an atrium generally need fire engineering review and building approval.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B and BS 9999 cover atria, including when they may connect floors and what smoke control they need, with smoke control components to the BS EN 12101 series; Approved Document K covers guarding and glazing; higher-risk residential atria fall under the Building Safety Act 2022.
- United States. International Building Code Section 404 governs atriums, requiring sprinklers and smoke control designed and tested under Section 909 and NFPA 92; guards follow Section 1015 and overhead glazing Chapter 24; alterations need fire department review.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire engineering report and atrium smoke design.
- Integrated smoke control test reports.
- Glass schedules for roof and balustrades.
- Maintenance access strategy and equipment certification.
- Leak and condensation history.
- Records of alterations within the atrium.

- Balustrade and edge protection certificates.
- Comfort and condensation complaints by level.
- High-level lighting and detector maintenance records.

pages.title: Localised HVAC
pages.question: How do split systems, VRF, rooftop units and heat pumps fail, and when does refrigerant or electronics end their life?
pages.answer: Localised systems end their life on electronics, outdoor coils and refrigerant. Inverter boards fail after power disturbances and parts for older models disappear; outdoor coils corrode in salt air; flare joints leak; R22 units are almost unserviceable and R410A faces rising costs. VRF puts large refrigerant charges in occupied rooms and needs concentration limits and leak detection. Gas rooftop units risk carbon monoxide from cracked heat exchangers.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about localised hvac; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Split systems, multi-head systems, heat pumps, underfloor heating

sources.title: Section 608 of the Clean Air Act

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Localised HVAC is heating and cooling equipment that serves a room, a dwelling or a tenancy rather than a whole building: split systems and multi-head splits, ducted reverse-cycle systems, variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems, packaged rooftop units, heat pumps for space and water heating, evaporative coolers, and hydronic or electric underfloor heating. It is the dominant system in Australian houses and apartments, in smaller offices and retail everywhere, and in much of the United States.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall-mounted split system | Houses, apartments, small offices | Cheap, short-lived; electronics and outdoor coils fail |
| Multi-head split | Apartments, small offices | One outdoor unit, several indoor; whole system fails together |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | Australian houses and townhouses | Indoor unit in the roof space; ductwork and zoning |
| Variable refrigerant flow (VRF/VRS) | Offices, hotels, apartments from the 2000s | Large refrigerant charges piped through the building; branch boxes; proprietary controls |
| Packaged rooftop unit | Retail, industrial, US commercial | Self-contained; often gas heating; exposed to weather |
| Air-source heat pump | Houses and small commercial; replacing boilers | Space heating and hot water; refrigerant rules apply |
| Evaporative cooler | Australian houses in dry climates | Pads, pump and fan on the roof; water quality |
| Underfloor heating | Houses, apartments, some commercial | Hydronic pipes or electric mats in slabs; long life, hard to repair |

Ownership is often split. In strata buildings, indoor units belong to the lot, outdoor units sit on common property roofs or balconies, and refrigerant pipework passes through common property. In offices, tenants may own and maintain their own units. Replacement, access and refrigerant leaks then involve several parties.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Equipment | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall-mounted split | 10 to 15 years | Electronics; coastal exposure |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | 12 to 18 years | Run hours; roof space heat |
| VRF outdoor units | 15 to 20 years | Compressor; coastal exposure |
| VRF indoor units and branch boxes | 15 to 20 years | Electronics; fans |
| Packaged rooftop units | 15 to 20 years | Weather; coil corrosion; heat exchanger |
| Air-source heat pumps | 15 to 20 years | Cycling; coastal exposure |
| Evaporative coolers | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; pads; corrosion |
| Underfloor heating pipe in slab | 40 years and more | Pipe type; oxygen barrier |
| Underfloor electric mats | 20 to 30 years | Damage at installation |

What shortens life:

- Coastal air on outdoor coils and casings.
- Poor installation: refrigerant flare joints that leak, pipework not pressure tested, condensate drains without fall.
- Outdoor units crammed together or boxed in, recirculating hot air.
- Electrical supply problems: surges and voltage dips damage inverter electronics.
- No maintenance: filters and coils never cleaned.
- Obsolete refrigerants.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Refrigerant leaks and obsolescence

Splits leak at flare joints and brazed connections; VRF systems, with long runs and many joints, can lose large charges. Equipment on R22 is now hard to service anywhere, and units on R410A face rising refrigerant costs as HFCs are phased down; newer units use R32 and other lower-GWP refrigerants that are mildly flammable (A2L) and need different installation rules.

### Electronics failure

Inverter boards, sensors and communication boards fail, often after power disturbances. Parts for older models stop being available, and a single board failure can make a ten-year-old unit uneconomic to repair.

### Outdoor coil corrosion

Aluminium fins corrode and separate from tubes in salt air; capacity falls on the hottest and coldest days. Units within a few hundred metres of surf can fail in under ten years without coated coils.

### Condensate leaks

Indoor unit drains block or lose fall; condensate pumps fail; water leaks onto walls, ceilings and floors.

### VRF-specific risks

VRF systems put a large refrigerant charge into pipework running through occupied spaces.
