Codes limit how much refrigerant may be in a room relative to its volume, and require leak detection and other measures for small rooms. Systems are proprietary: controls, branch boxes and parts tie the building to one manufacturer.

### Rooftop unit risks

Gas-fired rooftop units have heat exchangers that crack with age, risking carbon monoxide entering the supply air; economisers seize; casings leak water into the building.

### Evaporative cooler faults

Pads clog with minerals; pumps fail; water stagnates in the tank; casings corrode; drains and bleed fail. Water must be managed to limit scale and microbial growth.

### Underfloor heating faults

Hydronic underfloor circuits lose flow from sludge, especially where older plastic pipe without an oxygen barrier lets oxygen into the system; pipe damaged by later fixings leaks into the slab. Electric mats fail where damaged at installation, and the fault must be located before the floor is lifted.

### Compressor failure

Compressors fail from low refrigerant charge (overheating), liquid refrigerant returning to the compressor (slugging), short cycling on oversized units, and electrical faults. In inverter units the compressor is usually outlived by the electronics; in older fixed-speed units it is usually the end.

### Ducted system faults

Ducted reverse-cycle systems in roof spaces suffer from the same ductwork faults as larger systems: flexible ducts kink, tear and disconnect, roof space heat degrades insulation, and zone dampers fail. A failing ducted system often has a sound unit and failed ductwork.

### Heat pump hot water

Heat pump water heaters store water at lower temperatures than gas or electric units; they rely on periodic boost cycles to control Legionella. Units with failed boost elements or controls set too low carry that risk.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### Outdoor units

- Nameplate data: year and refrigerant.
- Coil corrosion; fins flattened or missing.
- Units crowded together or against walls.
- Oil stains at pipe joints (refrigerant leaks).
- Pipe insulation degraded by UV.
- Rust on casings and mounting frames.

### Indoor units

- Water stains below indoor units.
- Dust and mould on filters and coils.
- Noise; error codes on controllers.

### In the records

- Installation dates; refrigerant type and charge.
- Service and repair records; repeated regassing.
- Strata by-laws on air conditioning.
- Energy rating labels.

- Outdoor units on balconies or roofs added piecemeal, with pipes and cables run across façades.
- Noise from outdoor units near bedroom windows of neighbours.
- Condensate discharged onto roofs, balconies or footpaths.
- Electrical isolators corroded or missing.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit regassed repeatedly | Refrigerant leak | Leak test |
| Capacity loss on hot days | Coil corrosion or hot air recirculation | Coil condition; siting |
| Unit dead after a storm | Electronics failure | Error codes; board replacement availability |
| Water stains below indoor unit | Blocked drain or failed pump | Drain inspection |
| Carbon monoxide alarm near a rooftop unit supply | Cracked heat exchanger | Combustion inspection |

| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit runs continuously and never reaches setpoint | Undersized, low refrigerant, or fouled coils | Load calculation; refrigerant pressures; coil condition |
| Unit starts and stops every few minutes | Oversized or controls fault | Load; thermostat location |
| Ducted system weak in some rooms | Disconnected or kinked flexible duct | Roof space inspection |
| Many units of the same age failing together | End of life across the population | Installation dates; parts availability |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracked heat exchanger on a gas rooftop unit; refrigerant leak in a small room without detection | safety | Isolate now |
| Unit failed serving a critical space | failure | Repair or replace now |
| R22 equipment where servicing is restricted | deadline | Replace before the next major repair |
| Coil corrosion, leaks, drain faults | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Units at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| Refrigerant type unknown; VRF compliance unknown | check | Inspect |
| Normal wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services contractor or engineer; for strata and multi-tenant buildings, the inventory is the most important output because ownership is fragmented.

- Inventory of every indoor and outdoor unit: type, make, model, year, refrigerant and charge, capacity, location, area served, and owner (lot, tenant or common property).
- Sample condition inspection of outdoor coils, casings, pipe insulation, mounting frames, electrical isolators, indoor units, drains and filters.
- Refrigerant review: repeated regassing in service records, leak testing, and the refrigerant's servicing and supply outlook.
- VRF assessment: system charges against the smallest rooms served, leak detection and alarms where required, branch box and controller support, refrigerant pipework condition.
- Combustion inspection of gas-fired rooftop units, including heat exchanger inspection.
- Noise assessment where outdoor units are near neighbouring dwellings.
- Electrical capacity where heat pumps are replacing gas heating.
- Siting review: recirculation, access for maintenance, roof and balcony loads, waterproofing penetrations.

The report should give a full inventory with condition and remaining life, refrigerant position, safety items, ownership, and a replacement strategy (like for like, consolidation, or a central system).

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Repair or replace: repair is usually worthwhile for drains, fans and sensors; a failed compressor or main board on a unit more than about ten years old, or on R22, usually means replacement.
- Leak repair with pressure testing, not repeated regassing.
- Coil protection: factory-coated or treated coils near the coast; relocation away from salt spray where possible.
- Replacement with current refrigerants (R32 and other A2L refrigerants, or natural refrigerants) and installation to the safety requirements for A2L equipment; higher efficiency units.
- VRF compliance: leak detection and alarms, or reconfiguration to reduce charges, where refrigerant concentration limits are exceeded in small rooms.
- Rooftop units: heat exchanger replacement or unit replacement where cracks are found; economiser repairs.
- Consolidation: replacing many individual splits with VRF or a central system, which also clears façades and balconies.
- Noise control: acoustic enclosures, relocation, or quieter units where neighbours are affected.
- Strata coordination: by-laws setting standards for units on common property and a planned replacement programme.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is priced per unit for splits and ducted systems, per system for VRF, and per unit for rooftop units, with crane hire for rooftop and high-level outdoor units. Refrigerant recovery and disposal, electrical upgrades, structural support for new plant, roof and waterproofing works at penetrations, and making good to finishes add to each replacement. In strata buildings, costs split between lot owners and the owners corporation according to ownership.

Individual unit replacement is lifecycle and, for small units, often treated as a recurring allowance rather than discrete lines. Safety items are immediate; refrigerant-driven replacement can carry a deadline.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Refrigerant work requires an Australian Refrigeration Council licence; equipment safety follows AS/NZS 5149 and, for A2L refrigerants, AS/NZS 60335.2.40; energy labelling and minimum efficiency are set under the Greenhouse and Energy Minimum Standards (GEMS) scheme. State noise regulations restrict air conditioner noise at neighbouring residences, particularly at night. In strata schemes, by-laws govern outdoor units on common property.
- United Kingdom. The GB fluorinated gas regulations govern refrigerants and leak checks; heat pumps installed for government grants need MCS certification; Approved Document L sets efficiency; permitted development rules and noise limits apply to air-source heat pumps on dwellings.
- United States. EPA Section 608 governs refrigerant handling; A2L equipment follows UL 60335-2-40 and the model mechanical codes; Department of Energy minimum efficiency standards apply; the Technology Transitions rule restricts higher-GWP refrigerants in new residential and light commercial equipment.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Inventory of units with installation dates, refrigerants and owners.
- Service and repair records, including regassing.
- VRF design documents, refrigerant charges and leak detection details.
- Combustion inspection records for gas rooftop units.
- Strata by-laws and approvals for units on common property.
- Noise complaints.
- Electrical supply capacity records where heat pumps are planned.

pages.title: Main Electrical Supply
pages.question: How do main switchboards, transformers and supply equipment fail, and when does capacity rather than condition decide replacement?
pages.answer: Main supply equipment fails invisibly until it fails catastrophically. Terminations loosen and overheat; breakers seize when never operated and lose maker support; HV insulation degrades by partial discharge; transformer oil breaks down. Open-bus and fused boards expose workers to arc flash. Thermography under load and breaker testing find the faults. Capacity often decides replacement first: electrification, cooling and EV charging run out of supply before the board wears out.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about main electrical supply; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: HV and LV switchgear, transformers, main switchboards

sources.title: NFPA 70B Standard for Electrical Equipment Maintenance

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
The main electrical supply brings power into the building and splits it to the sub-mains: the network connection, any high-voltage switchgear and transformers the owner is responsible for, the low-voltage main switchboard with its main switch and protective devices, metering, power factor correction, surge protection and the main earthing arrangement. Distribution beyond the main switchboard, emergency power and solar have their own pages.

| Component | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HV switchgear (ring main units, circuit breakers) | Buildings with their own substation: large offices, hospitals, campuses, industrial | Insulation breakdown (partial discharge); oil-filled units leak; SF₆ units leak a potent greenhouse gas; mechanisms seize |
| Transformers (oil-filled or dry-type) | Owner-operated substations | Insulation ageing; oil degradation; leaks; older units may contain PCBs |
| LV main switchboard | Every building | Hot terminations; ageing breakers; unsupported devices; inadequate arc-fault containment; water in the switchroom |
| Air circuit breakers and moulded case breakers | Main and large sub-main protection | Mechanisms seize when never operated; trip units drift |
| Metering | Network meters; check meters; embedded network meters | Ownership and accuracy disputes |
| Power factor correction | Commercial and industrial | Capacitor failure and fire; older units may contain PCBs |
| Earthing and bonding | Every building | Corroded electrodes; disconnected bonds |
| Surge protection | Main and critical boards | Devices reach end of life after surges and stop protecting |

Era tells a lot. Boards from before the 1980s often have open busbars, rewireable or cartridge fuses, and asbestos-based arc shields or backing boards. Boards from the 1980s and 1990s have breakers whose makers no longer support them. Modern boards are built to defined forms of separation and with arc-fault containment. Capacity is the other dimension: a board in good order can still be the constraint on electrification, cooling upgrades and electric vehicle charging.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LV main switchboard | 30 to 40 years | Switchroom environment; loading; maintenance |
| Air and moulded case breakers | 20 to 25 years before support ends | Operation and testing; manufacturer support |
| Oil-filled transformers | 30 to 50 years | Loading; oil condition; cooling |
| Dry-type transformers | 25 to 35 years | Heat; dust |
| HV switchgear | 30 to 40 years | Insulation; type (oil, SF₆, vacuum) |
| Power factor correction capacitors | 10 to 15 years | Harmonics; heat |
| Surge protection devices | Until they absorb enough surges; check indicators | Surge exposure |
| Incoming cables | Life of the building | Overload; damage |

What shortens life:

- Heat, damp and dust in switchrooms; switchrooms used as storerooms; water pipes over boards.
- Loose terminations, which heat, oxidise and get worse.
- Breakers that are never operated, whose mechanisms seize.
- Load growth past ratings.
- Harmonics from electronic loads, which overheat neutrals, transformers and capacitors.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Connection overheating

Bolted connections at busbars, breakers and cable lugs loosen with thermal cycling, vibration and poor installation; resistance rises, the joint heats, oxidises and loosens further. Aluminium conductors are especially prone. Overheating ends in an arc fault or fire, and the early stage is visible only on a thermographic survey under load.

### Insulation ageing and partial discharge

Insulation in HV switchgear, transformers and cables degrades with heat, moisture and electrical stress. In HV equipment, partial discharge (small sparks within voids in insulation) erodes it from within until it fails. It can be detected by testing long before failure.

### Protective device failure and obsolescence

Breakers protect against overload and fault; if they do not open, a fault becomes a fire. Mechanisms seize when never exercised; electronic trip units drift; and breakers whose makers have stopped supporting them cannot be repaired. Changes to the installation over the years can leave devices that no longer discriminate, so a minor fault trips the main supply.

### Arc-flash hazard

Older open-bus boards and boards without arc-fault containment expose anyone working on or near them to arc flash: an explosive release of energy during a fault. This is a direct hazard to electricians and the reason for de-energised working rules and arc-flash studies.

### Transformer deterioration

Transformer oil absorbs moisture and breaks down; insulation paper ages; overheating and internal faults generate gases in the oil that can be measured. Leaks are an environmental and fire risk. Transformers made before about 1980 may contain PCBs.

### Capacity constraint

Maximum demand may already be close to the supply rating. Electrification of heating, larger cooling plant, data loads and electric vehicle charging all add load, and network supply upgrades take months to years. The main switchboard is often where capacity runs out first.

### Water in the switchroom

Basement switchrooms flood, and pipes or gutters above boards leak. Water on a switchboard is an immediate hazard and a common cause of long outages.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the switchroom

- Board type and era from the nameplate; open busbars; fuses; asbestos labels.
- Discolouration, burn marks or melted insulation at terminations.
- Warm surfaces; hum or buzzing; smell of hot insulation.
- Water staining, pipes overhead, damp; storage in front of the board.
- Missing covers, unlabelled circuits, open escutcheons.
- Surge protection status indicators.
- Transformer oil leaks; bund condition.

### In the records

- Thermographic surveys and their findings.
- Breaker testing and maintenance records.
- Periodic inspection and test reports.
- Maximum demand data and the supply agreement.
- Transformer oil tests; HV partial discharge tests.
- Single-line diagrams; protection studies; arc-flash study.
- Asbestos and PCB registers.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hot spot at a termination on thermography | Loose or overloaded connection | Temperature rise against adjacent phases; torque check after isolation |
| Hot spot across a whole circuit | Overload | Load measurement against rating |
| Hot neutral | Harmonics or unbalanced load | Harmonic measurement |
| Main breaker trips for faults on final circuits | Loss of discrimination | Protection study |
| Breaker fails to trip on test | Seized mechanism or failed trip unit | Primary or secondary injection test |
| Rising gases in transformer oil | Internal overheating or arcing | Dissolved gas analysis pattern |
| Partial discharge readings on HV gear | Insulation deterioration | Repeat testing; trend |
| Network refuses additional load | Supply capacity reached | Maximum demand; supply agreement |

> A switchboard with signs of overheating, water exposure, or missing covers over live parts is a safety finding. Do not judge a board as sound because it is working: the faults that matter are invisible until it fails.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposed live parts; burning or overheating; water on or above the board; PCB oil leaking | safety | Isolate or protect now |
| Main board or transformer failed; building without supply | failure | Restore now; temporary supply |
| Periodic inspection and testing due | deadline | At the interval set by the regulation or standard |
| Thermographic hot spots; breakers failing tests; unsupported devices; partial discharge | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Board at end of life; open-bus or fused boards | lifecycle | Plan replacement |
| Capacity unknown for electrification or EV charging; no recent thermography | check | Assess |
| Normal maintenance | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer or licensed electrical contractor leads; HV equipment needs an HV-qualified specialist.

- Records review: single-line diagrams, supply agreement, maximum demand data, maintenance and test records, previous inspection reports.
- Visual inspection of the switchroom and boards, covers off where safe to do so.
- Thermographic survey under significant load.
- Breaker testing: operation and trip testing by primary or secondary injection.
- Insulation resistance and earth testing.
- HV testing: partial discharge, insulation, oil analysis including dissolved gases and PCB content.
- Protection and discrimination study; arc-flash study where the board is worked on live.
- Capacity assessment: measured maximum demand against supply and board ratings, with planned loads added.
- Hazardous materials: asbestos and PCB sampling.

The report should state whether each component is to be maintained, modernised or replaced, the capacity headroom, safety items, and any supply upgrade needed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Re-terminate and torque hot connections found by thermography, then re-survey to confirm.
- Breaker maintenance: exercise, clean and test breakers on a cycle; retrofit unsupported breakers with supported units designed to fit the existing board.
- Protection review: reset or replace devices to restore discrimination.
- Arc-flash mitigation: arc-flash studies and labelling, remote operation and racking, arc-fault detection, maintenance switches that speed tripping during work, or board replacement.
- Switchroom works: remove water pipes from above boards, clear storage, add bunding, drainage and flood protection, ventilate or cool the room, restrict access.
- Board replacement with a staged changeover, temporary supply or generators, and out-of-hours shutdowns; often sized for future electrification.
- Transformer works: oil filtering and drying, gasket and bushing repairs, replacement where tests show advanced deterioration, and PCB removal under hazardous waste rules.
- HV works: replacement of oil-filled switchgear with vacuum or SF₆-free alternatives; partial discharge monitoring.
- Supply upgrade: application to the network early, since lead times are long; demand management, load shifting, batteries and solar as interim measures.
- Surge protection renewal and coordination at main and critical boards.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing, thermography and studies are lump sums, with thermography and breaker testing recurring. Repairs and breaker retrofits are itemised per device. Board replacement is a lump-sum project including temporary supply, out-of-hours shutdowns, cabling changes and commissioning, and can be large relative to the board itself. Transformer and HV works are lump sums, with oil disposal and PCB handling where relevant. Supply upgrades carry network contributions and long lead times, and belong with the electrification, cooling or EV charging project that needs them.

Replacement is lifecycle; safety, periodic testing and arc-flash compliance are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Where capacity is uncertain, the usual shape is two-part: a capacity and condition assessment first, then a conditional board and supply upgrade envelope.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Installations follow AS/NZS 3000, which includes arc-fault containment requirements for larger switchboards; assemblies are built to AS/NZS 61439; periodic verification follows AS/NZS 3019; safe work on low-voltage equipment follows AS/NZS 4836 and the work health and safety regulations, which restrict live work; customer-owned HV installations carry additional obligations under state electrical safety laws; supply upgrades follow the distribution network service provider's connection rules.
- United Kingdom. BS 7671 governs installations and periodic inspection produces an Electrical Installation Condition Report; the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require systems to be maintained safe and restrict live work; switchgear follows BS EN 61439; SF₆ is a regulated fluorinated gas; supply upgrades follow the distribution network operator's process.
- United States. NFPA 70 (the National Electrical Code) governs installations; NFPA 70B, now a mandatory standard, sets maintenance intervals and condition assessment; NFPA 70E sets electrical safety and arc-flash requirements, including labelling; OSHA enforces electrical safety at work; PCB transformers are regulated by the EPA.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Single-line diagram and switchboard drawings.
- Supply agreement, network capacity and maximum demand data for at least a year.
- Thermographic surveys and maintenance records for the main switchboard.
- Breaker test records.
- Periodic inspection and test reports.
- Transformer oil test results and HV partial discharge test records.
- Arc-flash study and protection coordination study.
- Asbestos and PCB registers.
- Planned load additions: electrification, cooling, EV charging, tenant loads.

pages.title: Main Entrance & Reception Areas
pages.question: How do building entrances and reception areas fail, and which entrance findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Entrances fail first on safety and access, then on image. Wet polished floors with short or worn matting make the entry the building's main slip location; automatic and revolving doors hurt people when sensors drift; heavy doors, revolving-only entries and high desks exclude people with disability; security turnstiles that do not release on alarm block escape. Then finishes date long before they wear out, and a tired entrance drags down the whole building's market position.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about main entrance & reception areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, joinery, reception desks, wayfinding, architectural features

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
The main entrance and reception is where people arrive: the entry doors and any draught lobby, entry matting, the reception or concierge desk, security turnstiles and access control, seating, wayfinding, and the finishes that set the building's first impression. Functionally it has to admit people safely and easily in all weather, control who goes further, welcome visitors and people with disability, and let everyone out fast in an emergency. It is the most heavily used and most visible space in most buildings, and its condition shapes how tenants, buyers and visitors judge the whole asset.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry doors | Automatic sliding, swing or revolving doors; glazed manual doors | Safe operation, accessibility, weather control, egress |
| Draught lobby and matting | Double doors with a lobby; recessed entrance matting | Keeping wind, rain and grit out; slip prevention |
| Reception and concierge | Desk joinery with a lowered section, seating | Accessibility, presentation, security sightlines |
| Security | Turnstiles, access control, CCTV, intercom | Control without blocking escape |
| Floor and wall finishes | Stone, terrazzo, timber, feature walls | Slip resistance, durability, appearance |
| Lighting | Feature and general lighting | Welcome, visibility for security, transition from daylight |
| Wayfinding and signage | Directories, lift signage, statutory signs | Finding lifts, tenancies and exits |

Entrances are refurbished more often than any other base-building space because they carry a building's market position. A tired entrance in an otherwise sound building is one of the most common reasons owners refurbish ahead of the services cycle.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entrance refurbishment (finishes, desk, lighting) | 10 to 15 years | Market positioning; wear |
| Automatic door operators | 10 to 15 years | Cycles; maintenance; weather |
| Revolving doors | 20 to 30 years with overhaul | Use; maintenance |
| Entrance matting | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Stone and terrazzo floors | 30 to 50 years with honing and sealing | Traffic; grit; cleaning |
| Turnstiles and access control | 10 to 15 years | Technology; vendor support |
| Reception joinery | 10 to 20 years | Use; style |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Market expectations for hospitality-style lobbies, end-of-trip access and amenity, which date older entrances quickly.
- Grit and water tracked in when matting is undersized or worn, which scratches floors and makes them slippery.
- Door cycles: automatic doors in busy entrances open thousands of times a day.
- Security upgrades retrofitted without regard to egress, access or appearance.
- Weather exposure where there is no draught lobby or canopy.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Slips at the entrance

Polished stone, terrazzo and glazed tiles become slippery when wet, and entrances are where rain arrives. Undersized or worn matting, no draught lobby, cleaning products that leave residues, and sealers that polish the surface turn the entrance into the building's most common slip location.

### Automatic and revolving door hazards

Automatic doors that close on people, swing doors without safeguarding, and revolving doors that do not stop when obstructed injure people, especially children and older users. Sensors drift out of adjustment, safety beams fail and doors are left on settings that suit throughput rather than safety.

### Access barriers

Heavy manual doors, revolving doors without an adjacent accessible door, steps or thresholds, reception desks with no lowered section, and no hearing augmentation exclude people with disability from the first space they meet.

### Security that blocks escape

Turnstiles, locked doors and access-controlled entries must release on fire alarm and power failure. Security added after construction often fails this, or creates queues and pinch points in an evacuation.

### Weather, draughts and comfort

Entrances without draught lobbies let wind and cold or hot air in, chilling reception staff, wasting energy and driving revolving or air curtain retrofits. Stack effect in tall buildings can make doors hard to open and lobbies draughty.

### Market dating

Finishes, lighting and joinery date long before they wear out. An entrance that looks old signals an old building, regardless of the condition of the services behind it.

### Wayfinding failure

Directories that are out of date, lifts hidden from the entry, and missing signs for accessible routes and amenities confuse visitors and undermine the welcome.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On a walk-through

- Matting worn, curled, undersized or missing; water and grit marks on floors beyond it.
- Scratched, dull or patchy stone floors; slip incidents reported.
- Automatic doors that close quickly on people, revolving doors without a working stop, door sensors misaligned.
- A revolving door with no adjacent accessible swing or sliding door.
- Reception desk without a lowered section; no hearing loop signage.
- Turnstiles without a wide accessible gate or fire release; queues at peak.
- Draughts felt at the desk; staff heaters under the reception counter.
- Dated finishes, lighting and directories.

### In the records

- Slip and trip incident records.
- Automatic and revolving door maintenance and safety checks.
- Access control fire release tests.
- Access audit.
- Refurbishment history.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slips concentrated inside the entry on wet days | Matting too short or worn; slippery finish | Wet slip resistance test; matting length |
| Floor dull in a path from the door | Grit tracked past inadequate matting | Matting review |
| Door strikes reported | Sensors or safety settings out of adjustment | Door safety check against the standard |
| Draughts and doors hard to open in winter | Stack effect or no draught lobby | Pressure and airflow observation |
| Visitors unable to find lifts or tenants | Wayfinding and sightlines | Observation; directory currency |
| Turnstiles stay locked in an alarm test | Fire interface fault | Interface test |

> Entrance problems are usually either safety and access (doors, slips, egress) or market and image. Fix the first regardless of budget; time the second with leasing strategy.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsafe automatic or revolving doors; slippery entry with incidents; security that does not release on alarm | safety | Rectify now |
| Entry doors failed, building insecure or inaccessible | failure | Repair now |
| Access or security requirements triggered by works or a complaint | deadline | By the required date |
| Worn matting and floors; draughts; outdated directories | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Entrance at the end of its refurbishment cycle or below market | lifecycle | Plan refurbishment with leasing strategy |
| No access audit; door safety unchecked | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or interior consultant leads, with an access consultant, a door specialist and security and fire consultants as needed.

- Walk-through at peak times to see queues, door behaviour, matting performance and wayfinding in use.
- Slip resistance testing of floors wet and dry, against the classification needed for an entrance.
- Door safety check of automatic, swing and revolving doors against the relevant standard: sensors, safety beams, closing speeds and forces, stop functions.
- Access audit of the entry sequence: approach, doors, thresholds, desk, hearing augmentation and signage.
- Security and egress review: turnstiles and access-controlled doors tested for release on alarm and power loss, and evacuation capacity.
- Comfort review: draughts, temperatures and stack effect at the desk and doors.
- Market review against competing buildings and the building's target grade.

The report should separate safety and access items from presentation and market items, and give a programme for both.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Matting: recessed entrance matting long enough to remove water and grit before people reach hard floors.
- Floor treatment: hone and treat stone for wet slip resistance, change cleaning products, or replace finishes in the wet zone.
- Door safety upgrades: sensors and safety beams to current standards, closing speeds reset, revolving door stops and an adjacent accessible door.
- Draught lobby or air curtain to control wind, stack effect and energy loss.
- Accessible reception: lowered desk section, hearing loops, seating, clear signage.
- Security integration: wide accessible gates, fire release on all locked devices, and evacuation capacity checked.
- Wayfinding: updated digital or fixed directories and clear sightlines to lifts.
- Refurbishment of finishes, lighting and joinery to reposition the building.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Matting, door safety upgrades, signage and desk modifications are itemised and relatively modest. Draught lobbies and revolving door installations are lump sums with façade work. Floor treatment is by area; replacement by area with weekend or overnight work in occupied buildings. A full entrance refurbishment is a lump-sum project, often the most visible capital spend in a leasing strategy.

Safety and access items are code compliance; door operators and matting are lifecycle on short cycles; refurbishment is repositioning capital timed with leasing.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 5007 covers powered doors for pedestrian access and egress; the National Construction Code and AS 1428.1 set access requirements for entrances, doors and counters; AS 4586 classifies slip resistance; security doors on egress paths must meet the code's egress provisions.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 16005 covers safety in use of power-operated pedestrian doors; Approved Document M and BS 8300 set access; the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 require doors and floors to be safe; the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments.
- United States. ANSI/BHMA A156.10 covers power-operated pedestrian doors and A156.27 revolving doors; the 2010 ADA Standards govern accessible entrances, doors and counters; NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern egress through security devices.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Slip, trip and door incident records.
- Automatic and revolving door maintenance and safety check records.
- Access audit for the entrance sequence.
- Access control and turnstile fire release test records.
- Entrance refurbishment history and any repositioning plans.
- Cleaning specifications for entrance floors.
- Visitor and tenant feedback on arrival experience.

pages.title: Maintenance Access Areas
pages.question: How do ceiling voids, hatches, platforms and confined spaces fail, and why does poor access matter?
pages.answer: Maintenance access fails dangerously or silently. Workers fall through ceilings and roof spaces with no walkways, through open hatches and from unsafe ladders; confined spaces kill when entered without testing and controls; hidden asbestos, wiring and heat injure people in voids. Where access is poor, maintenance is skipped and equipment fails. Identify confined spaces, guard hatches and provide catwalks to every item needing service.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about maintenance access areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes and safety provisions

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Maintenance access areas are the spaces people enter only to maintain the building: ceiling voids, roof spaces, crawl ways, plant platforms and catwalks, access hatches, fixed ladders, service walkways and confined spaces such as tanks and pits. Functionally they must let maintenance be done safely and conveniently. When they do not, maintenance is skipped or done dangerously: people fall through ceilings, off platforms and from ladders, are overcome in confined spaces, or disturb asbestos they did not know was there.

| Type | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling voids | Above suspended ceilings in most buildings | Falls through ceilings; asbestos; live wiring |
| Roof spaces | Pitched roofs in houses and low-rise | Falls between joists; heat; insulation hazards |
| Access hatches | Ceilings, roofs, floors | Falls through open hatches; unsafe ladders |
| Fixed ladders and stairs | Plant platforms, roofs, pits | Falls; non-compliant geometry |
| Platforms, catwalks and walkways | Plant rooms, atria, roofs | Missing guardrails; corrosion |
| Confined spaces | Tanks, pits, ducts, sumps, voids | Toxic or oxygen-deficient atmospheres |

Good access is designed in from the start; most problems arise in older buildings and wherever plant was added later.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel platforms and ladders | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Access hatches | 20 to 30 years | Hinges; seals; damage |
| Walkway boards in roof spaces | 20 to 40 years | Decay; damage |
| Guardrails | 25 to 40 years | Fixings; corrosion |
| Fitness for current plant locations | Changes when plant is added | Plant added without access |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Plant added in places with no designed access.
- Corrosion of ladders and platforms on roofs and in damp plant areas.
- Insulation and services covering walkways and joists.
- Locked or lost access, so people improvise.

Access provisions rarely wear out first; they become inadequate because plant is added or moved without access being designed, and because equipment in voids multiplies over decades of fit-outs.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Falls through ceilings and roof spaces

Suspended ceilings and plasterboard cannot carry people. Workers in ceiling voids and roof spaces step between supports or onto ceilings and fall through, often onto occupied spaces below. Roof spaces filled with insulation hide joists.

### Open hatches and unsafe ladders

Open ceiling and roof hatches without guarding are fall holes; portable ladders used to reach hatches slip; fixed ladders without cages or fall arrest, or with wrong geometry, injure users.

### Confined spaces

Tanks, pits, sumps and some ducts can contain toxic gases or lack oxygen. Entering without testing, ventilation, permits and rescue arrangements kills workers and rescuers.

### Hidden hazards

Ceiling voids and roof spaces may contain asbestos, loose-fill insulation, live and damaged wiring, hot surfaces and vermin. Workers who do not know they are there disturb them.

### Platform and walkway failures

Platforms and walkways without guardrails, with corroded grating or loose fixings, and plant placed close to roof edges without protection create fall hazards.

### Neglect from poor access

Equipment that is hard to reach is not maintained: filters, dampers, valves and lights in difficult voids are left until they fail.

### Heat and exhaustion in roof spaces

Roof spaces in hot climates reach temperatures that cause heat stress within a short time, especially in insulated and poorly ventilated roofs; work is unsafe in the middle of the day in summer.

### Electrical hazards in voids

Damaged cables, unprotected joints, old wiring and foil insulation in contact with wiring can electrocute workers in ceiling and roof spaces.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Plant above ceilings with no catwalks or access panels; footprints or damage on ceiling tiles.
- Roof spaces without walkway boards; insulation over joists.
- Hatches without guardrails or with damaged ladders.
- Fixed ladders without cages or fall arrest.
- Corroded platforms and missing guardrails.
- Confined spaces without signs or locks.
- Asbestos labels in voids, or suspect materials.

### In the records

- Confined space register.
- Asbestos register covering voids.
- Access equipment certification.
- Incident records.
- Maintenance records showing skipped tasks.

- Footprints on insulation or damage to plasterboard ceilings below roof spaces.
- Foil insulation near wiring; old rubber-insulated wiring in roof spaces.
- Hatches painted shut or blocked by furniture.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken ceiling tiles under plant | People standing on the ceiling to reach equipment | Access review |
| Filters and dampers neglected above ceilings | No practical access | Maintenance records |
| Workers using portable ladders to roofs | No fixed access | Observation |
| Unsigned pits and tanks | Confined spaces not identified | Register review |

> Confined spaces, unguarded hatches and ceilings that people stand on are serious fall and life hazards. Identify, sign and control them before the next maintenance visit.

If maintenance records show tasks skipped or delayed for the same equipment, the cause is often access, not the contractor. If damage to ceilings and finishes appears below the same equipment repeatedly, workers are improvising their own access.

Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unidentified confined spaces; unguarded hatches; no safe access to plant above ceilings or on roofs | safety | Rectify before next access |
| Access equipment damaged or unusable | failure | Repair now |
| Certification of anchors, ladders or platforms due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Corrosion; missing walkways; poor lighting | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Access equipment at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No access audit | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Access findings are graded on the consequence if someone uses the access as it stands today: a fall through a ceiling or a confined space entry without controls is a safety grade even if nobody has been hurt yet.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A health and safety consultant or building surveyor with the maintenance contractors.

- Access audit of every item of plant and service needing maintenance: how it is reached and what protection exists.
- Confined space survey and register.
- Hatch, ladder and platform inspection against standards.
- Hazard check in voids: asbestos, wiring, insulation, heat.
- Maintenance record review for skipped tasks.

The report should list hazards and a plan for safe access.

The audit should start from the maintenance schedule: for every task, ask where the equipment is and how someone gets to it safely.

- Roof space survey: walkways, clearances, hazards, ventilation and temperature.
- Electrical safety check of wiring and insulation contact in voids.
- Contractor interviews: maintenance staff know which items are hard or dangerous to reach.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Catwalks and walkways in ceiling voids and roof spaces to every item needing maintenance, with lighting.
- Access panels located under equipment so it can be reached from below.
- Hatch guarding and compliant fixed ladders with fall protection.
- Platforms and guardrails on roofs and in plant rooms.
- Confined space controls: signs, locks, register, entry procedures and rescue plans.
- Relocation of plant to accessible positions at replacement.
- Hazard removal: asbestos, damaged wiring, loose insulation.

- Work scheduling to avoid roof spaces in the heat of the day.
- Access documentation: drawings showing access points, routes and hazards for each item of plant, given to every contractor.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Access works are itemised: catwalks by length, hatches, ladders and platforms per item. Confined space controls are low cost. Plant relocation is part of replacement projects. Safety items are code compliance and prevent costly incidents.

Access works are modest compared with the cost of a fall or confined space incident, and they also reduce maintenance time and missed tasks, so they often pay for themselves. Relocating plant to accessible positions is cheapest when done as part of a planned replacement. Confined space signage, locks and procedures cost little.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Work health and safety regulations govern falls and confined spaces, with codes of practice; AS 1657 covers fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders; AS/NZS 2865 covers confined spaces.
- United Kingdom. The Work at Height Regulations 2005 and Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 apply; BS 5395 and BS EN ISO 14122 cover fixed access.
- United States. OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D covers walking-working surfaces and ladders, and 1910.146 permit-required confined spaces.

In all three countries, duties for safe access fall on whoever controls the building as a workplace, including when the work is done by contractors; designers also have duties to provide safe maintenance access in new work and alterations (for example under the UK Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 and Australian work health and safety duties for designers). Incidents involving falls or confined spaces lead to regulator investigation and prosecution.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Confined space register and procedures.
- Asbestos register covering ceiling voids and roof spaces.
- Access equipment certification.
- Incident and near-miss records.
- Maintenance records showing skipped tasks.

- Drawings showing access to plant above ceilings and on roofs.
- Contractor feedback on access difficulties.
- Work at height and confined space procedures.

pages.title: Masonry/Brickwork
pages.question: What goes wrong with brick and block façades, what does each defect look like, and how serious is it?
pages.answer: Masonry façades fail at the hidden steel and at the joints, not in the brick. Corroding ties crack the outer leaf horizontally at regular tie courses; corroding lintels and shelf angles crack brickwork over openings and at floor lines; brick growing against a shrinking concrete frame bows the panels between floors. Even-width cracks near corners are usually movement and benign; tapering cracks through openings point to the ground. Read the crack pattern first, then its width.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about masonry façades; it describes how these walls behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Pointing, cracking, efflorescence, structural stability

sources.title: BS 8221-1:2012 Cleaning and surface repair of buildings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Masonry walls take four main forms, and the form decides what can go wrong. Solid walls, one to two bricks thick and bonded with headers, dominate pre-1930 stock in Britain and Australia and early twentieth-century buildings in the United States. They have no cavity and rely on thickness and soft lime mortar to absorb and release moisture. Cavity walls, two leaves with a gap between them held together by metal ties, became standard in Britain from the 1920s and in Australian multi-storey and commercial work through the mid twentieth century. Brick veneer, a single outer leaf tied back to a timber or steel frame, has been the dominant Australian house and low-rise form since the 1950s. On framed buildings, masonry is cladding: an outer leaf carried at each floor on steel shelf angles or on the slab edge and tied back to the frame.

Bond pattern tells you the form from the street. Header courses (bricks laid end-on, showing their short face, in Flemish or English bond) mean a solid wall. Stretcher bond with no headers means a cavity or veneer, and therefore ties, which are the commonest hidden failure in masonry. Snapped half-bricks laid to imitate headers in stretcher work are a known trap; the rhythm is usually too regular and the heads often look slightly short.

| Era | Typical form | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before about 1920 | Solid brick or stone, lime mortar, timber or iron lintels behind arches, slate or no damp-proof course | Rising damp and salt attack at the base; decayed timber lintels; cement repointing damaging soft brick |
| 1920s to 1970s | Cavity walls with galvanised mild-steel ties: flat fishtail or vertical-twist strip, wire butterfly; black ash mortar in parts of Britain | Tie corrosion now advanced in exposed and coastal positions; strip ties crack the wall as they rust, wire ties thin silently; black ash mortar accelerates both |
| 1950s to 1980s | Concrete-framed buildings clad in brick on shelf angles or slab edges, often with no compressible joint under the angle | Bowing, spalling and horizontal cracking at floor lines as the frame shortens and the brick grows |
| 1900s to 1940s, United States | Steel frame encased in solid masonry with no cavity or drainage | Rust jacking of spandrel beams and columns, cracking and displacement along floor and column lines |
| 1980s onward | Stainless or exposure-rated ties, cavity trays, weep holes, movement joints | Lower risk; failures are mostly workmanship: missing or misplaced ties, mortar-bridged cavities, omitted joints |

Brick type governs movement. Fired clay bricks expand permanently as they take up moisture after leaving the kiln, quickly in the first months and slowly for decades after. Calcium silicate and concrete bricks and blocks do the opposite and shrink. A wall of either needs movement joints, sized and spaced for its material, and the two must not be mixed in one panel without allowing for the difference. Mortar governs durability. Lime mortar is softer and more permeable than the brick, so the joint weathers and is renewed while the brick survives. Cement mortar is harder and less permeable; laid against soft brick it forces moisture and salts out through the brick face and the brick fails instead of the joint.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fired clay brick | 100 to 150 years and more | Shortened by salt crystallisation, frost and hard cement pointing |
| Lime mortar joints | 50 to 100 years sheltered; 30 to 50 years exposed | Exposure, roof drainage, rising damp |
| Cement mortar joints | 40 to 70 years | Cracking at movement rather than erosion; sulfate attack where wet |
| Galvanised mild-steel ties (before about 1980) | 30 to 60 years; as little as 15 to 25 years in marine exposure or black ash mortar | Zinc consumed once the mortar carbonates and stays damp |
| Stainless steel ties | Life of the building | Workmanship: omitted, misplaced or bridged ties |
| Galvanised steel lintels and shelf angles | 40 to 80 years | Coastal exposure, water held behind them, missing cavity trays |
| Bitumen or polymer damp-proof course | 50 years and more | Bridging by raised ground, paving, render or garden beds, rather than material failure |
| Injected chemical damp-proof course | 20 to 30 years | Product, installation and salt loading |

What shortens life:

- Exposure. Elevations facing the prevailing rain, sites within a few kilometres of surf, and industrial atmospheres keep walls wetter and consume galvanising faster. The same building can have ties failing on one elevation and sound on another.
- Water management faults. Overflowing gutters, missing copings and sills without drips, blocked weep holes and absent cavity trays put water exactly where ties and lintels sit.
- Missing movement joints. Long runs of clay brick without joints, and brick cladding on concrete frames without soft joints under the shelf angles, crack and bow as the materials move against each other.
- Hard repointing and impermeable coatings. Cement pointing on lime-built walls, and paints or renders that trap moisture, move decay into the brick.
- Bridged damp-proof courses. Raised paths and garden beds, render taken down over the damp-proof course, and debris in the cavity carry ground moisture past the barrier.
- Cavity wall insulation retrofits. Fill injected into cavities in exposed locations can carry rain across to the inner leaf and keep ties wet.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Wall tie corrosion

Ties hold the outer leaf to the inner leaf or frame. Galvanised mild-steel ties lose their zinc once the surrounding mortar carbonates and stays damp, then the steel rusts. Rust occupies several times the volume of the steel it replaces. In the outer leaf bed joint that expansion lifts the brickwork above, and because ties are laid at regular vertical spacing (450 mm in British practice, about every sixth course) the wall cracks horizontally in a regular pattern. Strip ties (fishtail and vertical twist) jack and crack the wall. Wire ties mostly thin and snap with little expansion, so they can lose restraint with no visible sign. The end result in both cases is an outer leaf free to bulge, and under wind suction, to fall.

### Lintel and shelf angle corrosion

Steel lintels over openings and shelf angles carrying cladding at each floor corrode where water reaches them, usually because cavity trays and stop ends are missing or weep holes are blocked. Corrosion lifts the brickwork over the lintel and opens a crack along its bearing; as the flange thins the brickwork drops and the opening head deflects. Behind the arches of older buildings, timber lintels rot unseen until the arch drops.

### Frame shortening against brick growth

A concrete frame shortens over its first decades through creep and shrinkage. Clay brick grows. Where brick cladding is built tight to the underside of each shelf angle or slab edge, with no compressible joint, the frame unloads onto the brick panel below. The brick at the angle line crushes and spalls, panels bow outward between floors, and corners crack where the two elevations push against each other.

### Moisture and thermal movement

Long runs of clay brickwork without movement joints expand and push past corners and returns, producing vertical cracks near corners, cracks at short returns and brickwork sliding outward on the damp-proof course at the base (oversailing). Concrete block and calcium silicate shrink and crack vertically at openings and mid-panel. These cracks are usually even in width and stop growing once the material has stabilised.

### Foundation movement

Settlement, subsidence and the seasonal swelling and shrinking of reactive clay soils distort the wall. Cracks run diagonally through brick and mortar, taper (wider at one end), pass through openings, and are accompanied by sticking doors and windows, sloping floors and cracking internally on the same line. On reactive clay they open and close with the seasons; trees, leaking drains and changes to garden watering are the usual triggers.

### Sulfate attack

Soluble sulfates from clay bricks, ground water or flue gases react with cement in wet mortar and render, forming expansive compounds. Mortar swells, softens and whitens; the wall grows vertically and cracks along most bed joints, not only at tie courses. Chimneys, parapets, rendered walls and walls in wet ground are the usual places.

### Frost and salt damage

Water freezing in saturated brick, and salts crystallising as walls dry, break off brick faces (spalling) and turn surfaces powdery. Salt damage dominates in Australian stock at the base of walls with failed damp-proof courses and in coastal walls; frost damage dominates in Britain and the colder United States in parapets, chimneys and exposed copings. Hard cement pointing concentrates both in the brick.

### Damp

Rising damp is ground moisture drawn up a wall without a working damp-proof course, carrying salts that deposit in a band up to about a metre high. Penetrating damp is rain driven through solid walls, defective pointing, or across a cavity bridged by mortar droppings, debris on ties or retrofit insulation. Both decay plaster, timber in contact with the wall, and embedded steel.

### Rust jacking of embedded steel

In early steel-framed buildings the columns and spandrel beams are wrapped in solid masonry with no drainage. Water reaching the steel rusts it, and the rust pushes the masonry outward along column and floor lines, cracking corners and displacing brick and stone, often first at parapets where exposure is greatest.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Horizontal cracks at regular vertical spacing across an elevation; on a veneer or cavity wall this is the tie signature.
- Bulging or bowing panels, best seen by sighting along the wall at a low angle or in raking light; floor-line bowing on framed buildings.
- Brickwork lifted at eaves or verges, or a gap opening under the roof edge.
- Stepped cracks rising from the ends of lintels, rust staining below lintels and shelf angles, dropped arches.
- Diagonal tapering cracks through openings; distorted window heads.
- Spalled brick faces, mortar eroded or proud of the brick, mismatched patch repairs and repointing in a different colour.
- Vegetation in joints, overflowing gutter staining, white salt deposits and lime runs below defective details.
- Weep holes buried by paving or garden beds; render carried down over the damp-proof course.

### Close up on site

- Mortar that is soft enough to rake out with a key or crumbles to the touch; white, swollen mortar in most joints (sulfate).
- Hollow sound or movement when brick faces are tapped; loose bricks at parapets and corners.
- Crack width and whether it tapers; whether the crack passes through bricks or follows joints; displacement across the crack face.
- Rust at lintel bearings, compressed or missing sealant under shelf angles, spalling along the angle line.
- A salt tide line and eroded brick just above ground; damp-proof course visible or bridged.

### Inside the building

- Damp, blown plaster and salt bloom on the inside face of external walls, highest at the base (rising) or random and weather-related (penetrating).
- Cracks on the internal face on the same line as external cracks: this points to movement of the whole wall, not only the outer leaf.
- Sticking doors and windows, floor slopes and cornice gaps on the same line as external cracking: foundation movement.
- Decayed skirting and floor timbers against external walls.

### In the records

- Repeated repointing or crack repair on the same elevation, which means the cause was never addressed.
- Leak logs concentrated on one elevation, at window heads, or at each floor line.
- Previous façade inspections with unsafe or safe-with-repairs findings, and make-safe hoarding or netting invoices.
- Original specifications naming the tie type and lintel material; an absent tie specification on a building of the right era.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
Most masonry defects show as cracks, and the pattern of the crack identifies the cause far more reliably than its width. Read the pattern first, then the width.

| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal cracks at regular intervals, about every sixth course, outer leaf only | Wall tie corrosion | Worst on exposed elevations and higher up, where less load resists the lift; ties located by metal detector coincide with the cracks; inner face uncracked |
| Horizontal cracks in most bed joints, white swollen mortar, wall growth | Sulfate attack | Every course affected, not only tie courses; chimneys, parapets, rendered or wet walls; can affect both leaves; mortar soft when probed |
| Horizontal crack and outward bow repeated at each floor line of a framed building | Frame shortening; no soft joint under the shelf angle | Repeats floor by floor; brick spalled at the angle; no sealant line, or crushed sealant, under the angle |
| Stepped crack rising from a lintel end, horizontal crack along the lintel, brick lifted or dropped over the opening | Lintel corrosion | Rust at the bearing; crack widest at the lintel; opening frame itself square |
| Diagonal crack tapering wider at top or bottom, through openings, continuing below the damp-proof course | Foundation movement | Crack passes through bricks in a continuous line; sticking doors, floor slopes, matching internal cracks; seasonal movement on reactive clay; nearby trees or leaking drains |
| Vertical crack of even width near a corner or at a short return; brickwork oversailing at the base | Clay brick expansion or thermal movement | Long run without movement joints; no distortion of openings; width does not change across seasons |
| Vertical cracks at openings and mid-panel in blockwork or calcium silicate brick | Drying shrinkage | Material type; cracks widest early in life and then stable |
| Powdery brick, eroded mortar and salts in a band at the base | Rising damp with salt attack | Tide line up to about a metre; bridged or absent damp-proof course; worse behind garden beds and paving |
| Spalled faces high on exposed walls, parapets and chimneys | Frost damage, or hard cement pointing on soft brick | Cold climate; mortar proud of recessed brick; damage concentrated next to hard pointing |
| Cracking and displacement along column and floor lines of an early steel-framed building | Rust jacking of embedded steel | Rust staining at the crack; corners and parapets first; brick pushed outward rather than dropped |

> Wire ties corrode by thinning with little expansion, so they can fail without cracking the wall. On a cavity wall or veneer of the right era in a marine or exposed position, the absence of tie cracking does not clear the ties; it sends the item to investigation.

Two patterns are often confused. Tie cracking and sulfate cracking are both horizontal: tie cracks repeat only at tie courses and only in the outer leaf; sulfate cracks appear in most joints and the mortar itself is changed. Foundation cracks and movement cracks can both start at openings: foundation cracks taper and distort the opening; movement cracks are even and leave it square.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date, as façade inspection ordinances do), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, displaced or bulging brickwork over a footpath, entrance or occupied area; parapet or chimney out of plumb; outer leaf detached from ties | safety | Make safe immediately (exclusion zone, netting or take-down), engineer within days, repair within months |
| Displaced lintel with dropped brickwork; cracks 15 mm and wider; active water entry damaging the structure behind | failure | Repair now; propping where load-bearing |
| Tie corrosion cracking; lintel corrosion cracking over openings; floor-line bowing on a framed building; cracks 5 to 15 mm; persistent penetrating damp | condition | Programme repair in the near term, ahead of the next façade inspection cycle where one applies |
| Mortar eroded or friable over large areas; scattered spalling; damp-proof course bridged without salt damage yet; galvanised ties of the at-risk era with no cracking | lifecycle | Renewal on a planned cycle; combine with access for other façade work |
| Tie-era cavity wall in exposed or marine position with no record of tie condition; cracks of unknown cause; damp of unknown source | check | Investigate first; size the works from what the investigation finds |
| Hairline to 1 mm cracks of even width; historic movement shown stable; efflorescence on new work | nil | Monitor; cosmetic repair once shown stable |

Crack width scales are a useful second step. The BRE Digest 251 scale in Britain and the masonry damage categories in Appendix C of AS 2870 in Australia both grade damage by width: category 0 under 0.1 mm, 1 up to 1 mm, 2 up to 5 mm, 3 from 5 to 15 mm, 4 from 15 to 25 mm, with BRE adding 5 above 25 mm. Category 0 to 1 is normally cosmetic, 2 is moderate and usually repairable, 3 and above indicates significant movement needing structural attention.

> Width is not the whole answer. A 3 mm crack from tie corrosion is more serious than a 3 mm expansion crack, because the first keeps opening and the second does not. Grade the cause, then use width to set urgency within it.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads the survey; a structural engineer joins where there is bulging, lean or suspected foundation movement; a façade engineer leads on framed buildings and on buildings under a façade ordinance. In New York the inspection must be made by a Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector.

- Visual survey of every elevation, close up from access where defects or public areas warrant it, with a crack map recording location, pattern, width and taper.
- Tie inspection. Locate ties with a metal detector, drill and inspect by borescope, and remove a brick or tie at representative positions to examine the embedded section, where corrosion is worst. Weight sampling to the most exposed elevations and upper storeys; extend it when corrosion is found. BRE Digest 401 sets out the approach in British practice.
- Mortar analysis where sulfate attack is suspected, or to specify matching repointing mortar.
- Plumb and bulge survey by laser or plumb line where panels look out of line; record for comparison.
- Crack monitoring with tell-tales or gauge studs for at least twelve months, covering a full wet and dry season on reactive clay, before concluding a crack is stable.
- Lintels and shelf angles: covermeter to locate, opening up at bearings to see section loss and tray detail.
- Hammer tapping of faces and parapets over public areas, removing anything loose at the time.
- Moisture: calcium carbide or gravimetric samples at depth. Electrical moisture meters read salt as water and overstate rising damp; they show distribution, not diagnosis.
- Thermography to show wet zones, cavity fill voids and bridged areas.

The report should state the form of wall, the tie type and condition by elevation and height, lintel and shelf angle condition, crack causes with the evidence for each, anything made safe, and repairs by priority with extents measured, not estimated.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Remedial ties. Stainless helical or resin-anchored ties drilled through the outer leaf into the inner leaf or frame, at the spacing the standard requires, with extra ties at openings, corners and the top of walls. Strip ties that are expanding must be removed or cut back from the outer leaf, or the jacking continues; wire ties can usually be left in place.
- Rebuilding. Panels bulged beyond what ties can restrain, or with bricks displaced, are taken down and rebuilt on new ties.
- Lintels. Replace in stainless steel or galvanised to the exposure class, with a cavity tray, stop ends and weep holes over; prop the brickwork above during the work.
- Shelf angles and floor lines. Cut out the mortar bed beneath each angle and form a soft joint of compressible filler and sealant; inspect and treat the angle and its fixings; where angles have lost section, replace them, which requires propping the cladding.
- Movement joints. Saw-cut and seal joints at corners and in long runs; tie across where panels have been freed.
- Repointing. Rake out to a depth of about twice the joint width, and repoint in a mortar no stronger than the brick; lime mortar for lime-built walls.
- Damp. Remove the bridging first (lower ground and paving, cut render back above the damp-proof course, clear debris from cavities); then a new damp-proof course where the old one has failed, sawn-in or injected; replaster internally in salt-resistant systems.
- Embedded steel. Open up along the affected lines, clean or replace and protect the steel, and rebuild with flashing and drainage the original lacked.
- Foundation movement. Address the cause (drains, trees, watering) and monitor; underpinning is reserved for movement that continues after the cause is removed.

Interactions: tie and lintel work, repointing and shelf angle joints share the same access and are best packaged by elevation; cavity insulation may need to be extracted where it bridges; older renders and paints may hold hazardous materials that set the method.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with a rate for each probe or opening. Remedial ties and repointing are measured by wall area; lintels by opening; soft joints, damp-proof courses and movement joints by linear metre; rebuilding by area. Access is often the largest single component on multi-storey façades, which is why works are packaged elevation by elevation. Make-safe protection recurs until the repair is done.

The usual register shape is two-part: the investigation as a check line, and a conditional works envelope sized from what it finds. Ties, lintels and shelf angles are lifecycle items; repointing is repairs and maintenance on a long cycle; ordinance inspections and make-safe works are code compliance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 3700 Masonry structures and AS 4773 Masonry for small buildings; wall ties are rated to exposure classes under AS/NZS 2699.1, and masonry units are tested to AS/NZS 4456. AS 2870 governs residential footings and gives the crack damage categories. There is no periodic façade inspection regime; on strata buildings the façade is common property and belongs in the capital works plan.
- United Kingdom. Approved Documents A and C set structural and moisture requirements; design follows BS EN 1996 with PD 6697 guidance on movement joints, workmanship BS 8000-3, and cleaning and repair BS 8221-1 and BS 8221-2. BRE Digests 251 (crack classification) and 401 (replacing wall ties) are the working references. On leasehold blocks the works are service-charge items subject to section 20 consultation; higher-risk buildings sit under the Building Safety Act 2022.
- United States. The International Building Code calls up TMS 402/602 for masonry; ASTM E2270 sets the practice for periodic façade inspection. New York City's Façade Inspection and Safety Program requires a critical examination of buildings over six storeys every five years, with Cycle 10 filing windows running from February 2025 to February 2029 across three sub-cycles; Chicago, Boston, San Francisco and several other cities run comparable ordinances. The Brick Industry Association's Technical Notes are the standard practice references for ties, movement and repair.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Previous façade inspection reports and any ordinance filings, with their unsafe and repair findings.
- Drawings and specifications showing the wall form, tie type, lintels and shelf angles.
- Records of tie replacement, lintel replacement, repointing and crack repairs, with dates, extents and warranties.
- Any crack monitoring data and engineer's reports on movement or foundations.
- Damp-proof course installation records and guarantees, and any cavity insulation retrofit records.
- Leak and damp logs by elevation, and make-safe hoarding or netting records.
- Heritage listing and conservation constraints, which set materials and methods.

pages.title: Occupational Health & Safety (OHS)
pages.question: Which safety provisions in a building protect occupants and workers, and which gaps are serious hazards?
pages.answer: Workplace safety in a building rests on safe access to plant, sound stairs, slip-resistant floors, safe glazing, controlled confined spaces, and records that tell people what they are working on. The serious gaps are plant reached by climbing or portable ladders, unidentified confined spaces, slippery entries and wet areas, unmarked or unsafe glass doors, and contractors working without registers or permits. Falls on stairs and floors are the most common serious injuries.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about occupational health & safety (ohs); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Safe access provisions, handrails, statutory signage

sources.title: Model WHS laws and codes of practice

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
This element covers the safety provisions built into the fabric of a building and its management that protect occupants, workers and contractors: safe access to plant and roofs, stairs and handrails, slip-resistant surfaces, safety glazing and manifestation on glass, confined space identification, statutory and safety signage, the health and safety records that must be kept for the building, and the systems for managing contractors. It sits behind many other elements: roof safety, balustrades, lifts, plant and hazardous materials each have their own pages, and this page covers what ties them together and the provisions not covered elsewhere.

| Provision | Where it applies | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access to plant and services | Plant rooms, roofs, risers, ceiling voids | Ladders without cages or fall protection; plant reached by climbing |
| Stairs and handrails | All buildings | Uneven risers; worn or slippery nosings; missing handrails; low balustrades |
| Floor slip resistance | Entries, wet areas, ramps, external paving | Polished or wet surfaces; wrong finishes for the location |
| Glazing safety | Doors, sidelights, low-level glass | Ordinary glass in critical locations; no manifestation on glass doors |
| Confined spaces | Tanks, pits, ducts, voids | Not identified, signed or controlled |
| Safety signage | Plant, hazards, emergency equipment | Missing, faded or wrong |
| Building safety records | All workplaces and managed buildings | Missing or out of date: registers, manuals, the health and safety file |
| Contractor management | All managed buildings | No induction, permits or hazard information |

Duties sit with whoever manages or controls the building as a workplace, in Australia the person conducting a business or undertaking and those with management or control of a workplace, in Britain the employer and those in control of premises, and in the United States the employer under OSHA. Owners of tenanted buildings usually retain duties for common areas, plant and structure.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair nosings and treads | 10 to 25 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Anti-slip treatments | 1 to 5 years | Traffic; cleaning products |
| Fixed ladders and platforms | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Glass manifestation | 5 to 15 years | Cleaning; damage |
| Safety signs | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage |
| Records and registers | Must be kept current | Changes to the building |

What shortens life, or effectiveness:

- Heavy traffic wearing stairs and floors.
- Cleaning regimes that polish floors or strip treatments.
- Changes to the building without updating records and signs.
- Plant added without safe access.

Records have no wear life but go out of date every time the building changes, which is the commonest way they fail.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Unsafe access to plant

Plant installed on roofs, high walls and in ceiling voids without fixed ladders, platforms and fall protection is reached by portable ladders or climbing, which causes falls. New plant is often added without access being designed.

### Stair hazards

Uneven risers, worn and slippery nosings, missing contrast on edges, missing handrails, and balustrades below current heights cause falls, the most common serious injury in buildings.

### Slippery floors

Polished stone, glazed tiles and smooth finishes at entries, in wet areas and on ramps become slippery when wet or contaminated; cleaning products and sealers make them worse. Slip resistance can be measured and compared with the level needed for the location.
