### Glazing hazards

Glass doors and full-height glazing without manifestation are walked into; ordinary annealed glass in doors and low-level panels breaks into dangerous shards. Older buildings often have glass that would not meet current safety glazing rules.

### Confined spaces

Tanks, pits, sumps, ducts and voids with limited entry and poor ventilation can hold toxic or oxygen-deficient atmospheres. Deaths occur when people enter unidentified confined spaces without controls, and when rescuers follow them.

### Missing safety records

Asbestos registers, plant registers, confined space registers, operation and maintenance manuals, and the health and safety file (in Britain) are needed for anyone working safely on the building. Where they are missing or out of date, contractors work blind.

### Unmanaged contractors

Contractors without induction, permits or hazard information disturb asbestos, enter confined spaces, work at height without protection and isolate systems unsafely.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Plant reachable only by portable ladder or climbing; roof hatches without guardrails.
- Stairs with worn nosings, uneven risers, missing handrails or contrast.
- Polished or glazed floors at entries and wet areas; mats curling.
- Glass doors without manifestation; cracked or annealed glass in doors.
- Pits, tanks and voids without confined space signs or locks.
- Missing or faded safety signs at plant and hazards.

### In the records

- Asbestos, plant and confined space registers.
- Health and safety file or building manual.
- Contractor induction and permit records.
- Incident and injury records.
- Slip resistance test results.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ladder marks on walls near plant | No designed access to plant | Inspection |
| Repeated slips at an entry | Floor finish unsuitable when wet | Slip resistance test |
| Falls on one stair | Uneven risers or worn nosings | Measurement |
| People walking into glass doors | Missing manifestation | Inspection |
| Contractors unaware of hazards | No induction or registers | Records |

> Unidentified confined spaces and plant reachable only by climbing are serious hazards. Identify, sign and control them before anyone next needs access.

Incident clusters are the best guide: several slips at one entrance, or falls on one flight, point to that surface or stair rather than to the people using it.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unprotected access to plant at height; unidentified confined spaces; dangerous glazing; slippery entries | safety | Rectify now |
| Injury-causing defects | failure | Repair now |
| Register reviews and statutory inspections due | deadline | At the required interval |
| Worn stairs, faded signs, ageing treatments | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Stair finishes and fittings at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No registers or building safety file | check | Compile |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A health and safety consultant or building surveyor with safety expertise leads, with specialists for slip testing, glazing and confined spaces.

- Access audit of every plant item, roof area, riser and ceiling void that needs maintenance, recording how it is reached and what protection exists.
- Stair survey: consistency of risers and goings, nosing condition and contrast, handrails on both sides where required, balustrade heights and openings.
- Slip resistance testing of floors at entries, wet areas, ramps and external paving, wet and dry, against the classification needed for each location.
- Glazing survey: safety glass markings in doors and low-level panels, and manifestation on glass doors and full-height glazing.
- Confined space survey: identify every tank, pit, sump, duct and void that meets the definition, and record entry points, hazards and controls.
- Records review: asbestos, plant and confined space registers, operation and maintenance manuals, the health and safety file, and their currency.
- Contractor management review: inductions, permits to work, isolation procedures and hazard information.
- Incident review: where and how injuries and near misses have occurred.

The report should list hazards by risk, compliance gaps, missing records, and a prioritised programme.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Fixed access to plant: caged ladders or ladders with fall arrest, platforms with guardrails, walkways and roof hatches with guardrails.
- Stair repairs: replace worn nosings with slip-resistant, contrasting nosings, add handrails, raise balustrades where people are at risk.
- Slip remedies: anti-slip treatments, replacement finishes in wet and entry areas, recessed entry matting, and cleaning regimes that do not polish floors.
- Glazing: replace annealed glass in critical locations with safety glass; apply manifestation at the right heights.
- Confined spaces: signs, locked covers, a register and entry procedures.
- Signage at plant, hazards and emergency equipment.
- Records: compile and maintain registers, manuals and the safety file, and make them available to contractors.
- Contractor system: inductions, permits to work and isolation procedures.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and slip testing are lump sums, with slip testing recurring where floors are treated. Fixed access works are priced per item: ladders, platforms, walkways and guardrails. Stair works per flight; floor treatments and replacement finishes by area; glazing per pane; signage per sign. Compiling registers and a safety file is a lump sum, then a recurring update cost. Contractor management systems are an operating cost.

Most items are code compliance; worn stairs and finishes are lifecycle; treatments and signage are repairs and maintenance; serious hazards are immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The model work health and safety laws place duties on persons conducting a business or undertaking and those with management or control of workplaces; codes of practice cover managing the risk of falls, confined spaces and the work environment and facilities; AS 1657 covers fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders, AS 4586 slip resistance classification and AS 1288 glazing.
- United Kingdom. The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 cover floors, stairs and glazing; the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require a health and safety file for the building; the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 apply; Approved Document K covers stairs, guarding and glazing.
- United States. The OSH Act and OSHA standards for walking-working surfaces (29 CFR 1910 Subpart D) and permit-required confined spaces (1910.146) apply; building codes govern stairs and safety glazing; ANSI A326.3 sets dynamic slip resistance testing of hard surface flooring.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Asbestos, plant and confined space registers.
- Health and safety file or building manual, with operation and maintenance manuals.
- Contractor induction, permit and isolation procedures.
- Incident and injury records, including slips and falls.
- Slip resistance test results.
- Roof and plant access records and safety system certificates.
- Glazing schedules for doors and low-level panels.

pages.title: Partitioning Systems
pages.question: How do internal partitions fail, and when does a partition matter for fire safety?
pages.answer: Partitions carry no structural load but may carry fire and acoustic ratings, which they lose when services penetrate them or when they stop at the ceiling instead of the slab. Partitions built tight to deflecting slabs crack; meeting rooms leak sound over ceilings; full-height glass without manifestation is walked into; operable walls wear their tracks and jam or drop. Check the fire strategy before removing or penetrating any partition.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about partitioning systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fixed and operable partitions, performance requirements

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Partitioning systems divide space within a building: plasterboard on steel or timber studs, demountable and glazed office partitions, operable walls in meeting and function rooms, toilet cubicle partitions, and non-loadbearing masonry walls. Partitions carry no structural load, but they can be fire-rated, acoustically rated, or both, and they decide how well a space works for privacy, sound and layout flexibility. Most partitions in commercial buildings belong to tenant fit-outs and change at every lease.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasterboard stud walls | Offices, apartments, all building types | Damage; cracking at joints; acoustic leakage |
| Fire-rated plasterboard walls | Compartment and corridor walls, risers | Penetrations; walls not to slab |
| Acoustic partitions | Meeting rooms, apartments, hotels | Gaps above ceilings; services penetrations |
| Glazed and demountable partitions | Offices | Glass safety; manifestation; acoustic seals |
| Operable walls | Meeting and function rooms, schools, hotels | Track and mechanism failure; seals; safety |
| Toilet cubicle partitions | Amenities | Moisture swelling; hardware |
| Masonry internal walls | Older buildings | Cracking; alterations |

For assessment, the important question about any partition is its role: dividing space only, separating sound, or separating fire. The answer decides whether a defect is cosmetic, a comfort issue or a life-safety issue.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Type | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasterboard partitions | Life of the fit-out or longer | Damage; alterations |
| Glazed partitions | 15 to 25 years | Fit-out changes; hardware |
| Operable walls | 15 to 25 years with servicing | Use; track wear |
| Toilet partitions | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; abuse |
| Acoustic and fire performance | Until next penetration or alteration | Services works; fit-outs |

What shortens life, or performance:

- Services penetrations that break fire and acoustic ratings.
- Fit-out changes that remove or alter walls without understanding their role.
- Slab deflection crushing or cracking partitions without deflection heads.
- Moisture in plasterboard near wet areas.

In offices, partitions are usually removed and rebuilt with each fit-out, so their life is the lease term rather than their material life.

Rated partitions in the base building, such as corridor and riser walls, last as long as the building but lose performance with each penetration.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Lost fire and acoustic rating

Rated partitions only perform if they run to the slab or a rated ceiling and every penetration is sealed. Cables, pipes and ducts added later, and walls stopped at the suspended ceiling, let fire, smoke and sound pass. Partitions are often assumed to be rated, or assumed not to be, without checking.

### Cracking from movement

Partitions built tight to slabs above crack and bow when the slab deflects; deflection heads that allow movement are missing or jammed.

### Acoustic complaints

Meeting rooms and apartments leak sound through gaps above ceilings, around services, under doors and through back-to-back outlets.

### Glazed partition hazards

Full-height glass without manifestation is walked into; older glazed partitions may not use safety glass.

### Operable wall failures

Operable walls are heavy, moving panels on overhead tracks. Tracks and carriers wear, panels drop or jam, seals fail so rooms leak sound, and panels have injured people when moved improperly.

### Damage and moisture

Plasterboard is damaged by furniture, trolleys and moves, and swells and grows mould where it gets wet.

### Fit-out removal of base-building walls

Fit-outs sometimes remove or alter partitions that are part of the base building's fire or acoustic design, such as corridor walls and riser enclosures, without realising their role. The loss only shows in a fire or in neighbour complaints.

### Services in partitions

Power, data and plumbing inside stud walls are cut into during alterations, and back-to-back outlets create sound and fire paths.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Partitions stopping at the ceiling when tiles are lifted.
- Unsealed penetrations through walls above ceilings.
- Cracks at partition heads under long spans.
- Glass without manifestation.
- Operable walls hard to move, leaning or with damaged seals.
- Damaged and patched plasterboard.

### In the records

- Fire strategy showing rated walls.
- Fit-out drawings and approvals.
- Acoustic complaints.
- Operable wall service records.

- Back-to-back power outlets in walls between apartments or meeting rooms.
- Corridor and riser walls altered by fit-outs.
- Water staining and swelling at the base of plasterboard near wet areas.
- Toilet partitions swollen or with broken hardware.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversations audible between meeting rooms | Gap above ceiling or services penetration | Ceiling void inspection |
| Cracking at the partition head | Slab deflection without a deflection head | Head detail inspection |
| Operable wall dragging or dropping | Track or carrier wear | Service inspection |
| Rated wall with open penetrations | Services works without fire stopping | Inspection |

> Before removing or penetrating any partition, check the fire strategy: partitions forming compartments, corridors or risers are fire-safety elements.

Decide first whether a partition is a fire, acoustic or plain dividing wall, because the same defect matters very differently depending on its role.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire-rated partitions breached; unsafe glazing; operable walls with failing tracks | safety | Rectify now |
| Partitions damaged or unusable | failure | Repair |
| Fire certification requiring rectification | deadline | As required |
| Acoustic leakage; cracking; damage | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Partitions at end of fit-out life | lifecycle | Replace with fit-out |
| Rated partitions not identified | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

The same open penetration is a safety finding in a compartment wall, a condition finding in an acoustic wall between meeting rooms, and nil in a plain dividing wall; grade by role, not appearance.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a fire engineer to identify rated partitions and an acoustic consultant where privacy or noise is the issue.

- Identify rated partitions from the fire strategy, fire engineering report and acoustic design, and mark them on plans, since fit-outs often blur which walls matter.
- Ceiling void inspection along rated partitions to check they run to the slab and that every penetration is sealed with a tested system.
- Head detail inspection where partitions crack, to check for deflection heads.
- Acoustic testing between rooms where complaints exist, with flanking paths traced.
- Glazing check for safety glass marks and manifestation.
- Operable wall inspection by the manufacturer or a specialist: tracks, carriers, panels, seals and safe operation.

The report should give a plan of rated partitions, defects in each, and a remediation plan coordinated with fit-out cycles.

Where drawings are missing, ratings may need to be inferred from construction, which takes opening up and specialist judgement.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Fire stopping of every penetration in rated partitions with tested systems, and extension of partitions to the slab where they stop at the ceiling.
- Acoustic sealing above ceilings, around services and at outlets, with ceiling barriers where walls cannot be extended.
- Deflection heads fitted or freed where slab movement cracks partitions.
- Safety glass and manifestation on glazed partitions.
- Operable wall servicing on a schedule, with replacement where tracks or panels are failing.
- Labelling of rated partitions above ceilings so trades know what they are penetrating.
- Repairs to damaged plasterboard, with moisture-resistant board near wet areas.

- Fit-out controls requiring fire and acoustic review before base-building walls are altered.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Fire and acoustic sealing is priced per penetration or by length of partition, with access above ceilings driving cost. Partition replacement is priced by area and usually coincides with fit-outs, when it is cheapest. Operable wall servicing recurs; replacement is a lump sum per wall. Labelling of rated walls is inexpensive and prevents future breaches.

Fire safety items are code compliance; acoustic and finish repairs are condition items; replacement is lifecycle and often a tenant cost.

Identifying rated walls once, on plans and on site, avoids repeated investigation at every fit-out.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets fire resistance levels and sound insulation requirements, including between apartments and between units and corridors; AS 1530.4 sets fire testing; AS 1288 governs glazing including manifestation; fit-outs that alter partitions need approval.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B governs fire separation and Approved Document E sound insulation, including pre-completion testing in new homes; BS EN 1364 covers fire testing of non-loadbearing walls; Approved Document K covers glazing manifestation.
- United States. The International Building Code sets fire partitions and fire barriers and sound transmission requirements in dwelling units; ASTM E90 and E336 cover sound testing; tenant improvements need permits and fire review.

Tenancy fit-out guides should identify which walls tenants may not alter.

Strata by-laws restrict wall changes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire strategy and plans showing rated partitions.
- Fit-out drawings and approvals.
- Acoustic reports and complaints.
- Operable wall service records.
- Fire stopping records for partition penetrations.
- Glazing schedules for partitions.

- Tenant fit-out guide and rules on altering walls.
- Records of neighbour noise complaints.

- Strata approvals for wall alterations.

pages.title: Passenger & Goods Lifts
pages.question: How do lifts fail, when do they need modernisation rather than maintenance, and which faults are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Lifts are modernised in stages: controls, drives and doors at 15 to 20 years, machines and ropes at 25 to 35. Unsupported controllers are the usual trigger, shown by rising breakdowns and long waits for parts. Doors cause most breakdowns. The safety faults are door interlocks, brakes and unintended movement, levelling trip hazards, and emergency phones that no longer connect as copper lines are retired. Buried hydraulic cylinders corrode and leak.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about passenger & goods lifts; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Hoist machinery, control systems, door operators, car interiors, safety gear

sources.title: ASME A17.1 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Passenger and goods lifts move people and goods between floors. A lift comprises the drive machine and brake, the controller, suspension (steel ropes or coated belts), car and counterweight, guide rails, landing and car doors with their operators and interlocks, safety gear and overspeed governor, buffers in the pit, the car interior and fixtures, emergency communication, and interfaces to fire systems. In apartment buildings the lifts are usually the largest single sinking fund item; in offices they shape tenant experience every day.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geared traction | Offices and apartments, 1950s to 1990s | Worm or helical gear between motor and sheave; gearbox wear; oil |
| Gearless traction | Taller and newer buildings | Efficient; long-lived machines; controllers set the modernisation cycle |
| Machine-room-less (MRL) | Most new buildings from the 2000s | Machine in the shaft; access for maintenance is the constraint |
| Hydraulic | Low-rise buildings, goods lifts | Cylinder in the ground or beside the car; oil leaks; slow in cold |
| Goods and service lifts | Retail, hospitals, hotels, industrial | Heavy use; door and floor damage |
| Fire-fighting and evacuation lifts | Tall buildings | Protected power, controls and lobbies; additional testing |

Lifts are modernised in stages rather than replaced: controls, drives and door operators at 15 to 20 years; car interiors when the building is refurbished; machines, ropes, guides and safety gear at 25 to 35 years. Each stage brings the components it touches up to the current standard, which often adds work such as unintended car movement protection or accessibility features.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controllers and drives | 15 to 20 years | Manufacturer support; electronics |
| Door operators and equipment | 15 to 20 years | Traffic; abuse; maintenance |
| Geared machines | 25 to 35 years | Gear wear; lubrication |
| Gearless machines | 30 to 40 years | Bearings; brake |
| Suspension ropes | 10 to 20 years | Trips; sheave condition; lubrication |
| Hydraulic cylinders | 25 to 30 years | Corrosion of buried cylinders; seals |
| Car interiors | 10 to 20 years | Use; style |
| Guide rails, buffers and safety gear | 30 to 40 years | Rarely limiting; must be tested |

What shortens life:

- Heavy traffic, especially goods and hospital lifts and lifts serving car parks.
- Door abuse: doors forced, struck by trolleys and held open.
- Water in the pit from groundwater or failed sumps, corroding buffers, rails and safety gear.
- Hot, dusty machine rooms that age electronics.
- Call-out-only maintenance instead of planned preventive maintenance.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Controller and drive obsolescence

Controllers and drives are the usual trigger for modernisation. When the manufacturer stops making parts and the programming tools are proprietary, a single board failure can stop a lift for weeks. Lifts from the 1980s to early 2000s are commonly in this position now.

### Door faults

Doors cause most breakdowns and many injuries. Operators, tracks, rollers, gibs and interlocks wear; doors are struck by trolleys and forced by users; sensors that stop doors closing on people fail or are misaligned. Interlocks that let a landing door open without the car present are a fall hazard.

### Rope and sheave wear

Steel ropes wear and develop broken wires, rouge (red dust from internal wear) and diameter loss; sheave grooves wear unevenly, which accelerates rope wear and causes slippage. Ropes are replaced on measured condition.

### Brake and unintended movement

Brakes wear and their linings contaminate; a failed brake can let a car move with doors open. Newer standards require protection against unintended car movement, and modernising the controls usually brings this requirement with it.

### Levelling faults

Cars that stop above or below the floor create trip hazards, a common cause of injury to elderly passengers and a sign of drive, brake or hydraulic valve problems.

### Hydraulic cylinder failure

Buried hydraulic cylinders corrode from outside where groundwater reaches them; seals leak oil into the ground. Older single-bottom cylinders can fail suddenly. Oil leaks are an environmental issue, and replacing a buried cylinder means excavating the pit.

### Emergency communication failure

Trapped passengers must be able to call for help. Lift phones on copper lines stop working as networks are retired; batteries fail; phones are disconnected after maintenance.

### Fire service and evacuation functions

Fire service recall and fire-fighter control must work with the fire alarm and protected power supply. Interfaces broken by fire panel or lift upgrades leave lifts that do not home or cannot be used by fire-fighters.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Controller nameplate and era in the machine room or control cabinet.
- Doors: damage, slow or jerky operation, gaps, sensors.
- Levelling at each floor; trip edges.
- Ride quality: vibration, noise, jerking at starts and stops.
- Emergency phone: test call, line type, signage.
- Pit: water, oil, debris.
- Machine room: temperature, oil leaks, housekeeping, rope condition visible at the machine.

### In the records

- Call-out and breakdown history per lift.
- Entrapment records.
- Maintenance contract and scope.
- Modernisation history and recommendations.
- Registration and periodic inspection certificates.
- Rope test results.

- Fixtures: worn buttons, failed indicators and missing audio announcements, which show the age of the controls and accessibility gaps.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakdowns rising each year, long waits for parts | Controller obsolescence | Parts support status; call-out records |
| Most call-outs for doors | Door equipment wear or abuse | Call-out coding; door inspection |
| Car stops above or below floor level | Drive, brake or valve problems | Levelling measurements |
| Red dust on ropes | Internal rope wear | Rope inspection and measurement |
| Oil in the pit or ground near a hydraulic lift | Seal or cylinder leak | Oil consumption; cylinder test |
| Phone silent on test | Line retired, disconnected or battery failed | Line type; test |

> A landing door that can be opened without the car present, a car that moves with its doors open, or an emergency phone that does not connect are safety failures. Take the lift out of service until fixed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door interlock faults; brake faults; unintended movement; emergency communication not working; levelling trip hazards | safety | Remove from service until fixed |
| Lift out of service; entrapments recurring | failure | Repair now |
| Periodic inspection or registration due; copper line retirement | deadline | At the prescribed date |
| Rising breakdowns; worn doors and ropes; hydraulic leaks | condition | Repair or modernise in the near term |
| Controls, drives or machines at end of life | lifecycle | Plan staged modernisation |
| No condition audit; modernisation history unknown | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An independent lift consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor present; independence matters because the contractor may also bid for the modernisation.

- Records review: breakdowns and entrapments per lift over two to three years, maintenance scope and hours, modernisation history, inspection certificates.
- Machine room or control cabinet inspection: controller, drive, machine, brake, governor, ropes and sheaves.
- Shaft and pit inspection from the car top and pit: guides, doors, interlocks, counterweight, buffers, water and oil.
- Performance testing: door times, levelling accuracy, ride quality, waiting times at peak.
- Safety testing as the standard requires: safety gear, governor, buffers, brake, unintended movement protection.
- Parts support: written advice from the manufacturer on controller and drive support.
- Code gap review: accessibility, fire service functions, communications and unintended movement against current standards.

The report should give a staged modernisation scope and timing per lift, safety defects, and whether the maintenance contract is adequate.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Controls and drive modernisation, usually with door operators and fixtures, which cures most reliability problems and brings in regenerative drives and unintended movement protection.
- Door package: new operators, tracks, rollers, interlocks and full-height light curtains.
- Rope replacement with sheave regrooving or replacement.
- Machine replacement with gearless machines at the end of geared machine life.
- Hydraulic cylinder replacement with protected or holeless designs, or conversion to traction.
- Car interior refurbishment, with accessible controls and audio and braille indicators.
- Emergency communication upgrade to digital or cellular with battery backup.
- Maintenance contract with defined preventive scope, response times and parts support.
- Staggered programmes in multi-lift buildings so one lift is always in service.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Modernisation is priced per lift per stage, and is usually programmed lift by lift. Builders' work (machine room alterations, electrical supply, fire interfaces, pit works) adds to each stage. Rope replacement recurs on condition. Hydraulic cylinder replacement includes excavation. Temporary loss of service in single-lift buildings can require temporary arrangements for residents with limited mobility.

Modernisation stages are lifecycle; safety items and inspections are code compliance; ropes and repairs are repairs and maintenance; communication migration carries a deadline where lines are being retired.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Lifts are registered plant under state work health and safety regulations, with periodic inspection in some states; the AS 1735 series, now adopting the ISO 8100 and EN 81 based standards, governs design and modernisation; the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010 set accessibility for new and upgraded lifts.
- United Kingdom. The Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 require thorough examination of passenger lifts at least every six months; BS EN 81-20 and 81-50 govern new lifts and modernisation, including unintended car movement protection; BS EN 81-80 guides improving existing lifts; BS EN 81-28 covers remote alarms; fire-fighting lifts follow BS EN 81-72.
- United States. ASME A17.1 governs new lifts and A17.3 existing lifts, with annual inspections and periodic load tests set by state and city elevator authorities; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessibility; fire service recall and fire-fighter operation are required.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Breakdown, call-out and entrapment records per lift.
- Maintenance contract and scope.
- Registration and periodic inspection certificates.
- Modernisation history and outstanding recommendations.
- Manufacturer parts support advice for controllers and drives.
- Rope and safety test results.
- Emergency phone line details and test records.
- Sinking fund forecast for the lifts in strata buildings.

pages.title: Passive Fire Protection
pages.question: How does passive fire protection fail, how do you find the breaches, and which findings put lives at risk?
pages.answer: Passive protection fails by alteration and use, not age. Every cable, pipe and duct added through a fire wall is a potential breach; risers and ceiling voids above corridors are the worst. Fire doors fail when closers break, doors are wedged open, seals are painted over, and residents replace flat entrance doors with unrated ones. Walls that stop at the ceiling and damaged steel protection are found only by looking above ceilings and behind linings.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about passive fire protection; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fire-rated doors, walls, ceilings, structural protection

sources.title: NFPA 80 Fire Doors and Other Opening Protectives

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Passive fire protection is the fabric of the building that contains fire and smoke and keeps the structure standing long enough for people to escape and fire-fighters to work: fire-resisting walls, floors and ceilings that divide the building into compartments; fire doors and their hardware; fire-resisting glazing; protection of penetrations where services pass through; cavity barriers and fire stopping in concealed spaces; and fire protection of the structure itself. It does nothing until a fire, and it is broken every time a building is altered.

| Element | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire-resisting walls and floors | Divide the building into compartments; protect stairs, shafts and escape routes | Holes cut for services; walls stopped at the ceiling instead of the slab |
| Penetration seals | Restore fire resistance where pipes, cables and ducts pass through | Missing, unrated or damaged seals; new services added |
| Fire doors and doorsets | Close openings in fire-resisting walls | Gaps, failed closers, damaged seals, propped open, wrong hardware, replaced with non-rated doors |
| Fire-resisting glazing | Light and visibility through fire-resisting elements | Replaced with ordinary glass; frames and beads changed |
| Fire-resisting ceilings and shafts | Protect structure and voids | Tiles removed, access panels unrated |
| Cavity barriers | Stop fire spreading through concealed cavities, including façades | Missing, misplaced or open |
| Structural fire protection | Keep steel and other structure from losing strength | Spray-applied coatings damaged; intumescent paint chipped or overcoated |
| Fire dampers | Close ducts at compartment walls | Covered on the ductwork page |

A building's passive fire protection is defined by its fire strategy or fire engineering report, which sets the compartments, fire-resistance levels and escape routes. Without that document, nobody knows which walls and doors matter. Many older buildings have no current strategy, and many performance solutions rely on passive elements that later works have undone.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry and concrete compartment walls and floors | Life of the building | Penetrations; alterations |
| Plasterboard fire-resisting walls | Life of the building if intact | Damage; services penetrations |
| Penetration seals | 20 to 30 years if undisturbed | Further works; product |
| Fire doors | 20 to 30 years with maintenance | Use; abuse; maintenance |
| Door closers and hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Intumescent seals | 10 to 20 years | Painting over; damage |
| Intumescent coatings on steel | 15 to 25 years | Damage; moisture; overcoating |
| Spray-applied fire protection | Life of the building if undisturbed | Damage; water |

What shortens life:

- Alterations: every cable, pipe and duct installed after construction is a potential breach.
- Fit-outs that move walls, add doors and remove ceilings.
- Daily use: doors wedged open, closers disconnected, seals damaged by trolleys.
- Maintenance by trades who do not know which elements are fire-rated.
- Water on spray-applied and intumescent protection.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Breached penetrations

The most common passive fire defect in existing buildings is an unsealed or improperly sealed penetration: cables pushed through holes in fire walls, pipes surrounded by expanding foam that is not fire-rated, ducts without dampers, holes left after services were removed. Risers, plant rooms and ceiling voids above corridors are the worst areas. Each breach lets fire and smoke move between compartments.

### Walls not built to the slab

Fire-resisting walls must run from floor slab to floor slab or to a fire-rated ceiling. Walls that stop at the suspended ceiling, or that had their top sections removed for services, leave a path for fire over the top. This is often found only by lifting ceiling tiles.

### Fire door failures

Fire doors fail through use: closers disconnected or broken so doors do not close; doors wedged or propped open; gaps at edges larger than allowed; intumescent and smoke seals painted over, damaged or missing; non-rated hinges, locks and vision panels; doors cut down to clear new floor finishes; and, in apartment buildings, flat entrance doors replaced by residents with non-rated doors. A fire door that does not close fully is not a fire door.

### Glazing replacements

Broken fire-resisting glazing replaced with ordinary glass, or beads and frames replaced with untested parts, loses its fire resistance entirely.

### Missing cavity barriers

Concealed spaces in walls, floors, roofs and façades need barriers to stop fire travelling unseen. Missing or misplaced cavity barriers in façades and in timber-framed construction have allowed fire to spread rapidly through buildings.

### Damaged structural protection

Spray-applied fire protection on steel is knocked off by later trades, fixings and services; intumescent coatings are chipped, overpainted with incompatible paint, or weathered where exposed. Unprotected steel loses strength quickly in fire.

### Unverified products and certification

Fire stopping and door products must be installed as tested. Untested combinations, products used outside their tested range, and missing certification leave the protection unproven. Older protection may contain asbestos.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the building

- Holes and unsealed gaps around services in risers, plant rooms and above ceilings.
- Expanding foam around pipes and cables in fire walls.
- Fire doors propped or wedged open; closers disconnected; doors not closing fully into the frame.
- Gaps at door edges; seals painted, damaged or missing; non-rated hardware.
- Fire door labels or tags missing or illegible.
- Ordinary glass in fire-resisting screens and doors.
- Walls stopping at the ceiling line when tiles are lifted.
- Damaged spray protection on steel; chipped intumescent coatings.

### In the records

- Fire strategy or fire engineering report, including performance solutions.
- Compartmentation drawings.
- Fire door register and inspection records.
- Fire stopping records, with photographs and product details.
- Annual fire safety statements or essential safety measures reports.
- Asbestos register.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke spread between floors in a fire or drill | Breached riser penetrations or walls not to slab | Riser and ceiling void survey |
| Doors do not close fully | Failed or disconnected closer, binding, obstruction | Door inspection |
| Gaps of several millimetres at door edges | Wear, distortion or poor installation | Gap measurement against the standard |
| Foam in penetrations | Untested sealing | Product identification |
| Flat entrance doors of different designs | Resident replacements | Door survey |
| Exposed steel with patches of protection | Damage by trades | Structural protection survey |

> Passive fire protection is only as good as its weakest breach. A single unsealed riser or a fire door that does not close can let smoke reach every floor, so surveys must be thorough rather than representative in risers, stairs and escape routes.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair or escape route doors not closing; breached riser or stair penetrations; fire doors wedged open; flat entrance doors not fire-rated in apartment buildings | safety | Rectify now; fire watch or interim measures where needed |
| Fire door checks and annual certification due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Widespread penetration breaches; walls not to slab; damaged structural protection | condition | Remediation programme in the near term |
| Doors and hardware at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No fire strategy; compartmentation unknown | check | Fire strategy and compartmentation survey |
| Minor door adjustments | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire engineer or passive fire specialist leads, working from the fire strategy; where there is no strategy, the investigation begins by establishing one.

- Strategy review: compartments, fire-resistance levels, escape routes and performance solutions.
- Compartmentation survey above ceilings, in risers and plant rooms, recording every penetration and its seal, with photographs.
- Fire door survey of every door on escape routes and compartment lines, including all flat entrance doors in residential buildings: closing, gaps, seals, hardware, glazing, labels.
- Structural protection survey of exposed and concealed steel.
- Product identification against tested systems and certification.
- Asbestos sampling of older protection.

The report should give a register of defects by location with photographs, prioritised by risk, and the strategy those defects affect.

- Escape route check: door closing, glazing and wall integrity on every stair and protected corridor.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Fire stopping of every breach with tested systems, recorded with photographs and product data.
- Fire door repair: closers, seals, hardware, adjustment; replacement of doors that cannot be repaired; certified doorsets for flat entrances.
- Hold-open devices linked to the fire alarm where doors need to stay open in use.
- Wall completion to slab where walls stop at the ceiling.
- Glazing replacement with tested fire-resisting glass and frames.
- Structural protection repair with compatible products.
- Fire strategy update and compartmentation drawings.
- Management: permits for works that penetrate fire-rated elements, and regular door checks.

- Labelling: identify fire-resisting walls above ceilings and in risers so trades know what they are penetrating.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Fire stopping is priced per penetration or per riser floor. Door repair and replacement per door. Structural protection repair by area. Fire strategy preparation is a lump sum. Access above ceilings and in risers, and work in occupied buildings, drive cost.

Safety rectification and certification are code compliance; door and hardware replacement is lifecycle; ongoing door checks are repairs and maintenance.

Fire door surveys of whole apartment buildings are lump sums priced per door.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets fire-resistance levels and compartmentation; AS 1530.4 sets fire-resistance testing, AS 4072.1 penetration seals, AS 1905.1 fire doors; AS 1851 sets fire door inspection; passive elements are essential safety measures with annual certification; AS 4655 covers fire safety audits.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B sets requirements; the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual best-endeavour checks of flat entrance doors in residential buildings over 11 metres; the Fire Safety Act 2021 brings flat entrance doors and external walls into the responsible person's duties; BS 8214 covers fire doors.
- United States. International Building Code Chapter 7 governs fire-resistance-rated construction; NFPA 80 requires annual inspection of fire doors, and NFPA 105 smoke doors; firestop systems are tested to ASTM E814 and UL 1479.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire strategy or fire engineering report, including performance solutions.
- Compartmentation drawings.
- Fire door register and inspection records.
- Fire stopping records with photographs.
- Annual fire safety statements or essential safety measures reports.
- Asbestos register.
- Permits for works that penetrated fire-rated elements.

- Fire door certification for replaced doors.
- Records of resident door replacements in apartment buildings.

pages.title: Pavements & Hardstand
pages.question: How do car parks, driveways and paving fail, and how do you tell surface wear from structural failure?
pages.answer: Pavements fail when water gets in. Asphalt oxidises and block-cracks, then water through the cracks softens the base and potholes form. Alligator cracking in wheel paths means the base has failed and surface treatments will not fix it. Concrete panels step at joints when subgrade pumps out; pavers sink where bedding washes out. Trip hazards in pedestrian areas are the safety finding. Crack sealing and resealing are far cheaper than rebuilding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about pavements & hardstand; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Car parks, driveways, pedestrian paving (asphalt/concrete/pavers)

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Pavements and hardstand are the external trafficked surfaces of a site: car parks, driveways, loading and truck hardstand, service roads, footpaths and plazas. They are asphalt, concrete or segmental pavers over a base course and subgrade, with kerbs, edge restraints, line marking, wheel stops, and the drainage that keeps water out of the structure. Suspended car park decks are structure and have their own page; this page covers pavements on the ground.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asphalt (flexible) pavement | Car parks, roads, driveways | Ages by oxidation; cracks; rutting under heavy loads; needs resealing |
| Concrete (rigid) pavement | Truck hardstand, loading areas, service roads | Long life; joints and cracking; settlement |
| Segmental pavers (concrete, clay, stone) | Footpaths, plazas, driveways, residential | Settlement and rocking; edge restraint; weeds |
| Permeable pavements | Newer sites with stormwater controls | Clogging reduces infiltration |
| Sprayed seal and gravel | Rural and industrial yards | Stone loss; potholes |

Water is the main enemy of pavements: once it gets through cracks into the base and subgrade, the pavement loses support and fails under traffic. Drainage, crack sealing and resealing protect the investment far more cheaply than rebuilding.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asphalt wearing course | 15 to 20 years, with resealing at 7 to 10 | Traffic; sun; water |
| Asphalt pavement structure | 20 to 40 years | Base condition; drainage; loads |
| Concrete pavement | 30 to 40 years | Joints; subgrade; loads |
| Segmental pavers | 25 to 40 years | Bedding; edge restraint; traffic |
| Line marking | 2 to 5 years | Traffic; product |
| Kerbs and edge restraints | 30 to 50 years | Impact; settlement |

What shortens life:

- Water entering cracks and saturating the base and subgrade.
- Heavy vehicles on pavements designed for cars, such as trucks, garbage trucks and cranes.
- Poor drainage and ponding.
- Tree roots lifting pavements and pavers.
- Deferred resealing, which lets asphalt oxidise and crack.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Asphalt ageing and cracking

Asphalt binder hardens and becomes brittle in sun and air. The surface greys and ravels, then cracks in blocks. Once cracks open, water enters and accelerates failure.

### Fatigue (alligator) cracking

Interconnected cracking in wheel paths, like crocodile skin, means the pavement structure is failing under repeated loads, usually because the base is weak or wet. It cannot be fixed by surface treatment.

### Rutting and shoving

Heavy or slow-moving loads, and soft asphalt in heat, push the surface into ruts and ripples, which hold water.

### Potholes

Potholes form where water and traffic break out cracked asphalt and pump out base material. They grow quickly in wet weather.

### Concrete pavement faults

Joints spall and lose sealant; panels crack across corners; panels settle and fault (step) at joints where the subgrade has softened or been pumped out.

### Paver settlement and displacement

Pavers settle where bedding washes out or the base was inadequate; they rock, spread and lose joints where edge restraints fail; roots lift them; weeds grow in joints.

### Trip hazards

Steps between slabs, lifted pavers, broken edges and potholes in pedestrian areas trip people, especially the elderly and people with impaired vision. Many public liability claims start here.

### Edge and kerb failure

Unsupported pavement edges break away where vehicles run off them, and broken kerbs let edges crumble and water enter the base.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Greyed, ravelled asphalt; block cracking; alligator cracking in wheel paths.
- Potholes, patches, ruts and ponding after rain.
- Concrete panels cracked, spalled at joints, or stepped.
- Pavers rocking, sunken or lifted, with weeds and open joints.
- Trip edges on footpaths and around services pits.
- Faded line marking and missing wheel stops.
- Tree roots lifting surfaces.

### In the records

- Pavement design and construction records.
- Resurfacing and resealing history.
- Trip and fall incident claims.
- Drainage drawings.

- Water ponding against kerbs and in low spots for hours after rain, showing where the base is being saturated.
- Patches of different ages and materials, recording where the pavement has failed before.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Block cracking across the whole surface | Asphalt ageing | Age; no wheel-path pattern |
| Alligator cracking in wheel paths | Structural failure of the base | Cores; deflection testing |
| Ruts in truck routes | Overloading or weak asphalt | Traffic type; asphalt mix |
| Potholes after rain | Water through cracks into base | Crack pattern; drainage |
| Stepped concrete panels | Subgrade softening or pumping | Water at joints; voids |
| Sunken pavers near pits or edges | Bedding washout or edge failure | Lift pavers; inspect |

> Fatigue cracking in wheel paths means the pavement structure has failed. Resealing or overlaying it without repairing the base wastes money; the cracks return quickly.

The pattern of cracking is the key to treatment: random block cracking across a whole area is age and can be sealed; cracking confined to wheel paths, truck turning areas and loading zones is structural and needs the base repaired; cracks along the line of a buried service or near a tree point to those causes.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip hazards in pedestrian routes; large potholes in traffic areas | safety | Make safe now: patch, grind or barricade |
| Pavement failure in operational truck areas | failure | Repair now |
| Accessible parking or routes not compliant | deadline | Rectify as required |
| Cracking, ruts and ponding without failure | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Surface at end of life; resealing due | lifecycle | Reseal or resurface on cycle |
| Pavement capacity for current traffic unknown | check | Assess |
| Minor wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A civil or pavement engineer for larger pavements; a building surveyor for small sites.

- Condition survey mapping distress types and extent, scored using a pavement condition index method so areas can be ranked and tracked.
- Trip hazard survey of pedestrian routes, measuring height differences.
- Cores and test pits to measure asphalt thickness, base quality and subgrade.
- Deflection testing on heavy-duty pavements to measure structural capacity.
- Drainage review: falls, pits, ponding and subsoil drains.
- Traffic review: vehicle types and loads now using the pavement.
- Accessibility check of accessible parking, kerb ramps and routes.

The report should give a condition map, priorities, recommended treatments by area, and a resurfacing programme.

Pedestrian trip surveys are best repeated annually on busy sites, so that hazards are found before they cause claims.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Crack sealing to keep water out of sound pavements.
- Resealing asphalt with seal coats or thin overlays on a cycle.
- Patching: full-depth repair of failed areas, including base.
- Mill and overlay where the base is sound.
- Reconstruction where the base has failed, designed for current traffic.
- Concrete joint repair and panel replacement; slab lifting by grout.
- Relaying pavers with new bedding and edge restraints.
- Trip hazard removal by grinding, lifting or replacing.
- Drainage improvements.
- Line marking renewal.

- Kerb and edge repair with new edge restraints where pavements are breaking away.
- Heavy-duty sections rebuilt in concrete where trucks turn and stand, the zones that fail first in asphalt car parks.
- Permeable pavement maintenance: vacuum sweeping to restore infiltration.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Crack sealing is priced by length; resealing, overlays and reconstruction by area; patching by area and depth; pavers by area; line marking by length or per bay. Traffic management and night work in operating sites add cost.

Resealing and resurfacing are lifecycle on a cycle; patching and crack sealing are repairs and maintenance; trip hazards are immediate; accessibility rectification is code compliance.

Resurfacing in a busy car park is usually staged so parking remains available.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Austroads guides cover pavement design and maintenance; AS 2890.1 covers parking facilities and AS 1428 access; councils and owners carry public liability for trip hazards, often using a threshold of around 20 millimetres for intervention.
- United Kingdom. BS 7533 covers paving with pavers and flags; highways authorities use intervention levels for trips; the Equality Act 2010 and Approved Document M set access; occupiers have duties under the Occupiers' Liability Acts.
- United States. ASTM D6433 sets the pavement condition index method; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessible routes and parking, including limits on changes in level; AASHTO guides pavement design.

In all three jurisdictions, owners and occupiers owe a duty of care to people using their pavements, and documented inspection and repair is the main defence to trip claims; strata and condominium car parks and driveways are typically common property.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Pavement design and construction records.
- Resurfacing, resealing and repair history.
- Trip and fall incident and claim records.
- Drainage drawings.
- Traffic and vehicle use, especially heavy vehicles.
- Accessibility audit for external routes and parking.

- Trip hazard survey records and repair actions.
- Permeable pavement maintenance records where present.

pages.title: Plant Rooms
pages.question: How do plant rooms fail as spaces, and why do replacement routes matter so much?
pages.answer: Plant rooms fail around the equipment as much as in it. Storage blocks access, exits and switchboard clearances; refrigerant and gas detection lapses; switch rooms overheat; basement rooms flood, often with water pipes over switchboards; access by ladder and hatch injures staff. The costliest failure appears at replacement: plant boxed in by later walls and services must be cut out. Plan the route before the plant reaches end of life.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about plant rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Floor treatments, wall finishes, equipment access, safety systems, environmental controls

sources.title: ASHRAE 15 Safety Standard for Refrigeration Systems

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Plant rooms house the equipment that runs the building: chiller and boiler rooms, pump rooms, switch rooms and substations, generator rooms, tank rooms, air handling plant rooms, and open roof plant areas. Each element of equipment has its own page; this page covers the room as a space. Functionally a plant room must let equipment run safely, let people maintain it, and let equipment be replaced at the end of its life. The last point is often forgotten: plant rooms built around equipment that later cannot be removed turn a routine replacement into demolition.

| Provision | Why it matters | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access and egress | Safe entry and escape; restricted access | Single doors; blocked exits; poor stairs and ladders |
| Replacement route | Getting equipment in and out | Plant boxed in by later walls, services or equipment |
| Ventilation and temperature | Combustion air, cooling, refrigerant and gas safety | Overheating; refrigerant accumulation; CO |
| Drainage and bunding | Water, oil and chemicals contained and drained | No bunds; blocked drains; flooding |
| Fire separation | Contain fires in boiler and switch rooms | Penetrations; doors propped |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Safe work and escape | Dark rooms; failed emergency lights |
| Clearances and housekeeping | Safe working space around equipment | Storage; restricted clearances at switchboards |
| Noise and vibration control | Protect neighbours and structure | Failed isolators; complaints |
| Signage and safety equipment | Hazard warning and response | Missing signs, gas detection, eyewash |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Provision | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room fabric and floors | Life of the building | Water; chemicals; alterations |
| Ventilation fans and louvres | 15 to 25 years | Run hours; corrosion |
| Refrigerant and gas detection | 5 to 10 years; sensors calibrated annually | Sensor drift |
| Bunds and drainage | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Lifting beams and equipment | Life of the building with periodic inspection | Certification |
| Floor coatings | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; spills |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Equipment added over time until there is no space or route left.
- Storage of materials, chemicals and redundant equipment.
- Water from leaks, floods and condensation.
- Refrigerant changes that bring new safety requirements.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### No replacement route

Chillers, boilers, switchboards and generators were often lifted in before walls and floors were completed, and later services, partitions and equipment block the way out. At replacement, owners face cutting openings in walls and slabs, crane lifts or breaking equipment down, adding cost and time that a route plan would have avoided.

### Refrigerant and gas accumulation

Refrigerants leaking in chiller rooms can displace oxygen or be toxic or flammable depending on type; leak detection, alarms and emergency ventilation are required. Boiler rooms without adequate combustion air or with flue leaks accumulate carbon monoxide.

### Overheating

Switch rooms, communications rooms and plant rooms with inadequate ventilation overheat, shortening equipment life and causing trips.

### Flooding

Basement plant rooms flood from burst pipes, failed sumps and storms, putting switchboards, pumps and generators out of action at once. Water pipes above switchboards are a recurring defect.

### Storage and clearances

Plant rooms used as storerooms block access to equipment and escape, add fire load and violate working clearances at switchboards.

### Unsafe access

Plant reached by fixed ladders without cages, through ceiling hatches, or across roofs without edge protection injures maintenance staff; single exits from large plant rooms trap people in emergencies.

### Noise and vibration

Failed vibration isolators and inadequate acoustic treatment transmit noise and vibration to occupied spaces and neighbours.

Rooftop plant areas add exposure: corrosion, weather damage to equipment and access hazards at roof edges.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Storage, rubbish and redundant equipment in plant rooms.
- Equipment that could not be removed without demolition: no doors, hatches or lifting points large enough.
- Temperature high in switch rooms; ventilation louvres blocked.
- Refrigerant and gas detectors present, calibrated and alarming to the BMS.
- Water pipes over switchboards; flood marks; sump alarms.
- Bunds missing under oil and chemical stores.
- Dark corners; emergency lighting failures; missing signage.

### In the records

- Plant room drawings and replacement routes.
- Refrigerant registers and leak detection calibration.
- Flood history.
- Lifting equipment certification.
- Noise complaints.

- Rooftop plant without walkways or edge protection.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trips and failures of electrical equipment in summer | Overheated switch room | Temperature logging |
| Refrigerant alarms or low charge | Leaks in a poorly ventilated room | Leak detection records |
| No route for a chiller replacement | Plant boxed in after installation | Dimensions against openings |
| Equipment corroded at low level | Flooding or chronic damp | Flood history |
| Noise complaints from occupied floors | Failed isolators or acoustic breaches | Vibration measurements |

> Plant rooms with refrigerant or combustion hazards must have working detection and ventilation. Storage in plant rooms and blocked exits are safety findings.

Separate room problems (access, ventilation, flooding, storage) from equipment problems, which belong on each equipment page.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed refrigerant or gas detection; blocked exits; storage at switchboards; water over switchboards | safety | Rectify now |
| Plant room flooded or overheated causing outages | failure | Restore now |
| Detector calibration and lifting equipment certification due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Poor housekeeping; noise; worn floors and coatings | condition | Improve in the near term |
| No replacement route for major plant | lifecycle | Plan the route before the next replacement |
| Plant room conditions never assessed | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

A missing replacement route is not urgent today but becomes a major cost and delay at the next replacement, so it belongs in the capital plan now.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer leads, with the mechanical, electrical and fire maintenance contractors, and a structural engineer where replacement routes need openings or lifting.

- Room-by-room inspection: access and second exits, clearances at switchboards and plant, housekeeping, ventilation openings, drainage, bunding, lighting, emergency lighting, signage and safety equipment.
- Replacement route study for each major item: dimensions and weights against doors, corridors, lifts, hatches, floor capacity and crane access, recording what would need to be removed.
- Detection testing: refrigerant, gas and carbon monoxide sensors calibrated and alarming to the building management system, with emergency ventilation triggered.
- Temperature logging in switch rooms, communications rooms and enclosed plant rooms through a hot period.
- Flood risk review: pipes over electrical equipment, sumps and pumps, floor levels against flood paths.
- Noise and vibration measurement where neighbours or occupants complain.

The report should list safety items, give a replacement route for each major item with any enabling works, and set out room improvements.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Housekeeping rules: no storage in plant rooms, regular checks, and removal of redundant equipment.
- Replacement routes: knock-out panels, removable louvres, roof hatches, lifting beams and floor strengthening, built before the replacement is due.
- Detection and emergency ventilation for refrigerants, gas and carbon monoxide, with alarms to the building management system.
- Cooling for switch and communications rooms.
- Flood protection: reroute water pipes away from electrical equipment, add upstands, sumps and alarms.
- Bunds and drainage for oil, fuel, chemicals and water.
- Safe access: stairs instead of ladders where practicable, caged ladders and platforms, second exits from large rooms.
- Acoustic and vibration treatment: isolator replacement, acoustic linings and enclosures.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Housekeeping and signage cost little. Detection, ventilation, cooling and flood protection are lump sums per room. Replacement route works are lump sums that are far cheaper before a replacement than during one, and should be carried in the capital plan alongside the plant they serve. Access improvements are itemised.

Safety items are code compliance; route provision is lifecycle planning tied to major plant replacement.

Flood damage to a basement switch room typically costs far more than the protection that would have prevented it.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 5149 governs refrigerating systems safety including machinery rooms; AS/NZS 3000 sets switchboard clearances; AS 1657 covers fixed ladders and platforms; work health and safety laws govern plant room access.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 378 governs refrigerating system safety; BS 7671 sets switchgear access; the Work at Height Regulations and Workplace Regulations apply; gas safety regulations cover boiler rooms.
- United States. ASHRAE 15 governs refrigerant safety in machinery rooms; NFPA 70 sets working clearances; OSHA governs access; the International Mechanical Code covers boiler room ventilation.

In all three countries, workplace safety law places duties on whoever controls plant rooms to keep them safe for maintenance workers, including contractors.

Insurers also inspect plant rooms and may set conditions on housekeeping and flood protection.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Plant room drawings and replacement route studies.
- Refrigerant registers and detection calibration records.
- Flood and leak history.
- Lifting equipment certificates.
- Noise complaints.
- Plant room housekeeping and access procedures.

- Weights and dimensions of major plant.
- Records of past plant replacements and how they were done.

- Insurer survey reports on plant rooms.

pages.title: Plant Screens & Parapets
pages.question: How do parapets and plant screens fail, how do you read a leaning parapet, and when is it a falling hazard?
pages.answer: Parapets are exposed on every face and lean when frost and sulfate attack swell one face, or when a concrete roof slab expands and pushes them out, cracking the wall at roof level and the corners. Open coping joints and a missing damp-proof course send water down into the wall. Plant screens fail at fixings through the membrane and in wind. A parapet out of plumb or with loose copings over a street is a falling hazard until assessed.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about plant screens & parapets; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cladding, coping, structural condition

sources.title: 1 RCNY 103-15 Periodic observation of building parapets

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Parapets are the low walls that rise above the roof at its edge: masonry, concrete or framed, finished with a coping. Plant screens are the walls, louvres and panels that hide rooftop plant and are usually steel framed and fixed to the roof structure. Both are exposed on every face, both carry high wind loads at the edge of the building, and both stand over the street or a public area on many buildings.

A parapet does several jobs: it terminates the roof membrane and supports its flashing, it can serve as the guardrail for roof access if it is high enough, and on many buildings it is a fire separation or carries ornament. Its coping sheds water off the top; a damp-proof course under the coping stops water going down into the wall.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid masonry parapet with stone or brick coping | Pre-war commercial, residential and institutional | Lean, frost and sulfate attack, loose copings |
| Cavity or veneer parapet | Mid twentieth century onward | Tie corrosion, water into the cavity from the coping |
| Concrete parapet | Concrete-framed buildings | Reinforcement corrosion at low cover; cracks at movement joints |
| Framed parapet with metal capping | Modern commercial and residential | Capping fixings; water into framing |
| Plant screen on steel posts | Offices, retail, apartments | Fixings through the membrane; wind |
| Acoustic screen | Buildings near residences | Heavy panels; fixings and wind |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry parapet | 60 to 100 years | Two-sided exposure; damp-proof course under coping |
| Stone and concrete copings | 40 to 80 years | Joints; fixings |
| Metal cappings | 20 to 40 years | Coastal exposure; fixings |
| Plant screen framing | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; fixings through the membrane |
| Louvres and cladding on screens | 20 to 30 years | Fixings; wind |

What shortens life:

- Two-sided exposure: parapets get wetter and colder than the wall below.
- No damp-proof course under the coping and open coping joints.
- Expansion of the roof slab on concrete-roofed buildings.
- Fixings through the membrane for screens and cappings.
- Screens added without engineering for wind loads.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Lean and bowing

Parapets lean when frost, sulfate attack and wetting expand one face more than the other, and when the roof slab or structure behind pushes or pulls them. Tall unrestrained parapets are cantilevers from the roof level and fail in wind when their mortar is weak.

### Roof slab expansion

A concrete roof slab heats and expands more than the walls below it. Where the parapet and wall are built tight against the slab, the slab pushes them outward, cracking the wall horizontally at roof level and at the corners and displacing the parapet.

### Coping failure

Coping joints open, water runs into the wall below, and copings loosen and slide. Stone copings crack at their fixings; metal cappings lift in wind when fixings corrode.

### Roof junction leaks

The membrane turns up the inside face of the parapet; where the upstand is low, the termination fails or the flashing pulls out, water enters at the roof edge and appears inside at the top of external walls.

### Screen fixing failure

Screen posts are bolted through the membrane to the structure or to plant platforms. Corroded bases, loose bolts and fixings designed for less wind than the screen now carries let louvres and panels loosen and blow off.

### Tie corrosion in cavity parapets

Cavity parapets are wet on both leaves and the ties in them corrode first. With little load on top to hold the outer leaf, it lifts and leans more readily than the wall below.

### Concrete parapets

Concrete upstands and parapets carry reinforcement close to both faces; carbonation and chlorides reach it quickly. Spalling follows the bars, and corner cracks open where the parapet has no movement joints.

### Parapets as edge protection

Where people work on the roof, a parapet often serves as the guardrail. Many older parapets are lower than fall protection rules require, and some have been lowered in past repairs; they then need guardrails added.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Parapets visibly out of plumb; bowing along the roof line.
- Horizontal cracks in the wall just below roof level; cracks at corners at the top of the building.
- Copings displaced, open joints, vegetation; missing cappings.
- Loose or missing louvres; screens added since construction.

### On the roof

- Cracks and open joints in parapet masonry on the roof side.
- Membrane upstand height and termination; flashings pulled away.
- Screen post bases corroded; bolts loose; louvre blades rattling.

### Inside the building

- Damp at the top of external walls under the parapet.
- Cracks in top-floor walls at slab level.

### In the records

- Parapet observation reports where required.
- Screen engineering.
- Coping and flashing repair records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parapet leaning, joints open on one face | Differential frost or sulfate expansion | Mortar soft and white on the wet face |
| Horizontal crack at roof level, parapet pushed out, corners cracked | Roof slab expansion | Concrete roof slab bearing on the wall; no slip joint |
| Damp at the top of walls inside | Coping joints, missing damp-proof course or roof junction | Water test at copings and upstand |
| Loose louvres after storms | Screen fixing or design for wind | Fixings corroded or undersized |

> A parapet over a street that is out of plumb, or has loose copings, is a falling hazard. Treat it as unsafe until an engineer has assessed it.

Reading the direction of lean helps. Sulfate and frost attack lean the parapet towards the drier side, often away from the weather. Slab expansion pushes outward, with a horizontal crack at the slab line and stepped cracks at the corners. A parapet leaning inward over the roof may have lost its ties to the structure behind.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parapet leaning or bowing over a public area; loose copings; screens loose | safety | Make safe now: remove, restrain or exclude below |
| Annual parapet observation due (New York) | deadline | Annual |
| Leaks at the roof junction or copings | failure | Repair now |
| Open coping joints; cracked masonry without lean; corroded screen bases | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Copings, cappings and screens at age | lifecycle | Renew on cycle |
| Screens with no engineering; parapet used as roof edge protection with unknown height | check | Assess |
| Minor weathering | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A façade or structural engineer inspects close up.

- Plumb survey of parapets.
- Close inspection of copings, joints and the roof face.
- Opening up under copings to find the damp-proof course.
- Screen fixing inspection and wind load check.
- Water testing of the roof junction.

The report should state parapet height and plumb by elevation, coping condition, the presence of a damp-proof course and ties, screen fixing adequacy against current wind loads, and any parapets that do not meet edge protection height.

- Coping removal at sample positions to inspect the damp-proof course, dowels and fixings, and the wall head below.
- Height measurement of parapets against edge protection requirements wherever people access the roof.
- Moisture readings on internal walls below the parapet to map water entry.
- Cover and carbonation testing on concrete parapets.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Rebuild leaning parapets with a damp-proof course and restraint ties to the roof.
- Reset copings with new joints and fixings; metal cappings with proper fixings.
- Slip joints where slab expansion is the cause.
- Renew upstands and flashings.
