- Re-engineer screens with new fixings or independent frames.

- Restraint: steel or stainless ties and brackets connecting the parapet back to the roof structure where rebuilding is not needed.
- Guardrails on top of or behind low parapets where roof access needs edge protection.
- Concrete repair to spalled concrete parapets with an anti-carbonation coating.

- Coping replacement with weathered and throated copings, dowelled and with sealed or lead-tray joints.
- Metal cappings with concealed fixings, joint covers and a fall to the roof side.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Parapet and coping work is priced by linear metre; screens per bay or as a lump sum. Scaffold or access dominates. Observations recur annually where required.

Rebuild is lifecycle; make-safe and observations are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Parapet works over a street need scaffold or edge access with footpath protection and permits, which can exceed the cost of the masonry itself. Screen re-engineering is usually a lump sum per screen with crane hire. Restraint ties are priced per tie. Annual parapet observations, where required, are a small recurring compliance cost.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Masonry follows AS 3700 and wind actions AS/NZS 1170.2, called up by the National Construction Code; where a parapet is the roof edge protection, its height must meet the fall protection requirements under the work health and safety regulations and AS 1657.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document A and the Eurocodes (BS EN 1996, BS EN 1991-1-4) apply; parapets used as edge protection fall under the Work at Height Regulations 2005.
- United States. New York requires annual observation of parapets facing a public right of way under 1 RCNY 103-15, with a plumbness check; International Building Code Section 705.11 covers fire parapets; ASCE 7 sets wind loads.

Rebuilding heritage parapets and their ornament needs heritage consent in all three jurisdictions, which sets materials and methods.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Parapet observation and façade inspection reports.
- Screen engineering.
- Coping and flashing repair records.

- Wind load design for screens.
- Roof access and edge protection records.

- Heritage listing.
- Records of roof works that disturbed parapet flashings.
- Council or insurer notices about falling masonry.
- Previous coping repairs and the materials used.

pages.title: Portable Fire Equipment
pages.question: How does portable fire equipment fail, and what does it say about a building's fire safety management?
pages.answer: Portable equipment fails by being missing, discharged, out of date or wrong for the hazard: water extinguishers next to switchboards, no wet chemical or blanket at commercial cooking, units hidden behind furniture. Older foam units contain PFAS and are being withdrawn. Each item is cheap, but the pattern is telling: a building with lapsed extinguisher servicing and wrong types usually has gaps elsewhere in its fire safety.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about portable fire equipment; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fire extinguishers, fire blankets

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Portable fire equipment is the first-attack equipment occupants use on a small fire: fire extinguishers, fire blankets, and the signage and mountings that make them findable. It is selected for the fire risks in each area, placed at set travel distances and near exits, and serviced on prescribed intervals. It is cheap, numerous and easily neglected, and in many buildings its records are the most reliable indicator of how fire safety is managed overall.

| Type | Suited to | Not suited to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water | Paper, wood, textiles (Class A) | Electrical equipment; cooking oils; flammable liquids |
| Foam (AFFF and fluorine-free) | Class A and flammable liquids (Class B) | Cooking oils; live electrical equipment in some types; older AFFF contains PFAS |
| Carbon dioxide | Electrical equipment; flammable liquids | Class A fires (no cooling); confined spaces |
| Dry powder (ABE) | Most fires including electrical | Cooking oils; indoor use where powder damages equipment and visibility |
| Wet chemical | Cooking oil and fat fires (Class F/K) | Most other uses |
| Fire blankets | Small cooking fires; clothing fires | Larger fires |

Placement follows the hazard: wet chemical and blankets in kitchens, carbon dioxide near switchboards and electrical equipment, water or foam for general areas, powder in car parks and workshops. In Australia, extinguishers are common in all commercial buildings; in Britain they are part of the responsible person's risk assessment; in the United States they are required by the fire code in most occupancies.

Extinguishers are rated by the fire classes they can tackle, and the classes differ slightly by jurisdiction: Class A ordinary combustibles, Class B flammable liquids, Class C flammable gases in Australia and Britain (electrical fires in the United States), electrical fires as Class E in Australia, and cooking oils and fats as Class F in Australia and Britain and Class K in the United States. Labels show the classes and ratings, and selection should follow them rather than colour alone.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Equipment | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stored-pressure extinguishers | 10 to 20 years with periodic pressure testing | Corrosion; damage; test results |
| Carbon dioxide extinguishers | 20 years and more with pressure testing | Cylinder testing |
| Hoses and horns | 5 to 10 years | Cracking; UV |
| Fire blankets | 7 to 10 years | Damage; packaging |
| Signage and mounting | 10 to 20 years | Fading; damage |

What shortens life:

- Exposure: outdoor, car park and coastal locations corrode cylinders and fittings.
- Tampering and misuse: extinguishers used as door stops or discharged.
- Missed servicing, which leaves discharged or depressurised units in place.

Units in sheltered indoor positions last much longer than those in car parks, loading docks and external areas; marine environments corrode cylinders and fittings within a few years.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Missing, discharged or empty units

Extinguishers are moved, stolen, used and not replaced, or slowly lose pressure. Gauges in the red, broken tamper seals and missing units are the commonest findings.

### Wrong type for the hazard

Water extinguishers next to switchboards, powder in kitchens without wet chemical, and no blanket at cooking areas leave occupants with equipment that is dangerous or ineffective for the likely fire. Fit-outs that change the use of rooms rarely change the extinguishers.

### Obstruction and visibility

Extinguishers behind furniture, in cupboards, without signage, or mounted too high are not used in an emergency.

### Deterioration

Cylinders corrode, hoses crack, pins and seals go missing, and labels fade. Pressure testing at set intervals catches cylinders that are no longer safe.

### PFAS-containing foam

Older foam extinguishers contain PFAS and are being withdrawn; disposal must follow environmental rules.

### Coverage gaps

Travel distances grow when layouts change; new hazards (battery charging, kitchens, workshops) arrive without equipment.

### Lithium-ion battery hazards

E-bikes, scooters, tools and battery storage bring lithium-ion battery fires, which reignite and release toxic gases and are not reliably controlled by ordinary extinguishers. Charging areas in car parks, bike stores and apartments need hazard-specific measures: separation, detection, and guidance on what to do, rather than more extinguishers.

Misuse also matters: extinguishers used as door stops, moved to where staff find them convenient, or partly discharged and replaced on the bracket without being serviced.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Extinguisher at each required location, mounted, signed and unobstructed.
- Gauge in the green; tamper seal and pin intact.
- Service tag with the last date and the next due.
- Type matched to the hazard nearby.
- Blankets in kitchens; wet chemical at commercial cooking.
- Corrosion, damaged hoses, faded labels.

### In the records

- Routine service records and register by location.
- Pressure testing dates.
- Annual fire safety certification.
- Fire risk assessment (Britain).

- Extinguishers moved from their signed locations.
- Missing fire blankets in staff kitchens.
- Equipment near charging areas for e-bikes and scooters.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gauge in the red | Discharged or leaking | Weight or pressure check |
| Service tags out of date | Servicing lapsed | Records |
| Water extinguisher beside a switchboard | Wrong type for the hazard | Hazard review |
| Empty brackets | Missing or used unit | Register |
| Kitchen without blanket or wet chemical | Coverage gap | Hazard review |

> Portable equipment is a reliable indicator of fire safety management: a building where extinguishers are out of date, missing or wrongly placed usually has gaps elsewhere.

Patterns matter more than single units: many out-of-date tags point to a lapsed contract; many wrong types point to fit-outs that changed uses without a fire risk review.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong type at a high hazard (water at switchboards, none at commercial cooking); discharged units in high-risk areas | safety | Replace now |
| Routine service due | deadline | Six-monthly in Australia; annually in Britain and the United States, with monthly checks |
| Missing, damaged or depressurised units | condition | Replace in the near term |
| Units at end of life or failing pressure tests | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No register; placement not reviewed after fit-outs | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire equipment contractor or fire safety consultant.

- Location survey against requirements and travel distances.
- Hazard match of each unit to the hazards nearby.
- Condition check: gauge, seals, hose, cylinder, mounting, signage, service tag.
- Records review: service and pressure test dates.
- PFAS foam identification.

The report should list each location with its status, missing or wrong units, and the next service and test dates.

Where lithium-ion charging is present, the survey should also identify charging locations and whether the fire risk assessment or fire strategy addresses them.

- Records cross-check: compare the register with what is on site, unit by unit.
- Hazard review of new uses since the last survey: kitchens, battery charging, workshops, storage.

Survey results are best recorded on floor plans so gaps in coverage are visible at a glance.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Replace missing, discharged, damaged and failing units.
- Re-select types to match hazards.
- Relocate and sign units so they are visible and within travel distance.
- Replace PFAS foam units with fluorine-free or other types.
- Register and service contract covering every unit.

- Lithium-ion charging areas: designated, separated charging locations with detection and clear procedures.
- Training for wardens and staff on which extinguisher to use and when not to.

- Mounting and protection: brackets at the right height, cabinets in exposed or vandal-prone locations.
- Signage to current standards so units can be found in smoke.

- Fire risk review after any change of use, so equipment follows the hazard.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing is a recurring contract priced per unit. Replacement is per unit. Pressure testing recurs per unit at set intervals. These are small individually and often carried as a recurring allowance. Servicing and safety replacements are code compliance; replacement at end of life is lifecycle.

Replacing units in bulk at the end of their life is usually cheaper than piecemeal replacement after failed pressure tests. Disposal of PFAS foam units adds a hazardous waste cost.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code requires portable fire extinguishers in many building classes; AS 2444 governs selection and location; AS 1851 sets six-monthly service and periodic pressure testing; they are essential safety measures with annual certification.
- United Kingdom. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires appropriate fire-fighting equipment based on the fire risk assessment; BS 5306-8 covers selection and positioning, and BS 5306-3 maintenance, with an annual basic service and extended services or overhauls at five or ten years depending on type.
- United States. NFPA 10 governs selection, installation, inspection and maintenance: monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance, six-yearly internal maintenance for stored-pressure dry chemical units, and hydrostatic testing at five or twelve years depending on type; the International Fire Code sets where extinguishers are required.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Register of extinguishers and blankets by location and type.
- Service and pressure test records.
- Annual fire safety certification or fire risk assessment.
- Foam extinguisher product data and PFAS status.
- Records of fit-outs or changes of use that added new hazards.
- Policies for e-bike, scooter and battery charging.

pages.title: Power Distribution
pages.question: How does power distribution fail, what are the warning signs, and when is rewiring needed?
pages.answer: Distribution fails by insulation, connections and alteration. Rubber-insulated wiring from before the 1960s perishes to bare conductors and must be replaced; aluminium branch wiring in some US houses of 1965 to 1973 overheats at devices. Missing or untested RCDs leave people unprotected from shock. Tenant fit-outs add unrecorded circuits and breach fire stopping. Harmonics from electronic loads overheat shared neutrals.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about power distribution; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Distribution boards, sub-mains cabling, tenant/sub-metering

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Power distribution takes electricity from the main switchboard to the points of use: sub-main cables and busducts in risers, distribution boards on each floor or tenancy, final circuits to outlets, lighting and equipment, residual current devices (RCDs) and other protection, metering for tenants and services, and the trays, ladders and conduits that carry cables. It is the most altered part of a building's electrical system, because every fit-out touches it.

| Era | Typical wiring | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before about 1950 | Vulcanised India rubber (VIR) insulated cables; lead-sheathed cables; knob-and-tube in the United States | Rubber insulation perishes and crumbles off the conductor; replacement is the only remedy |
| 1950s to 1960s | Tough rubber sheathed (TRS) cables; early PVC | Brittle sheathing; lighting circuits often without an earth conductor |
| 1965 to 1973, United States | Aluminium branch circuit wiring in some houses | Connections at outlets and switches overheat; a recognised fire risk |
| 1960s onward | PVC insulated and sheathed cables; steel conduit in commercial work | Long-lived if not overheated or damaged |
| 1990s onward | Low-smoke zero-halogen cables in some buildings; RCD protection on socket circuits | Current practice |

| Component | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-main cables | Risers, basements, ceiling spaces | Overload; damage; joints; fire stopping where they pass compartments |
| Busducts (busways) | Riser distribution in towers and industrial buildings | Joints loosen and overheat; tap-off units disturbed |
| Distribution boards | Each floor, tenancy and plant area | Ageing devices; no RCDs; unlabelled alterations; added sub-boards |
| Final circuits and accessories | Throughout | Loose terminals; damaged outlets; overload |
| RCDs and RCBOs | Distribution boards | Absent in older installations; failing to trip if never tested |
| Sub-metering | Tenancies, plant, embedded networks | Inaccurate or unread meters; recharge disputes |
| Cable support systems | Ceiling spaces, risers | Overloaded trays; unsupported cables draped on ceilings |

Metering and ownership vary by building type. In multi-tenant commercial buildings the owner may meter tenants with check meters or recharge by area. In apartment buildings, residents are either supplied by the network directly or through an embedded network owned by the building, which carries its own regulatory and consumer obligations.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PVC wiring | 40 to 60 years | Heat; overload; damage |
| Rubber-insulated wiring | Past its life wherever found | Replace |
| Distribution boards | 25 to 40 years | Device support; alterations; environment |
| Busducts | 30 to 40 years | Joint maintenance; loading |
| RCDs and RCBOs | 15 to 25 years | Testing; surges |
| Socket outlets and switches | 20 to 30 years | Use; loose terminals |
| Sub-meters | 15 to 25 years | Technology; communications |

What shortens life:

- Heat: cables bundled together, run through insulation or in hot ceiling spaces and plant rooms lose capacity and age faster.
- Overload from added equipment, power boards and extension leads.
- Alterations by tenants and contractors without records or proper protection.
- Harmonics from electronic loads overheating shared neutrals.
- Mechanical damage by other trades in ceilings and risers.
- Moisture in basements, car parks and external areas.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Insulation breakdown

Rubber insulation hardens, cracks and falls away with age and heat, leaving bare conductors in light fittings, switches and ceiling spaces. Disturbing old cables during renovation accelerates the breakdown. PVC insulation that has been overheated becomes brittle and discoloured around terminations and in bundles.

### Connection failures

Terminals at outlets, switches, joint boxes and boards loosen with thermal cycling and poor workmanship; resistance and heat rise until the accessory scorches or ignites. Aluminium branch wiring in United States houses of 1965 to 1973 does this at devices not rated for aluminium; remediation with approved connectors or rewiring is the accepted fix.

### Absent or failed RCD protection

RCDs disconnect a circuit when current leaks to earth, protecting people from electric shock. Older installations often have none, or only on some circuits; devices that are never tested can fail to trip. Wet areas, outdoor circuits and portable equipment circuits are where the absence matters most.

### Busduct joint failure

Busduct sections are joined with bolted connections that must be torqued and checked. Loose joints overheat and fail; tap-off units opened or moved by tenants are a common source of faults.

### Undocumented alterations

Fit-outs add circuits and sub-boards, remove or bypass protection, reuse old cables, and leave boards without circuit schedules. Over time nobody knows what a breaker controls, and isolation for maintenance becomes unsafe.

### Harmonics and neutral overheating

Computers, LED drivers and variable speed drives draw distorted current. On three-phase circuits that share a neutral, some harmonic currents add rather than cancel, so the neutral can carry more current than the phases and overheat, particularly in older installations with reduced neutrals.

### Fire-stopping breaches

Every time cables are pulled through fire-rated walls, floors and riser slabs, the fire stopping is disturbed. Unsealed penetrations let fire and smoke spread between compartments; risers in older buildings are often riddled with them.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### At distribution boards

- Board type, age and maker; rewireable fuses, cartridge fuses or breakers; RCDs present on which circuits.
- Circuit schedules present and accurate; boards added by tenants.
- Discolouration, burn marks, melted insulation, a smell of hot plastic.
- Missing blanks and covers exposing live parts.

### In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces

- Rubber-insulated cables, especially at light fittings and old switches.
- Unsupported cables draped over ceilings; damaged sheathing.
- Unsealed cable penetrations in risers and walls.
- Scorched or warm outlets and switches; flickering lights.
- Daisy-chained power boards and extension leads, signs that circuits are too few.

### In the records

- Periodic inspection and test reports with observations and their codes.
- RCD test records.
- Circuit schedules and as-built drawings.
- Thermographic surveys of boards and busducts.
- Metering arrangements and any embedded network documents.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crumbling insulation at light fittings and switches | Perished rubber-insulated cable | Inspection; era of the building or rewiring |
| Warm or scorched outlets and switches | Loose terminal, overload, or aluminium wiring | Thermography; inspection of terminals |
| RCD trips intermittently | Earth leakage from appliances or damp, or an ageing RCD | Insulation resistance test; RCD test |
| Breakers trip under normal load | Circuit overloaded by added equipment | Load measurement |
| Neutral hotter than phases | Harmonics | Harmonic measurement |
| Unlabelled breakers and added boards | Undocumented alterations | Inspection against drawings |
| Smoke spread between floors in a fire drill or fire | Unsealed riser penetrations | Riser inspection |

> A working installation is not a safe one. Periodic inspection and testing exist because insulation breakdown, failed RCDs and loose terminals give no warning until they cause a shock or a fire.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perished rubber wiring; exposed live parts; scorched accessories; no RCD on wet area or outdoor circuits; aluminium branch wiring without remediation | safety | Isolate, make safe or rewire now |
| Circuits or boards failed | failure | Repair now |
| Periodic inspection and testing due | deadline | At the interval set by the regulation or standard |
| Overheating terminations; unsupported devices; unsealed penetrations; missing schedules | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Wiring and boards at the end of their life | lifecycle | Plan rewiring floor by floor or with fit-outs |
| No periodic inspection on record; wiring type unknown | check | Inspect and test |
| Minor defects | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed electrical contractor or electrical engineer carries out a periodic inspection and test.

- Visual inspection of boards, a sample of accessories and accessible wiring, with covers off where safe.
- Testing of a representative sample of circuits: insulation resistance, earth continuity, polarity, earth fault loop impedance, and RCD operation times.
- Wiring type survey to identify rubber-insulated, aluminium or other at-risk wiring.
- Thermographic survey of distribution boards and busduct joints under load.
- Load and harmonic measurement where overload or neutral heating is suspected.
- Fire-stopping survey of risers and penetrations.
- Documentation review: circuit schedules, drawings, metering.

The report should list observations by severity code, sample results extrapolated to the installation, wiring types and extent, boards needing replacement, fire-stopping breaches, and the next inspection date.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Rewiring of rubber-insulated and other end-of-life circuits, usually floor by floor or tenancy by tenancy.
- Aluminium wiring remediation with approved connectors at every device, or rewiring.
- RCD protection added to circuits without it, or boards upgraded to RCBOs.
- Board replacement where devices are unsupported or boards are unsafe.
- Busduct maintenance: torque checks and joint replacement.
- Neutral upgrades or harmonic filtering where neutrals overheat.
- Fire stopping of every penetration with tested systems, recorded with photographs.
- Documentation: circuit schedules, labelling and as-built drawings.
- Additional circuits where loads have outgrown the installation.

- Load management: redistribute circuits and add submains where boards are overloaded.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Periodic inspection and testing is a recurring lump sum. Rewiring is priced per circuit, per floor or per tenancy, with ceiling access and making good often the largest component. Boards are priced per board. RCD upgrades per circuit or per board. Fire stopping per penetration or per riser. Busduct joint work per joint.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; rewiring and board replacement are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Rewiring is usually best timed with fit-outs, when ceilings are open.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Installations follow AS/NZS 3000, with periodic verification to AS/NZS 3019; RCD protection is required on new and altered circuits; electrical safety regulators in each state set licensing and notification. Embedded networks in residential buildings are regulated by the Australian Energy Regulator and state rules.
- United Kingdom. BS 7671 governs installations and requires RCD protection on socket circuits; periodic inspection results in an Electrical Installation Condition Report, required at least every five years for privately rented homes in England; the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require installations to be maintained safe.
- United States. NFPA 70 (the National Electrical Code) governs installations, including GFCI and AFCI protection; NFPA 70B sets maintenance; the Consumer Product Safety Commission publishes guidance on aluminium branch wiring remediation.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Periodic inspection and test reports with observations.
- RCD test records.
- Circuit schedules and electrical as-built drawings.
- Thermographic surveys of boards and busducts.
- Rewiring records and dates.
- Fire-stopping records for risers.
- Metering and embedded network arrangements.

- Records of electrical fires, scorching or tripping incidents.
- Tenant fit-out electrical certificates.

pages.title: Public Amenities
pages.question: How do shared toilets and end-of-trip facilities fail, and when are there too few?
pages.answer: Amenities fail on water, numbers and management. Membranes and wastes leak into the floor below; dry traps and scaled urinals cause odour; little-used showers become Legionella risks. Densified floors outgrow fixture numbers and end-of-trip demand outstrips bikes, lockers and showers. Accessible toilets turned into storerooms leave people without facilities. Refurbish as a whole block, with membranes, every 15 to 20 years.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about public amenities; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Floor/wall finishes, partitions, fixtures, vanities, accessories in toilets and end-of-trip

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Public amenities are the shared toilets, accessible toilets, showers, change rooms, end-of-trip facilities, parents' rooms and tea points in commercial, institutional and mixed-use buildings. They are among the most heavily used and most judged spaces in a building: tenants rate buildings on their amenities, codes set how many fixtures are needed for the occupancy, and failures (leaks, odour, broken fixtures, shortages) are noticed immediately. Functionally they must provide enough fixtures for the people in the building, stay hygienic, be accessible, and not leak into the floors below.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sanitary fixtures | Toilets, urinals, basins, showers | Numbers for the occupancy; reliability; water use |
| Wet area waterproofing | Membranes under floors and up walls | Leaks to floors below |
| Partitions and cubicles | Toilet partitions, doors and hardware | Corrosion, damage, privacy |
| Finishes | Tiles, vanities, mirrors, accessories | Hygiene, durability, appearance |
| Ventilation | Exhaust to every room | Odour and moisture removal |
| Accessible facilities | Accessible toilets and showers, ambulant cubicles | Compliance, availability |
| End-of-trip | Bike parking, lockers, showers, drying rooms | Capacity against demand |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amenities refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Wear; market; leaks |
| Wet area membranes | 15 to 25 years | Installation; movement |
| Tapware and flush valves | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |
| Toilet partitions | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; damage |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| End-of-trip lockers and fittings | 10 to 15 years | Use |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Higher occupancy densities than the amenities were designed for.
- Rising market expectations for end-of-trip and quality.
- Water leaks through membranes and around fixtures.
- Vandalism and heavy use in public buildings.

Amenities are among the first spaces tenants judge, and their refurbishment is often brought forward for leasing reasons even when fixtures still work.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Leaks to floors below

Amenities leak through failed floor membranes, around floor wastes, at wall junctions, from cisterns, flush valves and pipework in ducts, and from overflowing urinals and blocked drains. Leaks show on ceilings of the floor below and damage tenancies.

### Too few fixtures

Codes set fixture numbers by occupancy. When floors are densified, queues and complaints follow, and the building no longer meets the occupancy it is let for. End-of-trip facilities sized for a few cyclists are overwhelmed as commuting changes.

### Odour

Odours come from failed exhaust, dry floor waste traps in little-used rooms, blocked or scaled urinals, sealant and grout harbouring bacteria, and leaks soaking substrates.

### Little-used showers and outlets

Showers in end-of-trip facilities and accessible bathrooms that are rarely used become dead legs where Legionella can grow, then aerosolise when used.

### Accessible facilities unavailable

Accessible toilets used as storerooms, locked with keys staff cannot find, or with layouts and fittings that do not meet requirements leave people with disability without facilities.

### Wear and damage

Partitions swell and corrode, hardware breaks, tiles crack, grout discolours, and accessories go missing.

### Drainage blockages

Toilets and urinals block from paper, wipes and scale, overflowing onto floors and into the floor below. Recurrent blockages in one block often point to a defect in the stack or branch rather than misuse.

In shared buildings, amenities on one floor often serve several tenants, so a single failure affects many people.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Ceiling stains below amenities on the floor beneath.
- Odour on entry; dry floor wastes; scaled urinals.
- Queues at peak; complaints about numbers.
- Swollen or corroded partitions; broken locks.
- Accessible toilets cluttered or locked.
- End-of-trip bike racks and lockers full; showers queued.
- Cracked tiles and failed grout around wastes.

### In the records

- Leak and plumbing call-out history.
- Occupancy figures against fixture numbers.
- Cleaning and hygiene complaints.
- Legionella management for showers.
- Refurbishment history.

- Water marks around WC pans and at floor wastes, showing leaks or overflows.
- Tenant or visitor complaints about cleanliness and odour.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stain on the ceiling below a toilet block | Membrane failure or pipe leak | Flood test; dye test; duct inspection |
| Odour in a lightly used room | Dry floor waste trap | Trap inspection |
| Odour near urinals | Scale and blockage or failed waterless cartridges | Inspection |
| Queues at peak | Fixtures below the occupancy now on the floor | Count against code ratios |
| Cubicle partitions swelling at the base | Moisture and cleaning water | Material type |

> Amenities problems usually come down to water (leaks, traps, Legionella), numbers (ratios, end-of-trip demand) or management (cleaning, storage). Each needs a different fix.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella risk from little-used showers; accessible facilities unavailable | safety | Flush, disinfect, restore now |
| Leaks damaging floors below; amenities closed | failure | Repair now |
| Fixture numbers below code for current occupancy | deadline | Before occupancy increases or as required |
| Worn fixtures and finishes; odour; partition damage | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Amenities at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Occupancy against fixtures unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a hydraulic engineer and access consultant.

- Leak investigation: flood tests, dye tests and duct inspections.
- Fixture count against code ratios for current and planned occupancy.
- End-of-trip review against demand and market expectations.
- Ventilation check.
- Legionella review of little-used outlets.
- Access audit of accessible facilities.
- Condition survey of fixtures, partitions and finishes.

The report should give leak causes, capacity against occupancy, safety items and a refurbishment plan.

A building surveyor leads, with a hydraulic engineer for leaks and drainage, an access consultant, and the cleaning contractor for hygiene issues.

- Leak investigation: flood tests of floors, dye tests of fixtures and wastes, and inspection of service ducts for leaking cisterns, valves and joints.
- Fixture count against the code ratios for current and planned occupancy, floor by floor, including accessible and ambulant facilities.
- End-of-trip review: bike spaces, lockers, showers and drying against current use and market expectations.
- Ventilation check of exhaust rates to every room.
- Legionella review of little-used showers and outlets, with temperature checks and flushing records.
- Access audit of accessible toilets and showers.
- Condition survey of fixtures, tapware, partitions, finishes and accessories.

The report should give the cause of each leak, capacity against occupancy, safety items, and a staged refurbishment plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Leak repair: re-membrane, repair wastes and joints, fix pipes in ducts.
- Capacity: add fixtures or end-of-trip facilities, often within a refurbishment.
- Odour control: trap primers, exhaust repair, urinal maintenance.
- Flushing regimes for little-used showers.
- Accessible facilities cleared, upgraded and kept available.
- Refurbishment with durable, water-efficient fixtures.

- Leak repair: re-membrane floors with correct falls and waste flanges, repair joints and replace cisterns and valves in ducts.
- Capacity increases: add fixtures or convert space, often as part of a whole-floor or core refurbishment.
- End-of-trip expansion: more bike spaces, lockers and showers to match demand.
- Odour control: trap primers or water-based seals for dry wastes, exhaust repairs, urinal maintenance regimes.
- Flushing regimes for little-used showers and outlets, with records.
- Accessible facilities cleared, upgraded to current layouts and kept available.
- Refurbishment with durable, water-efficient fixtures and moisture-resistant partitions.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Amenities are refurbished as lump sums per block or per floor, including membranes, finishes, fixtures and partitions, with out-of-hours work. Leak repairs are itemised. End-of-trip facilities are lump sums. Refurbishment is lifecycle; capacity upgrades for occupancy can be code compliance; leaks are failures.

Leaks often cost more in damage to the floor below than in the repair itself, so early repair is economical. Refurbishments are usually carried out floor by floor while other floors' amenities remain available.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets sanitary facility numbers by building class and occupancy, and accessible facilities under AS 1428.1; wet areas follow the code's waterproofing provisions.
- United Kingdom. BS 6465 sets the scale of sanitary provision; Approved Documents G and M apply; the Workplace Regulations 1992 require suitable facilities.
- United States. The International Plumbing Code sets minimum fixture counts by occupancy; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessible facilities.

Lease terms in all three countries often promise amenities to a standard or ratio, so shortfalls can be a leasing issue as well as a code one.

In all three countries, workplace health and safety law also requires employers to provide adequate, clean and accessible facilities for workers, independent of building code fixture counts, and health authorities may have additional requirements for shower hygiene and Legionella in public buildings.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Leak and plumbing call-out history.
- Occupancy figures by floor.
- End-of-trip usage data.
- Legionella management records.
- Access audit.
- Refurbishment history.

- Fixture schedules by floor.
- Cleaning specifications and complaint records.
- Flood test results after previous repairs.
- Lease clauses on amenities and end-of-trip provision.

- Plumbing maintenance contract and response times.

pages.title: Pumping Systems
pages.question: How do booster, sump and sewage pumping systems fail, and when do they threaten the building?
pages.answer: Pumping systems fail at their controls and power. Floats tangle and foul, pumps ragging with wipes trip out, and most sump and sewage pumps have no backup power, so they stop in the same storm that floods the basement, often reaching switchboards, lifts and fire pumps. Booster sets fail when pressure vessels lose their charge. A sump without a monitored alarm or backup power is a flood waiting to happen.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about pumping systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Domestic cold/hot water booster pumps, sump pumps

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Hydraulic pumping systems move water where gravity and mains pressure cannot: domestic water booster sets that raise pressure to upper floors, stormwater sump pumps that keep basements and car parks dry, sewage ejectors that lift waste from below the sewer, lift pit pumps, and the pits, controls, alarms and rising mains that go with them. Fire pumps have their own page.

| Type | Where it is found | Consequence of failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domestic water booster set (multiple pumps, variable speed, pressure vessels) | Apartment and office towers | Low or no water pressure on upper floors |
| Stormwater sump pumps | Basements, car parks, below-ground loading docks, lift pits | Basement flooding, often reaching switchrooms and plant |
| Sewage ejectors and pump stations | Basement toilets, kitchens and plant below the sewer | Sewage overflow; health hazard; odour |
| Groundwater dewatering pumps | Basements below the water table | Uplift and flooding; structural risk |
| Lift pit pumps | Lift pits | Water damage to lift equipment |

Many sump and sewage pumps have no backup power, so they stop in the same storm that knocks out the mains supply and floods the basement. In basement car parks and plant rooms, a failed sump pump can put the main switchboard, lifts and fire pumps under water.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster pumps | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; water quality |
| Variable speed drives | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Pressure vessels | 10 to 15 years | Diaphragm life; charge pressure |
| Submersible stormwater pumps | 10 to 15 years | Silt and debris; run hours |
| Sewage pumps | 8 to 15 years | Rags and wipes; H2S corrosion |
| Float switches and level controls | 5 to 10 years | Fouling; tangling |
| Concrete pits | 30 to 50 years | H2S attack in sewage pits |
| Control panels and alarms | 15 to 20 years | Damp; vendor support |

What shortens life:

- Silt, debris and rags drawn into pumps.
- Hydrogen sulphide in sewage pits corroding concrete, steel and electrical equipment.
- Short cycling from failed pressure vessels or poor level settings.
- No maintenance because pumps are out of sight.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Level control failure

Float switches tangle, stick or foul with grease and debris; level sensors drift. The pump either does not start, letting the pit overflow, or runs dry and burns out. A high-level alarm is the last line of defence, and it is often not monitored.

### Blockage and ragging

Sewage pumps block with wet wipes, rags and fats; stormwater pumps block with silt, leaves and litter washed down ramps. Pumps trip on overload and the pit fills.

### Loss of power

Sump and sewage pumps without generator or battery backup fail in power outages, which often coincide with storms. Basements then flood exactly when the drainage is most needed.

### Booster set failures

Pressure vessels lose their charge and diaphragms fail, so pumps start and stop constantly; drives fail; one pump fails and the others cannot meet peak demand; controls lose their settings. Upper floors get low pressure or none.

### Hydrogen sulphide

Sewage in pits produces hydrogen sulphide, which corrodes concrete and metal and is lethal in confined spaces. Pits need ventilation, and entering them is confined space work.

### Check valve failure

Check valves on rising mains stick open, letting water run back into the pit, so pumps cycle continuously; or stick closed, so pumps run against a closed valve.

### Capacity shortfall

Pits and pumps sized for the original catchment are overwhelmed when ramps, courtyards or new connections are added, or when rainfall intensities increase.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Water marks and silt lines on basement walls; corrosion at the base of switchboards and equipment.
- Pit lids: condition, odour, ventilation.
- Pumps: duty and standby both present; run hours; noise.
- Alarm panels: high-level alarm, monitoring connection.
- Booster set: number of pumps running, pressure gauges, vessel condition.
- Low pressure complaints on upper floors.

### In the records

- Pump maintenance and pit cleaning records.
- Flood incident history.
- Alarm monitoring arrangements.
- Backup power arrangements.
- Pump and pit design capacities.

- Silt, leaves and litter on car park ramps and grates feeding the sump, and the condition of silt traps.
- Odour around sewage pits and corrosion of fittings near them, signs of hydrogen sulphide.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basement flooded after a storm with a power outage | Sump pumps without backup power | Power arrangement; incident timeline |
| Basement flooded in rain with power on | Blocked pumps, failed floats or undersized pit | Pump inspection; capacity check |
| Booster pumps starting every few seconds | Failed pressure vessel or diaphragm | Vessel charge pressure |
| Upper floors low pressure at peak times | Booster capacity or a failed pump | Pressure logging; pump status |
| Sewage pump tripping repeatedly | Ragging from wipes and rags | Pump inspection |
| Pumps cycling with no inflow | Check valve letting water run back | Valve inspection |

> A basement sump with no monitored high-level alarm and no backup power is a flood waiting for the right storm. The consequence often reaches the main switchboard, lifts and fire pumps.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sump serving switchrooms or lift pits with failed pumps or alarms; sewage pit with no ventilation or failed lid | safety | Restore now; temporary pumping |
| Pumps failed; flooding or no water to upper floors | failure | Repair now |
| Worn pumps, failed pressure vessels, fouled floats | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Pumps at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No backup power or alarm monitoring; capacity unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or pump contractor; confined space procedures for pit entry.

- Inventory of every pumping system, pit, pump, control and alarm.
- Function test: start and stop levels, duty and standby changeover, high-level alarm and its monitoring.
- Pump condition: insulation resistance of motors, impeller wear, run hours.
- Pit inspection: silt, grease, concrete condition, H2S levels, ventilation.
- Booster testing: pressures at top floors at peak demand, vessel charge, drive faults.
- Capacity review: catchment, rainfall intensity and pump capacity.
- Power review: backup supply for critical pumps.

The report should list each system with its condition, flood risk, alarm and power arrangements, and works needed.

- Drawdown test: measure how quickly each pump empties the pit against its rated capacity, which shows wear and blockage that a simple start test misses.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Controls: replace floats with reliable level sensors; set alarms to a monitored system.
- Backup power: generator connection or battery backup for critical sumps.
- Pump replacement with vortex or cutter pumps for sewage.
- Pit cleaning on a schedule; silt traps on ramps.
- Pressure vessel replacement and recharge.
- Check valve replacement.
- Pit refurbishment: H2S-resistant linings, ventilation, lockable lids.
- Capacity upgrade: larger pumps, additional pumps, bigger pits.
- Flood protection of switchrooms below ground.

- Duty and standby alternation so both pumps share run hours and a failed standby is found before it is needed.
- Education and screening for sewage systems: signage about wipes and fats, and macerators or screens where ragging recurs.
- Variable speed booster sets replacing fixed-speed pumps, with correctly sized pressure vessels, to cut energy and pressure fluctuation.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance and pit cleaning recur. Pump replacement is per pump. Controls and alarms per system. Backup power per system or as part of a generator project. Pit refurbishment and capacity upgrades are lump sums. Booster set replacement is a lump sum with temporary supply.

Replacement is lifecycle; repairs and cleaning are repairs and maintenance; flood protection works and alarms may be risk-driven or code compliance.

Temporary pumping during replacement is a separate line where the pit cannot be left unattended.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3500.1 covers water boosters, AS/NZS 3500.2 sanitary pumps and AS/NZS 3500.3 stormwater pumps; confined space entry follows AS 2865 and the work health and safety regulations.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document H covers drainage; BS EN 12056-4 covers wastewater lifting plants; the Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 govern pit entry.
- United States. The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes cover sumps, ejectors and booster pumps; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 governs permit-required confined spaces.

In all three jurisdictions, sewage pumping into the public sewer may also be subject to the utility's connection conditions, and flooding of basements from failed pumps is commonly excluded from or limited under insurance where maintenance cannot be shown. Strata and leasehold buildings usually treat sump and booster systems as common property, maintained by the owners corporation or landlord.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Pump maintenance and pit cleaning records.
- Flood incident history.
- Alarm monitoring arrangements.
- Backup power arrangements.
- Pump and pit design data.
- Upper floor pressure complaints.

- Insurance claims for basement flooding.
- Drawdown or capacity test results.
- Hydraulic drawings showing pits, catchments and rising mains.

- Pressure vessel charge records and booster set service reports.

pages.title: Rainwater Systems
pages.question: How do gutters, box gutters and downpipes fail, and how do you tell a maintenance problem from a capacity problem?
pages.answer: Rainwater goods are small in cost and large in consequence. Box gutters and internal outlets that overflow spill inside the building, so the overflow is as important as the gutter. Leaks only in heavy storms are capacity problems that cleaning will not fix; leaks in any rain are perforation or joints. Gutters rust along the sole where debris and water stand; the cleaning regime sets their life. Roofs extended or re-roofed often carry goods sized for a smaller catchment.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about rainwater systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Gutters, downpipes, scuppers, overflow systems, rainwater heads

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Rainwater systems collect water from the roof and carry it to the stormwater drainage: eaves gutters, box gutters, valley gutters, sumps, rainwater heads, scuppers, overflows, downpipes and internal stacks, siphonic systems, and the connections at ground level. On large metal roofs, box gutters run the length of the building between bays or behind parapets, inside the building envelope; on apartment and office buildings with flat roofs, outlets feed internal downpipes in risers.

Every system is designed for a rainfall intensity and a catchment. Its weak point is what happens when it is overwhelmed. An eaves gutter that overflows spills outside the building. A box gutter or internal outlet that overflows spills inside it, unless it has an overflow sized to take the full flow. Buildings extended, re-roofed or fitted with larger plant decks often have rainwater systems sized for the original roof, and rainfall intensities used in design have increased in many regions.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eaves gutters and external downpipes | Houses, low-rise, older buildings | Corrosion, blockage, overflow at the wall |
| Box gutters | Industrial and commercial metal roofs; parapeted roofs | Overflow and leaks inside the building |
| Valley gutters | Pitched roofs | Debris and overflow under the covering |
| Internal outlets and stacks | Flat roofs, apartments, offices | Leaks in risers and ceilings; blockage |
| Siphonic systems | Large commercial roofs from the 1990s | Blockage changes the hydraulics; design-dependent |
| Cast iron and lead rainwater goods | Heritage buildings | Cracking, joint failure, theft of lead |
| Asbestos cement downpipes and gutters | Mid-century buildings | Hazardous material on replacement |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zinc-aluminium steel eaves gutters | 20 to 30 years | Cleaning regime; leaf litter; coastal exposure |
| Box gutters | 15 to 30 years | Fall; water standing; foot traffic; cleaning |
| Cast iron goods | 100 years and more with painting | Paint cycle; joint failure; frost |
| PVC downpipes | 30 to 50 years | UV; impact |
| Aluminium and copper gutters | 30 to 60 years | Contact with other metals |
| Internal stacks and outlets | 30 to 50 years | Joints; outlet clamping rings |

What shortens life:

- No cleaning regime, especially with trees over the roof: the single largest determinant of gutter life.
- Flat or back falls in box gutters, keeping them wet.
- Dissimilar metals and copper or lead run-off.
- Foot traffic in box gutters used as walkways to plant.
- Undersized outlets and missing overflows, which turn every blockage into an internal flood.
- Ground-level damage to downpipes from vehicles and trolleys.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Inadequate capacity

Gutters, outlets and downpipes sized for a smaller catchment or lower rainfall intensity overflow in heavy storms. Box gutters without overflows, or with overflows smaller than the outlet they protect, overflow into the building. Siphonic systems depend on their design flow; a blockage or an added catchment changes their behaviour.

### Blockage

Leaves, sediment, bird nests, balls and debris block outlets and sumps. Leaf guards that are not maintained make it worse. A blocked outlet holds water in the gutter, which then overflows, ponds and corrodes the gutter sole.

### Corrosion

Steel gutters corrode along the sole where water and debris stand, at laps and at sumps. Box gutters perforate and leak inside, often first at sumps and stop ends. Cast iron cracks at joints and from frost; its joints fail where the paint has gone.

### Joint and connection failure

Joints in internal stacks fail inside ceilings and risers; outlet clamping rings loosen from the membrane; downpipes disconnect from the drain at ground level and discharge against footings.

### Ponding load

Water held on a roof by blocked outlets adds load. On light steel roofs, deflection holds more water, and the process can end in collapse. Codes in all three jurisdictions now treat secondary drainage and rain loads explicitly for this reason.

### Cast iron and lead goods

Cast iron gutters and downpipes crack from frost and impact and leak at joints once the paint has gone; lead rainwater heads and gutters are stolen, leaving water discharging against the wall.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Vegetation and debris in gutters and box gutters; ponding at sumps.
- Staining on walls below gutter lines and at downpipe joints; overflow marks on fascias.
- Downpipes disconnected, damaged or discharging onto walls, paths or lower roofs.
- Trees overhanging the roof.
- Overflows missing from box gutters and parapet roofs.

### On the roof

- Corrosion along gutter soles, at laps and at sumps; perforations.
- Falls in box gutters: water standing after rain.
- Outlet size against the gutter and catchment; overflow presence and size.
- Leaf guards blocked; outlet grates missing.

### Inside the building

- Water staining along the line of box gutters on purlins, ceilings and walls; leaks during heavy rain only.
- Staining and leaks at internal stacks in risers and ceilings.
- Damp at the base of walls where downpipes discharge.

### In the records

- Gutter cleaning contract and log.
- Leak register, especially leaks in heavy storms.
- Drawings or hydraulic report showing design rainfall, catchments, outlets and overflows.
- Records of roof extensions, re-roofing or added plant decks.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks inside along the box gutter line, only in heavy storms | Overflow: undersized outlet or no overflow | Overflow absent or small; outlet capacity below the catchment's design flow |
| Leaks inside along the box gutter line in any rain | Perforated gutter or failed joint | Corrosion or open joint at the leak position |
| Staining down a wall from an eaves gutter | Blocked or corroded gutter overflowing at that point | Debris or perforation above the stain |
| Leaks at an internal stack in a riser | Joint failure or outlet clamp loose | Water test at the outlet; joint inspection |
| Damp and washouts at the base of a wall | Downpipe disconnected from the drain | Pipe ends above ground; drain blocked |
| Rust along the gutter sole, sound elsewhere | Water standing from poor fall or blockage | Water present after rain; debris |

> Leaks that occur only in the heaviest storms are capacity problems, not maintenance problems. Clearing the gutters will not stop them; outlets and overflows must be resized.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding on a light roof with visible deflection; box gutter overflowing onto electrical equipment | safety | Clear and drain now; isolate equipment; engineer for deflection |
| Perforated box gutters or failed internal joints leaking into the building | failure | Repair or replace now |
| Box gutters without adequate overflows; undersized outlets after roof changes | condition | Upgrade in the near term |
| Gutters and downpipes at age, corroding without perforation | lifecycle | Replace on cycle, often with the roof covering |
| Storm leaks of unknown cause; roof extended or re-roofed since the system was designed | check | Hydraulic capacity check |
| Debris in gutters, minor staining | nil | Clean and set a regime |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A roof plumber inspects condition; a hydraulic engineer checks capacity where the roof has changed or storm leaks occur.

- Visual inspection of every gutter, sump, outlet and downpipe, with falls checked after rain or by level.
- Capacity check of box gutters, outlets and overflows against the catchment and current design rainfall intensity.
- Water testing of internal outlets and stacks.
- CCTV of internal stacks and the connections to stormwater.
- Hazardous material check on asbestos cement goods before removal.

The report should list runs needing replacement, any capacity shortfall and the fix, and the cleaning cadence the roof needs.

- Box gutter measurement: falls, sole width and depth against the catchment.
- Rainfall data: current published design intensity for the location, which may exceed what the system was designed for.
- Riser inspection of internal stacks through access panels.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Cleaning regime with leaf guards maintained; quarterly where trees overhang.
- Repairs: reseal joints, replace sections, refix brackets.
- Replacement of gutters and downpipes, usually with the roof covering.
- Box gutter upgrade: replace with correctly falling, larger gutters; add sumps and rainwater heads.
- Overflows: add or enlarge overflows to discharge outside the building.
- Additional outlets and downpipes where capacity is short.
- Spreaders and diverters where downpipes discharge onto lower roofs.

- Rainwater heads to collect and redistribute flow into downpipes.
- Trace heating of gutters and outlets in snow regions.
- Licensed replacement of asbestos cement gutters and downpipes.
- Secondary drainage on parapet roofs where codes require it.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is rate-based on linear metre and profile, with sumps, rainwater heads and overflows itemised. Capacity upgrades are lump-sum design-and-construct items. Cleaning is a recurring maintenance contract. Gutters are often replaced with the roof covering and may sit inside that register line.

Replacement is lifecycle; capacity upgrades are lifecycle or code compliance where overflows are missing; cleaning and minor repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Where trees overhang a roof, cleaning may need to be quarterly; it is still the cheapest protection the roof has.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Roof drainage design follows AS/NZS 3500.3, called up by the National Construction Code, with box gutters and overflows sized to the design rainfall intensity for the location; SA HB 114 guides the design of eaves and box gutters. A change of roof area or plant deck requires the system to be rechecked.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document H (H3) covers rainwater drainage; BS EN 12056-3 sets roof drainage layout and calculation. Sustainable drainage requirements can apply where discharge arrangements change.
- United States. International Plumbing Code Chapter 11 covers storm drainage, including secondary (emergency overflow) drainage for roofs where parapets or other construction would trap water; ASCE 7 sets rain loads, including ponding.

Gutters and downpipes on common property are owners corporation items in Australian strata schemes and service-charge items on British leasehold blocks.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Gutter cleaning contract and log.
- Leak register, noting which leaks occur in heavy storms.
- Roof drainage drawings or hydraulic design report.
- Records of roof extensions, re-roofing or plant decks added.
- Roof plumber or leak investigation reports.

- Tree management records.
- Records of leaks from internal stacks.

pages.title: Recreational Facilities
pages.question: How do playgrounds, courts and shared recreation facilities fail, and which findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Recreation facilities fail first on safety. Most playground injuries are falls, so surfacing displaced, compacted or worn under equipment is the key finding; entrapment gaps, protrusions and broken parts are next. Courts crack through to trip lines as their bases move; gym cables fray; barbecues leak gas and build up grease. Close unsafe equipment until fixed; renew surfaces and equipment on predictable cycles.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about recreational facilities; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Swimming pools, tennis courts, playgrounds

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Recreational facilities are the shared amenities on a site: playgrounds, tennis and multi-sport courts, gyms, barbecue areas, outdoor fitness equipment, and swimming pools and spas (whose water systems are covered on the specialist hydraulics page). In apartment buildings and retirement villages they are common property and a significant part of the sinking fund; in schools, hotels and public sites they carry public safety obligations.

| Facility | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Playgrounds | Apartments, schools, childcare, parks, shopping centres | Falls onto inadequate surfacing; entrapment; equipment failure |
| Tennis and multi-sport courts | Apartments, schools, clubs | Surface cracking and trips; fencing; lighting |
| Gyms | Apartments, offices, hotels | Equipment failure; flooring; ventilation |
| Barbecue and outdoor kitchen areas | Apartments, parks | Gas safety; burns; hygiene |
| Outdoor fitness equipment | Parks, apartments | Wear; surfacing |
| Pools and spas | Apartments, hotels, schools | See specialist hydraulics |

Each facility type has its own safety standard and inspection expectations, and many sites are inspected only when something breaks. In shared residential buildings, the duty of care for these facilities sits with the owners corporation, landlord or operator, and the condition of play equipment and courts is often the first thing residents and buyers notice.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Playground equipment | 10 to 20 years | Use; materials; weather |
| Impact-absorbing surfacing | Loose fill topped up yearly; rubber 7 to 15 years | Wear; displacement |
| Tennis court surfaces | 7 to 15 years; resurfacing more often | Surface type; cracking |
| Court fencing and nets | 15 to 25 years; nets 2 to 5 | Corrosion; damage |
| Gym equipment | 7 to 12 years | Use; maintenance |
| Barbecues | 8 to 15 years | Use; cleaning |

What shortens life:

- Heavy use and vandalism.
- Weather and coastal exposure.
- Lack of inspection and maintenance.
- Ground movement under courts.

Facilities used by the public or by many residents wear far faster than identical equipment in a private garden, and coastal and hot climates shorten the life of plastics, rubber and coatings.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Inadequate impact surfacing

Most playground injuries are falls. Loose fill (bark, sand) displaces away from under equipment and compacts; rubber surfacing wears and hardens. Surfacing that is too thin or hard for the fall height turns falls into serious head injuries.

### Entrapment and protrusions

Gaps of certain sizes between parts trap heads, fingers and clothing; protruding bolts and broken parts snag and cut. Standards set the dimensions that avoid them.

### Equipment wear and failure

Bearings, chains, swing hangers and moving parts wear; timber rots; steel corrodes at the base; fixings loosen. Failures happen under load.

### Court surface cracking

Asphalt and concrete court bases crack from shrinkage and ground movement; cracks reflect through acrylic surfaces and create trip lines; drainage problems leave puddles and moss.

### Gym equipment and environment

Cables, pulleys and weight stacks wear; treadmills fail; poor ventilation and hygiene affect users; heavy equipment on upper floors may exceed floor loads.

### Barbecue hazards

Gas leaks, faulty ignition and grease build-up cause fires and burns; poor cleaning creates hygiene issues.

### Lighting and access

Poorly lit courts and play areas used in the evening cause falls and security problems; gates on play areas that do not self-close let small children reach roads, pools and car parks.

### Shade structures

Shade sails and canopies over play areas fail at fixings and masts in high winds, and unshaded equipment in hot climates gets hot enough to burn.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Loose fill displaced or thin under equipment; worn or hard rubber surfacing.
- Broken, worn or missing parts; exposed bolts; rust at bases; splintered timber.
- Court cracks, puddles, moss and damaged nets and fences.
- Gym equipment with frayed cables or out of service.
- Barbecues with grease build-up and damaged hoses.
- Missing signage on age groups and use.

### In the records

- Playground inspection records.
- Equipment manufacturer and installation certificates.
- Court resurfacing history.
- Gym service contracts.
- Incident records.

- Play area gates that do not self-close or latch.
- Hot metal and plastic surfaces in direct sun.

- Play equipment designed for older children installed where toddlers play, with no signage on age groups.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare ground under swings and slides | Loose fill displaced | Depth measurement |
| Rubber surfacing hard to the touch | Aged surfacing | Impact attenuation test |
| Cracks repeating through court surfaces | Base movement or shrinkage | Crack mapping |
| Equipment wobbling | Loose fixings or rotted posts | Inspection |
| Frayed gym cables | Wear | Inspection |

> Playground equipment over inadequate surfacing, or with entrapment gaps or broken parts, should be closed until fixed. Most serious playground injuries come from falls and entrapment.

Separating wear from design is important: equipment that is worn needs repair; equipment whose design no longer meets the standard (for example, fall heights above what the surfacing can absorb) needs replacement or redesign.

Incident records are a useful guide: repeated injuries at one item point to its design or surfacing, while scattered minor incidents usually reflect normal use.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inadequate surfacing; entrapment hazards; broken equipment; gas leaks | safety | Close and fix now |
| Facility out of use | failure | Repair |
| Periodic inspections due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn equipment; court cracking | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Equipment and surfaces at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No inspection records | check | Inspect |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Closing a facility is often the right immediate response: a play unit taped off for a week while surfacing is topped up is far better than a serious fall onto compacted ground.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A qualified playground inspector leads on play equipment; court and sports surface contractors, gym equipment servicers and licensed gas fitters cover their areas.

- Playground inspection against the current standard: free height of fall, surfacing type, depth and impact attenuation (tested in place where rubber surfacing is old), entrapment and finger traps, protrusions and sharp edges, structural integrity of posts and fixings, and wear of moving parts.
- Court inspection: cracking pattern and its cause, surface wear and slip resistance, drainage, fencing, nets and posts, and lighting levels.
- Gym inspection: equipment condition and service history, flooring, ventilation and floor loading for heavy equipment.
- Barbecue and outdoor kitchen inspection: gas connections and appliances, electrical safety, grease and hygiene.
- Shade structure check: fixings, masts and fabric.
- Records review: inspection frequency, incidents and complaints.

The report should list immediate safety actions, items to close, and a renewal programme by facility.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Surfacing: top up and rake loose fill to the depth needed for the fall height; replace hardened or torn rubber surfacing; extend surfacing to the full fall zone.
- Equipment: replace broken and worn parts, tighten and cap fixings, remove items that cannot be made compliant, and replace whole play units at the end of their life.
- Courts: treat cracks, resurface, rebuild bases where cracking is structural, and repair fencing, nets and lighting.
- Gyms: service and replace equipment, and check floors for heavy items.
- Barbecues: clean, service and replace units; check gas compliance.
- Gates and shade: self-closing gates, shade structures engineered for wind.
- Inspection regime: routine visual checks, operational inspections and an annual comprehensive inspection, recorded.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections recur at routine, operational and annual intervals. Loose fill top-ups recur yearly; rubber surfacing is replaced on its cycle. Play equipment replacement is a lump sum per play area including surfacing; court resurfacing is per court, with base reconstruction a larger lump sum. Gym equipment is replaced per item on a rolling cycle. In strata buildings these are common property sinking fund items.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4685 sets requirements for playground equipment and AS 4422 for impact-attenuating surfacing; councils, schools and owners corporations commonly follow their inspection regimes; barbecues on gas follow AS/NZS 5601.1.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 1176 covers playground equipment, including routine, operational and annual inspections, and BS EN 1177 impact-attenuating surfacing; the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents and others carry out annual inspections; occupiers' liability law applies.
- United States. ASTM F1487 covers public playground equipment and ASTM F1292 surfacing impact attenuation; the Consumer Product Safety Commission's Public Playground Safety Handbook is widely used; accessibility of play areas is set by the 2010 ADA Standards.

Insurers in all three countries commonly require evidence of regular inspection of play and recreation facilities.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Playground inspection reports at each required frequency.
- Equipment manufacturer certificates and installation records.
- Surfacing impact test results.
- Court resurfacing and repair history.
- Gym equipment service contracts and records.
- Barbecue gas compliance certificates.
- Incident and complaint records.

- Insurance requirements for recreation facilities.
- Shade structure engineering certificates.

pages.title: Residential Units/Guest Rooms
pages.question: How do apartments and guest rooms fail as places to live, and who is responsible in strata buildings?
pages.answer: Units fail on safety, health and neighbours. Missing or non-interconnected smoke alarms and entry doors that do not close are safety findings; weak exhaust and indoor drying cause condensation and mould; bathroom and laundry leaks damage the unit below; hard floors laid over carpet cause noise complaints. Units also slide below rental minimums or brand standards. In strata, establish whether each defect is common property or the owner's before deciding who pays.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about residential units/guest rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Kitchens, bathrooms, living areas, bedrooms — all finishes and fixtures

sources.title: Housing Health and Safety Rating System

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Residential units and guest rooms are where people live and sleep: apartments in strata, build-to-rent and student buildings, and rooms in hotels, serviced apartments and aged care. As a functional space, a unit must be safe to sleep in, healthy (dry, ventilated, warm or cool enough), quiet enough to live beside neighbours, and of a standard that suits the market or brand. For capital planning, the key question is who is responsible: in strata buildings most of the unit interior belongs to the owner, while structure, external walls, windows and shared services may be common property; in rented and hotel buildings, the operator carries everything.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen | Cabinetry, benchtop, appliances, exhaust | Function, condition, ventilation |
| Bathroom and laundry | Fixtures, waterproofing, exhaust | Leaks to units below; mould |
| Living and bedrooms | Floor and wall finishes, joinery, doors | Wear, acoustics, condition |
| Windows and balcony doors | Framed glazing, seals | Leaks, draughts, condensation, security |
| Heating and cooling | Split systems, ducted systems, heaters | Comfort, ownership, refrigerant |
| Smoke alarms and fire separation | Interconnected alarms, fire-rated entry door and walls | Life safety |
| Hot water | Individual or central | Temperature control, Legionella |

Hotels refresh rooms on brand-driven cycles: soft furnishings every five to seven years and case goods and bathrooms every ten to fifteen, set out in brand standards and property improvement plans. Build-to-rent operators turn units over between tenancies. Strata owners refurbish their own units on their own timing, which leaves shared issues such as noise and wet area leaks between neighbours.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen cabinetry and benchtops | 15 to 25 years | Use; moisture; style |
| Appliances | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Bathroom refurbishment | 15 to 25 years | Waterproofing; wear |
| Carpet | 8 to 12 years | Use; tenancy turnover |
| Hard floors | 20 to 30 years | Wear; acoustics |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Tenancy turnover |
| Hotel soft goods | 5 to 7 years | Brand standards |
| Hotel case goods and bathrooms | 10 to 15 years | Brand standards |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Moisture from cooking, showers and drying clothes indoors without adequate exhaust.
- Tenancy turnover and guest use.
