- Owner alterations in strata buildings, especially hard floors and bathroom renovations.
- Rising standards for rental minimums, energy and brand quality.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Wet area leaks to neighbours

Bathroom, laundry and kitchen leaks through failed membranes, shower screens, wastes and appliance connections are the most common source of damage between units. In strata, determining whether the cause is common property or the owner's fixture decides who pays.

### Condensation and mould

Units with weak or unused bathroom and kitchen exhaust, clothes dried indoors, poor heating and cold window frames grow mould on ceilings, window reveals and wardrobes. It is a health issue, and in rented housing a legal one.

### Noise between units

Impact noise from hard floors laid over carpet, plumbing noise, and airborne noise through party walls generate complaints. Hard floor replacements without acoustic underlay are a common cause, and strata by-laws often regulate them.

### Smoke alarms and fire separation

Smoke alarms missing, disconnected, out of date or not interconnected leave sleepers unwarned. Entry doors that do not close or have been replaced, and penetrations through walls between units, let fire and smoke spread.

### Window and balcony door leaks

Window and sliding door seals, sills and tracks leak and let draughts in, damaging floors and finishes.

### Falling below minimum or brand standards

Rental minimum standards, housing quality regimes and hotel brand standards set requirements for heating, ventilation, security and condition. Units can fall below them without any single failure.

In aged care and student buildings, intensive use and occupants with particular needs accelerate wear and raise safety expectations further.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In a sample of units

- Mould on ceilings, reveals and wardrobe backs; exhaust fans weak or switched off.
- Water staining on ceilings from the unit above.
- Hard floors in upper units, with noise complaints below.
- Smoke alarm type, date and interconnection.
- Entry door closers and seals.
- Leaks and draughts at windows and balcony doors.
- Worn kitchens, bathrooms and carpets.

### In the records

- Leak and defect history by unit.
- Noise complaints and by-law breaches.
- Smoke alarm compliance records.
- Mould complaints and remediation.
- Brand audits and property improvement plans for hotels.
- Rental standard compliance records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould on ceilings in bathrooms and bedrooms | Condensation from inadequate exhaust and heating | Fan airflow; humidity logging; occupant habits |
| Stain below a bathroom after showers | Membrane or shower screen leak | Flood and dye tests |
| Stain below a bathroom constantly | Pipe leak | Pressure test; inspection |
| Impact noise complaints after a renovation | Hard floor without acoustic underlay | Floor construction; acoustic test |
| Water at window sills in storms | Seal or sill failure | Water test |

> In strata buildings, the cause of a defect decides who pays, so investigation must establish whether the source is common property or within the owner's lot before repair.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing or failed smoke alarms; entry doors not self-closing in apartment buildings; severe mould | safety | Rectify now |
| Leaks damaging neighbours | failure | Repair now |
| Rental minimum standards, smoke alarm laws or brand deadlines | deadline | By the required date |
| Mould, noise complaints, worn finishes | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Kitchens, bathrooms and soft goods at end of cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish on cycle |
| No unit sample inspected | check | Inspect |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects a representative sample of units, with acoustic, mould, leak and fire specialists as needed; for hotels, the brand's quality auditor's findings are a key input.

- Unit sample inspection: kitchens, bathrooms, laundries, floors, windows and balcony doors, smoke alarms, entry doors and ventilation, in units of each type, floor and orientation, weighted to those with complaints.
- Leak investigations with flood tests of showers and floors, dye tests of fixtures, and pressure tests of pipework, to separate common property from owner causes.
- Ventilation and moisture assessment: measured exhaust airflows, humidity logging over a week, and thermal imaging of cold spots.
- Acoustic testing of impact and airborne sound where complaints exist, against the code at the time and current standards.
- Smoke alarm and entry door compliance check against current law, which may be stricter than when the building was built.
- Ownership review: strata plan, by-laws and lot boundaries, or lease and management agreements.

The report should separate owner, common property and operator items, state safety and health findings, and give a refurbishment plan by unit type.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Smoke alarms: interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom and hallway where required, hard-wired or with ten-year sealed batteries.
- Entry doors: self-closing, sealed fire-rated doors where the building requires them, replacing owner-fitted doors that do not comply.
- Ventilation: stronger ducted exhaust in bathrooms, laundries and kitchens, with humidity or run-on controls so it actually runs.
- Wet area rectification: re-waterproof bathrooms and laundries, replace shower screens and seals, repair wastes.
- Acoustic controls: by-laws requiring tested underlays for hard floors, and acoustic remediation where complaints are upheld.
- Windows and doors: replace seals and rollers, repair sills, and adjust or replace balcony doors.
- Refurbishment cycles: kitchens, bathrooms, flooring and paint on planned cycles in rented and hotel stock, timed with vacancies.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Unit works are priced per unit and grouped by type. In hotels, rooms are refurbished floor by floor to keep revenue flowing, with soft goods and case goods on separate cycles. In build-to-rent, works are timed with tenancy turnover. In strata, common property items fall to the owners corporation and lot items to owners, and leaks often lead to cost recovery between them.

Smoke alarms and doors are code compliance with deadlines; leaks are failures; refurbishment is lifecycle; mould remediation is condition or safety depending on extent.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. State laws set smoke alarm requirements (Queensland requires interconnected photoelectric alarms in all dwellings by 1 January 2027), rental minimum standards (for example Victoria's), and strata management; the National Construction Code sets fire separation, sound insulation and ventilation for apartments; strata legislation defines lot and common property boundaries.
- United Kingdom. The Housing Health and Safety Rating System assesses hazards in homes; the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 gives tenants rights; Awaab's Law sets timescales for social landlords to deal with damp and mould; smoke and carbon monoxide alarm regulations apply to rented homes; leasehold law sets landlord and leaseholder responsibilities.
- United States. The International Property Maintenance Code and local housing codes set habitability standards; HUD inspects assisted housing under its national standards; condominium law and declarations define unit and common element boundaries; hotel brands set property improvement plans.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Leak and defect records by unit, with causes and who paid.
- Noise complaints and by-law breaches.
- Smoke alarm compliance records.
- Mould complaints and remediation records.
- Strata plan, by-laws and lot boundary definitions.
- Brand audits and property improvement plans for hotels.
- Refurbishment history by unit type.

pages.title: Retail Tenancies (Base-Build)
pages.question: How do retail tenancies fail as lettable space, and which tenancy findings belong to the landlord?
pages.answer: Retail tenancies fail on fit more than condition. Food, fitness and service tenants need exhaust risers, grease waste, power and water that many shells lack, and retrofitting them is costly. Repeated fit-outs breach demising walls and alter sprinkler and detection coverage. Food tenancies leak, smell and block drains. Poor make-good hands shells back in bad order. Separate landlord provision, tenant obligations and market fit: each has a different fix and payer.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about retail tenancies (base-build); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Base-building elements, services integration, structural finishes

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Retail tenancies are the shops, food outlets, gyms and service premises let to tenants in shopping centres, high streets, office podiums and mixed-use buildings. As a functional space, a retail tenancy is judged on whether the base building provides what the current and likely future tenants need: the right shell, frontage and depth, and service connections for power, water, drainage, grease waste, exhaust, gas and air conditioning. The landlord usually provides the shell and service stubs; the tenant fits out within it and must make good at lease end. Many problems arise where that boundary is unclear or where the base building was set up for a different kind of tenant.

| Provision | Typical base-building scope | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shell | Slab, walls, ceiling or soffit, demising walls | Condition, fire separation, flatness |
| Shopfront | Glazed frontage, doors, signage zone (landlord or tenant) | Weather, security, presentation |
| Power and data | Supply to a tenancy board, metered | Capacity for the tenant type |
| Water and drainage | Water and sewer stubs; grease waste for food | Location and capacity; grease treatment |
| Exhaust and ventilation | Kitchen exhaust riser for food; general exhaust | Whether food tenants can operate |
| Air conditioning | Base supply, condenser water, or space for tenant units | Capacity and connection points |
| Fire services | Sprinklers, detection and warning extended into the tenancy | Coverage after each fit-out |
| Gas | Metered supply for food tenants | Capacity; future electrification |

The retail mix has shifted toward food, health, gyms and services, which need more power, exhaust, grease waste, water and structural capacity than the fashion shops many centres were designed around. Tenancies without these provisions are harder to let.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant fit-out | 5 to 10 years | Lease term; brand refits |
| Shopfronts | 15 to 25 years | Damage; centre refurbishment |
| Base-building service provisions | 25 to 40 years | Tenant mix changes |
| Demising walls and fire separation | Life of the building if maintained | Penetrations by fit-outs |
| Centre or precinct refurbishment | 10 to 15 years | Competing centres; retail trends |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Changes in tenant mix, especially toward food and fitness, which need services the tenancy lacks.
- Repeated fit-outs that penetrate demising walls and alter fire services.
- Poor make-good that leaves services, ceilings and floors in poor order for the next tenant.
- Water damage from tenant equipment and leaks.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Service shortfalls for the tenant type

A tenancy without a kitchen exhaust riser, grease waste connection, adequate power or water cannot take a food tenant, and retrofitting these through floors above, roofs or common areas is costly and sometimes impossible. Gyms need structural capacity and acoustic separation; medical tenants need specialised services. The lack of provisions shows up as vacancy and lower rents.

### Fire separation and services after fit-outs

Each fit-out penetrates demising walls and ceilings for services, relocates sprinkler heads and detectors, and changes layouts. Fire separation between tenancies and from common areas degrades unless every fit-out is checked; sprinkler and detection coverage may not follow the new layout.

### Leaks and water damage

Food tenancies, salons and gyms use water heavily; leaking equipment, floor wastes and wet floors damage the slab, adjacent tenancies and floors below.

### Grease, odour and exhaust

Food tenancies without adequate grease treatment block drains; inadequate exhaust spreads odour into malls and neighbouring premises and causes complaints from residents in mixed-use buildings.

### Make-good failures

Tenants leaving without proper make-good leave behind redundant equipment, damaged floors and ceilings, capped services and altered fire services; disputes are common where lease terms are vague.

### Centre-level obsolescence

Tenancies can be in good condition but in a centre or street that has lost trade. Configuration matters too: very deep, narrow tenancies, or poor frontage and visibility, are hard to let regardless of condition.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Vacant tenancies and the kinds of tenants that have left; types now trading nearby.
- Service provisions visible in shell tenancies: exhaust risers, grease waste points, power boards, condenser water connections.
- Penetrations through demising walls and ceilings; altered sprinkler heads and detectors.
- Water staining on slabs and ceilings below food tenancies.
- Odour in malls or neighbouring premises.
- Redundant equipment and damage left in vacated tenancies.

### In the records

- Tenancy schedule with leases, expiries and make-good terms.
- Fit-out guides and design criteria for tenants.
- Fit-out approvals and fire services certification after each fit-out.
- Trade waste agreements for food tenants.
- Complaints about odour and leaks.
- Vacancy and leasing history.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Food tenants unable to take vacant shops | No exhaust riser, grease waste or capacity | Services survey against fit-out guide |
| Fire alarm faults after each new tenancy | Fit-outs altering detection without proper reprogramming | Fire services records |
| Odour complaints in a mall | Exhaust inadequate or discharging near intakes | Exhaust survey |
| Blocked drains downstream of food court | Grease treatment inadequate | See trade waste page |
| Shells handed back in poor order | Weak make-good clauses or enforcement | Lease review; condition reports |
| Long vacancy in good condition shells | Configuration, trade area or rent | Leasing evidence |

> Separate base-building provision (what the landlord must supply), tenant condition (what the tenant must return) and market fit (what tenants want). Each is fixed by a different party and budget.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire separation breached between tenancies; sprinkler or detection coverage missing after fit-out | safety | Rectify before trading continues |
| Leaks damaging adjacent tenancies or structure | failure | Repair now |
| Lease, health or trade waste obligations requiring works | deadline | By the required date |
| Service provisions inadequate for current market; make-good shortfalls | condition | Upgrade at vacancy or lease renewal |
| Shopfronts and centre finishes at end of cycle | lifecycle | Refurbish with centre strategy |
| Services capacity per tenancy unknown | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or retail building consultant leads, with services and fire engineers and the centre's leasing team.

- Tenancy services survey: power, water, drainage, grease waste, exhaust, gas and air conditioning provision to each tenancy, against the fit-out guide and the tenant types sought.
- Fire separation and services review of a sample of tenancies and every vacant one: demising wall penetrations, sprinkler and detection coverage, egress.
- Make-good inspections at each lease end against the lease, with photographs.
- Leak and odour investigation where complaints exist.
- Leasing review: vacancy, tenant mix trends and why tenancies are hard to let.
- Lease review: base-building and tenant responsibilities, make-good and fit-out obligations.

The report should separate landlord capital, tenant obligations and market repositioning, and identify tenancies needing services upgrades to be lettable.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Services upgrades: kitchen exhaust risers, grease waste connections, larger power supplies and condenser water, installed when tenancies are vacant and ideally for groups of tenancies at once.
- Fire separation and services rectification after each fit-out, enforced through fit-out approval and sign-off.
- Fit-out guide updated so tenants know what is provided and what they must do.
- Make-good enforcement: clear lease clauses, condition reports at entry and exit, and claims where needed.
- Reconfiguration: merging or splitting tenancies to suit demand.
- Shopfront and centre refurbishment as part of a repositioning strategy.

- Separate metering of power, water and gas to every tenancy so outgoings are recovered accurately.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Services upgrades are lump sums per tenancy or per group, often justified by higher rents from food and service tenants. Fire separation rectification is itemised. Reconfiguration is a lump sum with demolition and new demising. Make-good shortfalls are recoverable from outgoing tenants where leases allow. Centre refurbishment is a large lump-sum repositioning project.

Fire safety items are code compliance; services upgrades and reconfiguration are repositioning capital; shopfronts are lifecycle; tenant damage is recoverable.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. State retail leases legislation (for example in New South Wales and Victoria) governs disclosure, outgoings and some fit-out and make-good matters; fit-outs need approval under the National Construction Code; food premises must meet the Food Standards Code premises requirements; trade waste agreements apply to food tenants.
- United Kingdom. Fit-outs need building regulations approval; food premises must meet food hygiene regulations and local authority requirements for extraction and odour; dilapidations practice governs lease-end obligations; planning use classes affect which tenants can trade.
- United States. Tenant improvements need permits under the International Building Code (mercantile occupancy); food establishments follow state health codes based on the FDA Food Code; the 2010 ADA Standards apply to public accommodations.

Mixed-use buildings add residential neighbours, so odour, noise and hours conditions in planning approvals often constrain food and entertainment tenants in all three countries.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Tenancy schedule with leases, expiries and make-good terms.
- Fit-out guide and tenant design criteria.
- Services provision schedule per tenancy.
- Fit-out approvals and fire services certificates after each fit-out.
- Trade waste agreements and odour complaints.
- Vacancy history and leasing agent feedback.
- Make-good condition reports.

- Planning conditions on uses, hours and extraction.

pages.title: Roof Coverings
pages.question: How do roof coverings fail, what does each failure look like, and when does a covering need repair rather than replacement?
pages.answer: Roof coverings fail at their edges, laps, fixings and junctions, not in the field. Coated steel rusts from laps and the bottom metre above the gutter; underside rust with a sound top means condensation. Tile roofs fail at ridge bedding, valleys and fixings; scattered slipped slates mean the nails have rusted through. Asbestos cement weathers to exposed fibre and is fragile at any age. Most leaks start at flashings and penetrations, so find the junction before condemning the sheet.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof coverings; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Slate, tiles, flagstones, shingles, sheet metal (copper, zinc, lead, steel)

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A roof covering is the weathering layer on a pitched or low-pitched roof: profiled and standing-seam metal sheet, clay and concrete tiles, natural and fibre cement slate, asphalt and timber shingles, and traditional fully supported metals (lead, copper, zinc). Flat roof membranes have their own page. The covering works with what lies under and around it: battens or purlins, sarking or underlay, flashings at walls and penetrations, ridge and hip cappings, valleys, and the gutters it drains to. Most leaks arrive at those junctions rather than through the field of the roof.

| Covering | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coated steel sheet (zinc-aluminium, pre-painted) | Industrial and commercial roofs everywhere; Australian houses since the 1960s | Light, fast; life set by coating and exposure; fails at laps, cut edges and fixings |
| Galvanised corrugated iron | Australian houses and sheds before about 1970 | Zinc consumed; rust at laps and nail holes |
| Asbestos cement sheet (corrugated and Super Six) | Industrial, agricultural and some housing, 1920s to 1980s | Fragile; weathers to exposed fibre; replacement is licensed removal |
| Concrete tiles | Houses and townhouses from the 1950s | Durable body; surface erodes; ridge bedding and pointing fail first |
| Terracotta tiles | Houses throughout; heritage stock | Very durable; glazed or unglazed; frost damage in cold climates |
| Natural slate | Heritage stock in Britain, Australia and the north-eastern United States | Century material; nails and battens fail first |
| Fibre cement slate | Housing from the 1970s in Britain; earlier types contain asbestos | Shorter life; delamination and curling |
| Asphalt shingles | Most United States houses | Granule loss, curling and wind damage; insurers drive replacement |
| Lead, copper and zinc | Heritage roofs, domes, bays, flashings everywhere | Long life if detailed correctly; fail by fatigue, creep and underside corrosion |
| Standing-seam metal | Commercial and architectural roofs | Concealed fixings; clips and thermal movement |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Covering | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zinc-aluminium coated steel, benign inland | 40 years and more | Coastal exposure halves it; industrial air; ponding at laps |
| Coated steel within about a kilometre of surf | 15 to 25 years | Unwashed areas under eaves and laps corrode first |
| Galvanised iron | 30 to 50 years | Zinc thickness; exposure |
| Asbestos cement sheet | 40 to 60 years before it weathers to fibre | Exposure; lichen; foot traffic |
| Concrete tiles | 50 years and more; bedding and pointing 20 to 30 | Surface erosion; frost |
| Terracotta tiles | 80 years and more; bedding and pointing 20 to 30 | Frost; poor-quality batches |
| Natural slate | 80 to 150 years; nails 50 to 100 | Slate quality; nail material |
| Fibre cement slate | 25 to 40 years | Product generation |
| Asphalt shingles | 15 to 30 years | Heat, UV, hail, wind |
| Lead | 80 to 100 years when bays are sized correctly | Bay size, fixing, underside condensation |
| Copper | 70 to 100 years | Thickness; acid run-off |
| Zinc | 40 to 80 years | Underside ventilation |

What shortens life:

- Coastal, industrial and geothermal atmospheres, especially on unwashed surfaces under eaves and laps where salt is not rinsed off by rain.
- Low pitch and ponding at laps, end laps and behind penetrations.
- Dissimilar metals: copper or lead run-off onto zinc-aluminium steel, steel fixings in aluminium, inert catchment debris.
- Condensation on the underside of metal roofs over humid spaces: pools, cool rooms, laundries, uninsulated sheds.
- Foot traffic to plant and solar arrays; plant mounted directly on sheeting.
- Heavier replacement coverings on structures designed for lighter ones, such as concrete tiles replacing slate.
- Neglected gutters and valleys that back water up under the covering.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Coated metal corrosion

Sheet steel corrodes from the edges and laps inward. The coating chalks and loses gloss, then cut edges, end laps and fixing holes show red rust, then the sheet perforates where water and debris sit, usually in the bottom metre above the gutter, at end laps and around penetrations. Underside corrosion from condensation can perforate a roof that looks sound from above.

### Fixing failure

Screws back out under thermal cycling, washers perish, and the hole elongates. Lifting sheets then admit water and can be torn off in wind. Concealed clips on standing-seam roofs can bind and tear seams if thermal movement was not allowed for.

### Tile roof failure

Tile bodies rarely fail. What fails is the system around them: ridge and hip cappings lose their bedding and pointing and become loose; valley irons corrode; tiles slip when nails or battens fail; broken tiles go unreplaced; sarking tears and deteriorates. Concrete tiles erode at the surface and become porous; poor-quality terracotta spalls in frost.

### Slate failure

Slates fail by "nail sickness": the iron nails rust through and slates slip out of place, usually scattered across the roof rather than in lines. Poor slate delaminates and flakes. Battens decay where the underlay has failed. Fibre cement slates curl, crack and delaminate.

### Asbestos cement weathering

The cement matrix erodes and lichen roots into it, exposing fibre on the surface. Sheets become brittle and crack at fixings; they cannot bear a person's weight at any age. Coating can extend the life of sound sheet but not of eroded sheet, and pressure cleaning is prohibited.

### Lead, copper and zinc

Lead creeps and cracks by thermal fatigue when bays are oversized or fixed too rigidly; it corrodes from the underside where condensation forms, and white carbonate appears at laps. Zinc corrodes from the underside where unventilated. Copper is durable but its run-off attacks other metals.

### Asphalt shingle ageing

Shingles lose their mineral granules, curl at edges, crack, and lose wind resistance as the sealant strips age. Hail bruises them. The end is usually determined by an insurance inspection rather than a leak.

### Flashings and junctions

Wall flashings pull out of their chases; apron and step flashings lift; valley gutters overflow; penetration flashings crack around pipes and plant. These junctions are where most roof leaks start.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Colour change across bays, patches in a different material, rust at laps and bottom edges, sections already replaced.
- Slipped, missing or broken tiles and slates; scattered slipped slates (nail sickness); lines of slipped tiles (battens).
- Ridge and hip cappings with missing pointing or out of line; lichen and vegetation in valleys.
- Grey, lichen-covered corrugated sheet on industrial roofs of the relevant era: likely asbestos cement.
- Sagging ridgelines and roof planes (structure; see Roof Structure).
- Debris in valleys and gutters; staining under gutter lines.

### On the roof

- Fixings: backed out, rusted, missing washers; elongated holes.
- Lap condition: corrosion at end laps and side laps; perforations at the gutter edge.
- Flashings lifted, chases open, sealant failed.
- Tiles cracked under foot traffic routes; loose cappings.
- Surface erosion of concrete tiles; fibre exposed on asbestos cement.

### In the roof space and below

- Daylight through the covering; rust and perforation on the underside of sheets.
- Condensation drips and staining on the underside, uniform across the roof in cold weather.
- Water staining on battens, trusses and ceilings, localised under defects.
- Torn or missing sarking and underlay.

### In the records

- Re-roofing dates and extents; warranties.
- Leak register; roof maintenance and gutter cleaning records.
- Hazardous materials register entries for the roof.
- Insurance inspections and storm claims.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust at laps and the bottom metre of sheets, field sound | Normal edge and lap corrosion of coated steel | Corrosion concentrated where water lingers; coating chalked |
| Underside corrosion with a sound top surface | Condensation | Humid space below; no vapour control; uniform pattern; worse in winter |
| Corrosion stripe below a copper pipe, flue or lead flashing | Dissimilar metal run-off | Source above the stripe |
| Leaks in rain, staining localised under a junction | Flashing or penetration failure | Water test reproduces it |
| Scattered slipped slates across the roof | Nail sickness | Nails rusted through on slates lifted |
| Line of slipped tiles or slates | Batten failure | Batten decayed or broken below |
| Loose ridge cappings, mortar on the ground and in gutters | Ridge bedding and pointing failure | Cappings move by hand |
| Roof plane sagging between trusses or rafters | Structure, often from a heavier covering | Covering weight vs original; see Roof Structure |
| Shingles curled with granules in the gutters | Age | Uniform across slopes; worse on the sunniest |

> Every asbestos cement roof and most translucent sheets are fragile at any age. Their condition is a fall-through hazard before it is a weathertightness issue, and no-one should walk on them.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose sheets, tiles or cappings at an edge over public areas; storm damage; fragile roof accessed without protection | safety | Secure or remove now; stop access |
| Active leaks damaging structure, insulation or interiors; perforated sheets | failure | Repair now; replacement of failed bays |
| Lap and edge corrosion short of perforation; loose ridges; nail sickness spreading | condition | Programme repair or partial replacement in the near term |
| Covering at the end of its expected life with no current leaks | lifecycle | Plan replacement |
| Grey corrugated or Super Six sheeting with no hazardous materials register entry | check | Identify before any work; sets the method and cost |
| Chalking coatings, minor lichen, isolated cracked tile | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A roof plumber, roofing contractor or building surveyor with safe access inspects. For large metal roofs and asbestos cement roofs, the inspection is planned around fragility and edge protection.

- Aerial imagery and drone survey for extent, material, patching and the pattern of corrosion across bays.
- Close inspection of laps, fixings, flashings, penetrations, valleys and the gutter edge, with sample fixings removed.
- Underside inspection from the roof space or plant deck for corrosion, condensation and daylight.
- Coating thickness readings where a coating or restoration is being considered.
- Tile and slate sampling: lift and examine fixings and battens; check sarking.
- Hazardous material sampling of sheeting, felt and mastics where the era warrants.
- Water testing of suspected leak points.

The report should give an extent plan, remaining life by zone, the junctions needing work now, any fragile areas, and the hazardous materials position.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Repairs: replace failed fixings with oversized screws, reseal laps, replace individual sheets or tiles, rebed and repoint ridges, renew flashings.
- Coating or restoration of sound but weathered metal sheet; not an answer to perforation or failed fixings.
- Partial replacement of the failed bays, often the lower run above the gutter or the coastal-facing slope.
- Full replacement, with new battens or purlins where needed, sarking, flashings, safety systems and gutters.
- Re-slating with new stainless or copper nails and reused or new slates.
- Asbestos cement replacement by licensed removal, with edge protection and safety mesh during works.
- Condensation control: vapour control and insulation below metal roofs over humid spaces.

Interactions: re-roofing triggers insulation upgrades in some jurisdictions, renewal of roof safety systems, and replacement of gutters and flashings; it is the natural time to deal with solar mounting and plant penetrations.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a lump sum. Repairs are itemised per sheet, per tile area, per linear metre of ridge or flashing. Replacement is priced by roof area for the covering, with separate lines for battens or purlins, sarking, flashings, safety systems and gutters. Asbestos cement replacement adds licensed removal, air monitoring and disposal. Access and edge protection are significant on any roof.

Where condition is unverified, the usual shape is two-part: inspection first, then a replacement envelope that falls away if the inspection finds the covering sound. Replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; asbestos removal carries a code compliance element.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 1562.1 for metal roof cladding, AS 2050 for roof tiles and AS/NZS 4200.1 and 4200.2 for sarking; wind actions follow AS/NZS 1170.2, with much heavier fixing in cyclonic regions. Asbestos cement roofs fall under the work health and safety asbestos regulations, with licensed removal above set quantities; pressure cleaning of asbestos roofs is banned in several states.
- United Kingdom. BS 5534 governs slating and tiling for pitched roofs; lead sheet work follows the industry's rolled lead manual and BS EN 12588. Renovating a large part of a roof is a controlled service under the Building Regulations, and Approved Document L requires the thermal performance to be upgraded where more than half of the element is renovated. Listed and conservation-area roofs carry material constraints.
- United States. International Building Code Chapter 15 governs roof assemblies, with Section 1512 setting when a roof may be re-covered over an existing one; asphalt shingles follow ASTM D3462 and wind uplift ratings; hail resistance is rated under UL 2218. Insurers increasingly set the replacement point for shingle and metal roofs through age-based underwriting.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Date and extent of the last re-roofing or sectional replacement, with invoice or warranty.
- Roof maintenance and gutter cleaning records.
- Leak register and any leak investigation report.
- Hazardous materials register entries for roof sheeting, felts and mastics.
- Roof plan showing penetrations, plant, solar and the safety system.
- Product and coating specification for metal roofs.
- Insurance roof inspections and storm claims.

pages.title: Roof Safety Systems
pages.question: How do roof safety systems fail, how do you judge whether a roof can be safely accessed, and what findings stop access?
pages.answer: Roof safety systems fail first on paper: anchors and lines past their inspection date cannot be used, however sound they look. Physically, anchors pull from thin sheeting, corroded purlins and soft membranes; static lines lose tension; a deployed energy absorber means the system has been shock loaded. The commonest real gap is coverage: plant and gutters near unprotected edges or fragile roof lights. Guardrails and walkways come before harness systems everywhere.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof safety systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fall arrest anchors, static lines, access walkways

sources.title: Managing the risk of falls at workplaces

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Roof safety systems let people reach and work on roofs without falling: anchor points, horizontal static lines, guardrails and edge protection, walkways and platforms, fixed ladders and stairs, roof hatches, and protection over fragile surfaces. They are how an owner meets the duty to provide safe access for maintenance of the roof, gutters, plant and façade, and they are only useful if they are certified, inspected, matched to the work that needs doing, and backed by a rigging plan.

All three jurisdictions apply the same order of control: avoid work at height where possible; prevent falls with collective measures that need no user skill (guardrails, walkways, platforms, covers); then use work restraint, which stops a person reaching the edge; and only then fall arrest, which stops a fall after it starts. Fall arrest needs trained users, enough clearance below the anchor, and a rescue plan, because a person suspended in a harness must be recovered quickly.

| Component | What it does | Typical forms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-point anchors | Attachment point for restraint or fall arrest | Cast-in or through-bolted to concrete; purlin-mounted on metal roofs; clamp-on to standing seam; deadweight on membranes |
| Horizontal static lines | Continuous attachment along a route | Stainless cable with terminal anchors, intermediates and an energy absorber |
| Guardrails | Collective edge protection | Fixed through the roof, clamped to parapets or standing seams, or freestanding counterweighted |
| Walkways and platforms | Safe route over the roof; protection over fragile areas; level standing at plant | Aluminium or GRP grating on supports; with handrails at edges |
| Fixed ladders and stairs | Access between levels | Caged ladders, ladders with vertical lifelines or rails, ship ladders, stairs |
| Roof hatches | Access from inside to the roof | Hatch with handholds, guardrail around the opening on the roof |
| Fragile surface protection | Prevent falls through roof lights and sheets | Mesh under sheets, covers, guardrails around |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stainless anchors and static lines | 20 to 30 years | Fixing substrate; coastal exposure; certification |
| Galvanised anchors | 15 to 25 years | Coastal exposure |
| Energy absorbers | Replace after any deployment; otherwise with the system | Shock loading |
| Fixed guardrails | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; fixings through the roof |
| Freestanding guardrails | 20 to 30 years | Counterweight and feet condition; movement |
| Aluminium walkways | 25 to 40 years | Supports; slip resistance |
| Fixed ladders | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion of rungs and fixings |

What shortens life:

- Lapsed inspection, which makes a sound system unusable on the day it lapses.
- Roof works: re-roofing or membrane replacement that disturbs or removes anchors and does not recertify them.
- Coastal and industrial exposure on fixings and lines.
- Substrate deterioration: anchors into corroded purlins or thin sheeting, or deadweights on deteriorated membranes.
- Plant added without extending the system.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Lapsed inspection and certification

Anchors, static lines and fall arrest equipment must be inspected by a competent person at set intervals, and some must be proof-load tested on installation and when disturbed. A system past its inspection date cannot lawfully be used. This is the commonest failure, and it gives no physical sign.

### Anchorage failure

Anchors are only as strong as what they are fixed to. Anchors fixed only to roof sheeting, or to purlins that have lost section, can pull out under a fall; clamp-on anchors loosen on standing seams that have moved; deadweight anchors slide on wet or soft membranes and are only rated for specified roof slopes and surfaces. Through-fixed anchors leak and corrode at the penetration.

### Static line faults

Cable tension falls, intermediates detach, terminations corrode, and energy absorbers deploy after a shock load. A deployed absorber means the system has arrested a fall or been overloaded and must be withdrawn until replaced and recertified.

### Fall clearance and swing

A fall arrest system needs enough clear distance below the anchor for the lanyard, the absorber, the harness stretch and the person's height. Anchors placed too far back from an edge create a swing fall into the building or the ground; anchors too low leave insufficient clearance on low roofs. These are design faults visible only on a site plan.

### Coverage gaps

Plant, gutters, roof lights and roof edges that need maintenance lie outside the reach of the system, or require a worker to pass an unprotected edge to reach it. Plant added after the system was designed is the usual cause.

### Guardrail and walkway faults

Guardrails are too low, lack mid-rails or toe boards, or have loose fixings; freestanding guardrails shift on membranes; walkways lose slip resistance and their supports damage the membrane; ladders corrode and lose rungs; hatches lack handholds or protection around the opening at the top.

### No system

Many older buildings have no roof safety system at all, and their roofs are reached by ladder over the gutter.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From aerial imagery

- Guardrails, walkways and anchors visible; plant, gutters and roof lights close to edges with no edge protection.
- Fragile roof lights with no mesh, covers or guardrails.
- Roof hatch location and whether a guardrail surrounds it.

### On the roof

- Inspection tags: current, overdue or missing on each anchor and line.
- Rigging plan displayed at the roof access point showing anchors, routes and restrictions.
- Corrosion at anchors, terminations and fixings; slack static lines; deployed energy absorbers.
- Guardrail heights, mid-rails, toe boards and fixings; freestanding guardrail feet and weights.
- Ladder rungs, cages or lifelines; hatch handholds and opening protection.
- Anchor positions relative to edges, plant and roof lights.

### In the records

- Anchor register with each item's location, type, installation date and inspection history.
- Installation certificates, load test records and design documentation.
- Rigging plan and rescue plan.
- Contractor permits and safe work method statements for roof access.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you find | What it means | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tags overdue or missing | System cannot be used | Last inspection date against the required interval |
| Energy absorber extended or indicator showing | System has been shock loaded | Indicator; withdraw from use |
| Anchors fixed to sheeting only | Anchorage capacity doubtful | Installation records; inspection of fixing |
| No rigging plan at the access point | Users cannot use the system correctly | Absent or out of date against the current roof |
| Plant or gutters near an edge outside the system's reach | Coverage gap | Site plan against maintenance needs |
| Anchors set back from an edge with a long drop | Swing fall or clearance problem | Fall clearance calculation |
| Anchors removed or covered after re-roofing | System disturbed | Re-roofing date against recertification records |

> A roof safety system is assessed against the work done on the roof. A clean, certified system that does not reach the plant that is serviced every quarter is still a finding.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant, gutters or roof lights maintained regularly at an unprotected edge or fragile surface; deployed absorber still in service | safety | Stop access until protection is in place; withdraw shock-loaded components |
| Anchors or lines uncertified, failed, or disturbed by roof works | failure | No use until recertified or replaced |
| Periodic inspection due | deadline | At least every 12 months under AS/NZS 1891.4; as required in Britain and the United States |
| Corrosion without failure; loose guardrail fixings; worn walkways | condition | Repair in the near term |
| System at the end of its service life | lifecycle | Replace, usually with re-roofing |
| No system on a roof that needs maintenance access; coverage unknown after plant changes | check | Access assessment and design |
| Minor wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A competent height safety inspector inspects; a height safety engineer designs new systems and assesses coverage.

- Records review: anchor register, certificates, load tests, rigging plan.
- Item-by-item inspection of anchors, lines, guardrails, walkways, ladders and hatches, with pass or fail recorded and tags updated.
- Proof load testing of anchors where the standard requires it, on installation and after disturbance.
- Coverage assessment: every item that needs maintenance mapped against the system, with routes from the access point.
- Fall clearance check for fall arrest anchors.
- Substrate check: purlins, decks and membranes under anchors.

The report should give a site plan with every item and its status, the next inspection date, coverage gaps, and a recommended design hierarchy for new work.

- Access procedures: contractor permits, inductions and the record of who accesses the roof and why.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Recertify items that pass inspection.
- Replace failed anchors, deployed absorbers and corroded components.
- Collective protection first: guardrails at edges near plant and gutters, walkways to plant, platforms at plant, covers or guardrails around roof lights.
- Extend or redesign anchor and line systems to reach all maintained items, with restraint preferred over arrest.
- Ladders and hatches: replace corroded ladders, add ladder safety systems, add guardrails and handholds at hatches.
- Rigging and rescue plans updated and displayed.
- Coordinate with re-roofing so systems are reinstated and recertified.

- Signage at access points stating the system, its limits and the rigging plan.
- Equipment compatibility: confirm users' lanyards and connectors suit the installed system.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a recurring cost per item. Replacement is priced per anchor, per metre of static line or guardrail, per metre of walkway, and per ladder or hatch. New systems are lump-sum design-and-install items. Re-roofing usually carries a line for reinstatement and recertification.

Inspection, recertification and new systems are code compliance; replacement at end of life is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Preparing and updating the rigging plan is a small lump sum each time the system or roof changes.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The model work health and safety regulations and the Safe Work Australia code of practice on managing the risk of falls set the duty and the hierarchy; AS/NZS 1891.4 requires anchors and fall arrest equipment to be inspected by a competent person at intervals not exceeding 12 months; AS/NZS 5532 covers single-point anchor devices and AS 1657 fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders.
- United Kingdom. The Work at Height Regulations 2005 set the duty and hierarchy, including identification and protection of fragile surfaces; BS 7883 covers the design, installation and inspection of anchor systems, BS EN 795 anchor devices, and BS 8610 anchor system specification.
- United States. OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D governs walking-working surfaces in general industry, with 1910.28 setting where fall protection is needed (including rules for work on low-slope roofs by distance from the edge), 1910.29 guardrails and ladder safety systems, and 1910.140 personal fall protection; fixed ladders over 24 feet must have ladder safety or personal fall arrest systems, with cages phased out by 2036; 1910.27 requires rope descent anchorages to be inspected annually and certified at least every ten years; 1926 Subpart M covers construction work; ANSI/ASSP Z359 sets fall protection standards.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Anchor register and inspection certificates with dates.
- Installation certificates and load test records.
- Rigging plan and rescue plan.
- Records of re-roofing and plant changes since the system was installed.
- Contractor access procedures for the roof.

- Training records for people who use fall arrest systems.
- Plant maintenance schedules showing who accesses the roof and how often.

pages.title: Roof Structure
pages.question: How do roof structures fail, what are the warning signs, and when is a sagging or altered roof dangerous?
pages.answer: Roof structures fail from water, alteration and added load. Pitched cut roofs spread at the eaves when ties are missing or a heavier covering goes on: the ridge dips and wall tops crack and lean out. Trusses fail where webs are cut or plates back out. Cold-formed purlins corrode along gutter lines and buckle under added plant. RAAC planks can fail suddenly. A gap between ceiling and internal walls that opens seasonally is usually truss uplift, not a structural defect.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof structure; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Primary framing (trusses, rafters), substrate, sarking

sources.title: Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC) panels: investigation and assessment

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
The roof structure carries the covering, the plant and services on and under it, wind and snow, and in some buildings ceilings and people. It includes the primary framing (trusses, rafters, portal frames, beams, slabs), secondary members (purlins, battens, ceiling joists), bracing and tie-downs that resist wind uplift and racking, and the connections between them.

| Form | Where it is found | Critical points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cut timber roof: rafters, ridge, purlins, collar ties, ceiling joists | Houses before about 1970; heritage stock | Rafter spread where ties are missing; decay at wall plates; heavier re-covering |
| Nail-plated timber trusses | Australian houses and low-rise from the 1970s; widespread elsewhere | Nail plates backing out; webs cut by trades; bracing and tie-downs |
| Steel portal frame with cold-formed purlins | Industrial and logistics; retail sheds | Purlin corrosion at eaves and gutters; bolted connections; bracing; overload by plant |
| Steel trusses | Older industrial, institutional and commercial | Corrosion at bearings and gutters; riveted connections |
| Concrete roof slab | Apartments and offices | Waterproofing over it; deflection; reinforcement corrosion; plant loads |
| Precast and lightweight planks, including RAAC | Britain especially, 1950s to 1990s; some elsewhere | Low bearing, cracking, moisture; reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete can fail with little warning |
| Timber and steel decks to flat roofs | Commercial and residential flat roofs | Decay or corrosion from leaks; deflection causing ponding |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Structure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber roof framing, dry | 80 to 120 years and more | Leaks, condensation, termites and borers |
| Nail-plated trusses | Life of the building if dry and unaltered | Moisture at plates; alterations |
| Steel portal frames | 50 to 80 years | Coatings; corrosion at bases and eaves |
| Cold-formed purlins | 30 to 60 years | Coating mass; condensation; coastal exposure; gutter leaks |
| Concrete roof slabs | 60 to 100 years | Membrane maintenance; cover; chlorides |
| RAAC planks | Designed for 30 years and now past it | Moisture; bearing length; cracking |

What shortens life:

- Water: leaking coverings, gutters and membranes, and condensation in unventilated roofs.
- Alterations: webs and braces cut for ducts and loft conversions, chimney breasts removed below, hatches cut through members.
- Added load: plant, solar arrays, water tanks, heavier replacement coverings, hung services and storage on ceiling joists.
- Termites and borers in timber in Australia, and furniture beetle and death-watch beetle in old British oak and softwood.
- Coastal exposure on purlins, cleats and bolts.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Roof spread

A pitched cut roof pushes outward at the eaves under load. Ceiling joists or collar ties restrain it; where they are missing, too high, poorly fixed or removed, the rafters spread, the ridge drops and the tops of the walls are pushed out. Re-covering a roof designed for slate with heavier concrete tiles is a common trigger.

### Truss defects

Nail plates back out where timber shrinks and gets wet; webs cut by trades take a member out of the truss; missing or loose bracing lets trusses lean; tie-downs that do not reach the wall frame fail under uplift. Truss uplift, where bottom chords bow up seasonally with moisture changes, opens a gap between ceilings and internal walls; it is common and usually not structural.

### Decay and insect attack

Timber at wall plates, valleys, box gutter lines and under leaks decays; termites attack from the ground up through walls into the roof; borers attack sapwood. Decay concentrates at bearings, where loss of section is most serious.

### Steel corrosion

Purlins and cleats corrode at the eaves and along box gutter lines, under translucent sheets and where condensation drips. Portal frame bases corrode where they sit in wet ground or are buried by raised floor levels. Section loss in cold-formed purlins, which are thin to start with, quickly reduces capacity.

### Overload and instability

Plant, solar arrays and tanks added without checking the structure overload purlins and slabs. Cold-formed purlins buckle sideways when their bridging or fly bracing is removed or never installed. Ponding from blocked gutters loads light roofs past capacity.

### Concrete slab deterioration

Roof slabs deteriorate when their membrane fails: water and chlorides reach the reinforcement, which corrodes and spalls the soffit. Long-term deflection causes ponding, which accelerates membrane failure.

### RAAC

Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete planks are light, weak and permeable. With moisture, cracking, short bearings or corroding reinforcement they can fail suddenly. Where present they are a structural safety matter regardless of appearance.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Ridgeline dipping or roof plane sagging between trusses or rafters.
- Walls bowing out at eaves level; cracks at the top of external walls near the corners.
- Plant, solar arrays and tanks added on roofs; ponding.

### In the roof space

- Nail plates lifted; webs or braces cut or missing; trusses out of plumb.
- Decay at wall plates, valleys and under leaks; termite workings and mud leads; borer holes and frass.
- Rafters spreading at the wall plate; collar ties or ceiling joists detached.
- Corrosion of purlins, cleats and bolts; buckled or twisted purlins.
- Hung services, storage and water tanks on ceiling joists.

### Inside the building

- Ceiling cracks along the line of the wall plate; gaps between ceilings and internal walls (truss uplift).
- Spalling and rust staining on concrete roof slab soffits; deflection.
- In industrial buildings, purlins visibly sagging or twisted, rust along gutter lines.

### In the records

- Truss design certificates and layouts; structural drawings.
- Engineering for plant, solar and tanks added to the roof.
- Termite inspection and treatment records.
- Records of re-covering, alterations and loft conversions.
- RAAC surveys where the building is of the relevant era and type.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ridge dipped, walls pushed out at the eaves, cracks at wall tops | Roof spread | Rafter feet moved on the plate; ties missing or detached; heavier covering |
| Roof plane sagging between supports | Undersized or overloaded rafters or purlins | Covering weight; member sizes; added loads |
| Gap between ceiling and internal walls, opens and closes seasonally | Truss uplift | Trusses sound; movement seasonal; bottom chord bow |
| Ceiling cracks along the wall line on top floors | Truss uplift or roof spread | Spread if walls lean out; uplift if seasonal and walls plumb |
| Purlins twisted or buckled near plant | Overload or missing bracing | Plant added; bridging missing |
| Corrosion along the box gutter line | Gutter leaks | Staining continues to the gutter above |
| Rust staining and spalls in lines on slab soffits | Reinforcement corrosion from membrane failure | Membrane defect above; cover low |

> Additions to a roof need a structural check before they go on, not after. Plant, solar arrays and tanks on light steel and timber roofs are a common cause of overload, and the roof can look normal until it is not.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visible sag with cracking, buckled purlins, RAAC with cracking or moisture, decayed bearings, active termite damage to members | safety | Prop or restrict use now; engineer within days |
| Rafter spread pushing walls; corrosion with section loss; overload from added plant | failure | Strengthen or relieve load now |
| Cut webs or missing bracing; corrosion without section loss; decay in non-critical members | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Coatings on steel portal frames and purlins at age | lifecycle | Recoat on cycle |
| Plant or solar added with no engineering on record; possible RAAC; termite risk with no inspection | check | Structural assessment or inspection first |
| Truss uplift gaps; minor surface rust | nil | Monitor; cosmetic repair with flexible details |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads, with a timber pest inspector for timber roofs in termite areas.

- Roof space inspection of all accessible members, connections, bearings and bracing.
- Level survey of ridges and roof planes; plumb of walls at eaves.
- Section measurement on corroded steel; probing of timber for decay.
- Load assessment of existing and proposed plant, solar and tanks against capacity.
- Concrete testing of slab soffits: cover, carbonation, chlorides.
- RAAC identification and assessment to the Institution of Structural Engineers guidance where planks may be present.
- Timber pest inspection to AS 4349.3 in Australia.

- Moisture readings in timber at bearings and under leaks.
- Tie-down inspection in cyclonic regions.
- Deflection measurement under plant against design limits.

Sampling is weighted to bearings, valleys, box gutter lines and areas under plant, where decay, corrosion and overload concentrate.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restore ties and bracing: new collar ties or ceiling ties, steel straps, reinstated bracing and webs.
- Strengthen members: sister rafters and purlins, add purlins, steel plates on trusses.
- Replace decayed members and treat for termites with a management system.
- Steel repair: treat and recoat, replace corroded purlins and cleats.
- Support plant on independent frames bearing on primary structure.
- Concrete repair of slab soffits after fixing the membrane.
- RAAC: propping, additional bearing, or replacement of the planks.
- Tie-down upgrade in high wind regions, often at re-roofing.

- Bracing and bridging for cold-formed purlins.
- Propping as an interim measure while strengthening is designed.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Engineering assessment is a lump sum. Repairs are itemised per member or connection; strengthening and plant frames are lump sums; purlin replacement is by length and usually done with re-roofing. Termite management recurs annually. RAAC remediation is a lump-sum project with propping as an immediate cost.

Strengthening for added loads is code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; recoating steel is lifecycle; the assessment is the check line that sizes everything else.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 1684 for timber framing, AS 1720.1 for timber structures, AS 4440 for nail-plated trusses, AS 4100 and AS/NZS 4600 for steel, and AS/NZS 1170 for actions; termite management follows AS 3660.1 and inspections AS 4349.3.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document A and the Eurocodes (BS EN 1995 for timber, BS EN 1993 for steel, BS EN 1991 for actions) apply; the Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on identifying and assessing RAAC, and the government has published guidance for building owners.
- United States. International Building Code Chapters 16 (loads), 22 (steel) and 23 (wood), with ASCE 7 for actions and ANSI/TPI 1 for trusses; the International Existing Building Code governs alterations and added loads.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Structural drawings and truss certificates.
- Engineering for plant, solar arrays and tanks on the roof.
- Termite inspection and treatment records.
- Records of re-covering, alterations and loft or roof-space conversions.
- RAAC survey for buildings of the relevant type and era.
- Leak history, since leaks drive most decay and corrosion.

pages.title: Sanitary & Drainage Systems
pages.question: How do sanitary plumbing and drains fail, and how do you tell a blockage from a defect?
pages.answer: Drainage fails by roots, ground movement and corrosion. Roots enter clay joints and crack pipes; ground movement displaces joints and leaks undermine footings; cast iron stacks corrode from inside along the crown; pitch fibre collapses. Repeated blockages at one place mean a defect, which CCTV finds. Wet area waterproofing fails at wastes and junctions. Missing backflow protection lets sewer surcharge flood basements.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sanitary & drainage systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Pipework, fixtures, fittings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Sanitary and drainage systems carry waste water from fixtures to the public sewer: sanitary fixtures (toilets, basins, sinks, showers, urinals), traps, above-ground pipework and stacks, vents that protect trap seals, in-ground drainage, inspection openings and access chambers, and the connection to the sewer. Wet area waterproofing in bathrooms and showers is included because its failure presents as a drainage problem. Stormwater drainage, trade waste and pumped systems have their own pages.

| Material | Typical era | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron | Before about 1970 in all three countries; later in some US buildings | Internal corrosion, especially at the crown of horizontal pipes; cracking; joint failure |
| Galvanised steel waste | Mid twentieth century | Corrosion and blockage |
| Vitrified clay with mortar or rubber joints | Below ground, before about 1980 | Root intrusion and joint displacement; cracking |
| Asbestos cement | Below ground and stacks, mid century | Cracking; hazardous on removal |
| Pitch fibre (Orangeburg in the US) | Below ground, 1950s to 1970s | Deforms and collapses |
| uPVC and HDPE | From the 1970s | Long-lived; joints and supports; noise |

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron stacks and drains | 50 to 75 years | Water chemistry; hydrogen sulphide |
| Clay drains | 50 to 100 years if undisturbed | Trees; ground movement |
| Pitch fibre drains | Past life wherever found | Replace |
| PVC drains | 50 years and more | Ground movement; installation |
| Sanitary fixtures | 20 to 40 years | Use; vandalism; style |
| Tapware and cisterns | 10 to 20 years | Water quality; wear |
| Wet area membranes | 15 to 25 years | Installation; movement |

What shortens life:

- Tree roots seeking water through joints in clay and older pipes.
- Ground movement from reactive clays, settlement and nearby excavation.
- Fats, oils, wipes and debris flushed into the system.
- Hydrogen sulphide corroding cast iron and concrete from inside.
- Poor wet area waterproofing installed with the building.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Root intrusion and joint failure

Roots enter through joints in clay and older pipes, grow into mats that catch debris, and crack and displace pipes as they thicken. Joints displaced by ground movement leak into the ground, undermining foundations and paving, and let roots in.

### Cast iron corrosion

Cast iron corrodes from the inside, worst along the crown of horizontal pipes where hydrogen sulphide gas collects, and along the invert where water runs. Pipes crack lengthwise and leak in ceilings and walls; many mid-century apartment buildings are now replacing cast iron stacks.

### Collapse and deformation

Pitch fibre pipes deform into ovals and collapse; asbestos cement and clay crack under load or ground movement. Collapsed drains cause blockages, leaks into the ground and subsidence.

### Blockages

Fats, wipes, sanitary products and debris block drains, especially at bellies (sags) where water and solids sit. Repeated blockages at the same place usually point to a defect in the pipe.

### Venting failures

Vents protect trap seals from being siphoned. Blocked, removed or undersized vents let traps empty, bringing sewer gas and odour into the building; air admittance valves fail closed or open.

### Wet area leaks

Bathroom and shower waterproofing fails at floor wastes, wall-floor junctions and around penetrations; water soaks into floors and walls, rots timber, corrodes steel, and leaks into the floor below. In apartment buildings it is among the most common defects.

### Sewer surcharge and backflow

When the public sewer surcharges in heavy rain, sewage can back up into the lowest fixtures. Overflow relief gullies and backflow valves protect against this; where they are missing or below floor levels set incorrectly, basements and ground floors flood with sewage.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Pipe materials in risers, ceilings and plant rooms; cracks and rust on cast iron.
- Odour of sewer gas in bathrooms and corridors.
- Slow drains and gurgling fixtures.
- Damp, stained or swollen skirtings and floors around showers and toilets.
- Cracked tiles and failed grout at shower floors.
- Wet patches, subsidence or lush growth over drain runs outside.
- Inspection openings and chambers: accessible, covers intact.

### In the records

- CCTV drain surveys.
- Blockage and plumber call-out history by location.
- Defect claims for wet areas.
- Sewer authority correspondence.
- As-built drainage drawings.

- Repeated plumber visits to the same stack or drain run, recorded by unit or tenancy.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated blockages at the same place | Root intrusion, belly or collapse | CCTV survey |
| Sewer gas odour in a bathroom | Dry trap, failed vent or cracked pipe | Smoke test |
| Leaks from ceilings under bathrooms | Wet area membrane failure or pipe leak | Flood test; dye test |
| Cast iron stacks leaking along their length | Internal corrosion | Inspection; pipe section |
| Sewage in the basement in heavy rain | Sewer surcharge without backflow protection | Event timing; relief gully levels |
| Subsidence over drain lines | Leaking or collapsed drain undermining soil | CCTV |

> Repeated blockages are a symptom, not the problem. A CCTV survey of the drain is cheaper than a year of call-outs.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sewage leaking into occupied spaces; sewer gas in occupied rooms; no backflow protection in flood-prone basements | safety | Rectify now |
| Collapsed drains; blocked stacks; wet area leaks damaging structure | failure | Repair now |
| Root intrusion, corrosion, displaced joints | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Cast iron and clay at end of life; pitch fibre | lifecycle | Plan replacement or relining |
| No CCTV; repeated blockages of unknown cause | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed plumber or drainage contractor leads; a hydraulic engineer joins for larger buildings, stack replacement programmes and where drainage is implicated in subsidence.

- CCTV survey of in-ground drains and the main stacks, with each defect coded to the industry system (WSA 05 in Australia, the MSCC in Britain, NASSCO PACP in the United States), located by distance and depth, and recorded on a plan.
- Smoke testing of stacks and vents to locate leaks, dry traps and the source of sewer odours.
- Dye and flood testing of bathrooms and showers to separate membrane failure from pipe leaks.
- Cast iron sampling: remove a short section from representative stacks to measure remaining wall thickness, which sets the replacement horizon for the whole building.
- Backflow review: levels of overflow relief gullies and the lowest fixtures against the sewer, and the presence of backflow valves.
- Fixture survey for condition, water efficiency and accessibility.

The report should give the condition of each drain run and stack with defects located, the cause of recurring blockages, wet area findings, backflow risk, and options for relining, repair or replacement.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Relining drains and stacks with cured-in-place liners, which avoids excavating under slabs and opening finishes in occupied apartments, provided the host pipe is still round and continuous.
- Patch repairs at isolated defects such as a single displaced joint or root entry point.
- Excavation and replacement where drains have collapsed, are badly displaced, or are pitch fibre.
- Root management: cutting and jetting as interim measures, followed by relining or replacement to stop recurrence.
- Stack replacement in apartment buildings, programmed riser by riser with temporary arrangements for residents.
- Wet area rectification: strip tiles and screed, re-waterproof with correct falls, upturns and waste flanges, and retile.
- Vent repairs, including replacement of failed air admittance valves.
- Backflow protection: overflow relief gullies at the right level and backflow valves on low fixtures.
- Fixture replacement with water-efficient fittings, reducing water use and sometimes drain loading.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
CCTV surveys and smoke tests are lump sums per building or per run. Relining is priced by length and diameter; excavation and replacement by length and depth, with surface reinstatement (paving, landscaping, slabs) often the largest part. Stack replacement is priced per stack or per floor, with access through apartments and making good of finishes. Wet area rectification is priced per bathroom. Blockage clearing is reactive maintenance whose frequency tells you where capital is needed.

Replacement and relining are lifecycle; patch repairs and clearing are repairs and maintenance; backflow protection and wet area rectification can be code compliance or defect items.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3500.2 governs sanitary plumbing and drainage, including overflow relief gullies; AS 3740 governs wet area waterproofing in houses and the National Construction Code in other buildings; plumbing is licensed and certified; wet areas are a leading strata defect.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document H governs drainage; BS EN 12056 covers gravity drainage inside buildings and BS EN 752 drains outside; private sewers transferred to water companies in 2011 changed responsibility for shared drains.
- United States. The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes govern drainage; some regions require sewer lateral inspection and repair on sale or renovation; NASSCO sets pipeline condition coding.

- Ownership. In all three jurisdictions the boundary between owner and utility responsibility matters: in Australia the sewer connection point and boundary trap; in Britain, the 2011 transfer of private sewers and lateral drains to water companies; in the United States, private laterals up to the main. Strata and condominium buildings treat stacks and shared drains as common property, while fixtures and wet areas within units are often the owner's.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- CCTV drain surveys with coded defect reports and plans.
- Blockage and plumber call-out history by location.
- Wet area defect claims, flood test results and rectification records.
- As-built drainage drawings and sewer connection details.
- Sewer authority or utility correspondence, including lateral inspection notices.
- Records of relining, stack replacement or excavation repairs.
- Cast iron wall thickness test results where stacks are cast iron.

pages.title: Sealants & Joints
pages.question: How do façade sealant joints fail, how do you read a failed joint, and when does it need a programme rather than patching?
pages.answer: Sealants are the shortest-lived element on most façades and set the weathertightness of every panel and window. Read the failure: sealant peeled clean from one face is an adhesion problem from preparation; a split down the middle is over-extension or age; a skin of substrate pulled off means the substrate is weaker than the sealant. Original sealant on a panel façade past 15 years is due for a full programme, whatever it looks like from the ground.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sealants & joints; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Structural, weather, and expansion joints

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Sealant joints are the weathertight line between every panel, every window frame and every movement joint in a façade, and between the façade and the roof, balconies and podium. A joint is designed to move: panels expand and contract with temperature, frames deflect under wind, and concrete structures shorten. The joint is a system of a sealant bead, a backing rod that sets its depth and shape, and a bond breaker so the sealant sticks only to the two sides of the joint and not to the back.

| Type | Typical use and era | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polysulphide | Precast and curtain wall joints, 1950s to 1980s | Durable when young, hardens with age; early products in some buildings contain PCBs |
| Oil-based mastic and butyl | Older window perimeters and glazing | Hardens and cracks; low movement capacity |
| Polyurethane | Concrete and precast joints from the 1970s | Good adhesion to concrete; UV sensitive; can soften or chalk |
| Silicone | Glazing, curtain wall, panel joints from the 1970s | Excellent UV and movement durability; can stain porous stone; does not take paint |
| Hybrid (silyl-modified polymer) | General façade use from the 2000s | Paintable, good adhesion; durability between polyurethane and silicone |
| Acrylic | Internal and low-movement joints | Low movement capacity; not for exposed movement joints |
| Preformed seals and gaskets | Curtain walls, expansion joints, precast | Compression seals; life set by material and compression set |
| Fire-rated sealants | Joints in fire-separating walls and floors, slab edges | Part of the fire separation; tested as a system |

Joint geometry decides life as much as product.
