A good movement joint has a bead roughly half as deep as it is wide, an hourglass profile thinner at the centre, adhesion on two faces only, and a width sized for the movement the joint must take. Joints made too narrow, too deep, or bonded to the back (three-sided adhesion) fail early whatever the product.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Sealant | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silicone on well-designed joints | 15 to 25 years | Joint design; surface preparation; exposure |
| Polyurethane | 8 to 15 years | UV exposure; joint movement |
| Hybrid polymer | 10 to 20 years | Product grade; exposure |
| Polysulphide | 15 to 25 years originally; most surviving examples are past life | Age-hardening |
| Acrylic | 5 to 10 years in exposed positions | Not a façade movement sealant |
| Preformed compression seals | 15 to 25 years | Compression set; UV |

What shortens life:

- Exposure: north and west elevations in Australia, south and west in the northern hemisphere, and any elevation with heavy wind-driven rain.
- Poor joint design: joints too narrow for the movement, beads too thick, no backing rod or bond breaker.
- Poor preparation: dust, release agents on precast, old sealant residue, wet or cold substrates, missed primer.
- Incompatibility between new sealant and old, or between sealant and coatings, gaskets or stone.
- Horizontal joints that hold water, and joints at the bottom of sloped surfaces.
- Patching new sealant over old, which bonds to the old bead rather than the substrate.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Adhesive failure

The sealant peels away from one face of the joint, leaving a clean substrate. It is caused by poor surface preparation, missing primer, contamination such as precast release agents or old sealant residue, or a substrate that was wet or dusty at installation. Adhesive failure usually starts early in the life of the joint and appears along long runs.

### Cohesive failure

The bead splits along its middle while staying bonded to both faces. It means the joint has moved more than the sealant can take, the bead is too thin at its centre, or the sealant has aged and lost elasticity. Cohesive failure late in life is the expected end of a well-installed joint.

### Substrate failure

The sealant stays intact but pulls a skin of concrete, render or stone off the joint face. The substrate is weaker than the sealant, often because a high-modulus sealant was used on a weak or carbonated surface.

### Hardening and surface breakdown

UV and heat drive out plasticisers and break down the surface. The bead hardens, crazes and cracks, loses the ability to stretch, and eventually splits at the first big movement. Polysulphides and older polyurethanes harden most; silicones least.

### Three-sided adhesion

Without a bond breaker or backing rod, sealant bonds to the back of the joint as well as its sides. It cannot stretch, so it tears at the first opening of the joint, often within a few years.

### Staining and compatibility

Some silicones bleed fluid into porous stone and concrete, leaving a dark band either side of the joint. Dirt pick-up darkens soft sealants. Incompatible sealants soften, discolour or fail to cure when applied over or next to another product.

### Hazardous content

Polysulphide and some other sealants applied from the 1950s to about 1980 may contain polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), which also migrate into adjacent concrete and masonry. Removal is then a hazardous materials operation.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Dark staining or efflorescence below joints; streaking down panels from horizontal joints.
- Sealant in several colours and ages, which means patching rather than a programme.
- Visible gaps at panel corners and window perimeters; daylight through joints from inside.

### Close up on site

- Gaps between sealant and substrate along one face (adhesive failure) or splits down the centre of the bead (cohesive failure).
- Crazing, chalking, cracking and hardness: an aged bead does not spring back when pressed.
- Bead dimensions: very thin or very thick beads, sealant smeared over the face rather than in the joint.
- Sealant bonded to old sealant rather than the substrate; patching over failed joints.
- Fluid staining on stone and concrete beside silicone joints.
- Fire-rated joints at slab edges and through walls: missing, gapped or replaced with non-rated material.

### Inside the building

- Damp, staining and mould at window heads, sills and reveals, and on the inside of external walls at joint lines.
- Leaks that worsen in wind-driven rain and recur after local patches.

### In the records

- Date of the last sealant programme and the product used; no programme on a panel façade older than 15 years is itself a finding.
- Leak log by elevation and location; repeated patching at the same spots.
- Hazardous materials register entries for sealants on buildings of the PCB era.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
Where a joint has failed tells you why. Look at which face the sealant has left, and whether the substrate came with it.

| What you see | Cause | What it means for the remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sealant peeled cleanly from one face | Adhesive failure: preparation, primer or contamination | New sealant needs full removal of old material, cleaning and priming; test adhesion before the programme |
| Split down the middle, bonded both sides | Cohesive failure: over-extension or ageing | Check joint width against movement; if the joint is too narrow, a different sealant or joint design is needed |
| Sealant intact, skin of substrate pulled off | Substrate failure | Lower-modulus sealant; substrate repair; possibly a bridge seal over the joint |
| Hard, crazed bead with fine cracks | Age and UV | Full replacement on cycle |
| Torn across the back as well as split | Three-sided adhesion | Reinstate backing rod or bond breaker in the new joint |
| Failure concentrated on one or two elevations | Exposure | Programme can be staged by elevation |
| Failure everywhere within a few years of a programme | Workmanship or product | Warranty claim; test adhesion; review specification |

> A joint that looks intact can still have lost adhesion. Pull a tab of sealant by hand at a sample of joints before deciding a façade is sound; adhesion loss is often only visible when tested.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed fire-rated joints at slab edges or through fire-separating walls | condition | Repair with a tested system in the near term; it is a fire compliance item |
| Failed joints with water entering and damaging finishes, fixings or framing | failure | Repair now; locate leaks by water testing |
| Widespread adhesive or cohesive failure with no damage yet | condition | Programme replacement in the near term, by elevation |
| Original sealant past 15 years on a panel or precast façade, no programme on record | lifecycle | Full programme due; test a sample to confirm timing |
| Sealants on a building of the PCB era with no hazardous materials survey | check | Test before any removal; sets the method of the programme |
| Isolated failures at a few joints | nil | Local repair in routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer or sealant consultant leads, using rope access or building maintenance units for close access.

- Close-up survey of a representative sample of joints on every elevation, recording failure mode, hardness, bead size and the percentage of joint length failed.
- Adhesion testing by the hand pull method in ASTM C1521 at a sample of joints on each elevation and substrate.
- Joint measurement: width, depth and movement, compared with the movement capacity of the proposed product.
- Compatibility and adhesion test patches of the proposed sealant on each substrate, left to cure and pulled before the programme starts.
- PCB sampling of sealants on buildings of the 1950s to 1980 era before any removal.
- Water testing where leaks are being traced.

The report should state the sealant type and age, failure mode and extent by elevation, adhesion results, joint geometry problems, any hazardous content, and a specification and staging for the programme.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Cut out and replace: remove the old sealant completely, clean and prime the faces, install a new backing rod and bond breaker, and apply and tool new sealant to the right profile. This is the standard programme.
- Bridge or overband seals: a preformed silicone strip bonded over the joint where the old sealant cannot be fully removed, the joint is too narrow, or the substrate is weak.
- Joint redesign: widen joints that are too narrow for their movement, or change to a lower-modulus product.
- Fire-rated joints: replace with a tested system matched to the joint width, movement and required rating.
- Hazardous sealants: removal under a hazardous materials method, including treatment of contaminated adjacent substrate.

Interactions: sealant programmes share access with façade inspections, glazing work and cleaning, and are most economical when combined; adjacent coatings may need to be renewed at the same time.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Survey and testing are a lump sum with rates per test. Sealant replacement is measured by linear metre of joint by joint type, with bridge seals and fire-rated joints priced separately. Access is usually the dominant cost on multi-storey façades. PCB removal adds containment, disposal and substrate treatment.

The programme recurs: a façade resealed today will need it again within one to two decades on exposed elevations. It is coded as lifecycle; patching is repairs and maintenance; fire-rated joint repairs are code compliance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Fire-rated joints follow the National Construction Code with fire resistance tested to AS 1530.4 and installed to AS 4072.1; façade sealants are specified to the ISO 11600 classification of movement capability. On strata buildings, façade joints are common property and a frequent sinking-fund omission.
- United Kingdom. BS 6213 guides the selection of construction sealants, BS 6093 the design of joints, and BS EN ISO 11600 classifies sealants by movement capability; fire-stopping falls under Approved Document B. On leasehold blocks a sealant programme is a service-charge item subject to section 20 consultation.
- United States. ASTM C920 specifies elastomeric joint sealants, ASTM C1193 guides their use and ASTM C1472 the calculation of joint movement; ASTM C1521 sets the adhesion test. The EPA publishes guidance on PCBs in caulk in buildings built or renovated between 1950 and 1979. Façade ordinances record sealant condition as part of each examination.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Date, extent, product and contractor of the last sealant programme, and its warranty.
- Façade inspection reports noting joint condition by elevation.
- Leak log and maintenance log.
- Façade specification naming sealants, coatings and panel finishes, for compatibility.
- Hazardous materials register, including any PCB testing.
- Fire-stopping records for slab edges and fire-separating joints.

pages.title: Service Corridors
pages.question: How do back-of-house service corridors fail, and why are they a fire safety concern?
pages.answer: Service corridors are often required exits, yet they become overflow storage for pallets, stock and bins, and exit doors are locked for security. Trolleys gouge walls and damage low services; overhead pipes leak unnoticed; waste spills bring pests into tenancies. Blocked exits and locked exit doors are fire safety breaches; mark no-storage zones, provide storage elsewhere, and protect walls and services at trolley height.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about service corridors; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, utility integration, safety systems

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Service corridors are the back-of-house routes that connect loading docks, kitchens, plant rooms, waste rooms, stores and tenancies out of public view. They carry trolleys, pallets, waste and staff, and overhead they usually carry the building's services. In shopping centres and many commercial buildings, they are also the required fire exits from tenancies, so they must stay clear even though they are used as overflow storage. Functionally a service corridor must allow goods and people to move safely, protect the services above it, keep fire separation and exits intact, and stay secure from the public.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor | Sealed concrete, vinyl or epoxy | Trolley and pallet jack traffic; spills; cleaning |
| Walls and protection | Blockwork or plasterboard with corner guards and rails | Impact damage |
| Doors | Fire doors, tenancy back doors, security doors | Fire separation; security; egress hardware |
| Overhead services | Ducts, pipes, cable trays, sprinkler mains | Leaks; impact; access |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Utility lighting | Visibility; egress |
| Signage | Exit signs, tenancy identification | Egress and deliveries |

Because they are out of public view, service corridors are a reliable indicator of how well a building is really managed, and inspectors often go there first.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor coatings | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; spills; cleaning |
| Wall protection | 10 to 20 years | Impact |
| Fire and security doors | 15 to 25 years; hardware sooner | Abuse; traffic |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Damage |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Overflow storage from tenants and operations.
- Trolley and pallet jack impact on walls, doors and services.
- Spills from waste and kitchens.
- Neglect because the public never sees them.

Back-of-house corridors are refurbished far less often than public spaces, so their condition often lags the rest of the building by a decade or more. Their fitness depends more on management than on materials: a corridor in poor repair but kept clear is safer than a freshly painted one full of pallets.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Blocked exits

Pallets, stock, bins and equipment left in service corridors narrow or block the exits that tenancies and staff rely on in a fire. In shopping centres this is one of the most common fire safety breaches found by inspectors.

### Fire door abuse

Doors along service corridors are propped for deliveries, damaged by trolleys and fitted with security locks that do not release, compromising both fire separation and escape.

### Impact damage

Walls, corners, door frames and low services are struck by trolleys, pallet jacks and bins; sprinkler pipes and ducts damaged at low height leak or fail.

### Service leaks

Pipes, drains and ducts overhead leak into the corridor; because few people see the space, leaks run for a long time.

### Hygiene and pests

Waste spills, food residue and damp floors attract pests that then move into tenancies and kitchens.

### Security

Back doors left open, broken locks and unmonitored access let the public and intruders into back-of-house areas.

### Lost access to services

Overhead valves, dampers and cable trays above service corridors are reached by ladder from the corridor; when stock, racking or tenant equipment occupies the space, maintenance becomes difficult and isolations in an emergency are slow.

### Odour and ventilation

Waste, kitchen exhaust leakage and poor ventilation make service corridors smell, and odours migrate into tenancies and public areas through doors and gaps.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Pallets, stock and bins in corridors; exits partly or fully blocked.
- Fire doors propped or damaged; security locks on exit doors.
- Gouged walls and broken corner guards at trolley height.
- Leaks and staining from overhead services.
- Spills, odour and pest evidence.
- Dark sections; failed emergency lights and exit signs.

### In the records

- Fire safety inspection findings and orders.
- Incident records.
- Pest control reports.
- Security incident logs.

- Trolleys, cleaning machines and waste bins parked permanently in the corridor.
- Valves and isolation points obscured by stored goods or racking.
- Unauthorised people in back-of-house areas.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridors used as stores | Insufficient storage for tenants or operations | Storage provision review |
| Doors damaged at trolley height | No protection or poor door selection | Inspection |
| Pests in tenancies near the corridor | Waste spills and gaps in corridor walls | Pest reports |
| Exit doors locked | Security concerns overriding egress | Security review |

> Service corridors that serve as exits must stay clear and openable. Storage in exit corridors is a fire safety breach, not a housekeeping issue.

Recurrent problems in one section usually point to a particular tenant or operation; problems throughout point to a building-wide shortage of storage or poor management. Matching problems to users decides whether the fix is a lease enforcement or a building change.

Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exits blocked; exit doors locked; fire doors propped | safety | Clear and rectify now |
| Leaks or service damage | failure | Repair now |
| Fire safety inspections due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Impact damage; hygiene; poor lighting | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Finishes and protection at end of life | lifecycle | Renew |
| Egress role of corridors not documented | check | Review |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Because service corridors are often exits, findings about storage and doors are graded as safety even when the corridor is in poor condition otherwise; condition items can wait, egress cannot.

Repeat breaches by the same tenant are a management finding as well as a safety one.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a fire safety consultant and the centre or facilities manager.

- Corridor walk at operational times: storage, door positions, damage, leaks, hygiene, lighting and security.
- Egress review: which corridors are required exits, their widths, and the hardware on exit doors.
- Fire door and security interface test.
- Services survey overhead for leaks, damage and access.
- Storage demand review with tenants and operators.

The report should list egress breaches, damage and a management and works plan.

- Use mapping: who uses each corridor, for what and when, including delivery and waste schedules.
- Access to services check: whether isolation valves, dampers and boards can be reached quickly.
- Hygiene and pest review with the pest control contractor.

Inspections at different times of day show the true condition: corridors are often cleared for audits and refilled afterwards.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Clear exits and mark no-storage zones on floors and walls, with regular checks and enforcement through leases.
- Provide storage elsewhere so corridors are not used for it.
- Impact protection: corner guards, buffer rails and door protection plates at trolley height, and guards for low services.
- Door hardware: fire doors with hold-open devices where deliveries require, and security locks that release on alarm.
- Durable finishes: sealed or epoxy floors and washable walls.
- Leak repair and drip protection.
- Pest proofing and waste management.

- Lease enforcement: clauses requiring tenants to keep corridors clear, with notices and recovery of clearance costs.
- Ventilation improvements to remove odours.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Management measures are low cost. Impact protection and door hardware are itemised. Floor coatings by area. Corridor works are usually done out of hours. Safety items are code compliance; finishes and protection are lifecycle.

Impact protection installed once is cheaper than repeated repairs to walls, doors and services. Clearing and enforcement is an operating cost, partly recoverable from tenants. Finishes are renewed on long cycles because the space is out of public view. Fire safety orders for blocked exits can bring penalties and closures far costlier than providing storage.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets egress requirements, and fire safety inspections by councils and fire services commonly find blocked back-of-house exits in shopping centres; retail leases can make tenants responsible for keeping corridors clear.
- United Kingdom. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires escape routes to be kept clear; the responsible person must manage back-of-house routes.
- United States. NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code require exit access to be kept clear and exit doors openable; fire marshals inspect.

In all three countries, fire services and building authorities can issue orders and fines for obstructed exits, and in serious cases close premises until they are cleared. Insurers may treat repeated egress breaches as poor risk management. Retail and commercial leases commonly give landlords the right to clear obstructions and recover costs from tenants, but only if the clauses are used.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire safety inspection reports and any orders.
- Egress drawings identifying exit corridors.
- Lease clauses on back-of-house use.
- Incident and security logs.
- Pest control reports.

- Delivery and waste schedules.
- Notices issued to tenants for obstructions.
- Records of clearance costs recovered.
- Building management plan for back-of-house areas.

pages.title: Skylights, Dormers & Glazed Atria
pages.question: How do skylights, roof sheets and atrium roofs fail, and when are they a safety hazard?
pages.answer: Roof lights are first a fall-through hazard and second a weathertightness item. Polycarbonate and fibreglass sheets yellow and become brittle with UV and cannot bear a person at any age; an unprotected roof light on a roof people walk on is a safety finding regardless of condition. Leaks come from kerb flashings and atrium seals at the bottom of slopes. Overhead glass must hold together when broken; older atria with monolithic toughened or wired glass may not.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about skylights, dormers & glazed atria; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Framing, glazing, seals, flashings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
This element covers every opening in a roof that lets in light, and the structures built up from the roof plane to do it: in-plane translucent sheets in profiled roofs, framed and domed skylights on kerbs, roof windows, patent glazing, glazed atrium roofs, lanterns, and dormers.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-plane polycarbonate or fibreglass sheets | Industrial and warehouse roofs | Fragile: fall-through; UV embrittlement |
| Domed acrylic or polycarbonate on kerbs | Commercial flat roofs, schools | Embrittlement; kerb flashings |
| Roof windows | Houses and loft conversions | Flashings; seals; condensation |
| Patent glazing | Older industrial, stations, institutions | Bars corroding; wired glass; seals |
| Glazed atrium roofs | Shopping centres, offices, institutions | Overhead glass; seals; structural steel |
| Lanterns | Heritage buildings | Timber decay; leaded joints |
| Dormers | Houses and heritage stock | Cheeks, flashings and support |

Overhead glass must hold together when broken. Codes require laminated glass, or toughened glass with a protective screen, in sloped and overhead glazing. Older atria often have wired glass or monolithic toughened glass that would not meet that requirement now.

Era and use shape what to expect. Warehouses and factories from the 1960s onward carry in-plane fibreglass and later polycarbonate sheets, often in regular runs across the roof, and many of them sit in asbestos cement roofs of the same era. Schools and commercial flat roofs carry domed acrylic or polycarbonate skylights on timber or metal kerbs. Shopping centres of the 1980s and 1990s carry large atrium and mall roofs of patent glazing or curtain wall sections. Victorian and Edwardian buildings carry lanterns and patent glazing with lead or putty seals.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polycarbonate sheeting | 10 to 20 years | UV protection grade; exposure |
| Fibreglass sheeting | 15 to 25 years | Resin and gel coat |
| Acrylic domes | 15 to 25 years | UV; impact |
| Atrium framing | 30 to 50 years | Coatings; drainage |
| Atrium seals and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | UV; movement |
| Roof windows | 25 to 40 years | Flashings; hardware |
| Dormers | With the roof; cheeks and flashings 30 to 50 years | Cladding and flashings |

What shortens life:

- UV: polycarbonate and fibreglass yellow, craze and become brittle.
- Hail and impact.
- Poor kerb and flashing details.
- Condensation on cold frames and glass.
- Debris on atrium roofs blocking gutters.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Fragility and fall-through

Translucent roof sheets and skylights cannot take a person's weight, and polycarbonate becomes more brittle as it ages. Falls through fragile roofs and roof lights are a leading cause of deaths in roof work in all three jurisdictions. An unprotected roof light on any roof that people walk on is a hazard regardless of condition.

### UV embrittlement

Polycarbonate and fibreglass yellow, haze and lose strength; fibreglass loses its surface and exposes fibres. Light transmission falls.

### Kerb and flashing leaks

Kerbs that are too low, flashings that are lapped the wrong way, and sealant-only details leak. In-plane sheets leak at laps with the adjacent metal where profiles do not match or fixings fail.

### Seal and gasket failure in atria

Atrium glazing leaks at gaskets, pressure plates and glazing bar joints, often at the bottom of slopes where water collects.

### Overhead glass failure

Monolithic toughened glass in overhead positions can break spontaneously and fall. Wired glass cracks from rusting wire and thermal stress. Laminated glass stays in place.

### Dormer failure

Dormer cheeks, sills and flashings leak; timber decays; dormers added in conversions can lack adequate support from the roof structure.

### Condensation

Single-glazed skylights and uninsulated aluminium frames are the coldest surfaces in the roof. In humid spaces (pools, kitchens, bathrooms, crowded malls) condensation forms on them, runs down and drips, and is often mistaken for a leak. Thermally broken frames and insulated glazing reduce it.

### Atrium structure

Atrium roofs are carried on steel or aluminium frames that are themselves exposed to water from failed seals and condensation. Corrosion at gutters and bearings, and movement of the supporting structure, load the glazing and open joints.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From aerial imagery

- Number and layout of roof lights; discoloured, yellowed or patched sheets.
- Roof lights without mesh, covers or guardrails on roofs with plant or walkways.
- Debris and staining on atrium roofs.

### On the roof

- Yellowing, crazing and brittle surfaces; cracks at fixings.
- Kerb height and flashing condition; sealant-only details.
- Gasket shrinkage and pressure plate condition on atrium glazing.
- Glass type markings on overhead glass.

### Inside the building

- Leak staining around skylights and along atrium glazing bars.
- Condensation drips from frames.
- Cracked or broken overhead panes.

### In the records

- Product data and non-fragility certificates.
- Glass schedule for atria; replacement records.
- Leak logs.
- Fall protection installation records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yellow, hazy roof sheets | UV embrittlement | Age; brittle surface |
| Leaks around a skylight kerb | Kerb flashing detail | Water test |
| Leaks at the bottom of atrium slopes | Gasket or pressure plate failure | Seals shrunk; water test |
| Drips from frames in cold weather, no rain | Condensation | Cold frames; humid space |
| Cracked overhead pane with no impact | Thermal stress, wire corrosion or nickel sulphide | Glass type and fracture pattern |

> Treat every roof light and translucent sheet as fragile unless a certificate shows otherwise. Age makes them weaker, not stronger.

Fracture patterns in overhead glass follow the same reading as in vertical glazing: a pair of small fragments at a point of origin inside toughened glass points to a nickel sulphide inclusion; a single crack meeting the edge at right angles points to thermal stress; cracks radiating from a point point to impact. In wired glass, cracks starting at the edge with rust staining mean the wire has corroded where the edge was not sealed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unprotected fragile roof lights where people work; overhead glass that is not laminated over occupied areas, with breakage history | safety | Protect now: mesh, covers, guardrails or restrict access |
| Leaks damaging interiors | failure | Repair now |
| Embrittled sheets; seals at end of life | condition | Replace in the near term |
| Roof lights at age | lifecycle | Replace on cycle, usually with the roof covering |
| Overhead glass of unknown type in an atrium | check | Identify glass type |
| Minor discolouration | nil | Clean |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A roofing surveyor inspects from safe access; a façade engineer inspects atrium glazing.

- Inventory of every roof light with type, size, condition and protection.
- Fragility assessment from product data.
- Glass identification in atria and overhead glazing.
- Water testing of kerbs and glazing joints.
- Structural inspection of atrium framing.

The report should give a roof light inventory with type, fragility, protection and condition; atrium glass types and any non-laminated overhead glass; leak paths found by testing; and the protection needed before anyone next works on the roof.

- Light transmission and discolouration readings where daylight performance matters.
- Atrium structure inspection of steel, gutters and bearings from access equipment.
- Incident review: falls and near misses on the roof.

Every roof light is recorded, not a sample, because one unprotected fragile sheet is enough to cause a fall.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Protection: safety mesh under sheets, covers or guardrails around skylights, walkways that avoid them.
- Replacement with non-fragile rated products.
- Kerb rebuild with proper flashings.
- Atrium reglazing with laminated glass and new seals.
- Dormer repair: new flashings, cheeks and support.

Interactions: roof light replacement on industrial roofs is usually done with the roof covering, and with asbestos cement roofs it is part of the licensed removal; atrium reglazing needs protection and closures below; protection works are often the cheapest and most urgent part of any roof light scope.

- Kerb upstands raised to current heights with new flashings.
- Interim covers and exclusion zones where replacement is delayed.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is priced per unit or by area; protection per unit or by length of guardrail. Access dominates. Atrium reglazing is a lump-sum project with protection to the floor below.

Fall protection is code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Safety mesh, covers and guardrails are inexpensive per roof light and should not wait for replacement. Atrium reglazing needs protection decks or scaffolds over occupied floors and out-of-hours work, which often exceed the cost of the glass. Industrial roof lights are usually replaced in the same contract as the roof covering, with licensed asbestos removal where the surrounding sheeting contains it.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4285 covers skylights; AS 1288 overhead glazing; the work health and safety regulations and the Safe Work Australia code of practice on falls require fragile surfaces to be protected.
- United Kingdom. The Work at Height Regulations 2005 require fragile surfaces to be identified and protected; the Advisory Committee for Roofsafety publishes the standard test for non-fragility (ACR[M]001); BS 5516 covers sloped glazing.
- United States. International Building Code Section 2405 covers sloped glazing and skylights; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.28 and 1926.501 require skylights to be protected by covers, guardrails or screens.

In Britain, the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require fragile surfaces to be identified to anyone working on the roof. In strata and leasehold buildings in all three jurisdictions, roof lights over individual dwellings may belong to the dwelling while the roof is common property, which decides who pays.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Product data and non-fragility certificates.
- Glass schedules for atria.
- Leak logs.
- Fall protection installation and inspection records.

- Records of any falls or near misses on the roof.
- Hazardous materials register for adjacent roof sheeting.
- Atrium maintenance and cleaning records.

- Asbestos register for surrounding roof sheeting.
- Atrium structural inspection records.

pages.title: Slab on Ground
pages.question: How do ground slabs and warehouse floors fail, and which defects matter?
pages.answer: Fine shrinkage cracks are normal. What matters is movement and joints: curled panel edges rock and break under forklifts; open joints lose their arrises; fill settles and clay moves, dishing slabs and tilting racking; moisture rising through slabs without vapour barriers destroys new flooring. Never cut a slab before scanning for post-tensioning tendons. Warehouse floors must also be judged against the flatness the current racking and forklifts need.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about slab on ground; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Structural condition, joints, surface integrity

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A slab-on-ground is a concrete floor cast directly on prepared ground, usually over a vapour barrier and compacted fill. In houses it is often also the footing, stiffened with edge and internal beams. In warehouses and industrial buildings it is a heavy-duty working surface carrying racking, forklifts and stored goods, with joints to control cracking and surface tolerances set for the equipment that runs on it.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stiffened raft and waffle pod slabs | Australian houses on reactive clays | Edge movement; cracking; termite entry at penetrations |
| Conventional slab with thickenings | Houses and low-rise | Settlement of fill; shrinkage cracking |
| Post-tensioned slab | Houses on expansive soils in the US; some commercial | Tendons must not be cut; corrosion at anchorages |
| Industrial floor slab, jointed | Warehouses, factories, retail | Joint damage from wheels; curling; flatness |
| Jointless steel-fibre slab | Modern warehouses | Random cracking; flatness |
| Older slabs without vapour barriers | Pre-1970s buildings | Moisture through the slab; rising damp; flooring failure |

Warehouse floors are increasingly specified for flatness because very narrow aisle forklifts and tall racking need level surfaces; a floor that was fine for its original use can be inadequate for a new tenant's equipment.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete slab | Life of the building | Ground movement; load; moisture |
| Industrial joints and arrises | 10 to 25 years | Wheel traffic; joint design |
| Joint sealants and fillers | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; movement |
| Vapour barrier | Life of the slab if intact | Damage at construction |
| Floor hardeners and coatings | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; chemicals |

What shortens life:

- Hard-wheeled forklifts crossing open joints, which break the edges.
- Loads beyond design: heavier racking, point loads, storage.
- Soil movement beneath the slab: reactive clay, fill settlement, leaking pipes.
- Moisture rising through slabs without vapour barriers.
- Chemicals: acids, sugars and oils attacking concrete surfaces.

The slab itself outlasts almost everything on it; the joints, surface and the ground beneath decide how long it stays serviceable for its use.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Shrinkage cracking

Concrete shrinks as it dries. Fine random cracks and cracks at re-entrant corners are normal; they matter only if they widen, displace or let water and termites through.

### Curling

Slabs dry faster at the top than the bottom, so panel edges lift (curl). Joints then rock under traffic, break down and crack the slab beneath the curled edge.

### Joint deterioration

Forklift wheels hammer open joints, breaking the arrises (edges); sealants fail; load transfer dowels are missing or ineffective so panels move independently. Broken joints damage forklifts and goods and become trip hazards.

### Settlement and heave

Poorly compacted fill settles; reactive clay shrinks and swells; leaking under-slab pipes soften the ground. Slabs crack, dish or dome, and pull away from walls.

### Moisture and flooring failure

Moisture vapour rising through slabs without vapour barriers, or with damaged ones, debonds adhesives, swells timber and blisters vinyl and epoxy coatings. It is a common cause of flooring failure when old slabs get new finishes.

### Post-tensioned tendon damage

Tendons in post-tensioned slabs carry very high forces. Drilling or cutting into them during alterations can release them violently and weaken the slab; anchorages corrode where water reaches them.

### Surface deterioration

Dusting, scaling and delamination of weak or poorly finished surfaces; chemical attack in food and industrial plants; abrasion in heavy-traffic aisles.

### Termite entry

In termite regions, cracks, slab edges and service penetrations are hidden entry routes for subterranean termites into wall framing.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Crack pattern: fine random, at re-entrant corners, along a line, or widening and displaced.
- Joints: broken arrises, rocking panels, failed sealant, trip edges.
- Floor levels: dishing, doming, steps; racking out of plumb.
- Damp patches, efflorescence and blistered or debonded floor finishes.
- Gaps between slab and walls; skirtings lifting.
- Termite mud tubes at slab edges and penetrations.

### In the records

- Slab design and loading, including racking and forklift loads.
- Flatness specifications and surveys.
- Post-tensioning drawings.
- Floor finish failure history.
- Termite inspection records.

- Forklift operators avoiding certain joints or aisles, and goods damaged in transit across the floor, which are early operational signs of joint failure.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fine random cracks, no displacement | Drying shrinkage | Pattern; age; stability |
| Panel corners rocking at joints | Curling | Level survey across joints |
| Broken joint edges in forklift aisles | Wheel impact on open joints | Joint width; forklift wheel type |
| Slab dished near the centre or edges dropping | Settlement or clay shrinkage | Level survey; soil investigation |
| Floor finish blistering or debonding | Moisture vapour through the slab | In-situ relative humidity testing |
| Racking leaning | Floor out of level or settlement under baseplates | Survey |

> Never drill, core or saw a slab until the absence of post-tensioning tendons and embedded services has been confirmed by drawings and scanning. Cutting a tendon is dangerous and weakens the slab.

Cracks that widen, displace or step across their length are moving; cracks that stay hairline and even are not. Gauge studs across a few representative cracks for several months settle the question.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip edges in walkways; settlement under racking causing lean; damaged post-tensioning | safety | Isolate area and fix now |
| Slab broken up in operational aisles | failure | Repair now |
| Joint deterioration; curling; moisture-driven flooring failures | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Joint sealants and surface treatments at end of life | lifecycle | Renew on cycle |
| Slab capacity or flatness unknown for a new use | check | Survey and assess |
| Fine shrinkage cracks | nil | Seal where needed |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural or pavement engineer, with a flooring specialist for moisture problems.

- Crack and joint mapping across the floor.
- Level and flatness survey against the tolerance the use requires.
- Joint condition: arris damage, load transfer, rocking under load.
- Moisture testing by in-situ relative humidity probes before new flooring.
- Cores for thickness, strength and reinforcement.
- Scanning by ground-penetrating radar for tendons and services before cutting.
- Under-slab services: CCTV and pressure testing where leaks are suspected.
- Load assessment against racking and equipment loads.

The report should give the condition, flatness and capacity against the use, causes of distress, and repair options.

- Joint movement monitoring with gauges where panels appear to be moving, to separate curling from settlement.
- Termite inspection at slab edges, penetrations and expansion joints in termite regions.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Joint repair: rebuild broken arrises with polymer or epoxy mortars, install steel armoured joints in heavy-traffic aisles, and fill with semi-rigid fillers.
- Curl correction: grout under lifted panels and grind high edges.
- Crack repair by routing and sealing or epoxy injection.
- Slab lifting and stabilisation by grout or polyurethane injection.
- Grinding and toppings to restore flatness.
- Moisture mitigation with surface membranes before new flooring.
- Local replacement of broken panels.
- Termite management at slab edges and penetrations.

- Load management: relocate heavy racking or point loads away from weak areas, add baseplates to spread loads, or restrict loads until strengthening.
- Coatings and hardeners renewed in chemical and abrasion zones to protect the surface.
- Under-slab pipe repair by relining or rerouting above the slab, avoiding breaking out the floor.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Joint repairs are priced by linear metre; armoured joints by length; panel replacement by area; grinding and toppings by area; moisture membranes by area. In operating warehouses, out-of-hours work and racking relocation add significantly.

Joint and surface renewal are repairs and maintenance or lifecycle; tenant-driven flatness upgrades sit with the tenancy; safety fixes are immediate.

Repairs timed around tenant shutdowns or between leases are usually far cheaper than work in a fully operating warehouse.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 2870 governs residential slabs and AS 3600 concrete structures; Concrete Institute and CCAA guides cover industrial floors; AS 3660.1 covers termite management at slab edges and penetrations.
- United Kingdom. The Concrete Society's TR34 sets industrial floor design and flatness; BS 8204 covers screeds; BS EN 1992 concrete design.
- United States. ACI 360 covers slabs on ground and ACI 302.1 floor construction; PTI publishes design of post-tensioned slabs on expansive soils; ASTM F2170 sets in-situ moisture testing.

In all three jurisdictions, warehouse leases commonly specify the floor loading and flatness a tenant may rely on, and fit-out works that cut or core the slab need engineering approval. Racking installers and operators also have safety obligations for racking on uneven or damaged floors under workplace safety law, which can force floor repairs at short notice.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Slab design, loading and flatness specification.
- Post-tensioning drawings.
- Flatness and level surveys.
- Floor finish failure history.
- Termite inspection records.
- Racking and forklift specifications.
- Previous repair records.

- Lease clauses on floor loading and flatness.
- Racking inspection reports noting floor issues.
- Records of coring, cutting or slab penetrations.

pages.title: Smoke Management Systems
pages.question: How do smoke management systems fail, and how do you know they will keep escape routes clear?
pages.answer: Smoke systems fail as systems, not components. Interfaces to the fire alarm and AHUs break, so fans do not start or AHUs feed the fire floor. Pressurised stairs drift too high (doors cannot be opened) or too low (smoke enters) as doors, seals and relief dampers change. Exhaust systems lose make-up air. Fans and dampers that run only in tests seize. Only an integrated test proves the system.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about smoke management systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Stair pressurisation, smoke spill fans, smoke curtains

sources.title: NFPA 92 Standard for Smoke Control Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Smoke management systems keep escape routes clear of smoke and give fire-fighters usable access. Smoke, not flame, kills most people in building fires, so these systems are central to life safety in tall, large and complex buildings. They include stair and lift shaft pressurisation; smoke exhaust from atria, malls and large spaces; zone smoke control using the air conditioning in fire mode; car park smoke exhaust and jet fan systems; smoke curtains and smoke doors; natural smoke vents (automatic opening vents in residential corridors and stairs); and the fire fan control panel and fire-rated wiring that run them.

| System | Where it is found | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair pressurisation | Tall buildings in Australia, Britain and the US | Fans push air into stairs so smoke cannot enter when doors open |
| Zone smoke control | Offices with central air conditioning | Fire floor exhausted, adjacent floors pressurised, using AHUs in fire mode |
| Atrium and mall smoke exhaust | Shopping centres, atria, large halls | Fans or vents remove smoke from high level to keep a clear layer above people |
| Car park smoke and heat exhaust | Enclosed car parks | Ducted exhaust or jet fans move smoke to exhaust points |
| Smoke curtains | Atria, lift lobbies, shopfronts | Fabric barriers that drop on alarm to contain smoke |
| Automatic opening vents (AOVs) | Residential corridors and stairs, especially in Britain | Vents open on alarm to release smoke |
| Fire fan control panel | Buildings with mechanical smoke control | Manual override for fire-fighters, status indication |

Smoke systems are designed together with the building: door positions, leakage paths, air make-up and the fire detection cause-and-effect. Changes to any of these (new doors, new seals, enclosed atria, altered AHUs) can stop a system working as designed even though every fan runs.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke exhaust and pressurisation fans | 20 to 25 years | Rarely run; motor and bearing condition |
| Smoke dampers and actuators | 15 to 20 years | Rarely operated; seize |
| Fire fan control panels | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Smoke curtains | 15 to 20 years | Fabric; motors; batteries |
| AOV actuators and controls | 15 to 20 years | Weather; operation |
| Fire-rated cabling | Life of the building | Damage; alterations |

What shortens life:

- Disuse: fans and dampers that run only in tests seize.
- Building changes that alter leakage and air paths.
- Controls replacement that moves fire functions onto non-fire-rated systems.
- Incomplete testing that checks components but not the system.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Interface and control failures

Smoke systems start on a signal from the fire detection system. Changes to the fire panel, BMS or AHU controls break interfaces so fans do not start, start in the wrong mode, or AHUs keep supplying air to the fire floor. Fire functions moved onto a building management system that is not designed for fire duty may not work in a fire.

### Pressure too high or too low

Pressurised stairs must hold smoke back without making doors too hard to open: Australian, British and US standards cap door opening forces, at about 110, 100 and 133 newtons respectively. New door seals, closers and lobbies raise pressures until doors cannot be opened by occupants; failed relief dampers, missing doors and new openings drop pressures so smoke enters.

### Make-up air failures

Exhaust systems need replacement air to move smoke. Make-up air paths blocked by new shopfronts, closed doors or failed inlet vents reduce exhaust to a fraction of design.

### Equipment seizure

Fans, dampers, curtains and vents operated only in tests seize, lose belts, or have motors that fail; smoke dampers corrode; curtains snag on new fittings.

### Architectural changes

Atria enclosed with new floors, malls subdivided, car parks partitioned for storage, and stair doors held open all change smoke behaviour against the design.

### Incomplete testing

Testing fans and dampers individually does not show the system works. Only an integrated test, with the fire alarm triggering the full sequence and pressures, airflows and door forces measured, does.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the building

- Fire fan control panel showing faults or manual overrides.
- Stair doors hard to open, whistling or slamming during tests.
- Smoke curtains obstructed by fittings; smoke dampers inaccessible.
- Make-up air louvres blocked; car park storage blocking jet fans.
- Fans with belts missing or corroded casings.

### In the records

- Fire engineering report and smoke control design.
- Integrated test reports, with pressures, airflows and door opening forces.
- Routine service records for fans, dampers, curtains and vents.
- Cause-and-effect matrix.
- Annual certification.

- Relief dampers in stairs stuck open or closed.
- Fire fan control panel without current labelling or zone plans.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair doors cannot be opened during a test | Pressure too high (new seals, failed relief) | Door opening force measurement |
| Smoke in stairs during a drill | Pressure too low or fans not starting | Pressure measurement; interface test |
| AHUs supply air to the fire floor in a test | Cause-and-effect fault | Integrated test |
| Atrium smoke fills too low in modelling or tests | Make-up air shortfall or enclosure changes | Airflow measurement; layout review |
| Fans run but dampers stay shut | Seized dampers or actuator failure | Damper inspection |

> A smoke system that has not passed an integrated test since the last major change to the building should be treated as unproven, even if every fan runs on its own.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System does not start on alarm; stair doors cannot be opened; stair pressurisation failed; AOVs not opening | safety | Rectify now; interim measures |
| Routine and integrated testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Fans or dampers failed | failure | Repair now |
| Equipment worn; partial interface faults | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Equipment at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No integrated test since changes | check | Integrated test |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire engineer leads, working from the fire engineering report or smoke control design, with a mechanical services engineer and the fire services contractor. Testing is done out of hours, with the fire brigade and monitoring centre notified.

- Design review: the smoke control design basis, performance criteria (pressures, airflows, smoke layer heights), cause-and-effect, and any performance solutions that rely on the system.
- Change review: every alteration since design that could change smoke behaviour or air paths, including new doors and seals, enclosed atria, subdivided malls, car park storage, and replaced AHUs or controls.
- Equipment inspection: fans (bearings, belts, motors, temperature rating), smoke dampers and actuators, relief dampers, curtains, vents, fire fan control panel, fire-rated cabling and power supplies.
- Integrated test initiated from the fire alarm in each smoke zone: confirm the full sequence starts, AHUs switch correctly, dampers move, curtains drop, vents open, and fire-fighters' overrides work.
- Measurement: stair pressure differentials with doors open and closed, door opening forces at every stair door, exhaust and make-up airflows, and car park jet fan coverage.
- Secondary power: confirm the system runs from the emergency supply where required.

The report should state whether the system meets its design performance today, list every failed function and measurement, identify changes that have compromised it, and set out rectification or redesign.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Repair interfaces and update the cause-and-effect matrix; return fire functions from general building management controls to fire-rated controls where they were moved.
- Rebalance stair pressurisation: adjust fan speed, add or repair barometric relief dampers, or add variable speed control, so pressure holds smoke back and door opening forces stay within limits.
- Restore make-up air: reopen or add inlet paths, automate inlet doors and vents, remove obstructions.
- Replace equipment: fans with temperature-rated units, seized dampers and actuators, curtain motors and batteries, vent actuators.
- Car parks: clear storage and partitions from jet fan paths; reposition or add fans.
- Redesign after major alterations, with a fire engineer revising the design and performance solution.
- Testing regime: routine component tests plus a full integrated test annually and after any change.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and integrated testing are recurring costs; integrated tests need several trades present out of hours. Interface and controls repairs are itemised or lump sums. Equipment replacement is per item, with temperature-rated fans and dampers costing more than standard equipment. Rebalancing is a lump sum. Redesign after alterations is a lump-sum fire engineering and construction project, usually carried by the alteration that caused it.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code sets smoke hazard management by building class and height (Part E2); AS 1668.1 sets the design of smoke control systems and the door opening force limit for pressurised stairs; AS 1851 sets routine service; smoke control systems are essential safety measures with annual certification; performance solutions often rely on them.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document B and BS 9999 and BS 9991 set requirements; the BS EN 12101 series covers smoke control components, including pressure differential systems in BS EN 12101-6; the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require higher-risk residential buildings to report defects in key fire safety equipment; responsible persons must keep systems maintained.
- United States. International Building Code Section 909 governs smoke control; NFPA 92 sets design and testing, with dedicated systems tested semi-annually and non-dedicated systems annually; NFPA 101 limits door opening forces; NFPA 4 covers integrated testing of fire protection and life safety systems.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fire engineering report and smoke control design, including performance solutions.
- Commissioning report and latest integrated test report, with measured pressures, airflows and door forces.
- Routine service records for fans, dampers, curtains, vents and the fire fan control panel.
- Cause-and-effect matrix.
- Annual certification.
- Records of alterations since the system was commissioned.

pages.title: Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
pages.question: How do rooftop solar systems fail, and what risks do they bring to the roof and building?
pages.answer: Solar arrays fail at their electronics and connections more than their panels. Inverters fail at 10 to 15 years and generation stops silently. Mismatched or wet DC connectors and rooftop DC isolators arc and start roof fires. Panels degrade slowly, faster with hot spots and cracks. Arrays leak at penetrations, hide the roof covering, add load, and must be removed for re-roofing. Burnt connectors or isolators mean isolate now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about solar photovoltaic (pv) systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Panels, inverters, mounting frames

sources.title: Rapid shutdown and PV requirements (NFPA 70 Article 690)

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A solar photovoltaic system generates electricity from sunlight. It comprises modules (panels) on mounting frames, DC cabling and connectors, DC isolators, inverters (string inverters, microinverters or optimisers with a central inverter) that convert DC to AC, AC connection to a switchboard, metering, monitoring, and often batteries. Systems on roofs interact with the roof covering, structure, lightning protection and fire-fighting access.

| Form | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residential rooftop with string inverter | Houses | Small; inverter is the weak point |
| Microinverters or optimisers | Houses and commercial from the 2010s | Module-level electronics on the roof; more parts, better shading performance |
| Commercial rooftop arrays | Warehouses, retail, offices | Large; penetrations or ballast on the roof; roof replacement interaction |
| Ballasted arrays on flat roofs | Commercial flat roofs | No penetrations; weight and wind uplift |
| Battery systems | Houses and commercial | Fire risk; location and separation rules |
| Building-integrated PV | Façades and canopies | Part of the envelope |

Ownership varies. Arrays may be owned outright, leased, or installed under a power purchase agreement with a third party that owns the equipment and holds rights over the roof; these arrangements constrain re-roofing and sale.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modules | 25 to 30 years, losing about half a per cent of output a year | Quality; heat; defects |
| String and central inverters | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Microinverters and optimisers | 15 to 25 years | Heat on the roof |
| Mounting frames | 25 to 30 years | Coastal exposure; fixings |
| DC connectors and isolators | 10 to 25 years | Installation quality; water ingress |
| Batteries | 10 to 15 years | Chemistry; cycling; heat |

What shortens life:

- Poor installation: mismatched connectors, cables on roof surfaces, isolators exposed to sun and water.
- Heat on inverters mounted in sun or in hot rooms.
- Coastal exposure on frames and fixings.
- Shading and soiling that cause hot spots.
- Wind on poorly fixed or ballasted arrays.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### DC connection and isolator fires

DC circuits on roofs carry high voltages that arc when a connection is poor. Mismatched connectors from different manufacturers, poorly crimped connectors, and rooftop DC isolators that take in water have caused roof fires. In Australia, rooftop DC isolators were a known fire source and are no longer mandatory under the current PV array standard.

### Inverter failure

Inverters are the commonest failure: electronics fail from heat, surges and age, typically within 10 to 15 years. A failed inverter stops generation without any visible sign on the roof.

### Module degradation and defects

Modules lose output slowly; defects accelerate it: hot spots from cell cracks or shading, potential-induced degradation, delamination, moisture ingress, junction box failures, and microcracks from hail or foot traffic.

### Roof interaction

Penetrations for mounting leak if poorly flashed; frames trap debris and water; roof coverings under arrays cannot be inspected or maintained; re-roofing requires removal and reinstatement of the array. Arrays add load the roof structure must carry, and ballasted arrays can shift in wind.

### Frame and fixing corrosion

Dissimilar metals, poor fixings and coastal air corrode frames and clamps; modules can come loose in wind.

### Battery risks

Lithium battery systems can enter thermal runaway, producing fire and toxic gases; location, separation and ventilation rules apply.

### Grid compliance and export limits

Inverters must meet grid connection standards and network settings; older inverters may not meet current requirements, and export limits may constrain output.

### Bypass diode and junction box failures

Bypass diodes in module junction boxes let current pass shaded or damaged cells; when they fail, sections of a module overheat or stop producing. Junction boxes that lose their seal let in water and can arc.

### Soiling, birds and debris

Dust, bird droppings and leaves reduce output and create hot spots; birds nesting under arrays damage cabling and block drainage on the roof below.

### Fire-fighting constraints

Arrays generate DC voltage whenever there is light, so fire-fighters cannot simply isolate them. Without rapid shutdown, labelling and clear access pathways, fire services may limit roof operations on buildings with arrays.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On the roof

- Discoloured, cracked or burnt modules; hot spots on thermal imaging.
- Cables lying on the roof surface; connectors in water.
- Burnt or discoloured DC isolators and connectors.
- Corroded frames and clamps; loose modules.
- Debris and bird nesting under arrays.
- Leaks below mounting penetrations.

### At the inverter

- Error lights and fault codes.
- Inverter in direct sun or a hot room.
- Monitoring showing zero or reduced generation.

### In the records

- Generation data against expected output.
- Installation certificates and compliance documents.
- Roof structural assessment for the array.
- Power purchase or lease agreements.
- Battery installation and compliance records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No generation; inverter fault light | Inverter failure | Error codes; monitoring |
| Output below expected | Shading, soiling, degradation or string fault | String measurements; thermal imaging |
| Burn marks at isolators or connectors | DC arcing | Inspection |
| Hot cells on thermal image | Cell cracks or shading | Thermography; electroluminescence |
| Roof leaks under the array | Mounting penetrations | Water test |

> Burnt or discoloured DC isolators and connectors are a fire hazard. The array should be isolated by a qualified person until repaired; DC wiring stays live while the sun shines.

Comparing strings tells you more than the total: one weak string points to a fault in that string; uniform decline points to soiling, degradation or the inverter.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Burnt connectors or isolators; exposed live DC; loose modules; battery overheating | safety | Isolate now |
| Inverter failed; no generation | failure | Repair or replace now |
| Degradation, corrosion, leaks | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Inverters at end of life; array at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| Roof structure not assessed; PPA terms unknown | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Clean and maintain |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A licensed solar installer or electrical engineer.

- Generation analysis against expected output for the system size, orientation and weather.
- Visual and thermographic inspection of modules, connectors, isolators, cabling and frames.
- String testing: open-circuit voltage, current, insulation resistance.
- Inverter inspection and fault history.
- Roof inspection: penetrations, covering under the array, structural capacity.
- Compliance check against grid connection and installation standards.
- Contract review: ownership, leases, PPAs.

- Electroluminescence imaging where cracks or hail damage are suspected.
- Earth fault and insulation testing of DC circuits.
- Battery inspection: location, separation, ventilation, detection and the battery management system's fault history.
- Fire service access: rapid shutdown, labelling and roof pathways where required.

The report should state generation performance against expectation, safety defects, roof and structural effects, compliance, and the remaining life of inverters and modules.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Replace connectors and isolators with matched, correctly installed parts.
- Inverter replacement.
- Module replacement for defective modules.
- Cable management off roof surfaces.
- Frame repairs and refixing.
- Cleaning.
- Array removal and reinstatement for re-roofing.
- Battery relocation or separation to meet rules.

Interactions: re-roofing under an array means removal, storage and reinstatement by a licensed installer, recommissioning, and often updating to current standards; batteries may need relocation; lightning protection must bond the array.

- Labelling and shutdown: labels for fire services and rapid shutdown where codes require it.
- Monitoring with alerts so failed inverters are found within days, not months.

- Bird proofing around array edges to stop nesting and cable damage.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inverter replacement is priced per inverter and recurs at 10 to 15 years, so it belongs in the register as a recurring line. Module replacement is per module, often limited by matching availability. Connector, isolator and cabling remediation is priced per string. Array removal and reinstatement for re-roofing is a lump sum that can be a large share of a re-roofing project and should sit in the roof line. Monitoring and cleaning recur. Batteries are replaced on their own cycle.

Inverter and battery replacement are lifecycle; DC fire-risk rectification is immediate; repairs and cleaning are repairs and maintenance. Under a power purchase agreement, many of these costs sit with the system owner, and the register should say so.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 5033 governs PV array installation, and its current edition no longer requires rooftop DC isolators; AS/NZS 4777.1 and 4777.2 cover inverter installation and grid performance; AS/NZS 5139 covers battery installation and location; installers must be accredited under the national solar accreditation scheme; network service providers set export limits and connection requirements.
- United Kingdom. BS 7671 Section 712 covers PV installations; the IET Code of Practice for grid-connected solar PV sets practice; MCS certification is needed for most incentive schemes; connection follows Engineering Recommendations G98 and G99; fire-safety guidance addresses PV on roofs.
- United States. NFPA 70 Article 690 governs PV systems, including rapid shutdown at the roof to protect fire-fighters; UL 61730 lists modules and UL 1741 inverters; IEEE 1547 sets interconnection; the International Fire Code sets rooftop access pathways and setbacks.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Installation certificates, single-line diagrams and compliance documents.
- Generation monitoring data since installation.
- Inverter, module and workmanship warranties.
- Roof structural assessment for the array.
- Ownership, lease or power purchase agreement terms, including roof access and re-roofing provisions.
- Network connection approval and export limits.
- Battery installation compliance and location records.
- Maintenance and cleaning records.

pages.title: Specialised Occupancy Areas
pages.question: How do laboratories, clinical spaces and teaching rooms fail, and which findings are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Specialised spaces fail when their critical services drift or their use changes. Fume cupboards lose containment as exhaust weakens; emergency showers go untested and deliver stagnant water; medical gas systems are altered without certification; isolation rooms lose pressure; classrooms echo and get stuffy as occupancy rises. Spaces converted to new uses without upgraded services fall short. Fume cupboard, safety shower, medical gas and ligature findings are safety-critical.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialised occupancy areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Classrooms, lecture theatres, laboratories, wards, purpose-built spaces

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Specialised occupancy areas are purpose-built spaces whose function sets demanding requirements: classrooms and lecture theatres in education buildings, laboratories in research, education and industry, and wards, treatment rooms and clinical spaces in healthcare and aged care. Each depends on services and finishes that ordinary space does not need, such as fume extraction, emergency showers, medical gases, nurse call, infection-control finishes, acoustic performance and controlled ventilation. They are judged on whether they still meet the standards of their use, which change faster than the buildings that house them.

| Space | Critical provisions | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classrooms | Acoustics, ventilation, daylight, power and AV | Noise and reverberation; stuffiness; worn finishes |
| Lecture theatres | Raked seating, AV, egress, acoustics, ventilation | Ageing AV; seating; air supply for full rooms |
| Teaching and research laboratories | Fume cupboards, exhaust, gases, emergency showers and eyewash, chemical storage, acid-resistant drainage | Exhaust performance; untested safety showers; chemical storage |
| Hospital wards and clinical rooms | Medical gases, nurse call, infection-control finishes, pressure-controlled rooms | Gas system compliance; finishes; isolation room pressures |
| Aged care rooms | Nurse call, accessible bathrooms, tempered water, falls prevention | Nurse call coverage; scalding risk; trip hazards |
| Mental health spaces | Ligature-resistant fittings and safe design | Ligature points; damaged fittings |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laboratory fit-out and fume cupboards | 15 to 25 years | Research needs; exhaust performance |
| Emergency showers and eyewash | 15 to 20 years | Testing; water quality |
| Medical gas outlets and alarms | 15 to 25 years | Compliance; clinical change |
| Nurse call systems | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Classroom refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Pedagogy; technology |
| Lecture theatre AV | 7 to 10 years | Technology |
| Clinical finishes (sheet vinyl, wall protection) | 10 to 20 years | Cleaning regimes; damage |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Changing use: new research, teaching methods or models of care that the space was not built for.
- Rising standards for safety, infection control and ventilation.
- Intensive cleaning with aggressive chemicals in clinical areas.
- Technology turnover in AV, nurse call and laboratory equipment.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Laboratory exhaust and containment

Fume cupboards must draw air in at a set face velocity to contain fumes. Exhaust fans that weaken, dampers that drift, too many cupboards on one system, and changes to room supply air reduce containment, exposing users to chemicals. Discharge stacks too low or near intakes re-entrain exhaust into the building.

### Emergency showers and eyewash

Safety showers and eyewash stations that are not run regularly deliver stagnant, contaminated or no water when needed; those with blocked paths or no tempered water are unusable in an emergency.

### Medical gas failures

Oxygen, medical air, vacuum and other gases are life-critical. Leaks, failed alarms, incorrectly labelled outlets, and works without permits create clinical and fire risks. Medical gas systems need specialist testing and certification after any change.

### Infection control

Damaged finishes, open joints in flooring, porous surfaces, and isolation rooms that have lost their pressure differentials undermine infection control in healthcare and aged care.

### Acoustics and ventilation in teaching spaces

Classrooms with long reverberation and noisy ventilation make speech hard to understand; rooms with low outdoor air become stuffy as occupancy rises, with measurable effects on learning.

### Ligature and patient safety

In mental health and some aged care settings, fittings that can be used as ligature points, and damaged or replaced fittings that reintroduce them, are serious patient safety risks.

### Change of use without upgrades

Laboratories converted from offices, wards repurposed, and classrooms subdivided without upgrading services often fall short of what the new use requires.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Fume cupboard test labels and face velocity indicators; alarms sounding or silenced.
- Safety showers and eyewash blocked, untested, or without test tags.
- Chemicals stored on benches and floors rather than in ventilated cabinets.
- Medical gas outlets, alarms and zone valves: labelling, damage, test records.
- Damaged clinical flooring and walls; open seams.
- Classrooms that echo or are stuffy when full.
- Nurse call points missing or not working; ligature points in sensitive areas.

### In the records

- Fume cupboard performance tests.
- Safety shower and eyewash test logs.
- Medical gas certification and permits.
- Isolation room pressure monitoring.
- Nurse call test records.
- Accreditation reports.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fume cupboards alarming low flow | Exhaust fan, damper or balancing problem | Face velocity and duct tests |
| Chemical odours in corridors | Exhaust re-entrainment or containment failure | Smoke tests; stack location |
| Brown water from safety shower | Stagnation from infrequent testing | Test log |
| Isolation room pressure alarms | Door seals, supply and exhaust balance | Pressure monitoring |
| Classroom complaints of noise and fatigue | Reverberation, ventilation noise or low outdoor air | Acoustic and CO₂ measurement |
