> Fume cupboards that fail containment tests, untested emergency showers, and medical gas faults are safety findings. Take the equipment out of use until tested and repaired.

Most findings in these spaces trace back either to drift in a critical service that was once right, or to a change of use the services never followed; the first needs testing and rebalancing, the second needs a design review.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fume cupboards failing containment; untested or blocked safety showers; medical gas faults; ligature points in mental health areas | safety | Take out of use and rectify now |
| Critical service failed (exhaust, gases, nurse call) | failure | Restore now |
| Statutory testing, certification or accreditation due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Worn finishes; acoustic and ventilation shortfalls | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Fit-out and specialist equipment at end of life | lifecycle | Refurbish |
| Use changed without a review of services | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer with specialists for laboratories, medical gases, acoustics or healthcare engineering, working with the users' safety officers.

- Use review: what each space is now used for against what it was designed for.
- Laboratory safety testing: fume cupboard face velocity and containment, exhaust system capacity, stack discharge, safety showers and eyewash, chemical storage and gas systems.
- Healthcare engineering review: medical gas testing and certification, isolation room pressures and air changes, nurse call coverage, infection-control finishes.
- Teaching space review: reverberation time, background noise, CO₂ in use, lighting and AV.
- Patient safety review for ligature risk in relevant settings.
- Records and accreditation review.

The report should list safety items for immediate action, compliance and accreditation status, and a refurbishment programme aligned with users' plans.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Laboratory exhaust: rebalance, replace fans, add variable air volume fume cupboard controls, raise or relocate stacks.
- Safety showers and eyewash: weekly activation, tempered supply, clear access, replacement where faulty.
- Chemical storage: ventilated, segregated cabinets and stores.
- Medical gases: repairs and certification by specialists under permit.
- Infection-control finishes: seamless flooring with coved skirtings, cleanable wall protection.
- Isolation rooms: restore pressures and monitoring.
- Teaching spaces: acoustic treatment, quieter ventilation, increased outdoor air, updated AV.
- Ligature-resistant fittings in sensitive areas.
- Refurbishment matched to the current use.

- Change-of-use upgrades: when a space is repurposed, bring its exhaust, gases, drainage, finishes and safety equipment up to the new use before occupation, not after.
- Permit systems for work on medical gases, laboratory exhaust and isolation rooms, so changes are controlled and recertified.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing and certification recur. Safety rectification is itemised per item. Laboratory and clinical refurbishments are lump sums per room or suite, usually large because of services, and constrained by the need to keep research, teaching or care going. Teaching space upgrades are per room. Specialist equipment is often owned by the user rather than the building, so ownership must be settled.

Safety and certification are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle; upgrades for a change of use sit with that change.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 2243 covers safety in laboratories and AS 2243.8 fume cupboards; AS 4775 covers emergency eyewash and showers; AS 2896 covers medical gas systems; the National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards and aged care quality standards apply; AS/NZS 2107 sets recommended acoustic levels for interiors including classrooms.
- United Kingdom. Health Technical Memoranda set healthcare engineering standards, including HTM 02-01 for medical gases and HTM 03-01 for ventilation; BS EN 14175 covers fume cupboards; Building Bulletin 93 sets acoustic design for schools and Building Bulletin 101 ventilation.
- United States. NFPA 99 covers healthcare facilities including medical gases; ANSI Z358.1 sets weekly activation of emergency showers and eyewash; ASHRAE 110 tests fume cupboard performance; ANSI S12.60 covers classroom acoustics; accreditation bodies such as The Joint Commission inspect healthcare facilities.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Fume cupboard and laboratory exhaust test records.
- Safety shower and eyewash test logs.
- Medical gas certification and permit records.
- Isolation room pressure monitoring records.
- Nurse call test and maintenance records.
- Accreditation and inspection reports.
- Acoustic and ventilation assessments of teaching spaces.

- Records of changes of use and the engineering reviews that accompanied them.

pages.title: Specialist & Non-Standard Features
pages.question: How should bespoke features such as indoor pools, saunas and cellars be recorded and assessed?
pages.answer: Specialist features are recorded so they count in a building's capital picture, but they are kept out of cohort comparisons so they do not distort benchmarks. Judge them mostly by their effect on the rest of the building: indoor pools, spas, saunas and cellars push moisture into walls and roofs; pools and aquariums overload floors; water near electrics is a hazard; bespoke systems become unrepairable when suppliers disappear.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist & non-standard features; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Genuinely unique one-off elements with no standard home \u2014 capture for completeness only; excluded from cohort convergence

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Specialist and non-standard features are the bespoke items some homes and buildings contain that do not fit any other element: wine cellars, home cinemas, indoor pools and spas, saunas and steam rooms, home lifts, safe rooms, recording studios, large aquariums, smart home systems, heritage and artistic features, and similar. In the Moyne Ross framework this element is a capture-only holding pen: items are recorded so they are counted in a building's capital picture, but they are kept out of cohort comparisons, because averaging a wine cellar or an aquarium across buildings would distort the benchmarks for everything else.

| Feature | Main risks to the building | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Indoor pools and spas | Humidity, condensation and corrosion in the building fabric; chemical storage; load | Plant, dehumidification, structure, safety |
| Saunas and steam rooms | Moisture and heat in walls and ceilings; electrical | Vapour control, ventilation, electrical |
| Wine cellars | Cooling equipment; condensation in walls | Climate control, vapour barriers |
| Home cinemas and studios | Electrical and heat load; acoustic construction | Ventilation, power |
| Large aquariums and water features | Floor load; leaks; electrical near water | Structure, leak protection |
| Home lifts | See accessibility lifts | Servicing, safety |
| Smart home and automation systems | Obsolescence; cyber; dependency on one integrator | Platform, support, documentation |
| Heritage and artistic features | Specialist repair; fragility | Significance, conservation needs |

Recording them consistently, even when rare, keeps nothing out of the building's capital story.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Feature | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pool and spa plant | 8 to 15 years | Chemicals; use |
| Sauna heaters and steam generators | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |
| Cellar cooling units | 8 to 12 years | Run hours |
| Smart home platforms | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support |
| Aquarium systems | 10 to 15 years | Maintenance |

What shortens life:

- Moisture escaping into the building fabric.
- Specialist suppliers leaving the market.
- Lack of documentation, so new owners cannot maintain features.

The life of specialist features is less predictable than ordinary elements because it depends on bespoke products, specialist suppliers and the care of each owner. Many are removed rather than replaced when they reach the end of their life, particularly when new owners do not value them.

Smart systems often age fastest.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Moisture damage to the building

The most serious risk from many specialist features is to the rest of the building: indoor pools, spas, saunas, steam rooms and cellars generate moisture that, without vapour control and ventilation, condenses in walls and roofs, rotting timber, corroding steel and growing mould.

### Structural load

Pools, spas, aquariums and heavy equipment add large loads that the floor may not have been designed for.

### Electrical and fire hazards

Water near electrical equipment, sauna heaters near combustible linings, and high electrical loads in cinemas and studios create shock and fire risks.

### Specialist obsolescence

Bespoke systems depend on specialist suppliers and integrators; when they disappear, features cannot be repaired.

### Lost knowledge

Features installed by previous owners often come without manuals or records, leaving new owners unable to maintain them safely.

### Chemical and air quality

Indoor pool chemicals and their by-products corrode metalwork, fixings and ventilation equipment and affect air quality throughout the house if the pool hall is not separated and ventilated.

### Insurance and valuation

Some features increase insurance risk or limit insurer appetite, and their effect on value varies widely: features that one buyer values, another sees as a liability.

### Occupant safety

Saunas, steam rooms and pools carry burns, slips and drowning risks; safe rooms and lifts can trap occupants without communication.

Each feature also adds maintenance burden that few owners plan for.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Condensation, mould or corrosion around pools, spas, saunas and cellars.
- Sagging or cracked floors under heavy features.
- Electrical equipment near water.
- Proprietary control panels without documentation.
- Unusual features with no records.

### In the records

- Approvals and engineering for features.
- Manuals and supplier details.
- Service records.

- Corrosion of fixings, light fittings and ventilation around pools.
- Steam or chemical odour in other parts of the house.
- Feature controls that no one in the household knows how to operate.
- Removed features with services capped and left behind.

- Dehumidifiers running constantly near the feature.

- Rust staining or efflorescence on walls next to pools and saunas.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould and rot around an indoor pool | Inadequate dehumidification and vapour control | Humidity logging; fabric inspection |
| Floor deflection under a spa or aquarium | Load beyond design | Engineering check |
| Feature cannot be repaired | Supplier gone | Supplier search |
| Tripping circuits | Electrical faults in wet areas | Electrical test |

> Record specialist features so they are counted, but judge them by their effect on the rest of the building. The fabric damage they cause usually matters more than the feature itself.

Ask first whether the feature is damaging the rest of the building; that usually matters more than the feature's own condition.

A feature's age is less telling than its surroundings.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical hazards near water; overloaded floors; pool and spa safety failures | safety | Isolate now |
| Feature failed; moisture damaging the building | failure | Repair now |
| Statutory inspections of pools or lifts due | deadline | As required |
| Condensation; ageing plant | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Feature at end of life | lifecycle | Replace or remove |
| Feature undocumented | check | Record and assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Because these features are excluded from cohort averages, their grading matters for the individual building only; the moisture, load and electrical risks they create for the building are graded the same way as any other finding.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor records and assesses each feature, bringing in specialists for pools, electrical safety, structure and building physics as needed.

- Inventory of every specialist feature with type, age, supplier, approvals and documentation.
- Building fabric check around moisture-producing features: humidity logging, moisture readings, thermal imaging and inspection of roof spaces and walls.
- Structural check of floors carrying heavy features.
- Electrical safety test of wet-area and high-load installations.
- Supplier and support check for bespoke systems.

The report should record each feature for the capital picture, state any risks it poses to the building, and recommend keep, repair, replace or remove.

Capture-only recording does not mean light assessment: the risks to the building still need checking.

Owners' knowledge of operation should be recorded too.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Moisture control: dehumidification, ventilation and vapour barriers for pools, saunas, steam rooms and cellars.
- Structural strengthening or load reduction under heavy features.
- Electrical rectification with RCD protection and separation from water.
- Documentation: compile manuals, supplier details and maintenance requirements.
- Platform replacement for unsupported smart home systems with open alternatives.
- Removal of features that cost more to keep than they are worth.

- Separation of pool halls and steam rooms from the rest of the building with sealed doors and their own ventilation.
- Safety measures: barriers, alarms, emergency stops and communication where people could be trapped or injured.
- Decommissioning with services made safe and fabric repaired.

- Monitoring: humidity and leak sensors around moisture-producing features so damage is caught early.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Costs vary widely and are bespoke: specialist servicing recurs, moisture control and strengthening are lump sums, and removal is a lump sum with making good. These items are recorded in the building's capital picture but excluded from cohort averages.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; building damage repairs are condition items.

Removal often costs less than continued repair and may add value.

Specialist servicing often requires the original supplier.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Building approval is needed for many features; pools and spas follow AS 1926 for barriers and state registration; electrical work follows AS/NZS 3000, including wet area zones.
- United Kingdom. Building regulations apply to structural, electrical and ventilation aspects; BS 7671 governs electrical installations in pools and saunas.
- United States. Local building and electrical codes apply, with NFPA 70 covering pools, spas and saunas; pool barriers follow the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code.

In all three countries, many specialist features need building approval, and features installed without it can affect insurance, sale and certification. Pools and spas carry barrier and safety rules regardless of how they are classified in the capital picture, and electrical work in wet areas is tightly regulated. Heritage features may be protected by listing.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Approvals and engineering for each feature.
- Manuals and supplier contacts.
- Service records.
- Electrical certificates.
- Records of moisture problems.

- Insurance terms affected by the feature.
- Heritage listing where relevant.
- Records of moisture or corrosion damage around the feature.
- Decommissioning records for removed features.

- Operating instructions held by the owner.

pages.title: Specialist Hydraulics
pages.question: How do pools, recycled water systems and water features fail, and which findings are life-safety issues?
pages.answer: Specialist hydraulics fails on safety before condition. Pool and spa outlets without compliant covers or with single drains can trap and drown; pool gates that do not self-close and latch defeat child barriers; chlorine and acid stored together can release gas; recycled and rainwater pipes connected to drinking taps contaminate the supply; spas and fountains grow Legionella. Shells, finishes and plant then wear on predictable cycles.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist hydraulics; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Pool filtration, recycled water systems

sources.title: Managing health and safety in swimming pools (HSG179)
Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Specialist hydraulics covers water systems beyond ordinary supply and drainage: swimming pools and spas with their filtration, heating and chemical dosing plant; rainwater harvesting and recycled or greywater systems that supply toilets, irrigation and cooling; water features and fountains; and irrigation systems. Each brings its own hazards: drowning and suction entrapment, toxic chemicals, cross-connection of non-drinking water into drinking supplies, and Legionella from aerosols.

| System | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swimming pools and spas | Apartment buildings, hotels, gyms, schools, aged care, leisure centres | Drowning, suction entrapment, chemical exposure, microbial contamination, slips |
| Pool plant rooms | With every pool | Chlorine gas from mixed chemicals, confined spaces, electrical hazards in wet areas |
| Rainwater harvesting | Houses, schools, commercial buildings | Cross-connection with drinking water; mosquitoes; contamination |
| Recycled and greywater systems | Green-rated commercial buildings, precincts with third-pipe networks | Cross-connection; treatment failure; odour |
| Water features and fountains | Lobbies, plazas, landscaping | Legionella from aerosols; slips; electrical |
| Irrigation | Landscaping, green roofs and walls | Backflow into drinking water; leaks onto membranes |

Recycled and harvested water is carried in separately identified pipes (purple or lilac in Australia and the United States, with marked pipes in Britain) and must never be connected to drinking water outlets. Most cross-connections are created years after construction by plumbers who did not recognise the pipe.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete pool shells | 30 to 50 years | Waterproofing; ground movement; chemical balance |
| Pool surface finishes (render, tiles, membranes) | 10 to 20 years | Water chemistry; maintenance |
| Pool filters | 10 to 15 years; media 5 to 10 | Backwashing; water quality |
| Pool pumps and heaters | 8 to 15 years | Chemicals; run hours |
| Chemical dosing equipment | 8 to 12 years | Corrosive environment |
| Rainwater tanks | 20 to 40 years | Material; sediment |
| Recycled water treatment plant | 15 to 20 years; membranes and lamps sooner | Maintenance; feed quality |
| Irrigation systems | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage; controllers |

What shortens life:

- Poor water chemistry in pools, which etches finishes, corrodes metalwork and damages plant.
- Corrosive plant rooms where chlorine fumes attack electrical equipment, steel and controls.
- Neglected treatment of recycled and harvested water, which lets systems foul and smell.
- Ground movement and leaking pool shells that undermine surroundings.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Suction entrapment

Pool and spa outlets with single drains, missing or broken covers, or flow rates too high for the cover can trap hair, limbs or bodies against the outlet, causing drownings and serious injuries, particularly to children. Dual drains, compliant covers and safety vacuum release systems prevent it; older pools often lack them.

### Chemical hazards

Chlorine and acid stored or dosed together, or mixed by accident during deliveries, release chlorine gas. Plant rooms without ventilation, bunding, separation of chemicals and signage put staff and the public at risk; dosing failures overdose or underdose pools.

### Microbial contamination

Pools and spas with poor filtration, disinfection or turnover grow bacteria and parasites; spas are the highest risk because of warm water and aerosols, and are a known source of Legionella.

### Cross-connection

Recycled, greywater and rainwater pipes connected to drinking water outlets, or drinking water top-up connections without backflow protection, contaminate the drinking supply. The risk grows with every later alteration.

### Pool barrier failures

Pool fences and gates that do not self-close and self-latch, gaps under or through fences, and climbable objects placed nearby defeat the barriers that prevent child drownings.

### Pool shell and finish failure

Pool shells crack and leak through ground movement and failed waterproofing; finishes etch, delaminate and loosen tiles; leaks undermine surrounding paving and structures, and on podium pools leak into car parks and plant below.

### Water features and aerosols

Fountains and water features recirculate warm water and create aerosols; without treatment and cleaning they grow Legionella and have caused outbreaks.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Pool outlet covers: present, intact, secured, compliant labels; number of drains.
- Pool fences and gates: self-closing and self-latching, heights, gaps, climbable objects nearby.
- Plant room: chemical storage separation, bunding, ventilation, smell of chlorine, corrosion of equipment.
- Pool surfaces: etching, loose tiles, cracks, water loss.
- Recycled and rainwater pipes and outlets: colour and labelling, signage at taps.
- Water features: cleanliness, slime, foam, treatment equipment.
- Staining or leaks under podium pools.

### In the records

- Pool water testing logs.
- Pool barrier compliance certificates.
- Chemical safety data and storage register.
- Recycled water validation and testing.
- Water feature Legionella management.
- Leak and repair history.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pool losing water beyond evaporation | Shell crack, plumbing leak or failed finish | Bucket test; dye test; pressure testing |
| Corroded equipment and electrical panels in the plant room | Chlorine fumes from poor storage or ventilation | Inspection |
| Cloudy water and complaints of irritation | Filtration or chemical dosing problems | Water testing; turnover check |
| Purple pipe connected to a basin or kitchen tap | Cross-connection | Dye or tracer testing |
| Gate that does not latch | Hinge or latch failure | Inspection |
| Slime and foam in water features | Inadequate treatment | Water testing |

> Missing or broken pool outlet covers and pool gates that do not self-close and latch are life-safety failures. Close the pool or spa until they are fixed.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsafe pool outlets; pool barriers failed; chemical storage able to release chlorine gas; cross-connection to drinking water; Legionella in a spa or feature | safety | Close, isolate or rectify now |
| Pool or treatment plant failed; podium pool leaking into structure | failure | Repair now |
| Pool barrier inspection or registration due | deadline | By the regulatory date |
| Worn finishes, ageing plant, corroded equipment | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Plant and finishes at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No water management plan; no barrier certificate | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A pool and aquatic specialist, hydraulic engineer and, for water quality, a water hygiene specialist.

- Pool safety inspection: outlet covers and their ratings, number and spacing of drains, safety vacuum release systems, signage, depth markings and lifesaving equipment.
- Barrier inspection against the applicable standard: height, gaps, gates, latches, non-climbable zones, and any certificate or registration requirements.
- Plant room inspection: chemical storage and segregation, bunding, ventilation, dosing controls, electrical condition, confined space status.
- Water quality review: testing logs, turnover rates, filtration performance, disinfection levels; laboratory sampling where needed.
- Leak investigation of pool shells and pipework by bucket, dye and pressure tests.
- Cross-connection survey of recycled, greywater and rainwater systems by tracing and dye testing.
- Water feature review under a Legionella risk assessment.

The report should state safety defects and immediate actions, regulatory compliance, water quality management, plant condition and remaining life, and a capital plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Outlet upgrades: compliant anti-entrapment covers, dual drains or safety vacuum release systems, and flow rates within the cover rating.
- Barrier rectification: self-closing and self-latching gates, heights and gaps fixed, climbable objects removed, and certification obtained.
- Plant room upgrades: separated and bunded chemical storage, ventilation, automatic dosing with alarms, signage and emergency procedures.
- Pool refurbishment: shell repairs, new waterproofing, finishes, tiles and coping.
- Filtration and plant replacement sized to the bather load and turnover required.
- Cross-connection removal, with backflow protection on drinking water top-ups and clear labelling.
- Treatment upgrades for recycled water systems, with validation and monitoring.
- Water feature treatment and cleaning regimes, or decommissioning.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Water testing, plant maintenance and barrier inspections recur. Outlet and barrier rectification are lump sums and usually urgent. Plant room upgrades and pool refurbishment are lump sums, with refurbishment closing the pool for weeks. Pool plant replacement is per item. Recycled water plant overhauls are lump sums with membrane and UV lamp replacement on cycles.

Safety and barrier rectification are code compliance; refurbishment and plant replacement are lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance. In apartment buildings, pools are often one of the largest sinking fund items.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Pool barriers follow AS 1926.1 with state registration and certification regimes (for example in New South Wales and Queensland); outlets follow AS 1926.3; public pools are regulated by state health departments; recycled and rainwater systems follow AS/NZS 3500.1 and state health guidelines.
- United Kingdom. HSG179 sets health and safety guidance for swimming pools, and the Pool Water Treatment Advisory Group (PWTAG) sets water treatment practice; rainwater harvesting follows BS EN 16941-1 and BS 8515; the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations govern cross-connections.
- United States. The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act requires anti-entrapment drain covers on public pools and spas; the Model Aquatic Health Code and state health codes govern public pools; ASHRAE 188 covers Legionella risk in features and spas; plumbing codes cover non-potable water systems.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Pool barrier compliance certificates and registration.
- Pool water testing logs and health department inspection reports.
- Outlet cover specifications and installation dates.
- Chemical storage register and safety data sheets.
- Recycled or rainwater system validation and testing records.
- Water management plan covering spas and features.
- Pool refurbishment and leak history.

pages.title: Specialist Suppression Systems
pages.question: How do gaseous, pre-action and other specialist suppression systems fail, and when do agent rules end their life?
pages.answer: Specialist suppression fails at the room and the rules. Gaseous systems discharge into rooms that no longer hold gas because cables and doors were added, so the fire reignites. Halon, HFC agents and PFAS foams are restricted, ending the life of sound systems. Carbon dioxide systems kill if safeguards fail. Panels left in manual stop discharge. Kitchen systems fail when nozzles are greased up and links not replaced.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist suppression systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Gaseous (Inergen, FM-200), pre-action systems

sources.title: NFPA 2001 Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Specialist suppression systems protect spaces and hazards where ordinary sprinklers are unsuitable or insufficient: data and communications rooms, switchrooms, archives, museums, heritage buildings, commercial kitchens, flammable liquid stores, aircraft hangars and industrial processes. They use gas, water mist, foam, wet chemical or water released only after detection confirms a fire.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inert gas (IG-541, IG-55, nitrogen, argon) | Data rooms, archives, switchrooms | Lowers oxygen to suppress fire; safe for occupants at design concentrations; large cylinder banks |
| Chemical clean agents (HFC-227ea, FK-5-1-12) | Data rooms, telecoms, control rooms | Compact; HFC-227ea is subject to HFC phase-down; FK-5-1-12 supply changed after a major producer stopped making PFAS |
| Halon | Legacy systems in some aviation, defence and older installations | Ozone-depleting; banned for new use; restricted to critical uses |
| Carbon dioxide | Unoccupied machinery spaces, industrial | Lethal at extinguishing concentrations; strict safeguards |
| Pre-action sprinklers | Data rooms, freezers, heritage | Pipes dry until detection opens a valve, then heads operate |
| Deluge | Transformers, process hazards | Open heads; all discharge together |
| Water mist | Heritage, hotels, machinery spaces | Fine droplets; less water; system-specific design |
| Kitchen wet chemical | Commercial cooking hoods | Suppresses cooking oil fires; linked to gas and power shutdown |
| Foam systems | Hangars, fuel stores, industrial | Older foams contain PFAS and are being phased out |

Gaseous systems only work if the protected room holds the gas for the required time. Every cable, pipe and door added to the room after commissioning can let the gas escape, so room integrity is as important as the cylinders.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas cylinders and valves | 20 to 30 years with periodic hydrostatic testing | Pressure testing intervals; corrosion |
| Detection and control panels | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Pre-action valves | 20 to 30 years | Maintenance; water quality |
| Kitchen system cylinders and links | Fusible links replaced at least annually | Grease; heat |
| Foam concentrate | 10 to 20 years | Storage; type; regulation |
| Water mist pumps and nozzles | 15 to 25 years | Water quality; nozzle blockage |

What shortens life:

- Room integrity lost by later penetrations and doors.
- Agent regulation: halon, HFC and PFAS controls end the useful life of systems that are mechanically sound.
- Panel obsolescence.
- Grease on kitchen system nozzles and links.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Loss of room integrity

Gaseous systems are designed to hold an extinguishing concentration for a set time. New cable penetrations, raised floor and ceiling changes, gaps under doors, and new ductwork let the gas leak away, so the fire reignites when the concentration falls. A door fan integrity test shows whether the room still holds.

### Agent obsolescence and regulation

Halon production ended in developed countries in 1994; remaining systems must be decommissioned or justified. HFC-227ea is being phased down with other HFCs. A major producer of FK-5-1-12 stopped making PFAS products, changing supply. Older firefighting foams contain PFAS and are being banned or restricted in Australia, Britain, the European Union and many US states, with clean-up obligations.

### Occupant safety

Carbon dioxide systems kill people who are in the room when they discharge; pre-discharge alarms, time delays, lock-off valves and signage must work. Inert gas systems lower oxygen to levels that are safe only for short exposures at design concentration.

### Detection and control faults

Systems release only when detection confirms a fire, usually from two detectors. Faulty detectors, disabled panels, and abort or manual release switches left in the wrong position stop discharge or cause accidental discharge.

### Pre-action faults

Pre-action pipework that holds water from tests corrodes; supervisory air leaks; valves fail to trip.

### Kitchen system faults

Nozzles blocked with grease, fusible links not replaced, appliances moved from under nozzles, and gas shutoff interlocks bypassed.

### Change of use

A room fitted out for one use and later used for another (more equipment, storage, people) can outgrow its design.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Cylinder labels: agent, fill date, test date; pressure gauges.
- Panel faults; isolations; manual or lock-off positions.
- New penetrations and gaps in protected rooms; doors without seals or closers.
- Warning signs and alarms at protected rooms.
- Kitchen nozzles greasy or out of position.
- Foam concentrate type and labels.

### In the records

- Design and agent quantity calculations.
- Room integrity test reports.
- Service and cylinder test records.
- Halon or foam registers and decommissioning records.

- Room doors fitted without closers or seals after works.
- Raised floors and ceilings opened for cabling.
- Abort and manual release switches without labels or covers.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room integrity test fails | Penetrations and gaps added | Door fan test |
| Halon cylinders present | Legacy system | Labels |
| Foam concentrate of older type | Likely PFAS-containing foam | Product data; testing |
| Panel in manual or isolated | Left after works or a false discharge | Panel status |

> A gaseous system in a room that no longer holds gas will discharge and fail to put the fire out. Room integrity must be retested after any works that penetrate the room.

A protected room that fails its integrity test after recent works points to the works; one that fails without recent works points to ageing seals, doors and dampers.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon dioxide safeguards failed; system isolated in a protected room; kitchen system disabled | safety | Rectify now |
| Room integrity failed | failure | Seal now |
| Halon, HFC or PFAS foam requiring decommissioning or replacement under rules | deadline | By the regulatory date |
| Servicing and integrity testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Panel or detection ageing | condition | Repair |
| System at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Design basis unknown after change of use | check | Review |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer leads, with a suppression specialist for the system type and, for kitchens, the hood and suppression contractor.

- Design review: hazard, agent, design concentration and hold time, room volume, and whether the room's use, contents and occupancy have changed.
- Room integrity test by door fan for gaseous systems, predicting hold time against the design, with leaks located by smoke pencil or thermal imaging.
- Cylinder and agent inspection: weight or pressure against the label, hydrostatic test dates, valves, discharge pipework and nozzles, mounting.
- Detection and control test: detectors, two-stage confirmation logic, pre-discharge alarms, time delays, abort and manual release, lock-off valves, interfaces to air handling shutdown and dampers.
- Occupant safety review for carbon dioxide and inert gas systems: signage, alarms, lock-off procedures, room access controls.
- Regulatory review of the agent: halon status, HFC phase-down, foam PFAS content and any decommissioning or clean-up obligations.
- Pre-action checks: supervisory air, low-point drains, internal condition, trip test.
- Kitchen system inspection: nozzle positions against current appliances, grease, fusible links, gas and power shutdown interlocks, manual release.

The report should state whether the system will suppress a fire in the room as it now is, the safety position, the agent's regulatory status, and works or replacement needed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Restore room integrity: seal every penetration with tested products, fit door seals and closers, seal raised floors and ceilings, then retest.
- Recalculate and recharge where room volume or use has changed.
- Replace regulated agents: decommission halon through approved channels; plan replacement of HFC-227ea systems; move to inert gas or other permitted agents, which may need more cylinder space and pressure relief venting.
- Replace PFAS foam with fluorine-free foam, with full system cleaning and disposal of old concentrate and rinse water under environmental rules.
- Panel and detection replacement with supported equipment.
- Safety measures for carbon dioxide: lock-off valves, alarms, signage, procedures, or replacement with a safer agent.
- Pre-action corrosion control: nitrogen supervisory gas, drainage, pipe replacement.
- Kitchen systems: reposition nozzles to match appliances, replace links, restore interlocks, clean regularly.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing, room integrity testing and cylinder testing recur. Room sealing is a lump sum per room. Agent replacement is a lump-sum project per protected space, including new cylinders, pipework, nozzles, pressure relief and commissioning. Halon decommissioning and PFAS foam replacement carry disposal and clean-up costs that can be significant. Kitchen system servicing recurs, with replacement per hood.

Servicing, integrity and safety rectification are code compliance; agent replacement driven by regulation is a deadline item; system replacement at end of life is lifecycle.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 4214 and ISO 14520 cover gaseous systems; AS 1851 sets routine service including room integrity checks; halon is controlled under the ozone protection legislation with use only under permit; several states and the Commonwealth restrict PFAS firefighting foams; kitchen suppression follows the relevant Australian Standard and AS 1851.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 15004 and BS ISO 14520 cover gaseous systems; halon use is restricted to listed critical uses; HFC agents fall under fluorinated gas regulations; PFAS foam restrictions apply under UK and EU chemical rules; kitchen systems follow LPS 1223.
- United States. NFPA 2001 covers clean agent systems, including annual enclosure integrity checks; NFPA 12 carbon dioxide with strict personnel safety requirements; NFPA 17A wet chemical systems; NFPA 11 foam; EPA and state rules restrict PFAS foams; NFPA 13 and 25 cover pre-action systems.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Design and agent quantity calculations.
- Room integrity test reports with hold times.
- Service, cylinder weight and hydrostatic test records.
- Detection and control test records.
- Halon register and decommissioning records; foam product data and PFAS status.
- Carbon dioxide safety procedures and lock-off records.
- Kitchen system service records and link replacement dates.
- Records of works in protected rooms.

pages.title: Storage & Archive Areas
pages.question: How do storerooms and archives fail, and which storage findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Stores fail through what is put in them. Compactus and archives overload upper floors; goods stacked to the ceiling block sprinklers; plastics and batteries outgrow sprinkler designs; incompatible chemicals stored together without bunding or ventilation risk toxic gas and fire; e-bikes charged in basement cages start fires. Archives under pipes or in damp basements are destroyed by leaks and mould. Most fixes are management, but floor overloads and chemical hazards need action now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about storage & archive areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Flooring, wall systems, environmental controls, access

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Storage and archive areas hold goods, records and materials: general storerooms, paper and media archives, compactus and mobile shelving rooms, cleaners' stores, chemical and dangerous goods stores, and resident and tenant storage cages in basements. Functionally a store must carry its load, keep its contents safe from fire, water, pests and theft, keep hazardous materials segregated, and not obstruct escape or fire protection. Stores are easy to overlook because they are rarely visited, yet they concentrate fire load, floor load and hazardous materials in one place.

| Type | Where it is found | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General storerooms | All building types | Fire load, sprinkler clearance, egress, housekeeping |
| Archives and compactus rooms | Offices, councils, law firms, hospitals | Floor loading; water protection; environmental control |
| Cleaners' and chemical stores | All managed buildings | Segregation, ventilation, spill containment |
| Dangerous goods stores | Industrial, laboratories, pool plant, workshops | Separation distances, bunding, signage, ventilation |
| Resident and tenant storage cages | Apartment and office basements | Fire load; sprinkler coverage; lithium batteries; security |
| Rack storage in warehouses | Logistics and retail | Sprinkler design; racking safety; floor flatness |

In apartment buildings, resident storage cages in basements are common property spaces filled with private belongings, so fire and battery risks there are shared by everyone in the building.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mobile shelving and compactus | 20 to 30 years | Load; track wear |
| Storage cages | 20 to 30 years | Damage; corrosion in damp basements |
| Chemical storage cabinets | 15 to 25 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Archive environmental control | 15 to 20 years | Equipment life |
| Fitness for the stored contents | Changes whenever contents change | New uses; denser storage |

What shortens fitness for purpose:

- Denser or heavier storage than the room was designed for, such as compactus added to an office floor.
- Changes in what is stored, from paper to plastics, from tools to lithium batteries, without reviewing fire protection.
- Water from pipes running overhead and basement flooding.
- Neglect in rooms nobody visits.

sections.heading: How the space fails
sections.markdown:
### Floor overload

Compactus and mobile shelving full of paper impose loads far above ordinary office floor loads. Installed on upper floors without engineering, they cause cracking and deflection and, in extreme cases, threaten the floor.

### Fire load and sprinkler obstruction

Stores concentrate combustible material. Storage stacked close to sprinkler heads blocks their spray; high-piled plastics exceed what the sprinkler system was designed for; doors to stores are propped; and stores without detection let fires grow unseen.

### Lithium-ion batteries

E-bikes, scooters and batteries stored and charged in basement cages and stores are a growing fire source; such fires are intense, produce toxic gases and can reignite.

### Water damage

Archives and stores under pipework, plant rooms, wet areas or in flood-prone basements suffer leaks and floods that destroy records and stock. Archives should never sit under water pipes.

### Dangerous goods incompatibility

Chemicals stored together that react (such as pool chlorine and acids, oxidisers and flammables), without bunding, ventilation or separation, can release toxic gas, cause fires or contaminate drains.

### Archive environment

Paper, film and media need stable temperature and humidity; damp basements grow mould, and pests (silverfish, rodents) damage records.

### Egress and access

Stores overflowing into corridors and stairs, and blocked access to fire equipment, valves and switchboards, are common in buildings where storage is scarce.

Basement stores also sit where floods arrive first, so stored contents and the services that pass through stores are at combined risk.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Storage within the clearance zone under sprinkler heads; stacked to the ceiling.
- Compactus and heavy shelving on upper floors; cracks or deflection in the floor.
- Pipes running above archives and stores; water staining on boxes.
- Chemicals stored together without bunding or segregation; corroded containers.
- E-bikes and batteries in basement cages; charging cables run to outlets.
- Mould on boxes or walls; pest evidence.
- Storage spilling into corridors, stairs and plant rooms.

### In the records

- Floor loading design and approvals for compactus.
- Dangerous goods register and manifest.
- Sprinkler design basis.
- Leak and flood history.
- Building rules on storage cages and charging.

- Fire doors to stores propped open to make access easier, and stores left unlocked.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor cracks under a compactus room | Overload beyond design | Load calculation against design |
| Sprinklers blocked by stacked goods | Housekeeping and inadequate storage space | Clearance measurement |
| Corroded fittings near a chemical store | Fumes from incompatible or unventilated storage | Inventory; ventilation check |
| Mould on archive boxes | Damp basement or poor ventilation | Humidity logging |
| Water-stained boxes | Leaks from overhead pipes | Pipe route survey |

> Overloaded floors, blocked sprinklers, incompatible chemicals and battery charging in basement stores are safety findings, not housekeeping.

Most storage findings come from a mismatch between what the store was designed for and what is now in it, so begin by recording the actual contents and their weight and combustibility.

Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor overload; incompatible dangerous goods; storage blocking sprinklers or egress; battery charging in cages | safety | Remove or rectify now |
| Flood or leak damaging stored contents | failure | Stop the water now |
| Dangerous goods notification or manifest due | deadline | As required |
| Damp, pests, poor housekeeping | condition | Improve in the near term |
| Shelving and cages at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| Storage loads and contents unknown | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

Storage findings are graded by consequence: a store whose contents could start, feed or spread a fire, overload a floor, or release toxic gas is a safety grade; a damp or untidy store of inert goods is a condition grade.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a structural engineer for heavy storage, a fire engineer for storage hazard and sprinkler adequacy, and a dangerous goods specialist where chemicals are stored.

- Storage survey of every store: contents, height, density, clearances to sprinklers, access to fire equipment and egress.
- Floor load assessment for compactus, archives and heavy storage against the floor's design.
- Sprinkler adequacy review against the actual stored commodity and height.
- Dangerous goods review: inventory, quantities, compatibility, separation, bunding, ventilation, signage, and notification thresholds.
- Water risk review: pipes above stores, flood levels, drainage.
- Environmental monitoring in archives: temperature, humidity, pests.
- Battery charging review in basement stores and cages.

The report should list safety findings by store, the capacity and suitability of each, and works and management changes.

sections.heading: Remedies and refurbishment
sections.markdown:
- Load control: relocate heavy storage to ground floors or over beams, strengthen floors, or limit shelving density.
- Sprinkler clearance: marked maximum stacking heights, and sprinkler upgrades where the stored hazard has outgrown the design.
- Dangerous goods stores: segregated, bunded and ventilated cabinets or rooms, with signage, spill kits and a current register.
- Water protection: reroute pipes, add drip trays and leak detection, raise storage off floors in basements.
- Archive environment: dehumidification, stable temperature, pest control.
- Battery policy: ban charging in cages and stores, provide designated charging rooms with detection.
- Housekeeping rules enforced with regular checks.

- Records digitisation to reduce paper archives and their floor and fire loads.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Most storage findings are fixed by management at little cost. Floor strengthening and sprinkler upgrades are lump sums. Dangerous goods cabinets and stores are itemised. Archive environmental control is a lump sum with running costs. Leak protection is itemised. Safety items are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle.

Digitising or offsiting archives can avoid floor strengthening and free valuable space. Dangerous goods non-compliance can bring regulatory penalties and insurance consequences that far exceed the cost of proper stores.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Work health and safety regulations govern hazardous chemicals, with AS 1940 for flammable liquids and AS 3780 for corrosives; state laws set dangerous goods notification thresholds; AS/NZS 1170.1 sets floor loads for storage; sprinkler design for storage follows AS 2118.1.
- United Kingdom. The Dangerous Substances and Explosive Atmospheres Regulations 2002 (DSEAR) and COSHH govern chemicals; BS EN 1991-1-1 sets storage loads; the responsible person must manage fire risk in stores.
- United States. OSHA hazard communication and flammable liquid standards and NFPA 30 govern chemical storage; NFPA 13 sets sprinkler design for storage; ASCE 7 sets storage live loads.

Insurers in all three countries commonly set conditions on storage heights, battery charging and chemical storage.

Records retention laws may also apply.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Floor loading design and approvals for heavy storage.
- Dangerous goods register and manifest.
- Sprinkler design basis for storage areas.
- Leak and flood history affecting stores.
- Building rules on storage cages and battery charging.
- Archive environmental monitoring records.

- Insurer conditions on storage.
- Inventory of stored contents by room.

pages.title: Stormwater Drainage
pages.question: How do site stormwater systems fail, and why do buildings flood in large storms?
pages.answer: Stormwater systems fail by blockage and obstruction. Litter, sediment and roots block pits and pipes; detention tanks lose storage and orifices block; treatment devices fill and bypass. Buildings flood in big storms most often because overland flow paths have been blocked by fences, walls and landscaping, sending water into basements and ground floors. Many detention systems carry legal maintenance obligations on title.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about stormwater drainage; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Surface pits, pipes, on-site detention/retention systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Stormwater drainage collects rainwater from roofs and paved areas and carries it to the public system or to on-site treatment and storage: surface pits and grates, channel drains, underground pipes, subsoil drains, on-site detention tanks that hold water and release it slowly, retention and harvesting tanks, gross pollutant traps and treatment devices, bioretention basins and swales, and the overland flow paths that carry water safely when pipes are full. Roof gutters and downpipes have their own page.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surface pits and grates | Car parks, paved areas, landscaping | Blockage; broken grates; trip and wheel hazards |
| Underground pipes | All sites | Root intrusion; cracking; displacement; sediment |
| Subsoil drains | Behind retaining walls, under pavements, around footings | Silting and root blockage |
| On-site detention (OSD) tanks | Newer urban sites in Australia, Britain and the US | Orifice blockage; sediment; access; legal maintenance obligations |
| Gross pollutant traps and treatment devices | Car parks and commercial sites | Full of litter and sediment; bypassing |
| Bioretention and swales | Newer sites with water-sensitive design | Clogging; planting loss; erosion |
| Overland flow paths | All sites | Blocked by fences, walls and landscaping |

Stormwater is designed for a storm of a given size. When pipes and pits are full, water must flow safely across the surface along overland flow paths, away from buildings. Fences, walls, landscaping and new structures that block those paths send floodwater into buildings, basements and car parks.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete and PVC stormwater pipes | 50 years and more | Roots; ground movement; installation |
| Clay and older pipes | 50 to 80 years | Roots; joint failure |
| Pit structures and grates | 30 to 50 years | Traffic loads; corrosion |
| On-site detention tanks | 50 years and more | Maintenance; access |
| Treatment device media and filters | 1 to 5 years | Sediment load |
| Subsoil drains | 15 to 30 years | Silting; roots |

What shortens life:

- Sediment and litter from car parks, construction and landscaping.
- Tree roots entering joints.
- Traffic over pits and grates not rated for it.
- Lack of maintenance of detention and treatment devices.

The pipes usually outlast the building; the maintainable parts (grates, treatment media, detention screens and orifices) set the real maintenance cycle.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Blockage

Leaves, litter, sediment and debris block grates, pits and pipes; water then ponds on pavements, enters buildings and basements, and overflows into neighbouring land.

### Root intrusion and pipe damage

Roots enter pipe joints and grow into masses that block flow and crack pipes; ground movement displaces joints; pipes crushed by traffic or construction collapse.

### On-site detention failure

Detention tanks release water through small orifices that block with debris; tanks fill with sediment and lose storage; access covers are buried or sealed. Failed detention increases flooding downstream and on the site itself, and in many places the owner has a legal obligation to maintain it.

### Treatment device failure

Gross pollutant traps and filters fill with litter and sediment and then bypass, discharging pollutants; clogged media stops working.

### Blocked overland flow paths

Fences, retaining walls, landscaping, sheds and raised paving built across overland flow paths force floodwater into buildings and basements during large storms.

### Subsoil drain failure

Silted or root-blocked subsoil drains let groundwater build up behind retaining walls, under slabs and around footings, causing damp, heave and wall failure.

### Illegal connections

Stormwater connected to the sewer overloads it in storms; sewer connected to stormwater pollutes waterways. Both are breaches.

### Capacity shortfall

Systems sized for older rainfall data or smaller paved areas are overwhelmed when sites are extended, paved over, or when design rainfall intensities are revised upward.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Ponding on paved areas and around pits after rain; silt and debris marks.
- Grates broken, missing or sitting proud; pits full of sediment.
- Water entering basements, car parks or ground floors in storms.
- Fences, walls and landscaping across low points.
- Detention tank access covers missing, buried or sealed.
- Treatment devices overflowing or full.

### In the records

- Stormwater drawings and design.
- On-site detention design and maintenance obligations.
- Cleaning and maintenance records.
- Flood history.
- CCTV surveys.

- Erosion, scour and sediment fans at outlets and on slopes below the site.
- Water discharging onto neighbouring land or footpaths from the site.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding at one pit after every storm | Blocked pit or pipe | Inspection; CCTV |
| Site floods in large storms only | Overland flow blocked or system capacity exceeded | Flow path review; design capacity |
| Detention tank never empties or empties instantly | Blocked orifice or missing orifice plate | Inspection |
| Repeated blockage downstream of trees | Root intrusion | CCTV |
| Damp behind retaining walls and under slabs | Blocked subsoil drains | Inspection; flushing |

> Floodwater entering basements and ground floors in storms is often a blocked overland flow path or detention system rather than a pipe problem. Check the surface first.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken or missing grates in traffic or pedestrian areas; flooding into switchrooms or basements | safety | Make safe now |
| Collapsed pipes; blocked system causing flooding | failure | Repair now |
| On-site detention maintenance required by title or council | deadline | As required |
| Sediment build-up; roots; failing devices | condition | Clean and repair in the near term |
| Treatment media and devices at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No drawings; detention obligations unknown | check | Investigate |
| Normal | nil | Routine cleaning |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A civil or hydraulic engineer, with a drainage contractor for cleaning and CCTV.

- Drawings and obligations review: stormwater design, detention and treatment requirements, and any covenants or council conditions.
- Pit and pipe inspection: lift grates, measure sediment, CCTV pipes.
- Detention tank inspection: access, orifice plates, screens, sediment, storage volume.
- Treatment device inspection: litter and sediment levels, media condition.
- Overland flow path survey: obstructions and levels against design.
- Subsoil drain flushing and inspection.
- Connection check for illegal cross-connections.

The report should state system condition, flood risk, compliance with detention and treatment obligations, and a maintenance plan.

- Capacity check of the system against current design rainfall and the paved area now draining to it, especially after extensions.
- Storm observation: where practicable, observe the site in heavy rain to see where water actually goes.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Cleaning programme: scheduled cleaning of grates, pits, pipes, detention tanks and treatment devices, with extra visits after storms and leaf fall.
- Pipe repairs: root cutting as an interim, then relining or excavation and replacement of damaged pipes.
- Grate replacement with load-rated grates suited to the traffic, and heel-safe and bicycle-safe patterns in pedestrian areas.
- Detention restoration: clear or replace orifice plates and screens, remove sediment, and reinstate accessible covers so maintenance can be done.
- Overland flow path restoration: remove, lower or open fences, walls and landscaping that block flow, and regrade where needed so water passes the building safely.
- Subsoil drain renewal behind retaining walls and under pavements.
- Capacity upgrades: larger pipes and pits, additional inlets, or added detention where flooding recurs.
- Treatment device servicing and media replacement.
- Correct illegal connections between stormwater and sewer.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Cleaning and inspection recur, often annually and after major storms, and are best carried as recurring maintenance. Pipe repairs are priced by length; relining by length and diameter; grates and pits per item. Detention restoration is a lump sum, often modest unless access must be rebuilt. Overland flow path works range from minor fence changes to regrading. Capacity upgrades are lump-sum civil projects. Treatment media is replaced on a cycle.

Cleaning is repairs and maintenance; detention and treatment compliance is code compliance; flood protection works are risk-driven; replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3500.3 covers stormwater drainage; Australian Rainfall and Runoff sets design rainfall and flood guidance; councils impose on-site detention and water quality conditions, often backed by covenants on title requiring owners to maintain them.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document H covers rainwater drainage; the CIRIA SuDS Manual sets sustainable drainage practice; planning conditions and, in Wales, statutory approval regimes require SuDS and their maintenance.
- United States. Local stormwater codes and permits under the Clean Water Act set on-site management; maintenance agreements are often recorded against property; plumbing codes cover building storm drainage.

In strata and condominium schemes in all three countries, site stormwater, detention and treatment systems are common property, and maintenance obligations recorded on title bind the owners corporation; failure to maintain can lead to council orders and liability for flooding of neighbours.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Stormwater drawings and design.
- On-site detention and treatment obligations, covenants and maintenance plans.
- Cleaning and maintenance records.
- CCTV surveys.
- Flood history.
- Council correspondence on stormwater.

- Records of flooding events and insurance claims.
- Council orders or notices about stormwater.
- Records of site extensions or paving since the stormwater design.

pages.title: Structural Core
pages.question: How do cores, shear walls and bracing fail, and how do alterations undermine a building's stability?
pages.answer: Lateral systems rarely wear out; they are cut and removed. Cores and shear walls collect openings for services and doors until capacity is lost; bracing is removed from warehouse bays and fit-outs for new layouts; steel bracing connections corrode. Soft-storey buildings over open parking are especially vulnerable in earthquakes. Missing bracing in a portal frame or significant unengineered core openings need temporary bracing and an engineer now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about structural core; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Lift and stair core walls, shear walls, bracing systems

sources.title: ASCE 41 Seismic Evaluation and Retrofit of Existing Buildings

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
The structural core and bracing system keep a building upright against sideways forces: wind, earthquake and the small imperfections that would otherwise let a frame sway and buckle. In multi-storey buildings this is usually a concrete core around lifts and stairs, sometimes with additional shear walls; in steel buildings it may be braced bays or rigid moment frames; in low-rise sheds and houses it is bracing in walls and roofs. Because these elements carry little vertical load, their importance is easy to overlook when cutting openings or removing walls.

| System | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete lift and stair cores | Offices and apartments of most eras | Openings cut for services and doors; construction defects |
| Concrete shear walls | Apartments, car parks, mid-rise | Penetrations; removal in alterations |
| Steel braced frames | Steel buildings, warehouses, portal frames | Bracing removed; corroded connections |
| Moment-resisting frames | Steel and concrete buildings | Connection detailing in older seismic design |
| Timber wall and roof bracing | Houses and low-rise | Bracing panels removed or cut in renovations |
| Transfer structures | Podiums and mixed-use buildings | High loads; alterations; detailing |

Seismic design requirements have tightened over time in all three countries, most heavily on the US west coast. Older buildings in seismic regions, including soft-storey buildings with open ground floors over parking, can have lateral systems far weaker than current standards require.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete cores and shear walls | Life of the building | Alterations; durability |
| Steel bracing and connections | Life of the building if protected | Corrosion; removal |
| Timber bracing panels | Life of the building if kept | Renovations; decay |
| Seismic retrofit elements | Life of the building | Maintenance; damage in earthquakes |

Lateral systems rarely wear out. What shortens their effective life is change:

- Openings and penetrations cut through cores and shear walls for doors, ducts and pipes.
- Bracing removed in fit-outs and alterations, often because it obstructs a new layout.
- Corrosion of steel bracing and connections in exposed or damp areas.
- Added height or mass that increases lateral loads.
- Earthquake damage that weakens the system for the next event.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Openings and penetrations

Core and shear walls are cored and cut for new services, risers and doors throughout a building's life. Each opening removes concrete and may cut reinforcement; several near each other, or near wall ends and corners, can significantly reduce capacity and create weak points. Cores are often more penetrated than any other element.

### Bracing removed

In warehouses, bracing bays are removed or relocated for new doors and racking; in offices, braced partitions are removed in fit-outs; in houses, bracing walls are removed to open up living areas. Without bracing, frames sway and can buckle or collapse in wind or earthquake.

### Connection corrosion and detailing

Steel bracing connections corrode where water collects; older moment frame connections in seismic regions were found after the 1994 Northridge earthquake to fracture in a brittle way and have since been the subject of retrofit guidance.

### Soft and weak storeys

Buildings with open ground floors (for parking or shopfronts) beneath stiffer upper floors concentrate earthquake movement in the ground storey, which can collapse. Many such buildings in California have been required to retrofit.

### Construction defects

Cores and walls can have cold joints, honeycombing and poorly compacted concrete, particularly at congested reinforcement, and later reveal these through leaks and cracking.

### Cracking and movement

Diagonal cracking in shear walls and cores indicates shear distress; cracking at the base or at openings can indicate overload or settlement; excessive sway in wind shows reduced stiffness.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Openings, cores and chases in lift and stair core walls; new risers and doors through shear walls.
- Missing bracing in warehouse bays; bracing rods slack, bent or disconnected.
- Diagonal cracking in core and shear walls.
- Occupants noticing sway in wind in taller buildings.
- Open ground floors under residential floors in seismic areas.
- Corrosion at bracing connections and base plates.

### In the records

- Structural drawings showing the lateral system.
- Records of coring and openings with engineering.
- Fit-out drawings showing bracing changes.
- Seismic evaluations and retrofit orders.
- Post-earthquake inspections.

- Penetrations in core walls grouped closely together around new risers, or near wall ends and corners, where they matter most.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Many cores and openings through a lift core | Accumulated service penetrations | Survey against drawings; engineering review |
| Warehouse bay without the bracing shown on drawings | Bracing removed for doors or racking | Drawing comparison |
| Diagonal cracks in a shear wall | Shear distress from overload, settlement or past earthquake | Engineering assessment |
| Slack or bent bracing rods | Movement, impact or corrosion | Inspection |
| Noticeable sway in wind | Reduced stiffness or design limits | Monitoring; assessment |

> Never cut, core or remove core walls, shear walls or bracing without a structural engineer's design. Their importance is not obvious from the loads they carry day to day.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bracing removed in a portal frame building; significant openings in cores without engineering; earthquake damage | safety | Brace temporarily and engineer now |
| Shear distress cracking | failure | Repair and strengthen now |
| Seismic retrofit required by ordinance | deadline | By the ordinance date |
| Corroded bracing connections; minor unengineered penetrations | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Protective coatings on exposed bracing at end of life | lifecycle | Recoat on cycle |
| Lateral system unknown; seismic adequacy unassessed in seismic regions | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads; a seismic specialist joins in seismic regions.

- Drawing review to identify the lateral system and compare it with the building as it now is.
- Penetration survey of cores and shear walls, with scanning to locate reinforcement before any new coring.
- Bracing survey in steel and timber buildings for missing, altered or damaged members.
- Condition survey for cracking, corrosion and concrete defects.
- Structural analysis of lateral capacity with the openings and changes accounted for.
- Seismic evaluation to the recognised method for existing buildings in seismic regions.
- Monitoring of sway or crack movement where concerns exist.

The report should state the lateral system's adequacy, the effect of alterations, any urgent measures, and strengthening options.

Where drawings are missing, the lateral system may have to be inferred from the structure itself, which takes opening up and scanning.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Temporary bracing wherever bracing has been removed, until permanent replacement.
- Reinstated or relocated bracing designed by an engineer to suit the new layout.
- Strengthening around openings with steel frames, fibre-reinforced polymer or added concrete.
- Seismic retrofit: new shear walls or braced frames, strengthened connections, soft-storey strengthening, base isolation for important buildings.
- Connection repair and recoating of corroded bracing.
- Concrete repair of defects and cracks.
- Controls on future penetrations: a permit system and penetration register for cores and shear walls.

- Post-earthquake assessment and repair: rapid safety evaluation, then detailed assessment and repair of damaged elements before reoccupation.
- Documentation: mark core and shear walls on fit-out drawings and on site so trades know not to cut them.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment and analysis are lump sums. Temporary bracing is an immediate cost. Strengthening and seismic retrofit are lump-sum projects, often large, which may require tenants to vacate. Bracing reinstatement in warehouses is per bay. Penetration management is a low-cost procedure that avoids large future costs.

Safety items are immediate; ordinance retrofits carry deadlines; strengthening is a condition or code compliance item; recoating is lifecycle.

Seismic retrofits often attract incentives or are tied to ordinance timetables, which affect funding and programme.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 1170.2 sets wind actions and AS 1170.4 earthquake actions; AS 3600 and AS 4100 govern concrete and steel; the National Construction Code requires structural adequacy for alterations; earthquake design has applied nationally since the 1990s.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document A, including requirements to avoid disproportionate collapse, and the Eurocodes govern design; seismic design is rarely required; the Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on appraisal of existing structures.
- United States. ASCE 7 sets wind and seismic loads and ASCE 41 the seismic evaluation and retrofit of existing buildings; the International Existing Building Code governs alterations; Los Angeles and San Francisco require soft-storey and non-ductile concrete retrofits.

Insurance and lending in seismic regions increasingly depend on a building's seismic assessment in all three markets where earthquake risk is material.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Structural drawings showing the lateral system.
- Records of coring and openings in cores and shear walls, with engineering.
- Fit-out and alteration drawings affecting bracing.
- Seismic evaluations, retrofit orders and completion records.
- Post-earthquake inspection reports.
- Penetration permits or register.

- Earthquake insurance terms and any seismic assessment used for lending.

pages.title: Structural Frame
pages.question: How do concrete, steel and timber frames deteriorate, how do you read the cracks, and when is a frame unsafe?
pages.answer: Frames deteriorate where protection fails. Carbonation reaches thin-covered steel and cracks concrete along the bars; chlorides from accelerators, vehicles or sea air pit reinforcement with little warning, worst in car parks. Alkali-silica reaction map-cracks concrete. Steel corrodes where water reaches it, including encased steel behind masonry. Alterations cut openings, cores and tendons. Cracks around columns on top of flat slabs can signal punching shear and need urgent attention.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about structural frame; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Concrete, steel, composite, or timber-framed columns, beams, primary supports

sources.title: CROSS: Collaborative Reporting for Safer Structures
ACI 562 Code for Assessment, Repair and Rehabilitation of Existing Concrete Structures
