sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
The structural frame is the skeleton of columns, beams and their connections that carries a building's floors, roof and envelope to the foundations. Frames are reinforced concrete (cast in place or precast), structural steel, composite steel and concrete, timber (sawn, glulam and, increasingly, cross-laminated timber), or combinations. The frame's condition depends on what protects it: concrete cover protecting reinforcement, coatings and fire protection on steel, and dryness for timber.

| Type and era | Where it is found | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel frame encased in masonry or concrete, 1900s to 1940s | Early offices, warehouses, department stores | Hidden corrosion of encased steel; rust jacking of the encasement |
| Reinforced concrete with calcium chloride accelerators, 1950s to 1970s | Offices, car parks, apartments | Chloride-induced reinforcement corrosion, often aggressive |
| High alumina cement concrete, 1950s to early 1970s (Britain) | Precast beams in schools, offices, industrial roofs | Strength loss with age and moisture |
| Large panel precast systems, 1960s to 1970s | Residential towers, especially in Britain | Robustness of joints; progressive collapse risk |
| Post-tensioned concrete, 1970s onward | Car parks, offices, apartments | Tendon corrosion; damage during alterations |
| Multi-storey car park flat slabs, 1960s to 1990s | Car parks | Chlorides from vehicles; punching shear at columns |
| Modern concrete and steel frames, 1990s onward | Most commercial and residential | Usually sound; issues come from alterations and water |
| Mass timber (glulam, CLT), 2010s onward | New offices, schools, apartments | Moisture during construction and in service; connections |

The era and type of frame tell you where to look. Car parks deserve particular attention: they combine exposed concrete, chlorides carried in on vehicles, water ponding and cycles of wetting and drying, and some older designs are vulnerable to punching shear failure around columns.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete frame | Life of the building, often 100 years and more | Cover; carbonation; chlorides; water |
| Car park decks and ramps | 30 to 60 years before major repair | Chlorides; drainage; protection coatings |
| Structural steel frame, protected | Life of the building | Coating and fire protection; water |
| Exposed steel | 25 to 50 years between major recoating | Corrosivity of the environment |
| Timber and mass timber frames | Life of the building if dry | Moisture; connections; fire protection |
| Protective coatings and membranes on concrete | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; UV; product |

What shortens life:

- Low cover to reinforcement, which lets carbonation and chlorides reach the steel early.
- Chlorides: added as accelerators in older concrete, carried in on vehicles from salted roads, or from sea air.
- Water: leaking roofs, failed membranes, ponding car park decks and blocked drainage.
- Alterations: openings cut, columns removed, tendons cut, loads changed.
- Fire, which weakens concrete, steel and timber.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Carbonation-induced corrosion

Concrete protects steel through its alkalinity. Carbon dioxide from the air slowly neutralises it from the surface inward; when this carbonation front reaches the reinforcement and moisture is present, the steel corrodes. The rust expands, cracking and spalling the concrete along the bars. It is slow, widespread and most common where cover is thin.

### Chloride-induced corrosion

Chlorides break down the protective layer on steel even in alkaline concrete, producing localised pitting that can remove a large part of a bar's section with little surface sign. It is the main cause of serious deterioration in car parks, marine structures and concrete built with chloride accelerators, and can be structurally significant before spalling appears.

### Alkali-silica reaction

Some aggregates react with alkalis in cement to form a gel that swells with moisture, cracking concrete in a map pattern and sometimes causing expansion that distorts elements. It develops over decades and needs moisture.

### High alumina cement and other problem concretes

High alumina cement concrete, used in British precast beams in the 1950s to 1970s, loses strength as it converts with age, heat and moisture, and led to collapses in the 1970s. Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete planks are covered on the roof structure page.

### Punching shear

In flat slabs without beams, the slab around each column carries very high shear. Reinforcement corrosion, deterioration and added load (soil and landscaping on podium decks, resurfacing) can lead to a slab punching through around a column, and once one column fails the load can cascade. Older car parks and podiums are the main concern.

### Steel corrosion

Steel frames corrode where water reaches them: perimeter columns and beams behind leaking façades, steel encased in masonry, connections and base plates in damp basements, and exposed steel in car parks and industrial buildings.

### Alterations

Openings cut through slabs and walls, cores drilled for services, columns removed, beams notched, post-tensioning tendons cut, and heavier loads from new uses all change how the frame carries load. Many are done without engineering.

### Fire damage

Fire spalls concrete and reduces the strength of exposed reinforcement, buckles and weakens steel, and chars timber. The structure may stand after a fire with reduced capacity.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Cracks running along the line of reinforcement, with rust staining; spalled concrete exposing bars.
- Map cracking with gel deposits, suggesting alkali-silica reaction.
- Cracks radiating around columns on the top of car park and podium slabs, and deflection near columns.
- Water ponding on car park decks; failed joints and membranes; staining on soffits.
- Corroded steel at bases, connections and perimeter; rust bleeding through encasement.
- Sagging beams or slabs; cracks in partitions below.
- Openings, cores and cut elements not shown on drawings.

### In the records

- Structural drawings and calculations.
- Previous condition surveys, concrete testing and repairs.
- Records of alterations and their engineering.
- Car park inspection reports where required.
- Fire history.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracking and spalling along bars across a facade or soffit | Carbonation-induced corrosion | Carbonation depth at the steel; low cover |
| Localised spalling in a car park, especially near joints and drains | Chloride-induced corrosion | Chloride content at bar depth; half-cell potentials |
| Map cracking with white gel | Alkali-silica reaction | Petrographic examination of cores |
| Cracking around columns on the top of a flat slab | Punching shear distress | Engineering assessment; deflection survey |
| Rust bleeding through masonry at column lines | Encased steel corrosion | Opening up |
| Diagonal cracks near beam supports | Shear distress | Engineering assessment |
| Vertical cracks at mid-span soffits | Flexural cracking from load or loss of capacity | Load review; reinforcement check |

> Cracking around columns on the top surface of flat slabs, especially in older car parks and on podiums carrying soil or landscaping, can indicate punching shear distress. It needs an engineer urgently and may require propping.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Punching shear distress; significant section loss at critical members; spalling over occupied areas; post-fire damage | safety | Prop, exclude and engineer now |
| Corrosion with loss of section in members; cut tendons | failure | Repair or strengthen now |
| Statutory car park or milestone inspection due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Corrosion and spalling without significant section loss; ASR; failed car park membranes | condition | Repair programme in the near term |
| Protective coatings and membranes at end of life | lifecycle | Renew on cycle |
| Problem concretes possible; alterations unengineered; no survey of a car park | check | Assess |
| Isolated minor cracking | nil | Monitor |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer experienced in existing structures leads, with a concrete testing specialist for durability.

- Desk study: drawings, calculations, construction era and materials, previous surveys and repairs, alterations and their approvals.
- Visual and hammer survey of exposed surfaces, mapping cracks, spalls, rust staining and delamination.
- Cover survey by covermeter or radar, and reinforcement location before any drilling.
- Carbonation depth testing at a sample of locations.
- Chloride profiles from dust samples at increasing depths to the reinforcement.
- Half-cell potential and resistivity mapping to locate active corrosion in chloride-contaminated areas.
- Cores for strength and petrographic examination for alkali-silica reaction, high alumina cement and other problems.
- Opening up at representative locations to measure section loss of bars and steel members.
- Structural assessment of capacity against current loads, including punching shear for flat slabs.
- Monitoring of deflection and crack movement where needed.

The report should state the deterioration mechanisms, their extent and rate, structural capacity, safety issues and a repair and protection strategy with timing.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Patch repair: break out damaged concrete, clean or replace reinforcement, and reinstate with repair mortars to recognised repair principles. Patches in chloride-contaminated concrete can accelerate corrosion next to them (the incipient anode effect) unless combined with other protection.
- Cathodic protection: impressed current or galvanic anode systems that stop corrosion in chloride-contaminated concrete, widely used in car parks and marine structures.
- Electrochemical treatments: realkalisation of carbonated concrete and chloride extraction.
- Protective coatings and membranes: anti-carbonation coatings on facades and traffic membranes on car park decks to keep water and chlorides out.
- Drainage: fix falls, outlets and joints on car park decks to stop ponding.
- Strengthening: fibre-reinforced polymer wraps and plates, steel plates and brackets, additional columns or beams, punching shear reinforcement.
- Steel repair: blast, repair and recoat; replace badly corroded members; open up and treat encased steel.
- Fire damage repair after assessment.
- Load control: restrict loads, remove surcharge from podiums.
- Demolition and replacement where repair is uneconomic or the structure is unsafe.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum, with testing rates per sample. Patch repair is priced by area or volume of concrete, with access, propping and protection of the area below as major components; repairs in occupied car parks are phased by bay. Cathodic protection is priced by area with monitoring that recurs for its life. Membranes by area, recurring on their cycle. Strengthening is priced per element or as a lump sum.

The usual shape is two-part: investigation first, then a repair programme sized from it, often phased over years. Repairs to stop active deterioration are condition items; membranes and coatings are lifecycle; statutory inspections are deadlines; safety items are immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 3600 governs concrete structures, AS 4100 steel and AS 1720 timber; repairs follow recognised concrete repair practice; strata buildings carry structural repairs as common property, and New South Wales adds duties for building defects in apartment buildings.
- United Kingdom. The Eurocodes (BS EN 1992 concrete, 1993 steel, 1995 timber) govern design and BS EN 1504 concrete repair and protection; the Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on appraising existing structures; the Building Safety Act 2022 adds structural safety duties for higher-risk buildings; CROSS collects structural safety reports.
- United States. ACI 562 governs assessment and repair of existing concrete structures and the International Existing Building Code alterations; New York City requires periodic inspection of parking structures, and Florida requires milestone structural inspections of condominium buildings of three or more storeys and structural integrity reserve studies.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Structural drawings and calculations.
- Previous structural surveys, concrete testing and repair records.
- Records of alterations, openings and coring, with engineering.
- Car park condition surveys and statutory inspection reports.
- Cathodic protection monitoring records where installed.
- Fire history and any post-fire assessments.
- For strata buildings, capital works or reserve study entries for structural repair.

pages.title: Sub-floor & Crawlspace
pages.question: How do sub-floors and crawlspaces fail, and what causes decay and pest damage beneath floors?
pages.answer: Sub-floors fail when they get damp. Raised ground levels, paving and extensions block vents; leaks and downpipes wet the ground; timber then rots at stumps, bearers and joist ends. Termites enter through stumps and bridged barriers; in damp climates dry rot spreads through masonry. Uneven, springy floors and musty smells are the early signs. Remove the moisture source before replacing timber.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sub-floor & crawlspace; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Soil condition, ground vapour barriers, sub-floor ventilation

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
A sub-floor or crawlspace is the space beneath a suspended ground floor: timber floors on bearers, joists and stumps or piers in older Australian houses; suspended timber ground floors on sleeper walls with air bricks in British terraces and semis; and crawlspaces under timber floors in American houses. The space must stay dry and ventilated, or the timber above decays and pests thrive.

| Form | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber floor on stumps or piers, open sub-floor | Australian Victorian, Federation and inter-war houses; Queenslanders on high stumps | Stump decay and sinking; termites; ventilation |
| Suspended timber floor on sleeper walls with air bricks | British houses before about 1950 | Blocked air bricks; joist end decay; dry rot |
| Vented crawlspace | Older American houses | Humidity, mould, decay |
| Conditioned or encapsulated crawlspace | Newer and retrofitted US houses | Depends on vapour barrier and dehumidification |
| Concrete suspended ground floor with void | Some modern buildings | Ventilation; services; ground gases |

Ventilation is usually the deciding factor. Ground levels raised by paving and gardens, extensions built over vents, and air bricks blocked with debris or paint turn a dry sub-floor into a damp one.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber stumps | 30 to 60 years | Moisture; termites; treatment |
| Bearers and joists | 60 to 100 years if dry | Ventilation; leaks; pests |
| Ant caps and termite barriers | 20 to 50 years; chemical barriers 5 to 10 | Bridging; disturbance |
| Vapour barriers | 20 to 30 years | Damage; coverage |
| Sub-floor vents and air bricks | Life of the building if kept clear | Blockage |
| Crawlspace dehumidifiers | 8 to 12 years | Run hours |

What shortens life:

- Blocked ventilation from raised ground levels, paving and extensions.
- Water from leaking plumbing, overflowing downpipes and poor site drainage reaching the sub-floor.
- Insufficient clearance between ground and timber.
- Bridged termite barriers.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Wet rot

Timber that stays above about 20 per cent moisture decays. Joist ends bearing on damp walls, bearers over wet ground, and stumps at ground level go first. Decayed timber is soft, cracked across the grain and darkened.

### Dry rot

In Britain and other damp climates, dry rot (Serpula lacrymans) spreads from damp timber across masonry and through walls, destroying floors and joinery well away from the original source. It is identified by white strands, orange-brown fruiting bodies and cuboidal cracking.

### Termites and borers

Subterranean termites, a major risk across most of Australia and the southern United States, enter through the sub-floor via stumps, piers and bridged barriers, hollowing timbers from inside. Borers attack sapwood in drier conditions.

### Stump failure

Timber stumps rot and sink, concrete stumps crack and lean, and floors become uneven, springy and cracked. Restumping is a standard Australian repair.

### Humidity and mould

Poorly ventilated crawlspaces grow mould, which affects indoor air above, and allow condensation on cold surfaces and services.

### Radon and ground gas

In radon-affected areas, gas collects in crawlspaces and enters the house through the floor. Ventilation and sealing reduce it.

### Services in the sub-floor

Leaking pipes, disconnected drains and damaged wiring in sub-floors cause decay, contamination and hazards. Older sub-floors may hold asbestos debris.

Insulation added beneath floors without care can also trap moisture against timber or block vents, turning an energy upgrade into a decay problem.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From inside and outside

- Floors uneven, springy or sloping; cracks in plaster at floor level.
- Vents and air bricks blocked, buried or painted over; ground levels close to or above floor framing.
- Musty smell inside; mould on skirtings.
- Mud tubes on stumps, piers and walls; damaged timber at the surface.

### In the sub-floor

- Soft, cracked or stained timber at stumps, bearers and joist ends.
- Standing water, damp soil, leaking pipes.
- Ant caps missing or bridged.
- White strands or fruiting bodies of fungus.
- Clearance from ground to timber.

### In the records

- Timber pest inspections and treatment records.
- Restumping records.
- Damp and timber treatment guarantees.
- Radon tests.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uneven floors in a house on timber stumps | Decayed or sunken stumps | Sub-floor inspection |
| Soft joist ends at external walls | Wet rot from damp walls or blocked vents | Moisture readings |
| White strands across masonry and fruiting bodies | Dry rot | Identification |
| Hollow timbers with mud | Termites | Inspection; termite detection |
| Musty smell and mould | Poor ventilation or damp ground | Humidity and ventilation check |
| Damp only below one area | Plumbing leak or downpipe discharge | Inspection |

> Active termites and dry rot are progressive and spread unseen. Both need specialist identification and treatment, and the source of moisture must be removed.

Decay concentrated under bathrooms, kitchens and laundries points to plumbing leaks or failed wet area waterproofing above; decay along external walls points to blocked vents, high ground levels or damp walls; decay spread evenly across the sub-floor points to general ventilation failure.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor collapse risk from decay or termites; radon above action levels | safety | Prop and remediate now |
| Active termites; dry rot; failed stumps | failure | Treat and repair now |
| Blocked ventilation; damp; decay starting | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Stumps and chemical barriers at end of life | lifecycle | Restump; renew barriers |
| No timber pest inspection; inaccessible sub-floor | check | Inspect |
| Normal | nil | Routine inspection |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A timber pest inspector and building surveyor; a structural engineer for extensive decay.

- Sub-floor inspection of stumps, piers, bearers, joists, and ground, with probing and moisture readings.
- Timber pest inspection to the relevant standard, with non-invasive detection where needed.
- Ventilation assessment: vent area, cross-flow, blockages, clearances.
- Level survey of floors.
- Plumbing and drainage check for leaks.
- Radon test in affected areas.
- Asbestos check for debris and old materials.

The report should state timber condition, pest activity, causes of damp, and repairs.

- Access: where crawl access is too low or blocked, small access openings or camera inspection may be needed to see critical areas such as joist ends under bathrooms and kitchens.
- Fungus identification by a specialist where decay is found, distinguishing wet rot from dry rot, because the treatment and extent of removal differ.
- Termite monitoring with in-ground stations or detection equipment where activity is suspected but not seen.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Ventilation: clear and add vents; lower ground levels; mechanical sub-floor ventilation where cross-flow is poor.
- Fix water sources: plumbing leaks, downpipes, site drainage.
- Restumping and replacement of decayed bearers and joists.
- Termite management: chemical barriers or baiting, ant caps, removing bridges.
- Dry rot treatment: remove the moisture source, cut out affected timber well beyond visible damage, treat masonry.
- Ground vapour barriers.
- Crawlspace encapsulation with dehumidification in suitable climates.
- Radon mitigation.

- Access openings so the sub-floor can be inspected in future, which is a requirement for effective termite management in Australia.
- Under-floor insulation installed so it does not block ventilation or trap moisture.
- Asbestos removal of debris and old materials in the sub-floor by licensed contractors.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections recur annually in termite regions. Restumping is priced per stump or per house. Timber replacement by length. Termite barriers by perimeter length, recurring. Ventilation works itemised. Encapsulation by area.

Restumping and timber replacement are lifecycle or repairs; termite management recurs; active infestations are immediate.

Access is the main cost driver: low, obstructed or partly enclosed sub-floors make every task slower, and extensions over old sub-floors may require floors to be lifted from above. Dry rot remediation can extend into walls, plaster and joinery well beyond the floor. Annual timber pest inspections and periodic barrier renewal should be carried as recurring lines in termite regions.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 3660.1 sets termite management for new buildings and AS 3660.2 for existing ones; AS 4349.3 covers timber pest inspections; the National Construction Code sets sub-floor ventilation and clearance.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document C covers resistance to moisture, including ventilation of suspended floors; the Property Care Association publishes guidance on timber decay and dry rot; the UK Health Security Agency maps radon.
- United States. The International Residential Code sets crawlspace ventilation or conditioning; termite protection is required in many regions; the EPA recommends radon testing and mitigation.

Pre-purchase timber pest inspections are standard in Australian residential sales, and termite damage and dry rot often affect insurance and lending in all three countries; many insurance policies exclude termite damage, so prevention and inspection carry the risk.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Timber pest inspection reports and treatment records.
- Restumping and sub-floor repair records.
- Damp proofing and timber treatment guarantees.
- Radon test results.
- Plumbing leak history.

- Pre-purchase or periodic building and pest inspection reports.
- Records of extensions built over the sub-floor.
- Insurance terms on termite and decay damage.
- Asbestos register for older houses.

pages.title: Sub-metering
pages.question: How do sub-metering systems fail, and when do metering errors become a billing or compliance problem?
pages.answer: Sub-metering fails quietly. Current transformers are installed with the wrong ratio, on the wrong circuit or reversed; fit-outs move circuits so meters measure the wrong tenancies; communications fail and data stops. Reconciling sub-meters against the main meter exposes most errors quickly. Meters used to bill tenants or residents must meet legal measurement rules, and embedded networks carry regulatory obligations; monitoring-grade meters used for billing invite disputes.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sub-metering; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Enhanced energy and water sub-metering for monitoring and reporting

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Sub-metering measures electricity, water, gas and thermal energy below the utility meter: by tenancy, apartment, floor, plant item or end use. It serves two different purposes with different requirements. Billing meters charge tenants or residents for what they use and must meet legal metrology rules; monitoring meters show where energy and water go, support ratings and catch faults, and need accuracy and reliable data but not legal approval. Many buildings have meters installed for one purpose being used for the other.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electricity sub-meters with current transformers | Tenancies, floors, plant | Wrong ratios, reversed polarity, wrong circuits |
| Whole-current electricity meters | Apartments, small tenancies | Communications; accuracy approval for billing |
| Water sub-meters | Apartments, tenancies, cooling towers, irrigation | Mechanical wear; batteries in pulse units |
| Gas sub-meters | Tenancies, kitchens, plant | Approval; access |
| Thermal (heat and chilled water) meters | Heat networks, shared plant | Sensor accuracy; flow meter fouling |
| Embedded network meters | Apartments and shopping centres where the owner on-sells energy | Regulatory obligations; billing systems |
| Data loggers and gateways | Most networked metering | Communications failure; data gaps |

Metering also underpins compliance: ratings, disclosure and building performance standards rely on accurate whole-building and end-use data, and metering errors can misstate a building's performance to buyers, tenants and regulators.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electronic electricity meters | 15 to 20 years | Technology; communications |
| Mechanical water meters | 10 to 15 years before accuracy drops | Volume passed; water quality |
| Battery-powered meter communications | 5 to 10 years | Battery life |
| Thermal meters | 10 to 15 years | Sensor drift; flow meter fouling |
| Data gateways and software | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support; networks |

What shortens life, or usefulness:

- Fit-outs that move circuits without updating which meter measures what.
- Communications that fail silently, leaving data gaps.
- Vendor platforms that close or change.
- Network changes, such as retirement of older mobile networks used by meter modems.

Meter hardware usually outlasts the communications and software around it, which is where most metering systems fail first.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Current transformer and wiring errors

Electricity sub-meters that use current transformers are commonly installed with the wrong ratio programmed, transformers on the wrong phase or circuit, or polarity reversed. The meter then reads a fraction, a multiple or the wrong load entirely, sometimes for years.

### Mapping drift

After fit-outs and alterations, circuits are moved between boards and meters no longer measure the areas their labels say. Tenants are billed for each other's use, and plant energy is attributed to the wrong place.

### Data gaps

Meters keep counting but communications fail, batteries die, or gateways lose connection; monitoring dashboards show gaps or flat lines that nobody notices.

### Legal metrology non-compliance

Meters used to bill tenants or residents generally need approved patterns and verification under national measurement law. Monitoring-grade meters used for billing expose owners to disputes and regulatory action.

### Accuracy decline

Mechanical water meters under-read as they wear; thermal meters drift as temperature sensors age and flow meters foul.

### Embedded network obligations

Owners who on-sell electricity or gas through embedded networks take on regulatory obligations for metering, billing, hardship and customer protections. These are tightening in several Australian states.

### Missing meters

Loads added after the metering design (new plant, EV chargers, tenant equipment on common supply) are often not metered at all, so the main meter and sub-meters never reconcile and costs are absorbed by the owner or spread unfairly.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Meters without clear labels of what they measure.
- Meters showing zero or impossible readings.
- Dead displays on battery-powered meters.
- Boards altered since metering was installed.

### In the data

- Sub-meter totals that do not add up to the main meter.
- Flat lines or gaps in data.
- Tenancy consumption that does not match occupancy or hours.
- Negative readings on current transformer meters.

### In the records

- Metering schedule and single-line diagrams.
- Meter pattern approvals and verification certificates for billing meters.
- Recharge and billing records, and tenant disputes.
- Embedded network registrations and exemptions.

- Tenants or residents questioning their bills, often the first sign of mapping or ratio errors.
- Ratings that change sharply without a physical change to the building.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-meters add up to much more or less than the main meter | Ratio, polarity or mapping errors, or missing meters | Reconciliation; spot load checks |
| Negative or reversed readings | Current transformer installed backwards | Inspection |
| Tenant consumption far from expected | Wrong circuits measured | Load tracing |
| Data flat for weeks | Communications or battery failure | Gateway status |
| Billing disputes | Mapping errors or unapproved meters | Audit |

> Reconciling sub-meters against the main meter is the quickest test of a metering system. Any significant unexplained difference means something is wrong in the meters, the mapping or the data.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing with unapproved meters or under embedded network rules not met | deadline | Rectify to the legal requirement |
| Metering system failed; no data for billing | failure | Restore now |
| Mapping errors; ratio and polarity faults; data gaps | condition | Correct in the near term |
| Meters at end of life or on retiring networks | lifecycle | Replace |
| No reconciliation or metering schedule | check | Audit |
| Accurate and reconciled | nil | Routine |

Metering findings are rarely about physical safety; their weight comes from money and compliance, because errors in billing meters affect every tenant's charges and errors in monitoring meters undermine ratings and performance standard reporting.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer or metering specialist, with legal advice where billing or embedded networks are involved.

- Metering audit: inventory of every meter with type, approval, location, what it measures and how it communicates.
- Reconciliation of sub-meters against the main meter over a representative period.
- Spot checks of current transformer ratios, polarity and the circuits measured, by clamp measurement.
- Mapping verification against current single-line diagrams and tenancy layouts.
- Data review for gaps and failures.
- Compliance review of billing meters and embedded network obligations.

The report should give a corrected metering schedule, faults found, compliance status and a remediation plan.

Reconciliation over several weeks, comparing sub-meter totals with the main meter by hour, separates constant errors (ratios, missing meters) from intermittent ones (communications, failing meters).

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Correct installation faults: ratios, polarity and circuit allocation.
- Update mapping and labelling after fit-outs, and make this part of every fit-out sign-off.
- Replace meters that are not approved for billing, are inaccurate or are on retiring networks.
- Improve communications and set alarms for data gaps.
- Add meters where ratings or performance standards need end-use data.
- Embedded network compliance or exit, depending on obligations and economics.

- Commissioning standard: require every new or moved meter to be commissioned with a clamp-meter check of ratio, polarity and circuit, and recorded in the metering schedule.
- Validation rules in the data platform that flag gaps, flat lines, negative readings and reconciliation differences automatically.
- Tenant recharge corrections: recalculate past bills where errors are found, and agree adjustments.
- Open data formats so metering data can move between platforms when vendors change.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Meter corrections are itemised. Meter replacement and additions are per meter plus installation and communications. Data platforms are recurring subscriptions. Errors corrected in tenant recharges can produce refunds or recoveries.

Billing compliance is code compliance; metering for ratings is often code compliance or improvement; replacement is lifecycle; corrections are repairs and maintenance.

Correcting long-standing billing errors can involve refunds to tenants for overcharging or unrecovered costs for undercharging, which may exceed the cost of fixing the meters.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Meters used for trade must meet national measurement law administered by the National Measurement Institute; embedded networks are regulated by the Australian Energy Regulator with state rules, and Victoria is restricting new embedded networks in residential buildings; NABERS requires metering to rate buildings; the National Construction Code requires energy monitoring facilities in larger new buildings.
- United Kingdom. The Measuring Instruments Regulations 2016 govern billing meters; the Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations 2014 require meters on heat networks; Approved Document L and CIBSE TM39 guide metering in non-domestic buildings.
- United States. State public utility commissions regulate sub-metering and re-billing of utilities to residents; weights and measures authorities oversee meter accuracy; benchmarking and building performance standards in many cities require whole-building data that sub-metering supports.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Metering schedule and single-line diagrams.
- Meter approvals and verification certificates for billing meters.
- Reconciliation reports.
- Tenant recharge methods and disputes.
- Embedded network registrations, exemptions and compliance records.
- Data platform contracts and access.

- Commissioning records for each meter.
- Data platform validation reports.
- Records of loads added since metering was designed.

pages.title: Terminal Units
pages.question: How do fan coils, VAV boxes and chilled beams fail, and how do you assess hundreds of them?
pages.answer: Terminal units fail by population. Fan coil condensate drains block and leak into ceilings; VAV dampers stick and airflow sensors drift, so zones get too much or too little air; reheat valves stick and heat and cool together. Chilled beams drip when water is below room dew point. Behind most comfort complaints is a mix of failed actuators, drifted sensors and controls overrides. Assess them by sample and controls data, not one by one.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about terminal units; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: FCUs, VAV boxes, chilled beams

sources.title: Guideline 36: High-Performance Sequences of Operation for HVAC Systems

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Terminal units deliver heating and cooling to individual zones from the central plant and air handling system. They are numerous: a single office floor can have dozens, and a tower hundreds. Their condition is assessed as a population, by sample and by controls data, rather than one by one.

| Type | Where it is found | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan coil unit (FCU), two-pipe or four-pipe | Offices, hotels, apartments, from the 1960s | A fan blows room air over chilled and heating water coils; condensate drains from a pan |
| Variable air volume (VAV) box, with or without reheat | Offices from the 1980s | A damper varies supply air to a zone; a controller reads airflow and room temperature |
| Fan-powered VAV box | Offices, especially in the United States | VAV box with a fan mixing plenum air |
| Active chilled beam | Offices and laboratories from the 2000s | Primary air induces room air over a chilled water coil; no fan, no drain |
| Passive chilled beam or chilled ceiling | Offices | Natural convection over chilled water coils or panels |
| Induction unit | Offices of the 1960s and 1970s | High-pressure primary air induces room air over a coil; perimeter units under windows |
| Perimeter heating: radiators, convectors, trench heaters | All building types | Hot water or electric heating at the façade |
| Constant volume reheat boxes | Older offices, laboratories | Constant airflow with reheat |

Terminal units are where the tenant meets the building's systems, so they are often relocated, added and altered in fit-outs. Lease make-good obligations frequently cover them, and their ownership and maintenance responsibility can be split between owner and tenant.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan coil units | 15 to 20 years | Fan motors; coils; drain pans |
| FCU fan motors | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| VAV box casing and damper | 20 to 30 years | Rarely limiting |
| VAV controllers and actuators | 10 to 15 years | Electronics obsolescence |
| Airflow sensors | 10 to 20 years, with recalibration | Dust fouling; drift |
| Chilled beams | 25 to 30 years | Coil cleaning; condensation control |
| Induction units | 25 to 35 years | Mostly at end of life now |
| Control valves and actuators | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |

What shortens life:

- Blocked condensate drains on fan coils.
- Lack of filter maintenance in fan coils.
- Poor water treatment, which blocks small coils and valves.
- Fit-out changes that relocate units, cut ductwork and lose commissioning.
- Obsolete controllers that cannot be replaced like for like.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Fan coil condensate failures

Fan coil drain pans block with dust and slime, overflow, and drip into ceilings and onto fit-outs; pans corrode; drain pipework sags and holds water. Water damage to ceilings below fan coils is one of the commonest maintenance calls in office buildings, and the pans are also a microbial growth site.

### Fan coil fan and coil faults

Fan motors fail and bearings get noisy; filters clog and dust fouls coils; small coils block with sludge from poorly treated water; valves stick.

### VAV box faults

Damper actuators fail, leaving boxes stuck open or closed; airflow sensors foul and drift so the controller delivers the wrong airflow; reheat valves stick open so the box heats and cools at once, wasting energy; controllers lose communication or become unsupported. Many problems hide behind controls overrides.

### Chilled beam condensation

Chilled beams have no drain. If the chilled water supply is colder than the room dew point, they condense and drip. They depend on dew point control and on dry primary air; failures of either cause dripping.

### Induction unit faults

Induction units at the perimeter suffer blocked nozzles, fouled coils, noisy high-pressure primary air and leaking valves. Many are fifty years old, and some contain asbestos in linings and insulation.

### Controls and commissioning drift

Over years of fit-outs and maintenance, setpoints drift, schedules are overridden, zones are put in manual, and units fight each other (one heating while its neighbour cools). The equipment works but the building performs badly.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### In the building

- Stained ceiling tiles below fan coils; water marks on fit-outs.
- Hot and cold complaints concentrated in particular zones.
- Noise from fan coils; draughts from diffusers.
- Musty smells from fan coils.

### At the units (sample)

- Drain pans: standing water, slime, corrosion.
- Filters: overloaded, missing.
- Coils: dust, corrosion, leaks.
- Actuators: position against command.
- Labels and controller types; asbestos in induction units.

### In the BMS

- Zones in manual override.
- VAV boxes at full open (starved) or minimum (oversupplied).
- Reheat valves open while cooling.
- Controllers offline.
- Temperature trends showing persistent deviations.

### In the records

- Maintenance logs and reactive call-outs for leaks and comfort.
- Test and balance reports after fit-outs.
- Controller types and support status.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling stains below fan coils | Blocked or overflowing condensate drain | Drain pan inspection |
| Zone too hot, VAV box at full open | Box undersized for the load, or upstream supply starved | Airflow measurement; load change |
| Zone too cold, VAV box at minimum | Minimum airflow too high or reheat failed | Settings; reheat valve |
| Heating and cooling at the same time | Reheat valve stuck or controls fighting | BMS trends |
| Dripping from chilled beams | Chilled water below room dew point | Water temperature; humidity; dew point control |
| Many zones in manual override | Controls problems worked around | BMS point list |

> Terminal units are assessed as a population. A sample inspection plus controls data tells you more than inspecting every unit, and the controls data usually shows where the problems are.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water leaking onto electrical equipment; asbestos in deteriorating induction units | safety | Isolate now |
| Widespread leaks damaging fit-outs | failure | Clear drains and repair now |
| Many units with failed actuators, drifted sensors or blocked drains | condition | Programme in the near term |
| Units at end of life; unsupported controllers | lifecycle | Plan replacement, often floor by floor |
| No sample inspection; controls data unavailable | check | Sample inspection and controls audit |
| Isolated faults | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with the controls contractor operating the BMS during the inspection.

- Sample inspection of a representative share of units of each type on each floor, weighted to areas with complaints and leaks: drain pans and drains, filters, coils, fans and motors, valves and actuators, controllers, casing and insulation.
- Functional testing through the BMS: command a sample of VAV dampers, valves and fans and confirm the response at the unit; read airflow and temperature against setpoints.
- Controls audit: overrides, alarms, offline controllers, trend data for zone temperatures and VAV damper positions, controller models and vendor support.
- Airflow measurement at a sample of VAV boxes and diffusers; comparison with test and balance records.
- Comfort survey and complaint analysis to locate problem zones.
- Asbestos check of induction units and older fan coils.
- Fit-out review: changes to layouts, ceilings and ductwork since commissioning.

The report should give fault rates by type and floor, controller support status, the controls faults found in the trends, safety items, and a strategy: repair and recommission, retrofit controls, or replace floor by floor.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Drain programme: clean and treat fan coil drain pans and drains on a schedule; fix falls and traps; condensate overflow switches on units above sensitive areas.
- Fan motor upgrade to electronically commutated motors, cutting energy and noise.
- Coil cleaning and filter regime.
- Controls retrofit: replace unsupported unitary controllers and actuators with open-protocol controllers, often in the same programme as a BMS upgrade.
- Airflow sensor recalibration and test and balance.
- Recommissioning: setpoints, deadbands, schedules, and sequences to stop simultaneous heating and cooling.
- Chilled beam protection: dew point control and condensation sensors.
- Replacement floor by floor, timed with lease expiries and fit-outs, sometimes moving from fan coils to VAV or chilled beams.
- Induction unit replacement with asbestos removal and new perimeter systems.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Sample inspection and controls audits are lump sums. Repairs and motor replacements are per unit. Controls retrofits are per unit or per floor. Replacement is per unit or per floor including ceiling works, ductwork and pipework connections, controls and commissioning, and is usually timed with tenancy changes. Lease make-good obligations can carry part of the cost of units altered by tenants.

Replacement is lifecycle; repairs, recommissioning and drain maintenance are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 1668.2 sets ventilation and AS/NZS 3666 microbial control for air-handling systems including terminal units; NABERS Energy and Indoor Environment ratings reflect terminal unit and controls performance; lease make-good clauses commonly address tenant alterations to terminal units.
- United Kingdom. Approved Documents F and L apply; the British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations for office conditions; BESA TR/19 covers hygiene; air-conditioning energy inspections apply to systems over 12 kW.
- United States. ASHRAE 55 sets thermal comfort, 62.1 ventilation and 90.1 energy, and Guideline 36 sets VAV and other terminal sequences; state energy codes such as California's Title 24 add requirements.

Asbestos rules in all three jurisdictions govern work on older induction units and fan coils with asbestos-containing linings or insulation.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Maintenance logs and reactive call-out records, especially for leaks and comfort.
- Test and balance reports, original and after fit-outs.
- BMS point lists and trend data for zones and terminal units.
- Controller types, firmware and vendor support status.
- Asbestos register for older units.
- Fit-out records and lease make-good obligations.
- Comfort survey or complaint records.

pages.title: Trade Waste Systems
pages.question: How do grease arrestors and other trade waste devices fail, and when do they put the building in breach?
pages.answer: Trade waste devices fail by being too small, too full or bypassed. An arrestor sized for a café cannot treat a busy restaurant; missed pump-outs leave grease and solids filling the tank and turning septic; hydrogen sulphide corrodes concrete and baffles until grease passes straight through; fit-outs connect dishwashers around it. Utilities then issue notices and fines. Blockages downstream of an arrestor point at the arrestor; upstream, at kitchens or drains.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about trade waste systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Grease arrestors, interceptors

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Trade waste systems treat liquid waste from commercial and industrial activities before it enters the public sewer, so fats, oils, solids and chemicals do not block sewers or harm treatment plants. They are governed by agreements or consents with the water utility that set what may be discharged, how it must be treated, and how often treatment devices must be emptied and sampled.

| Device | Where it is found | What it removes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease arrestors (grease traps, grease interceptors) | Restaurants, food courts, hotels, hospitals, schools, aged care | Fats, oils and grease from kitchens |
| Oil and silt interceptors (light liquid separators) | Car parks, car washes, workshops, fuel areas, loading docks | Oils, fuels and sediment |
| Silt and plaster traps | Workshops, dental and craft rooms | Solids |
| Lint traps | Commercial laundries | Fibres |
| Neutralising or dilution pits | Laboratories, schools, hospitals | Acids and alkalis |
| Dosing and pre-treatment plant | Industrial processes | Process contaminants |

Most arrestors are concrete, steel or plastic tanks in the ground or in basements, with baffles that slow the flow so grease floats and solids settle. They work only if they are sized for the flow and emptied before they fill. When a tenancy changes from a café to a high-volume restaurant, the arrestor that served the café can be overwhelmed.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete grease arrestors | 20 to 40 years | Hydrogen sulphide and acid attack on concrete |
| Steel arrestors | 15 to 25 years | Internal corrosion |
| Plastic and fibreglass arrestors | 25 to 40 years | Ground movement; lid damage |
| Oil interceptors | 25 to 40 years | Alarms; baffles; coalescer media |
| Baffles and internal fittings | 10 to 20 years | Corrosion |
| Access covers | 15 to 30 years | Traffic loads; corrosion |

What shortens life:

- Infrequent pump-outs, which leave acidic, septic waste in contact with concrete and steel for long periods.
- Hot water and chemical cleaners discharged into arrestors, which carry grease straight through and attack the tank.
- Traffic loads on covers not rated for vehicles.
- Undersizing for the current use, so devices are overloaded continuously.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Overload and undersizing

An arrestor sized for a small café cannot treat the flow from a commercial kitchen. Grease passes through to the sewer, blocking the building's drains and the public sewer, and the utility issues notices or fines. Food court and multi-tenancy buildings often have shared arrestors whose capacity was set for an earlier tenant mix.

### Missed pump-outs

Arrestors must be emptied at a frequency set by the utility or the agreement. When pump-outs lapse, grease and solids fill the tank, overflow to the sewer, and turn septic and odorous.

### Corrosion of the tank

Hydrogen sulphide and acids from decomposing waste attack concrete above the liquid line and corrode steel baffles and fittings. Corroded baffles let grease pass straight through; failed walls leak into the ground.

### Bypasses and wrong connections

Dishwashers, floor wastes and sinks connected around the arrestor, or arrestors bypassed after blockages, discharge untreated waste. Connections added in fit-outs are a common source.

### Odour and gas

Septic arrestors release odours into kitchens, basements and public areas through failed seals and lids. Hydrogen sulphide makes arrestor pits dangerous confined spaces.

### Cover failures

Covers in car parks and service lanes crack and break under vehicles, creating trip and fall hazards and letting stormwater in.

### Oil interceptor faults

Oil interceptors fill with oil and silt, alarms fail, and coalescer media clog. A full interceptor discharges oil to the sewer or stormwater system, which is an environmental offence.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Arrestor location, size and covers; odour around lids.
- Fat build-up in kitchen drains and frequent blockages downstream of kitchens.
- Pump-out labels or dockets; date of the last service.
- Oil interceptor alarms and level indicators.
- Cracked or rocking covers in trafficked areas.
- Dishwashers and floor wastes connected directly to the sewer.

### In the records

- Trade waste agreement or consent with discharge limits.
- Pump-out dockets and frequency.
- Utility notices, sampling results and fines.
- Tenant kitchen specifications.
- Drain blockage history.

- Kitchen staff pouring fat, oil and food scraps into sinks rather than collecting them, a management issue that overloads even well-sized arrestors.
- Sewer overflows or utility crews attending blockages in the street outside the building.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease blockages in drains downstream of the arrestor | Arrestor undersized, full or with corroded baffles | Size against flow; pump-out dates; internal inspection |
| Grease blockages upstream of the arrestor | Kitchen practices or drain defects | CCTV; kitchen practices |
| Strong odour at lids | Septic arrestor from infrequent pump-outs, or failed seals | Pump-out records; seal inspection |
| Utility notice for high fats in discharge | Overload or bypass | Sampling; connection survey |
| Oil sheen at stormwater outlets from a car park | Full or bypassed oil interceptor | Interceptor levels |
| Broken covers | Covers not rated for traffic | Cover rating |

> Grease blockages downstream of an arrestor point at the arrestor; blockages upstream point at kitchen practices or the drains. The location tells you which to fix.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken covers in trafficked areas; hydrogen sulphide exposure; oil discharging to stormwater | safety | Make safe and contain now |
| Arrestor overflowing; sewer blocked | failure | Pump out and clear now |
| Utility notice or agreement requiring upgrade or sampling | deadline | By the utility's date |
| Corroded baffles and tank; undersized for current use | condition | Repair or upgrade in the near term |
| Arrestor at end of life | lifecycle | Replace |
| No trade waste agreement; capacity not checked after tenancy changes | check | Assess |
| Normal | nil | Routine pump-outs |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber with liquid waste contractor support; confined space procedures for entry.

- Inventory of every pre-treatment device, its size, material, age and what it serves.
- Capacity check of each arrestor against the current kitchen fixtures, meals and flow, using the utility's sizing method.
- Internal inspection after pump-out: walls, baffles, inlet and outlet fittings, seals and covers.
- Connection survey by dye testing to confirm every fixture that should discharge through the arrestor does, and nothing bypasses it.
- Records review: trade waste agreements, pump-out frequency against requirements, utility sampling and notices.
- Oil interceptor checks: levels, alarms, media and outlet condition.
- Cover load ratings against the traffic over them.

The report should state compliance with the utility's requirements, capacity against current use, condition, bypasses, and the works and pump-out frequency needed.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Pump-out regime set to the utility's requirement and the actual loading, with dockets kept on site.
- Upsizing or additional arrestors where tenancies have outgrown the existing devices, usually as a condition of the new tenancy.
- Internal repair: replace corroded baffles and fittings; reline concrete tanks with acid-resistant linings.
- Replacement with plastic or fibreglass units where concrete or steel tanks have failed.
- Connection corrections: route dishwashers, floor wastes and sinks through the arrestor and remove bypasses.
- Heavy-duty covers rated for the traffic, with gas-tight seals.
- Oil interceptor servicing: emptying, media replacement and alarm repair.
- Tenant obligations: lease clauses requiring tenants to maintain their devices and fund upgrades their use requires.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Pump-outs recur at the required frequency and are usually a tenant or service charge cost. Internal repairs and relining are lump sums per device. Replacement or upsizing is a lump sum including excavation in kitchens, basements or car parks, which can disrupt tenants. Utility fees and fines are operating costs that capital works avoid. Cover replacement is per cover.

Utility-required upgrades carry deadlines; replacement is lifecycle; pump-outs and repairs are repairs and maintenance; tenant-driven upsizing should sit with the tenancy.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. Water utilities set trade waste requirements through agreements or permits, with arrestor sizing, pump-out frequencies and sampling (for example Sydney Water and the Melbourne retailers); AS/NZS 3500.2 governs the plumbing; confined space entry follows AS 2865.
- United Kingdom. Discharges of trade effluent need consent from the water company under the Water Industry Act 1991; grease separators follow BS EN 1825 and light liquid separators BS EN 858; local authorities enforce on food premises where fats block sewers.
- United States. Local pretreatment programmes under the Clean Water Act and municipal fats, oils and grease ordinances set requirements; plumbing codes set grease interceptor sizing; oil separators follow local and environmental rules.

Lease terms matter in all three jurisdictions: in multi-tenant buildings, the agreement is often in the owner's name while tenants generate the waste, so leases should allocate pump-out, upgrade and fine costs to the tenant whose use requires them.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Trade waste agreements, permits or consents, with discharge limits.
- Pump-out dockets for the last two years.
- Utility notices, sampling results and any fines.
- Drawings showing arrestors and the fixtures connected to them.
- Tenant kitchen fit-out specifications.
- Drain blockage history downstream of kitchens.
- Oil interceptor service and alarm records.

pages.title: Upper Floor Slabs & Structures
pages.question: How do upper floors fail, and when does a change of use overload them?
pages.answer: Floors fail from overload, alterations and water. Mobile shelving, archives, plant and water features can exceed design loads; concrete floors keep deflecting for years and crack partitions below; coring without scanning cuts post-tensioning tendons; water corrodes composite decking; timber joists are notched by trades and decay at damp bearings. Check design loads against current use before accepting heavy tenants or equipment.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about upper floor slabs & structures; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Concrete, composite, or timber-joisted floor structures

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Upper floors carry occupants, furniture, partitions, storage and equipment and transfer them to beams, walls and columns. They are reinforced concrete flat slabs or beam-and-slab floors, post-tensioned slabs, precast hollowcore planks, composite slabs on steel decking, timber joists and boards, and, more recently, cross-laminated timber panels. Each has characteristic weaknesses: deflection and cracking in concrete, tendons in post-tensioned slabs, bearings in precast, corrosion of decking, and notching, decay and bounce in timber.

| Type | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete flat and beam-and-slab floors | Offices, apartments, institutions | Deflection; cracking; corrosion in wet areas |
| Post-tensioned slabs | Offices, apartments, car parks from the 1970s | Tendons cut during alterations; anchorage corrosion |
| Precast hollowcore planks | Commercial and residential from the 1970s | Bearing length; cutting; water in cores |
| Composite slabs on steel decking | Steel-framed offices and car parks | Decking corrosion; holes cut through ribs |
| Timber joists and boards | Houses, terraces, older commercial | Notching and drilling; decay at bearings; bounce |
| Cross-laminated timber | New mid-rise buildings | Moisture; vibration; fire protection |

Floors are designed for imposed loads that depend on use: offices, homes, assembly areas, storage, libraries and plant rooms all differ. A change of use or tenant can put loads on a floor that were never designed for it, particularly compactus and mobile shelving, archives, server racks, gym equipment and water tanks.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete floors | Life of the building | Water; alterations; overload |
| Post-tensioned slabs | Life of the building if tendons protected | Water at anchorages; alterations |
| Hollowcore planks | Life of the building | Bearings; cutting |
| Composite decking | 40 to 80 years | Corrosion where wet |
| Timber joists | 80 to 150 years if dry | Decay; notching; insects |
| Floor screeds and toppings | 20 to 50 years | Cracking; debonding |

What shortens life:

- Overload from changed uses, storage and heavy equipment.
- Alterations: openings cut, cores drilled, joists notched for services.
- Water from leaking wet areas, roofs and plant.
- Long-term creep in concrete, which keeps deflections growing for years.

Floors rarely reach the end of their structural life; their limits come from the loads placed on them and the holes cut through them.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Deflection and creep

Concrete floors continue to deflect for years after construction as concrete creeps. Long spans and thin slabs sag; partitions below crack, doors bind, and on balconies and podiums water ponds. Deflection is usually a serviceability problem, but large or increasing deflection can signal loss of capacity.

### Overload from changed use

Mobile shelving, archives, plant, water features and heavy equipment can exceed design loads by a wide margin. Overloaded floors crack and deflect, and in extreme cases fail.

### Post-tensioned tendon damage

Drilling and coring into post-tensioned slabs without scanning can cut tendons, releasing them violently and removing part of the slab's capacity. Water reaching unbonded tendon anchorages at slab edges corrodes them.

### Hollowcore and precast issues

Precast planks need adequate bearing on supports; short bearings and planks cut near their ends for services are vulnerable. Water trapped in hollow cores freezes or corrodes strands.

### Composite decking corrosion

Steel decking under composite slabs corrodes where water leaks through from wet areas, car park decks or roofs, losing its role as reinforcement.

### Timber floor defects

Joists are notched and drilled by plumbers and electricians, cutting through critical zones; joist ends decay where they bear on damp walls; floors are springy or bouncy where joists are undersized or have lost strutting; insects attack timber.

### Vibration

Light, long-span floors in timber, steel and post-tensioned concrete can be lively under footfall, a comfort problem that matters for sensitive uses such as laboratories and hospitals.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Floors noticeably sloping or sagging; ponding on balconies and podiums.
- Cracks in partitions and ceilings below; doors binding.
- Cracks on slab soffits; rust staining from decking or reinforcement.
- Heavy storage, mobile shelving, plant or water features on upper floors.
- Cored holes and cut openings in slabs.
- Notched and drilled joists; springy floors; decay at joist ends.

### In the records

- Structural drawings with design loads.
- Post-tensioning drawings.
- Records of coring and openings.
- Change of use approvals.
- Floor loading notices.

- Load notices on floors and racking, or their absence where heavy storage is present.
- Patched or filled holes in slabs whose history is unknown.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sagging mid-span and cracked partitions below | Creep deflection or overload | Level survey; load review |
| Cracks under heavy storage areas | Overload | Loads against design |
| Broken concrete around a cored hole | Tendon or reinforcement cut | Scanning; drawings |
| Rust staining on decking soffits | Water through the slab above | Leak source above |
| Springy timber floor | Undersized joists, lost strutting, or notching | Inspection |
| Lively floor under footfall | Low stiffness and mass | Vibration measurement |

> Never core, drill or cut into a floor slab until tendons and reinforcement have been located by drawings and scanning. Cutting a post-tensioning tendon is dangerous and reduces capacity.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floors overloaded beyond design; cut tendons; severe decay at joist bearings | safety | Remove loads or prop now |
| Significant deflection or cracking from overload or damage | failure | Strengthen or repair now |
| Decking corrosion; notched joists; creep deflection affecting finishes | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Screeds and toppings at end of life | lifecycle | Renew |
| Design loads unknown for current or proposed use | check | Assess capacity |
| Minor shrinkage cracking | nil | Monitor |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer, with scanning specialists for coring and concrete testing as needed.

- Load review: current and proposed uses against design loads, including specific heavy items.
- Level survey of deflections, repeated over time where growth is suspected.
- Scanning of slabs to locate tendons and reinforcement.
- Condition survey of soffits, decking, bearings and timber.
- Opening up of timber floors to inspect joists and bearings.
- Vibration measurement for sensitive uses.
- Capacity assessment for the intended use.

The report should state floor capacity against use, condition, any overload or damage, and strengthening options.

- Load testing in special cases where calculations cannot confirm capacity, carried out under engineering control.
- Cores and concrete testing to confirm strength and reinforcement where drawings are missing.

Investigations are best timed before a lease commits to a use, so capacity limits are known at negotiation.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Load control: relocate heavy items over beams and columns, limit storage, post load notices.
- Strengthening: fibre-reinforced polymer on concrete, added steel beams, additional supports.
- Tendon repair by specialists where tendons have been cut or anchorages corroded.
- Decking repair and stopping leaks from above.
- Timber floor repair: sister or replace joists, restore strutting, repair bearings, replace decayed timber.
- Vibration control: added stiffness or mass, tuned mass dampers for special cases.
- Penetration controls: scanning and engineering for every new hole.

- Tenant controls: lease clauses setting floor load limits and requiring engineering approval for heavy equipment and storage.
- Screed and topping replacement where cracked or debonded toppings add load without strength.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment is a lump sum. Strengthening is priced per element or as a lump sum. Timber repairs per joist or per area. Load relocation is an operational cost. Scanning per area or per location.

Strengthening for a new use sits with the change of use; repairs are condition items; safety items are immediate.

The cost of a heavy-use tenancy often includes structural strengthening that should be recovered through the lease rather than absorbed by the owner. Scanning before every coring job is inexpensive compared with repairing a cut tendon.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 1170.1 sets imposed floor loads by use; AS 3600 governs concrete and AS 1684 and AS 1720 timber; a change of use needs building approval showing the structure is adequate.
- United Kingdom. BS EN 1991-1-1 sets imposed loads; Approved Document A applies to material changes of use; the Concrete Society publishes guidance on post-tensioned floors.
- United States. ASCE 7 sets live loads; the International Existing Building Code governs changes of occupancy; ACI 318 governs concrete design.

In all three jurisdictions, leases and building management rules commonly set floor loading limits, and strata or condominium by-laws restrict alterations that cut slabs. Changes of use (for example, office to residential, or office to laboratory) trigger structural review under each country's rules for existing buildings, and may require strengthening before approval. Post-tensioned slabs need specialist contractors for any repair or alteration.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Structural drawings with design loads.
- Post-tensioning drawings.
- Coring and opening records.
- Change of use approvals.
- Floor load notices and tenant equipment schedules.

- Lease clauses on floor loads.
- Engineering approvals for heavy tenant equipment.
- Deflection monitoring records where available.
- Timber pest and decay reports for timber floors.

pages.title: Ventilation Systems
pages.question: How do car park, kitchen, laboratory and toilet exhaust systems fail, and which failures are safety findings?
pages.answer: Dedicated ventilation fails on hazards, not comfort. Kitchen ducts accumulate grease beyond the hood and catch fire; car park CO sensors drift so fans do not start, or run constantly and mask the fault; fume cupboards lose face velocity and alarms get silenced. Toilet exhaust ducts disconnect and dump moisture into voids. Large exhaust without make-up air pulls flue gases back into buildings. Most of these systems have prescribed testing or cleaning intervals.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ventilation systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Car park, toilet, miscellaneous exhaust, kitchen exhaust, fume cupboards

sources.title: NFPA 96 Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Ventilation systems here are the dedicated supply and exhaust systems that serve particular spaces and hazards, separate from the general air conditioning: car park ventilation, toilet and bathroom exhaust, commercial kitchen exhaust, laboratory fume cupboards and fume extraction, garbage room and plant room exhaust, local exhaust ventilation for workshops, and whole-dwelling mechanical ventilation in apartments. Smoke exhaust and stair pressurisation for fire are covered on the fire services pages.

| System | Where it is found | What it protects against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car park ventilation (ducted or jet fans), often with CO control | Basement and enclosed car parks | Carbon monoxide and vehicle exhaust |
| Toilet and bathroom exhaust | All buildings | Odour and moisture; mould |
| Commercial kitchen exhaust (hood, grease filters, ductwork, fan) | Restaurants, hotels, hospitals, schools | Grease, heat, smoke; grease fires in ductwork |
| Fume cupboards and lab exhaust | Laboratories, schools, hospitals | Toxic and flammable vapours |
| Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) | Workshops, industrial processes | Dust, fume and vapour at source |
| Garbage and plant room exhaust | Apartments, commercial | Odour; heat; refrigerant |
| Whole-dwelling mechanical ventilation (MVHR, continuous extract) | Newer apartments, especially in Britain | Indoor air quality and condensation in airtight dwellings |
| Make-up air | Kitchens, labs, large exhaust systems | Balances exhaust so the building is not starved of air |

Many of these are life-safety or occupational health systems with statutory testing regimes: car park ventilation and kitchen exhaust are commonly essential safety measures; fume cupboards and LEV have periodic test requirements; kitchen exhaust cleaning frequencies are prescribed by standards and insurers.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust fans (general) | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; corrosion in wet exhaust |
| Car park jet fans | 15 to 20 years | Moisture; exhaust contaminants |
| CO sensors | 5 to 10 years, with calibration | Sensor technology; drift |
| Kitchen exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Grease; heat |
| Kitchen exhaust ductwork (welded steel) | 25 to 40 years | Cleaning access; grease fires |
| Fume cupboards | 15 to 25 years | Chemicals; sash mechanisms; controls |
| MVHR units | 15 to 20 years | Filter maintenance; fan motors |

What shortens life:

- Grease build-up in kitchen exhaust.
- Corrosive vapours in laboratory and wet area exhausts.
- Lack of maintenance on systems that run out of sight.
- Changes of use: a car park converted to storage, a kitchen with heavier cooking, a lab with new chemicals.
- Disconnected ductwork in risers and ceilings.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Car park ventilation failures

Carbon monoxide sensors drift or fail, so fans either do not start when they should (CO builds up) or run continuously (wasting energy and masking the fault). Jet fans corrode in damp basements and are disabled when noisy. Supply air paths are blocked by storage or doors kept shut.

### Kitchen exhaust grease

Grease condenses in hoods, filters, ductwork and fans. Without regular cleaning to the full length of the duct, it accumulates to the point where a flare-up at the cooker ignites the duct. Kitchen duct fires spread through buildings, which is why cleaning frequencies are set by cooking volume and type.

### Fume cupboard failures

Face velocity falls as fans wear, ducts leak or the building's pressure regime changes; sashes stick; alarms are silenced; cupboards are used for chemicals they were not designed for. Exhaust discharged too low or near intakes re-enters the building.

### Toilet and bathroom exhaust failures

Fans fail, ducts disconnect in ceilings and risers, and moisture is discharged into roof spaces and voids instead of outside, causing mould and decay.

### Make-up air imbalance

Large exhaust without matching make-up air puts the building under negative pressure: doors slam or resist opening, flues backdraught (pulling combustion gases into the building), and dust and contaminants are drawn in through the envelope.

### Exhaust re-entry

Exhausts discharging near air intakes, operable windows or terraces re-enter the building. Kitchen odour, car park fumes and laboratory vapours are the usual complaints.

### Dwelling ventilation failures

MVHR filters are never changed, fans are switched off by residents because of noise, and boost controls do not work; condensation and mould follow in airtight apartments.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Car park: CO sensor locations and calibration labels; jet fans running or dead; storage blocking airflow.
- Kitchen: grease on hoods, filters and accessible duct sections; fan casing grease; cleaning labels.
- Labs: fume cupboard test labels, face velocity alarms, sash condition.
- Bathrooms: fans running; condensation and mould; discharge points on façades and roofs.
