- Exhaust discharges relative to intakes and windows.
- Doors slamming or hard to open (pressure imbalance).

### In the records

- Essential safety measure records for car park and kitchen exhaust.
- Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates and frequencies.
- Fume cupboard and LEV test reports.
- CO sensor calibration records.
- Complaints of odour or fumes.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car park fans never run | CO sensors failed or disabled | Calibration records; sensor test |
| Car park fans always run | Sensors failed safe, or controls overridden | BMS; sensor test |
| Grease visible in ducts beyond the hood | Cleaning frequency or extent inadequate | Cleaning records; inspection |
| Fume cupboard alarms silenced | Low face velocity | Face velocity test |
| Mould in bathrooms and roof spaces | Exhaust failed or discharging into voids | Fan and duct inspection |
| Odour in occupied areas | Exhaust re-entry or negative pressure | Discharge locations; pressure test |
| Flue spillage from appliances | Negative pressure from exhaust | Combustion and pressure test |

> Kitchen exhaust ductwork with grease beyond the hood, car park ventilation that does not respond to carbon monoxide, and fume cupboards that fail face velocity tests are safety findings, not maintenance items.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease build-up in kitchen ductwork; car park ventilation not responding to CO; fume cupboard failing test; flue spillage from negative pressure | safety | Stop use or clean and repair now |
| Kitchen exhaust cleaning, fume cupboard or LEV testing due | deadline | At the prescribed interval |
| Fans failed; exhaust disconnected | failure | Repair now |
| Sensors drifting; fans worn; poor balance | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Systems at end of life | lifecycle | Replace on cycle |
| No records for safety-related systems | check | Test and inspect |
| Normal wear | nil | Routine maintenance |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer, with specialists for kitchen exhaust, fume cupboards and LEV.

- Records review: essential safety measures, cleaning certificates, test reports, calibration records.
- Car park: CO sensor tests with calibration gas, fan operation, airflow paths.
- Kitchen exhaust: inspection of hood, filters, the full length of ductwork through access panels, fan; grease depth measured.
- Fume cupboards: face velocity and containment testing to the relevant standard; alarm function.
- LEV: thorough examination and test of capture and airflow.
- Toilet exhaust: sample airflow checks; riser and duct inspection.
- Pressure regime: building pressure relative to outside; make-up air.
- Discharge review: distances to intakes and windows.

The report should give the status of every safety-related system, test results, cleaning adequacy, and recommended works.

- Smoke test of exhaust discharges to see where plumes travel.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Car park: replace and calibrate CO sensors; repair or replace jet fans; clear airflow paths.
- Kitchen exhaust: clean the full system; add access panels; set cleaning frequency to cooking volume; replace fans; fire suppression in hoods.
- Fume cupboards: repair fans and ductwork; rebalance; replace cupboards; raise discharge stacks.
- Toilet exhaust: reconnect ducts; replace fans; extend discharges outside.
- Make-up air: add or rebalance.
- Discharge relocation away from intakes.
- MVHR: maintenance programmes; quieter fans; resident guidance.

Interactions: kitchen exhaust changes often require fire-rated duct enclosures and access panels through finished spaces; fume cupboard and lab exhaust changes need the whole lab pressure regime rebalanced; car park changes interact with smoke exhaust and fire systems.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Kitchen exhaust cleaning, fume cupboard and LEV testing, and CO sensor calibration are recurring contracts at prescribed frequencies. CO sensor replacement and fan replacement are itemised. Kitchen exhaust duct replacement, access panel installation and fire-rated enclosures are lump sums. Fume cupboard replacement is per cupboard, with ductwork and controls. Discharge relocation and make-up air systems are lump sums.

Testing, cleaning and safety rectification are code compliance and recur; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS 1668.2 sets ventilation including car parks with CO control; AS 1668.1 covers kitchen exhaust fire aspects; AS/NZS 2243.8 governs fume cupboards; car park and kitchen exhaust systems are commonly essential safety measures maintained under AS 1851 and state regulations.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document F; BESA TR/19 Grease sets kitchen extract cleaning frequencies; COSHH requires LEV thorough examination at least every 14 months; fume cupboards follow BS EN 14175.
- United States. NFPA 96 sets kitchen exhaust inspection frequencies (monthly for solid fuel cooking, quarterly for high volume, semi-annually for moderate, annually for low volume); the International Mechanical Code covers car park ventilation; ANSI/ASSP Z9.5 covers laboratory ventilation.

Planning conditions often govern kitchen exhaust discharge and odour control in all three countries.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Essential safety measure records and annual statements for car park and kitchen exhaust.
- Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates showing the extent cleaned, with frequency.
- Fume cupboard face velocity and containment test reports.
- LEV thorough examination reports.
- CO sensor calibration records and car park ventilation test records.
- Complaint records for odour, fumes or doors.
- Mechanical drawings showing exhaust discharge locations and air intakes.

pages.title: Verandahs, Balconies & Balustrades
pages.question: How do balconies, decks and balustrades fail, what are the warning signs, and which findings mean closing them?
pages.answer: Balconies fail where you cannot see: corroding top steel at the root of a concrete cantilever, decayed ledgers on timber decks, rusting post bases inside slab pockets, membranes leaking at thresholds. A cantilever tip lower than its root with cracking along the wall line, a balustrade that moves under hand pressure, or a missing toughened glass panel means closing it now. Older balustrades below current height are a risk even where upgrade is not mandated.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about verandahs, balconies & balustrades; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Structural integrity, railings, posts, decorative features

sources.title: BS 8579:2020 Guide to the design of balconies and terraces

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Balconies, verandahs and decks are elevated platforms attached to or projecting from a building, and balustrades are the barriers that stop people falling from them. They combine structure, waterproofing and a life-safety barrier in one element, often over occupied space or a footpath, which is why their failures are among the most serious on any building.

| Form | Where it is found | Critical points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cantilevered concrete slab continuous with the floor | Apartments and offices from the 1950s | Top reinforcement near the upper surface, under the tiles and membrane; the root where the slab passes the wall line |
| Steel or precast balconies bolted or hung on the frame | Apartments from the 1990s | Connection brackets and bolts; thermal break connectors |
| Timber deck on a ledger fixed to the house | Houses and townhouses | Ledger fixing to the wall; joist hangers; post bases; fasteners in treated timber |
| Post-supported balcony or verandah | Houses, heritage terraces, low-rise | Post bases and footings; beam connections; roof drainage on verandahs |
| Heritage verandah with cast iron or timber | Victorian and Edwardian terraces in Australia; heritage stock elsewhere | Cast iron corrosion and fracture; timber decay at post bases and floor edges |
| Juliet balcony | Apartments and houses | Fixings of a balustrade across an opening with no platform |

Balustrades are steel, aluminium, timber, masonry, wire or glass. Glass balustrades are either framed, point-fixed with clamps or spigots, or frameless in a base channel; the glass is toughened, laminated or toughened laminated. Older balustrades were often lower than current codes require and had horizontal rails children can climb; current codes in all three jurisdictions set minimum heights, limit openings, and in Australia restrict climbable elements where the fall is large.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete cantilever slab | 50 to 80 years and more | Cover to top steel; waterproofing over it; chloride exposure |
| Steel balcony frames and brackets | 40 to 60 years | Coating cycle; coastal exposure; water at connections |
| Timber deck structure | 15 to 30 years | Timber species and treatment; ground clearance; fastener corrosion |
| Membrane under tiles | 15 to 25 years | Falls, threshold height, outlets |
| Tiles and bedding | 20 to 30 years | Membrane condition; movement joints |
| Steel balustrades | 25 to 40 years | Paint or galvanising; post-base detail |
| Aluminium balustrades | 30 to 50 years | Finish; fixings; dissimilar metals |
| Glass balustrade fittings and glass | 25 to 40 years | Clamp and spigot corrosion; glass type; edge damage |

What shortens life:

- Water at the wrong level: flat or reversed falls, blocked outlets, low thresholds that let water run back to the door and the structure.
- Hollow posts cast into or grouted onto slabs, which fill with water and rust from inside.
- Treated timber with copper-based preservatives (ACQ and similar) that corrode plain galvanised nails, screws and hangers.
- Coastal exposure and spray from pools.
- Alterations by occupants: tiles laid over membranes without care, planters, spas, enclosures, fixings drilled through the membrane.
- Overloading: heavy planters, hot tubs and crowding on timber decks.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Cantilever reinforcement corrosion

A concrete cantilever carries its load in the top reinforcement, close to the upper surface. Water passing a failed membrane, chlorides from coastal air or old calcium chloride additives, or low cover lets that steel corrode. It loses section unseen at exactly the point of highest stress, the root at the wall line. The slab cracks along the wall line on its top surface, then rotates and sags at its tip; spalling appears on the soffit edge and at the front face.

### Ledger and connection failure

Timber decks most often collapse at the ledger, the beam fixed to the house wall. Nails withdraw, bolts corrode, and water trapped between ledger and wall decays both. Joist hangers corrode in treated timber. Collapse is sudden and typically happens when the deck is crowded.

### Membrane and threshold failure

Balconies over occupied space depend on a membrane under the tiles. It fails at the threshold where the door sill meets the balcony, at upstands, at outlets and at balustrade post fixings drilled through it. Water leaks into the unit below, saturates the screed, and on concrete balconies reaches the reinforcement.

### Balustrade post-base corrosion

Steel posts set in pockets or core holes in the slab fill with water, rust from inside, and burst the concrete around the base. The post looks sound above the floor and is loose at its root. Bolted base plates corrode under the plate.

### Glass balustrade failure

Monolithic toughened glass can break spontaneously from nickel sulphide inclusions and falls out of the frame as fragments, leaving no barrier. Laminated glass stays in place when broken. Clamps and spigots loosen and corrode; glass in base channels can rotate when the channel fixings or packers fail.

### Decay of timber verandahs and decks

Post bases in contact with soil or paving, floor board ends, and beams where water lodges decay first. Termites attack timber in contact with the ground in Australia.

### Cast iron and heritage elements

Cast iron lace, brackets and columns corrode and are brittle: they crack rather than bend, and a rusted fixing can let a heavy section fall. Verandah gutters and roofs overflow onto posts and floors.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From the street and from aerial imagery

- Balcony slab edges drooping relative to the floor line above or below; tips lower than roots.
- Spalling and rust staining on slab soffits and front edges; efflorescence on soffits.
- Rust at the base of balustrade posts; posts out of line; missing glass panels; replaced glass in a different tint.
- Balustrades visibly below the height of their neighbours or with horizontal rails.
- Timber decks with sagging joists, staining at the house wall line, decayed post bases.
- Heritage verandahs with missing lace, leaning posts, sagging beams.

### Close up on site

- Cracking on the top surface along the wall line; drummy tiles; tiles cracked in a line parallel to the wall.
- Movement of balustrades when pushed by hand; corrosion at post bases and clamps; cracked concrete around post pockets.
- Threshold height: water ponding against the door sill; falls towards the building.
- Ledger fixing type and condition; rust on hangers and fasteners; soft timber when probed.
- Glass type markings on balustrade panels; edge chips in toughened glass.

### Inside the building

- Leaks, staining and swelling of floor finishes at the balcony door; damp ceilings in the unit below.
- Cracks in internal finishes near the slab root on cantilevers.

### In the records

- Strata defect claims and leak logs concentrated at balconies.
- Balustrade certificates and glass specifications; any engineer's report on balconies.
- Occupant alteration approvals: tiling, enclosures, spas, planters.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crack along the wall line on the top surface; tip of the slab lower than its root | Top reinforcement corrosion or overload in a cantilever | Half-cell and cover readings at the root; chloride or carbonation at bar depth; rotation measured by level |
| Spalling on the soffit and front edge | Corrosion of edge and bottom bars | Rust staining along bar lines; low cover |
| Rust and burst concrete at a balustrade post base, post loose | Water in hollow post or pocket | Post moves at the root under hand pressure; water inside when drilled |
| Deck separating from the wall; bounce; stained wall line | Ledger fixing failure and decay | Nails or corroded bolts at the ledger; soft timber behind |
| Leak to the unit below at the door line | Membrane failure at the threshold | Flood test at the threshold; low or reversed upstand |
| Drummy and cracked tiles over the whole balcony | Membrane failure with saturated bedding | Flood test; moisture in the screed |
| Missing glass panel with fragments below | Spontaneous breakage of monolithic toughened glass | Glass marked toughened, not laminated; no impact |

> Rotation of a cantilever is a structural warning. A balcony whose tip has dropped relative to its root, with cracking along the wall line on top, should be closed to use until an engineer has assessed it.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Balustrade that moves under hand pressure, missing glass panel, loose post; cantilever rotation or root cracking; decayed or loose deck ledger | safety | Close or barricade immediately; engineer within days |
| Leaks damaging the structure or units below; spalling exposing reinforcement | failure | Repair now; extent from investigation |
| Post-base corrosion without looseness; membrane leaks without structural damage; fastener corrosion on decks | condition | Programme repair in the near term |
| Membranes and coatings at age without leaks | lifecycle | Renewal on cycle |
| California exterior elevated element inspection due; strata order | deadline | Timing set by the statute or order |
| Balustrades below current height or with climbable rails, compliant when built; monolithic toughened glass balustrades at height | check | Assess risk by use and fall height; upgrade where children use the space or where the risk warrants |
| Cosmetic coating wear, isolated drummy tile | nil | Routine care |

> Codes rarely require existing compliant balustrades to be upgraded, but a balustrade below current height or with climbable rails on an apartment balcony is a foreseeable risk. Upgrade is usually justified where children use the space and the fall is large.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads, with a waterproofing consultant for membranes. On apartment buildings, a sample of balconies is inspected, weighted to the most exposed and oldest; every timber deck and every glass balustrade over a public area is inspected.

- Level survey of cantilever tips against roots to detect rotation.
- Hammer survey of soffits, edges and tiles; cover and half-cell potential surveys at the root; chloride and carbonation testing at bar depth.
- Opening up at thresholds, outlets and post bases; removal of tiles at the root where corrosion is suspected.
- Flood testing of membranes.
- Load testing of balustrades to the design horizontal load where fixings are doubtful.
- Ledger inspection from below, with probing of timber and removal of a sample fastener.
- Glass identification of balustrade panels.

The report should state for each balcony inspected the structural condition, rotation measured, membrane condition, balustrade compliance with the code at the time and current code, and urgent actions.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Concrete repair: break out, treat or replace reinforcement, reinstate to a recognised repair standard; strengthening with additional steel or external brackets; replacement of the balcony where section loss at the root is severe.
- Re-membrane: remove tiles and screed, correct falls and threshold upstands, new membrane and outlets, re-tile.
- Post bases: cut out and rebuild with drained or solid posts on surface-mounted plates above the membrane.
- Balustrades: refix or replace; raise height with extensions; infill climbable sections; replace monolithic toughened glass with laminated or heat-soaked laminated glass.
- Timber decks: new ledger with through-bolts and lateral load connectors, new joists and hangers with compatible fasteners, or full rebuild.
- Heritage verandahs: repair cast iron with matching castings, replace decayed timber in kind, restore roof drainage.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is priced per balcony with a lump sum for testing. Works are priced per balcony unit for concrete repair and re-membrane, per linear metre for balustrades, and per square metre for membranes and tiling. Access by scaffold or swing stage dominates on multi-storey buildings, and work inside occupied units adds time and cost.

Two-part lines are normal. Balustrade upgrades and statutory inspections are code compliance; membranes are lifecycle; concrete and fixing repairs are repairs and maintenance, or lifecycle when replacement is needed; make-safe is immediate.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code requires barriers where a fall is 1 m or more, at least 1 m high (865 mm on stair flights), with openings that do not pass a 125 mm sphere and no climbable elements between 150 mm and 760 mm where the fall is more than 4 m. Glass in barriers follows AS 1288, external membranes AS 4654.2 and imposed loads AS/NZS 1170.1. Balconies are a leading item in strata defect claims; New South Wales adds duties under the Design and Building Practitioners Act 2020.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document K sets guarding heights (1100 mm for external balconies and edges of floors in most buildings) and limits openings to 100 mm where children may be present; BS 6180 covers barriers and BS 8579 the design of balconies and terraces. Regulation 7(2) restricts combustible materials in balconies of relevant buildings.
- United States. International Building Code Section 1015 requires guards of 42 inches where the drop exceeds 30 inches, with a 4-inch sphere limit, and Section 1607 sets guard loads; the International Residential Code allows 36-inch guards in houses. California requires periodic inspection of exterior elevated elements: every six years for apartment buildings under SB 721 and every nine years for condominiums under SB 326.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Structural drawings of balconies and decks; balustrade certificates and glass specifications.
- Membrane specification and warranty; flood test records.
- Any engineer's report on balconies, and statutory inspection reports where required.
- Leak logs and defect claims concentrated at balconies.
- Records of occupant alterations: tiling, enclosures, planters, spas.
- Maintenance records for outlets, coatings and timber decks.

pages.title: Water Conservation
pages.question: Where do buildings waste water, and how do you find and fix it?
pages.answer: Most avoidable water use is leaks, timed urinal flushing and poorly controlled cooling towers, not fixture choice. Night flow on the main meter with the building empty reveals leaks and timed urinals in minutes. Efficient fixtures help, but very low flows on old drains cause blockages and weak showers invite tampering. Rainwater and recycled systems that fail quietly revert to mains water. Metering that someone reads holds the savings.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about water conservation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Water-efficient fixtures (WELS rated), rainwater harvesting

sources.title: Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Water conservation covers the measures that reduce a building's water use: efficient taps, showers, toilets and urinals; leak detection and repair; cooling tower water management; efficient irrigation; rainwater harvesting and water recycling (whose systems are covered on the specialist hydraulics page); and metering that shows where water goes. In offices and commercial buildings, cooling towers, toilets and leaks dominate use; in apartments, showers, toilets and leaks.

| Measure | Where it is found | Watch points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Efficient taps and showerheads | All buildings | User satisfaction; tampering |
| Dual flush and efficient toilets | All buildings | Cistern leaks; drainage carry in old pipes |
| Waterless and efficient urinals | Commercial and public buildings | Odour and maintenance; old timed flushing systems |
| Leak detection and metering | Larger buildings | Meters not read; data ignored |
| Cooling tower water management | Buildings with water-cooled chillers | Bleed control; cycles of concentration |
| Efficient irrigation | Landscaped sites | Leaks; running in rain |
| Rainwater harvesting and recycling | Newer buildings | Treatment; cross-connection |

Labelling schemes help choose fixtures: the Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme is mandatory in Australia, the Unified Water Label is used in Britain, and WaterSense is the US Environmental Protection Agency's voluntary label.

Water conservation also reduces energy, because heating, pumping and treating water all use it; in buildings with large hot water loads, efficient showerheads cut gas or electricity use as much as water.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Measure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tapware and showerheads | 10 to 20 years | Water quality; use |
| Toilets and cisterns | 20 to 30 years; internals 5 to 10 | Valve and seal wear |
| Urinal controls | 10 to 15 years | Sensors; batteries |
| Water meters | 10 to 20 years | Accuracy; batteries |
| Irrigation controllers | 8 to 12 years | Technology |

What shortens savings:

- Silent leaks in cisterns and pipes.
- Timed urinal flushing running day and night.
- Tampering with flow restrictors by dissatisfied users.
- Unread meters, so waste goes unnoticed.

Water savings decay quickly without maintenance: a cistern valve that starts to pass, a urinal sensor that fails into continuous flushing, or a restrictor removed by a tenant can undo years of savings within weeks, and nothing visible signals it except the meter.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Leaks

Leaking cisterns, dripping taps and hidden pipe leaks waste large volumes silently. In many buildings leaks are a significant share of total use, and night flow on the main meter is the simplest test.

### Urinal flushing

Older urinals on timed cisterns flush around the clock whether used or not; replacing them with sensor or waterless systems is one of the largest savings in commercial buildings.

### Cooling tower water

Cooling towers lose water by evaporation and bleed; poor water treatment forces excessive bleed. Bleed control tied to conductivity and good treatment raises cycles of concentration and cuts water use.

### Low flows in old drains

Very low-flush toilets on long, shallow-graded or old drains can leave solids behind, causing blockages; water efficiency must be matched to the drainage.

### User dissatisfaction

Showers with poor spray and taps with weak flow lead users to remove restrictors or complain until fixtures are replaced.

### Alternative water system failures

Rainwater and recycled systems that fail revert to mains top-up, so the saving disappears without anyone noticing.

### Irrigation waste

Irrigation running on fixed timers in rain, broken sprinklers and leaking drip lines waste water outdoors, often the largest use on landscaped residential sites in summer.

### Kitchen and process use

Commercial kitchens, laundries and process equipment such as single-pass cooling of refrigeration and ice machines can use large volumes; single-pass cooling in particular wastes water continuously and is prohibited in some places.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site and in data

- Night flow on the main meter when the building is empty.
- Cisterns running or trickling into pans.
- Urinals flushing in empty toilets.
- Cooling tower overflow or constant bleed.
- Irrigation running in rain.

### In the records

- Water bills and meter data.
- NABERS Water or similar ratings.
- Fixture schedules.
- Cooling tower water treatment reports.

- Wet ground, lush patches or water running in gutters on dry days, which suggest buried leaks.
- Equipment discharging cooling water continuously to drain.
- Rainwater tanks overflowing while the building draws mains water, showing the harvesting system is not connected or working.
- Showerheads and taps with restrictors removed.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Night flow with the building empty | Leaks or timed urinals | Night flow test; isolate zones |
| Water use rising with no change in occupancy | New leak | Sub-meters |
| High cooling tower water use | Poor bleed control | Treatment records |
| Blockages after toilet replacement | Low flows in old drains | CCTV; drain grades |

| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Summer peaks in water use | Irrigation or cooling towers | Sub-meters; seasonal pattern |
| Constant flow from equipment | Single-pass cooling | Inspection of kitchen and plant |
| Tanks full but mains use unchanged | Harvesting system not supplying end uses | Pump and valve checks |

Comparing water use per occupant or per square metre with benchmarks shows whether a building is unusually wasteful before any detailed investigation.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cross-connection of recycled water to drinking water | safety | Isolate now |
| Major leak | failure | Repair now |
| Water restrictions or rating requirements | deadline | As required |
| Leaks, timed urinals, poor tower control | condition | Fix in the near term |
| Fixtures at end of life | lifecycle | Replace with efficient fixtures |
| No water audit | check | Audit |
| Normal | nil | Monitor |

Water findings are rarely urgent for safety, but a large hidden leak can damage structure and finishes, which raises it to a failure grade.

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or water auditor leads, with the cooling tower water treatment contractor and landscape contractor where relevant.

- Water audit: consumption broken down by end use (amenities, cooling towers, irrigation, kitchens, process) from bills, sub-meters and fixture counts.
- Night flow test: read the main meter over a period when the building is empty to quantify leaks and continuous flows.
- Fixture survey: flow rates of taps and showers, flush volumes, urinal controls, and condition of cistern valves and seals.
- Cooling tower review: bleed control, cycles of concentration, overflow and drift.
- Irrigation audit: leaks, overspray, controllers and rain sensors.
- Alternative water check: whether rainwater and recycled systems are actually supplying their end uses.
- Drainage check before installing very low-flush fixtures on old drains.

The report should identify the largest uses and losses, quick fixes, fixture upgrades, and a metering and monitoring plan.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Leak repair of cisterns, taps and pipework, followed by leak alarms on sub-meters.
- Urinal controls: sensor flushing or waterless urinals in place of timed cisterns.
- Efficient fixtures chosen for user satisfaction as well as rating, to avoid tampering.
- Cooling tower bleed control by conductivity with good water treatment.
- Irrigation upgrades: drip irrigation, smart controllers and rain sensors.
- Alternative water restoration: repair harvesting and recycling systems so they supply their end uses.
- Metering with alarms on night flow and unusual consumption.
- Drain upgrades where low-flow fixtures cause blockages.

- Single-pass cooling replacement with air-cooled or closed-loop equipment in kitchens and plant.
- Tenant engagement: share consumption data and include water clauses in leases.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Leak repairs and urinal controls are small itemised costs with quick paybacks. Fixture replacement is per fixture, usually timed with refurbishment. Cooling tower controls and irrigation upgrades are lump sums. Metering is per meter plus a monitoring subscription.

Leak repair is repairs and maintenance; fixture replacement is lifecycle; ratings and restrictions can create deadlines.

Water savings often also cut sewer charges and the energy used to heat and pump water, so paybacks are usually better than the water bill alone suggests.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme requires labelling of taps, showers, toilets and urinals; NABERS Water rates offices; water utilities and states impose restrictions in droughts; plumbing codes set minimum efficiency for new fixtures.
- United Kingdom. Approved Document G sets a water efficiency limit for new homes; the Unified Water Label grades fixtures; BREEAM rewards water efficiency in non-domestic buildings; water companies offer audits.
- United States. WaterSense labels efficient fixtures; federal and state standards set maximum flow rates, with stricter limits in states such as California; some cities require water benchmarking alongside energy.

In all three countries, strata and condominium buildings commonly have a single water meter, so individual waste is shared by all owners; sub-metering apartments changes behaviour and is required or encouraged in some places.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Water bills for at least two years.
- Sub-meter data and night flow readings.
- NABERS Water or similar ratings.
- Fixture schedules with ratings.
- Cooling tower water treatment reports.
- Irrigation controller settings and records.
- Alternative water system maintenance records.

- Records of leaks found and repaired.
- Any water efficiency plan or audit.

pages.title: Water Supply
pages.question: How do building water supplies fail, and which failures put drinking water quality or the building at risk?
pages.answer: Water supply fails by corrosion, pressure and contamination. Galvanised steel narrows and runs brown; copper pinholes in some waters; brass fittings in plastic systems dezincify; polybutylene fails. The safety findings are about water quality: backflow devices that are untested or missing on hazard connections, cross-connections from alterations, lead service pipes and solder, and Legionella in cold storage tanks. Seized isolation valves turn small leaks into building-wide outages.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about water supply; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Incoming services, storage tanks, backflow prevention devices

sources.title: Legionnaires' disease: the control of legionella bacteria in water systems (L8)

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Water supply covers drinking and service water from the utility connection to the outlets: the incoming main and meter, backflow prevention devices that stop building water flowing back into the public supply, pressure-limiting valves, storage and break tanks, distribution pipework, risers and isolation valves, sub-meters, and cold water to fixtures and equipment. Hot water plant and booster pumps have their own pages.

| Material | Typical era and use | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead | Service pipes in older housing: Britain before about 1970, US lead service lines into the 1980s | Lead in drinking water; replacement programmes in Britain and the United States |
| Galvanised steel | Pre-1970s in all three countries; some commercial risers later | Internal corrosion and tuberculation; brown water; falling flow |
| Copper | Most buildings from the 1950s onward | Long-lived; pinhole pitting in some waters; erosion at high velocity |
| Polybutylene | US and some Australian housing, late 1970s to mid 1990s | Fittings and pipe failures; often replaced proactively |
| PEX and other plastics | From the 1990s | Durable; brass fittings can dezincify; UV degradation if exposed |
| Ductile iron and PE | Large incoming mains and site services | Corrosion of iron; joint failures; ground movement |

In apartment and commercial buildings, water often passes through break tanks and booster pumps before reaching upper floors. Tenancies and apartments are sub-metered, and the owner's infrastructure stops at each lot's isolation valve or meter. Where a building has cooling towers, irrigation, fire services or process water, backflow devices separate each hazard from the drinking supply.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copper pipework | 50 years and more | Water chemistry; velocity; installation |
| Galvanised steel pipework | 40 to 60 years, often less | Water chemistry; internal corrosion |
| PEX pipework | 50 years and more | UV exposure; fittings |
| Brass fittings in plastic systems | 10 to 30 years | Dezincification in aggressive waters |
| Backflow prevention devices | 15 to 25 years with annual testing | Water quality; debris; maintenance |
| Pressure-limiting valves | 10 to 20 years | Debris; diaphragms |
| Cold water storage tanks | 20 to 40 years | Material; lining; access and cleaning |
| Isolation valves | 15 to 30 years | Rarely operated; seize |

What shortens life:

- Aggressive water chemistry that pits copper, dezincifies brass and corrodes steel.
- High pressure without limiting valves, which stresses joints and fittings and causes water hammer.
- High velocity in undersized pipes, causing erosion at bends and fittings.
- Stagnation in tanks and dead legs, which affects water quality.
- Ground movement on buried services.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Internal corrosion

Galvanised steel corrodes from the inside: the zinc is consumed, the steel rusts and builds tubercles that narrow the bore, flow falls, and water runs brown after periods of no use. Copper can pit in certain waters, producing pinhole leaks that recur along the same runs. Brass fittings in plastic systems can lose zinc (dezincification), becoming porous and weak, and leak or fail.

### Backflow and cross-connection

Where building water connects to a hazard (cooling towers, fire systems, irrigation, laboratories, chemical dosing, boilers), a drop in mains pressure can draw contaminated water back into the drinking supply. Backflow devices prevent it only if they work; devices that are not tested can fail open without any sign. Unprotected cross-connections created by alterations are a public health risk.

### Pressure problems

High mains pressure without limiting valves bursts flexible hoses, wears tap washers and valves, and causes water hammer: the banging when valves close fast, which loosens supports and fatigues joints. Low pressure at upper floors points to booster problems, undersized risers or corroded pipes.

### Storage tank contamination

Cold water storage tanks with poor lids, missing insect screens and sediment build-up allow contamination; warm tanks in roof spaces and plant rooms grow Legionella. Tanks that are oversized for current use hold water too long.

### Lead in drinking water

Lead service pipes and lead solder in older plumbing release lead into water, especially after it has stood. In the United States, federal rules now require lead service lines to be identified and replaced; in Britain, water companies and owners share responsibility for lead pipes on either side of the boundary.

### Hidden leaks

Leaks under slabs, in walls and in ceiling voids waste water, damage finishes and structure, and are found through rising consumption or damp. Polybutylene and failed fittings are common sources.

### Seized isolation valves

Valves never exercised seize, so a leak on one floor means shutting down the building. This turns small repairs into major outages.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### On site

- Pipe materials visible in plant rooms, risers and under fixtures.
- Brown water on opening taps; low flow at upper floors or far outlets.
- Water hammer noise; loose pipe supports.
- Green or white crusting on brass fittings (dezincification).
- Backflow devices: test tags, leaks from relief ports, bypasses.
- Tank lids, screens, overflows and condition.
- Damp and staining on walls and ceilings near pipe runs.

### In the records

- Water consumption trends, especially night-time use.
- Backflow device register and test certificates.
- Leak and repair history by location.
- Water quality testing, including lead where relevant.
- Tank cleaning and inspection records.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brown water after periods of no use | Corroding galvanised steel | Pipe material; internal inspection of a removed section |
| Repeated pinhole leaks in copper on the same runs | Pitting corrosion from water chemistry | Leak history; water analysis; pipe section examination |
| Leaks at brass fittings in a plastic system | Dezincification | Fitting examination; product type |
| Banging when taps close | Water hammer from high pressure or fast-closing valves | Pressure measurement |
| Night-time water use with the building empty | Hidden leak or running cisterns | Meter readings; leak detection |
| Backflow device leaking from the relief port | Fouled or failed check valves | Device test |

> Backflow devices fail without visible signs. A device that has not been tested in the last year should be treated as unproven, and in some jurisdictions the water utility can disconnect the supply until it is tested.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed backflow device on a high-hazard connection; unprotected cross-connection; lead above drinking water limits; Legionella in cold storage | safety | Isolate or rectify now; notify the utility or health authority where required |
| Burst main or major leak; no water to the building | failure | Repair now |
| Backflow testing due; lead service line replacement under a programme | deadline | At the prescribed interval or date |
| Galvanised corrosion, recurring copper leaks, dezincification, seized valves, high pressure | condition | Repair in the near term |
| Pipework at end of life | lifecycle | Plan replacement, often riser by riser |
| Pipe materials unknown; no backflow register | check | Survey |
| Normal | nil | Routine |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber leads, with a water treatment specialist where corrosion or quality is in question.

- Materials survey of incoming services, risers, branches and fittings.
- Backflow audit: every hazard connection identified, with the device type checked against the hazard rating and tested.
- Pressure and flow measurement at the incoming main, at the top floors and at remote outlets.
- Water quality testing: lead and copper at outlets after standing; Legionella and bacterial counts in storage.
- Pipe sampling: remove sections of corroded or leaking pipe for examination.
- Leak detection: meter tests, acoustic and thermal methods for hidden leaks.
- Tank inspection: internal condition, lids, screens, temperatures.
- Valve operation: exercise isolation valves and record those that fail.

The report should state pipe materials and condition, backflow compliance, pressure and flow adequacy, water quality, leaks and a replacement strategy.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Backflow: install or upgrade devices to suit each hazard, and set up annual testing.
- Pressure control: pressure-limiting valves and water hammer arrestors.
- Replacement of galvanised, polybutylene and pitting copper pipework, riser by riser with temporary supplies.
- Fitting replacement with dezincification-resistant brass.
- Lead removal: replace lead service pipes and remove lead solder where testing warrants.
- Tank works: clean, reline, fit sealed lids and screens, or remove redundant tanks.
- Valve replacement so floors and risers can be isolated individually.
- Leak repairs and smart metering to find future leaks quickly.

- Water quality management: flushing programmes for little-used outlets and dead legs, and removal of redundant branches so water does not stagnate.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Backflow testing recurs annually per device; device replacement is per device. Pipe replacement is priced by length or per riser, with access, finishes and temporary supply as major components in occupied buildings. Valve replacement is per valve. Tank works are lump sums. Lead service line replacement is a lump sum and may be shared with the utility under its programme.

Backflow and water quality compliance are code compliance; pipework replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. AS/NZS 3500.1 governs water services and backflow prevention, with testing of devices under AS 2845.3 typically required annually by the water utility; plumbing work is licensed and certified in each state; pressure-limiting valves are required where mains pressure is high.
- United Kingdom. The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 (and Scottish byelaws) govern fittings and backflow protection, with WRAS approval of products; the HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 covers Legionella control in cold water systems; water companies and owners have lead pipe replacement responsibilities on either side of the boundary.
- United States. The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes govern water supply; states and utilities run cross-connection control programmes with annual testing of backflow assemblies; the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements require water systems to replace lead service lines over the coming decade.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Backflow device register and test certificates.
- Water consumption data, ideally by sub-meter.
- Leak and repair history.
- Water quality test results, including lead where relevant.
- Tank cleaning and Legionella records.
- Hydraulic drawings showing pipe materials and isolation.
- Utility notices about lead pipes or backflow.

- Pressure readings at the incoming main and upper floors.

pages.title: Waterproofing Membranes
pages.question: How do flat roof and deck membranes fail, how do you tell a detail failure from a failed roof, and when must a roof be stripped rather than patched?
pages.answer: Membranes fail at details first: upstands, terminations, outlets and penetrations, then seams. Leaks in a line point to seams; one leak under a penetration is a detail repair; leaks that move around and continue after rain mean wet insulation, which keeps leaking after every patch and rules out recovering. EPDM shrinks and tears at upstands; old PVC turns brittle. Establish whether the insulation is wet before choosing repair, recover or replace.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about waterproofing membranes; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: TPO, PVC, EPDM, Bitumen, liquid-applied membranes

sections.heading: What it is and how it is built
sections.markdown:
Waterproofing membranes are the continuous waterproof layers on flat and low-slope roofs, podiums, plant decks, terraces, planters and balconies. They sit on a structural deck, usually with insulation above or below, and are often hidden under ballast, paving on pedestals, soil or tiles. The membrane turns up at parapets and walls, terminates under flashings, and is penetrated by outlets, plant supports and balustrade posts.

| Type | Typical use and era | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-up roofing (BUR): bitumen and felt in layers | Commercial flat roofs, 1950s to 1990s | Thick, robust; surface ages and crazes; blisters between plies |
| Modified bitumen sheet (SBS, APP), torch-on or self-adhered | Commercial and residential roofs from the 1980s | Durable; laps are the weak line; heat at installation |
| Mastic asphalt | British flat roofs and decks, long history | Very durable when protected; cracks with movement |
| Single-ply TPO | Commercial roofs from the 2000s | Heat-welded seams; reflective; product generations vary |
| Single-ply PVC | Commercial roofs from the 1980s | Welded seams; plasticiser loss causes shrinkage and embrittlement in older products; incompatible with bitumen and some foams |
| EPDM rubber | Commercial roofs from the 1980s | Taped or glued seams; shrinks with age, pulling at perimeters |
| Liquid-applied (polyurethane, acrylic, PMMA, polyurea) | Balconies, wet areas, roof restoration | Seamless; life set entirely by film thickness and preparation |
| Cementitious and crystalline | Planters, basements, water tanks | Rigid; cracks with movement |

How insulation is arranged decides how failure plays out. In a warm roof the insulation is above the deck and under the membrane; a leak saturates the insulation, which then holds water across a wide area. In an inverted roof the insulation is above the membrane, protecting it, and is held down by ballast. In a cold roof the insulation is below the deck, and condensation in the deck or void becomes the risk.

sections.heading: Service life and what shortens it
sections.markdown:
| Membrane | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-up roofing | 15 to 25 years | Surfacing and maintenance; ponding |
| Modified bitumen, protected | 20 to 30 years | Ballast or paving above it |
| Modified bitumen, exposed | 15 to 20 years | UV; foot traffic |
| Mastic asphalt, protected | 30 years and more | Movement; solar protection |
| TPO | 15 to 25 years | Product generation; seam quality |
| PVC | 15 to 25 years | Plasticiser loss; compatibility |
| EPDM | 20 to 30 years | Seam method; shrinkage |
| Liquid-applied coatings | 8 to 20 years | Film thickness; preparation; product |

What shortens life:

- Ponding from flat or reversed falls, deflecting decks and blocked outlets.
- Foot traffic and plant on unprotected membranes; plant installed later through the membrane without proper penetration details.
- UV exposure on membranes intended to be protected.
- Movement at upstands, deck joints and changes of material.
- Roots in planters and green roofs without a root barrier.
- Incompatible materials: PVC in contact with bitumen or polystyrene; solvents on EPDM.

sections.heading: How it fails
sections.markdown:
### Failure at details

Membranes rarely fail first in the open field. They fail at upstands where the membrane turns up a wall and is terminated, at outlets, at penetrations and at changes of level. Terminations pull out of their chases or bars; upstands are too low and water rises above them; outlets corrode or detach from the membrane.

### Seam and lap failure

Single-ply seams that were under-welded or contaminated open over time; EPDM tape and adhesive seams debond; bitumen laps lift. Seam failures run in lines across the roof.

### Blisters and splits

Moisture or air trapped between layers or under the membrane expands in heat and forms blisters, which crack when walked on. Splits form over deck joints, at insulation board edges and where the membrane is stressed by thermal shock or movement.

### Surface ageing

Bitumen surfaces craze (alligatoring), lose their mineral surfacing and harden. PVC loses plasticiser, shrinks and becomes brittle. EPDM shrinks and pulls at its perimeter, bridging across the angle at upstands until it tears.

### Wet insulation

In warm roofs, water entering through any defect spreads through the insulation below the membrane. Wet insulation loses its thermal value, adds load, rots timber decks, corrodes steel decks and fixings, and keeps feeding leaks long after the original defect is repaired. It is the most expensive hidden failure on a flat roof, because the roof cannot simply be re-covered.

### Wind uplift

Mechanically fastened single-ply membranes rely on fasteners into the deck. Corroded or under-specified fasteners, and corners and perimeters with too few, let the membrane billow and tear in wind.

### Liquid coating failure

Liquid membranes fail where they were applied too thin, over damp or dusty substrates, or across cracks that move. They crack, peel and blister, often over the whole area, and the cause is usually the original application.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.markdown:
### From aerial imagery

- Ponding marks and dark rings where water has stood; vegetation in ballast and at outlets.
- Patches in different materials; areas of new membrane; coatings over old membranes.
- Plant added since the roof was laid, with its supports through the membrane.
- Lifted or billowing single-ply at corners and perimeters after wind.

### On the roof

- Open seams and laps; blisters; splits over deck joints and board edges.
- Upstands lower than the water line; terminations pulled out; sealant at terminations failed.
- Outlets corroded, blocked, detached or set above the membrane level.
- Soft or spongy areas underfoot: wet insulation beneath.
- EPDM bridging at upstands; brittle PVC that cracks when folded.
- Wrinkles and ridges in the membrane over moving insulation boards.

### Below the roof

- Staining, blistering paint and efflorescence on soffits; drips at deck joints.
- Corrosion of steel deck and fixings visible from below.
- Leaks that continue for days after rain stops: water held in insulation.
- In car parks under podiums, staining and corrosion in lines along joints.

### In the records

- Membrane specification, installer and warranty, with date.
- Leak register and repair history; repeated repairs in different places.
- Roof surveys, core reports and moisture surveys.

sections.heading: Telling causes apart
sections.markdown:
| What you see | Most likely cause | What confirms it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single leak under a penetration or upstand | Detail failure | Water test or electronic leak detection at the detail |
| Leaks in a line across the roof | Seam failure | Probing seams finds open laps along the line |
| Leaks moving around, continuing after rain | Wet insulation spreading water | Cores show saturated insulation; thermography shows wet areas |
| Spongy areas underfoot | Wet insulation | Cores and moisture survey |
| Membrane pulled tight at upstands, tearing at the angle | EPDM shrinkage | Membrane bridges the angle; field is slack-free |
| Membrane cracks when folded; shrinkage at laps | PVC plasticiser loss | Age and product; cracking at stress points |
| Blisters over the field | Trapped moisture or poor adhesion | Blisters cut show moisture; not structural on their own |
| Liquid coating peeling over large areas | Application thickness or substrate | Film thickness readings; substrate condition |

> A dry membrane over wet insulation will keep leaking after every repair. Before patching, recovering or coating a warm flat roof with a leak history, establish whether the insulation is wet.

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | Situation | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Membrane torn or lifted by wind; ponding loading a light deck | safety | Secure and drain now; engineer where deck deflects |
| Active leaks damaging structure, services or interiors; saturated insulation | failure | Repair or replace now; extent from moisture survey |
| Seam opening, failing details, membrane ageing with isolated leaks | condition | Repair details and seams in the near term; plan replacement |
| Membrane at end of life, no leaks | lifecycle | Plan replacement |
| Leak history on a warm roof with no moisture survey | check | Moisture survey and cores before choosing repair, recover or replace |
| Minor surface ageing, isolated dry blister | nil | Routine maintenance and outlet clearing |

sections.heading: Investigation and testing
sections.markdown:
A roofing consultant or building surveyor leads, with a specialist leak detection contractor where needed.

- Visual survey of the field, seams, upstands, terminations, outlets and penetrations, with a plan of defects.
- Core cuts to identify the build-up, membrane type and layers, and insulation condition; cores sealed after.
- Moisture survey by infrared thermography at night, capacitance or impedance meters on a grid, or nuclear moisture gauges.
- Electronic leak detection (low-voltage or high-voltage methods) to locate breaches, including under ballast or overburden; ASTM D7877 guides the methods.
- Flood testing of balconies and small decks, checking deck capacity first.
- Seam probing on single-ply roofs.
- Fastener pull-out tests on mechanically fastened roofs.

The report should state the build-up, membrane type and age, defects and their locations, the extent of wet insulation, and whether the roof can be repaired, recovered or must be stripped.

sections.heading: Remedies and what they involve
sections.markdown:
- Detail repairs: renew upstands, terminations, outlets and penetration flashings; often the best value on an otherwise sound field.
- Seam repair: reweld or re-tape seams, or overlay with cover strips.
- Recover: a new membrane over the old, only where the insulation is dry, the deck sound, and the code allows the extra layer.
- Restoration coatings over sound ageing membranes to extend life; not over wet insulation.
- Strip and replace: remove membrane and wet insulation, repair the deck, correct falls with tapered insulation, new membrane and outlets.
- Drainage: add outlets and overflows, correct falls, clear and maintain outlets.
- Protection: walkways to plant, raised plant supports, protection boards under pavers.

Interactions: replacing a membrane usually means lifting and reinstating whatever sits on it, which can cost more than the membrane; insulation upgrades may be required; roof safety systems and plant supports are renewed with it.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Moisture surveys and cores are lump sums. Detail repairs are itemised per outlet, penetration or linear metre of upstand. Replacement is priced by area with separate lines for strip-out, wet insulation removal, deck repair, new insulation and falls, upstands and outlets, and reinstatement of ballast, pavers, planters and plant. Reinstatement is often the largest component on terraces and podiums.

The usual shape where leaks exist and insulation status is unknown is two-part: moisture survey, then a conditional envelope that is a detail repair if the insulation is dry and a strip-and-replace if it is wet. Replacement is lifecycle; detail repairs and outlet clearing are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: Standards and jurisdiction
sections.markdown:
- Australia. The National Construction Code calls up AS 4654.1 and AS 4654.2 for external above-ground membranes; roof drainage follows AS/NZS 3500.3. On strata buildings, roof, podium and balcony membranes are usually common property and a leading head of defect claims; New South Wales and Victoria have statutory defect and warranty periods for waterproofing.
- United Kingdom. BS 6229 sets the code of practice for flat roofs with continuously supported coverings, BS 8217 covers reinforced bitumen membranes and BS 8218 mastic asphalt; Approved Document L applies thermal upgrades on renovation, and Approved Document B and regulation 7(2) bear on roof build-ups on relevant buildings.
- United States. International Building Code Chapter 15 governs roof assemblies and re-covering; single-ply membranes follow ASTM D6878 (TPO), D4434 (PVC) and D4637 (EPDM); ASTM D7877 guides electronic leak detection. Insurers commonly require FM Approvals ratings for wind uplift and fire.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
- Membrane specification, installer and warranty, with installation date.
- Leak register, repair history and any leak investigation or moisture survey.
- Roof drawings showing falls, outlets, overflows and the build-up.
- Records of plant added through the roof since installation.
- Outlet cleaning and roof maintenance schedule.
- Defect claims and expert reports inside statutory defect periods.

docs.title: How we use AI
docs.kind: The practice
docs.blurb: How AI fits inside the Moyne Ross system, and where it stops.
docs.text: AI one part of system model does not do arithmetic maths MR Index final decision professional judgement quality checks AI and the practice | Moyne Ross Moyne Ross Approach Insights About Portal Start your strategy Moyne Ross / AI Judgement, given room How AI changes building and capital advice, where it stops, and who stands behind the result. “The slow part of building advice was never the judgement. It was everything around it.” Moyne Ross The argument Most of a surveyor’s time has gone into producing the report: finding records, reading them, measuring, pricing, assembling. The judgement clients actually rely on was fitted into whatever time was left. AI changes that balance. It can take on the reading, the cross-checking and the first draft, at a scale no person can match, so professional time moves to where it matters: the building, the evidence that is missing, and the decision in front of you. That is why Moyne Ross was built. 01 Reading at scale A building leaves traces everywhere: planning records, permits, imagery, listings, maintenance logs, past reports. Few assessments read them all, and fewer read them against each other. The MR engine searches, reads and compares that evidence together, alongside any documents you share. Where sources agree, confidence rises. Where they conflict, the conflict is recorded rather than smoothed over. Every finding is held as documented, observed or inferred , so you can see what kind of claim it is. More evidence, read more carefully, before anyone forms a view. 02 How the engine works The engine was built around the real work of assessing a building, and it keeps each part of that work in its proper hands. Evidence Research and your documents establish the asset, its history and known works. Gaps stay visible. Assessment One framework across structure, services and space: condition, action, cost basis, timing and confidence. Calculation Costs, horizons and the MR Index are calculated by code from structured inputs, not written by the model. Checks More than forty automated checks look for gaps, contradictions and claims the evidence cannot support. Review A chartered surveyor reviews the assessment before it is issued as advice. The model proposes. The platform calculates. The surveyor decides. Each step leaves its working on the page, so it can be questioned afterwards. See what that looks like inside the Capital Register . 03 Every number shows its working A capital figure is only as good as what sits behind it. In a Moyne Ross strategy, every priced line carries its cost basis: the scope assumed, the quantities, what is included and excluded, the date, and how firm the footing is. Where a figure is a planning allowance rather than a quote, it says so. Where the evidence stops short, the register prices the inspection and goes no further. Confident language is not allowed to outrun the evidence, and the checks are built to catch it when it tries. Honest uncertainty is more useful than false precision. 04 What it changes for you Your building’s strategy, usually within a working day, from its address alone, looked over before release. Because the production is faster, the conversation can start earlier and go further. A different holding period, a refurbishment, a change of use: alternatives can be explored together within the agreed brief, with the register as the shared reference. And the record stays live. New evidence, a quotation or a change of plan can be brought in and the strategy updated, rather than the work going stale in a document. You also work with fewer layers. The person who built the engine is the person who reviews your building and talks it through with you. 05 Where the line is AI does not inspect your building. It does not certify compliance, perform the final arithmetic, calculate the MR Index or take responsibility for the instruction. A Capital Strategy issued as professional advice is reviewed and approved by the responsible chartered surveyor for its agreed purpose. A desktop assessment and an inspection-supported assessment rest on different evidence, and the strategy says which it is. The engine extends judgement. It never replaces it. 06 Accountable, by design RICS’s Responsible use of artificial intelligence in surveying practice standard took effect on 9 March 2026. It informs how Moyne Ross works: appropriate use, data and provider assessment, professional judgement, clear communication with clients, and accountability. Moyne Ross is not currently an RICS-regulated firm, and this page does not claim RICS approval or certification of the engine. For any instruction, you can ask how material AI outputs were assessed, which assumptions affect their reliability, and whether further verification is needed. The extent of professional indemnity cover, including for AI-assisted work, is addressed before an instruction is accepted; this page does not itself confirm cover. The detail Systems, data and your choices The practical arrangements behind the approach above. Open any section. The systems we use We use large language models to assist with research and analysis. They are general-purpose systems; Moyne Ross supplies the building methodology, evidence rules and output structure. The platform supports different providers, including Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini) and OpenAI, depending on the feature and selected configuration. The provider used for a confidential instruction forms part of the processing arrangements explained to the client. A new provider is not authorised to receive private material merely because the platform can connect to it. Relevant changes are disclosed before the affected processing, with permission obtained where required. Data retention and model-training terms differ by provider, product and account settings. We do not promise that information is retained only while a response is generated. Our Privacy & Cookie Policy explains this distinction and how to ask about the arrangements for your instruction. Issued strategies and working outputs An issued Capital Strategy records the professional advice for the agreed instruction. Where the portal offers interactive AI tools, such as chat or a generated working report, their status is different: those responses and reports may not have been individually reviewed or adopted as advice. If a working output suggests a material new conclusion, ask us to review it and, where appropriate, incorporate it into the advice or a revised strategy. Generating a report does not by itself make its contents a newly issued professional opinion. The scope, permitted reliance and any further work are governed by your client agreement and instruction. How we manage uncertainty AI can produce convincing but incorrect statements, miss relevant evidence or give undue weight to a weak source. An apparently precise cost is still only as reliable as its scope, quantity, rate and assumptions. Our approach combines: Evidence distinctions: separating documented information, observations and inference, with gaps and uncertainty kept visible. Structured assessment: consistent coverage of building fabric, services and the spaces they support, within the agreed scope. Separate calculations: code-based cost roll-ups and MR Index scoring from the structured assessment. Automated checks: checks for structural, arithmetic and completeness problems, alongside advisory signals that inform review. Professional judgement: consideration of the material findings, their limitations and their suitability for the client’s decision. Further investigation: identifying questions that require better records, site evidence or the appropriate specialist. These measures reduce risk; they do not eliminate uncertainty or guarantee that every issue is identified. The speed of generation does not determine whether an assessment is suitable to rely on. How we handle your data AI services may receive relevant asset documents, images, questions and assessment context, and may process them outside Australia. Private and confidential material requires an appropriate processing basis and express written permission before submission. We seek to minimise unnecessary personal information and address restrictions on third-party material before it is used. The permissions for delivering an instruction are distinct from permission to publish a client case study or use identifiable material for model development. See our Privacy & Cookie Policy for providers, overseas processing, retention, research use and your choices. Your questions and choices You can ask which AI systems are involved, why they are used, what their relevant limitations are and how they affect your work. We will provide an appropriate written explanation, including relevant reliability reasoning and safeguards, while respecting security, confidentiality and third-party rights. You can also contest a proposed use of AI, request correction or raise a complaint through our contact form . We aim to acknowledge concerns within five business days and give a substantive response within twenty business days, or explain when a response will follow. The complaints process in our Terms sets out the next steps. AI is integral to an engine-generated Capital Strategy. A wholly AI-free version of that product is not offered. If you have restrictions on a provider or particular information, raise them before sharing the material so we can consider whether a different evidence basis or scope can meet your needs. Updated 24 October 2026. Moyne Ross / AI Better evidence. More time for judgement. One person accountable. Start with an address. We’ll read the building before anything else is agreed. docs.title: The MR Index
docs.kind: Methodology
docs.blurb: The decision layer: how much attention a building needs, and how soon, from MR 1 to MR 5.
docs.text: MR Index score band MR 1 MR 2 MR 3 MR 4 MR 5 rating condition elements attention how serious how soon no costs capital position The MR Index | Methodology Reference | Moyne Ross Moyne Ross Approach Insights About Portal Start your strategy Methodology / The MR Index The MR Index How much of the building needs attention, how serious it is and how soon. One reading, on a scale from MR 1 to MR 5. Every Capital Strategy carries one. This page explains what the Index is reading, how a building ends up on a band, and what the band is telling you. How it is read ↓ Start your strategy → One reading, five bands Illustrative building · forty elements Element by element Each square is one element of the building Needs nothing Needs a check Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon Reads as MR 3 · Mid-cycle refresh 01 Why a single score A Capital Register runs to forty lines or more. The first question anyone asks of it is simpler than that: how bad is it? The MR Index answers that first. It gives back one position for the decade ahead, so an owner, a board or a buyer sees the shape of what is coming at a glance, then turns to the register for the why. Condition, not cost A large building is not marked down for being large, and an expensive repair counts for no more than a cheap one of the same seriousness. The costs stay in the register, for planning. The same way, every time The band is worked out from the register itself, line by line. Nobody decides it, and it does not drift as prices move. It tells you where the building stands. What to do about it is the conversation that follows. 1 Minimal 2 Routine 3 Mid-cycle 4 Elevated 5 Major 02 Three questions, every element By the time the register is complete, every element of the building, from the footings to the fire panel, has been looked at and judged. The Index asks the same three things of each one. Does it need attention? Over the next ten years, will this element need work, need someone to look before anyone can say, or need nothing at all? Works A check Nothing How serious? If it were left, what would it cost the building: its safety, its function, its value? Essential Important Planned Routine How soon? Is this a matter for the coming year, the middle of the decade, or later? Within a year Years two to five Years six to ten 03 The band reads the whole building Picture the building as a field of squares, one for each element. Light up the ones that need attention, more strongly the more serious and the sooner. The band is a reading of that whole picture. A building with a few faint squares late in the decade reads lightly. A building where most of the field is lit, much of it strongly, reads heavily. Three examples, drawn to the same scale: MR 1 Minimal requirements MR 3 Mid-cycle refresh MR 5 Major intervention Needs nothing Needs a check Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon Illustrative buildings of forty elements. A real register commonly reads between thirty and fifty. 04 The five bands The reading lands on one of five bands. Each describes a kind of decade, not a verdict on the building. Where the lines between them fall is set against buildings Moyne Ross has assessed, and reviewed as that library grows. MR 1 Minimal requirements Little needs attention, and nothing serious any time soon. MR 2 Routine profile What is needed is routine or already planned, and spread across the decade. MR 3 Mid-cycle refresh A clear set of elements needs attention, some of them important. This decade needs a plan. MR 4 Elevated programme Serious elements need attention, often within a few years, or too many questions are still open. MR 5 Major intervention So much of the building needs serious, early attention that the decision itself changes. 05 What the Index is, and is not The Index says what condition a building is in. It is not a verdict on whether the building is good, beautiful or worth buying. Not a valuation A prime building in a tightly held precinct can read MR 5 and still be the right acquisition. A heritage building often reads heavily simply because so much of it deserves care. Nor is the Index a cost estimate; the register carries the costs. Same band, different decisions Someone holding for ten years reads an MR 4 one way; someone weighing a refurbishment or a change of use reads it another. The Index is the shared starting point. The plan comes from your objectives. Since October 2026 The Index has read condition rather than cost since October 2026. Earlier strategies were banded from cost-weighted measures, still kept for reference, and any of them can be read again under the current method. Five bands. See where yours sits. Send us an address. The first read comes back with the building’s band and the register behind it, before anything is agreed.
