Separating how much an item matters from when it needs action is the most useful discipline in capital planning.  capital expenditure timing risk capital plan Capital Register year one capexcapital expenditure timing risk capital plan Capital Register year one capex capex timing versus risk what belongs in year 1 capex immediate costs building risk is not timing capital plan horizons 1 yr 2-5 yr 6-10 yrcapex timing versus risk what belongs in year 1 capex immediate costs building risk is not timing capital plan horizons 1 yr 2-5 yr 6-10 yrcapex timing versus risk what belongs in year 1 capex immediate costs building risk is not timing capital plan horizons 1 yr 2-5 yr 6-10 yr Capital plans often confuse two different questions. How much does this item matter? And when does something need to be done about it? The first is about consequence. The second is about the item’s condition, remaining life and the window in which intervention makes sense.

When the two are merged, every serious item drifts into year one. The near-term budget swells, credibility falls, and owners learn to discount the plan. Keeping them separate is one of the main disciplines of the Moyne Ross Capital Register.  Research note

The timing discipline described here is the Moyne Ross Capital Register method. Professional guidance in building surveying and technical due diligence, including RICS standards, distinguishes urgent works from planned works and leaves the timing of intervention to professional judgement; it does not prescribe the one-year, two-to-five-year and six-to-ten-year horizons Moyne Ross uses. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the ISO 15686 factor method for service life.

## Three horizons, one question

A Moyne Ross register expresses timing in three horizons: within one year, years two to five, and years six to ten. The near-term horizon is protected. An item belongs there only when the whole intervention window falls inside the next twelve months.

The test is simple to state: why must this happen within twelve months? If the honest answer is “because it is important”, the item probably belongs later, with monitoring or investigation now. If the answer is “because it is failing, unsafe, non-compliant with a current obligation or about to cause consequential damage”, it belongs now.

Every dollar in the first year should be able to answer one question: why must this happen within twelve months?

## Consequence is carried separately

Consequence still matters. In the register it is carried by impact, on its own scale, and by the item’s description of what failure would mean. A fire system with modest remaining life may be impact four and still a two-to-five-year replacement, with inspection and testing confirmed now. A lift with serious safety implications may need immediate attention. The impact rating tells the reader why the item matters. The timing tells them when to act.

This is consistent with the way professional guidance treats the question. The RICS approach to building surveys and technical due diligence distinguishes urgent works within a short period from planned works over longer horizons, and leaves the timing of intervention to professional judgement on the evidence. Risk is not treated as the same thing as expenditure timing.

## Why a published life is not a date

Service life planning has an international standard, and it makes the same separation this paper argues for. ISO 15686 estimates a component’s life by starting from a reference life and adjusting it for the conditions it actually faces. The factors ISO 15686 uses to adjust a reference service lifeFactorWhat it coversExample that shortens or lengthens lifeAQuality of the componentA premium coating against a basic oneBDesign levelSheltered detailing against an exposed oneCQuality of installationSealant joints prepared properly or notDIndoor environmentA dry office against a humid plant roomEOutdoor environmentAn inland site against a coastal oneFConditions of usePlant running continuously against part-timeGMaintenance levelA planned regime against reactive repair

ISO 15686-1, service life planning: the factor method. Factors are judgements, not constants.

The factor method is a reminder that timing is an estimate about a particular component in particular conditions, which is why the register records the evidence behind each timing rather than a table value alone. Consequence is a different question, and it stays on its own scale.

## Two worked rows

Consider two rows from an office register. The first is a fire detection system: twenty-two years old, functioning, with parts becoming harder to source. Impact is high, because the system protects life. But it passes its tests and its intervention window opens in three to four years when parts support lapses. Timing: two to five years, with annual testing confirmed in the first year. The second is a section of roof membrane: fifteen years old, with active leaks over a tenancy and staining spreading. Impact is moderate. Timing: within one year, because the window for intervention is now, before consequential damage.

A risk-weighted plan would put the fire system first and the roof second. A timing-disciplined plan puts the roof in the first year and the fire system in the middle years, with testing now. Both items are still visible and both are taken seriously. The first-year budget is smaller and every dollar in it can say why it is there.

## Checks are not works

Many near-term actions are not works at all. They are investigations, surveys or tests that resolve uncertainty: a roof survey, a facade inspection, a hazardous materials survey, a structural assessment. These can and should sit in the first year, with their own small cost, while the works they may lead to sit later as conditional allowances. Treating the check as the works overstates year one. Ignoring the check understates risk.

[Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know) develops how conditional allowances are carried without inflating the base programme.

## Why it matters for decisions

A plan that separates timing from risk is more useful to an owner. It shows the true near-term commitment, which is usually smaller and more defensible than a risk-weighted plan would suggest. It shows which items need watching rather than spending. And it lets the owner bring items forward for strategic reasons, a tenant’s requirement, a refurbishment, a sale, rather than because the plan defaulted them there.

It also produces a better rating. The [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) reads consequence and timing separately too, and attention needed soon weighs more than attention needed later in the decade. A building does not look worse simply because it has important systems; it looks worse when important systems need attention soon.  In the register

Every row carries impact and timing as separate fields; first-year items are limited to those whose intervention window falls inside twelve months, with checks recorded separately from the works they may lead to.   Key signal

Separating consequence from timing keeps first-year capital credible: an important item may need investigation now and works later.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors](https://www.rics.org/), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What should be included in first-year capital expenditure?

Items whose intervention window genuinely falls within twelve months, such as failing or unsafe elements and current compliance obligations, plus investigations needed to resolve important uncertainty.

### Where does a high-consequence but sound item belong in a capital plan?

In the horizon that matches its condition and remaining life, with its impact rating showing why it matters, and with monitoring or testing in the near term if appropriate.

docs.title: Deferred Maintenance Is Debt Without a Statement
docs.kind: Part IV: How capital should behave
docs.blurb: Deferring necessary work does not remove the cost; it moves it forward with interest in the form of further deterioration, consequential damage, construction inflation and compliance upgrades that larger works may trigger. Because none of this appears in accounts or valuations until it is discovered, deferred maintenance behaves like unrecorded debt.

Why is deferred maintenance described as a hidden liability in commercial buildings?  Deferring necessary work does not remove the cost; it moves it forward with interest in the form of further deterioration, consequential damage, construction inflation and compliance upgrades that larger works may trigger. Because none of this appears in accounts or valuations until it is discovered, deferred maintenance behaves like unrecorded debt. Deferring necessary work does not remove the cost; it moves it forward with interest in the form of further deterioration, consequential damage, construction inflation and compliance upgrades that larger works may trigger. Because none of this appears in accounts or valuations until it is discovered, deferred maintenance behaves like unrecorded debt. Deferring necessary work does not remove the cost; it moves it forward with interest in the form of further deterioration, consequential damage, construction inflation and compliance upgrades that larger works may trigger. Because none of this appears in accounts or valuations until it is discovered, deferred maintenance behaves like unrecorded debt.  Every postponed repair is a liability that accrues interest: deterioration, consequential damage, rising prices, triggered compliance. Unlike real debt, nobody sends a statement. Every postponed repair is a liability that accrues interest: deterioration, consequential damage, rising prices, triggered compliance. Unlike real debt, nobody sends a statement.  deferred maintenance hidden liabilities building condition capital expenditure asset managementdeferred maintenance hidden liabilities building condition capital expenditure asset management deferred maintenance cost increase deferred maintenance liability cost of delaying building repairs maintenance backlog commercial property consequential damage from deferraldeferred maintenance cost increase deferred maintenance liability cost of delaying building repairs maintenance backlog commercial property consequential damage from deferraldeferred maintenance cost increase deferred maintenance liability cost of delaying building repairs maintenance backlog commercial property consequential damage from deferral When a company borrows, it records the debt. Interest accrues on a schedule. Lenders send statements. Analysts can see the liability and price it.

When a building owner defers necessary work, something similar happens with none of the paperwork. The obligation does not disappear. It sits in the building, growing, until someone discovers it, usually at the least convenient moment.  Research note

The debt analogy is a thesis. The mechanisms it describes, accelerated deterioration after protection fails, consequential damage, construction cost escalation and compliance triggered by larger works, are general building practice observations; their size varies widely between buildings and elements. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the NHS England backlog series and the published evidence on the 1:5:200 ratio and the law of fives.

## How the interest accrues

Deferred maintenance accrues interest in four ways. First, deterioration accelerates: a failing roof membrane lets water into insulation and structure, a cracked sealant lets air and water behind a facade, corrosion spreads once protection is lost. Second, consequential damage spreads the cost beyond the original element: the roof leak becomes a ceiling, a switchroom, a tenant’s stock.

Third, prices move. As [The Building That Has to Earn Its Hedge](/insights/the-building-that-has-to-earn-its-hedge) describes, construction costs can rise faster than general inflation. Fourth, larger works trigger compliance. Replacing a system late, as part of a bigger intervention, can bring upgrades into scope that a timely replacement might have avoided.

Deferred maintenance compounds. By the time it shows, the principal is larger and the interest has been running for years.

## The largest public example

The clearest published record of deferral accumulating is the NHS estate in England, which reports its maintenance backlog every year through the Estates Returns Information Collection. It is a public estate, not a commercial portfolio, but the mechanism is the same one this paper describes. NHS England estate: the cost to clear backlog maintenanceYearBacklogContext2018/19£6.5 billion2024/25£15.9 billionUp 15.7% in a year; high-risk backlog £3.5 billion, up 28%2025/26£17.3 billionNow above the £14.4 billion annual cost of running the estate; high-risk backlog £3.7 billion

NHS England Estates Returns Information Collection, as reported by BCIS (2024/25) and NHS England Digital (2025/26).

Two features matter for any owner. The backlog more than doubled in six years while investment continued, because deferred items degrade into more serious ones; the high-risk category grew fastest. And the backlog now exceeds the annual cost of running the estate. That is what a building’s statement looks like when the interest has been compounding for years.

## The ratios to avoid

Two numbers are often quoted to dramatise deferral, and neither should be relied on. The 1:5:200 ratio, said to relate a building’s construction cost to its maintenance cost and to the cost of the people in it, began as a passing remark in a 1998 Royal Academy of Engineering paper with no data behind it. When researchers at the University of Reading tested it against three office buildings in 2004, they found something closer to 1:0.4:12.

The law of fives, which holds that every pound of deferred maintenance becomes five of repair and then twenty-five of renewal, comes from 1984 work on concrete durability. It is a useful heuristic for reinforced concrete exposed to chlorides. It is not a measured ratio for roofs, plant or services. The honest version of the argument does not need either number: it needs the register to show what each deferral does to the item’s condition, timing and cost.

## Not all deferral is bad

Deferral is sometimes the right answer. A system may have more life than its age suggests. A building may be heading for redevelopment, making investment in some elements wasteful. An owner may choose to run a system to failure where failure is low-consequence and replacement is quick.

The difference is between conscious and unconscious deferral. Conscious deferral is a decision, recorded with its reason and its risk. Unconscious deferral is the absence of a decision. The first is asset management. The second is accumulating debt without knowing the balance.

## Recording a deferral properly

A conscious deferral can be recorded on the register in a few words: the item, the reason, the risk accepted, the monitoring in place and the trigger that would end the deferral. For example: chiller two beyond typical life; deferred because the tenant’s lease expires in eighteen months and the replacement specification depends on the next use; risk of failure accepted with temporary hire as contingency; monthly performance logging; replace on failure or at lease end, whichever comes first.

Five lines like that turn a hidden liability into a managed one. They also tell the next owner, lender or adviser exactly what was decided and why, which is what distinguishes asset management from neglect.

## Why the statement never arrives

Valuations rarely reflect deferred maintenance in detail. Income capitalisation, as [The Cap Rate Doesn’t See the Roof](/insights/the-cap-rate-does-not-see-the-roof) argues, does not see the physical building directly. Annual accounts record maintenance spent, not maintenance owed. Condition reports, where they exist, are often out of date. The liability shows up only when a buyer, lender, insurer or failure forces it into view.

This is why the backlog in ageing commercial stock is so hard to measure, and why it surprises owners so often.

## Writing the statement

The remedy is to write the statement yourself. A register that records, element by element, what work is due, when, at roughly what cost and with what confidence is, in effect, a schedule of the building’s physical liabilities. Items consciously deferred are recorded as such, with their reasons. Items unknown are recorded as uncertainty.

Once the debt is visible, it can be managed like debt: prioritised, scheduled, refinanced in time, or reflected in price. Invisible, it can only be discovered.  In the register

Deferred items appear as condition-driven rows with timing pulled toward the near term and impact reflecting consequential damage; conscious deferrals carry their reasoning in the action field.   Key signal

Deferred maintenance accrues interest through deterioration, consequential damage, cost inflation and compliance triggers, and it stays invisible until a register makes it a statement.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors](https://www.rics.org/), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Cost to clear NHS backlog maintenance nears £16 billion](https://www.bcis.co.uk/news/cost-to-clear-nhs-backlog-maintenance-nears-16-billion/), BCIS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Exposing the myth of the 1:5:200 ratio relating initial cost, maintenance and staffing costs of office buildings](https://www.arcom.ac.uk/-docs/proceedings/ar2004-0373-0381_Hughes_et_al.pdf), Hughes, Ancell, Gruneberg and Hirst, ARCOM 2004. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [The cost of deferred maintenance: the law of fives](https://knottlab.com/cases/the-cost-of-deferred-maintenance-the-law-of-fives/), Knott Laboratory. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is it ever sensible to defer building maintenance?

Yes, when the decision is conscious and recorded: for example where a system has more life than expected, where redevelopment is planned, or where failure is low-consequence. The problem is unrecorded deferral.

### Why do valuations miss deferred maintenance?

Income-based valuation methods focus on rent and market yields and usually include only general allowances for capital, so element-level backlog rarely appears until due diligence or failure reveals it.

Each line has a condition, an action, a cost basis, timing, impact and confidence.

It is tempting to read that as a report: here is what the building needs. We think it is better read as a set of forty decisions, most of which are still open.  Research note

The figure of around forty material lines is typical of Moyne Ross registers for mid-sized commercial buildings; the methodology reference shows registers of forty-six elements. Larger and more complex assets carry more. Deepened 4 November 2026 with published service lives (Menlo Park Fire Protection District, consistent with ASHRAE), ASHRAE’s public service life database and NBS. CIBSE’s 2026 economic life tables are a paid resource and were not reproduced.

## Every line is a choice

For each line, an owner has real options. Act now or later. Investigate before committing. Repair rather than replace. Replace like for like or upgrade. Stage the work across years. Combine it with another item. Pass it to a tenant under the lease. Accept the risk and run the element to failure.

The register recommends a course for each, based on evidence and judgement. But the best course depends on things the register cannot know alone: the owner’s plans, hold period, tenants, appetite for disruption and capital availability. That is why [bringing the owner’s intentions to bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear) changes the strategy without changing the building.

## Forty clocks

Each decision has a clock attached: the period over which an element typically lasts before it needs renewal. Published service lives give a starting point, though not a verdict on any particular building. Typical service lives of commercial building elementsElementTypical life (years)ElementTypical life (years)Single-ply roof membrane15 to 20Built-up asphalt roof18 to 25Metal roof panels25Metal curtain wall40Centrifugal chiller23 to 28Hot-water boiler (steel)24 to 25Packaged rooftop unit15Built-up air handling unit30VAV box17 to 25Building controls (digital)20Traction lift (gearless)50Lift controller20Switchboards and switchgear30Transformer30Fire detection and alarm15Sprinklers25Domestic water piping30Water heater10Car park structure, exposed30Car park structure, covered40

Menlo Park Fire Protection District facility condition assessment, Appendix 4 (US, consistent with ASHRAE service life data). UK practice uses the CIBSE Guide M11 economic life tables.

Laid side by side, the clocks explain why a building is forty decisions rather than one. A roof membrane, a set of chillers and a fire panel installed in the same year will each want renewal at a different time, and a capital plan that bundles them into one event either spends too early on some or too late on others.

## Lives are distributions, not dates

A published life is an average, and averages hide a spread. ASHRAE’s public database illustrates it well. For centrifugal chillers, the units that had actually been replaced had a median life of 25 years, but most units in the sample were still running, so the median for all units could only be stated as more than 25. Survival depends on duty, maintenance and environment.

NBS makes the same point for British practice: life expectancy tables give single figures, while research into component lives shows wide distributions, with most mechanical and electrical components averaging a little over 20 years. That is why the register records each element’s observed condition and evidence, not only its age. A chiller at 26 years with a clean maintenance history is a different decision from one at 18 with repeated failures.

## Decisions interact

Many decisions depend on others. The roof should usually be renewed before solar goes on. The switchboard may need replacing before heating is electrified. Facade works and window replacement share access equipment, so doing them together saves money. A lift modernisation may wait for a lobby refurbishment. Fire upgrades may be triggered by another project.

## Mapping the dependencies

A useful exercise is to draw the dependencies between the register’s lines. Roof before solar. Switchboard before electrified heating and charging. Hazardous materials survey before any works that disturb fabric. Facade inspection before facade allowance. Lobby refurbishment and lift modernisation together. Fire upgrades with any major refurbishment. Controls before plant optimisation.

Once drawn, most registers reduce to a handful of chains and a scattering of independent items. The chains are where sequencing creates or destroys value. The independent items can be timed on their own merits. Seeing the shape makes the decisions far easier to discuss with an owner than a list of forty rows.

## Decisions change

Decisions also change over time. A tenant announces it will leave. A survey resolves an uncertainty, up or down. A regulation tightens. A chiller performs better than expected. Each new piece of information reopens some decisions and closes others. A register that is updated as this happens remains useful. One that is not becomes a historical document within a year or two.

## Where the value sits

The most valuable part of capital advice is rarely the first document. It is the ongoing work of making these decisions well: which to make now, which to defer consciously, which to reopen when evidence changes. That is the argument of [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record) and, in its fullest form, [Physical Assets Under Management](/insights/physical-assets-under-management).

It also suggests a question to ask of any building beyond what it needs: who is making its forty decisions, and how well.  In the register

Each row’s action field records the recommended choice; dependencies between rows, such as roof before solar or switchboard before heat pumps, are recorded in the cost basis and timing.   Key signal

A Capital Register is a network of interacting decisions that change with evidence, so its value lies in ongoing decision-making rather than in a one-off report.

- [Service life data query: public database](https://weblegacy.ashrae.org/publicdatabase/system_service_life.asp?selected_system_type=2), ASHRAE. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How many items does a typical commercial building capital register contain?

It varies with size and complexity, but a mid-sized commercial building commonly carries a few dozen material lines, often around forty, across structure, envelope, services and space.

### Why does the order of capital works matter?

Many works depend on or share costs with others, such as renewing a roof before installing solar or upgrading a switchboard before electrifying heating. Good sequencing reduces cost, disruption and rework.

As a result, two buildings with similar income can carry very different capital requirements that the headline valuation does not distinguish.

How do commercial property valuations account for future capital expenditure? How do commercial property valuations account for future capital expenditure? How do commercial property valuations account for future capital expenditure?  Capitalisation and discounted cash flow valuations focus on income and market yields, and usually treat future capital expenditure through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-by-element view. As a result, two buildings with similar income can carry very different capital requirements that the headline valuation does not distinguish. Capitalisation and discounted cash flow valuations focus on income and market yields, and usually treat future capital expenditure through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-by-element view. As a result, two buildings with similar income can carry very different capital requirements that the headline valuation does not distinguish. Capitalisation and discounted cash flow valuations focus on income and market yields, and usually treat future capital expenditure through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-by-element view. As a result, two buildings with similar income can carry very different capital requirements that the headline valuation does not distinguish.  Income-based valuation is built to price rent, not concrete. Capital requirements enter as broad allowances, if at all, which leaves a gap between what a building is worth on paper and what it will cost to own. Income-based valuation is built to price rent, not concrete. Capital requirements enter as broad allowances, if at all, which leaves a gap between what a building is worth on paper and what it will cost to own.  cap rate property valuation capital expenditure allowance discounted cash flow due diligencecap rate property valuation capital expenditure allowance discounted cash flow due diligence does valuation include capex capex in discounted cash flow property capitalisation rate and building condition valuation versus capital requirement capex deduction valuationdoes valuation include capex capex in discounted cash flow property capitalisation rate and building condition valuation versus capital requirement capex deduction valuationdoes valuation include capex capex in discounted cash flow property capitalisation rate and building condition valuation versus capital requirement capex deduction valuation A capitalisation rate is a compact idea. Take a building’s net income, divide by a market yield, and you have a value. Discounted cash flow adds time: project income and costs, discount them, add an exit value. Both methods are sensible ways to price an income stream.

Neither is designed to see a roof. Physical condition enters these models indirectly, through rent, vacancy, a general allowance or a deduction for known works. The building itself is mostly invisible.  Research note

Valuation practice is governed by professional standards, including the RICS Valuation Global Standards (the Red Book) and International Valuation Standards, both in current editions effective from 31 January 2025. Valuers do consider condition and capital needs; the point here is that income-based methods usually reflect them through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-level programme. Practice varies by valuer, asset and market. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the 2025 valuation standards and a summary of how capital enters valuations.

## Where capital hides in a valuation

Future capital needs enter valuations in a few ways. A deduction for known immediate works, often taken from a due diligence report. A general allowance in a cash flow, sometimes expressed per square metre or as a share of income. An adjustment to the yield to reflect a building’s age or grade. Each is a reasonable shortcut. None is a reading of what the building will actually need.

Two buildings with the same income, tenants and location can therefore be valued similarly while one faces a heavy programme of plant, facade and compliance works and the other does not.

The valuation says what the income is worth. The capital plan says what it will cost to keep earning it. Investors need both.

## What the valuation standards now ask

Valuation standards have been moving toward the building. The International Valuation Standards and the RICS Red Book Global Standards that incorporate them both took effect in their current editions on 31 January 2025. The Red Book edition added material on environmental, social and governance factors and on modelling, and valuers are expected to consider how such factors, including the physical characteristics of the asset, affect value.

What the standards do not do is supply the building evidence. A valuer can only reflect the capital position that is known to them, and in most valuations that evidence is a general allowance or a figure lifted from a due diligence report prepared for another purpose. How capital commonly enters a valuationMethodWhat it capturesWhat it tends to missDeduction for immediate worksKnown near-term costs from a reportAnything beyond the report’s horizon or scopeGeneral capital allowance in a cash flowA smoothed annual cost, often a share of incomeConcentration: a roof or facade falling due in one yearAdjusted yieldThe market’s view of risk in the asset classThe specific condition of this buildingBuilding-specific programmeTiming, size and uncertainty of each major itemLittle, if the evidence is current

Moyne Ross summary of common practice; valuation method varies by valuer, market and purpose.

## A worked comparison

Two neighbouring offices each produce two million dollars of net income on similar leases and are valued at a similar yield. The first had its central plant, roof and lifts renewed six years ago; its ten-year capital requirement is modest and falls mostly late in the decade. The second has original plant, a membrane at the end of its life and lifts due for modernisation; its ten-year requirement is several million dollars, mostly in years two to five.

A buyer pricing both on income and a general allowance pays nearly the same for each. A buyer who reads both registers sees that the present value of the second building’s programme is a material share of its price, and either negotiates or walks. The valuation was not wrong. It answered a different question.

## The acquisition moment

The gap matters most at acquisition. A buyer who prices a building on income and a general allowance, then discovers a large capital requirement after settlement, has overpaid by roughly the present value of the difference. A seller whose building has a lighter programme than its age suggests may be underpaid unless that is demonstrated.

This is why technical due diligence exists, and why its quality matters. The approaches in Australia, Britain and the United States differ, as [Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) sets out, but each aims to bring physical condition into the price.

## A second number

We think every investment decision on a commercial building benefits from a second number beside the valuation: a ten-year capital requirement, built element by element, split by horizon, with its cost basis and confidence visible. The two numbers answer different questions. Together they give a far better picture of value than either alone.

The [Melbourne office study](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) is an example. Its ten-year capital requirement, set beside its approved development pathway, changed the question from refurbishment to redevelopment. The valuation alone would not have shown that.

## Reading condition into value

Anyone relying on a valuation can ask how capital enters it, and whether that reflects the building or a generic assumption. Across a portfolio, buildings with similar yields may sit at very different points in their physical lives, and only the second number shows it.  In the register

A register’s ten-year total and its split across 1 yr, 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons is the second number to read beside a valuation.   Key signal

Income-based valuations treat capital through broad allowances, so a separate element-level ten-year capital requirement is needed to see what the building will actually cost to own.

## Sources

## Questions

### Do property valuations include future capital expenditure?

Usually in a general way, through deductions for known works, allowances in cash flows or yield adjustments. They rarely reflect an element-by-element view of what the building will need.

### Why compare a valuation with a ten-year capital requirement?

The valuation prices the income; the capital requirement shows what it will cost to keep that income. Two buildings with similar values can carry very different capital needs.

docs.blurb: Physical obsolescence is wear and deterioration; functional obsolescence is when a building no longer suits how it is used, such as layout, floor-to-floor height or controls; and economic or external obsolescence comes from changes outside the building, such as regulation, energy markets or demand. Condition surveys mostly capture the first, so capital plans need deliberate judgement to capture the other two.

Buildings stop being useful in three different ways: they wear out, they stop fitting how people use them, and the world around them changes. Each needs a different response. Buildings stop being useful in three different ways: they wear out, they stop fitting how people use them, and the world around them changes. Each needs a different response.  building obsolescence functional obsolescence stranded assets building lifecycle capital planningbuilding obsolescence functional obsolescence stranded assets building lifecycle capital planning types of building obsolescence functional obsolescence office economic obsolescence regulation building stranded asset building physical versus functional obsolescencetypes of building obsolescence functional obsolescence office economic obsolescence regulation building stranded asset building physical versus functional obsolescencetypes of building obsolescence functional obsolescence office economic obsolescence regulation building stranded asset building physical versus functional obsolescence When people say a building is obsolete, they usually mean one of three different things. It may be worn out. It may no longer suit the way people want to use it. Or the world around it may have changed in a way that makes it less valuable, even if nothing inside it has.

These three kinds of obsolescence often arrive together, but they are not the same, and treating them as the same leads to poor decisions.  Research note

The three-way classification of physical, functional and economic obsolescence, called external obsolescence in American appraisal practice and the International Valuation Standards, is long established in valuation and asset management. Regulatory examples cited are current at the review date: the expected EPC B standard for larger let non-domestic buildings in England and Wales from 2031, and New York’s Local Law 97 emissions limits. Deepened 4 November 2026 with vacancy-by-grade evidence from Australia and South East England and CBRE’s estimate of UK stock below EPC B.

## Physical: wearing out

Physical obsolescence is the familiar kind. Materials deteriorate, systems wear, components fail. A roof membrane loses waterproofing, a chiller loses efficiency and reliability, concrete spalls. This is what condition surveys measure and what most capital plans are built around.

Physical obsolescence is usually gradual and predictable within a range. Its response is maintenance, repair and replacement on a sensible schedule.

## Functional: no longer fitting

Functional obsolescence happens when a building, or part of it, no longer does what its users need, even if it is in good condition. A low floor-to-floor height that cannot fit modern services. A deep floor plate in a world that values daylight. A building management system that cannot integrate with current controls. Lifts that are reliable but too slow and too few for current occupancy patterns. A warehouse with insufficient clear height for modern racking.

A building can be in good repair and still be obsolete. Condition ratings alone will not show it.

Functional obsolescence is harder to see because it is relative to expectations, which change. Its responses are upgrade, reconfiguration or change of use, and sometimes acceptance that the building serves a different market than it once did.

## Economic: the world moves

Economic or external obsolescence comes from outside the building. Regulation tightens, as with minimum energy standards for letting in Britain or emissions limits in some American cities. Valuers in the United States and under the International Valuation Standards usually call this external obsolescence. Energy markets shift, making gas-dependent plant less attractive. Demand moves, as with secondary office stock in some cities. Insurance reprices physical risk.

This kind of obsolescence can arrive quickly and without any change in the building’s physical state. It is the source of most talk about stranded assets, and it often shortens the economic life of systems that are physically sound, as [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) describes for gas.

## Obsolescence shows up in vacancy first

The three kinds of obsolescence leave different traces, but the market reads them together, and the clearest place to see that is vacancy by grade. The market’s reading of obsolescenceEvidenceBetter spaceOlder or lower-grade spaceSourceSydney CBD office vacancy, January 2026Prime 13.2%Secondary 14.9%Property Council of AustraliaSouth East England office vacancyGrade A 1.7%Grade B rising from 10.6% to 11%Knight Frank, via Property WeekUK city-centre office stock below EPC B60% by floor area (August 2025)CBREMelbourne CBD office vacancy, July 202618.9% overall, the highest of the Australian capitalsProperty Council of Australia

Vacancy definitions differ between sources; read for direction rather than direct comparison.

The South East figures are the starkest: Grade A space is almost fully let while Grade B vacancy is rising. Physical condition, functional fit and regulatory exposure tend to cluster in the same older buildings, which is why the gap between grades widens rather than closes as markets recover.

## Recording obsolescence on the register

On a Moyne Ross register, physical obsolescence lives in the condition field. Functional and economic obsolescence surface elsewhere: in the action, where an upgrade replaces a like-for-like renewal; in the timing, where a regulatory date or a refrigerant phase-out brings a sound item forward; and in the cost basis, where the reason is stated in words. A reader can therefore filter the register for items driven by a changing world rather than by wear, and see how much of the programme each accounts for.

In some older buildings that share is large. It is also the part of the programme most open to judgement and to the owner’s intentions, which is why it belongs in the conversation rather than in a formula.

## Reading all three

A capital plan that only reads physical condition will consistently misjudge timing for the other two. A chiller in fair condition may need replacement within five years because of its refrigerant. A sound office floor may need reconfiguration to remain lettable. A well-maintained building may need an energy upgrade to stay legally lettable.

In a Moyne Ross register, condition records physical state, while action, impact and timing carry the judgement about functional and economic obsolescence. Making that judgement explicit, with its reasoning in the cost basis, lets an owner see which lines are driven by wear and which by a changing world.  In the register

Physical obsolescence lives in the condition field; functional and economic obsolescence surface through action, impact and timing, with their reasoning recorded in the cost basis.   Key signal

Condition surveys mostly see physical obsolescence, but functional and economic obsolescence increasingly decide when systems and buildings stop earning their place.

## Questions

### What is functional obsolescence in a commercial building?

It is when a building or system no longer meets users’ needs even though it is in reasonable condition, for example inadequate floor-to-floor height, poor daylight, insufficient lift capacity or outdated controls.

### Can regulation make a building obsolete?

Yes. Minimum energy standards, emissions limits and other rules can reduce a building’s lettability or value without any physical deterioration. This is often called economic or external obsolescence.

A buyer’s technical adviser walks the roof, opens the plant rooms, asks for maintenance records, compliance certificates and drawings, and writes a report. The report goes to the buyer’s board, lender and lawyers. Its findings become negotiating points.

The owner who sells is, in effect, being examined on the decisions made during the hold. Most do not prepare for the exam.  Research note

Due diligence practice in each market is described in Part VI. Vendor due diligence is common in larger British and European transactions and increasingly used elsewhere; its value depends on independence, scope and the ability of buyers and lenders to rely on it. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a pre-sale document set and what a buyer infers from each gap.

## What the buyer looks for

A buyer’s adviser is looking for three things. First, near-term capital needs that the buyer will have to fund soon after settlement. Second, deferred works that suggest the building has been under-maintained. Third, uncertainty: things that cannot be confirmed from the documents and site visit, which the buyer will either price conservatively or require the seller to resolve.

Each of these becomes money. Near-term works are usually deducted. Deferred maintenance can reduce confidence in the whole asset. Uncertainty is priced at its pessimistic end, because the buyer carries the risk after settlement.

Uncertainty is always priced by the party that will carry it. At sale, that party is the buyer, and buyers are not optimists.

## The documents a buyer’s adviser asks for

Whatever the market, the adviser’s first request is for documents, and the speed and completeness of the answer is itself evidence about how the building has been run. A pre-sale document setDocumentWhat it tells the buyerIf it is missingCompliance certificates and fire safety statementsStatutory systems are maintained and certifiedAssumed non-compliant until shown otherwiseMaintenance logs and service contractsHow plant has been looked after, and by whomPlant life is read from age alone, usually pessimisticallyHazardous materials registerWhat is present and how it is managedA survey becomes a condition of exchangeWarranties and recent worksWhat has been renewed and what is guaranteedRecent works are discounted as unprovenEnergy ratings and benchmarkingPerformance and exposure to performance rulesThe buyer prices the worst plausible ratingA current capital registerThe decade’s capital position, with its evidenceThe buyer builds one, from a sceptic’s brief

Moyne Ross practice. Due diligence scopes follow RICS, ASTM E2018 or local practice; see Due Diligence Across Three Markets.

The last row is the one owners can do most about. A register prepared before sale does not stop a buyer commissioning their own, but it changes the conversation from discovery to verification.

## Surprises cost more than facts

A known, well-explained capital requirement is usually priced close to its expected cost. The same requirement discovered late in a sale process can cost more, because it raises the question of what else might be missing, compresses the timetable and shifts negotiating power to the buyer. This is the practical meaning of [deferred maintenance as debt](/insights/deferred-maintenance-is-debt): the statement arrives at the worst moment.

## The record as an asset

An owner who has kept a living record of the building can sell it differently. The capital position is known and explained. Past works are documented. Deferral decisions are recorded with their reasons. Uncertainties have been investigated or are clearly described. The buyer’s adviser can verify rather than discover.

Vendor due diligence is the formal version of this, common in larger transactions in Britain and increasingly elsewhere. But a full vendor report is not the only route. A capital register maintained through the hold provides much of the same benefit, and it is ready when the decision to sell is made.

## A pre-sale reading

Twelve to eighteen months before a likely sale, an owner can read the building as a buyer’s adviser would. Which first-year items would be flagged, and can they be resolved or explained? Which uncertainties would be priced pessimistically, and could a modest investigation narrow them? Which compliance records are missing or out of date? Which deferrals would look like neglect without their reasoning? Which warranties, drawings and certificates are in the data room, and which are in someone’s head?

The answers usually produce a short programme of cheap, high-value actions. Completing them before marketing tends to repay itself many times over in a calmer process and a firmer price.

## Planning for the reader

The useful habit is to read the building periodically as a buyer would, well before any sale. What would an adviser flag? Which uncertainties could be resolved cheaply now? Which deferrals would be hard to explain? Which records are missing? Answering these questions during the hold costs little and protects price at exit.

It also improves the hold itself. Most of what a buyer wants to know is exactly what an owner should want to know anyway.  In the register

The 1 yr horizon and low-confidence rows are what a buyer’s adviser will focus on first; a register that already explains them turns discovery into verification.   Key signal

At sale, uncertainty is priced by the buyer at its pessimistic end, so an owner with a living capital record sells the building as a known quantity.

## Questions

### Does vendor due diligence increase sale price?

It does not change the building, but it can reduce surprise, shorten negotiations and stop uncertainty from being priced at its worst case. The benefit depends on the quality and independence of the information.

### What records should an owner keep for an eventual sale?

Maintenance and works history, compliance and certification records, drawings, warranties, surveys and a current capital plan explaining what is due, what was deferred and why.

Reading it as capital means asking what each part will ask of its owner, when, and how sure we are.  capital strategy building assessment Capital Register technical due diligence asset managementcapital strategy building assessment Capital Register technical due diligence asset management how to assess a commercial building capital needs building condition to capital plan reading a building as an investment structure services space assessment element by element capital assessmenthow to assess a commercial building capital needs building condition to capital plan reading a building as an investment structure services space assessment element by element capital assessmenthow to assess a commercial building capital needs building condition to capital plan reading a building as an investment structure services space assessment element by element capital assessment There are many ways to read a building. An architect reads form, light and intent. A building surveyor reads condition and defects. A valuer reads income and comparable evidence. An engineer reads loads and systems. All of these are useful, and all of them leave a question unanswered for an owner or investor: what will this building ask of my capital?

Reading a building as capital is the discipline of answering that question element by element.  Research note

This paper describes the Moyne Ross method as published in its Capital Register and MR Index references. The six-field row structure and the structure, services and space scope are Moyne Ross conventions, not industry standards. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of the three layers and ASTM’s own account of the limits of transactional condition assessments.

## Structure, services, space

Moyne Ross reads every building in three layers. Structure: frame, foundations, envelope, roof, the parts that hold the building up and keep weather out. Services: mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, fire, lifts and controls, the systems that make it work. Space: the internal environment, common areas, amenities and fit-out that make it usable.

Each layer has different lives, different failure modes and different relationships to value. Structure is long-lived but expensive and disruptive to fix. Services renew on shorter cycles and drive much of the capital in modern buildings. Space turns over fastest and is most closely tied to what occupiers will pay.

## The three layers in practice

Each layer carries its own typical elements, its own clocks and its own kinds of evidence. Laid out together, they show why a reading has to cover all three: a building can be sound in structure, tired in services and functionally dated in space at the same time. Structure, services and space: what each layer holdsLayerTypical elementsTypical clocksEvidence that usually reads itStructureFrame, foundations, slabs, roof structure, facade and its fixingsDecades; failures are rare but consequentialDrawings, structural reports, observed cracking or movement, the building’s era and typeServicesMechanical plant, electrical supply and switchboards, lifts, fire systems, hydraulics, controlsMostly 15 to 30 years, often on their second or third cyclePlant schedules, maintenance logs, compliance certificates, nameplates, energy dataSpaceFloor plates, ceiling heights, amenities, accessibility, fit-outSet by what occupiers need, not by wearPlans, leasing evidence, how comparable buildings are being used and let

Moyne Ross practice. Service clocks from published service-life data; see A Building Is Forty Decisions.

The layers interact in the register as well as in the building. A services renewal can be blocked by structure, for example where a new chiller is heavier than the roof was designed for. A space decision, such as converting to another use, can make a services renewal unnecessary. Reading as capital means reading those dependencies, not only the condition of each part.

## How it differs from a condition assessment

Condition assessments are well established, and the best of them are rigorous. The US standard guide for property condition assessments, ASTM E2018, was revised in January 2024 with more than 140 changes. But ASTM itself notes that the guide is designed for transactional use, supporting acquisitions and financing, and is less suited to asset management and capital planning; in 2024 it opened work on a separate standard for facility condition assessments for that reason.

That distinction is the one this paper draws. A condition assessment asks what state the building is in. A capital reading asks what that state will cost its owner, when, and how sure anyone can be, and it keeps asking as the building changes.

## Six things on every line

For each element, a capital reading records six things. Condition: what state it appears to be in, and on what evidence. Action: what should be done about it. Cost basis: how the planning allowance was built, what it includes and excludes, and how firm it is. Timing: when the intervention falls across the ten-year horizon. Impact: how much the element matters to the building’s function, safety and value. Confidence: how strong the evidence is.

A condition description tells you what is wrong. A capital reading tells you what to do about it, what it will roughly cost, when, why it matters and how sure we are.

These six things turn a physical observation into a decision-ready line. They also make every number challengeable, because the reasoning behind it is visible. The [Capital Register reference](/methodology/capital-register) shows a real row in full.

## One row, read slowly

The methodology reference shows a real row from a 1970s distribution warehouse: metal deck roofing across the older bays. Condition, from aerial imagery, describes severe oxidation, corrosion staining and coating breakdown, with past re-sheeting on the western bays. Action proposes staged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, preceded by a roofing consultant’s inspection. The cost basis gives a planning range for the area concerned, states the tax basis and base date and excludes purlins. Impact is four, essential. Confidence is medium. Timing places a small sum in the first year for the inspection and the main works in years two to five.

Each field answers a different question, and together they let an owner challenge any part of the reasoning: the area, the exclusion, the timing, the confidence. That is what reading as capital means in practice.

## From lines to a position

Individual lines add up to a capital position: a ten-year total, its split across the near term, the middle years and the later years, and its concentration in particular systems or issues. On top of the register, the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) places the building on a band from MR 1 to MR 5 by reading the register’s judgements: how much of the building needs attention, how serious and how soon.

The position tells an owner the shape of the next decade before the detail. The register tells them why.

## What reading as capital is not

It is not a valuation, although it informs one, as [The Cap Rate Doesn’t See the Roof](/insights/the-cap-rate-does-not-see-the-roof) argues. It is not a quantity surveyor’s cost plan, although it carries costs. It is not a dilapidations schedule or a compliance audit, although it touches both. And it is not a final diagnosis: where evidence is thin, it says so, and carries the uncertainty visibly.

It is a way of seeing the building that matches the decisions its owner actually has to make.  In the register

Every row carries the same six fields, condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence, so that each figure can be traced back to its evidence and reasoning.   Key signal

Reading a building as capital turns each element into a decision-ready line with its evidence and reasoning visible, which is what owners and investors actually need.

## Questions

### How is a capital reading different from a building condition report?

A condition report describes the state of elements and defects. A capital reading adds what should be done, how the cost is built, when it falls, how much it matters and how confident the evidence is, producing a decision-ready capital view.

### What are the three layers Moyne Ross uses to read a building?

Structure, services and space: the elements that hold up and enclose the building, the systems that make it work, and the internal environment and amenities that make it usable.

docs.blurb: Evidence should be graded by its source: documented evidence comes from records or supplied material, observed evidence from what is visible in available evidence, and inferred evidence from reasoning about era, type and context. Keeping these grades separate on every line prevents a reasonable inference from being treated as a confirmed fact and makes the confidence of each figure clear.

The roof is metal deck. The chillers were replaced around 2008. The facade panels are precast concrete. The building was completed in the mid-1970s. Some of those claims come from a document. Some come from what can be seen. Some are reasoned from context.

All three kinds are legitimate. The problem arises when they are mixed up, and an inference starts to behave like a fact.  Research note

The three evidence grades are published in the Moyne Ross Capital Register and llms.txt descriptions. The safeguard that a planning application or permit date alone does not establish a construction year is a Moyne Ross method rule. Deepened 4 November 2026 with examples of each evidence grade and the RAAC lifespan claim as a public example of inference hardening.

## Three grades

Documented evidence is supported by a record or supplied material: a drawing, a maintenance log, a compliance certificate, a survey, a permit with a clear scope, an owner’s confirmation. Observed evidence is visible in what is available to the assessment: a photograph, aerial or street imagery, a site inspection, a listing image. Inferred evidence is reasoned from era, type and contextual signals: a building of this age and type in this location probably has this kind of plant or these materials.

Each grade has a place. Inference is often the only evidence available for concealed elements, and it can be very good inference. It is still inference.

The danger is not inference. It is inference that has forgotten it is one.

## What each grade looks like

The grades are easiest to apply when each comes with examples of its evidence and of what would move it up. Evidence grades in practiceGradeTypical evidenceExampleWhat would upgrade itDocumentedDrawings, invoices, maintenance logs, compliance certificates, test resultsChillers replaced in 2015, per invoice and commissioning reportAlready the strongest grade; it can still be out of dateObservedInspection, photographs, imagery, nameplates seen in listing materialPonding visible on the roof in imagery from two separate yearsA document confirming the cause, or a closer inspectionInferredThe building’s era, type, location and comparable buildingsAsbestos-containing materials likely in a 1972 officeObservation, then a survey or test result

Moyne Ross practice.

## A public example of inference hardening

The clearest recent example of an inference hardening into fact is the 30-year lifespan widely attributed to reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete during the 2023 school closures in England. The figure was repeated across news reports, professional commentary and guidance. The Institution of Structural Engineers has since said the claim is misleading, traced to a 1995 exchange of correspondence, with no specific data behind it.

Every mechanism this paper describes is visible in that case: a figure repeated without its source, summarised without its caveats, and finally treated as an engineering fact. A register that grades evidence would have carried it as inferred and unsupported, and priced the investigation rather than the date. [What Age Conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals) sets out the case in full.

## How inference hardens

Inference hardens into assumed fact in predictable ways. It is repeated across documents without its source. It is summarised into a headline. It fills a field that has no way of saying how it was derived. An inferred construction year appears in a report, is copied into the next one, and becomes the building’s age.

Dates are a common example. A planning application or permit tells you that work was proposed or approved at a certain time. It does not, on its own, establish when a building was completed. A capital view that treats the permit date as the construction date may misjudge the age of every system in the building.

## Grades and confidence

Evidence grade feeds directly into confidence. A line whose condition and cost basis rest on documented evidence can carry high confidence. One resting on inference should carry lower confidence and, where the stakes justify it, an action to confirm. This is what lets an owner see where the capital position is firm and where it is soft.

It also shapes how uncertainty is priced, which is the subject of [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know).

## Three statements about one roof

Documented: “The roof was re-sheeted in 2014; invoice and scope supplied by the owner.” Observed: “Aerial imagery from 2015 onward shows a uniform new profile across the western bays.” Inferred: “Buildings of this type and era in this location typically had asbestos cement roofing originally; the eastern bays may retain it.” Each statement is useful. Each supports a different level of confidence. And each tells the reader what would strengthen it: the inferred statement points directly to a hazardous materials survey.

Keeping the grade visible stops the inferred statement from being read as the documented one six months later in someone else’s report.

## Why it matters more now

Assessments increasingly draw on public data, imagery and AI-assisted reading of documents. These tools are powerful at producing plausible statements. Plausibility is not evidence. A disciplined method has to keep asking of every claim: where did this come from? [What Public Evidence Can Tell You](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) discusses the limits of desktop reading, and the Moyne Ross [approach to AI](/ai) sets out how models are kept inside this discipline.  In the register

Each row’s condition text states its evidential basis, and confidence reflects whether the line rests on documented, observed or inferred evidence.   Key signal

Keeping documented, observed and inferred evidence separate on every line prevents plausible inference from hardening into assumed fact.

## Sources

## Questions

### Is inferred evidence unreliable?

Not necessarily. Inference from era, type and context can be well founded and is often the only evidence for concealed elements. It should simply be labelled as inference and carry appropriate confidence.

### Does a planning permit date show when a building was built?

Not on its own. A permit or application shows when work was proposed or approved. Completion needs a source that actually fixes or bounds the construction date.

A capital plan can carry an investigation allowance for the work needed to find out, a range for the possible outcome, a conditional allowance for works that depend on the investigation, and a confidence rating, so that the owner sees both the likely position and the size of what is unknown.

Foundations are buried. Structural timbers sit behind ceilings. Concrete hides its reinforcement. Cladding hides its fixings. Records go missing. In a desktop read, most of the building is unseen.

There are two common bad responses. One is silence: leave out what cannot be confirmed, and present a tidy number that understates the risk. The other is false precision: give the unknown a single confident figure as if it were known. Both mislead.  Research note

This paper describes the Moyne Ross approach to uncertainty: investigation allowances, ranges, conditional allowances kept distinct from anticipated expenditure, and confidence ratings. The heritage example draws on the published CMP 003 asset study. Deepened 4 November 2026 with AACE International’s estimate classification as a reference for how range width should track evidence.

## Four tools

A capital plan has four tools for carrying uncertainty honestly. An investigation allowance pays for finding out: a roof survey, a structural assessment, a hazardous materials survey. A range shows the spread of plausible outcomes rather than a single point. A conditional allowance carries works that will only be needed if the investigation finds a problem, kept distinct from anticipated expenditure. And a confidence rating tells the reader how firm each line is.

Used together, they let an owner see the likely capital position and, separately, the size of what is not yet known.

## How wide a range should be

Cost engineers have a long-standing way of saying how wide an estimate’s range should be: tie it to how much is known. AACE International’s cost estimate classification sets out the expected accuracy of an estimate by the maturity of the information behind it. Expected accuracy by estimate classClassInformation availableTypical low rangeTypical high rangeClass 5Concept only, very little definition−20% to −50%+30% to +100%Class 4Feasibility; limited definition−15% to −30%+20% to +50%Class 3Budget authorisation; meaningful definition−10% to −20%+10% to +30%Class 2Control estimate; substantial definition−5% to −15%+5% to +20%Class 1Bid or tender check; full definition−3% to −10%+3% to +15%

AACE International Recommended Practice 18R-97, cost estimate classification. Ranges are typical, not limits.

Two lessons carry straight into a capital plan. A range that is too narrow for the evidence is not more accurate, only more confident. And the ranges are asymmetric: when less is known, the upside risk is larger than the downside. That is why a register built from early evidence carries wide, upward-skewed ranges on the lines that matter, and why investigation is often the cheapest way to narrow them.

## The heritage example

The fire station in [The Economics of Heritage](/insights/the-economics-of-heritage) shows the pattern clearly. A significant share of near-term spend was investigation rather than remediation: foundations, roof structure, fire compliance. Beside it sat explicit worst-case ranges for the risks those investigations would resolve. The building was not presented as cheaper or more expensive than it was. It was presented as partly unknown, with a plan to find out.

The cost of an investigation is usually small beside the cost of being wrong. Pricing it explicitly is how a plan earns trust.

## Keeping the base honest

Conditional allowances need care. If every possible problem is added to the base programme, the plan becomes a worst case and loses credibility. If none is shown, the plan becomes a best case. The register keeps them separate: anticipated works in the base, conditional works beside it, each with its trigger. This is the same discipline as [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): checks can sit in the near term while the works they may lead to sit later.

## A worked uncertainty

A 1960s office has precast facade panels whose fixings cannot be seen. The register carries three lines. An investigation item in the first year: inspection of a sample of fixings from access equipment, with a modest cost. A base-programme item in years two to five: cleaning, sealant renewal and minor concrete repair, priced with a range. And a conditional allowance beside the programme, not inside it: remedial fixing works if the inspection finds corrosion, priced as a wide range with its trigger stated.

The owner sees the likely programme, the size of the unknown and the small cost of resolving it. After the inspection, the conditional line either disappears or moves into the base with a narrower range. Either way, the plan stays honest.

## Uncertainty in the rating

Uncertainty also belongs in the building’s overall position. In the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index), an element that needs a check, or a hazard suspected but not yet seen, is carried as an open question until it is resolved. A building with many open questions reads differently from one whose questions have been answered, and resolving them moves the band in whichever direction the evidence points.

What an owner gets from this is a clear list of what to investigate first. Resolving the largest uncertainties early usually narrows the range of the whole programme and makes every later decision easier.  In the register

Uncertainty appears as investigation items, ranges in the cost basis, conditional allowances kept distinct from anticipated works, and a confidence rating on every line.   Key signal

Honest capital plans show both the likely position and the size of the unknown, using investigation allowances, ranges, conditional allowances and confidence.

## Questions

### What is the difference between a provisional sum and a contingency?

Terms vary by market, but generally a provisional or conditional allowance is tied to a specific identified uncertainty, while a contingency is a general margin across a project. A capital plan is clearer when specific uncertainties are named.

### Why not include every possible defect in the capital plan?

Adding every possible problem to the base turns the plan into a worst case and undermines its credibility. Keeping conditional works separate, with their triggers, shows the likely position and the risk around it.

Much of that is still necessary for a final view. But a great deal can now be learned before anyone sets foot on site, from evidence that is publicly available.

This paper describes what that evidence can establish, what it cannot, and how Moyne Ross uses it as a first read.  Research note

## What the record shows

Aerial imagery shows roof form, materials, plant locations, solar, ponding, patch repairs and changes over time when historic imagery is available. Street-level imagery shows facades, windows, entrances, signs of movement or staining, and how a building has changed. Planning and permit records show what works were proposed or approved and when. Heritage registers show protections. Energy and emissions disclosure regimes, such as NABERS in Australia, EPCs in Britain and city benchmarking in the United States, show recorded performance for many buildings.

Sales and leasing material, annual reports, tenant announcements and published documents often add specifications, floor areas, plant details and recent works.

## Where the public record lives

The sources differ by market, but the categories are the same. The table names the main public sources a first read draws on and what each tends to say about capital.
