How are disclosure rules changing the information available about commercial buildings?  Disclosure regimes across Australia, Britain and the United States, including energy ratings at sale or lease, city benchmarking, fire safety records, climate-related reporting and reserve requirements for shared buildings, are making more of a building’s physical performance visible to buyers, tenants and lenders. As information asymmetry shrinks, physical facts become price signals, and owners who understand their buildings first gain an advantage. Disclosure regimes across Australia, Britain and the United States, including energy ratings at sale or lease, city benchmarking, fire safety records, climate-related reporting and reserve requirements for shared buildings, are making more of a building’s physical performance visible to buyers, tenants and lenders. As information asymmetry shrinks, physical facts become price signals, and owners who understand their buildings first gain an advantage. Disclosure regimes across Australia, Britain and the United States, including energy ratings at sale or lease, city benchmarking, fire safety records, climate-related reporting and reserve requirements for shared buildings, are making more of a building’s physical performance visible to buyers, tenants and lenders. As information asymmetry shrinks, physical facts become price signals, and owners who understand their buildings first gain an advantage.  Energy ratings, benchmarking, fire safety statements, climate reports, reserve studies: more of a building’s physical reality is becoming public. Disclosure shrinks the gap between what owners know and what markets price. Energy ratings, benchmarking, fire safety statements, climate reports, reserve studies: more of a building’s physical reality is becoming public. Disclosure shrinks the gap between what owners know and what markets price.  building disclosure energy benchmarking NABERS EPC information asymmetrybuilding disclosure energy benchmarking NABERS EPC information asymmetry commercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildingscommercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildingscommercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildings For most of the history of commercial property, sellers knew more about their buildings than buyers did. Condition, performance, past problems: these were private until due diligence dug them up, and even then only partly. Information asymmetry was a source of profit for those on the right side of it.

That gap is narrowing. Across our three markets, rules increasingly require building information to be published, disclosed at transaction or reported to investors.  Research note

Disclosure regimes cited: the Commercial Building Disclosure programme in Australia for office space of 1,000 square metres or more; Energy Performance Certificates on sale or letting in Britain, with Display Energy Certificates for larger public buildings; benchmarking ordinances and performance standards in a number of American cities, led by New York; and Florida’s requirement that condominium buyers receive milestone inspection reports and structural integrity reserve studies. Climate-related financial reporting is phasing in in Australia and Britain; in the United States the federal rule is proposed for rescission while California’s emissions reporting proceeds. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a comparison of building and climate disclosure by market.

## What is now visible

In Australia, most larger offices must disclose a NABERS Energy rating when sold or leased, and fire safety maintenance records are routinely requested. In Britain, Energy Performance Certificates are required on sale or letting and sit on a public register, and the minimum standards described in [our British note](/insights/britain-when-the-energy-rating-becomes-a-letting-rule) turn them into a letting condition. In the United States, many cities require large buildings to benchmark energy use annually, and several publish the results; cities with performance standards publish compliance data.

Climate-related financial reporting in all three markets is bringing physical and transition risk into investor documents. And for shared buildings, reserve and inspection requirements, such as those introduced in Florida after Surfside, put capital planning on the record.

## Disclosure at review

The direction is toward more disclosure, but not in a straight line, and the United States has moved backwards at federal level. Building and climate disclosure by marketMarketBuilding-level disclosureCorporate climate disclosureAustraliaCommercial Building Disclosure: offices of 1,000 m² and over disclose a NABERS Energy rating when sold or leasedMandatory climate reporting under AASB S2, phased in from financial years starting 1 January 2025United KingdomEnergy Performance Certificates on sale and letting; Display Energy Certificates for public buildingsUK Sustainability Reporting Standards published in February 2026; mandatory scope still being setUnited StatesLocal benchmarking in more than 35 jurisdictions; performance standards in about fifteenSEC proposed in May 2026 to rescind its climate disclosure rule; California’s SB 261 enjoined since November 2025

Australian Government; UK Government; Institute for Market Transformation; status at review.

For building owners the federal retreat in the United States changes less than it seems. The building-level rules that drive capital, benchmarking and performance standards, are local, and they continue to spread.

## From a number to a programme

Take a disclosed metric and ask what moves it. For an energy rating, the answer is usually a known list: controls and operation, lighting, heating and cooling plant, fabric, on-site generation. For a fire safety statement or essential safety measures record, it is the maintained condition of specific systems. For a reserve study, it is the remaining life of named components. In every case, the disclosed number is the output of physical elements that sit on a register.

An owner who holds that register can read the disclosure as a diagnosis and plan the works that change it. An owner who holds only the number can react to it. Over the next decade, as more of these numbers become public and more of them carry consequences for letting, finance and sale, the difference between those two positions will be worth a great deal.

## Physical facts become price signals

When information is public, it gets priced. Tenants compare energy ratings. Lenders build them into credit terms. Buyers screen out buildings below thresholds. Insurers use condition and resilience data. What was once a technical detail discovered late becomes a visible attribute that shapes demand from the start.

Disclosure does not change a building. It changes how quickly the market notices it.

## Disclosure is not a plan

Disclosure regimes publish outcomes: a rating, a benchmark, a compliance record. They do not say what to do about them, what it will cost, or in what order. A building with a poor rating has a problem everyone can see and a solution nobody has published.

That is where the advantage now lies. Owners who understand the capital path from a disclosed position to a better one, which systems, which sequence, what cost, what timing, can act before the market prices the gap against them. [It’s Not About Owning Data](/insights/its-not-about-owning-data) makes the broader point: as raw information becomes more available, value moves to the ability to turn it into decisions.

## Knowing first

The response that follows is to know your buildings at least as well as the market soon will: read disclosed metrics against the physical register, identify what drives each, and plan the works that would move them.

Disclosure also offers a screening layer across portfolios. It is a starting point, and the building behind each number still has to be read. Disclosure can contract as well as expand, and this note is reviewed every six months.  In the register

Disclosed metrics such as energy ratings and benchmarking results are read against the mechanical, electrical, controls and fabric rows that drive them, turning a published number into a sequence of works.   Key signal

As disclosure makes building performance public, advantage shifts to owners who understand the capital path behind each disclosed metric before the market prices it.

## Questions

### Does disclosure of energy ratings affect commercial property values?

It makes performance visible to tenants, lenders and buyers, which allows it to be priced. The effect depends on the market, the asset and how far the rating sits from thresholds that matter.

### Is a disclosed energy rating enough to plan upgrades?

No. A rating shows an outcome. Planning requires understanding which systems and fabric drive it, what works would improve it, and in what order and at what cost.

This final part is about how that world arrives at one building.

It arrives as a Capital Strategy.  Research note

This paper describes the Moyne Ross Capital Strategy as published in its methodology references. Scope, fees and timing for any engagement are agreed before work begins. Deepened 4 November 2026 with an account of the work from address to issued strategy, and a comparison with other building documents.

## Six connected parts

A Moyne Ross Capital Strategy has six connected parts. An executive summary in plain words: where the building stands, what matters most and what is still uncertain. The capital position: the ten-year total and how it falls across the next year, years two to five and years six to ten. The [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index): one band for the decade ahead, calculated from the register. The [Capital Register](/methodology/capital-register): every element of structure, services and space, row by row. The cost basis: how each number was built and how firm it is. And a living record: the building’s private place, updated as evidence and plans change.

Each part answers a different question. Together they let an owner see the shape of the decade, the reasons behind it and the decisions it contains.

## What Moyne Ross does, start to finish

The work starts with an address. Moyne Ross gathers the public evidence about the building: listing and marketing material, planning and permit history, energy ratings, imagery, heritage and overlay controls, and whatever the owner can share. From that evidence it builds the Capital Register, element by element, with every finding graded as documented, observed or inferred, and every cost carried with its basis. A surveyor reviews the register before anything is issued; the platform does the arithmetic, and the surveyor takes responsibility for the judgement.

The first read hears the building on its own terms, before the owner’s plans are brought to bear, so that the brief does not shape what the building is found to need. Then the strategy is set against the owner’s intentions: hold, improve, reposition or exit. What arrives is a Capital Strategy in six parts, and a private record of the building that is updated as evidence and plans change.

## How it differs from the documents a buyer already knows

Most owners have seen a condition report, a technical due diligence report or a valuation. A Capital Strategy borrows from each and replaces none of them. A Capital Strategy beside other building documentsDocumentThe question it answersHorizonWhat it producesCondition report or building surveyWhat state is the building in?NowDefects and condition, usually without a decade of costsTechnical due diligenceWhat should a buyer know before purchase?Typically 5 to 10 yearsFindings, risks and cost estimates for a transactionValuationWhat is the building worth?At the valuation dateA value, with capital treated as an allowanceDilapidations scheduleWhat must be put right at lease end?The lease termA schedule tied to lease obligationsCapital StrategyWhat will the building ask of its owner’s capital, when, why and how sure are we?Ten years, in three horizonsA reviewed register, an MR Index band and a living record

Moyne Ross summary. Terms and scope differ by market; see Same Thing, Different Name.

The difference that matters most is the horizon and the record. A report answers a question at a date. A Capital Strategy is built to keep answering as the building, the market and the owner’s plans change.

## What it is not

A Capital Strategy is not a valuation, a quantity surveyor’s estimate, a dilapidations schedule, a compliance certificate or a structural engineer’s report. It draws on the kinds of evidence those disciplines produce and points to where they are needed. Its job is narrower and, for an owner, more directly useful: to set out what the building will ask of its capital and how the owner might respond.

A Capital Strategy is the building expressed as decisions about money and time.

## What an owner does with one

Owners use a Capital Strategy in a few recurring ways. To budget: the horizons give a defensible near-term figure and a planning view of the decade. To prioritise: impact, timing and confidence show what matters most and what to investigate first. To decide: the register supports hold, improve, reposition and exit comparisons, as described in [Hold, Improve, Reposition or Exit](/insights/hold-improve-reposition-or-exit). To communicate: with lenders, insurers, co-owners and buyers. And to remember: kept current, the strategy becomes the building’s living record.

## How the thesis lands

Every force in this publication shows up somewhere in a register. [Electrification](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) in the switchboard and heating plant. [Physical climate risk](/insights/climate-as-physical-risk) in drainage and plant location. [Obsolescence](/insights/three-kinds-of-obsolescence) in the timing of sound systems that a changing world has overtaken. [Concealed conditions](/insights/what-age-conceals) in investigation allowances. A Capital Strategy is where these general arguments become specific lines, with specific evidence, for one asset.

Not every force bears on every building. Part of the work is deciding which do, and how much.

## Two movements

A Capital Strategy is built in two movements. The first hears the building as it is, from its address and the evidence available, without the owner’s plans shaping the read; [Hearing the Building as It Is](/insights/hearing-the-building-as-it-is) explains why. The second brings the owner’s intentions, records and knowledge to bear on the decisions the first read raises, which is the subject of [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).

Then the strategy keeps going. Buildings change, and so should the record of them.  In the register

The Capital Strategy is the register plus its readings: the summary, the capital position by horizon, the MR Index band and the cost basis behind each line.   Key signal

A Capital Strategy is where the general forces reshaping commercial property become specific, evidenced lines and decisions for one building.

## Questions

### How is a Capital Strategy different from a building condition report?

A condition report describes the state of the building. A Capital Strategy turns that and other evidence into a ten-year view of actions, costs, timing, impact and confidence, with an overall position and decisions for the owner.

### What horizons does a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy use?

Within one year, years two to five, and years six to ten, across a ten-year view.

The owner explains the plan: a refurbishment, a sale, a new tenant, a five-year hold. The adviser then reads the building in light of it.

That sounds efficient, and for some questions it is. But for the first read of a building’s capital position, we think it is the wrong order.  Research note

This paper states a Moyne Ross method principle: the first read is made on the building’s current, business-as-usual terms, and the owner’s intentions are applied afterwards. The observations about attention and briefing are general and drawn from practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of what the first read records and what it holds back.

## Briefs bend evidence

A brief tells the reader what matters before the reader has looked. An owner planning a sale may unconsciously steer attention away from issues a buyer will find. An owner planning a refurbishment may lead the adviser to discount systems the refurbishment would replace, even if the refurbishment never happens. A tenant’s fit-out plan may focus attention on one floor while the roof above it is the real story.

None of this requires bad faith. It is how attention works. Knowing the answer someone wants changes which questions get asked.

The first read should be the building speaking for itself. Everything else can be layered on once that voice has been heard.

## Business as usual

The Moyne Ross first read assumes the building continues in its current use, on its current terms. What is its condition? What will it need over ten years if nothing about its use changes? What is uncertain? This business-as-usual baseline is the reference against which every later plan can be measured.

It is built from the address and the evidence available, often [public evidence](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) at first, read with the discipline described in [Documented, Observed, Inferred](/insights/documented-observed-inferred). Its uncertainties are visible, and its conclusions are a starting point rather than a verdict.

## What the first read contains

A first read sets out the building’s profile as established from evidence: use, age and how it was dated, construction, size and the main systems. It sets out a ten-year register on business-as-usual terms, with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence on every line. It carries an overall capital position and MR Index band. And it states plainly what is uncertain and what would resolve it.

It does not assume a refurbishment, a sale or a new tenant. Those come next, and they are easier to reason about because the baseline is already there.

## What the first read holds back

The discipline of the first read is as much about what it leaves out as what it contains. The first read and what follows itThe first read recordsHeld back until the owner is heardThe building’s profile, dated from evidenceThe owner’s plans for use, tenancy and timingEvery element, graded documented, observed or inferredBudgets and preferred spending patternsA business-as-usual register: what the building needs in its current useOptions for refurbishment, repositioning or saleThe uncertainties and what would resolve themWhich uncertainties the owner wants resolved first

Moyne Ross practice.

Holding the second column back is not indifference to the owner. It is what makes the first column trustworthy: a baseline written before anyone said what they hoped it would show.

## The read changes the brief

One of the most useful things a first read does is change the questions. An owner who expected to discuss tenancy refresh learns that the facade and fire services are the dominant issue. An owner planning to sell learns that a cheap investigation now could remove the largest uncertainty a buyer would price. An owner thinking about electrification learns that the switchboard gates everything.

If the brief had come first, those findings might have been framed as peripheral. Coming first, the read sets the agenda for the conversation.

## Then the owner

Hearing the building as it is does not mean ignoring the owner. It means sequencing. Once the baseline exists, the owner’s plans, records, knowledge and constraints are brought to bear, line by line, on the decisions it contains. That second movement is described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).

The baseline stays on the record. It is what lets an owner see exactly what their plans change, and what they do not.  In the register

The first read produces a business-as-usual register: condition, action, timing and confidence on the building’s current terms, which later strategies are measured against.   Key signal

A first read made on the building’s own terms, before the owner’s plans are applied, avoids bending evidence and often changes what the brief should be.

## Questions

### Does a first read ignore what the owner knows?

No. It sets a baseline from the evidence before plans are applied. The owner’s records and knowledge can still improve that evidence, and their intentions are applied in the next stage.

### Why is a business-as-usual baseline useful?

It shows what the building needs if its use does not change, so the effect of any plan, refurbishment, sale or new tenant, can be measured against it clearly.

It does not tell them what to do. That depends on what they want from the building, and two owners of the same building can rightly reach very different answers.

This is the second movement of a Capital Strategy: bringing the owner’s intentions, records and knowledge to bear on the decisions the first read raises.  Research note

This paper describes the second movement of a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy. How intentions are applied in any engagement depends on the owner, the building and the agreed scope. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a grid of one register read under three intentions.

## Intentions change actions, not condition

An owner planning a deep refurbishment in three years should not replace a lobby finish now. An owner selling next year may resolve a large uncertainty before marketing. An owner holding for twenty years may bring a roof forward to install solar. A tenant committing to a long lease may change which systems matter and who pays for them. In each case the building’s condition is unchanged. The right action and timing are not.

This is why the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) reference says the same score can lead to different decisions. The capital position is a fact about the building. The strategy is a fact about the building and its owner together.

## Records sharpen the read

Owners also bring evidence. Maintenance logs, compliance records, drawings, recent works, warranties, surveys and tenant information can confirm, narrow or overturn lines from the first read. An inferred plant age becomes documented. A wide range for a facade becomes a narrow one after an inspection report is supplied. A suspected issue is closed.

The first read listens to the building. The second listens to the owner. A good strategy needs both voices, in that order.

## Three intentions, one building

Take a 1990s office with a mid-decade chiller replacement, a lobby in need of refresh and an energy rating below where the market is heading. An owner selling in eighteen months resolves the largest uncertainty, documents the plant, and leaves the replacement to the buyer with clear information. An owner holding for ten years replaces the chiller with electrified plant at the right moment, sequences the switchboard first and times the lobby with a lease event. An owner repositioning for a different tenant market brings plant, lobby and energy works together into one refurbishment.

The building is identical in all three. The register lines are the same. The actions and timing differ, and each strategy can be read against the same baseline.

## The same building under three intentions

The worked example in this paper is clearest as a grid: the same register lines, read under three different plans. One 1990s office, three intentionsRegister lineHold for ten yearsRefurbish in three yearsSell within eighteen monthsChiller replacement, mid-decadePlan and fund on its own clockFold into the refurbishment scopeDisclose with its evidence; consider early works only if they protect the priceLobby refreshDo it when the leasing case supports itDefer: the refurbishment replaces itA modest refresh may help presentationEnergy rating below the marketImprove controls and plant over the holdDesign the refurbishment to the target ratingExplain the pathway and its cost to buyersLow-confidence facade allowanceInvestigate early and refineInvestigate as part of designInvestigate before marketing so the buyer does not

Moyne Ross illustration. The condition of each line is the same in every column; only the action and timing change.

## Working through the decisions

Bringing intentions to bear means working through the register with the owner: which lines matter most to their plans, which decisions are urgent, which can wait, which depend on each other, and which need investigation before anyone can decide. [A Building Is Forty Decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) describes the shape of that work.

The outcome is a direction the owner can act on, with the reasoning visible: what will be done, when, why, and what remains open.

## Keeping the baseline

The baseline from the first read stays on the record beside the tailored strategy. That matters for two reasons. It shows the owner exactly what their plans change. And if the plans change, as they often do, the strategy can be re-tailored from the same baseline rather than rebuilt.

It also guards against a subtle risk: that a strategy shaped around an intention drops issues the intention made inconvenient. With the baseline visible, nothing disappears without a reason.  In the register

Tailoring changes the action and timing fields on affected rows and records the owner’s reason in the cost basis, while the business-as-usual baseline remains available for comparison.   Key signal

Owner intentions change the right action and timing on many lines without changing the building, so a strategy applies them to a stable baseline rather than replacing it.

## Questions

### Can two owners of the same building have different capital strategies?

Yes. Hold period, refurbishment plans, tenancy, sale timing and risk appetite all change the best action and timing for many items, even though the building’s condition is the same.

### What owner records improve a capital strategy most?

Maintenance and works history, compliance records, drawings, recent surveys, warranties and lease and tenant information typically narrow uncertainty and confirm or correct the first read.

Reports from different years, by different advisers, in different formats. Invoices for works. Certificates. Some drawings. A great deal of knowledge sits in the heads of a facility manager or a former owner, and leaves with them.

Buildings forget. Every few years someone has to rediscover them.  Research note

This paper describes how Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy as a versioned register in a private, invitation-only place for the owner. Retention and access arrangements are set out in the Moyne Ross terms and privacy policy. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of recurring regulatory evidence that refreshes a building record.

## Memory as an asset

A living record is a capital register that is kept current. When a survey arrives, the affected lines change. When works are done, they are recorded and the next cycle is set. When a plan changes, the strategy is re-tailored and the reason noted. Each version is kept, so the record shows how understanding of the building developed over time.

A building with a living record carries its knowledge with it. A building without one loses most of what anyone learned about it at every handover.

## Why it is worth keeping

The benefits compound. Decisions are made on current evidence rather than old reports. Uncertainty narrows over time instead of being re-estimated from scratch. Managers and advisers can change without the building losing its history. Lenders and insurers can be shown a credible picture. And at sale, as [What the Next Buyer Will Read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read) argues, the buyer verifies rather than discovers.

There is also a simpler benefit. Rediscovering a building every few years is expensive and slow. Updating a record is not.

## What keeps a record current

A record stays alive because the building keeps producing evidence. Much of it arrives on a regulatory calendar. Recurring evidence that refreshes a building’s recordEvidenceWhereHow oftenAnnual fire safety statementNew South WalesEvery yearEssential safety measures reportVictoriaEvery yearBuilding Energy Efficiency Certificate for offices of 1,000 m² and overAustraliaValid for up to 12 months, needed when space is sold or leasedFire risk assessmentEngland and WalesKept under regular review, and after significant changeEnergy benchmarking disclosureNew York City and other US jurisdictionsEvery yearFacade inspection for buildings over six storeysNew York CityEvery five years

State and city regulations as summarised at review; obligations depend on building type and size.

Each of these is a small update to the register if the record is kept, and a box of paper if it is not. The difference compounds: after a few cycles, a kept record knows the building better than any single report could.

## What a good record holds

A living record holds the current register with its reasoning; every previous version with what changed and why; completed works with their scope, date and evidence; investigations and their results; the decisions agreed with the owner; and the documents that support them, drawings, certificates, warranties, surveys. It is organised so that any line can be traced from today’s figure back to the evidence that produced it.

Kept this way, the record is useful to everyone who will ever have to make a decision about the building, which over its life is a long list.

## Versions and agreement

A living record needs discipline. Versions should be clear: what was known at each point and what changed. Anything shown together, a strategy, a report, a summary, should agree, which is why reports are best drawn from the register as views rather than written separately, as [The Register, Not the Report](/insights/the-register-not-the-report) explains. And updates should follow evidence, not convenience.

Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy in a private place for the owner, by invitation, where the current version, its history, the notes and what has been agreed sit together.

## Beyond the single owner

Over a long enough period, a building’s living record matters more than any single owner’s tenure. It is the baton described in [Patient Capital and the Long Building](/insights/patient-capital-and-the-long-building): the most useful thing one owner can pass to the next. It is also, in aggregate, how a practice learns. Every record that improves over time teaches something about how buildings of that kind actually behave.  In the register

A living register keeps every version, records completed works and resolved uncertainties on their rows, and carries the reasons for each change.   Key signal

A capital record kept current becomes the building’s memory, preserving knowledge across managers and owners and turning sale and finance into verification rather than discovery.

## Questions

### How often should a building capital plan be updated?

Whenever material evidence arrives, works are completed or plans change, with a periodic review even when nothing obvious has changed. The aim is that the record always reflects current knowledge.

### What should a living building record contain?

The current capital register with its reasoning, a version history, completed works, resolved and open uncertainties, supporting documents and the decisions agreed with the owner.

Every element of structure, services and space, each with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence. Read top to bottom, it can feel like an inventory. Read in the right order, it tells a story quickly.

This guide sets out the order we recommend. The [Capital Register reference](/methodology/capital-register) shows a real row from a 1970s distribution warehouse, which is a useful companion.  Research note

The worked row referred to is published in full on the Moyne Ross Capital Register methodology reference. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a field-by-field reading of the register row in the methodology reference.

## Start with the shape

Begin with the capital position: the ten-year total and its split across the first year, years two to five and years six to ten. The split says more than the total. A front-loaded programme means decisions now. A mid-decade bulge means planning time. A back-loaded programme means a building in a quiet phase that will not stay quiet.

Then read the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) band. It summarises how much of the building needs attention, how serious and how soon, in one position from MR 1 to MR 5. It is not a verdict on the building. It tells you what kind of decade to expect.

## Find the concentration and the gates

Next, see where the capital concentrates. Is it spread across many systems, or dominated by one, a roof, a facade, central plant? Concentration tells you where attention and investigation will pay off most.

Then look for gating items: single findings that could reshape the programme if confirmed. A structural question, a concealed facade issue, a hazardous material in the way of planned works. These usually sit as investigation items with conditional allowances, as described in [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know).

Read the shape before the rows. Most of what matters is visible in the split, the band, the concentration and the gates.

## One row, read field by field

The methodology reference shows a single row from an issued strategy: metal deck roofing across the older bays of a 1970s distribution warehouse. Reading it field by field shows what each part is for. Reading a register rowFieldWhat the row saysThe question it answersConditionSevere oxidation and coating breakdown across the older bays; water ingress risk to stock belowWhat state is it in, and what is the consequence if nothing is done?ActionStaged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, with a roofing consultant’s inspection firstWhat should be done, and in what order?Cost basisPlanning range $1.8 million to $3.4 million for 20,000 to 25,000 m², excluding GST, Q3 2026; purlins excludedHow was the figure built, and what does it leave out?Impact4, EssentialHow much does this matter to the building?ConfidenceMediumHow firm is the evidence?Timing$35,000 in year one; $2.6 million in years two to five; nothing in years six to tenWhen does the money fall?Item total$2.64 millionWhat does it add to the decade?

Moyne Ross Capital Register methodology reference.

Read together, the fields say something no single one does. The roof matters a great deal, but the money is not urgent: the first year buys an inspection, and the works follow once their scope is known. The exclusion of purlins is the line a buyer’s adviser would circle first.

## Read confidence and the near term

Filter for low-confidence lines. They show where the evidence is thin and where the capital position could move. Then read every first-year line and ask the question from [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): why must this happen within twelve months? A good register answers it on each row.

On the warehouse example in the reference, the roof row shows the pattern clearly: strong evidence from aerial imagery, a large exposure, a modest first-year amount for a roofing consultant’s inspection, and the main re-sheeting in years two to five.

## Five questions to ask any register
- Why must each first-year item happen within twelve months?
- Which single findings could reshape the programme, and what would it cost to resolve them?
- Where does the capital concentrate, and is that concentration supported by strong evidence?
- Which lines rest on inference, and does their confidence say so?
- Which lines depend on each other, and is the sequence right?

A register that answers these well is one an owner can act on. One that cannot is one to question.

## Finish with the cost basis

Finally, read the cost basis on the largest lines. How was each figure built? What scope, quantity and assumptions does it rest on? What is included and excluded? How firm is it? This is where you can challenge a number intelligently, and where an owner’s own knowledge, a recent quote, a known constraint, can sharpen it.

Read this way, a register of forty lines becomes a short list of questions worth asking. That list is usually the start of the conversation described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).  In the register

The reading order follows the register’s own structure: capital position by horizon, MR Index band, concentration by system, gating and low-confidence rows, first-year rows, then the cost basis on the largest lines.   Key signal

Reading a register from its shape to its evidence, split, band, concentration, gates, confidence, near term, cost basis, turns a dense schedule into a short list of decisions.

## Sources

## Questions

### What is the most important number in a capital register?

Usually not the total, but how it splits across the near term, middle years and later years, together with where it concentrates. Those show what kind of decisions the building will demand and when.

### How can an owner challenge a figure in a capital register?

By reading its cost basis: the scope, quantity, assumptions, inclusions, exclusions and confidence behind it, and testing them against the owner’s own knowledge, quotes or records.

It makes each option legible.  asset strategy hold or sell repositioning refurbishment capital allocationasset strategy hold or sell repositioning refurbishment capital allocation hold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit propertyhold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit propertyhold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit property However detailed the analysis, a capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. Broadly there are four paths. Hold it largely as it is and maintain it well. Improve it within its current use. Reposition it, for a different tenant market or a different use. Or exit.

The register does not choose between them. What it can do is make each option legible, so the choice rests on evidence rather than instinct.  Research note

The four-path framing is a general asset strategy convention. The redevelopment example draws on the published CMP 007 asset study. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the Marks & Spencer Marble Arch case as a public test of refurbishment against redevelopment.

## What the building needs regardless

Every option starts from the same base: what the building needs whatever path is chosen. Safety, current compliance obligations, items failing or causing damage. These are the floor. Even an owner who intends to sell must usually deal with some of them, or price them into the sale.

Above the floor, the paths diverge.

## Four paths, four programmes

Holding as is means following the business-as-usual register: renew systems as they come due, defer consciously where sensible, keep the building competitive within its current market. Improving means adding works that raise performance within the current use: better controls, an energy upgrade, a lobby, end-of-trip facilities. Repositioning means accepting a larger programme to reach a different market or use, a deeper refurbishment, a conversion, a change of tenant type. Exiting means deciding what to do before sale, which uncertainties to resolve and which works to leave to the buyer.

The same register supports all four paths. What changes is which lines are taken up, when, and what is added.

Each path also carries different risk. Holding exposes the owner to obsolescence. Improving exposes them to whether the market rewards the improvement. Repositioning exposes them to construction, approvals and leasing risk. Exiting exposes them to what [the next buyer will read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read).

## A simple comparison table

For each path, set out four figures from the register: the base programme every path must fund; the additional works the path implies; the conditional allowances still open; and the timing against leases. Add a short note on the main risk each path carries. On one page, an owner can see the capital implication of each option on the same evidence, which is usually enough to narrow the choice to one or two before any detailed feasibility work begins.

## When the building is not the answer

Sometimes the evidence points beyond all four. When the capital needed to keep a building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the land supports something else, redevelopment becomes the rational path, as [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) describes. A good capital strategy says so plainly when it is true.

## A public test of refurbish against rebuild

The most visible recent test of this decision is Marks & Spencer’s store at Marble Arch on London’s Oxford Street. The retailer applied in 2021 to demolish the 1930s building and replace it with a new nine-storey building of shops and offices, arguing that the existing store could not be adapted. Westminster approved the scheme, but the government called it in, and in July 2023 the then Secretary of State refused it, citing among other things whether refurbishment had been properly explored and the embodied carbon of demolition.

In March 2024 the High Court quashed that refusal, finding that national planning policy had been misapplied. In December 2024 the decision was remade and permission granted. The case did not settle the general question of retrofit against rebuild, but it made one thing plain: the case for redevelopment now has to be argued from evidence about the existing building, including what refurbishment could achieve and at what carbon and capital cost. The Marble Arch timelineDateEvent2021Application to demolish and rebuild; approved by Westminster City CouncilJune 2022Called in by the Secretary of StateJuly 2023Permission refused1 March 2024High Court quashes the refusal5 December 2024Permission granted on redetermination

Mishcon de Reya; Dezeen; CIBSE Journal.

For an owner weighing the four paths, the lesson is that exit by redevelopment is no longer a quiet choice in many cities. The register that shows what the existing building needs, and what it could become, is the evidence such a decision will be asked for.

## Choosing on evidence

Owners compare paths through the register: the base they must fund anyway, the additional programme each path implies, the uncertainty that remains, and the timing against leases and plans. The comparison does not need to be elaborate to be useful. What matters is that each option is costed and timed on the same evidence.

This is also where the ideas in Capital Made Physical become practical. Whether a building should be held, improved, repositioned or sold depends in part on the forces in [Part I](/insights/the-movement-to-real) and the futures in Part II. The register brings those general arguments down to one building’s options.  In the register

Options are compared on one register: the base rows every path must fund, the additional rows each path adds, and the conditional allowances that remain open under each.   Key signal

Hold, improve, reposition and exit each imply a different capital programme and risk, and a register makes them comparable on the same evidence.

- [High Court overturns Gove’s M&S decision](https://www.cibsejournal.com/news/high-court-overturns-goves-ms-decision/), CIBSE Journal. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What capital works must be done even if a building is being sold?

Typically safety issues, current compliance obligations and failing elements causing damage, or else they are priced into the sale. Discretionary improvements can usually be left to the buyer.

### When does redevelopment make more sense than refurbishment?

Often when the capital needed to keep the existing building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the site supports a more valuable use or form. The decision depends on the building, the land and approvals.

docs.kind: Part VII: From thesis to building
docs.blurb: Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced.

The argument of this publication ends with the case for treating physical assets the way capital treats money. The investment world manages financial assets continuously. Buildings are mostly advised on in episodes. The argument of this publication ends with the case for treating physical assets the way capital treats money.  asset management ongoing building advice living record capital decisions real assetsasset management ongoing building advice living record capital decisions real assets ongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancyongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancyongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancy A financial portfolio is never left alone for five years. It is monitored, rebalanced and reported on continuously. Decisions are made as information arrives. The manager is judged by outcomes over time.

Buildings, which are often a large part of those same portfolios, are usually treated differently. Advice arrives in episodes: a due diligence report at purchase, a condition survey at refinancing, a vendor report at sale. Between episodes, the building’s capital position drifts, and nobody is watching it as a whole.  Research note

This closing thesis describes a direction for building advice rather than a service offering. The comparison with continuing service arrangements for lifts and major plant refers to common industry practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the ISO 55000 asset management series and a comparison of episodic and continuous advice.

## Episodes and drift

Episodic advice made sense when assessing a building was slow and expensive, and when reports were the only practical output. Each engagement started from scratch, produced a document and ended. The knowledge it created aged on a shelf.

The cost of that model is drift. Systems age past their planned replacement. Uncertainties remain unresolved. Regulations change. Plans change. By the next episode, much of the previous advice is out of date and the building has to be rediscovered, which is the problem [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record) addresses.

## A different shape of advice

The tools now exist to change that shape. A building can be read quickly from evidence, held as a structured register, and kept current as things change. The expensive part of the old model, rediscovering the building, shrinks. What remains, and grows in importance, is judgement: deciding which of the building’s [forty decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) to make now, which to defer, which to reopen.

When reading a building becomes fast, the value moves to staying with it.

Other industries already work this way with physical equipment. Lifts, escalators and major plant are commonly maintained under continuing service arrangements by people who know the installed base intimately. The idea here is similar, applied to a building’s whole capital position rather than to one system.

## What would make it work

Continuous advice on a building’s capital position needs three things. A structured, versioned register that can be updated cheaply as evidence arrives. A method that keeps judgement visible and challengeable, so that changes are explained rather than asserted. And people who know the building well enough to notice what matters and to talk to its owner about it. The first two are now practical. The third is the part that cannot be automated, and the part owners value most.

## An established discipline, applied to buildings

Continuous management of physical assets is not new. Infrastructure owners, utilities and public estates have run it for decades, and it has an international standard: the ISO 55000 series on asset management, first published in 2014 and revised in 2024. Its premise is the one this paper argues for buildings: decisions about physical assets should be made over their whole life, from current evidence, and recorded so they can be reviewed. Episodic advice and continuous managementEpisodicContinuousTriggerA transaction, a lease event or a failureA calendar, and any new evidenceOutputA report at a dateA register kept current, with its historyUncertaintyFixed at the date of the reportNarrowed as evidence arrivesAcross a portfolioReports in different formats and datesComparable registers on one basisWho carries the knowledgeWhoever read the last reportThe record itself

Moyne Ross summary; asset management principles follow the ISO 55000 series.

Commercial property has been slow to adopt this way of working because its assets change hands and its advice is bought transaction by transaction. That is exactly why the record matters: it is the part of the discipline that survives a change of owner.

## Physical assets under management

Seen at portfolio scale, a set of live registers begins to look like assets under management: physical rather than financial, but held, monitored and decided on continuously. Each register improves as evidence accumulates. Across many buildings, patterns emerge about how real systems age, what works cost and which decisions paid off. That is the argument of [It’s Not About Owning Data](/insights/its-not-about-owning-data) carried to its conclusion: the advantage lies in turning evidence into decisions, repeatedly.

## Where the thesis ends

Capital Made Physical began with a claim that capital is turning back toward the physical, that buildings are becoming operating infrastructure rather than financial wrappers. If that is right, buildings deserve the continuous attention that capital gives to everything else it cares about.

That is the world this publication describes and the one Moyne Ross is built for: buildings read as capital, held as living records, and decided on with care over time, by people who know them. This is the most speculative paper in Capital Made Physical. Within a few years the evidence will show whether owners want continuous attention to their buildings and whether it can be delivered economically, and the paper will be rewritten either way.  In the register

In this model the register never closes: every row is a standing decision, revisited as evidence, markets and the owner’s plans change.   Key signal

As reading a building becomes fast, the value of building advice moves from producing documents to staying with the building and its decisions over time.

## Questions

### How is continuous building advice different from periodic condition surveys?

Periodic surveys produce a snapshot that ages until the next one. Continuous advice keeps a living register current and works through decisions as evidence and plans change, so knowledge accumulates instead of being rediscovered.

### Why compare buildings with financial assets under management?

Both are significant capital that changes value with time and circumstances. Financial assets are managed continuously; the argument is that physical assets increasingly warrant similar ongoing attention to their capital position.

How to read this register How To Read The Register One row, one element Each row is an element of the building: its condition, the action it needs, when that falls, what it is expected to cost, how much it matters and how firm the evidence is. Cost basis Every priced row carries the reasoning behind its number: the scope assumed, the quantities, what is included and excluded, the cost date and how firm the footing is. A planning allowance is presented as a planning allowance, not as a market price. Timing Every allowance carries an intervention window in years. The next-year column is reserved for work whose whole window sits inside the next twelve months. Any other window is shown, as a single placement, in the horizon that holds its midpoint; the window itself is stated in the cost basis. Evidence Desktop or inspection Unless this strategy records a site inspection, the assessment is desktop-based: public records, imagery and material supplied by the client. A desktop assessment cannot establish concealed conditions or replace an inspection where one is needed. Documented, observed, inferred Documented findings are supported by records or supplied material. Observed findings are visible in the evidence available. Inferred findings are reasoned from the building’s era, type and context, and are labelled as such. Where the evidence stops Where nothing yet supports a works figure, the register prices the investigation that would, and stops there. Where an inspection is included, its fee is a separate line added to the works midpoint rather than absorbed into the range. Impact Essential Critical to operation, life safety or compliance. Failure would risk shutdown, a safety incident or regulatory action. Important Significant effect on operation or commercial value. Failure would cause material disruption. Planned Standard lifecycle work within expected replacement cycles. Routine Minor work that can be deferred without material consequence. Confidence High Strong, asset-specific evidence for the scope. Any benchmark, quote or tender relied on is identified at item level. Medium Building-specific evidence combined with standard assumptions for buildings of this type and scale. Low Limited evidence, concealed elements or atypical systems. The range is wider, and the investigation that would narrow it is included. Work Codes CAP Capital expenditure: lifecycle replacement, restoration or end-of-life renewal. R&M Repair and maintenance beyond routine thresholds. BCC Building code compliance: statutory, certification or code-upgrade work. ENV Environmental: efficiency, carbon and environmental compliance. Costs Planning allowances Costs are planning allowances in the strategy currency at Q4 2026. Each row states its own inclusions, exclusions and treatment of preliminaries and tax; these are not assumed to be uniform across the register. Separate interventions Works are planned as discrete interventions unless a row says otherwise. Coordinated procurement may reduce duplicated access and preliminaries; no saving is assumed without project-specific evidence. Before commitment This Capital Strategy is a planning tool based on the evidence available at the time. It identifies likely capital needs, priorities and areas of uncertainty, but does not replace site inspection, detailed investigation, design, certification or specialist advice.
